# MARCUS TULLIUS CICE-
## RO’S DREAM
## OF SCIPIO,
### FROM THE SIXTH BOOK
### ON THE REPUBLIC.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'C' depicting a reclining figure in a classical garment within a landscape of foliage and trees.</image-desc>
WHEN I had come into Africa <note>Referring to the start of the Third Punic War in 149 BC</note>, serving as a Military Tribune <term>Military Tribune: a high-ranking officer in a Roman legion, often from the aristocratic class</term> (as you know) to the Fourth Legion under the Consul Manius Manilius <note>original: "Anitio Manilio cos."; a common Roman way of dating by the names of the presiding consuls</note>: nothing was more important to me than to meet Masinissa, a King most friendly to our family for just reasons <note>Masinissa was a Numidian king and a crucial ally of Scipio Africanus the Elder during the Second Punic War</note>. When I came to him, the old man embraced me and wept; and after a little while, he looked up to heaven and said: "I give thanks to you, supreme Sun, and to you, the rest of the heavenly beings <note>original: "cœlites"</note>, that before I depart from this life, I behold in my kingdom and within these walls Publius Cornelius Scipio <note>The narrator, Scipio Aemilianus, who was the adoptive grandson of the Great Africanus</note>, by whose very name I myself am refreshed: so never does the memory of that best and most invincible man <note>The elder Scipio Africanus</note> depart from my mind." Then I questioned him about his kingdom, and he me about our Republic <note>original: "Rep."</note>; and with many words exchanged on both sides, that day was spent by us. Later, however, having been received with royal hospitality, we prolonged our conversation far into the night, while the old man spoke of nothing except Africanus, and remembered not only all his deeds, but even his sayings. Then, when we departed for bed, a deeper sleep than usual embraced me, as I was both tired from the journey and had stayed awake late into the night. Here <note>Scipio prepares the reader for the shift from reality to the supernatural dream state</note> (I believe indeed because of what we had been talking about; for it usually happens that our thoughts and conversations produce something in sleep like that which Ennius <note>An early Roman poet</note> writes concerning Homer <note>The Greek poet; Ennius famously claimed Homer's ghost appeared to him in a dream</note>, about whom he was obviously very often thinking and speaking while awake), Africanus showed himself to me in that form which [was known to me] from [his image...] <note>Referring to the wax funeral masks or busts of ancestors kept in Roman homes</note>

<insert>ima</insert>gine of him, than from the man himself. When I recognized him, I truly shuddered; but he said: "Take heart, Scipio, and cast away your fear, and commit to memory what I shall say. Do you see that city, which, though forced by me to obey the Roman people, is renewing its former wars and cannot remain at rest?" (He was pointing out Carthage from a high place, full of stars, bright and clear.) "To attack which you now come almost as a simple soldier; this city you shall overthrow as **C O S.** <term>COS.: abbreviation for 'Consul', the highest elected political office in the Roman Republic</term> within these next two years, and that surname <note>The title 'Africanus'</note> will be won by your own merit, which you now hold as an inheritance from us. When you have destroyed Carthage, celebrated a triumph, and served as Censor <term>Censor: a high-ranking magistrate responsible for the census and public morality</term>, and have traveled as an envoy through Egypt, Syria, Asia, and Greece, you will be elected **C O S.** a second time while absent, and you will finish a great war by destroying Numantia <note>A city in Spain that resisted Roman rule for years</note>. But when you have been carried in your chariot to the Capitol, you will find the Republic <note>original: "Remp."/Respublica</note> thrown into confusion by the schemes of my grandson <note>Referring to the political reforms of Tiberius Gracchus, who was a cousin/kinsman to Scipio</note>. It is then, Africanus, that you must show your country the light of your spirit, your character, and your wisdom. But I see at that time a fork, as it were, in the path of destiny. For when your age has completed eight times seven circuits and returns of the sun <note>Meaning 56 years of age</note>, and when these two numbers—each of which is considered 'full' for different reasons—have fulfilled your fated sum in their natural circuit, the whole state will turn to you alone and to your name. The Senate, all good men, the allies, and the Latins will look to you. You will be the one on whom the safety of the state depends. To put it briefly, it will be necessary for you to restore the Republic as **D I C T.** <term>DICT.: abbreviation for 'Dictator', a magistrate with supreme authority granted during times of national crisis</term>, if you escape the impious hands of your own kinsmen." At this point, when Laelius had cried out and the others had groaned more loudly, Scipio, smiling gently, said: "Quiet, I beg of you, do not wake me from my sleep; let there be peace, and listen to the rest. But so that you may be more eager, Africanus, to protect the Republic, know this: for all those who have preserved, aided, or enlarged their fatherland, there is a certain [place in heaven...]"

<meta>This page continues the "Dream of Scipio" from Cicero’s *On the Republic*. Scipio Aemilianus is being addressed by his grandfather (by adoption), Scipio Africanus, who is explaining the divine nature of the cosmos and the rewards for those who serve their country.</meta>

### [OF SCIPIO]

...to be in heaven, and a fixed place where the blessed may enjoy eternal life. For there is nothing to that supreme God, who rules all this world, which is more acceptable among the things done on earth than those councils and gatherings of men joined by law, which are called states <note>original: "civitates". In this context, it refers to organized political communities or city-states.</note>. The rulers and preservers of these come from here, and to here they shall return.

At this point, although I was terrified—not so much by the fear of death as by the fear of treachery from my own kin <note>original: "insidiarum à meis". Scipio was famously found dead in his bed under suspicious circumstances, a fate this passage foreshadows.</note>—I asked nonetheless whether he himself lived, and my father Paulus <note>Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus, the biological father of Scipio Aemilianus.</note>, and others whom we think of as dead. "On the contrary," he said, "these are truly alive who have flown out from the chains of the body as if from a prison. Your so-called life is actually death. Why do you not look at your father Paulus coming toward you?"

When I saw him, I indeed shed a flood of tears. But he, embracing and kissing me, forbade me to weep. And as soon as I had suppressed my weeping and was able to speak, I said, "I beg you, most holy and excellent father, since this is truly life, as I hear Africanus say, why do I linger on earth? Why do I not hasten to come here to you?"

"It is not so," he said: "for unless that God, whose temple is all this which you behold, has freed you from those confinements of the body <note>original: "corporis custodijs", literally the 'guards' or 'custody' of the flesh.</note>, the way here cannot be open to you. For men are born under this law: to care for that globe which you see in the middle of this temple, which is called Earth. And a soul has been given to them from those eternal fires which you call constellations and stars, which, being spherical and round, and animated by divine minds <note>Ancient cosmology viewed the stars as living, rational beings or "divine minds."</note>, complete their circles and orbits with marvelous speed. Therefore, both you, Publius, and all pious men, must keep the soul in the custody of the body; nor must you depart from human life without the command of Him by whom the soul was given to you, lest you seem to have abandoned the human duty assigned by God. But like this, Scipio, as your grandfather here, and as I who fathered you, cherish justice and piety; which, while it is great toward parents and...

<meta>This page continues Scipio Africanus’s discourse to his grandson, Scipio Aemilianus. Having just explained that the soul is immortal and that statesmen earn a place in heaven, he now begins to describe the physical structure of the universe as seen from the celestial heights. ->### T H E  D R E A M<-

...to relatives, then it is greatest toward the fatherland. That life is the path to heaven, and to this gathering of those who have already lived and who, released from the bonds of the body, inhabit that place which you see. 

It was a circle shining with the most brilliant whiteness among the stars, which you (as you learned from the Greeks) call the Milky Way <note>original: "orbem Lacteum"</note>. As I gazed upon everything from that vantage point, all other things appeared magnificent and wonderful. Moreover, there were stars which we have never seen from this place [the Earth], and their sizes were such as we never suspected they could be. Among them, the smallest was that one furthest from the heaven and nearest to the Earth, which shone with a borrowed light <note>original: "luce lucebat aliena". This refers to the Moon, which reflects the light of the Sun.</note>. Furthermore, the spheres of the stars easily surpassed the Earth in size. Indeed, the Earth itself appeared so small to me that I felt ashamed of our empire, with which we touch only a mere point of its surface, as it were. 

While I gazed more intently at the Earth, Africanus said, "I beg you, how long will your mind be fixed upon the ground? Do you not see the sacred precincts <note>original: "templa". In the ancient Roman worldview, the entire sky was seen as a divine temple or a space marked out by the gods.</note> into which you have come? All things are connected by nine circles, or rather spheres <note>term: "globis". Cicero uses "orbes" and "globi" to describe the concentric shells of the geocentric universe.</note>. One of these is the outermost celestial sphere, which encompasses all the others: the supreme God himself, confining and containing the rest. Within this sphere are fixed those eternal courses of the stars that revolve. Beneath this are seven spheres which turn backwards with a motion contrary to that of the heaven. 

One of these spheres belongs to the planet which on Earth they call Saturn. Next is that radiance, prosperous and healthy for the human race, which is called Jupiter. Then comes the red one, terrible to the Earth, which you call Mars. Then, almost below the middle region, the Sun holds the place of leader, prince, and governor of the other lights; he is the mind and moderator of the universe <note>original: "mens mundi et temperatio"</note>, of such magnitude that he illuminates and fills all things with his light. Him follow, as companions, the courses of Venus and Mercury. In the lowest sphere, the Moon revolves, lit by the rays of the Sun. Below this, there is now nothing that is not mortal...

<meta>This page continues the vision of Scipio the Elder as he guides his grandson through the celestial spheres. Having previously described the Earth as a small, insignificant point in the cosmos, he now explains the distinction between the mortal realm and the eternal heavens, focusing specifically on the "Music of the Spheres"—the divine harmony produced by the motion of the planets.</meta>

->### O F  S C I P I O<-

...frail and fleeting, except for the souls given to the human race as a gift from the gods. Above the moon, all things are eternal. For that which is the middle and ninth sphere, the Earth, does not move; it is the lowest, <margin>* by movement</margin> and toward it all weights are carried by their own natural gravity <note>original: "nutu suo pondera". Cicero describes the geocentric view where the center of the Earth is the center of the universe, drawing all heavy objects toward it.</note>. 

As I gazed at these things in amazement, once I recovered myself, I asked, "What is this? What is this great and sweet sound that fills my ears?" 

"This," he replied, "is the sound which, joined by unequal intervals—yet nonetheless distinct in their proper proportions—is produced by the impulse and motion of the spheres themselves. By blending high-pitched notes with low ones, it creates uniform harmonies. For such great movements cannot be driven in silence; and nature dictates that the extremes on one side sound low, while on the other they sound high. For this reason, that highest circuit of the starry sky, whose revolution is swifter, moves with a high and sharp sound; however, this lowest lunar circuit moves with the deepest tone. For the Earth, the ninth sphere, remaining motionless, always stays fixed in the lowest seat, occupying the central place of the world. 

<margin>* of modes</margin> Now, those eight circuits—among which the power of two is the same—produce seven <note>original: "v i i"</note> distinct sounds separated by intervals. This number [seven] is almost the knot <note>term: "nodus". In this context, a binding element or a mathematical focal point that holds the structure of the universe together.</note> of all things. Learned men, having imitated this with strings and songs, have opened for themselves a path back to this place; just like others who, with outstanding talent during their human lives, have pursued divine studies. 

The ears of men, filled with this sound, have become deaf. Indeed, there is no duller sense in you; just as where the Nile rushes down from the highest mountains to those falls which are called the Catadupa <note>term: "Catadupa". The Greek-derived name for the Great Cataracts of the Nile; ancient writers claimed the roar was so loud the local inhabitants lost their hearing.</note>, the people who inhabit that place lack the sense of hearing because of the magnitude of the noise. But this sound, produced by the most rapid revolution of the whole universe, is so great that human ears cannot capture it; just as you cannot look directly at the sun, and your sight and sense are overcome by its rays." 

While I was marveling at these things, I nevertheless kept turning my eyes back to the Earth. Then Africanus said, "I per-" <note>catchword: "tio," indicating the next page begins with "sentio" (I perceive).</note>

# T H E  D R E A M

"I perceive," he said, "that you are even now gazing upon the seat and home of men. If it seems small to you—as it truly is—then you should always look upon these heavenly realms and despise those human things. For what fame can you achieve through the speech of men, or what glory is worth seeking? You see that the Earth is inhabited in rare and narrow places, and that between these very 'spots' where people dwell, vast wildernesses are scattered. And those who inhabit the Earth are not only so separated that nothing can flow between them from one group to another, but they stand relative to you partly slantwise <note>original: "obliquos"; this refers to people living in the same hemisphere but at a different latitude</note>, partly <margin>transverse</margin> transverse <note>original: "transuersos"; this refers to people living in the other hemisphere but at the same latitude</note>, and partly even directly opposite <note>original: "aduersos"; these are the "Antipodes," people living on the exact opposite side of the globe</note>. From these people, you can certainly expect no glory.

You see, moreover, that this same Earth is wreathed and surrounded by certain 'girdles' <note>original: "cingulis"; these are the five climate zones (Arctic, Antarctic, Torrid, and two Temperate zones) described in ancient geography</note>. Of these, you see that two—which are most distant from each other and supported on either side by the poles of the heavens—are frozen with frost; however, that middle and largest one is scorched by the heat of the sun. Two zones are habitable. Of these, the southern one—where those who dwell there plant their feet opposite yours <note>Referring to the inhabitants of the Southern Hemisphere</note>—has nothing to do with your race. 

Now, as for this other zone lying to the north where you dwell: see how small a portion of it belongs to you. For all the land inhabited by you—narrow at the poles and wider at the sides—is a small sort of island surrounded by that sea which you on Earth call the Atlantic, the Great Sea, or the Ocean. Yet you see how small it is, despite such a grand name. From these very lands that are known and cultivated, has your name, or that of any of us, been able to cross this Caucasus Mountains which you see, or swim across that river Ganges? Who in the remaining parts of the East, or the farthest reaches of the setting sun, or the regions of the North or South, will ever hear your name? With these regions cut away, you surely see in what narrow straits your glory seeks to spread itself. Even those who do speak of us, how long will they continue to do so? Furthermore, even if the [future] offspring...

their feet opposite yours, has no connection with your race. But even if the offspring of future generations should wish to pass down the praises of each of us, as received from their fathers, to their own descendants, nevertheless, because of the <term>floods and conflagrations</term> <note>original: "eluuiiones exustionesque"; Cicero refers to the Stoic belief that the earth is periodically destroyed and renewed by water and fire</note> of the earth, which must happen at certain fixed times, we are unable to achieve a glory that is even long-lasting, let alone eternal. What does it matter, then, if you are talked about by those who are born after you, when there was no mention of you by those born before you—who were no fewer in number and were certainly better men? This is especially true since, among those very people by whom our name can be heard, no one can maintain a memory lasting for even a single "year." For men commonly measure a year only by the return of the Sun, which is the movement of a single star. However, when all the stars have returned to the same point from which they once set out, and have restored the same configuration of the entire sky after long intervals, then that can truly be called a <term>Turning Year</term> <note>original: "annus uertens"; also known as the "Great Year" or "Platonic Year," the period of time it takes for all celestial bodies to return to their original relative positions</note>; I hardly dare to say how many generations of men are contained within it. For just as the sun once seemed to fail and be extinguished for men, at the moment when the soul of Romulus entered these very celestial realms, so when the sun shall fail again at the same point and the same time, then you may consider a year to be complete, with all the signs and stars recalled to their original starting point. Know that not even a twentieth part of this year has yet turned. Therefore, if you should lose hope of returning to this place, where all things exist for great and excellent men, what then is that human glory worth, which can hardly pertain to a small fraction of a single year? If, therefore, you wish to look upward and contemplate this seat and eternal home, you should not surrender yourself to the talk of the common crowd, nor place the hope of your affairs in human rewards; <term>Virtue</term> herself, by her own charms, ought to draw you toward true honor. Let others see to what they say about you—though they will talk regardless. All such talk, however, is both...

# THE DREAM

-> THE DREAM <-

...narrow straits <note>original: "angustijs"; the text begins mid-word, completing a sentence describing the small, inhabited portions of the Earth</note> of those regions which you see; nor has it ever been everlasting for anyone, for it is buried by the death of men and extinguished by the forgetfulness of posterity."

When he had said these things, I replied, "O Africanus <note>Scipio Africanus the Younger is addressing his adoptive grandfather, Scipio Africanus the Elder</note>, if indeed a path like a gateway to the entrance of heaven lies open to those who have served their country well, then—although I have followed in my father's footsteps and yours since I was a boy, and have not failed to uphold your honor—now, with such a great reward set before me, I will strive much more vigilantly."

And he said, "Strive indeed, and hold this truth: it is not you who are mortal, but only this body. For you are not what that physical form reveals; rather, the <term>mind</term> <note>original: "mens"; here referring to the rational soul or the true self</note> of each person is who they truly are, not that shape which can be pointed to with a finger. Know, therefore, that you are a god <note>original: "Deum... te esse"; Cicero follows the Platonic tradition of viewing the rational, self-moving soul as divine</note>: if indeed that which thrives, feels, remembers, and foresees is a god—that which rules, governs, and moves the body over which it is set, just as the supreme God rules this world. And just as the eternal God moves the world, which is in some part mortal, so the everlasting soul moves the fragile body.

For that which is always in motion is eternal. But that which communicates motion to something else, and which is itself moved from an outside source, must necessarily find an end to its life when it finds an end to its motion. Therefore, only that which moves itself never ceases to move, because it is never deserted by itself; moreover, for all other things that are moved, this is the source, the <term>principle</term> <note>original: "principium"; the primary cause or starting point from which everything else flows</note> of their movement. Now, a principle has no origin, for all things arise from a principle, while the principle itself cannot be born from anything else. It would not be a principle if it were produced from elsewhere. And if it never has a beginning, it certainly never dies. For if a principle were extinguished, it could not be reborn from another, nor could it create anything else from itself, since all things must necessarily arise from a principle. Thus it follows that the principle of motion arises from that which is moved by its own power. This can neither be born nor die; otherwise, the whole heaven would collapse and all nature would col- <note>The text cuts off mid-word "consistat," meaning to come to a halt or collapse</note>

<summary>In this pivotal passage, the Elder Scipio explains that the true human identity is the immortal mind, not the physical body. He argues for the soul's divinity and immortality based on its nature as a self-moving "principle" of life.</summary>

<keywords>immortality of the soul, divinity, self-motion, Scipio Africanus, Cicero, Macrobius, cosmic vision, philosophy of mind</keywords>

# OF SCIPIO

<meta>catchword: MACRO <note>This catchword refers to Macrobius, the 5th-century author whose commentary preserved this portion of Cicero’s "Republic" for the Middle Ages.</note></meta>

*...must necessarily come to a stop <note>original: "sistat"; completing the sentence from the previous page: "what is moved by an external force must necessarily stop when the force ends."</note>, and can find no force which might be moved by an initial impulse. Since, therefore, it is evident that what is moved by its own self is eternal, who is there who would deny that this nature has been granted to souls? For everything that is shaken by an external pulse is inanimate. But that which is an animal <term>animal</term> <note>original: "animal"; in Latin, this literally means "a thing possessed of 'anima' or soul," referring to any living, breathing being.</note> is moved by an internal motion of its own. For this is the proper nature and power of the soul. If the soul is the only thing among all others that moves itself, then it was certainly never born and is eternal. Exercise this soul in the best of pursuits.*

*The best cares are those for the safety of the fatherland <note>original: "salute patriae"; for a Roman like Cicero, the highest moral duty was service to the state.</note>; the soul, agitated and exercised by these, will fly more swiftly to this seat and its own home. And it will do this more quickly if, even then while it is still shut up in the body, it reaches outward and, contemplating those things which are outside, abstracts itself as much as possible from the physical form. # OF MACROBIUS
## AURELIUS THEODOSIUS
### The first book of the most elegant exposition on the Dream of Scipio, by a man of Consular and most illustrious rank.

->Chapter 1. What difference and what similarity exist between the books of Plato and Cicero concerning the Republic; and why the former chose the testimony of Er, and the latter the Dream of Scipio, for his work.<-

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'I' depicting a figure standing in a forest beside a large stag.</image-desc>
Between the books of Plato and Cicero, both of which were established concerning the Republic, Eustathius—my son, who is equally the sweetness and the glory of my life—we have observed at first glance this difference: that the former [Plato] organized a Republic, while the latter [Cicero] recounted one. The one discussed what a Republic ought to be; the other discussed how one was established by our ancestors. In this respect, however, Cicero’s imitation preserved the similarity of the work most especially: for just as Plato, at the conclusion of his volume, makes it known through a certain man returned to life <margin>Why either Plato introduced Er returning to life, or Cicero introduced Scipio aroused by a dream.</margin> (which he seemed to have left) what the state of souls is after they have put off their bodies—adding to this a significant description of the spheres and stars—so too is a vision of no dissimilar matters narrated by Cicero's Scipio, as it was presented to him during his rest. But why there was a need for either such a fictional account <note>original: "commento"; referring to Plato's Myth of Er.</note> or such a dream in these particular books, in which the authors were speaking of the state of Republics; and what purpose it served to describe circles, orbits, and spheres among the principles of governing cities, or to treat the measurements of the stars and the rotation of the heavens, seemed to me a matter worthy of inquiry.

<summary>Macrobius begins his commentary by comparing Plato’s "Republic" with Cicero’s "Republic," noting that while Plato imagined an ideal state, Cicero described an actual historical one. He questions why both authors chose to end their political works with mystical visions of the cosmos and the afterlife.</summary>

<header>BOOK I.</header>

...[ficti]tious <note>The text here completes the thought that the use of a dream or myth might seem like a "fictitious" or unnecessary addition to a serious work.</note> and perhaps it might seem so to others: lest we suspect that men excelling in wisdom, accustomed to sensing nothing but the divine in the search for truth, added something superfluous to such a refined work. A few things must therefore be said about this first, so that the intention of the work we are discussing may become clearly known. Plato, gazing deeply into the essence of all things and actions, observed in his entire discourse concerning the establishment of a Republic that the love of justice must be poured into the soul; without which not only a Republic, nor even a small gathering of men, but not even a small household will stand firm. 

Furthermore, to *instill <margin>*An old reading has "to implant" <note>original: "inoculandum"</note>; a metaphor drawn from the practice of grafting plants.</margin> this affection for justice in hearts, he saw that nothing would be as supportive as if the fruits of that justice did not seem to end with the life of a man. But how could it be shown that this fruit survives and lasts after a man, unless the immortality of the soul were first established? Once faith in the eternity of souls was established, he noticed that it followed that certain places must be assigned to them once they are released from the bond of the body, according to the consideration of their good or wicked merit. 

Thus in the *Phaedo* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the soul's final hours and its immortality.</note>, after the soul is asserted into the true dignity of its own immortality by the light of unassailable reasons, there follows a distinction of the places which are owed to those leaving this life, by that law which each person established for himself while living. So too in the *Gorgias* <note>A dialogue concerning rhetoric and the power of justice.</note>, after the discussion on behalf of justice is completed, we are reminded of the condition of souls after the body with the moral gravity and the persuasive charm of Socrates. 

He [Plato] therefore followed the same method attentively, especially in those volumes in which he undertook to form the state of a Republic. For after he gave the primacy to justice and taught that the soul does not perish after the living being, he finally asserted at the end of the work—through that myth <note>original: "fabulam"</note> (for so some call it)—where the soul goes after the body, or from where it comes to the body; so that the soul might know either the reward for justice cultivated or the punishment for it scorned, since souls are indeed immortal and destined to undergo judg[ment]... <meta>catchword: [judi]cium (judgment)</meta>

<header>BOOK I.</header>

...preface <note>original: "prafationem". This completes the word from the previous page.</note>; and finally, what response should be given to the objections, specifically regarding the part that is necessary for this work. Once these objections are weakened—which is an easy task—then whatever bite of envy has ever been aimed, or perhaps will be aimed, against the opinion of either Plato or Cicero, even regarding the Dream of Scipio, will be dissolved. The entire faction of the Epicureans <note>A school of philosophy that generally prioritized sensory experience and often mocked the metaphysical or allegorical "myths" used by Platonists.</note>, always straying from the truth with a consistent error and considering things they do not understand to be laughable, has mocked this sacred volume and the most majestic, serious matters of nature. Colotes <note>An Epicurean philosopher and student of Epicurus known for his polemics against other schools of thought.</note>, who is particularly notable for his talkativeness among the followers of Epicurus, even recorded in a book the bitter quibbles he directed at this subject. But we must omit the other things he wrongly criticized here (since they do not pertain to the Dream, which is the subject of our current discussion). We will pursue that specific slander which, unless it is stamped out, will remain a charge common to both Cicero and Plato. 

<margin>What Colotes the Epicurean objected to in Plato.</margin>
For he [Colotes] says that a philosopher ought not to devise a **fable** <note>original: "fabulam". In this context, it refers to a fictional or allegorical narrative used to illustrate a point.</note>, because no kind of fiction is appropriate for those who profess the truth. "For why," he asks, "if you wanted to teach us the concept of celestial things or the condition of souls, was this not handled with a simple and direct explanation? Instead, you sought out a character, devised a novel situation, and staged a complex scene of fiction, thereby polluting the very gateway of seeking the truth with a lie." Since these accusations, when thrown at Plato's Er <note>Referring to the "Myth of Er" from the end of Plato’s *Republic*, which Cicero modeled Scipio's dream after.</note>, also indict the rest of our dreaming **Africanus** <note>Scipio Africanus the Younger, the narrator of Cicero's vision.</note> (for in both cases, a character was chosen under a fitting premise to be a convenient messenger for these revelations), let us resist the pressure and refute the slander of this vain argument. Thus, by dissolving this one charge, the work of both authors may rightly retain its unharmed dignity. 

Philosophy does not reject all fables, nor does it accept them all.

<meta>This page continues Macrobius’s systematic defense of using fictional narratives in philosophy. He is responding to the Epicurean critique by establishing a hierarchy of "fables," distinguishing between those that are merely for entertainment and those that serve a higher pedagogical or "pious" purpose.</meta>

<header>ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO</header>

...admit often and willingly, it must be explained through the stages of divisions. **Fables**—a name which indicates a profession of falsehood—were invented either merely for the sake of pleasing the ear, or for the purpose of encouraging moral improvement <note>original: "in bonam frugem". Literally "into good fruit" or "harvest," a metaphor for a productive or virtuous life.</note>. They soothe the hearing, just as comedies do, like those Menander <note>A famous Greek dramatist known for "New Comedy" which focused on domestic life rather than politics.</note> or his imitators produced for the stage; or plots filled with the fictional misfortunes of lovers, a style in which Petronius Arbiter <note>The author of the "Satyricon."</note> practiced much, or in which we are surprised to find Apuleius <note>The author of "The Golden Ass."</note> sometimes amused himself. Philosophy banishes this entire category of fables, which professes only to delight the ear, from its sanctuary to the cradles of nurses.

However, among those fables that encourage the reader’s intellect toward a certain appearance of virtue, a second distinction is made. For in some, the plot itself is based on fiction, and the sequence of the narrative is woven together through lies: such are those **Aesopic fables**, famous for the elegance of their fiction. But in others, the plot is founded on the solidity of truth, yet this truth itself is presented through composed and fictional elements. This type is no longer called a "fable," but a **fabulous narrative** <term>narratio fabulosa: a story that uses a fictional outer shell to protect or convey a core of philosophical truth</term>. Examples include the sacred ceremonies of Hesiod and Orpheus <note>Legendary poets whose works dealt with the origins and genealogies of the gods.</note>, which tell of the ancestry or deeds of the gods, or the mystical teachings reported by the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras who used symbols and allegories to hide their philosophical doctrines from the uninitiated.</note>. 

Therefore, according to this second division we have mentioned, the first type—which is conceived of falsehood and told through falsehood—is foreign to books of philosophy. The latter type is further divided by another distinction. For when truth underlies the plot and only the narrative is "fabulous," there is more than one way to relate truths through fiction. Either the narrative is woven from things that are shameful and unworthy of the divine, or resemble monstrosities—such as gods committing adultery, or Saturn <note>The Roman equivalent of the Greek Titan Cronus.</note> cutting off the genitals of his father Caelus <note>The Roman personification of the sky, equivalent to the Greek Uranus.</note>, and Saturn himself then being cast into chains by the son who seized his kingdom. This entire category philosophers prefer to ignore <note>original: "nescire malunt" — literally "prefer not to know," suggesting they reject these crude or literal interpretations of myths as unworthy of serious thought.</note>. Or, the understanding of sacred matters [is presented] under a pious fiction—

<meta>catchword: ...under [the knowledge of sacred things]</meta>

### BOOK I.

...under a veil, where things are covered by honorable realities and dressed in names. And this is the only kind of fiction that the caution of a philosopher dealing with divine matters permits. Since, therefore, neither the reporter Er <note>A reference to the "Myth of Er" from the end of Plato’s *Republic*, where a soldier returns from the dead to describe the afterlife.</note> nor the dreaming Africanus <note>Scipio Africanus the Younger, whose dream is the subject of Cicero’s work.</note> causes any harm to the discussion—but rather the declaration of sacred things remains whole in its dignity, covered by these names—let the accuser at last, having been taught to distinguish between fables <note>meaning mere entertaining lies</note> and fabulous narratives <note>allegorical stories containing truth</note>, fall silent.

<margin>
When philosophers are accustomed to use fables.
*Or, instead of "also," another reading is "playful things."
</margin>
It must be known, however, that philosophers do not admit fabulous or even "permitted" fables into every discussion: they are accustomed to use them only when speaking of the soul, or of the spirits of the air or the heavens, or of the other gods. But when the discourse dares to raise itself toward the highest and principal God of all—who among the Greeks is called **the Good** <note>original: τἀγαθὸν (tagathon)</note> and the **First Cause** <note>original: ππρῶτον αἴτιον (proton aition)</note>—or toward the Mind, which the Greeks call **Nous** <note>original: νοῦν</note>, containing the original species of things which are called **Ideas** <note>original: ἰδέαι</note>, and which is born from and proceeds from the highest God: when, I say, they speak of these—the highest God and the Mind—they touch upon nothing fabulous at all. 

Instead, if they attempt to describe anything about these subjects—which exceed not only human speech but even human thought—they take refuge in analogies and examples. Thus Plato, when he was inspired to speak **concerning the Good** <note>original: περὶ τἀγαθοῦ (peri tagathou)</note>, did not dare to say what it is, knowing only this about it: that what it is like cannot be known by man. In the visible world, he found only the sun to be its closest likeness; and through this analogy, he opened a path for his discourse to raise itself toward things that cannot be comprehended. Therefore, antiquity fashioned no **image** <term>simulachrum: a physical statue or representation of a deity</term> for him, though images were established for other gods, because the highest God and the Mind born from him are as far beyond the soul as they are above nature; to that level, it is not permitted for any fables to reach. Regarding the other gods, however, as I have said, and the soul, they do not turn to fabulous things without reason, nor for the sake of entertainment, but because they know that an open [nakedness] is hostile to nature...

...and the explanation of itself. Just as Nature has withdrawn the understanding of itself from the common senses of men through a varied covering and veil of reality, so she has willed that her secrets be handled by the wise through fabulous narratives.
<margin>*by little cords <note>The main text uses "cuniculis" (tunnels), while the margin suggests "funiculis" (cords/lines).</note></margin>

## CHAPTER III.

### BOOK I.

b 2
<meta>catchword: Sky</meta>

<margin>Five kinds of dreams.</margin>
...stituted them to everyone. Let us now set forth the five kinds of dreams, so that it may become known to which category the dream we are discussing <note>Referring to the "Dream of Scipio" by Cicero, which Macrobius is commentating upon.</note> should be applied. Of all the things that people seem to see while sleeping, there are five principal types and names: there is the *onar* <note>Greek: ὄναρ</note> according to the Greeks, which the Latins call a *somnium* <note>An enigmatic dream requiring interpretation.</note>; or the *horama* <note>Greek: ὅραμα</note>, which is rightly called a *visio* <note>A prophetic vision of a future event.</note>; or the *chrematismos* <note>Greek: χρηματισμὸς</note>, which is named an *oraculum* <note>An oracle, where a parent or solemn person reveals the future.</note>; or the *enypnion* <note>Greek: ἐνύπνιον</note>, which is called an *insomnium* <note>A nightmare or non-predictive dream caused by daily stress.</note>; or the *phantasma* <note>Greek: φάντασμα</note>, which Cicero (whenever he had need of this name) called a *visum* <note>An apparition seen in the moment between waking and sleep.</note>. The last two of these, when they are seen, are unworthy of the care of interpretation, because they bring no divination: I mean the *insomnium* and the *phantasma*.

<margin>Insomnium <note>Literally "disturbed sleep" or nightmare.</note></margin>
For it is an *insomnium* whenever the care of a burdened mind, or body, or even of fortune—such as might have fatigued a person while awake—presents itself to them while sleeping. In the mind: if a lover sees himself either enjoying his delights or deprived of them; or if someone fearing a person who threatens them either with treachery or power seems to have either encountered them or escaped them in the imagery of his thoughts. In the body: if someone gorged with wine, or stuffed with food, or bloated, thinks he is being suffocated by the abundance or relieved by the weight; or on the contrary, if someone hungry for food or thirsty for drink seems to desire, seek, or even find it.

<margin>*instead of <note>This indicates a textual correction: "to be increased" rather than "to increase."</note></margin>
In fortune: when someone thinks that he, out of desire, is being increased* in power or office, or out of fear, is being stripped* of it. These and similar things, since they followed from the state of the mind just as they had preceded and disturbed the sleeper's rest, fly in along with sleep and vanish just as quickly. From this comes the name "Insomnium": not because it is seen through sleep (for this is common to this type as well as the others), but because it is believed to exist only in the sleep itself; while it is seen, it leaves behind no utility or significance after the sleep is over. That these *insomnia* are false, Virgil <note>original: "Maro," the family name of the poet Virgil.</note> did not fail to mention:

<margin>Book 6 of the Aeneid.</margin>
> *But the spirits of the dead send false dreams <note>original: "insomnia"</note> to the sky above.*

# ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

...presents itself. <note>Continuing the definition of *insomnium* from the previous page.</note> Calling the sky here the region of the living: because just as the gods are higher than us, so we are considered the "higher ones" to the dead. Describing love as well, the cares of which are always followed by nightmares <note>original: *insomnia*</note>, the poet <note>Virgil</note> says:
<margin>Aeneid, Book 4.</margin>
> His features and words remain fixed in her breast, 
> nor does care give peaceful rest to her limbs.

And after this:

> Anna, my sister, what nightmares <note>original: *insomnia*</note> terrify me and keep me in suspense?

<margin>Apparition.</margin>
An apparition <note>original: Φάντασμα (*phantasma*)</note>—that is, a "vision" <note>original: *uisum*</note>—occurs between wakefulness and deep sleep, in what is called the first mist of sleep. The person, who has barely begun to sleep and still believes themselves to be awake, seems to see forms rushing toward them or wandering about, differing from nature either in size or appearance, or various shifts in circumstances, whether joyful or turbulent. 

<margin>Ephialtes <note>A term for a "pressing" nightmare or incubus.</note>.</margin>
In this category is the *ephialtes* <note>original: ἐφιάλτης</note>, which popular belief thinks invades those resting, and who, feeling themselves pressed by its weight, are burdened. Since these two types <note>The *insomnium* and *phantasma*.</note> are accepted as being of no help in knowing the future, we are instructed in the art of divination by the three remaining types. 

<margin>Oracle.</margin>
And indeed, an oracle <note>original: *oraculum*</note> is when, in dreams, a parent or another holy and grave person, or a priest, or even a God, openly announces what will happen or not happen, or what should be done or avoided. 

<margin>Vision.</margin>
A vision <note>original: *uisio*</note>, however, is when someone sees something that will happen in exactly the same way it appeared. For example: a person seems to see a friend who is staying abroad (and whom they were not thinking about) having returned; they go out, meet the friend they saw, and embrace them. Or, while resting, one receives a deposit of money, and in the morning a petitioner meets them, entrusting money to their care and asking for it to be hidden in faithful custody.

<margin>The Dream and its five species.</margin>
That which is properly called a "dream" <note>original: *somnium*</note> is what covers its meaning with figures and veils it with obscurities, so that the significance of the thing shown cannot be understood without interpretation. What kind of thing this is, we do not need to explain, since everyone knows this from experience...

# BOOK I. 21

...that he may recognize what it is. Of this type <note>Referring to the *somnium* or enigmatic dream.</note> there are five species: it is either **personal**, **other-oriented**, **shared**, **public**, or **universal**. 

It is **personal** <note>original: *proprium*</note> when one dreams of oneself doing or experiencing something. It is **other-oriented** <note>original: *alienum*</note> when one dreams of another person. It is **shared** <note>original: *commune*</note> when one dreams of oneself together with another. It is **public** <note>original: *publicum*</note> when one imagines some sad or joyful event has happened to the city, the forum, the theater, or any public walls or activities. It is **universal** <note>original: *generale*</note> when one dreams of some change involving the sun's orb, the moon's sphere, the other stars, the heavens, or the whole of the earth.

<margin>To which category the Dream of Scipio should be referred.</margin>
This dream, however, which Scipio reported he had seen, embraces those three types which alone are considered authoritative, and it touches upon every species of the "enigmatic dream" itself. 

It is an **oracle**: because both [Aemilius] Paullus and [Scipio] Africanus—both equals, both holy and venerable, and both holding the priesthood—announced to him what was going to happen. It is a **vision**: because he beheld the very places where he would be after leaving the body, and what his future state would be. It is an **enigmatic dream**: because the "height" of the matters narrated to him, covered by a depth of wisdom, cannot be opened to us except through the science of interpretation. 

It is also referred to every species of the dream itself. It is **personal**: because he was led to the upper realms and learned of his own future. It is **other-oriented**: because he discovered the state which the souls of others had obtained. It is **shared**: because he learned that the same places were being prepared for himself as for others of similar merit. It is **public**: because he recognized the victory of his fatherland, the destruction of Carthage, his triumph at the Capitol, and the anxiety of future civil strife. It is **universal**: because, while still a living man, he perceived the heavens and the circles of the sky, the harmony of their rotation <note>This refers to the "Music of the Spheres," a Pythagorean concept that the movement of celestial bodies creates a divine musical interval.</note>—things new and unknown—and also the movements of the stars and lights, and the layout of the entire earth, by looking both upward and downward.

<margin>How a public dream is appropriate for Scipio while still a soldier.</margin>
Nor can it be said that a dream which was universal and public was not fitting for Scipio's person: because not yet to him...

...the highest office had fallen to him: indeed when, as he says himself, he was still considered almost a common soldier. For they say that dreams regarding the state of the city should not be held as true unless its ruler or a magistrate has seen them; or if not one, but many of the common people, have dreamed similar things. Therefore in Homer, when Agamemnon made public in the council of the Greeks the dream he had seen concerning the marshalling of the battle, Nestor—who himself helped the army no less with his wisdom than all the youth did with their strength—secured belief for the report. Nestor said: "Concerning the public state, we must believe a kingly dream; but if another had seen it, we would reject it as futile." <note>This refers to a scene in the *Iliad*, Book 2, where Nestor validates Agamemnon’s dream because of his status as king.</note> 

But it was not without reason that Scipio—even if he had not yet attained the consulship, nor was yet the commander of the army—should dream of the destruction of Carthage, of which he was to be the author. It was fitting that he should hear that victory would be made public through his service, and that he should even see the secrets of nature, being a man excelling no less in philosophy than in virtue. 

These things having been asserted—since earlier, citing Virgil as a witness to the falsity of certain dreams, we mentioned his verse drawn <note>original: *eruti*</note> from the description of the twin gates of sleep—if any should perchance wish to ask why the gate of ivory is assigned to false things and the gate of horn to true things, he will be instructed by the author Porphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher whose interpretations Macrobius frequently uses.</note>. In his commentaries, Porphyry says the following regarding this passage, which was first described by Homer under the same division: "All truth," he says, "lies hidden. Yet the soul, when it is somewhat free from the duties of the body during sleep, sometimes catches sight of it; sometimes it extends its vision, yet does not reach it."

<margin>*direct</margin>

->CHAPTER IV.<-

Having discussed the types and modes to which the *Dream of Scipio* is referred, let us now attempt to reveal the core meaning and the purpose of the dream itself—which the Greeks call the *skopos* <note>original: *σκοπὸν*</note>—before the specific words are examined. We should assert that the purpose of the present work pertains to this: as we already suggested at the beginning of this discourse, it is to teach us that the souls of those who have served the Republic <note>The Roman state (*Respublica*).</note> well are returned to heaven after their bodies, and there enjoy an eternity of happiness. For it was this specific occasion that prompted Scipio himself to narrate the dream, which he testified he had kept hidden in silence for a long time. For when Laelius <note>Gaius Laelius, a close friend of Scipio Aemilianus and a character in Cicero’s dialogues.</note> complained that no statues of Nasica <note>Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica Serapio, who led the senate against Tiberius Gracchus in 133 BCE.</note> had been placed in public as a reward for killing the tyrant, Scipio replied, among other things, with these words: "But although for the wise, the very consciousness of excellent deeds is the most ample reward for virtue; nevertheless, that divine virtue does not desire statues held fast by lead, nor triumphs with withering laurels, but certain more stable and more ever-fresh <note>original: *viridiora*, literally 'greener' or more vigorous.</note> kinds of rewards." 

"What, however, are those rewards?" asked Laelius. ### BOOK I.

<note>original: "nities", likely "planities" continued from the previous page</note> ...A surface, however, which the Greeks call <term>epiphaneia</term> <note>original: ἐπιφάνειαν; meaning the appearance or outer surface of an object</note>, is stretched out in length and width but lacks height; and we have already expressed by how many lines this surface is contained. Solidity in bodies, moreover, is established when height is added to these two. For when three dimensions are filled, it becomes a solid body, which they call <term>stereon</term> <note>original: στερεὸν; meaning a solid or three-dimensional shape</note>: such as a die, which is called a cube. If, however, you wish to contemplate the surface not of just one part, but of the whole body—which we propose to be a square (to discuss one example which will suffice)—now not four, but eight angles are gathered together. You notice this when you mentally behold another square, such as we previously described, placed higher above the first: so that the height, which that plane lacked, may be added; and with three dimensions filled, it becomes a solid body, which they call a <term>stereon</term>, in imitation of a die, which is called a cube.

<margin>Stereon. Cube.</margin>

From these things it is apparent that the number eight both is, and is held to be, a solid body. This is because among geometers, one holds the place of a point; two make the drawing of a line, which is constrained by two points, as we said above. Four points, however, placed opposite each other in two rows of two, express the appearance of a square when a line is cast from each point to the point opposite it. These four, as we said, when doubled and made into eight, describe two similar squares; these, being placed one above the other with height added, create the form of a cube, which is a solid body. From this it appears that number is more ancient than the surface and the lines from which we mentioned the surface consists, and more ancient than all forms. For from lines one ascends to number as if to something prior, so that it may be understood from the diverse numbers of lines which geometric forms are being described. ### CHAPTER VI.

It remains for our established reasoning to persuade us that the <term>septenary</term> <note>original: "septenarium"; the number seven</note> number also deserves to be called "full" by right. First, we cannot pass over this without wonder: that the two numbers which, when multiplied together, define the vital lifespan of a robust man, consist of an even and an odd number. <note>This refers to 7 and 8. In antiquity, 56 years (7 x 8) was often considered the "perfect age" or the climax of a man's life.</note> For that which is generated from the mixing of these numbers is truly perfect. In this system, the odd number is called "male," and the even number is called "female." Likewise, mathematicians honor the odd number with the title of "father" and the even number with that of "mother."

Hence, Plato's *Timaeus* <note>A famous Socratic dialogue by Plato that explains the creation of the universe through mathematics and geometry.</note> records that God, the creator of the **world-soul**, interwove its parts from the even and the odd—that is, from the double and triple numbers—so that there was an alternation of <insert>* otherwise: numbers</insert> exchange starting from the double up to eight, and from the triple up to twenty-seven. For these are the first **cubes** born on either side. Indeed, from the even numbers, two times two (which is four) creates a surface; but two times two times two (which is eight) forms a solid body. From the odd numbers, three times three (which is nine) produces a surface; and three times three times three (that is, three times nine, which is twenty-seven) equally produces the first cube of the other side.

From this, we are given to understand why these two numbers—I mean eight and seven—which were combined in the *Republic* <note>Referring to Cicero’s *The Republic*, of which "The Dream of Scipio" is the final part. It mentions the "perfect" number of years in a man's life.</note> for the calculation of the years of a perfect man, were judged the only ones suitable for creating the world-soul: for nothing following the Creator can be more perfect than they. ...by its lines, and in all bodies, we have shown. However, the proceeding treatise finds that numbers existed even before the **world-soul** <note>The *anima mundi*; an intrinsic spirit that many ancient philosophers believed brought life and order to the universe.</note>, and the most venerable reasoning of the *Timaeus*—a witness conscious of nature itself—expressed that the soul was woven from these numbers. Hence it is that the wise have not hesitated to pronounce that the soul is a **self-moving number**. <note>original: "animam esse numerum se mouentem"; a definition famously attributed to the philosopher Xenocrates.</note>

<margin>The first reason why the **septenary** <note>The number seven.</note> number is perfect, taken from its own parts.</margin>
Now let us see why the septenary number is considered "full" or "complete" by its own separate merit. So that its fullness may be more closely understood, let us first investigate the merits of the parts of which it consists, and then finally what the number itself is capable of. The septenary number consists of: either one and six; or two and five; or three and four. Let us examine the members of each of these combinations; from these, we shall confess that no other number is fruitful with such varied majesty. 

The first combination is composed of one and six. Now "one," which is called the <term>monad</term> <note>original: "monas"; from the Greek *monas*, meaning unity or the indivisible source.</note>—that is, **unity**—is simultaneously male and female, both even and odd. It is not a number itself, but the source and origin of numbers. This monad is the beginning and end of all things, yet it remains ignorant of its own beginning or end. It refers to the **Supreme God**, and it separates the understanding of Him from the number of subsequent things and powers; nor would you seek it in vain at the level of existence immediately below God. 

This is that **Mind**, born from the Supreme God, which, knowing nothing of the changes of time, exists always in the one eternity that is present. And since, being one, it is not countable, it nevertheless both creates from itself and contains within itself innumerable species of kinds. From there, if you incline the edge of your thought a little further, you will find this monad refers to the **soul**. For the soul, foreign to the contagion of "wild" matter <note>original: "syluestris materiae"; a reference to the Greek *hyle*, often translated as "forest" or "wood," referring to the raw, unformed substance of the physical world.</note>, owes itself only to its creator and to itself. Having obtained a simple nature, even when it pours itself into the immensity of the universe to provide life, it nevertheless enters into no divorce from its own unity. <margin>Why Pallas is called the <term>monad</term> <note>original: *monas*</note> by the poets.</margin>
She is called Pallas for this reason: because she proceeded from the offspring and multiplication of the monad alone, just as **Minerva** <note>The Roman equivalent of Pallas Athena.</note> is said to have been born from only one parent.

<margin>The power of the **senary** <note>The number six.</note> number.</margin>
The **senary**, however, which when joined with one makes the **septenary**, possesses a varied and manifold religious significance and power. First, because it is the only one among all the numbers below ten that consists of its own parts. We have preferred this one because, once mentioned, the dignity not only of the six but also of the seven will be equally established. <margin>Praise of the ternary and the quaternary.</margin>
*The third [pairing of the number seven] concerns **three** and **four**; let us consider how much power this holds. The first surface of a geometric body [derived] from an odd number consists of three lines: for by these, a triangular shape is enclosed. However, the first [surface] from an even number is found in four [lines]. Likewise we know, according to **Plato** <note>Macrobius refers here to the Pythagorean-Platonic tradition that views numbers as the literal building blocks of reality.</note>—that is, according to the secret of truth itself—that those things are bound together by a strong bond when an intervening mean <note>In ancient mathematics, a "mean" (medietas) is a value that sits between two extremes to create a proportion or harmony.</note> provides the firmness of the link. But when that mean itself is doubled, those things which are outermost are bound together not only tenaciously, but even indissolubly. Thus it happened to the first **ternary** <term>ternary</term> <note>The number three.</note> number that it received a middle [term] between two extremes by which it might be bound. But the **quaternary** <term>quaternary</term> <note>The number four.</note> was the first of all to obtain two means. Borrowing these from this number, God—the craftsman and founder of the worldly mass—bound the elements together with an indissoluble bond, just as it is asserted in **Plato's Timaeus** <note>The Timaeus is a famous Socratic dialogue that provides a mathematical explanation for the creation of the physical world.</note>. Nor could things so contentious and repugnant to one another, which by nature refuse communion—I speak of **earth** and **fire**—have been mixed otherwise, nor joined through such a yoke-like agreement, unless they were bound by the two middle links of **air** and **water**. For in this way, God the Maker connected elements very different from one another through the fitness of order, so that they might be easily joined. For since there were two qualities in each, He gave to each one such a second quality that it might find something kindred and similar to itself in that to which it adhered. **Earth** is dry and cold; but **water** is cold and moist. These two elements, although they are opposites through the "dry" and the "moist," are nevertheless joined through the common "cold." **Air** is moist and hot; and though it is the opposite of cold water because of its heat, it is nevertheless coupled through the conciliation of its partner, moisture. Above this is **fire**; since it is hot and dry, it rejects the moisture of the air through its dryness, but is connected through the fellowship of heat. And so it happens that*

Each of the elements embraces its two neighbors on either side with its individual qualities as if with certain arms. **Water** binds itself to **earth** through cold, and to **air** through moisture. **Air** is allied to water by a similar moisture, and to **fire** by heat. **Fire** is mixed with air because it is hot, and joined to earth by dryness. **Earth** endures fire through dryness and does not reject water because of cold. Yet this variety of bonds, if there were only two elements, would have possessed no firmness between them; if there were three, they would be knotted together by some link, though a less powerful one. But among **four**, there is an indissoluble binding, since the two extremes are bound together by two intermediaries. This will be more manifest if you place the very essence of the meaning, taken from **Plato's Timaeus** <note>Macrobius is paraphrasing Timaeus 31b-32c, where Plato explains that the universe must be a solid, and solids require two middle terms to be perfectly joined.</note>, in the middle.

<margin>This is an explanation of Plato's meaning, not his exact words.</margin>

> The principle of divine beauty, he says, demanded that the world be made such that it could be both seen and touched. It was certain, moreover, that nothing could be seen without the benefit of **fire**, nor touched without being solid; and nothing is solid without **earth**. Therefore, the Creator <term>fabricator</term> <note>Referring to the Demiurge, the divine craftsman in Platonic philosophy who shapes the material world.</note>, beginning to construct the whole body of the world out of fire and earth, saw that two things cannot be joined together without a middle bond to unite them; and the best bond is that which binds itself and the things to be bound together in equal measure. A single intermediary can suffice only when a surface <note>A two-dimensional plane.</note>, lacking depth, is to be bound. But where a deep dimension <note>A three-dimensional solid.</note> is constrained by bonds, the knot is not tied except by a double intermediary. Consequently, he wove **air** and **water** between fire and earth; and thus, through all things, a single and fitting bond of harmony ran, associating the diversity of the elements by the very equality of their differences. For as much as there is between water and air in terms of density and weight, just as much is there between air and fire. And again, what exists between air and water in terms of lightness and thinness, this same exists between...

Indeed, the space from the earth to the water is called **necessity** by natural philosophers <note>original: "physicis"</note>: because it is believed to bind and solidify that which is muddy and material within bodies.

<margin>* Menelaus, *Iliad* Book 7: "But may you all become water and earth."</margin>

Between the air and the fire, however, it is called **obedience**: because just as muddy and heavy things are joined to the higher ones by necessity, so higher things are coupled to the muddy ones by obedience, with harmony standing in the middle to provide the conjunction of both. Therefore, it is manifest that the completion <note>original: "absolutionem"</note> of bodies consists of these four elements and their three intervals. Thus these two numbers—I mean three and four—associated by such a manifold necessity of kinship among themselves, obey as servants of the treaty by consensus in forming the bodies of each. Nor do these two numbers provide a collaborative favor only in explaining bodies, but the Pythagoreans indeed venerate the number four, which they call the **tetractys** <term>tetractys</term> <note>A mystical triangular figure consisting of ten points arranged in four rows, representing the organization of the universe.</note>, as a sacred secret, as if it pertained to the perfection of the soul. # BOOK I.

He did not doubt that the number seven also consists of musical harmonies. Among these, the one called the **diapason** <note>original: διὰ πασῶν, literally "through all"; in modern music, the octave</note> is of no small power. This harmony consists of two others: the **diatessaron** <note>original: διὰ τεσσάρων, the interval of a fourth</note> and the **diapente** <note>original: διὰ πέντε, the interval of a fifth</note>. Moreover, the *diapente* is produced from the **hemiolios** <note>original: hemiolio; the ratio of 3:2</note>, and the *diatessaron* is produced from the **epitritos** <note>original: epitrito; the ratio of 4:3</note>. The first *hemiolios* is three, and the first *epitritos* is four; we shall explain more fully in its proper place what this signifies. Therefore, the *diatessaron* and *diapente* consist of these two numbers <note>three and four</note>, and from them the *diapason* harmony is generated. Whence Virgil, who was well-versed in every branch of learning, wishing to describe those who are fully and entirely blessed, said: *O thrice and four times blessed.* <note>Aeneid I.94. By combining 3 and 4, Virgil invokes the perfection of the number 7.</note>

# ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

<margin>Third.</margin> The architect-creator, through his providence, also placed the order of the seven wandering spheres <term>wandering spheres</term> <note>The "planets" in the geocentric model: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon.</note> beneath the star-bearing sphere and all that it contains. This was done so that they might both counter the rapid motions of the higher sphere <note>The "higher sphere" is the firmament or *primum mobile*, which was thought to rotate from East to West; the planets move in the opposite direction.</note> and govern all things below. 

<margin>Fourth.</margin> The number seven also moves the Moon, which is, as it were, the seventh among them, and regulates its course. Since this can be proven in many ways, let it first be shown by this: the Moon completes the circuit of the entire zodiac in nearly twenty-eight days. For although it returns to the Sun, from which it set out, over thirty days, it nonetheless spends only about twenty-eight days in its total circulation of the zodiac. In the remaining days, it catches up to the Sun, which had moved from the place where the Moon left it. For the Sun travels through one of the twelve signs in a full month. 

Let us suppose, then, that while the Sun is positioned in the first part of Aries, the Moon has emerged from its orb (as it were)—which we call being "born" <note>original: *nasci*; the "birth" of the moon refers to the New Moon, the beginning of a new cycle.</note>. After twenty-eight days and roughly seven hours, this Moon returns to the first part of Aries, but it does not find the Sun there. Meanwhile, by the law of its own progression, the Sun has moved further away. Therefore, the Moon is not yet thought to have returned to where it set out, because our eyes perceive its progress not from the first part of Aries, but from its relation to the Sun. Thus, in the remaining days—that is, two days, more or less—it follows the Sun, and then, moving once more under its orb and proceeding from there, it is said to be born again. 

<margin>Why the moon is born twice in Gemini.</margin> Consequently, it is almost never born twice in succession within the same sign, except in Gemini. There, this sometimes occurs because the Sun spends thirty-two days in that sign due to the height of the sign <note>The "height" refers to the Sun's apogee, where it appears to move more slowly through the zodiacal signs of summer, such as Gemini.</note>; it is very rare in others, occurring only if it proceeds from the Sun near the very first part of a sign. The origin of this number of twenty-eight days is the number seven. For if you proceed from one up to seven, adding each individual number to those that preceded it <note>1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 7 = 28. In Pythagorean numerology, this demonstrates how seven "generates" the lunar month.</note>, you will find that twenty-eight is born from seven. This number, which in four times seven

For in seven days, by traveling obliquely across the width from the edge of the northern boundary, it reaches the midpoint of the width, a location called the **ecliptic** <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The central line of the zodiac. While usually referring to the Sun's path, Macrobius uses it here to describe the Moon crossing the celestial equator.</note>. In the seven following days, it glides down from the middle to the lowest southern point. In another seven, it climbs back to the middle on its slanted path. In the final seven, it is restored to the northern summit. Thus, in those same four-times-seven days, it runs through the entirety of the zodiac’s length and width.

By similar arrangements of weeks, it also regulates the changes of its light by eternal law. For in the first seven days, it grows to the midpoint of a seemingly divided orb, and is then called **dichotomos** <term>dichotomos</term> <note>original: διχότομος; literally "cut in half." This refers to the First Quarter moon.</note>.

<margin>*Dichotomos*, that is, cut into a half-orb.</margin>

In the second seven days, by gathering its reborn fires, it now completes the whole orb and is then called "full." In the third seven, it becomes **dichotomos** again, when it is contracted by decreasing toward the midpoint. In the fourth seven, it is thinned out by the final reduction of its light. It is also distinguished throughout the whole month by seven changes, which the Greeks call **phaseis** <term>phaseis</term> <note>original: φάσεις; from which we get the word "phases."</note>: when it is born, when it becomes **dichotomos**, when it becomes

<margin>*Amphicyrtos*, that is, bulging on both sides.</margin>

**amphicyrtos** <term>amphicyrtos</term> <note>original: ἀμφίκυρτος; the "gibbous" moon, where more than half but not all of the face is illuminated.</note>, when it is full, and again when it is **amphicyrtos**, and once more **dichotomos**, and finally when it is deprived of all light to us. **Amphicyrtos** occurs when the light is beyond the diameter of the half-moon but before it is enclosed by the full circle; or, when decreasing from the full orb, it maintains a curved prominence of light between the midpoint and the fullness.

The greatest **revolution** <term>revolution</term> <note>original: *conuersio*; here referring to a completed cycle of time.</note> is that of the year according to the Sun; the middle is that of the month according to the Moon; and the smallest is that of the day according to sunrise and sunset. Indeed, every revolution is fourfold, and thus the number seven is established: that is, from the three types of revolutions and the four stages by which each one revolves. These are the four stages: first it becomes moist, then hot, then dry, and finally cold.

The greatest revolution—that of the year—is moist in the springtime, hot in the summer, dry in autumn, and cold through the winter. The middle revolution—the month—governed by the Moon, works such that the first **week** <term>week</term> <note>original: *hebdomas*; a seven-day period.</note> is moist, because the rising Moon is accustomed to stir up moisture; the second is hot, as the light in it now grows from its view of the Sun; the third is dry, being farther removed from its rising; and the fourth is cold, as its light now fails. The third revolution, which is that of the day according to sunrise and sunset, is arranged thus: it is moist until the first of the four parts of the day; hot until the second; dry until the third; and the fourth is already cold.

<margin>Seventh.</margin>The Ocean also maintains this number in its rising. For on the first day of the new Moon, the tide becomes more abundant than usual; it decreases slightly on the second; and the third sees it smaller than the second, and so by decreasing it reaches the seventh day. Again, the eighth day remains equal to the seventh; the ninth becomes similar to the sixth; the tenth to the fifth; the eleventh becomes equal to the fourth; the twelfth to the third; the thirteenth becomes similar to the second; and the fourteenth similar to the first. The third week does the same as the first; the fourth the same as the second.

<margin>Eighth.</margin>Finally, this is the number that causes a human being to be conceived, formed, delivered, to live, be nourished, and to be handed over through all the stages of life to old age—indeed, it is what makes them exist at all. For, to say nothing of the fact that nature has established that the womb, when not occupied by any force of seed, <note>Macrobius is referring here to the menstrual cycle, which typically follows a four-week (28-day) pattern.</note> [is cleansed] by this number of days...

The fifth completes the full increase of strength, as much as can exist in anyone, and in no way can anyone now become stronger than he is. Among boxers, finally, this custom is observed: those whom victories have already crowned should hope for nothing further regarding an increase in strength; those, however, who have remained devoid of this glory up to that point, should retire from the profession. Truly, six times seven years [age 42] preserve the strength previously gathered, nor do they allow any decrease to happen, except by accident. But from the sixth until the seventh seven-year period [ages 42 to 49], a decrease indeed occurs, but it is hidden, and does not betray its loss by an open failing.

Therefore, it is the custom of some republics that after the sixth period no one is forced into military service; in most, a proper discharge is granted after the seventh. It should be noted, indeed, that when the number seven multiplies itself [49], it creates an age which is properly held and called "perfect": so much so that a man of that age—as one who has already reached perfection and has not yet passed beyond it—is both fit for counsel and not considered a stranger to the exercise of strength. When, however, the decade <note>original: *decas*; the number ten.</note>—which is itself a most perfect number—is joined to the perfect number, that is, the heptad <note>original: *ἑπτάδι*; the number seven.</note>, so that either ten times seven or seven times ten years are counted [age 70]: this is believed by Natural Philosophers <note>original: *Physicis*; those who study the nature of the physical world.</note> to be the goal of living, and with this the perfect span of human life is bounded.
