# BOOK I.

<margin>that is to say</margin>
The number seven <note>original: *septenarius*</note>, which either borrows from its parts or exercises its power as a whole, is rightly held and called "full." And it has now been established—with absolute reason, I believe—why, for various causes, eight and seven are called "full" numbers. Now the meaning is this: when your age has completed its fifty-sixth year, which total will be fatal to you, the hope of public safety will look to you, and for the remedy of the common state of all good men, the dictatorship will be owed to your virtues: *but only if you escape the traps of your relatives.* For by "seven times eight of the sun’s turnings and returnings," he signifies fifty-six years. He calls the "turning and returning of the sun" a year: "turning" <note>original: *anfractum*</note> because of the circuit of the zodiac, and "returning" because the sun measures out the same signs every single year by a fixed law.

Signs and dreams about adversity are always obscure and shrouded. And yet there is always something beneath them by which the truth can be detected in some way, provided a diligent investigator is present.

### CHAPTER VII.

Here some wonder what that hesitation means—*If you escape*—as if a divine soul, having long ago returned to heaven and here especially professing knowledge of the future, could be ignorant of whether his grandson could or could not escape. But they do not notice that all signs or dreams have this law: they announce, threaten, or warn about adversities indirectly. And therefore, some things we pass by through caution; others are avoided through prayer and sacrifice <note>original: *litando*; the act of making an offering that results in a favorable omen</note>; there are others that are inescapable, which are turned aside by no art and no ingenuity. For where there is a warning, it is escaped through the vigilance of caution. What threats bring, the sacrifice of propitiation <note>original: *propitiationis*; an act intended to appease or regain the favor of a deity</note> turns away. Formal proclamations never come to nothing. At this point you might ask: "How then do we distinguish these things, so that we can grasp whether we must be cautious, or pray, or indeed simply endure?" But it is the task of the present work to suggest what kind...

<margin>Iliad 2</margin>
For instance, look at the Homeric dream sent by Jupiter <note>The Roman name for Zeus</note>, as it is told, to join battle with the enemy on the following day. Under an open promise of victory, it encouraged the king's hope <note>Agamemnon, leader of the Greeks in the Trojan War</note>. He, following it as if it were a divine oracle, joined the battle, lost many of his men, and returned to the camp only with great difficulty. Must we say then that a god commanded a lie? It is not so. But because the Fates had decreed that disaster for the Greeks, there lay hidden in the words of the dream a meaning which, if noticed, could have prepared him either to truly conquer or at least to be cautious. For the command was that the *entire* <note>original: *uniuersus*</note> army should be led forth. But he, content with only the general exhortation to fight, did not see what was commanded regarding the leading forth of the *entirety*; and since Achilles—who at that time, provoked by a recent injury, was resting from arms with his own soldiers—was left behind, the king went forward into battle, met the disaster that was destined, and cleared the dream of the accusation of lying, because he had not followed all the instructions. 

Maro <note>Virgil</note>, who was an imitator of Homeric perfection in all things, maintained an equal diligence of observation in such matters. [Macrobius posits] that there are four kinds of virtues: political <note>In this context, "political" virtues are "civic" or social virtues used to govern human society</note>, purgative <note>cleansing virtues that detach the soul from bodily concerns</note>, those of the purified soul, and exemplary <note>the divine archetypes of virtue existing in the Mind of God</note>. And since virtue makes men blessed, and that first kind of virtue is found in the governors of Republics, these men will therefore certainly be happy.

<margin>That men are made blessed by virtue alone.</margin>
Virtues alone make a person blessed, and by no other way does anyone obtain this name. Hence, those who think that virtues exist in none but those who practice philosophy declare that none besides philosophers are blessed. For calling the knowledge of divine things "wisdom" in the proper sense, they say that only those are wise who seek after higher things with the sharp focus of the mind, and grasp them with diligent sagacity in their seeking, and imitate those divine things as far as the clarity of their lives permits. And they say that the exercise of the virtues exists in this alone, whose duties they distribute thus:
<margin>The duties of the virtues according to the Stoics.</margin>
It belongs to **Prudence** <note>original: *Prudentiæ*. One of the four "cardinal virtues," here meaning the wisdom to see beyond the physical world.</note> to look down upon this world and all that is in it through the contemplation of divine things, and to direct every thought of the soul toward the divine alone. It belongs to **Temperance** to leave behind, as far as nature allows, all those things which the use of the body requires. It belongs to **Fortitude** for the soul not to be terrified as it withdraws from the body—led, as it were, by the guidance of philosophy—nor to shudder at the height of a perfect ascent to the higher realms. It belongs to **Justice** for the obedience of each individual virtue to agree upon this one path of its proposed goal. And so it happens that according to the steep cliff <note>original: *abruptum*. The professors of wisdom <note>This likely refers to Plotinus, a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a famous treatise *On Virtues*</note>, with Plato as their leader, arrange the degrees of these virtues in order, composed by a true and natural system of division. <margin>Four kinds of virtues according to the Platonists.</margin> "There are," he says, "four kinds of these fourfold virtues. Of these, the first are called **political**, the second **purifying**, the third belong to the **soul already purified**, and the fourth are **exemplary** <note>original: *exemplares*; these are the archetypal virtues as they exist in the Divine Mind</note>."

<margin>The first kind.</margin> And the **Political** virtues belong to man insofar as he is a social animal. By these, good men look after the Republic and protect cities; by these, they revere their parents, love their children, and cherish their neighbors; by these, they govern the safety of the citizens; by these, they protect allies with circumspect foresight and bind them with just generosity; <margin>Aeneid, Book 6</margin> and by these virtues, "they made others mindful of them through their merit" <note>original: *hisq; sui memores alios fecere merendo*. A quote from Virgil’s *Aeneid* (6.664) describing the inhabitants of the Blessed Fields in the underworld</note>.

It is the nature of political **Prudence** to direct everything the mind thinks or does according to the standard of reason, to will or do nothing except what is right, and to oversee human actions as if the gods were the judges. Within Prudence are found reason, understanding, circumspection, foresight, teachability, and caution.

It is the nature of **Fortitude** to lift the mind above the fear of danger, to fear nothing except what is shameful, and to endure bravely either adversity or prosperity. Fortitude provides magnanimity, confidence, security, magnificence <note>In the classical sense of "doing great things"</note>, constancy, tolerance, and firmness.

It is the nature of **Temperance** to desire nothing that must be regretted, to exceed the law of moderation in nothing, and to tame desire under the yoke of reason. Following Temperance are modesty, shame, abstinence, chastity, honesty, moderation, thrift, sobriety, and purity.

It is the nature of **Justice** to preserve for each person what is their own. From Justice come innocence, friendship, harmony, piety, religion, affection, and humanity.

By these virtues, the good man is made first a ruler of himself and then a ruler of the Republic, governing human affairs justly and with foresight, while not neglecting divine matters.

He did not say absolutely, "Nothing is more acceptable to that supreme God than cities," but he added: "at least of what happens on earth." He did this to distinguish those who begin from the heavenly spheres themselves from the rulers of cities, for whom a path to heaven is prepared through their earthly actions. Furthermore, what could be more precise or more careful than his definition of the word "cities"? "What else," he asks, "are those councils and assemblies of men joined together by law, which are called cities?" For once, even a band of slaves or a troop of gladiators were "assemblies and councils of men," but they were not "joined together by law." That alone is a just multitude whose collective whole consents to follow the law.

### BOOK I.

<margin>What the most ancient peoples thought the underworld to be.</margin>
*The pagan authors who established the sacred ceremonies denied that the underworld was anything other than the bodies themselves, in which the imprisoned souls suffer a prison foul with darkness, and horrid with filth and blood. This they called the sepulcher of the soul, the hollows of Dis* <note>original: "Ditis concaua"; referring to Pluto/Hades, the god of the underworld</note>*, and the underworld. And everything that mythic persuasion believed to exist there, they attempted to assign to ourselves and to these very human bodies: asserting that the river of*
<margin>What the rivers of the underworld signify.</margin>
*forgetfulness* <note>original: "obliuionis fluuium"; referring to the River Lethe</note> *is nothing other than the error of the soul forgetting the majesty of its prior life, which it enjoyed before it was thrust into a body, and believing that the only life is that within the body. By a similar interpretation, they thought **Phlegethon** represented the fires of anger and desires; **Acheron**, whatever we regret having done or said, according to the sad habit of human instability; **Cocytus**, whatever compels men to mourning and tears; and **Styx**, whatever plunges human souls into the whirlpool of mutual hatred.*
<margin>How the punishments of the underworld are to be understood.</margin>
*They also believed that the very description of punishments was taken from the actual experience of human social life. By the **vulture*** <note>A reference to the myth of Tityos, whose liver was eternally eaten by vultures as punishment.</note> *striking at the immortal liver, they wished nothing else to be understood than the torments of a conscience guilty of crime, which searches the interior vitals and tears at the very organs with the tireless reminder of the committed wickedness. It always stirs up anxieties if they should happen to try to rest, clinging to them as if the fibers were being reborn, sparing itself no mercy by this law: that with oneself as judge, no guilty person is acquitted, nor can one avoid their own sentence. Furthermore, those who are tortured by hunger while feasts are placed before their eyes, and who waste away from lack of food, are those whom the desire for acquiring more and more forces to not see the abundance they already have; they are paupers in the midst of affluence and suffer the evils of poverty amidst plenty, not knowing how to look back at what they have gained while they feel the need for what they must have. Finally, they believed those who hang stretched upon the spokes of **wheels** are those who provide for nothing with foresight, moderate nothing with reason, and nothing with virtue...*

He placed it with the point downward, looming over the head of that friend during a banquet. When the friend, seeing the danger of immediate death, began to despise those Sicilian and tyrannical riches, Dionysius said: "Such is the life you thought was happy; this is how we always see death looming over us. Consider then: how can anyone be happy who never ceases to be afraid?"

Here, he shifts from the "hell on earth" of the politicians to a more metaphysical discussion of the "two deaths"—the physical death we all know, and the spiritual "death" that occurs when a soul descends from the heavens into a human body.</meta>

# BOOK I.

->**BOOK I.**<-

They have handed down the teaching that there are two deaths: one of the soul, the other of the living creature. <margin>"Animal" here stands for the body.</margin> The living creature "dies" when the soul departs from the body; but they assert that the soul itself "dies" when it is scattered from the simple and indivisible source of nature into the members of the body. And because one of these deaths is manifest and known to everyone, while the other is detected only by the wise—with the rest of humanity believing it to actually be *life*—this is the reason why most people are ignorant of why we call the same God of death sometimes *Dis* and sometimes *Immitis* <note>original: "modo Ditem, modo Immitem". *Dis* is related to the Latin *dives* (rich), while *Immitis* means "unmerciful" or "harsh."</note>. For through the former—that is, the death of the living creature—the soul is released and sent back to the true riches of nature and to its own liberty, which the auspicious name *Dis* [the Rich One] indicates. But through the latter death, which the common people think is life, we testify by the horror of the name [*Immitis*] that the soul is driven from the light of its immortality into certain shadows of death.

For in order for a living creature to exist, it is necessary that the soul be bound within the body. Therefore the body is called *demas* <term>δέμας: Greek for "body," which Macrobius links to the word for "binding"</term>, that is, a "bond," and *soma* <term>σῶμα: the standard Greek word for "body"</term>, as if it were a *sema* <term>σῆμα: Greek for "sign" or "tomb"</term>, that is, the sepulcher of the soul. <margin>Plato's *Gorgias* and *Cratylus*.</margin> Whence Cicero, signifying both equally—that the body is a bond and the body is a sepulcher, which is the prison of those buried—says:
> Those who have flown out from the bonds of bodies as if from a prison.

Moreover, the Platonists said that the Underworld <note>original: *Inferi*</note> is not *in* bodies—that is, it does not begin from bodies—but they called a certain part of the world itself the seat of Dis, that is, the Underworld. <margin>The Underworld according to the Platonists, and its location.</margin> However, they published discordant views regarding the boundaries of that place, and their opinion was divided into three sects. For some divided the world into two parts: one which acts, and one which is acted upon. And they said that the part which acts, since it is immutable, imposes the cause and necessity of change upon the other; the part which is acted upon is that which is varied through change. And they said the immutable part of the world extends from the sphere called *aplanes* <term>aplanes: the "non-wandering" sphere of the fixed stars</term> down to the beginning of the lunar globe. The mutable part, however, they said extends from the moon down to the earth. And they say souls live as long as they re- [main] <meta>catchword: -main (siſt-)</meta>

...stay fixed; however, they die when they have fallen into the part capable of change. And for this reason, the space between the moon and the earth is called the place of death and of the underworld; the moon itself is the boundary of life and death. Souls flowing from there to the earth "die," while those moving from there toward the heights return to life. Nor is this thought without merit. For from the moon downwards begins the nature of perishable things <note>original: *caducorum*, referring to things that fall, decay, or are transitory</note>; from this point, souls begin to fall under the counting of days and under the rule of time. Finally, the natural philosophers <term>physici: ancient thinkers who studied the "physics" or natural laws of the universe</term> called her the "ethereal earth," and they named its inhabitants the "lunar peoples"; they have shown this to be so with many arguments which it would be too long to list now. Nor is there any doubt that the moon herself is the author and builder of mortal bodies—so much so that certain bodies experience growth as her light increases and are diminished as she wanes.

But lest a long-winded assertion about an obvious matter cause boredom, let us pass on to what others define regarding the location of the underworld. For others have preferred to divide the universe into three sets of four elements, so that in the first order are counted: earth, water, air, and fire (which is the clearer part of the air near the moon). Above these, again, are elements equal in number but of a purer nature: so that the moon stands for "earth" (which we said the natural philosophers called the "ethereal earth"), the sphere of Mercury is "water," the sphere of Venus is "air," and "fire" is in the Sun.

Indeed, the third order of elements is to be considered turned toward us in such a way that it makes earth the last; with the others reduced into the middle, the lowest extremity ends in "earth" just as the highest did. Therefore, the sphere of Mars is considered "fire," Jupiter "air," Saturn "water," and the starless sphere <term>aplanes: the Greek term for the outermost sphere of the fixed stars, which does not "wander" like the planets</term> is "earth." Antiquity has left us to understand that the Elysian Fields <note>the mythical paradise for the souls of the heroic and the virtuous</note> are in this sphere, assigned to pure souls. When a soul is sent from these fields into a body, it descends through the three orders of elements by a "triple death" until it reaches the body. ### BOOK I.

This is the second opinion regarding the soul when it is thrust into the body. However, others (for we have previously indicated that there are three different opinions among them) also divide the world into two parts, just as the first group did, but they do not divide it at the same boundaries. These thinkers want the sky, which is called the *fixed sphere* <note>original: *aplanes sphæra*, referring to the outermost shell of the universe containing the stars that do not "wander" like planets</note>, to be one part. They want the second part to consist of the seven spheres which are called "wandering" <note>the planets</note>, along with everything between them and the earth, and the earth itself. According to these men—whose reasoning is more favorable to their school—blessed souls, free from any contagion of the body whatsoever, possess the heavens. But when a soul looks down from that highest watchtower and perpetual light with a hidden desire for the body and for this which we call "life" on earth, it gradually slips down into the lower regions by the very weight of its earthly thought. 

<margin>Incorporeality</margin>

Nor is the clay-like body put on suddenly from a state of perfect incorporeality <note>the state of having no physical body</note>; rather, through gradual losses and a longer withdrawal from its simple and most absolute purity, the soul swells with a certain increase of a "starry body." For in each of the individual spheres that are situated below the heaven, the soul is clothed in an ethereal covering, so that through these stages it is reconciled to the company of this "shell-like" <term>testei: Macrobius uses this term to describe the physical body as a hard, crusty container or shell for the soul</term> garment. And so, the soul passes through as many "deaths" as the spheres it crosses until it reaches this state which is called life on earth.

### How the soul slips down from the higher part of the world to
### these lower regions.
->CHAPTER XII.<-

The order of its descent, by which the soul slips down from heaven into the lower regions of this life, is arranged as follows: the Milky Way <note>original: *lacteus circulus*</note> so embraces the Zodiac by meeting it in an oblique curve that it intersects it where the two tropical signs, Capricorn and Cancer, are located. Natural philosophers <term>physici: ancient thinkers who studied the "physics" or natural laws of the universe</term> have called these the "Gates of the Sun," because in both of them the sun’s further progress is inhibited by the opposing solstice, and a return is made for it to the path of the zone whose boundaries it never leaves. ## ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

<margin>Odyssey, Book 13 <note>The Latin text cites Book 5, but the famous description of the Cave of the Nymphs occurs in Book 13.</note></margin>
<margin>*withdrawal</margin>

...gates, the souls are believed to travel from heaven to the earth, and to return from the earth to heaven. Therefore, one is called the gate of men, and the other the gate of the Gods. Cancer is the gate of men, because through it the descent into the lower regions occurs; Capricorn is the gate of the Gods, because through it souls return to the seat of their own immortality and are restored to the number of the Gods. This is what Homer’s divine wisdom signifies in his description of the cave in Ithaca. Hence, Pythagoras also believes that the empire of Dis <note>the Underworld; Pluto</note> begins downward from the Milky Way, because souls falling from there seem already to have withdrawn from the celestial beings. He says that the nourishment of milk is offered to the newborn for this reason: because their first motion begins from the Milky Circle <note>the Milky Way</note> as they glide into earthly bodies. This is why it was said to Scipio regarding the souls of the blessed, after the Milky Way was shown to him: "Having set out from here, they return to this place." 

Therefore, while the souls about to descend are still in Cancer, they are still counted among the Gods, since having been placed there, they have not yet left the Milky Way. But when, by gliding downward, they reach Leo, they begin the first stage of their future condition. Because the first steps of birth and a certain apprenticeship of human nature are found in Leo, and since Aquarius is opposite to Leo and sets just as Leo rises, funeral rites are performed for the spirits of the deceased <note>original: *manibus parentatur*</note> when the sun holds Aquarius, as it is in a sign that is considered contrary or adverse to human life. 

From that point, then—that is, from the boundary where the Zodiac and the Milky Way touch—the soul, descending from its rounded shape (which is the only divine form), is drawn out into a cone as it flows downward, just as a line is born from a point and proceeds into length from a single unit. There, from its point which is the monad <note>the "One" or ultimate unity</note>, it comes into the dyad <note>the "Two" or duality</note>, which is the first extension <note>original: *protractio*</note>. This is the essence, both indivisible and divisible, which Plato expressed in the *Timaeus* when he spoke of the construction of the World Soul. For the soul of the world, just as the soul of an individual human, is divided by a method of division...

<meta>This page continues Macrobius’s commentary on the soul’s descent through the zodiac. Having just reached the sign of Leo, the soul begins its transition from a pure divine state to a physical one, encountering the "intoxication" of the material world.</meta>

### BOOK I.

[Souls] are found to be ignorant, if the simplicity of the divine nature is considered; yet they are capable, when that divine nature is spread through the parts of the world, and the soul is spread through the members of man. Therefore, when the soul is drawn toward the body, in this first stage of its production, it begins to experience a "wooded tumult" <note>original: "syluestrem tumultum." Macrobius uses the Latin "silva" (wood/forest) to translate the Greek "hyle" (matter), implying a chaotic, wild growth.</note>, that is, the influx of matter into itself. And this is what Plato noted in the *Phaedo*, that the soul is drawn into the body trembling with a new drunkenness; he wished this to be understood as a new drink of material flooding, by which the soul is stained and weighed down as it is led downward. The sign of this mystery is that starry Bowl of Father Liber <note>Liber Pater: an ancient Italian god of fertility and wine, later identified with the Greek Dionysus or Bacchus. The "Bowl" refers to the constellation Crater.</note>, 
<margin>The constellation of the Bowl is located between the Crow and the Snake <note>The constellations Corvus and Hydra.</note>.</margin>
located in the region between Cancer and Leo, signifying that drunkenness first occurs there for souls about to descend, as matter flows in. From this, forgetfulness, the companion of drunkenness, begins to creep secretly into the souls at that point. For if souls brought the memory of divine things—of which they were conscious in heaven—all the way to their bodies, there would be no disagreement among men concerning divinity. But indeed, all drink in forgetfulness as they descend: some more, others less. And therefore on earth, although the truth is not clear to everyone, nevertheless everyone has an opinion; for the origin of opinion is the failure of memory. Those, however, find the truth more easily who have drunk less of forgetfulness, because they easily remember what they knew before in that higher realm. Hence it is that what is called "reading" [*lectio*] among the Latins is called "re-cognition" among the Greeks:
<margin>re-cognition <note>original: "ἀνάγνωσις" (anagnosis).</note></margin>
because when we learn true things, we recognize those things which we knew by nature before the material influx intoxicated the souls as they entered the body. This, moreover, is *hyle* <term>hyle: the Greek word for matter, often described by Neoplatonists as a chaotic, flowing substance</term>, which formed the whole body of the world—which we see everywhere—once it was impressed with ideas. But its highest and purest part, by which divine things are either sustained or consist, is called nectar, and is believed to be the drink of the Gods; the lower and more turbid part, however, is the drink of souls. And this is what the ancients called the River Lethe <note>the mythological river of forgetfulness in the underworld.</note>.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the soul’s descent. Having previously mentioned the "Cup of Liber Pater" (Dionysus) as the source of the soul's intoxication with matter, Macrobius now explains the Orphic symbolism of this god and the specific faculties the soul acquires as it passes through each planetary sphere.</meta>

### ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

The followers of Orpheus suspect that Father Liber <note>Liber Pater: The Roman name for Dionysus or Bacchus. Macrobius is linking the Orphic myth of Dionysus being torn apart by Titans to the soul's division into individual bodies.</note> is to be understood as the **material mind** <note>original: "νοῦν ὑλικὸν" (nous hylikon). In Neoplatonism, this refers to the divine intellect as it begins to engage with and organize the material world.</note>, who, born from that indivisible source, is himself divided into individual parts. For this reason, it is handed down in their sacred rites that he was torn into limbs by Titanic fury and, after his fragments were buried, he emerged again as one and whole. This is because the **Mind** <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous). To Neoplatonists, the Mind is the second level of reality, below "The One" but above the Soul.</note>—which we have said is called "intellect"—by offering itself to be divided from its indivisible state and then returning from that division to its indivisibility, both fulfills the duties of the world and does not abandon the secrets of its own nature.

Therefore, with this first weight of material influx, the soul slips down from the zodiac and the Milky Way toward the spheres lying below. While it glides through these, it is not only clothed in each sphere (as we have already said) with an addition of a luminous body <note>This "luminous body" or *pneuma* is a sort of celestial envelope the soul wears to bridge the gap between pure spirit and heavy matter.</note>, but it also produces the specific motions that it will exercise [in the physical world]. 

In the sphere of **Saturn**, it acquires reasoning and intelligence, which they call the **logical and contemplative** <note>original: "λογιστικὸν θεωρητικὸν" (logistikon theoretikon).</note> faculty. 

In **Jupiter’s** sphere, it gains the power of acting, which is called the **practical** <note>original: "πρακτικὸν" (praktikon).</note> faculty. 

In **Mars**, it gains the heat of courage, which is named the **spirited** <note>original: "θυμικὸν" (thymikon). This relates to the "thumos," the part of the soul associated with anger, pride, and spiritedness.</note> faculty. 

In the **Sun**, it gains the nature of sensing and imagining, which they call the **sensory and imaginative** <note>original: "αἰσθητικὸν & φανταστικὸν" (aisthetikon and phantastikon).</note> faculty. 

In the sphere of **Venus**, it acquires the motion of desire, which is called the **appetitive** <note>original: "ἐπιθυμητικὸν" (epithymetikon).</note> faculty. 

In the orb of **Mercury**, it gains the power of pronouncing and interpreting what it feels, which is called the **interpretive** <note>original: "ἑρμηνευτικὸν" (hermeneutikon).</note> faculty. 

Finally, upon entering the globe of the **Moon**, it exercises the **vegetative** <note>original: "φυτικὸν" (phytikon).</note> faculty, which is the nature of planting and growing bodies. This lunar sphere is the last of the divine orbs, but it is the first in our earthly circles. 

For this [earthly] body, just as it is the dregs of divine things, so it is the first substance of a living creature. And this is the difference between earthly bodies and the superior ones—meaning the heavens, the stars, and the other elements: those higher bodies were summoned upward to the seat of the soul and earned immortality from the very nature of their region and their imitation of sublimity. However, the soul is led down into these earthly bodies, and therefore it is believed to "die" when it is enclosed in this decaying region and in the seat of mortality. Nor should it trouble you that concerning the soul, which we say is immortal...

# BOOK I.

<margin>hidden</margin>
we so often speak of death. Indeed, the soul is not extinguished by its own death, but is overwhelmed for a time; nor is the benefit of its perpetuity removed by this temporal immersion. When it has deserved it—having utterly eliminated the contagion of vice—it is purified and, restored to the light of everlasting life, it may return in its entirety to its original state. The definition of the life and death of the soul seems fully clear, which [the author] drew from the <margin>hidden</margin> sanctuaries of philosophy <note>original: "adytis philosophiae." An "adytum" was the innermost, most sacred part of a Greek temple, accessible only to priests. Macrobius uses this to suggest that Cicero's insights come from the deepest mysteries of thought.</note> through the teaching and wisdom of Cicero.

Man dies in two ways. First, if the soul leaves the body. Second, if the soul, while still remaining in the body, despises bodily allurements and casts off all pleasures and passions. Of these deaths, this latter one <note>This is the "philosophical death," a core concept in Neoplatonism where the soul "dies" to the physical world while the body is still alive, focusing entirely on the divine.</note> is to be sought by everyone, while the former is not to be summoned or hurried, but rather awaited until God himself releases the soul from the body.

->CHAPTER XIII.<-

But Scipio—through his sleep and in heaven, which is the reward granted to the blessed—encouraged by the promise of immortality, grew more and more firm in such glorious and distinguished hope after seeing his father, about whom he had asked whether he was still living, as he still seemed to doubt it. Therefore, he began to prefer death so that he might truly live. Not content with merely weeping upon seeing the parent he had believed was dead, as soon as he was able to speak, he first wished to prove that he desired nothing more than to remain with him now. Nevertheless, he did not decide to do what he desired before first consulting [his father]; one of these actions is an assertion of prudence, the other of piety. Now, let us examine the words of the one consulting and the one commanding:

> "I beg you," I said, "most holy and excellent father, since this is truly life—as I hear Africanus <note>Scipio Africanus the Elder, the grandfather of the dreamer, who appears earlier in the vision.</note> say—why do I delay on earth? Why do I not hasten to come here to you?" "It is not so," he replied. "For unless the God to whom this whole temple belongs—and everything you see—has freed you from those prison-guards of the body <note>original: "corporis custodiis." This reflects the Orphic and Platonic idea that the body is a prison (*soma sema*) or a place of detention for the soul.</note>, the way here cannot lie open for you."

### ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from the previous page's discussion on the purpose of human existence.</note> ...For humans were born under this law: to tend that sphere which you see in the middle of this **temple** <note>original: "templo hoc." The Stoics and Platonists often referred to the entire universe as a temple of the gods.</note>, which is called Earth. To them, a soul was given from those everlasting fires which you call stars and constellations; these, being spherical and round, animated by divine minds, complete their circles and orbits with marvelous speed. Therefore, Publius, you and all pious men must keep the soul in the custody of the body; nor must you depart from the life of men without the command of Him by whom the soul was given to you, lest you seem to have fled the duty assigned by God. *This is the school and teaching of Plato, who defines in the **Phaedo** <note>One of Plato's most famous dialogues, depicting the final hours of Socrates and his arguments for the immortality of the soul.</note> that a man must not die of his own accord. But in the same dialogue, he also says that death is to be sought by those practicing philosophy, and that philosophy itself is the practice of dying.*

<margin>The twofold death of man according to Plato: which of these is to be sought, which is not to be summoned, and the seven reasons for this.</margin>
These things therefore seem contrary to one another, but it is not so. For Plato recognizes two deaths for man. I do not repeat now what was said above—that there are two deaths, one of the soul and another of the living creature—but even for the living creature itself (that is, the human), he asserts two deaths: one provided by nature, the other by virtues. A man dies when the soul leaves the body, released by the law of nature. He is also said to die when the soul, while still situated in the body, despises bodily allurements—*through the teaching of philosophy*—and is stripped of the sweet traps of desires and all remaining passions. And this is what we noted above as happening from the **second order of virtues** <note>In Neoplatonism, these are the "purgative" or "cleansing" virtues (*virtutes purgatoriae*) that help the soul detach from the physical world.</note>, which are suited only to those practicing philosophy. Therefore, Plato says this death is to be sought by the wise; but that death which nature established for all, he forbids to be forced, inflicted, or summoned. He teaches that nature must be awaited, and he reveals the reasons for this prohibition, which he borrows from the common use of things in daily life.

*For he says that those who are thrust into prison by the command of a power...*

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Cicero’s "Dream of Scipio." On the previous page, Macrobius introduced the Platonic view of the soul's relationship to the body, emphasizing that the soul is a gift from the divine stars and must remain in the body until called away. This page details specific philosophical reasons why a person must not end their own life prematurely.</meta>

### BOOK I.

...that one ought not to flee from there, before the very power which enclosed us has permitted our departure.
<margin>First reason.</margin> For punishment is not avoided by a stealthy departure; rather, it is increased.
<margin>Second reason.</margin> He <note>Referring to Plato.</note> also adds this: that we are in the possession of the Gods, under whose guardianship and providence we are governed. Nothing, moreover, should be taken away from the place where the master had stationed his own property against his will.
<margin>Third reason.</margin> And just as one who snatches life from another’s slave <note>original: "mancipio." In Roman law, this refers to property held by legal right, here used as a metaphor for the human soul as God's property.</note> will not be free of crime, so too he who seeks an end for himself before the master commands it does not achieve absolution, but guilt.
<margin>Fourth reason.</margin> Plotinus <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) who expanded on these ideas in his "Enneads."</note> follows these seeds of the Platonic school more deeply. He says: "It is necessary that the soul, after the man dies, be found free from bodily passions <note>The "passions" (strong emotions like fear, lust, or anger) were thought to "weight down" the soul, preventing its ascent to the heavens.</note>." He who violently thrusts the soul out of the body does not allow it to be free. For he who prepares death for himself by his own will descends to this act either through weariness of necessity, or fear of someone, or hatred—all of which are counted among the passions. Therefore, even if the soul was pure of these stains before, it becomes stained by the very fact that it is forced out.
Next, he says that death ought to be a release of the soul from the body, not a bond.
<margin>Fifth reason.</margin> By a forced exit, however, the soul is bound more and more to the body. And in truth, for this reason, souls thus wrenched out wander for a long time around the body, or its grave, or the place where the hand was laid <note>That is, the site where the act of suicide or violence took place; popular belief held that such spirits became "unrestful" ghosts.</note>; whereas, on the contrary, those souls which in this life are dissolved from bodily bonds by the "death of philosophy" <note>This refers to the practice of mental and spiritual detachment from material desires while one is still physically alive.</note> are carried into the heavens and stars while the body still stands. And therefore he indicates that alone among voluntary deaths is the one to be praised which is achieved by the method of philosophy—as we said—not by the blade; by wisdom, not by poison.
<margin>Sixth reason.</margin> He also adds that natural death is the only kind where the body leaves the soul, not the soul the body. For it is established that a certain and fixed ratio of numbers <note>A Pythagorean concept: every life has a pre-destined numerical "span" or harmony; to break this is to disrupt the cosmic order.</note> associates souls with bodies. As long as these numbers remain, the body continues to be animated; but when they fail, soon the [secret]... <note>The text cuts off here; the word "arca" combined with the catchword "na illa" on the next page forms "arcana," meaning "secret" or "mysterious."</note>

# ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

...indeed, that force is dissolved by which the partnership itself <note>The "partnership" or "society" refers to the union of the soul and the physical body.</note> was maintained. And this is what we call fate and the fated spans of life. The soul itself, therefore, does not fail—since it is immortal and everlasting—but when the numbers <note>original: "numeris." In Pythagorean and Platonic thought, health and life spans were governed by mathematical proportions and cycles. When these cycles "fill up" or complete their circuit, the physical body can no longer sustain the soul's energy.</note> are fulfilled, the body decays. The soul is not exhausted by the act of giving life, but the body deserts its duty when it can no longer be animated. Hence the words of the most learned poet:
<margin>Aeneid, Book 6</margin>
> —I shall fulfill my number, and return to the shadows. <note>original: "Explebo numerum, reddarq; tenebris." This quote is from Virgil’s Aeneid, spoken by the ghost of Deiphobus to Aeneas in the underworld. Macrobius interprets "fulfilling the number" as completing one's allotted lifespan.</note>

This, therefore, is truly natural death: when the failure of its own numbers alone brings an end to the body, and not when life is wrenched from a body that is still fit to continue bearing it.
<margin>The seventh reason.</margin> Nor is the difference a slight one between dissolving life by nature or by one’s own will. For when the soul is deserted by the body <note>i.e., through natural death.</note>, it is able to retain nothing of the body within itself, provided it conducted itself purely while it was in this life. But when the soul is violently thrust out of the body, it exits because the bond has been broken, not loosened; thus, that very necessity becomes an occasion for "passion" <note>In ancient philosophy, "passion" (passio) refers to a state where the soul is "acted upon" by external or bodily forces, rather than acting of its own free will. A violent death forces the soul into a state of agitation.</note>, and it is stained by evils in the very act of breaking the bond.

He also adds this reason to the ones above for not perishing by one's own hand: "Since it is certain," he says, "that a reward is to be granted to souls in that other place according to the measure of perfection which each reached in this life, one must not rush the end of life while there is still the possibility of making further progress."

And this was not said in vain. For in the secret discussions regarding the return of the soul, it is said that those who sin in this life are like people falling on level ground, for whom it is immediately possible to rise again without difficulty. But souls departing this life with the filth of their sins are to be compared to those who have fallen into a sheer abyss from a high and steep place, from which there is never an opportunity to rise again. Therefore, one must use the granted spans of life so that there may be a greater opportunity for perfect purification.

"Therefore," <margin>An objection.</margin> you will say, "he who is already perfectly purified ought to lay hands on himself, since he has no reason to remain, because his progress <margin>* progress</margin>...

### BOOK I.

...requires nothing further, as one who has already reached the higher realms. Furthermore, he encounters the other consequences which the previous reasoning discussed. And this is why Paul <note>Aemilius Paullus, the father of Scipio Africanus the Younger. He appears in Scipio's dream to give him counsel from the afterlife.</note> forbids and drives back his son who is hastening to come to him in the hope of a truer life: lest the hurried desire for release and ascension bind him more tightly and delay him by this very passion. Nor does he say, "Because unless natural death arrives, you will not be able to die," but rather, "You will not be able to come here." For unless, he says, when God has freed you from these guardians of the body <note>original: "corporis custodijs." Macrobius views the body as a prison or a duty station that one cannot desert without divine permission.</note>, the way hither cannot lie open to you: because, having already been received into heaven, he knows that the entrance to the celestial dwelling does not lie open except to perfect purity. With equal constancy, death is neither to be feared when it comes by nature, nor is it to be forced against the order of nature. From these things which we have reported Plato and Plotinus to have pronounced concerning voluntary death <note>original: "uoluntaria morte," a common term for suicide in classical philosophy.</note>, nothing will remain obscure in the words of Cicero by which he forbids it.

Why this whole universe is called the temple of God. In what double sense the name of the soul is understood. And how the mind of man is said to be shared with the stars. ### ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

...by a wonderful [virtue]. Concerning the earth—why it is said to be a globe positioned in the middle of the universe—we shall discuss more fully when we speak of the nine spheres.

<margin>Why the world is called the temple of God.</margin>
Rightly indeed is the entire world called the temple of God, on account of those who think that God is nothing other than heaven itself and those celestial things we see. Therefore, to show that the omnipotence of the Highest God can scarcely be understood and never seen, he called whatever is subjected to human sight his "temple"—He who is perceived by the mind alone. This was done so that he who venerates these things as temples still owes the greatest worship to the Creator; and let whoever is brought into the service of this temple know that he must live according to the ritual of a priest. Whence also, as if by a certain public proclamation, he testifies that such great divinity dwells in the human race that he ennobles everyone with the kinship of a "starry mind."

<margin>That "mind" is understood in two ways.</margin>
It should be noted that in this passage he used the term "mind" both in its proper sense and in a loose sense. For "mind" <term>animus: here referring to the rational spirit</term> is properly the "intellect" <term>mens: the highest, most divine part of the human soul</term>, which no one doubts is more divine than the "soul" <term>anima: the life-giving principle that animates the physical body</term>. But sometimes we use the terms interchangeably, calling even the soul "mind." Therefore, when he says: "And a mind was given to these from those eternal fires," <note>original: "Hisq́; animus datus eſt ex illis ſempiternis ignibus"</note> he intends "intellect" to be understood, which is properly common to us and the heaven and the stars. But when he says: "The mind must be kept in the custody of the body," <note>original: "Retinendus animus eſt in cuſto-dia corporis"</note> he then names the soul itself, which is bound by the corporal prison, to which the divine intellect is not subject.

<margin>How the mind is common with the stars.</margin>
<margin>*Elsewhere, a part a little before.</margin>
Now, let us discuss according to the theologians <note>Macrobius refers to "theologians" as the Neoplatonic philosophers like Plotinus and Porphyry who treated cosmology as a divine science.</note> how the mind—that is, the intellect—is common to us and the stars. God, who both is and is called the First Cause, is the one ruler and origin of all things that are and that seem to be. He, out of the superabundant fertility of his majesty, created Mind from himself. This Mind, which is called *Nous* <note>original: "νοῦς" — the Greek term for the Divine Intellect or First Emanation.</note>, maintains a full likeness to its author insofar as it gazes upon the Father; but it creates the Soul <note>original: "animam"</note> from itself, looking back at what follows. Again, the Soul * [looks to] the Father...

<meta>This page continues the Neoplatonic discussion of the soul's descent from the divine realm into the material world. ->**BOOK I.**<-

<sig>C 3</sig>

[the soul] gazes upon, clothes itself in, and as its focus gradually turns back toward the construction of bodies, the incorporeal itself degrades. It possesses, therefore, both a most pure reason from the Mind out of which it was born, which is called <term>λογικὸν (logikon): the rational faculty</term>; and from its own nature it receives the seed for providing sensation and providing growth, of which one is called <term>αἰσθητικὸν (aisthētikon): the sensory faculty</term>, and the other <term>φυτικὸν (phutikon): the vegetative or growth faculty</term>. But of these, the first—that is, the rational—which it took as innate to itself from the Mind, is just as truly divine as it is suited only to divine things. The remaining two, the sensory and the vegetative, as they depart from divine things, so are they suited to things that are fleeting <note>original: "caducis", referring to things that are perishable or "fall" away from eternity</note>.

Therefore the soul, creating and building bodies for itself—for this reason nature begins from the soul, which the sages, in relation to God and the Mind, name <term>ὕλην (hūlēn): matter or substance</term> <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, each level of reality acts as the "matter" or substrate for the higher level that shapes it</note>—from that pure and most clear fountain of the Mind which it had drawn from the abundance of its origin at birth, it animated those divine or celestial bodies (I mean the heavens and the stars) which it built first. Divine minds were infused into all bodies that were formed into a rounded shape—that is, in the manner of a sphere. And this is what [Cicero] meant when, speaking of the stars, he said: "Which were animated by divine minds."

But descending into lower and earthly things, [the soul] discovered that the fragility of fleeting bodies could not sustain the pure divinity of the Mind; indeed, a part of it is scarcely suited even to human bodies alone. This is because they alone appear upright, as if they were withdrawing from the lowest depths toward the heights, and they alone easily look up to heaven as if always standing tall. Only in the [human] head is there the likeness of a sphere, which form we have said is alone capable of containing the mind. To man alone, therefore, did it infuse reason—that is, the power of the mind—whose seat is in the head. 

But it also inserted that twin nature of growing and sensing, because the human body is fleeting. And hence it is that man both possesses reason, and senses, and grows—and by reason alone has he deserved to surpass the other animals. These other animals, because they are always prone <note>leaning forward or face-down toward the ground</note> and by their very [nature of] looking down...

# ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

...departed from the higher realms with difficulty. Because they did not earn any likeness to the divine bodies in any part of themselves, they received nothing from the Mind <note>In this context, "Mind" (Latin: *Mens*) refers to the supreme cosmic intelligence, one level above the "Soul" (Latin: *Anima*)</note>, and therefore they lacked reason. They obtained only two faculties: sensation and growth. For if anything in them appears to imitate a likeness of reason, it is not reason, but memory—and not that memory mixed with reason, but the kind that accompanies the dullness of the five senses. We shall omit saying more about this now, as it does not pertain to the present work. 

The third order of earthly bodies is found in trees and plants, which lack both reason and sensation. Because only the function of growth thrives in these, they are said to live by this faculty alone. 

Virgil also expressed this order of things. For he both gave a soul to the world and, to attest to its purity, he called it "Mind." 

<margin>Aeneid, Book 6</margin>
*For the heavens*, he says, *and the lands, and the seas, and the stars, a spirit within nourishes* <note>original Latin: "spiritus intus alit" (Aeneid 6.726). Macrobius explains that this "spirit" is the world-soul</note>, that is, the soul. 

<margin>Aeneid, Book 8</margin>
Just as elsewhere he uses "soul" to mean a breath of air, as in: *As much as the fires and the souls <note>original: "animaeque". In this poetic context, it refers to the blasts of a blacksmith's bellows, but Macrobius uses it to show the word's range of meaning</note> are strong.* 

And so that he might assert the dignity of that world-soul, he testifies that it is "Mind": 

<margin>Aeneid, Book 6</margin>
*Mind moves the mass* <note>original: "Mens agitat molem" (Aeneid 6.727). One of the most famous descriptions of the divine force animating the universe</note>. Furthermore, to show that all living things consist of and are animated by this very soul, he added: *From there comes the race of men and of cattle*, and so forth. And to assert that the same vigor is always present in the soul, but that its use is dulled in living creatures by the density of the physical body, he added: *Insofar as harmful bodies do not slow them down*, and the rest. 

According to these principles, therefore, since Mind stems from the most high God, and Soul from Mind, and since Soul indeed both creates and fills with life all things that follow it; and since this one radiance illuminates all things and appears in the whole universe like a single face reflected in many mirrors arranged in a row; and since all things follow one another in continuous succession, degenerating in order as they descend to the lowest point; it will be found by one looking more closely that from the most high God down to the last...

<meta>This page continues Macrobius’s exploration of the cosmic hierarchy. Having previously discussed how the World-Soul animates the universe, he now explains the "Golden Chain" that links the divine realm to the human mind, concluding with a survey of how various ancient philosophers defined the nature of the soul.</meta>

->### BOOK I.<-

...for the torch of nature <note>original Latin: *facem* (torch/light). Many editions read *seriem* (series/chain), but Macrobius here emphasizes the illuminating connection of all things</note> binds itself together with mutual bonds in a never-interrupted connection. This is Homer’s "golden chain," which he records that God commanded to hang from heaven to the earth. 

Based on these words, it is established that among all earthly creatures, only man shares a common society of the mind—that is, of the soul—with heaven and the stars. This is why he says: *To these a soul was given from those eternal fires which you call stars and planets.* <note>Macrobius is quoting Cicero's "Dream of Scipio" here</note>. 

Yet, he does not mean that we are animated directly by those celestial and eternal fires themselves. For that fire, though divine, is still a body. We could not be animated by a body, even a divine one; rather, we are animated by that source from which those bodies—which are and appear divine—are themselves animated. This source is that part of the World-Soul which we previously stated consists of pure Mind. 

And therefore, after he said: *To these a soul was given from those eternal fires which you call stars and planets*, he immediately added: *Which are animated by divine minds.* He does this so that through "eternal fires," he signifies the body of the stars, but through "divine minds," he signifies their souls in a clear description, showing that the power of the Mind comes into our souls from them.

<margin>The opinions of the philosophers regarding the soul.</margin> 

It is not out of place for this discussion on the soul to conclude by containing the opinions of everyone who is seen to have pronounced a definition of the soul. 

**Plato** said the soul is an essence moving itself. 
**Xenocrates** called it a number moving itself. 
**Aristotle** called it an <term>entelechy</term> <note>original Greek: *entelecheia*. This term refers to the "actualization" or "complete reality" of a body that has the potential for life</note>. 
**Pythagoras** and **Philolaus** called it a harmony. 
**Posidonius** called it an Idea <note>referring to a Platonic Form or Archetype</note>. 
**Asclepiades** called it the harmonious exercise of the five senses. 
**Hippocrates** called it a thin spirit dispersed through the whole body. 
**Heraclitus of Pontus** called it light. 
**Heraclitus the Physicist** called it a spark of stellar essence. 
**Zeno** <note>original OCR: *Xenon*. Macrobius refers to Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoicism</note> called it a spirit fused to the body. 
**Democritus** called it a spirit inserted into atoms, with such a <margin>*ease</margin> facility of movement that the entire body is permeable to it. 
**Critolaus the Peripatetic** claimed it consists of a fifth essence...

...essence; Hipparchus <note>A Greek astronomer and philosopher</note> believed it was fire; Anaximenes, air; Empedocles and Critias, blood; Parmenides, a mixture of earth and fire; Xenophanes, of earth and water; <margin>*Boethus</margin> Boethus, of air and fire; and Epicurus, a form mixed from fire, air, and spirit <note>original Latin: *spiritu*, referring to a physical breath or wind</note>. Now let us see what these two names are, both of which he mentions when he says: **"Which you call constellations and stars."** For here, one thing is not being designated by two names, as is the case with "blade" and "sword." Rather, "stars" (*stellae*) are individual, 
<margin>What stars are. What constellations are.</margin> 
such as the five wandering ones <note>The five planets known to the ancients: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>, and the others which are carried alone and not mixed with others. "Constellations" (*sidera*), however, are those which are formed into a specific sign by the arrangement of several stars, such as Aries, Taurus, Andromeda, Perseus, or the Crown, and whatever types of varied forms are believed to have been received into the heavens. 
<margin>aster [ἀστὴρ], astron [ἄστρον].</margin> 
This is also the case among the Greeks, where *aster* [ἀστὴρ] and *astron* [ἄστρον] signify different things. Indeed, an *aster* is a single star, while an *astron* is a sign gathered from many stars, which we call a constellation. When he says the stars are "globular and round," he is not only describing the appearance of individual stars, but also of those which come together to form signs. For all stars, although they may differ somewhat in size, have no difference in their appearance. Through these two names, a "solid sphere" is described: it is not produced from a "globe" alone if roundness is lacking, nor from "roundness" alone if the globe is lacking; for the one term refers to the shape, and the other to the solidity of the body. 
<margin>Sphere.</margin> 
By "spheres" here, we mean the bodies of the stars themselves, all of which are formed with this appearance.

<meta>This page continues Macrobius’s linguistic and astronomical commentary on Cicero’s "Dream of Scipio." Having just distinguished between individual stars and grouped constellations, Macrobius now turns to the specific definitions of "orbits" and "circles" and explains the counter-intuitive motion of the planets.</meta>

-># BOOK I.<-
<margin>e 3</margin>

<margin>Orbit.</margin>
<margin>Circle.</margin>
<margin>Wandering stars.</margin>
...there are two names for two things. And indeed, these names are used differently elsewhere. For he <note>Referring to Cicero</note> used **orbit** <note>original Latin: *orbem*</note> in place of **circle** <note>original Latin: *circulo*</note>, as in the "milky orbit." And he used **orbit** for **sphere**, as in: "To you, the universe is composed of nine orbits, or rather, spheres." But those which gird the greatest sphere are also called **circles** <note>original Latin: *circi*</note>, as the following treatise will show. One of these is the Milky Way, of which he says: "A circle shining among the flames." But here, he intended for neither of these to be understood by the name of circle or orbit. Instead, in this passage, an **orbit** <term>orbis: here meaning a single, completed revolution of a celestial body</term> is one entire and completed revolution of a star: that is, its return to the same place after it has traversed the circumference of the sphere through which it moves. A **circle** <term>circus: here referring to the physical track or path of a planet</term>, however, is here the line encircling the sphere and making a kind of path, through which light runs in both directions, and within which the "lawful wandering" of the **wandering stars** <note>original: *uagantiū stellarū*; these are the planets</note> is contained.

The ancients called these "wandering" <note>the word "planet" comes from the Greek *planētēs*, meaning "wanderer"</note> because they are carried by their own course, and they revolve with a contrary motion from West to East, against the force of the greatest sphere—that is, the heaven itself. And indeed, the speed of all of them is equal, their motion similar, and their manner of walking is the same; but they do not all complete their **circles** and **orbits** in the same amount of time. And for this reason, the speed itself is wonderful: because although it is the same for all of them, and none of them can be either more rapid or slower than the others, they nevertheless do not all complete their circuit in the same space of time. The following sections will better teach us the cause of this unequal distance despite the same speed.

Here, he focuses specifically on the "Milky Circle" (the Milky Way), presenting various ancient scientific theories regarding its physical composition and purpose before transitioning to a broader discussion of the ten celestial circles.</meta>

### ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

<margin>The Milky Circle.</margin>
...which you (as you have learned from the Greeks) call the **Milky orbit**. <note>original Latin: *orbem lacteum*; we know this today as the Milky Way.</note> In the name of the "Milky Way," this "orbit" signifies the same thing as a "circle." The Milky Way is one of the circles that surround the heavens; besides it, there are ten others in number, about which we shall speak when a suitable discussion of that matter arises. Of all these, this is the only one visible to the eyes, while the other circles are understood more by thought than by sight. Regarding this Milky Way, many have held differing opinions; some have offered mythical explanations, while others have offered natural ones. But we, remaining silent on the myths, will mention only those things which seem to pertain to its nature.

Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle.</note> said that the Milky Way is a 
<margin>*alternatively: a joint,</margin>
*seam by which the two hemispheres of the heavens are fastened together into a solid sphere. Therefore, where the edges meet on both sides, a remarkable brightness is seen. Diodorus <note>Likely Diodorus of Alexandria, a mathematician and astronomer.</note> claimed it is a fire of a dense and solidified nature gathered into a single path along a curved boundary, concentrated by the separation of the world's structure; he argues it is thus visible to the viewer's gaze, whereas the rest of the celestial fire—having its light diffused by extreme thinness—is not presented to our sight. Democritus <note>The ancient "atomic" philosopher; his theory here is remarkably close to modern science.</note> claimed it consists of countless stars, all small, which are gathered together in a dense region; with the very narrow spaces between them hidden, and being close to one another on all sides, they display a continuous body of joined light through the scattering of light diffused everywhere. 

But Posidonius <note>A Stoic polymath and teacher of Cicero.</note>, whose definition has gained the most consensus, says that the Milky Way is an infusion of starry heat. He explains that its curve was made slanted, opposite the Zodiac, so that since the sun never leaves the boundaries of the Zodiac and would otherwise leave the rest of the sky devoid of its heat, this circle—receding obliquely from the sun's path—might temper the whole universe with its warm bend. In which parts it intersects the Zodiac has already been related above. So much for the Milky Way. There are, however, as we have said, ten other circles, one of which is the Zodiac itself, which out of these ten...

<meta>catchword: alone</meta>

<summary>Macrobius examines the Milky Way, presenting competing theories from ancient philosophers: as a structural seam of the universe, a concentration of celestial fire, a cluster of tiny stars (Democritus), or a source of heat to balance the sun's path (Posidonius).</summary>

<meta>This page continues Macrobius’s explanation of the celestial spheres, moving from the physical nature of the Milky Way to the geometry of the zodiac and the mathematical circles that define the heavens. ### BOOK I.

*The zodiac <note>The text continues from the previous page's discussion of the twelve signs.</note> alone was able to acquire width in the manner we shall describe. The nature of the celestial circles is that of an incorporeal line, which is conceived in the mind such that it is considered only by its length and cannot have width. But in the zodiac, the capacity for the signs of the constellations required width. Therefore, the amount of space that this wide dimension occupied by the extended stars was limited by two lines. A third line, drawn through the middle, is called the **ecliptic**, because when the sun and moon complete their courses together on that same line, a failure <note>The Latin "defectus" refers to an eclipse—a "failing" or "dropping out" of light.</note> of one of them must occur: of the Sun, if the moon then moves beneath it; of the moon, if it is then positioned opposite the Sun. For this reason, the Sun never fails except when it is the thirtieth day of the moon <note>The time of the New Moon.</note>; and the moon knows no failure except on the fifteenth day of its course <note>The time of the Full Moon.</note>. For it happens that either the Earth's shadow-cone stands in the way of the moon (positioned opposite the sun to borrow its usual light) when it is found on the same line, or the moon itself, passing under the Sun, repels its light from human sight by its own obstruction. In an eclipse, therefore, the Sun itself suffers nothing, but our sight is cheated. The moon, however, truly suffers through its own eclipse, by not receiving the light of the Sun, by whose benefit it colors the night. Knowing this, Virgil, the most skilled of all in the disciplines, said:*

<margin>Virgil, Georgics, Book 2.</margin>
> *The various eclipses of the sun, and the labors of the moon.* <note>original Latin: "Defectus Solis uarios, lunæq; labores." Virgil uses the word "labors" to describe the moon's struggle during an eclipse, a common poetic and scientific term in antiquity.</note>

*Therefore, although the drawing of three lines both encloses and divides the zodiac, antiquity wished for it to be called a single circle by the author of these names.*

<margin>The five parallels.</margin>
*Five other circles are called **parallels**. The middle and largest of these is the **equinoctial** <note>The celestial equator.</note>. Two are near the extremities, and are therefore short; one of these is called northern, the other southern. Between these and the middle are the two **tropics**, which are larger than the ones at the ends but smaller than the middle one, and they themselves form the boundary of the scorched zone <note>The torrid zone or tropics.</note> on both sides.*

<margin>The two colures.</margin>
*Besides these, there are two others called **colures**, to which an "incomplete rotation" gives their name <note>The word "colure" comes from the Greek "kolouros," meaning "dock-tailed" or "clipped," because these circles seem to be cut off at the poles and never complete a full visible circuit like the others.</note>. For they encircle the northern pole, and...*

# ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

<meta>catchword: locor</meta>

From there, <note>Referring to the poles of the heavens mentioned on the previous page.</note> they spread out in different directions and intersect each other at the highest point, and they divide the five parallels into four equal parts. They intersect the **zodiac** <term>zodiacus: the "circle of animals," the path the sun follows through the constellations</term> in such a way that one of them runs through **Aries** and **Libra**, while the other runs through **Cancer** and **Capricorn**. However, they are believed not to reach the southern pole. The two circles that remain to complete the aforementioned number of ten, the **meridian** and the **horizon**, are not drawn on celestial spheres because they cannot have a fixed location; rather, they vary according to the different position of the observer or inhabitant.

<margin>The Meridian circle.</margin>
For the **meridian** is that circle which the sun marks when it reaches the zenith <note>original: "verticem"</note> of men, thereby creating midday itself. Because the curvature <note>original: "globositas"</note> of the earth does not allow everyone's dwelling-place to be in the same position relative to the sky, the same part of the heavens does not look down upon everyone's zenith. Therefore, there cannot be a single meridian for everyone; instead, a unique meridian is created for each people directly above their own heads. Similarly, the line of sight of each individual creates their own horizon.

The **horizon** is a boundary of the sky, designated as if by a circle, encompassing what is seen above the earth. Because human sight cannot truly reach the actual edge of the world, the extent to which each person can see by looking around creates for them their own boundary of the sky that exists above the earth.

<margin>Note on human sight.</margin>
This horizon, which the view of each person marks out for themselves, cannot contain within its length more than three hundred and sixty **stades** <term>stadium: an ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 185 meters or 600 feet</term>.

<margin>Note: he uses "stadios" in the masculine gender, whereas properly it is called "stadia" in the neuter.</margin>
For the sight of one looking forward does not exceed one hundred and eighty stades. But when the power of sight reaches this distance, failing in its reach, it curves back into a circle. And so it happens that this number, doubled from both sides, creates the space of three hundred and sixty stades contained within one’s horizon. Thus, as much as you advance from the rear part of this space, just as much is taken from the <margin>* or otherwise: front</margin> \* inner part. Therefore, the horizon, however much...

<summary>Macrobius explains that while the celestial colures are fixed, the meridian and horizon are relative to the observer's location on the spherical Earth. He also provides a mathematical limit for the human visual horizon, calculated at 360 stades.</summary>

<keywords>meridian, horizon, colures, zodiac, geometry of the sphere, curvature of the earth, stades, optics, celestial circles</keywords>

...is changed by moving from place to place. Moreover, this view we mentioned is permitted either by a level plain on land or the calm openness of the sea, which offers no obstruction to the eyes. ## Why it happens that certain stars are never seen by us, and how great the size of all the stars is.

### CHAPTER XVI.

"From there, as I gazed upon everything, the rest of the sights seemed brilliant and wonderful. There were those stars which we have never seen from this place <note>original: "ex hoc loco"; meaning from Earth</note>, and their sizes were such as we never suspected. Among them, the smallest was that which, being furthest from heaven and nearest to earth, shone with a borrowed light <note>original: "luce lucebat aliena"; this refers to the Moon, which Macrobius and Cicero understood to reflect the light of the Sun</note>. Moreover, the spheres of the stars easily surpassed the size of the earth."

By saying: *From there, as I gazed upon everything*: he confirms what we said above, that the meeting of Scipio and his ancestors took place in the **Milky Way** <term>lacteo: the "milky" circle of the heavens where the souls of heroes were said to reside</term> itself during the dream. There are two main things which he says he admired regarding the stars: the novelty of some, and the size of all. We shall discuss the novelty first, and the size afterward. By fully and skillfully adding, *Which we have never seen from this place*, he shows the reason why they are not seen by us.

<margin>Why certain stars are always seen by us, and some never.</margin>
For the place of our habitation is so positioned that certain stars can never be seen from it. This is because the part of the sky in which they are located can never appear to those living here. For this part of the earth, which is inhabited by all humanity, as far as we can know...

<meta>catchword: ...we are,</meta>

<meta>This page continues Macrobius’s commentary on Cicero’s "Dream of Scipio." Having established the nature of the horizon on the previous page, Macrobius now explains why the curvature of the Earth prevents us from seeing the southern stars and discusses the immense size of the stars compared to the Earth.</meta>

...wherever we are, the sky rises toward the northern pole, and the spherical convexity of the earth plunges the southern pole deep down away from us. Since the sphere of heaven is always revolving around the earth from East to West, this pole which contains the **Septentriones** <term>Septentriones: the seven stars of the Great and Little Bears, used here to refer to the North Pole</term>, in whatever direction it is turned by the world's rotation, is always seen by us because it is above us, and it always shows:

> The Bears that fear to be dipped in the waters of the Ocean. <note>original: "Arctos Oceani metuentes æquore tingi"; a quote from Virgil’s Georgics 1.246. In the northern hemisphere, these constellations are circumpolar and never "set" or touch the horizon.</note>

The southern pole, on the other hand, is submerged once and for all because of the position of our habitation; it is never seen by us, nor does it show its stars, with which it is undoubtedly adorned. And this is what the poet [Virgil], conscious of the laws of nature itself, said:

<margin>Virgil, Georgics, Book 1.</margin>
> This pole is always high above us: but that other one, 
> black Styx and the deep spirits of the dead see beneath their feet. <note>original: "Hic uertex nobis semper sublimis: at illum / Sub pedibus Styx atra uidet, manesq; profundi." (Georgics 1.242-243). Virgil poetically suggests that the southern stars are visible only to the underworld.</note>

But while the roundness of the earth creates this difference for its inhabitants—making celestial regions appear either always or never—for someone who is located in the heavens, the entire heaven is undoubtedly visible. This is because there is no obstruction from any part of the earth, which, in its entirety, hardly occupies the space of a point in comparison to the vast magnitude of the heavens. Therefore, to Scipio, who had never happened to see the stars of the southern pole from the earth, they rightly caused a sense of wonder as if they were something new, since they were now seen with a free view, without the obstacle of the earth's bulk. And because he understood the reason why he had never seen them before, he said: *Moreover, there were those stars which we have never seen from this place.* By "this place," he refers demonstratively to the earth, upon which he stood while he was telling these things. 

Next follows the discussion of what he added: *And these were the magnitudes of them all, which we never suspected to exist.* Why men never suspected the true sizes which he saw in the stars, he himself revealed by adding: *Moreover, the spheres of the stars easily surpassed the size of the earth.*

<margin>Each individual star is larger than the entire earth.</margin>

For when would a man—unless one whom the teaching of philosophy has raised...

# BOOK I.

*...beyond man, indeed it made him a true man,* <note>original: "pra hominem, imò uerè hominem fecit." This likely refers to the transformative power of celestial knowledge mentioned on the preceding page.</note> *one might suspect that a single star is larger than the entire Earth; even though commonly each one seems scarcely able to equal the flame of a single torch? Therefore, their true magnitude will be believed to be established if it is proven that each individual star is larger than the whole Earth, which you may recognize in this way. Geometers* <term>Geometers: mathematicians specializing in the properties of space and shape</term> *have said that a **point** is that which, because of its incomprehensible smallness, cannot be divided into parts; nor is it called a part itself, but only a mark. Physicists* <term>Physicists: natural philosophers who studied the physical world and the cosmos</term> *have taught that the Earth, compared to the magnitude of the circle through which the Sun revolves, holds the measure of a point.* 

*How much smaller the Sun is than its own circle has been detected by the most manifest reasons of dimension. It is established that the measurement of the Sun holds the two-hundred-and-sixteenth part of the magnitude of the circle* <note>The ratio of 1:216 for the Sun's diameter relative to its orbit was a standard calculation in ancient Greek astronomy, used by figures like Aristarchus or Cleomedes.</note> *through which the Sun itself runs. Since, therefore, the Sun is a certain part of the circle, but the Earth is a point relative to the Sun's circle—which cannot be a part—by unhesitating judgment, it is established that the Sun is larger than the Earth, if a part is larger than that which, by its excessive smallness, cannot even take the name of a part. Indeed, it is certain that the circles of the higher stars are larger than the Sun's circle, if that which contains is larger than that which is contained—since this is the order of the celestial spheres, that each lower one is surrounded by a higher one. Hence he said the sphere of the Moon—being, as it were, the last from heaven and near to the Earth—is the smallest,* 
<margin>otherwise: of the sphere</margin> 
*while the Earth itself, as a point, truly fades away as the final thing. If therefore the circles of the superior stars (as we said) are grander than the circle of the Sun, and each of these is of such magnitude that it holds the measure of a part relative to its own circle: without doubt each is more ample than the Earth, which we predicted to be a point relative to the Sun's circle (which is smaller than the superior ones). Regarding the Moon, if it truly shines with borrowed light, following things will teach us.*
