# ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

### In what sense the highest god is named: and whether the stars, which they call fixed, are also moved by their own proper motion.

->CHAPTER XVII.<-

While <term>Scipio's</term> <note>Scipio Aemilianus, the Roman general and protagonist of Cicero's "Dream of Scipio."</note> gaze wandered through these sights with wonder, descending even to the Earth and lingering there as if on familiar ground, he was once again recalled to higher things by the warning of his grandfather, who showed him the very order of the spheres from the beginning of heaven in these words:
> All things are connected by nine circles, or rather spheres, of which one is the outermost heavenly sphere which encompasses all the others—the highest god himself, <note>In the Stoic and Neoplatonic view, the outermost sphere or "Primum Mobile" was often identified with the divine mind that contains all of existence.</note> confining and containing the rest. Within this are fixed the eternal revolving courses of the stars. Below this are seven spheres which turn backward with a motion contrary to that of the heaven. Of these, that which they call <term>Saturnian</term> <note>The planet Saturn, named for the god of time and agriculture.</note> on Earth occupies one sphere. Next is that radiance, prosperous and healthy for the human race, which is called <term>Jupiter's</term>. Then comes the red one, terrible to the Earth, which you call <term>Mars'</term>. Then, below the middle region, the <term>Sun</term> takes its place—the leader, prince, and moderator of the other lights, the mind and regulator of the world, of such great magnitude that it illuminates and fills all things with its light. Following the Sun as companions are the paths of <term>Venus</term> and <term>Mercury</term>. In the lowest sphere, the <term>Moon</term> revolves, ignited by the rays of the Sun. Below her, however, there is nothing except what is mortal and fleeting, except for the souls given to the human race by the gift of the gods. Above the moon, all things are eternal. For the Earth, which is the middle and ninth sphere, does not move; it is the lowest point, and toward it all weights are carried by their own gravity.

In this passage, a careful description of the entire world from the highest to the lowest has been gathered together, and a complete body of the universe is fashioned, which some have called <term>the All</term> <note>original Greek: "τὸ πᾶν"</note>—that is, "the whole." Whence...

# BOOK I.

<margin>The 6th book of the *Aeneid*.</margin>
And here he says: *All things are connected.* <note>original: "Connexa sunt omnia."</note> <term>Virgil</term> truly called it a "great body": *And it mingles itself with the great body.* <note>original: "Et magno se corpore miscet." This is a quote from Virgil's *Aeneid*, Book VI, describing how the divine spirit sustains the universe.</note> In this place, however, <term>Cicero</term> has bequeathed many things to be cultivated by us, having cast the seeds of inquiry. Concerning the seven subject spheres, he says: *Which turn backward with a motion contrary to that of the heaven.* <margin>He sets forth those things which must be explained in order.</margin> When he says this, he warns us to inquire whether the heaven itself turns; and whether those seven both turn and are moved with a contrary motion; or if the Platonic authority agrees with this order of the spheres which Cicero reports. Furthermore, if they are truly placed beneath, we must ask in what way the stars of all those spheres are said to survey the <term>zodiac</term>, <note>The belt of the heavens within which the sun, moon, and planets move.</note> since the zodiac is both a single thing and located in the highest heaven; and what reason causes the courses of some to be shorter and others longer within that one zodiac. For all these things must be asserted in the explanation of their order. And finally, by what reason they are carried toward the earth, just as he says: *All weights by their own inclination.* <note>original: "Omnia nutu suo pondera." This refers to the theory of gravity in the geocentric model, where heavy things naturally seek the center of the universe—the Earth.</note>

<margin>Why the heaven is moved.</margin>
The nature, power, and reason of the <term>World-Soul</term> <note>original: "mundanae animae." In Neoplatonism, the soul that animates the entire universe.</note> teaches that the heaven turns; its eternity is found in motion, because motion never leaves that which life does not desert; nor does life depart from that in which an ever-active vigor flourishes. Therefore, the celestial body—which the World-Soul fabricated for itself to be a sharer in its immortality so that it might never fail in living—is always in motion and knows not how to stand still, because the soul by which it is driven does not stand still itself. For since the essence of the soul, which is incorporeal, consists in motion, and the body of the heaven was the first of all things fabricated by the soul, the nature of motion undoubtedly migrated from the incorporeal into this first body. Its power, whole and uncorrupted, does not desert that which it first began to move. <margin>Why it is not driven in a straight motion but in a circle.</margin> Indeed, the motion of the heaven is necessarily revolving, because while it must always be moved, and there is no place beyond it to which it might extend its reach, it is driven by a perpetual continuation of returning into itself. Therefore, it runs within that which it can or has, and for it to "approach" is to be revolved.

because there is but one course for the sphere that encompasses all spaces and places: to rotate. But in this way, it always seems to follow the soul, which runs through the universe itself. Shall we say then that it never finds her [the soul], if it always follows her? On the contrary, it always finds her, because she is whole everywhere and perfect everywhere. Why then, if it finds what it seeks, does it not rest? Because she also knows no rest. For the sphere would stand still if it ever found the soul standing still. But since she, toward whose desire the sphere is drawn, always pours herself into the universe, the body [the heavens] always turns itself back toward her and through her. Let these few points among many, discovered with <term>Plotinus</term> as the authority, suffice concerning the mystery of celestial rotation. <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism. Macrobius relies heavily on his idea that the physical movement of the heavens is an expression of the soul’s desire for the divine.</note>

<margin>In what sense the outermost sphere is called the highest god.</margin> However, the fact that Cicero called this outermost globe, which revolves in this way, the "highest God," is not to be understood as if it were the <term>First Cause</term> and that most almighty God. For the globe itself, which is the heaven, is the handiwork of the Soul; the Soul proceeded from the Mind; and the Mind was created from God, who is truly supreme. But he called it "highest" in relation to the order of the others that are placed beneath it; hence he soon added: *Encompassing and containing the others.* <note>original Latin: "Arcens & continens cæteros."</note> He called it "God," however, not only because it is an immortal and divine being filled with the renowned reason from that purest Mind, but because it either creates or contains all the powers that follow that summit of the first omnipotence. Finally, the ancients called this very thing <term>Jupiter</term>, and among the theologians, Jupiter is the <term>World-Soul</term>. <note>The World-Soul (Anima Mundi) is a concept where the entire universe is viewed as a single living organism endowed with a rational soul.</note> From this comes that saying:

> From Jupiter is the beginning, O Muses; all things are full of Jupiter.

<margin>Eclogue 3. "Let us begin with Zeus." <note>original Greek: ἐκ Διὸς ἀρχώμεθα.</note> This principle was also used by Theocritus in his poem for Ptolemy. Whether the fixed stars are also moved by a certain motion of their own.</margin> Other poets borrowed this from <term>Aratus</term>, who, about to speak of the stars and deciding that the beginning must be taken from the heaven in which the stars reside, mentioned that one must start with Jupiter. <note>Aratus was a Greek poet famous for the *Phaenomena*, a poem about the constellations. Ancient scholars often interpreted his "Jupiter" as a metaphor for the divine order of the sky.</note> From this, <term>Juno</term> is called both his sister and his wife. For Juno is the Air; and she is called his sister because she [is formed] from the same seeds...

by whom the heaven and even the air were brought forth: the air is called a "wife" because it is subject to the heaven. To these points we must add that, besides the two great lights <note>The Sun and the Moon.</note> and the five stars which are called "wandering" <note>The planets: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>, some say all the rest are fixed in the heaven and move only with the heaven itself. <margin>Common tradition holds that this course takes fifteen thousand years; but Ptolemy’s calculation allows for 36,000 years. Others say more or less 25,200.</margin> Others (whose assertion is closer to the truth) have said that these stars also move by their own motion, in addition to being carried along by the rotation of the heaven; but because of the vastness of that outermost sphere, they complete a single circuit of their course over a number of ages exceeding belief. Therefore, no motion of theirs is perceived by man, since the span of a human life is not sufficient to detect even a brief point of such a slow advancement. Hence <term>Tullius</term> <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), the author of the original text Macrobius is commenting upon.</note>, who was well-acquainted with every school of thought approved by the ancients, touched upon both opinions at once by saying: **In which are fixed those eternal courses of the stars, which revolve.** <note>original: "In quo sunt infixi illi, qui uoluuntur, stellarum cursus sempiterni."</note> For he called them "fixed," yet did not remain silent about the fact that they "revolve."

->*The wandering stars move in a motion contrary to that of the heaven.*<-

### C H A P T E R XVIII.

Now let us seek, through arguments leading to the truth, whether those seven spheres placed beneath are carried along in a motion contrary to the rotation of the heaven, as he says. To those who are <margin>"The uninitiated in letters" refers to the unskilled or ignorant.</margin> uninitiated in learning—the "unprofessed" in letters—the idea that the Sun, the Moon, and the five stars named for their "wandering" <note>The word "planet" comes from the Greek *planetes*, meaning "wanderer."</note> actually proceed by their own motion from West to East (besides being dragged from East to West by the daily rotation of the heaven) seems unbelievable and like a miracle. But to those who look more closely, it will be established as so true that it can not only be grasped by the mind, but also proven to the eyes themselves. However, so that we may deal with one who stubbornly denies this, come now—whoever you are who pretends this is not clear—let us take everything that either stubbornness imagines for itself to undermine faith, or that truth itself suggests, and lay it out in parts.

We must decide whether these wandering stars <note>The five planets known to the ancients: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>, along with the two lights <note>The Sun and the Moon.</note>, are fixed in the sky like the other stars and show no motion of their own to our eyes—being carried along solely by the <margin>*of confusion</margin> force of the world’s rotation—or whether they also move by their own advancement. Again, if they do move, do they follow the path of the sky from East to West, traveling both by the sky’s motion and their own? Or do they revolve in a contrary retreat toward the East, moving away from the West? <margin>Point of the argument.</margin> Beyond this, I believe, nothing can either exist or be imagined. Now let us see which of these possibilities can be proven true. If they were fixed, they would never depart from the same station, but would always be seen in the same places, just like the other stars. For look at the <term>Vergiliae</term> <note>original: "Vergiliae"; the Roman name for the Pleiades star cluster.</note> among the fixed stars: they never disperse from their union, nor do they desert the <term>Hyades</term> <note>A cluster of stars in the constellation Taurus.</note> which are nearby, nor do they leave the neighboring region of Orion. The framework of the <term>Septentriones</term> <note>original: "Septentrionum"; the "Seven Oxen," referring to the constellations of the Great and Little Bears (Ursa Major and Minor).</note> likewise does not break apart. The <term>Serpent</term> <note>original: "Anguis"; the constellation Draco.</note> that glides between them does not change the embrace it has once wound around them. These wandering stars, however, are seen now in this region of the sky, now in that. And often, when two or more have met in one place, they are later separated both from the place where they were seen together and from each other. From this it is clear, with our own eyes confirming it, that they are not fixed in the sky. Therefore they move, and no one can deny what sight itself affirms.

We must therefore ask whether they revolve with their own motion from East to West, or in the opposite direction. But even as we ask this, not only the most manifest reason but sight itself will show us. For let us consider the order of the individual signs by which we see the <term>Zodiac</term> <note>The belt of the heavens divided into twelve signs, which the Sun, Moon, and planets appear to move through.</note> divided or distinguished, and let us take the beginning of that order from any one sign we choose. When Aries rises, Taurus emerges after it; Gemini follows this, then Cancer, and the rest in order. If these planets, therefore, proceeded from the East toward the West, they would not move from Aries into Taurus, which is located behind it, nor from Taurus into Gemini, the subsequent sign...

### BOOK I.

...would be rolled along; but they would proceed from <term>Gemini</term> <note>The Twins</note> into <term>Taurus</term> <note>The Bull</note>, and from Taurus into <term>Aries</term> <note>The Ram</note>, directly and in a motion harmonious with the world's rotation. Since, therefore, they revolve from the first sign to the second, from the second to the third, and from there to the rest which follow after, while the signs themselves are carried fixed in the sky: it is undoubtedly certain that these stars move not *with* the sky, but *against* the sky. 

To make this fully clear, let us provide evidence from the moon's course, which is more noticeable both for its brightness and its speed. After the moon has been renewed by departing from the Sun <note>The "New Moon" phase, when the Moon is positioned between the Earth and the Sun.</note>, it is seen near the West on about the second day, appearing close to the Sun which it recently left. After the Sun has set, the moon holds the edge of the sky, setting just after it. On the third day it sets later than on the second, and so daily it recedes further from the West, until on the seventh day it is seen in the middle of the sky at sunset. 

After another seven days, when the Sun sets, the moon rises; thus in the middle of the month, by receding from the West toward the East, it traverses half the sky—that is, one hemisphere. Again, after seven more days, at the time of sunset, it holds the peak of the hidden hemisphere <note>The part of the sky currently below the horizon from the observer's perspective.</note>. The proof of this is that it rises at midnight. Finally, when the same number of days have passed, it reaches the Sun once more, and the rising of both appears close together, as long as it moves again following the Sun, and by receding again little by little, always returning toward the East, it leaves the West behind. 

The Sun itself also moves in no other way than from West to East, and although it completes its retreat more slowly than the moon (since it takes as much time to traverse one sign as the moon takes to run through the whole <term>zodiac</term>), it nevertheless provides clear evidence of its motion, visible to the eyes. Let us suppose the Sun is in Aries; because this is an <term>equinoctial</term> sign, it makes the hours of sleep and day equal. When the Sun sets in this sign, we see <term>Libra</term>—that is, the Claws of the Scorpion <note>original: "Scorpij chelas"; in ancient astronomy, the constellation of Libra was often depicted as the outstretched claws of the neighboring Scorpio.</note>—soon rise.

After the Twins, the sun recedes into <term>Cancer</term> <note>The Crab</note>, and then, when it sets, Libra is seen in the middle of the sky. Thus it is established that after the sun has completed its journey through three signs—namely, <term>Aries</term> <note>The Ram</note>, Taurus, and Gemini—it has receded to the midpoint of the hemisphere. And while the sun sets in that very sign, Aries—in which the sun used to set six months earlier—immediately rises. We choose to point out its setting rather than its rising because the signs that follow after are visible after sunset. ### CHAPTER XIX.

<margin>What order the Sun holds among the planets.</margin>
Having established these points, a few words must be said regarding the order of the spheres. In this matter, **Cicero** may appear to disagree with **Plato**; for Cicero says the Sun's sphere is the fourth of seven—that is, located in the middle—while Plato records that it holds the second place upward from the Moon—that is, the sixth place from the top among the seven. **Archimedes** <note>The famous Greek mathematician and engineer</note> and the calculations of the **Chaldeans** <note>Babylonian astronomers and astrologers</note> agree with Cicero. Plato followed the **Egyptians**, the parents of all philosophical disciplines, who hold that the sun is located between the Moon and Mercury; however, they have grasped by reason and <margin>*elicited</margin> \*proclaimed <note>The Latin text uses *edixerint* ("proclaimed"), while the margin suggests the alternative *elicuerint* ("elicited" or "drawn out")</note> why it is believed by some that the Sun is above Mercury and above Venus. Indeed, those who hold that opinion do not wander far from the appearance of truth. Truthfully, the following reasoning persuaded them of this interchangeable opinion: from the sphere of **Saturn**, which is the first of the seven, down to the sphere of **Jupiter**, which is the second from the top, there is such a great distance of intervening space that the higher one completes the circuit of the zodiac in thirty years, while the one below it completes it in twelve years. Again, the sphere of **Mars** is so far removed from Jupiter that it performs the same course in two years. Now, **Venus** is so much lower than the region of Mars that a single year is enough for it to traverse the zodiac. Indeed, the star of **Mercury** is so very close to Venus, and the **Sun** so near to Mercury, that these three [complete] their heavens...

...they orbit in an equal space of time—that is, in a year, more or less. For this reason, **Cicero** called these two courses the "companions of the sun," because, in an equal span of time, they never recede far from it. The Moon, however, has moved so far downward from these that what they complete in a year, she herself finishes in twenty-eight days. Therefore, there was no disagreement among the ancients regarding the order of the three superior planets <note>The "outer" planets: Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars</note>, which an immense distance distinguishes clearly and manifestly; nor regarding the region of the moon, which is far removed from all the others. 

But the proximity of these three—Venus, Mercury, and the Sun—confused their order for some. This was the case among other [philosophers]. For the logic did not escape the skill of the **Egyptians**, which is as follows: The circle through which the sun runs is surrounded by the circle of **Mercury**, as the lower one. The higher circle of **Venus** also encloses that one. And so it happens that these two stars, when they run through the upper arcs of their circles, are understood to be located above the sun; but when they pass through the lower parts of their circles, the sun is considered to be above them. 

Therefore, to those who said their spheres were below the sun, this appeared to be the case from that course of the stars which sometimes (as we said) seems lower—which is indeed more notable because they then appear more clearly. For when they occupy the upper regions, they are more hidden by the sun’s rays. And thus that belief grew strong, and this order was adopted for use by almost everyone. 

<margin>*otherwise: a truer [order]</margin> However, a more perceptive observation has detected a * better order, which, beyond the investigation of sight, this reasoning also recommends: that it is necessary for the moon—which lacks its own light and borrows it from the sun—to be positioned below the source of its light. For this reasoning establishes that the moon does not have its own light, while all the other stars shine with their own: because those located above the sun are in the very purest **ether** <note>The "fifth element," believed by ancients to be the substance of the heavens, consisting of pure light and fire</note>, in which everything that exists is light that is natural and its own. This light, along with its fire, rests upon the sphere of the Sun in such a way that the zones of heaven, which

<margin>The moon shines with borrowed light.</margin>
...are far from the sun, they are oppressed by perpetual cold, as will be shown below. But the **Moon**, because she alone is beneath the sun and nearest to the region of transitory things <term>caduca: things that are subject to decay or falling, referring to the sublunary world</term>—which already lacks its own light—could not have light unless the sun were positioned above her, whom she reflects. In fact, because the earth is one part of the whole world, and the moon is one part of the ether <term>æther: the pure, fiery upper air of the heavens</term>, they have called the moon an "ethereal earth." However, she could not be immobile as the earth is: for in a sphere that revolves, nothing remains motionless except the center. Since the earth is the center of the world’s sphere, it alone remains immobile. Furthermore, the earth merely grows bright when it receives the Sun's light; it does not reflect it. The Moon, like a mirror, sends forth the light by which she is illuminated. This is because the earth is considered the "dregs" of air and water—elements which are themselves solid and dense—and therefore it is thickened to an extreme solidity, such that light cannot penetrate beyond its surface. Although the moon is also an endpoint <note>original: "finis" — here meaning a boundary or outer limit of the ethereal realm</note>, she is the endpoint of the most fluid light and ethereal fire. Therefore, although her body is denser than the other heavenly bodies, yet being much purer than the earth, she is penetrable to the light she receives—so much so that she emits it from herself again, though conveying no sensation of heat to us. This is because a ray of light, when it reaches us from its source—that is, from the sun—carries with it the nature of the fire from which it is born. But when it is poured into the body of the moon and reflects from there, it sends back only brightness, not heat. For even a mirror, when it casts a glare from the force of a fire placed far opposite it, shows only the likeness of the fire, lacking the sensation of heat.

Enough has been said regarding the order that **Plato** (or his authorities) gave to the **Sun**, or whom **Cicero** followed when he assigned it the fourth place, or what reasoning led to this difference of opinion, and why **Tullius** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the author of the *Dream of Scipio*</note> said: *In the lowest sphere, the moon, kindled by the sun's rays, revolves.* But on these matters...

# ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

<margin>Why he says the sun is "almost" the middle, and not absolutely so.</margin>
It must be added why Cicero—since he intends the Sun to be the fourth of the seven <term>the seven celestial bodies of the geocentric system: Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</term>, and the fourth among seven is, and is considered to be, exactly in the middle—did not call the Sun the middle abruptly, but instead said "almost the middle" with these words: <margin>*variant: the middle of the seven</margin> "Then, below, the Sun occupies the almost middle region." But this addition, which softens the statement, is not without purpose. For the Sun, holding the fourth place, will hold the middle region by number, but not by physical space. If he were speaking of the three highest and three lowest, the Sun is undoubtedly the middle by count. However, when the dimensions of the entire space occupied by the seven spheres are examined, the region of the Sun is not found to be located in the center of that space: because the Sun is further from the highest point than the lowest extremity is from the Sun itself. A brief demonstration will prove this without any winding debate. The star of Saturn, which is the highest, traverses the zodiac <term>the belt of the heavens through which the planets move</term> in thirty years; the Sun in the middle, in one year; the Moon, the last, in less than a full month. Therefore, there is as much difference between the Sun and Saturn as there is between one and thirty. There is as much between the Moon and the Sun as there is between twelve and one <note>The author is comparing the time it takes for orbits to complete: Saturn takes 30 times longer than the Sun, while the Sun takes roughly 12 times longer than the Moon</note>. From this it appears that the region of the Sun does not create an exact division of the whole space from top to bottom into two equal halves. But because Cicero was speaking here of the number, in which the fourth is truly the middle, he indeed pronounced it the middle; however, on account of the hidden dimensions of the spaces, he added the word "almost" to qualify this definition.

<margin>Where the names of the stars come from.</margin>
It should be noted that the fact that there is a "star of Saturn," and another "of Jupiter," and another "of Mars," is not an arrangement of nature, but a human convention <margin>Virgil, Georgics, Book 1</margin> which gave numbers and names to the stars. For he <note>Cicero</note> does not say "that which is Saturnian," but "that which they name Saturnian on earth"; and "that radiance which is said to be Jupiter’s," and "that which you call Martian." He expressed this so clearly in each instance to show that these names were not found in nature, but were human inventions adopted for the sake of making distinctions.

# BOOK I.

<margin>Why among the planets some are called favorable to us and others adverse.</margin>
Indeed, the fact that he called the brightness of Jupiter prosperous and salutary to the human race, and conversely, the reddish glow of Mars terrible to the earth: one description is drawn from the color of the stars—for Jupiter shines brightly, while Mars glows red—the other from the treatises of those who claim that adverse or prosperous things flow from these stars into human life. For they generally define that terrible things happen from the star of Mars, and salutary things from Jupiter. 

If anyone should perhaps seek a deeper cause as to why malevolence is attributed to divine beings—so that a star is called "malefic," as is the opinion regarding the stars of Mars and Saturn—or why a more notable "benignity" of Jupiter and Venus is held among the <term>genethliacos</term> <note>original: "genethliacos," referring to astrologers who cast horoscopes based on the moment of birth</note>: since there is but one divine nature, I will bring forward a reason read, as far as I know, in only one place. For Ptolemy, in the three books he composed *On Harmony*, revealed the cause, which I will briefly explain. 

He says there are certain numbers through which all things that suit one another are joined and fitted together, and a "yoke-like" competence <note>a state of being well-matched or harmonious</note> is formed; nor can anything agree with another except through these numbers. These are the <term>epitritus</term> <note>the sesquitertian ratio, 4:3</note>, <term>hemiolius</term> <note>the sesquialter ratio, 3:2</note>, <term>epogdous</term> <note>the sesquioctave ratio, 9:8</note>, <term>duplaris</term> <note>the double ratio, 2:1</note>, <term>triplaris</term> <note>the triple ratio, 3:1</note>, and <term>quadruplaris</term> <note>the quadruple ratio, 4:1</note>. I wish for you to accept these for now simply as the names of numbers. In the following sections, however, when we speak of the harmony of the heavens, we will more opportunely reveal what these numbers are and what they are capable of. For now, let it suffice to know that without these numbers, no binding, no concord can exist. 

Our life, however, is chiefly governed by the Sun and the Moon. For since these two faculties are proper to perishable bodies—to feel or to grow—the <term>αἰσθητικὸν</term> <note>original Greek: *aisthētikon*; the power of sensory perception</note>, that is, the nature of sensing, comes to us from the Sun; while the <term>φυτικὸν</term> <note>original Greek: *phutikon*; the vegetative power</note>, that is, the nature of growing, comes to us from the lunar sphere. Thus, by the benefit of both lights, this life we enjoy is established. Yet our social interaction and the outcome of our actions relate as much to these two lights as...

than is referred to the five wandering stars <note>The "wandering stars" are the planets, distinguished from the "fixed stars" of the constellations.</note>. But the intervention of these numbers (which we mentioned above) joins and associates some of these stars well with the lights; however, no connection of number applies others to the lights. Therefore, the stars of Venus and Jupiter are associated with both lights through these numbers: but Jupiter’s is joined to the Sun through all the ratios, and to the Moon through many; and Venus’s is added to the Moon through all, and to the Sun through many numbers. 

Hence, although both are believed to be beneficial, the star of Jupiter is more suited to the Sun, and Venus to the Moon. Therefore, they are more advantageous to our lives, being in concord by the law of numbers with the lights who are the authors of our life. The stars of Saturn and Mars, however, do not have such compatibility with the lights; yet, by some line of numbers, even if at the extreme, Saturn looks toward the Sun and Mars toward the Moon. For this reason, they are considered less advantageous to human life, as if they were not joined to the authors of life by a close numerical ratio. 

Why these planets themselves are nevertheless sometimes believed to provide wealth or fame to men must belong to another treatise; for here it suffices to have revealed the reason why one is considered terrible and another salutary. Indeed, Plotinus <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 204–270 AD). Macrobius is referencing his treatise *Enneads* 2.3.</note>, in the book entitled *Whether the Stars Act* <note>original: "Si faciunt astra"</note>, pronounces that nothing happens to men by the force or power of the stars. Instead, he suggests that those things which the necessity of the divine decree ordains for individuals are merely demonstrated through the transit, station, or retreat of these seven planets. He compares them to birds: just as birds, whether by flying past or standing still, unknowingly signify future events by their wings or their voice, so too do the stars. Thus, a planet may still rightly be called "salutary" or "terrible," since through the former we signify prosperous things, and through the latter, inconveniences.

Among these many names, however, which are spoken concerning the sun, speech is not being used recklessly nor for the sake of a parade of praise: rather, true realities are expressed by these terms. "Leader and prince," he says, "and moderator of the remaining lights, the mind of the world and its tempering." <note>This quote is from Cicero’s "Dream of Scipio," which this text is a commentary on.</note> Plato in the *Timaeus*, when he was speaking of the eight spheres, says this: *"In order that there might be a certain measure for the eight circuits of speed and slowness, and that it might be known: God, in the orbit above the earth, kindled a* <gloss>\* else: second</gloss> *second light, which we now call the sun."* <note>original: "secundum lumen accendit"</note> Do you see how this definition intends for the light of all the spheres to be found in the sun? But Cicero, knowing that the other stars also have their own light, and that only the moon (as we have already often said) lacks its own: clearing up the obscurity of this definition more clearly, and showing that the greatest light is in the sun, did not only say: 

<margin>Various names of the Sun.</margin>

"Leader, and prince, and moderator of the remaining lights": thus he also knows that the other stars are lights; but he calls this one the leader and prince, which Heraclitus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher (c. 535–475 BC) known for his theories on fire and constant change.</note> calls the source of celestial light. He is "Leader" [Dux], therefore, because he precedes all others in the majesty of his light; he is "Prince" [Princeps], because he stands out so much that, because he alone appears as such, he is called *Sol* [the Sun]. <note>The author is following an ancient etymological theory that the Latin word "Sol" (Sun) comes from "solus" (alone).</note> He is called "Moderator of the others" because he himself moderates their forward courses and their backward returns by a certain definition of space. For there is a certain definition of space such that when each wandering star <note>The "wandering stars" are the planets.</note> reaches it while receding from the sun, it seems to be driven backward as if it were forbidden to approach further; and again, when it has touched a certain part in its receding, it is recalled to the customary path of its direct course. Thus the force and power of the Sun moderates the movements of the remaining lights in an established dimension. He is called "Mind of the world" just as natural philosophers have called him the "heart of heaven." <note>original: "cor coeli"</note> This is surely because all things which we see happen through the heaven by a fixed law—day and night, and the shifting turns of length and brevity between both, and at certain times...

There is also this reason why he is rightly called the heart of heaven: because the nature of fire is always in perpetual motion and agitation. We have mentioned that the Sun is called the source of ethereal fire. Therefore, the Sun is in the ether what the heart is in a living creature: its nature is such that it never ceases from movement; for if there were even a brief cessation from its agitation by any chance, it would immediately destroy the creature. This covers why he called the Sun the mind of the world. But why he is also called the **Tempering of the world** <note>original: "Temperatio mundi." For it is most certain that not only the earth, but also heaven itself—which is truly called the "world"—is tempered by the Sun; so much so that its extremities, which have withdrawn furthest from the path of the Sun, lack every benefit of heat and grow numb in a single perpetuity of cold. This will be explained more clearly in what follows.

There is no doubt that this cannot be grasped unless the measurement of both the Earth and the Sun is discovered, so that the distinction may be made by comparison. And indeed, the dimensions of the Earth were easily established by the eyes with the help of reason. But they saw that the measurement of the Sun could not be found except through the measurement of the heaven through which it travels. Therefore, they decided they must first measure the heaven—that is, the Sun's path—so that through it they might recognize the scale of the Sun. 

But I ask, if anyone should ever be so idle or so free from serious business as to take these matters into their hands, let them not shudder at nor laugh at such a promise of the ancients as if it were close to insanity. For human ingenuity has made a path for itself toward a matter that seemed incomprehensible by nature, and discovered the scale of heaven through the earth. To make the reasoning behind this discovery clear, a few basic principles must first be stated so that the approach to what follows may be better prepared.

In every circle or sphere, the middle point is called the **center**.

# COMMENTARY ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

<margin>Diameter.</margin>
...ther. And this line, which divides a circle so equally, is called the <term>diameter</term> <note>original Greek: διάμετρος</note>. Likewise, every diameter of any circle, when tripled and with the addition of a seventh part of itself, creates the measurement of the circumference by which the circle is enclosed. That is, if the length of the diameter is seven inches, and you wish to know from this how many inches the circumference of that circle contains: you will triple the seven, making twenty-one. To these you will add a seventh part, which is one: and you will declare twenty-two inches to be the measurement of this circle whose diameter extends seven inches <note>Macrobius is describing the Archimedean approximation of Pi as 22/7, a standard geometric rule in antiquity.</note>. We could prove all these things with the most evident geometrical reasons, were it not that we believe no one doubts them, and we are careful not to extend this volume to an excessive length.

<margin>The shadow of the Earth.</margin>
It should also be known that the shadow of the Earth—which the sun, running in the lower hemisphere after its setting, forces to be cast upward, and from which darkness is created over the earth, called night—is multiplied sixty times in height from that measure which the diameter of the earth possesses. Reaching with this length toward the very circle through which the sun runs, it pours back darkness upon the earth by the exclusion of light. Therefore, it must be disclosed how great the diameter of the earth is, so that it may be clear what sixty times that measure can collect. Hence, with these preliminaries, let the discourse return to the treatment of measurements which it promised. By the most evident and

### CHAPTER XXI.

But since we have said that there are seven spheres placed beneath the heaven <margin>In what manner the stars of the interior spheres are said to travel in the signs of the zodiac.</margin>, with each outer sphere surrounding those it contains within, and since they are all far removed from the heaven and from each other, we must now ask: since there is only one zodiac, and it consists of stars fixed in the heaven, how can the stars of the lower spheres be said to travel in the signs of the zodiac? It is not difficult to find the reasoning, which lies at the very threshold of the question. ## BOOK I.

<note>The author is explaining how to divide a circle into twelve equal parts using lines.</note> Without a doubt, the passage of the lines will divide each of the individual spheres into twelve parts. Therefore, in whichever circle—whether it be the Sun, the Moon, or any of the wandering stars <note>original: "de uagis"; referring to the planets</note> traveling within it—when it comes to the space enclosed between the lines flowing down from the marks and letters **A** and **B**, it will be said to be in **Aries**. This is because, being positioned there, it will have the space of Aries (as designated in the zodiac) directly above its head, just as we have described. Similarly, into whichever part it moves, it will be said to be in the sign beneath which it is located.

And this very description will teach us, by the same brief explanation, <margin>Why some stars traverse the signs of the zodiac in a shorter time, others in a longer time.</margin> why some stars traverse the same zodiac and the same signs in a longer time, and others in a shorter time. For whenever many spheres are placed one within another: just as the one which is first is the largest, and the one which holds the last place is the smallest, so it is with those in the middle—the one closer to the top is larger than those below it, and the one nearer to the last is shorter than those above it. Therefore, among these seven spheres, the order of their position has assigned to each a degree of its own speed.

For this reason, the stars that travel through larger spaces complete their circuit in a more extended time; those that travel through narrow spaces, in a shorter time. For it is established that none among them proceeds more quickly or more slowly than the others. But since the motion of traveling is the same for all, the diversity of the spaces alone creates such a great difference in time. For—to pass over the middle ones for now so that the same things are not often repeated—the fact that **Saturn** encompasses and passes through the same signs in thirty years, while the **Moon** does so in twenty-eight days, the sole cause lies in the size of their circles: of which one is the largest, the other the smallest. Therefore, each of the other stars also either extends or contracts its time of traveling according to the measure of its space. At this point, a diligent investigator of things, having inspected the marks of the zodiac <margin>How the zodiac is divided into twelve parts.</margin> which the description (called upon to support our reliability) demonstrates, will ask: "But who actually discovered the twelve parts of the celestial circle,

...or created them, especially since no visible beginnings of the individual divisions are presented to our eyes? To this most necessary question, history itself shall provide the answer, recounting the deed by which the ancients both attempted and achieved so difficult a division. For the ancestors of the Egyptians—who are well known to have been the first of all men to dare to scrutinize and measure the heavens—took advantage of the perpetual serenity of their skies. Looking up with a free and unobstructed view, they discovered that while all the other stars and constellations are fixed in the heavens, only five stars <note>The five planets known to the ancients: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> wander along with the sun and the moon. They saw that these did not run through all parts of the sky at random or without a certain law governing their "wandering" <note>The word "planet" comes from the Greek word for wanderer.</note>; finally, they noted that these never deviated toward the northern pole, nor did they ever sink to the depths of the Southern Pole. Instead, they confined all their movements within the boundary of a single oblique circle <note>The Zodiac or Ecliptic.</note>. Yet they did not all go and return together; some reached the same place at different times. Furthermore, they saw some of these approach, others move backward, and sometimes they even appeared to stand still. After they saw these things happening among them, I say, they decided to establish certain parts within that very circle and to mark them with divisions. This was done so that there would be fixed names for the places in which the planets stayed, or from which they had departed, or to which they were about to return, so that they might announce these things to one another and transmit the knowledge to posterity. Therefore, having prepared two bronze vessels, one of which had its bottom pierced in the manner of a water-clock <note>original: "clepsydræ"</note>, they placed the one that was whole and empty underneath, with the other full of water placed above it, though with its opening initially blocked. They then observed one very bright and notable star among the fixed stars as it was rising. As soon as it first began to emerge, they immediately withdrew the blockage and allowed the water from the upper vessel to flow into the one placed below. It flowed until the end of that night and the following day, and into the second night, until that same star returned again to its Rising; and when...

This water was then divided into twelve equal parts by a reliable measurement: two other vessels of this capacity were provided, so that each would hold only one of those twelve parts. All the water was then poured back into its original vessel, the opening having first been closed; and of those two smaller vessels, they placed one beneath the full vessel and set the other nearby, ready and prepared.

With these things prepared, on another night, in that part of the sky through which they had learned by long-term observation that the sun, the moon, and the five wandering stars <note>The "five wandering stars" refers to the planets known to the ancients: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> travel—and which they later called the **Zodiac**—they watched for a constellation to rise, to which they later gave the name **Aries**. When that was full, they quickly removed and emptied it, and substituted the other similar one. They observed certain signs and noted them from memory among the stars of that place which were rising when the first vessel was filled; understanding that in the time it took for a twelfth part of the total water to flow, a twelfth part of the heavens had ascended.

Therefore, from that place where the water began to flow into the first vessel at the start of the rising, up to the place that was rising when that same first vessel was filled, they declared to be a twelfth part of the sky—that is, one **sign**. Likewise, when the second vessel was filled and quickly withdrawn, they again substituted the similar one they had previously emptied. They similarly noted the place that was emerging when the second vessel was filled; and from the end of the first sign to the place that was rising at the end of the second water-flow, the second sign was marked out. This was accomplished not in a single night, but in two; for the entire sky does not revolve in one night, but half of it turns during the day and the remaining half during the night. ### CHAPTER XXII. For what reason the Earth is immobile, and why all weights are carried toward it by their own inclination.

For that Earth, he says, which is the middle and the ninth, neither moves and is the lowest point, and all weights are carried into it by their own inclination <note>original: "nutu suo"; referring to the natural tendency or "nod" of objects to seek their place</note>. Truly, those are indissoluble causes which are bound together by mutual links; and while one cause creates the other, they are born from one another in turn in such a way that they are never separated from the embraces of their natural fellowship. Such are the bonds with which nature constrains the Earth. For all things are carried toward it for this reason: because, being the middle, it does not move; and it does not move for this reason: because it is the lowest point. Nor could it fail to be the lowest point, into which all things are carried.

Let this treatise explain each of these points, which the necessity of things has bound up inseparably within itself. *It does not move*, he says: for it is the center <note>original: "centron"; the geometric midpoint of the celestial spheres</note>. Now, we have said that in a sphere, only the center does not move, because it is necessary that a sphere moves around something immobile. He added: *It is the lowest*. This also is correct, for that which is the center is the middle. In a sphere, however, it is established that only that which is the middle is the bottom-most point. And if it is the lowest, it follows that it was truly said: *All things are carried into it*. For nature always leads weights down to the lowest point.

Indeed, it was brought about in the world itself that the Earth should be the lowest. Whatever was the purest and most liquid out of all the matter from which all things were made, that held the summit and was called the ether. That part which had less purity and contained some slight weight emerged as air and sank into the second place. After these things, that which was still indeed liquid, but now even to the point of touch...

<image-desc>Ornate initial S depicting a face or figure within its loop, with foliage.</image-desc>In the previous commentary, Eustathius—my son, dearer and more beloved to me than light itself—our discussion had proceeded as far as the course of the star-bearing sphere <note>The 'stellifera sphæra' refers to the highest heaven containing the fixed stars.</note> and the seven spheres situated beneath it; now, let us deliberate upon their musical melody. *What is this sound,* I ask, *that fills my ears, a song so sweet?* <note>Macrobius is quoting the character Scipio the Younger from Cicero's 'Dream of Scipio'.</note> *This is that sound,* he replied, *which, though separated by unequal intervals, is nevertheless divided by a reasoned proportion; it is produced by the impulse and motion of the spheres themselves, and by tempering high pitches with low, it creates various harmonies equally. For such great movements cannot be stirred in silence, and nature dictates that the extremes sound low on one side and high on the other. For this reason, that highest star-bearing course of heaven, whose revolution is more rapid, moves with a sharp, high-pitched sound; whereas this lunar and lowest course moves with the deepest sound. <page-num>113</page-num>
<header>BOOK II.</header>

## BOOK II.

The sounds of hammers, responding to one another in a certain fixed order, suddenly struck his ears. In these sounds, the low pitches harmonized with the high ones in such a way that each returned to the listener's sense with a steady proportion, and from the various strikes, a single unified consonance was born. Thinking that an opportunity was here offered to him to grasp with his eyes and hands what he had long sought in his thoughts, he approached the blacksmiths. Hovering over the work, he gazed quite curiously, noting the sounds that were produced from the muscles <note>original: "lacertis" - literally the upper arms or strength of the smiths</note> of each man. Since he thought the sounds should be attributed to the strength of the men, he ordered them to swap hammers with one another. When these were swapped, the diversity of sounds left the men and followed the hammers. Then he turned his entire attention to examining the weights of those hammers. And when he had noted for himself the difference in weight held in each, he ordered other hammers to be made exceeding those weights by more or less; but from the strikes of these, the sounds heard were by no means similar to the previous ones, nor were they so harmonious with one another. Then he realized that the concord of the voice <note>musical pitch</note> arises from the law of weights. Having collected the numbers in which the harmonious diversity of weights was contained, he turned his examination from hammers to strings. He stretched the intestines of sheep or the sinews of oxen by binding them with various weights, just as he had learned existed in the hammers. From these, such a harmony resulted as his previous observation, not noticed in vain, had promised—with an added sweetness which the resonant nature of strings provided. Here Pythagoras, having gained possession of so great a secret, discovered the numbers from which harmonious sounds are born. Thus, with strings arranged under this observation of numbers, some were stretched in concord with certain numbers and others with others, so that when one was struck with a plectrum <note>a small tool used to pluck strings, like a guitar pick</note>, another string—though placed far away, yet agreeing in its numbers—would sound at the same time. However, out of the entire innumerable variety of numbers, only a few...

<page-num>114</page-num>

<margin>Six numbers are found to be fit for creating music.</margin> Few and countable numbers have been found which are suitable among themselves for the creation of music. These are six in total: the <term>epitritus</term> <note>original: "epitritus"; a ratio of 4:3</note>, the <term>hemiolius</term> <note>original: "hemiolius"; a ratio of 3:2</note>, the double, the triple, the quadruple, and the <term>epogdous</term> <note>original: "epogdous"; a ratio of 9:8</note>.

<margin>Epitritus.</margin> The **epitritus** occurs when, of two numbers, the larger contains the whole of the smaller plus a third part of it: such as four to three. For in four there is three, plus the third part of three, which is one. This number is called the epitritus; from it is born the <term>symphony</term> <note>In this context, a "symphony" refers to a consonant musical interval.</note> which is called the **fourth** <note>original: "διὰ τεσσάρων" (dia tessarōn)</note>.

<margin>Hemiolius.</margin> The **hemiolius** occurs when, of two numbers, the larger contains the whole of the smaller plus its half: such as three to two. For in three there is two, plus their middle part, which is one. From this number, which is called the hemiolius, is born the symphony called the **fifth** <note>original: "διὰ πέντε" (dia pente)</note>.

<margin>Double.</margin> The **double** number occurs when, of two numbers, the smaller is counted twice within the larger: such as four to two. From this double number is born the symphony whose name is the **octave** <note>original: "διὰ πασῶν" (dia pasōn), literally "through all [notes]"</note>.

<margin>Triple.</margin> The **triple**, however, occurs when, of two numbers, the smaller is counted three times within the larger: such as three to one. From this number proceeds the symphony which is called the **octave plus a fifth** <note>original: "διὰ πασῶν, καὶ διὰ πέντε" (dia pasōn, kai dia pente)</note>.

<margin>Quadruple.</margin> The **quadruple** occurs when, of two numbers, the smaller is counted four times within the larger: such as four to one. This <margin>*in numbers.</margin> number creates the symphony which they call the **double octave** <note>original: "διὰ ὀκτὼ" (dia oktō), though usually referred to as the "disdiapason"</note>.

<margin>Epogdous.</margin> The **epogdous** is the number which contains within itself the smaller number plus its eighth part: such as nine and eight. Because in nine there is eight, plus their eighth part, which is one. This number gives birth to the sound which musicians have called a **tone**.

<margin>*semitone <note>original: "ἡμιτόνιον" (hēmitonion)</note></margin> Indeed, the ancients wished to call a sound smaller than a tone a **semitone**. But this is not to be understood as if it were thought to be exactly half a tone. For we do not even accept a "semivowel" in letters as being exactly half of a vowel. Furthermore, a tone, by its very nature, [cannot] be divided into two [equal parts]...

It has been discovered that this semitone differs from a full tone by the same distance that these two numbers differ from one another: that is, two hundred forty-three and two hundred fifty-six <note>The Pythagorean limma ratio of 256:243</note>. The ancient Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras who believed the universe was governed by numbers</note> used to call this semitone a *diesis* <note>original: "diefin"</note>; but later usage established that the name *diesis* should refer to a sound even smaller than a semitone. There are, therefore, five symphonies <note>consonant intervals</note>: that is, <margin>Five symphonies.</margin> the fourth <note>original: "διὰ τετράχορδον" (diatessaron)</note>, the fifth <note>original: "διὰ πέντε" (diapente)</note>, the octave <note>original: "διὰ πασῶν" (diapason)</note>, and the octave-plus-fifth <note>original: "διὰ πασῶν καὶ διὰ πέντε"</note>. The symphony of the fourth consists of two tones and a semitone—leaving aside the tiny fractions found in the addition so as not to create difficulty—and it arises from the *epitrite* ratio <note>The ratio 4:3</note>. The fifth consists of three tones and a semitone, and it arises from the *hemiolic* ratio <note>The ratio 3:2</note>. The octave consists of six tones and arises from the double ratio <note>The ratio 2:1</note>. But the octave-plus-fifth consists of nine tones and a semitone, and it arises from the triple ratio <note>The ratio 3:1</note>. The double octave contains twelve tones and arises from the quadruple ratio <note>The ratio 4:1</note>.

If the meaning of that work is applied to this present book, it will greatly assist us in understanding the words of Cicero, which seem obscure regarding the discipline of music. But lest that which is brought in to support another explanation be believed difficult in itself, we must first set forth a few points which may make the understanding of both clearer at once. Every solid body is extended in three dimensions: for it possesses length, width, and depth. A fourth dimension cannot be found in any body; rather, every solid body is contained within these three. Geometers, however, propose other bodies for themselves which they call **mathematical**, to be subjected only to thought, not to the senses. For they say a **point** is an indivisible body in which neither length, width, nor height can be detected, since it cannot be divided into any parts. This point, when drawn out, creates a **line**, which is a body of one dimension. For it is long without being wide or high, and it is contained by two points at each end, limiting only its length. If you double this line, you will create another mathematical body which is built of two dimensions, length and width, but lacks height. And this is what is called a **surface** <note>original: "superficies"</note> among them; it is contained by four points, that is, two for each line. If, however, these two lines are doubled so that two are placed above two below, depth is added, and from this a **solid body** is created. This will undoubtedly be contained by eight angles, as we see in a die, which is called by the Greek name *kybos* <note>original: "κύβος," meaning a cube</note>. To these geometric principles, the nature of numbers is applied. And the **monad** <note>original: "μονὰς," the number one or unity</note> is considered a point; because just as a point is not a body, but from itself creates...

# BOOK II.

Just as the unit <note>original: "monas"; the monad or the number one</note> creates bodies, so it is not called a number itself, but the origin of numbers. For the first number is found in two, which is similar to a line produced from a point under the double termination of that point. This number, two, when doubled, produces four from itself: in the likeness of a mathematical body, which is stretched out in length and breadth under four points. The number four itself, when doubled, produces eight: a number which imitates a solid body. Just as we said two lines placed upon two others create the complete solidity of a body through the dimension of eight angles. And this is what is said among the Geometers: "twice two, twice" <note>2 x 2 x 2</note> is already a solid body. Therefore, by an increase from an even number up to eight, there is the solidity of a body. For this reason, among the first principles, he assigned fullness to this number.

Now it is necessary to look at how this is achieved from an odd number as well. And because the unit is the origin of both even and odd numbers, the number three <note>original: "ternarius"</note> is believed to be the first line. This, when tripled, makes the number nine, which itself—as if from two lines—produces a body of length and breadth. Likewise, nine tripled provides the third dimension, and thus from the side of the odd number, a solid body is created in twenty-seven (which is "thrice three, thrice"), just as in the even number "twice two, twice" (which is eight) created solidity.

Therefore, to create a solid body on both sides, the unit is necessary, along with six other numbers—that is, three each from the even and the odd. From the even: two, four, eight; from the odd: three, nine, twenty-seven. Therefore, Timaeus <note>The speaker in Plato's dialogue of the same name</note> in Plato's work, when announcing the counsel of the divinity in the fabrication of the World Soul <note>original: "mundi anima"</note>, says that it was woven together through these numbers, which produce a cube (that is, the perfection of solidity) from both the even and the odd. This was not because he meant to signify that the soul had anything corporeal about it, but so that it might be able to penetrate the entirety of the universe by giving it life.

# ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

The fables of Orpheus and Amphion <note>Orpheus and Amphion were legendary Greek musicians; Orpheus was said to charm animals, while Amphion's music moved stones to build the walls of Thebes.</note>—one of whom was said to draw animals lacking reason, and the other even stones, by their songs—took their origin from this: because they were perhaps the first to draw together, through singing, either barbarian nations living without the cultivation of reason, or those as unmoving as stone and lacking all emotion, toward a sense of pleasure. And is it any wonder if music holds such dominion among men, when even birds—such as the nightingale and swans, and others of that kind—practice singing as if it were a disciplined art? Indeed, some creatures, whether birds or beasts of the land or water, run of their own accord into nets when invited by song; and the shepherd's pipe commands quiet to the flocks as they go out to pasture. Nor is this surprising. For we have stated previously that the causes of music are inherent in the World-Soul, with which it is interwoven. Moreover, the World-Soul itself provides life to all living things. <margin>*Aeneid*, Book 6</margin> *Hence comes the race of men and cattle, and the lives of flying things, and the monsters that the sea bears beneath its marble-like surface.* <note>original: "Hinc hominum, pecudumq; genus, uitaeq; uolantum, Et quæ marmoreo fert monstra sub æquore pontus."</note> Rightly, therefore, is every living thing captured by music, because the celestial soul, by which the universe is animated, took its origin from music. ...he thought that the distance from the Earth's surface to the Moon, from the Moon to Mercury, from Mercury to Venus, from Venus to the Sun, from the Sun to Mars, from Mars to Jupiter, and from Jupiter to Saturn followed a specific measure. He even believed he had measured the entire space from the orbit of Saturn up to the star-bearing heaven itself by calculation. However, this dimension proposed by Archimedes <note>Archimedes of Syracuse (c. 287–212 BC), though famous for engineering, also calculated the distances of the planets.</note> was rejected by the Platonists, as it did not preserve the double and triple intervals. They established that it should be believed that the distance from the Earth to the Moon is doubled from the Earth to the Sun; and as much as it is from the Earth to the Sun, it is tripled from the Earth to Venus; and as much as it is from the Earth to Venus, it is four times as much from the Earth to the star of Mercury; and as much as it is to Mercury from the Earth, it is nine times as much from the Earth to Mars; and as much as it is from the Earth to Mars, it is eight times as much from the Earth to Jupiter; and as much as it is from the Earth to Jupiter, it is twenty-seven times as much from the Earth to the orbit of Saturn. 

Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) who wrote commentaries on Plato's Timaeus.</note> included this Platonic persuasion in his books, in which he shed some light on the obscurities of the *Timaeus*. He noted that they believe these intervals exist in the body of the world according to the image of the soul's composition, which are filled by <term>epitrites</term> <note>A ratio of 4:3, known in music as a perfect fourth.</note>, <term>hemiolias</term> <note>A ratio of 3:2, known as a perfect fifth.</note>, <term>epogdoons</term> <note>A ratio of 9:8, a whole tone.</note>, <term>semitones</term>, and the <term>limma</term> <note>A small interval or "remainder" in the Pythagorean scale.</note>; and thus a harmony is produced. The logic of this, woven into the substance of the soul, is also inserted into the mundane body which is moved by the soul. Hence, the assertion of Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC); this likely refers to his "Dream of Scipio," which discusses the music of the spheres.</note> is learned and perfect in every respect: he says that the celestial sound is divided by unequal intervals, which are nonetheless <margin>nevertheless</margin> distinguished by a proportional logic.

How it happens that among the sounds of that celestial harmony, one is higher in pitch and another lower. What kind of melody is there, and why that sound is not heard by us.

nature dictates that the extremes on one side sound deep, while on the other side they sound sharp. For this reason, that highest, star-bearing circuit of heaven, whose revolution is more rapid, moves with a sharp, high-pitched sound; whereas this lunar and lowest sphere moves with the deepest tone. We have said that sound is never produced unless the air is struck. However, the blow itself determines whether the sound is brought forth as higher or lower: when it falls with great force and speed, it produces a sharp sound; if it is slower or <margin>or more gentle</margin> *more sluggish*, it produces a deeper one. An example is a rod striking the air: if it hits with a quick impulse, it sharpens the sound; if with a slower one, it strikes the ear with a deeper tone. We see the same in stringed instruments: if the strings are stretched with tighter tension, they sound sharp; if looser, they sound deeper. Therefore, the higher spheres—while they are turned with greater force according to their vast size, and while they are stretched by a spirit <note>The Latin 'spiritus' here refers to a vital breath or cosmic force that moves the celestial bodies.</note> that is stronger in its own <margin>or origin</margin> *region*—move with a sharp, high-pitched sound because of that very "more rapid revolution," as he calls it. But this lunar and lowest sphere moves with the deepest tone, because it is now turned by a spirit that grows faint at the extremity, and because of the narrowness by which the second-to-last sphere is confined, it is turned with a gentler force. We prove this likewise in flutes <term>tibijs: ancient reed instruments similar to an oboe or clarinet</term>, from whose holes near the mouth of the player a sharp sound is emitted, but from those far away and near the end, a deeper sound. Likewise, a sharper sound comes through wider holes, and a deeper one through narrow ones. The reasoning for both cases is the same: because the breath is stronger where it begins, and more failing where it ends. And because it drives a greater force through a larger hole, whereas the opposite happens in a narrower one and those placed far off; therefore, the highest sphere—both as it lies open to an immense extent and as it is urged on by a spirit that is stronger the closer it is to its origin—emits from itself a sharpness of sounds. The voice of the last sphere is now broken by the shortness of its space and by its distance. From this it is also more clearly proven that the spirit, as much as it recedes downward from its origin...

## ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

I do not think there is any limit to <note>original: "opinio"</note> opinion. However, one must pursue those matters by which the words you have undertaken to explain may become clear. For in a matter that is naturally obscure, he who pours out more words than necessary in explaining it only adds darkness and does not remove the density. Therefore, we shall make an end to this part of the treatise <margin>What kind of melody exists in the celestial bodies.</margin> by adding one thing we think worthy of knowing: Since there are three genera of musical melodies—the enharmonic, the diatonic, and the chromatic—the first has fallen out of use because of its excessive difficulty; the third is indeed infamous for its softness; hence the middle one, that is, the diatonic, is ascribed to the music of the world <note>The "music of the spheres" or the cosmic harmony.</note> by the teaching of Plato. Nor shall we place this among the things to be passed over: that although music is born from the perpetual revolution of the sky, we do not perceive it with a clear sense of hearing <margin>Why we do not perceive the harmony of heaven.</margin> because the sound is greater than can be received by the narrowness of human ears. For if the cataracts <note>original: "χάταδππα" (katadoupa). The author refers to the famous waterfalls of the Nile.</note> of the Nile shut out the magnitude of their crashing from the ears of the inhabitants, what wonder is it if the sound emitted by the impulse of the world's massive bulk exceeds our hearing? For it is not for nothing that he says: *What is this sound, so great and so sweet, that fills my ears?* Rather, he wished it to be understood that if the ears of one who feared to be present at celestial secrets were filled by the magnitude of the sound, it follows that the senses of other men cannot grasp the hearing of the worldly harmony. But now let us bring the treatise to the following matters.

The middle part of the Earth in which we exist is divided into five zones; and of these, only two are habitable, one of which is inhabited by us, while it is unknown what men dwell in the other; then, indeed, in the remaining half of the Earth there are the same zones, and among those, two are likewise inhabited by men.

<note>The following section is the commentary by Macrobius on the preceding passage.</note>
After the discourse of Tully <note>Cicero</note>—having been led through necessary matters fit for the present work—described the heavens which contain all things, the order and motion of the spheres placed beneath, the sound of celestial music unfolding its measures and numbers from that motion, and the air subject to the moon, it has now descended to the Earth. He has completed the description of the Earth itself, being sparing in words but fertile in facts. For by naming the "spots" of habitation, and among the inhabitants themselves some as interrupted and turned away, others as oblique and transverse, he has painted the sphericity of the terrestrial globe with words alone, not with colors. This also is not without the perfection of learning: that he does not allow us to err with others who believed the Earth was encircled by only one Ocean. For if he had said: "All the earth is a certain small island, surrounded by that sea," he would have given us to understand a single circuit of the Ocean. But by adding, "Which is inhabited by you," <note>original: *Quæ colitur à uobis*</note> he indicates the true division of that sea, about which we shall discuss a little later...

<margin>Concerning the five zones or circles of the Earth.</margin>
The Earth is the ninth and final sphere. It is divided by the horizon—that is, the "final circle," which we mentioned before. Therefore, the half in which we dwell is under that part of the sky which is above the Earth, and the remaining half is under that part which, as it revolves, descends to those places which seem lower to us. For being located in the middle, the Earth looks up at the sky from every part of itself. Therefore, its smallness in relation to the sky—

which is but a point—but its immense globosity in relation to us, is distinguished by regions pressed upon by turns by an excess of either cold or heat, with a twin temperament <note>the temperate zones</note> born between these diverse extremes. For both the northern and southern extremities are stiffened by perpetual frost. And these are like two belts with which the Earth is encircled, but short in circumference, as if girding the extremities. Both of these are impatient of habitation, because that glacial numbness provides life neither to animal nor to fruit. For the body is nourished by the same air that feeds the vegetation. The middle belt, and therefore the largest, is scorched by the eternal breath of continuous heat; the space which it occupies, both in its wide circuit and its great length, is rendered uninhabitable for living things by the excess of fervor. Finally, of the four quarters of our habitation, the East, the West, and the North are called by their own names because they have been known to us from our very beginnings. For even if the northern extremity is uninhabitable, it is nonetheless not far removed from us. But for the fourth quarter of our habitation, a specific cause gave it a different name, so that it was called <term>Midday</term><note>original: Meridies</note> rather than "Southern." This is because the "Southern" region properly belongs to that which proceeds from the other extremity, opposite the North; whereas this region is rightly called "Midday" because of the place where the day begins for us. For since the day begins to be felt from the middle of the Earth where the use of daylight exists, it was named *Meridies* as if it were a "Middle-day" <note>original: Medidies</note>, with only one letter changed.

# BOOK II.

<header>BOOK II.</header>

<margin>Why the South Wind <note>original: "Auster"</note> reaches us warm, even though it is cold at its origin.</margin>
is named. It must be understood, however, that the wind which reaches us from this pole—that is, the South Wind—is so icy at its origin that the North Wind <note>original: "Septentrio"</note>, which we find so commendably brisk, is comparable to it. But because it travels to us through the flame of the Torrid Zone <note>the equatorial region believed by ancients to be a belt of fire</note>, it becomes heated by the admixture of fire; thus, what begins as cold arrives as heat. For neither reason nor nature would allow that two poles, pressed by an equal intensity of cold, should emit currents of a dissimilar nature. There is no doubt that our North Wind also reaches those who live adjacent to the southern regions as a warm wind for the same reason, and that the South Wind soothes their bodies with the twin chill of its own breeze.

<margin>That the part of the Earth which is beneath our feet is also inhabited, and is divided just as ours is.</margin>
The same reasoning does not permit us to doubt that across that surface of the Earth which is considered "below" us, the entire circuit of the zones which are temperate here is maintained as temperate by the same path. Therefore, in that region as well, those same two zones, separated from one another, are similarly inhabited. Or let anyone who prefers to oppose this belief say what prevents such a distinction. For if we have the faculty of living in this part of the world which we inhabit—because, treading upon the ground, we look up at the sky above our heads; because the Sun both rises and sets for us; because we enjoy the surrounding air, the breath of which we inhale—why should we not believe that people live there as well, where the same things are always available? For those who are said to dwell there must be believed to breathe the same air, because the temperature is the same in the continuation of that same zonal circuit. The same Sun will be said to set for them at our sunrise, and it will rise when it sets for us. They will tread the ground just as we do, and will always see the sky above their heads. Nor should there be any fear that they might fall from the Earth into the sky, since nothing can ever fall upward. Furthermore, he depicted the inhabitants of the four habitations both by the relation of their site and by the very quality of their standing position. ### CHAPTER VI.
It remains for us to report on the dimensions of the Earth itself—how much has been granted for habitation and how much is uncultivated: that is, what the measurement of each individual zone <note>original: "cingulorum," literally "belts" or "girdles"</note> is. So that you may easily distinguish this, you must return to the description of the Earth's globe which we set down a little earlier: so that through the marks of the letters assigned to it, the logic of the dimensions may be more clearly explained. The entire globe of the Earth—that is, the circle which encloses the universal circumference, to which the letters A, B, C, and D are assigned—has been divided into sixty parts by those who have measured with reason. Moreover, that entire circumference contains two hundred and fifty-two thousand stadia <note>A stadium was an ancient unit of distance, roughly 185 meters; 252,000 stadia was the standard Eratosthenic calculation for Earth's circumference</note>. Therefore, each individual sixtieth part extends for four thousand two hundred stadia. And without doubt, half of it—which goes from D, through the East (that is, through A), all the way to C—contains thirty sixtieths, and one hundred and twenty-six thousand stadia. Truly, a fourth part—which is from A to C, beginning from the middle of the scorched zone <note>original: "perusta," referring to the Torrid Zone at the equator</note>—contains fifteen sixtieths, and sixty-three thousand stadia. Once the measurement of this fourth part is established, the full dimension of the entire circumference will be clear.

From A, therefore, to P—which is half of the scorched zone—it contains four sixtieths: which make sixteen thousand stadia, with the addition of eight hundred. Therefore, the entire scorched zone consists of eight sixtieths, and holds thirty-three thousand stadia, and six hundred besides. Furthermore, the width of our zone, which is temperate <note>original: "temperatus"</note>—that is, from P to O—contains five sixtieths, which make twenty-one thousand stadia. And the space of the frozen zone <note>original: "frigida"</note> from O to C contains six sixtieths, which hold twenty-five thousand two hundred stadia. From this fourth part of the world, the measurement of which is evidently...
