### That the same zones which are in the Earth exist also in the Heavens; and that the cause of this diversity is the Sun, which just as it causes heat by its approach, so it induces cold by its departure. CHAPTER VII. ###

Now that this previous discussion has reached its proper conclusion, let us now bring forward that which we promised to prove: that Virgil <note>original: "Maronem" referring to Publius Vergilius Maro</note> rightly assigned these belts <note>term: belts (cingulos) - used here interchangeably with "zones" to describe the latitudinal bands of the globe</note> to the heavens, and Cicero rightly assigned them to the earth; and that both said the same thing, not in disagreement, but in harmony. For the nature of the heavens has distinguished this balance or excess of temperature in different parts of the earth; and the quality of either cold or heat, which has once attached itself to any part of the ether <note>term: ether (ætheris) - the ancient term for the upper atmosphere or the substance of the celestial spheres</note>, infects that same part of the earth which it looks down upon as it circles around. And because they have called these diversities, which are bounded by certain limits, "zones" in the heavens, it is necessary that the same number of zones be understood here on earth as well. Just as in a very small mirror, when a large face is shown, the limbs or features maintain in that narrow space the same order which their own magnitude had arranged in the reality.

But here also we shall lessen the labor of asserting what is said by placing a picture before your eyes. For let the sphere of heaven be **A, B, C, D**. And let it enclose within itself the sphere of the earth, to which are assigned **S, X, T, V**. And let there be drawn in the sphere of heaven a northern circle from **I** to **O**. The summer tropic <note>original: "tropicus aestivus" - the Tropic of Cancer</note> from **G** to **P**. And the equinoctial <note>the Celestial Equator</note> from **B** to **A**. And the winter tropic <note>original: "tropicus hyemalis" - the Tropic of Capricorn</note> from **F** to **Q**. And the southern circle from **E** to **R**. Furthermore, let the zodiac be drawn from **F** to **P**. Again, in the sphere of the earth, let those same boundaries of the zones be drawn which we described above at **N, M, L, K**.

With these things thus depicted, it will be established without difficulty that the individual parts of the earth have borrowed their quality regarding excess or balance from the individual parts of heaven placed above their summit. For that which is above from **D** to **R**, looks down upon the earth from **S** to **K**. And that which is in the heavens from **R** to **Q**, infects that part of the earth...

Conversely, when it comes to the mark F, that is, to Capricorn, it creates winter for us by its withdrawal, and brings back summer to them by its proximity. Then, regarding the cardinal points <note>original: "cardinibus," referring here to the four directions or "hinges" of the world</note> through which the Sun enters any building, it never enters from the fourth. For a window receives the Sun from both the East and the West, since it looks out upon him as he rises and as he sets. It also receives him from the South, because the Sun's entire path lies in our Southern sky, as the previously presented diagram has shown. However, a Northern window never admits the Sun, because the Sun never approaches from point P to point O; instead, by always receding from P, he never reaches the boundaries of the North Pole. And for that reason, the Sun's ray is never poured in through this cardinal direction.

The shadow of any body also suffices to provide proof of this same matter. For the shadow falls toward the West when the Sun is rising, and toward the East when he is setting. At midday, however, because the Sun holds the South, the shadow is driven toward the North. But in our inhabited region, it is impossible for the shadow of any body to fall toward the South, because a shadow is always cast in the direction opposite to the Sun. Now, the Sun cannot be opposite to the South for us, since he never reaches the Northern boundaries. 

To be sure, since that scorched part <note>The "Torrid Zone" near the equator, which ancient geographers often thought was too hot for life, though the author notes here that the temperate edges are inhabited</note> which is near the temperate zone allows for inhabitants there—that is, beyond the tropic—whatever spaces are inhabited there cast a shadow toward the South at that time when the Sun holds the sign of Cancer <note>The Summer Solstice</note>. For then the Sun becomes Northern to them when he holds that tropic, because he has moved to the North of them. 

Furthermore, the city of Syene <note>Modern Aswan, Egypt</note>, which is the beginning of the province of Thebaid after the deserts of the upper mountains, is situated directly under the summer tropic itself. And on that day when the Sun enters a specific part of Cancer, at the sixth hour of the day <note>Noon</note>, because the Sun is then found directly over the very summit of the city, no shadow can be cast upon the ground there from any body. Even the pointer of the hemisphere that shows the hours, which they call a <term>gnomon</term> <note>original Greek: γνάμωνα; the vertical rod of a sundial</note>, cannot then create a shadow from itself. And this is what Lucan <note>The Roman poet Marcus Annaeus Lucanus</note> refers to:

Lucan <note>original: "canus" likely referring to Marcus Annaeus Lucanus</note> wished to speak of this, yet he did not, as it is held, explain it fully. For by saying:
<margin>a. Pharsalia <note>Referring to Lucan's epic poem on the Roman Civil War.</note></margin> —*And at Syene, which turns the shadows nowhere,*—
he indeed touched upon the matter, but he disturbed the truth. For it is not that it *never* turns the shadows, but only at one specific time, which we have reported according to its proper reasoning. Having related these things, it is established that the sun never exits the boundaries of the scorched zone: because the zodiac is slanted from tropic to tropic. The cause is therefore manifest why this zone is always subject to flames: namely, because the sun—the source and administrator of all ethereal flame—never leaves it. Therefore, both the furthest parts, that is, the northern and the southern, to which the heat of the sun never approaches, are necessarily oppressed by perpetual frost. Two zones, however (as we have said), are tempered on this side and that by the proximity of heat and cold. Finally, in this very zone which we inhabit, which is called entirely "temperate," those parts which are neighbors to the scorched belt are nevertheless hotter than the rest: such as Ethiopia, Arabia, Egypt, and Libya. In these places, the heat so thins the body of the surrounding air that it is either never, or only rarely, forced into clouds; and for that reason, there is almost no use for rain among them. Conversely, those regions which approach closer to the boundaries of the cold zone—such as the Maeotian marshes <note>The Sea of Azov</note>, the regions through which the Tanais <note>The Don River</note> and the Ister <note>The Danube River</note> flow, and all the places beyond Scythia, whose inhabitants antiquity called the Hyperboreans <note>Literally "those beyond the North Wind"</note>, as if by receding inward they had passed the origin of Boreas <note>The North Wind</note>—are oppressed by such nearly eternal frost that it is not easily explained how great the injury of excessive cold is there. However, the places which are in the middle of the temperate zone, since they recede far from both extremes, maintain a true and healthy temperature.

# BOOK II.

The subject now reminds us—since we have stated a fact that no one can refute, namely that each tropic <note>The Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn</note> forms the boundaries around the zodiac, and that the sun can never exceed either tropic by moving further upward or downward—that we should investigate the regions beyond the zodiac, that is, beyond the scorched zone <note>The torrid zone or 'perusta'</note> which is enclosed by the tropics, where the temperate zones <margin>begin</margin> take their place. We must ask what Virgil meant—a man never clouded by error in any branch of learning—when he wrote:

->Two zones are granted to weary mortals<- <margin>Georgics, Book 1</margin>
->By the gift of the gods, and a path is cut between them,<-
->Where the slanted order of the signs <note>The Zodiac</note> might turn itself.<-

For he seems to say in these verses that the zodiac is drawn through the temperate zones, and that the sun's course is carried through them; yet it is not right to even imagine this, because the sun's course never exceeds either tropic. 

Should we therefore consider what we mentioned before: that there are inhabitants within the tropics, in that scorched part which is neighboring the temperate zone? For Syene <note>Modern Aswan, Egypt</note> is directly under the tropic itself, while Meroë <note>An ancient city on the east bank of the Nile</note> recedes three thousand eight hundred stadia <note>A Greek unit of distance, roughly 600 feet</note> inward into the scorched zone from Syene. From there all the way to the land fertile with cinnamon, there are eight hundred stadia; and through all these spaces of the scorched zone, inhabitants enjoy life, though they are few. Beyond that, however, it is truly inaccessible because of the excessive heat of the Sun. 

Since, therefore, so much space within the scorched zone provides for life, it cannot be denied that there is an equal amount of space and equal mildness within the borders of the scorched zone near the neighboring temperate zone of the opposite side—that is, the land of the <term>Antoeci</term> <note>Those who live in the same longitude but opposite latitude</note>. For all things are equal on both sides. Therefore, we must believe that through the "poetic trumpet"—which always extols everything to a greater degree—he said the path of the Sun was cut through the temperate zones because, on both sides, the borders of the scorched zone are similar to the temperate ones in that they allow themselves to be inhabited. Or perhaps, by poetic license, he used a small part to represent a similar...

placed almost a similar particle <note>original: "particula"; referring here to a grammatical preposition or small part of speech</note>: and instead of "under both," did he prefer to say "through both"? For in truth, the path of the Zodiac <note>original: "ductus zodiaci"</note> reaches to and fro under both temperate zones; yet it does not go *through* both. <margin>Maro <note>Virgil</note> often borrowed such particles.</margin>

For the starry serpent <note>The constellation Draco</note> does not actually cut through the Bears: but while it both embraces them and comes between them, it revolves around them and between them, not through them. Therefore, our understanding can remain firm if we consider "through both" to be said for "between both," according to the custom of the poet himself; nothing else occurs to us for a defense beyond what we have said. Truly, since we have placed in the midst of our discussion those boundaries which the path of the Sun never exceeds—and it is manifest to all what Maro said, who is well known to be ignorant of error—it will be up to the ingenuity of individuals to find what more can be contributed toward resolving this question.

# BOOK II.

The crown <note>original: "corona"; referring to the Great Ocean</note> flows through the hot zone of the earth, encircling the upper and lower parts of the lands, imitating the curve of the equatorial circle. From the East, it pours back two gulfs: one toward the northern extremity, and another toward the southern. Likewise, from the West, two similar gulfs arise, which, having poured back toward both extremities mentioned above, meet those sent down from the East. When they are mixed with the greatest force and a more immense impact, and strike one another in turn, that famous ebb and flow <note>the tides</note> of the Ocean is born from that very collision of waters. And wherever the same occurs in our sea <note>the Mediterranean</note>, whether in narrow straits or perhaps on flat shores, it happens because of those very boundaries of the Ocean—which we now call the Ocean—because our sea flows inward from them. Furthermore, its truer channel (so to speak) occupies the scorched zone <note>the torrid zone at the equator</note>. And both the Ocean itself, which follows the equator, and the gulfs born from it, which imitate the horizon circle in the scope of their bending, divide the whole earth into four parts; and they make each individual habitation (as we said above) into islands. For flowing through the hot zone between us and the Southern people, and encircling the whole, and again surrounding the extremities of both regions with its borders, it creates two islands on the upper and two on the lower surface of the earth. Hence Cicero <note>original: "Tullius"; Marcus Tullius Cicero</note>, wishing this to be understood, did not say:
> All the earth is a certain small island; but rather, *All the earth which is inhabited by you is a certain small island*:

because each of the four habitations is made into a small island, with the Ocean surrounding them twice (as we have said).

The following diagram can place all these things before your eyes, from which you will see the origin of our sea (which is one part of the whole), and the source of the Red and Indian Seas, and you will find where the Caspian Sea originates—though I am not unaware that there are some who deny it an entry from the Ocean. Nor is there any doubt that into that [region] of the Southern race also...

### CHAPTER X.

**Furthermore**, even if the offspring of future men should desire to pass down to posterity the praises of each one of us received from their fathers: nevertheless, on account of the floods <note>original: "eluutiones"</note> and conflagrations <note>original: "exustiones" — referring to the ancient theory of periodic global destruction by water or fire</note> of the lands, which must happen at a certain time, we are able to attain not only no eternal glory, but not even a long-lasting one. The wise man places the fruit of virtue in his conscience; the less perfect man places it in glory. Hence, Scipio, desiring to instill perfection in his grandson, is the authority: that, content with the reward of conscience, he should not seek glory. In the seeking of which, since there are two greatest things that can be desired—that it should spread as widely as possible, and endure as long as possible—he has previously shown, by discussing the narrowness of our habitation, that only a very small particle of the whole earth (which holds the place of a point relative to the sky) is possessed by men of our race. How is the eternity of memory supported? Why, finally, has the experience of many things reached certain nations only in a recent age? For behold, the Gauls learned of the vine and the cultivation of the olive only when Rome was already growing up; yet other nations still remain ignorant of many things that have been discovered and found pleasing to us. All these things seem to contradict the eternity of the world, as they lead us to believe that each individual thing began gradually at a fixed beginning of the world. But *Philosophy* is the authority that the world has indeed always existed, with God as its founder, but not beginning from a point in time. Since time could not exist before the world, as nothing else creates time except the course of the Sun. Human affairs, however, for the most part often perish while the world remains, and rise up again, either by alternating floods or by recurring conflagrations <note>The author refers to the ancient theory of "Ekpyrosis" and "Kataklysmos"—periodic destruction by fire and water.</note>. The cause or necessity of this alternation is such: natural philosophers have taught that the ethereal fire is nourished by moisture. They assert that beneath the scorched zone of heaven, which the path of the sun—that is, the zodiac—occupies, the Ocean was placed by nature (as we described above), so that the entire breadth through which the Sun, along with the five wandering stars <note>The five planets known to the ancients: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> and the moon, runs back and forth, might have the sustenance of the moisture lying beneath it. And they wish this to be what Homer—the source and origin of all divine inventions—granted to be understood as truth by the wise under the cloud of a poetic fiction: that Jupiter, with the other Gods (that is, with the stars), set out for the Ocean, with the Ethiopians inviting him to a feast. <margin>Iliad, Book 1</margin> By this fabled image, they wish to show that Homer signified that nourishment for the stars is drawn from moisture; for this reason, he called the Ethiopians the kings who participate in the celestial feasts, because only the Ethiopians live around the shore of the Ocean, whom the proximity of the sun has scorched even to the appearance of a black color. Therefore, since heat is nourished by moisture, this alternation happens: that now heat, now moisture, overflows. For it happens that the fire, having been nourished to its greatest increase, overcomes the draught of moisture—

But soon, once the force of the heat is exhausted, strength gradually returns to the moisture; for when a great portion of the fire has been spent in the conflagrations, it consumes less of the reborn moisture. And so it happens that while the world remains, the cultivation of the lands—along with the human race—often perishes between the alternating excesses of heat and moisture; and, when a temperate balance is restored, it is renewed again. Yet, neither the deluge nor the conflagration ever entirely covers or completely burns up all lands or the entire human race. Certainly, in Egypt (as Plato confesses in the *Timaeus* <note>A reference to Plato's dialogue where an Egyptian priest explains to Solon that Egypt is protected from these disasters by the Nile</note>), an excess of moisture or heat has never caused harm. Whence it is that an infinite thousands of years are read of in the monuments and books of the Egyptians alone. Certain parts of the earth, therefore, surviving the slaughter, become a nursery for restoring the human race. And so it happens that men—not in a raw world, but themselves raw and ignorant of the culture whose memory the destruction intercepted—wander upon the lands. Gradually casting off the harshness of their wandering wildness, they allow for assemblies and gatherings as nature instructs them. Among them, there is at first a simplicity ignorant of evil and as yet inexperienced in craftiness, which provides the name of the "Golden Age" to those first centuries. Then, the more that practical use promotes the cultivation of things and arts, the more easily emulation creeps into their minds; which, beginning well at first, latently escapes into envy. And from this is born whatever the human race experiences in the centuries that follow. This, therefore, is the vicissitude <note>The natural change or succession of states</note> by which human affairs perish and return again while the world remains unharmed.

What does it matter if those who are born after you speak of you, when there was no mention of you by those born before—who were not only no fewer in number, but certainly better men? This is especially true since, among those very people by whom our name might be heard, no one can achieve a memory lasting even a single year. For men commonly measure the year only by the return of the sun, that is, of a single star. But in reality, when all the stars have returned to the same point from which they once set out, and have restored the same map of the whole sky after long intervals, then can that truly be called a "turning year" <note>The "Great Year" or Platonic Year, a cosmic cycle where all celestial bodies return to their original positions</note>; in which I hardly dare to say how many generations of men are contained. For just as the sun once seemed to fail and be extinguished for men when the soul of Romulus <note>The legendary founder of Rome</note> entered these very celestial temples, so when the sun fails again at the same part of the sky and at the same time, then—with all the constellations and stars recalled to the same starting point—consider a full year to have passed. Know that not even a twentieth part of this year has yet revolved.

<margin>The diversity of years.</margin>
He continues to do the same, persisting in his dissuasion of the desire for glory. Having shown above that glory is confined to narrow places, and even within those straits it is not eternal, he now teaches that it is not only devoid of perpetuity, but cannot even be extended to the limits of one full year. We shall explain the reasoning behind this assertion. A "year" is not only that which common usage now calls by that name; rather, the return of each light or star to the same place after measuring the entire circuit of the heaven is its own year. Thus a month is the year of the moon, within which it traverses the ambit of the sky. <note>original: "Interea magnum sol circuomuoluitur annum"</note>
Calling the sun's year "great" in comparison to the lunar year. For the courses of Venus and Mercury are nearly equal to the sun. But the year of Mars holds almost two years; for in that much time it circles the heavens. The star of Jupiter consumes twelve years, and Saturn thirty years in the same circuit. These things concerning the lights <note>the sun and moon</note> and the wandering stars <term>planets; from the Greek 'planetes' meaning wanderer</term>, as they are often reported, are already well known. But the year which is called "Worldly," which is truly the "turning year," because it is produced by the conversion of the full universe, is unfolded over the most extensive ages. The reasoning for it is such: All the stars and constellations which appear fixed in the sky—whose own motion human sight can never perceive or detect—nevertheless do move. And besides the revolving of the heaven by which they are always carried along, they also advance by their own approach <margin>*otherwise: they move forward</margin> so slowly that no man's life is long enough that, by continuous observation, he may detect a change made from the place in which he first saw them. Therefore, the end of the Worldly Year is when all the stars and all the constellations which the <term>aplanos; the fixed sphere of the stars</term> holds, have returned from a certain place to that same place, so that not even one star of heaven is in any other place than where it was; when all the others have moved from that place to which they returned, they have given an end to their year: so that the lights <note>sun and moon</note> along with the five wandering stars are in the same places and parts in which they were at the beginning of the Worldly Year. This, however, as the Natural Philosophers <note>original: "Physici"</note> maintain, happens after fifteen thousand years have passed. Therefore, just as the year of the moon is a month, and the year of the sun is twelve months, and the years of the other stars are those which we reported above: so fifteen thousand years, such as we now compute, make up the Worldly Year. That, therefore, is truly to be called the "turning year," which not only the sun...

They measure this not by the return of a single star <note>original: "unius astri"</note>, but by the return of all the stars in whatever part of the heavens they may be, concluding at the same place under the same description of the entire sky. For this reason, it is called the **World Year** <note>original: "mundanus dicitur"</note>, because the "world" is properly the name given to the heavens. Therefore, just as we call a solar year not only the period from the first of January <note>original: "Calendis Ianuarijs"</note> back to the same date, but also from the day following the first of January back to that same day—or indeed from any day of any month back to that same day—so too does each person establish the beginning of this World Year at whatever point they choose.

For example, Cicero has here established the beginning of the World Year for himself from the eclipse of the sun <note>original: "defectu solis"</note> which occurred toward the end of Romulus's life. And although solar eclipses have occurred very frequently since then, a repeated eclipse is not said to have completed the World Year. Rather, it will be fulfilled only when the sun, in eclipse, is itself in the same locations and degrees, and finds all the stars of the heaven and all the constellations back in the same positions where they were when it eclipsed at the end of Romulus's life.

Therefore, from the departure of Romulus, after fifteen thousand years (as the Natural Philosophers <note>original: "Physici"</note> assert), the sun will again eclipse in such a way that it is in the same sign and the same degree at the same starting point where it was under Romulus, with all the stars and signs having been recalled to their places.

For at the time when Scipio was campaigning in Africa, five hundred and seventy-three years had passed since the death of Romulus. In the six hundred and seventh year from the founding of the city <note>term: "ab urbe condita" (AUC) - the traditional Roman system for dating years from the founding of Rome</note>, this Scipio triumphed after the destruction of Carthage. From this number, if we remove the thirty-two years of Romulus's reign and the two years that passed between the dream and the end of the war, five hundred and seventy-three years remain from the death of Romulus until the time of the dream. Therefore, he [Cicero] noted reasonably and truly that not even a twentieth part of the World Year had yet turned. For that which flows from other bodies departs from them; but the flow of the elements never departs from the elements themselves. Therefore, in this world, no part is mortal according to the assertions of true reason. ## On the three modes of reasoning by which the Platonists asserted the immortality of the soul.

### CHAPTER XIII.

For that which is always in motion is eternal; but that which communicates motion to something else, and which is itself moved from elsewhere, must necessarily have an end of living when it has an end of motion. Therefore, only that which moves itself, because it is never deserted by itself, never indeed ceases to be moved; furthermore, for all other things that are moved, this is the source, this is the principle <term>principium: the fundamental origin or starting point</term> of moving. Moreover, there is no origin for a principle. For all things arise from a principle, but the principle itself cannot be born from any other thing. For it would not be a principle if it were produced from elsewhere. And if it never arises, it certainly never dies. For if a principle were extinguished, it would neither be reborn from another, nor would it create anything else from itself; clearly, it is necessary for all things to arise from a principle. Thus it happens that the principle of motion comes from that which is moved by itself. This, moreover, can neither be born nor die; otherwise, the whole heaven would collapse and all nature would necessarily stand still, nor is any force born by which it might be moved after being driven by a first impulse. Since it is clear, therefore, that what moves itself is eternal, who is there who would deny that this nature has been granted to souls? For everything that is driven by an external impulse is inanimate; but that which is <insert>a living being</insert> <margin>animal</margin> is moved by an interior and its own motion. For this is the proper nature and power of the soul; which, if it is the only one among all things that moves itself, it certainly was not born, and is eternal. This entire passage was translated word-for-word by Cicero from Plato's *Phaedo* <note>original: "de Phædone Platonis"; actually a famous passage from Plato's *Phaedrus* 245c, though often associated with the soul-doctrines in the *Phaedo*</note>, in which the immortality of the soul is asserted with the strongest arguments. And this is the summary of the arguments: that the soul is [free] from death...

These things having been premised, it is now necessary to reveal the <term>syllogisms</term> <note>A form of logical reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two assumed premises</note> by which the various followers of Plato reason concerning the immortality of the soul.

<margin>The reasonings of the Platonists concerning the immortality of the soul.</margin>For there are those who, through steps of syllogisms, arrive at a single end of proof, making for themselves a certain proposition for the following step from the conclusion of the preceding one; among whom this first one is: The soul is moved by itself; whatever is moved by itself is always moved. Therefore, the soul is always moved. The second syllogism follows, which is born from the end of the first: The soul is always moved; whatever is always moved is immortal. Therefore, the soul is immortal. And so, in two syllogisms, two things are proved: namely, that the soul is always moved (as in the first) and that it is immortal (as is gathered from the second). Others, however, proceed in their arguing up to a third step, as follows: The soul is moved by itself; that which is moved by itself is the principle <note>The "principle" or "source" (Latin: *principium*)</note> of motion. Therefore, the soul is the principle of motion. Again, from this conclusion a proposition is born: The soul is the principle of motion; that which is the principle of motion is not born <note>Meaning it has no beginning in time and was not created from something else</note>. Therefore, the soul is not born. In the third place: The soul is not born; that which is not born is immortal. Therefore, the soul is immortal. Others, indeed, [place] their entire reasoning in one...

### By what reasons Aristotle wished to show, against Plato, that the soul cannot be moved by itself.

->CHAPTER XIV.<-

<margin>Aristotle against Plato</margin>
But of all these reasonings, the final conclusion regarding the immortality of the soul can only stand for one who does not refute the first proposition—that is, that the soul moves of itself. For if this is not accepted in faith, all things that follow become weak. Indeed, the assent of the Stoics <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy that held the soul to be a physical, self-moving breath or 'pneuma'.</note> happens to fall in line with this. Aristotle, however, so far from acquiescing, endeavors to assert not only that the soul is not moved by itself, but that it is not moved at all. For he constructs his clever arguments to show that nothing moves of itself: so that even if he were to concede that something might do this, he would still confirm that this thing is not the soul. For if the soul, he says, is the principle of motion, I shall teach that it is impossible for the principle of motion to be moved. And thus he enters into the division of his art, so that he first teaches that in the nature of things there is something immobile, and then he attempts to show that this is the soul. It is necessary, he says, either that all things which exist are immobile, or all are moved: or some of these are moved, and some are not moved. Likewise, if we grant, he says, both motion and rest, it is necessary either that some things are always moved and others never moved: or that all things are at once sometimes at rest and sometimes moved. Of these possibilities, he says, let us seek which is more true. That all things are not immobile, sight itself is witness, because there are things whose motion we see: on the other hand, sight teaches that all things are not moved, by which we recognize things that are unmoved. But neither can we say that all things suffer motion at one time and are without motion at another: because there are things whose perpetual motion we see: as concerning

Regarding celestial bodies, there is no doubt. It remains, therefore, he says, that just as something is always moved, so there must be something that is always immobile. From these points, it is gathered that something immobile exists, and no one opposes or refutes this. For this is a true division of categories, and it is not repugnant to the Platonic school <note>The "Platonic school" refers to the followers of Plato, who argued that the soul is the source of its own motion.</note>. Nor does it follow that if something is immobile, this thing must be the soul. Nor does he who says the soul is moved by itself confirm that all things are moved; rather, he affirms the mode by which the soul is moved. If, however, there is something else that is immobile, it will have no bearing on what is affirmed regarding the soul.

<margin>Macrobius's response.</margin>

Aristotle himself, seeing this, after he taught that there is something immobile, wishes to say that this is the soul; and he begins to assert that there is nothing that can be moved by itself, but that all things which are moved are moved by another.

<margin>Everything that is moved is moved by another, according to the opinion of Aristotle.</margin>

If he had truly proved this, nothing would be left for the defense of the Platonic school. For how could it be believed that the soul is moved by itself, if it were established that nothing exists which can be moved by itself? In this Aristotelian argumentation, the order of division is woven as follows: Of all things that are moved, he says, some are moved through themselves <note>original: "per se"</note>, others by accident <note>original: "ex accidenti"; a technical term in logic referring to a property that is not essential to the subject.</note>. And those are moved by accident, he says, which, while they do not move themselves, are nevertheless in something that is moved: such as a bundle or a resting passenger in a ship; or even when a part is moved while the whole remains at rest: as if someone standing still were to move a foot, a hand, or the head.

<margin>Why the soul also cannot be moved by itself.</margin>

However, that which is moved through itself is that which is moved neither by accident nor in part, but the whole is moved at once: as when fire ascends to the higher regions. And regarding those things which are moved by accident, there is no doubt that they are moved by another. But I will prove, he says, that even those things which are moved through themselves are moved by another. For of all things, he says, which are moved through themselves, some possess the cause of motion within themselves: such as animals and trees, which are understood without doubt to be moved by another: namely, by a cause that lies hidden within them. For the cause of motion...

# BOOK II.

Reason separates that which is moved from the mover. Other things, however, are openly moved by something else—that is, either by force or by nature. For instance, we say that every javelin is moved; although it seems to be carried by its own motion once it has left the hand of the thrower, the origin of that motion is attributed to force. In this same way, we sometimes see the earth carried upward and fire downward, which an external impulse <note>original: "alienus impulsus"</note> undoubtedly compels. 

By nature, however, heavy things are moved when they fall downward of their own accord, or light things when they are carried upward. But it must also be said that these are moved by something else, even if it is uncertain by what they are moved. For Reason, he says, apprehends that there is "I know not what" which moves these things. For if they were moved spontaneously, they would also stop spontaneously. Furthermore, they would not always follow a single path; rather, they would move through various directions if they were carried by a spontaneous agitation. Since they cannot do this—but instead ascent is always assigned to light things and descent to heavy things—it appears that their motion is referred to a certain and established necessity of nature. These and similar points are those by which Aristotle believed he had proved that everything which is moved is moved by another. 

But the Platonists (as will be demonstrated a little later) have taught that these arguments are more clever than they are true. Now, his following division must be joined, by which he labors to show that the soul cannot be moved of itself, even if another thing were able to do this. And he borrows the first proposition of this matter from those things which he considers to have been established. <margin>Why the soul cannot be moved of itself, nor even be moved by another, and is therefore immobile.</margin> <margin>* to have stood firm</margin> For he says: Since, therefore, it is certain that everything which is moved is moved by another, without doubt that which moves first—because it is not moved by another (for it would no longer be considered "first" if it were moved by another)—it is necessary, he says, that it be said either to stand still or to move itself. For if it were said to be moved by another, that which moves it would also be said to be moved by another, and that in turn by another. This inquiry is destined to fall into infinity; you will never find the first beginnings if you always think that there is something else...

It remains, therefore, he says, that if that which first moves is not said to stand still, it must be said to move itself: and thus there will be in one and the same thing both that which moves and that which is moved. Since in every motion, he says, these three things are necessary: that which moves, that by which it moves, and that which is moved. Of these, that which is moved is only moved, and does not also move others, while that by which the motion occurs both is moved and moves; that which moves, however, is not itself moved: so that from these three a common middle ground is understood, while the two extremes are contrary to one another. For just as there is that which is moved and does not move, so there is, he says, that which moves and is not moved. This is why we said that since everything that is moved is moved by another, if this thing which moves is itself also moved, we will always be seeking the origin of this motion and will never find a beginning. Furthermore, if anything is said to move itself, it is necessary, he says, that we consider it to be moved either as a whole by the whole, or part by part, or a part by the whole, or the whole by a part: and yet that motion, whether it proceeds from the whole or from a part, will require another author for itself. From all these points, the entire Aristotelian reasoning is gathered into one, in this manner: Everything that is moved is moved by another. ## BOOK II.

For among *Geometers* <note>original: "Geometras"</note> the beginning of a line is said to be a point, not a line; among *Arithmeticians* <note>original: "Arithmeticos"</note> the beginning of a number is not a number. Likewise, the cause of birth is not itself born; and therefore the cause or beginning of motion <note>term: "motus" (motion/movement) — in this context, it refers to both physical movement and internal change</note> is not moved. Therefore the soul, which is the beginning of motion, is not moved. A *Third* argument is added:
It can never happen, he says, that concerning one and the same thing, at one and the same time, contraries pertaining to that same thing should occur. We know, moreover, that to move is to act, and to be moved is to be acted upon <note>original: "pati" (to suffer/undergo/be passive)</note>. And therefore, if something moves itself, two contraries would happen to it at once: both acting and being acted upon, which is impossible. The soul, therefore, cannot move itself.
He also says: If the essence of the soul were motion, it would never <margin>Fourth.</margin> rest from motion. For there is nothing that admits the contrary of its own essence. For fire will never be cold, nor will snow ever grow warm of its own accord. But the soul sometimes ceases from motion; for we do not see the body being moved at all times. Therefore, motion is not the essence of the soul, for it would then admit its own contrary.
He says further: If the soul is the cause of motion for others, it <margin>Fifth.</margin> cannot be the cause of motion for itself. For nothing, he says, is the cause of the same thing for itself as it is for another; just as a physician or a physical trainer does not provide the health or strength to themselves in the same way they provide it—the former to the sick, the latter to wrestlers.
He says likewise: Every motion requires an instrument for its <margin>Sixth.</margin> exercise, as the practice of individual arts teaches; therefore, it must be seen whether the soul also needs an instrument to move itself. But if that is judged impossible, then it will also be impossible for the soul to move itself.
He says likewise: If the soul is moved, it is moved without doubt <margin>Seventh.</margin> along with other movements both from a place and into a place. If this is so, it now enters the body, now departs again, and performs this frequently. But we see that this cannot happen; therefore the soul is not moved. To these he also adds: <margin>Eighth.</margin>

If the soul moves itself, it must necessarily move by some specific type of motion. Therefore, it either moves in space, or it moves by generating itself, or by consuming itself, or by increasing itself, or by diminishing itself. For these, he says, are the types of motion. Let us investigate how each of these might occur. If it moves in space, it either moves in a straight line or it rotates in a circle with a spherical motion. But no straight line is infinite. For whatever line is understood in nature is undoubtedly bounded by some end. If, therefore, the soul moves along a bounded line, it does not move forever. For when it reaches the end and returns from there back to the beginning, there must be an interval <note>original: "interstitium"</note> of motion during that very change of direction. Nor can it rotate in a circle. Because every sphere moves around something immobile, which we call the center. If, then, the soul moves in this way, it either has something immobile within itself—and thus it would follow that it does not move in its entirety—or if it does not have this within itself, another equally absurd conclusion follows: that the center is outside of it, which is impossible. It is established from these points, he says, that it does not move in space. Furthermore, if it generates itself, it follows that we must say it both exists and does not exist at the same time; if indeed it consumes itself, it will not be immortal. But if it either increases or diminishes itself, it will be found to be simultaneously both larger and smaller than itself. From these points he gathers the following syllogism <note>A logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</note>: If the soul moves itself, it moves by some type of motion; however, no type of motion is found by which it might move itself. Therefore, it does not move itself.

By these arguments, the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato's philosophy</note> defend their master against Aristotle, showing that there is indeed something which is moved by itself, and that this is necessarily the soul. Once these things are proven, Aristotle's first objection is weakened.

### BOOK II.
We must now prepare our arguments according to the followers of Plato, who have undermined the undertaking by which Aristotle attempted to wound the so true and so solid definition of his master <note>Aristotle was a student of Plato, though he famously disagreed with him on the nature of the soul</note>. Truly, I am not so forgetful of my own standing, nor so ill-disposed, as to resist Aristotle or support Plato solely from my own wit. Rather, I have gathered into one body of continuous defense those points which great men—who gloried in being called Platonists—left behind in their various works to showcase their efforts. I have also added whatever was right to feel or permissible to venture in understanding after them. 

Because there are two points which Aristotle attempted to assert: <margin>The refutation of Aristotle's argument, in which he wishes to show that whatever moves is moved by another. And this is the solution to the first objection.</margin> first, when he says there is nothing that is moved by itself; and second, when he confirms that the soul cannot be this thing. We must resist both points, so that it may be established that something *can* be moved by itself, and that it may become clear that the soul is this very thing. 

First, therefore, we must beware the deceptions of that division of his, in which he enumerates certain things that move by themselves. By showing that those things are also moved by another—that is, by a cause lurking within—he seems to himself to have proven that everything which moves, even if said to move by itself, is nevertheless moved by another. Now, part of this is true, but the conclusion is false. For we do not deny that there are some things which, while appearing to move by themselves, are known to be moved by another. However, this does not hold for *all* things that move by themselves, such that it is necessary for them to be moved by another. 

For when Plato says the soul moves by itself—that is, when he calls it <term>self-moving <note>original: *αὐτοκίνητον* (autokineton)</note></term>—he does not wish it to be numbered among those things which *seem* to move by themselves but are moved by a cause hidden within. For example, animals are moved by another cause, though a hidden one, for they are moved by the soul; or trees, whose mover is not seen, yet it is certain they are stirred by a nature lurking within them. But Plato says the soul moves by itself in such a way that it has no other cause, either

We <insert>shall explain</insert> how this is to be understood. We call fire hot, but we also say iron is hot; we call snow cold, and we name a stone cold; honey is sweet, but we also call mead <note>a fermented honey drink</note> sweet. Yet each of these signifies something different in different cases. For we understand the name of "hot" one way regarding fire, and another way regarding iron. Because fire is hot through itself, it does not become hot from another source; on the contrary, iron does not grow hot except from something else. That snow is cold or honey is sweet does not happen from elsewhere; however, the coldness in a stone or the sweetness in mead proceeds from the snow or the honey.

In the same way, both "standing still" and "being moved" are said of those things which either stand or move by themselves, as well as of those which are either brought to a halt or driven by another. But those things which happen to be moved or stopped by another also cease to stand and cease to move. However, for those things where "to be" and "to be moved" are the same thing, they never cease from motion; because they cannot exist without their own essence. Just as iron loses its heat, but fire truly never stops being hot.

Therefore, the soul is moved by itself; although animals or trees may seem to be moved by themselves. But for those things, even if it is hidden within, another cause—that is, the soul or nature—provides the motion; therefore they also lose that which they took from elsewhere. But the soul is moved by itself in such a way as fire is hot by itself, with no external cause either heating the fire or moving the soul. For when we call fire hot, we do not conceive of two different things—one which heats and another which is heated—but we call the whole thing hot according to <margin>one</margin> its *own nature. When we call snow cold, or honey sweet, we do not perceive one thing which provides the quality and another to which it is provided. So also when we say the soul is moved by itself, a double consideration of a mover and a moved does not follow, but we recognize its essence in the motion itself: because that which is in <margin>fire</margin>

# BOOK II.

Just as the name of "heat" is inherent to fire, the word "cold" to snow, and the designation "sweet" to honey, so must the term *self-moving* <note>original: "αὑτὸκίνητον" (autokinēton); a central concept in Platonic and Aristotelian philosophy describing a being that originates its own motion</note> be understood regarding the soul. This is what the Latin translation signifies as "to be moved by itself." Do not let it confuse you that "to be moved" is a passive verb. <margin>Removal of a quibble.</margin> In the case of the word "to be cut," two things are considered equally: that which cuts and that which is cut. Likewise, when we say "to be held," two things are understood: that which holds and that which is held. You might think that here, in the phrase "to be moved," there is a similar significance of two things—one which moves and one which is moved. Indeed, "to be cut" and "to be held" are passive states <term>passive state: "passio," referring to an action being acted upon a subject</term>; therefore, they embrace the consideration of both the doer and the sufferer.

However, while "to be moved" represents both considerations when spoken of things moved by another, it is different for that which is moved by itself so as to be *self-moving*. When such a thing is said "to be moved," because it moves from itself and not from another, no suspicion of a passive state can be understood. For even the word "to stand," though it does not appear to be a passive verb, signifies a passive state when it is said of something that stands because another has set it there—as in the line: "The spears stand fixed in the earth" <margin>Aeneid, 6. <note>Virgil, Aeneid, Book 6, line 652.</note></margin>. Thus, although "to be moved" sounds passive, when there is no external agent acting upon it, there can be no "sufferer" of the action.

To make it more absolutely clear that a passive state is signified by the understanding of things rather than mere words: behold, when fire is carried toward the heavens, it suffers nothing; but when it is carried downward, it undoubtedly suffers, because it does not endure this unless another force is impelling it. Although one and the same verb is uttered, we say that the passive state is sometimes present and sometimes absent. Therefore, "to be moved" is the same in significance as "to be hot." When we say iron is "hot," or a pen is "moved," we admit it is a passive state because the condition comes to each from elsewhere <margin>*originates <note>The author notes a correction from "peruenit" (reaches) to "prouenit" (originates/arises).</note></margin>. But when fire is said to be hot, or the soul is said to be moved—because the essence of the former is in heat and the essence of the latter is in motion—no place is left here for a passive state. # ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

...heaping up false accusations <note>original: "lumniam farciens," likely part of "calumniam" (calumny/false accusation) split from the previous page</note>, he contends that Plato himself also signified two things—that is, that which moves and that which is moved—by saying: **Therefore, only that which moves itself, because it is never deserted by itself, never indeed ceases to be moved.** And he openly proclaims that Plato expressed two distinct things with these words: that which moves, and that which is moved. But it seems to me that so great a man could have been ignorant of nothing; rather, in the exercise of such subtleties, he was winking at himself and playing a deliberate game. 

Otherwise, who would not notice that when something is said to "move itself," two separate entities are not to be understood? Just as when it is said *heauton timorein* <note>Greek: ἑαυτὸν τιμωρεῖν</note>, that is, **punishing oneself**: there is not one person who punishes and another who is punished. And when someone is said to destroy himself, to involve himself, or to free himself, it is not necessary for one to be the active agent and another to be the passive recipient. Instead, this alone is expressed by the understanding of this phrase: that he who punishes himself, or he who frees himself, has not received this from another, but is said to have either inflicted it or provided it for himself. 

So also regarding the **prime mover** <note>Greek: ἀρχικινήτου (archikinētou), referring to the "original source of motion"</note>, when it is said that "it moves itself," it is said for this purpose: to exclude the estimation of any other mover. Plato, wishing to remove this from the thought of the reader, expressed it by what he stated previously. For he says: **For that which is always moved is eternal; but that which brings motion to something else, and which is itself moved from elsewhere, must necessarily have an end of living when it has an end of motion.** 

What can be found more expressive than these words, which testify with clear significance that what moves itself is not moved from elsewhere? For he says the soul is eternal for this reason: because it moves itself and is not moved from elsewhere. Therefore, "to move itself" signifies only this: not to be moved by another. Nor should you think that the same thing moves and the same thing is moved <note>as if they were two separate parts</note>, but rather, to be moved without another mover is what it means to "move itself." It is clearly established, therefore, that not everything which is moved is moved by another. Therefore, the **prime mover** can avoid being moved by another; but not even by itself...

# BOOK II.

Indeed, it is moved in such a way that within itself there is one thing which moves and another which is moved, neither in its entirety nor in part, as he proposes; but for this reason alone it is said to move itself, lest it be thought to be moved by another. But even that Aristotelian division of motions (which we mentioned above) is more suited to a deceptive argument than a proving one, in which he says: "Just as there is that which is moved and does not move, so there is that which moves and is not moved." For it is established that everything whatever that is moved moves other things, as it is said, either the rudder moves the ship, or the ship moves the air surrounding it or the waves. What is there, indeed, that cannot push another thing while it is itself being moved? Therefore, if it is not true that those things which are moved do not move others, it does not follow that you may find something else which moves and yet is not moved.

Therefore, that division of motions brought forth by Plato in the tenth book of the *Laws* <note>original: "decimo de Legibus"</note> is more to be approved: "Every motion," he says, "either moves itself and other things, or is moved by another and moves other things." And the first refers to the soul, while the second refers to all bodies. Here, therefore, two motions are separated by their difference and joined by their association. They have this in common: that both the first and the second move other things. However, they differ in this: that the former is moved by itself, the latter by another. From all these points, which we have gathered and unearthed from the fertility of the Platonic senses, it is established that it is not true that everything which is moved is moved by another. Therefore, the "principle of motion" <note>term: *principium motus* — the starting point or source of movement</note> will not be said to stand for the purpose of pleading away the necessity of a further mover; because it can afterwards move itself (as we have said) without another moving it.

The syllogism <note>term: *syllogismus* — a logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</note> which had gathered its points from the previously mentioned varied and manifold division has therefore been weakened. That is: "The soul is the principle of motion; the principle of motion is not moved; therefore the soul is not moved." It remains that, because it has been established that something can be moved by itself without another moving it, the soul should be shown to be this very thing. This will be easily shown if we proceed from manifest and indubitable

We derive our arguments from things that are observable. In a human being, motion is provided either by the soul, or the body, or a mixture of both. And because there are three possibilities from which this inquiry proceeds: since it is established that this cannot be provided by the body, nor by the mixture, it remains beyond doubt that the human being is moved by the soul. Now let us speak of each individually, and first of the body. It is more manifest than needs to be asserted that no inanimate body is moved by its own motion. Moreover, there is nothing which, while being immobile itself, can move another thing. Therefore, the body does not move the human being. We must see whether perhaps the very mixture of soul and body provides this motion for itself. But because it is established that motion is not inherent in the body, if it is not inherent in the soul either, no motion can be produced from two things lacking motion: just as bitterness will not come from two sweet things, nor sweetness from two bitter things; nor will heat be born from a double cold, or cold from a double heat. For every quality increases when doubled; a contrary never emerges from duplicated similar things. Therefore, there will be no motion from two immobile things. Thus, the mixture will not move the human being. From this, an impregnable <term>syllogism</term> <note>A form of logical reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two assumed premises</note> is gathered from the indubitable light of conceded facts: A living creature is moved; moreover, either the soul, or the body, or a mixture of both provides motion to the living creature; but neither the body nor the mixture provides motion; therefore, the soul provides the motion. From these points, it appears that the soul is the beginning of motion: and the previous treatise taught that the beginning of motion is moved by itself. There is no doubt, therefore, that the soul is <term>self-moving</term> <note>original Greek: ἀυτοκίνητον (autokinēton)</note>, that is, it is moved by itself.

## BOOK II.

He says that the same qualities exist in their own beginnings as in those things which are born from them: and therefore the soul, which is the <term>beginning of motion<note>Latin: *initium motus*. The first cause or source from which all movement starts.</note></term>, is not itself moved, lest the beginning and that which is born from the beginning be the same thing; that is, lest motion should seem to have proceeded from motion. To these points, there is a ready and complete response. Because, even if we admit that principles and those things which come forth from principles sometimes differ from one another in some respect, they can nevertheless never be so contrary to each other as "standing still" and "being moved" are opposed. For if the beginning of white were called black, and if the starting point of moisture were dryness, then good would proceed from evil, and sweetness from a bitter beginning. But it is not so, because nature does not allow beginnings and their consequences to disagree to the point of total contrariety. However, one sometimes finds such a difference between them as is appropriate between an origin and its progression: as is the case here between the motion by which the soul is moved, and that by which it moves other things. For Plato did not simply call the soul "motion," but "motion moving itself." Therefore, what the difference is between self-moving motion and the motion by which it moves other things is plain to see. Inasmuch as the former is without an author <note>i.e., it has no external cause or creator of its movement</note>, while the latter is the author of motion for others. It is established, therefore, neither that beginnings and the things procreated from beginnings can differ so much as to be contrary to each other, nor that a moderate difference was lacking here. Therefore, the principle of motion—which he gathered by a clever conclusion—will not stand still. To these, a third objection followed (as we remember): <margin>The third objection repeated.</margin> that contrary things cannot happen to one thing at the same time; and because "to move" and "to be moved" are contrary to each other, the soul cannot move itself, lest the same thing should both be moved and be the mover. But the things asserted above dissolve this. Inasmuch as it was established that in the motion of the soul, two separate things—that which moves and that which is moved—are not to be understood: because to be moved by oneself is nothing other than to be moved without another moving it. There is no contrariety where that which happens is one; because it does not happen by one thing acting upon another, since the very motion of the soul is its

<margin>The fourth objection is repeated, which must also be refuted.</margin> The fourth objection is as follows. From this, as we have reported above, the fourth occasion for debate arose: If the essence of the soul is motion, he asks, why does it sometimes rest, when no other thing admits a contradiction to its own essence? Fire, whose <margin>*essence is heat,</margin> essence contains heat, never ceases to be hot. And because the coldness of snow is in its essence, it is never anything but cold. Therefore, by the same reasoning, the soul should never cease from motion. But I would like him to say: when does he suspect the soul ceases from motion? If by moving itself, he says, it also moves the body: it is surely necessary that when we see the body is not being moved, we understand the soul also is not moving. Against this, a twin defense is ready at hand. First, because the motion of the soul is not detected solely by whether the body is shaken. For even when no part of the body is seen to move in a human: nevertheless, thought itself—or in any animal, hearing, sight, smell, and the like—and even in rest itself, breathing and dreaming, all these are motions of the soul. Furthermore, who could call the body itself immobile, even while it does not seem to be shaken? Consider the growth of the limbs, or if the age of growing has already <margin>*passed its time*</margin> passed: consider the leaping of the heart <note>original: "saltus cordis"; referring to the heartbeat</note> which is impatient of any pause: consider the orderly digestion of food which, by natural dispensation, supplies juice <note>original: "succum"; the vital nutrients or chyle</note> between the veins and the organs: consider how the very collection of fluids <note>original: "collectio fluentorum"; likely referring to the circulation of humors or blood</note> bears witness to the perpetual agitation of the body. And therefore the soul is always moved by an eternal motion of its own, and the body also is always moved, so long as it is animated by the soul, which is the beginning and cause of its motion. <margin>The fifth objection is repeated, so that it may be dissolved.</margin> From this, the spark <note>original: "fomes"; literally tinder or fuel for an argument</note> of the fifth question arose for the same person. If the soul, he says, is the cause of motion for others, it cannot be the cause of motion for itself: because there is nothing that is the cause of the same thing for both itself and others. I, however, although I could easily prove that there are many things which are the cause of the same thing for both themselves and others, will nevertheless grant this to be true—lest I seem to oppose everything he asserts out of mere zeal—because even if held as true, it will not harm the assertion of the soul's motion.

# BOOK II.

For indeed, we call the soul the beginning of motion and its cause. Regarding the cause, we shall see later. In the meantime, it is established that every beginning exists within the thing of which it is the beginning; and therefore, whatever proceeds into any thing from its beginning is found in that beginning itself. Thus, the beginning of heat cannot fail to be hot. Who would deny that fire itself, from which heat passes into other things, is hot? But, he says, fire does not heat itself because by its very nature it is entirely hot. I hold exactly what I wanted: for neither does the soul move itself in such a way that there is a distinction between the motion and the mover; rather, it is moved by its own motion in its entirety, so that you can separate nothing that does the moving. 

These things said concerning the beginning shall suffice. But concerning the cause—since we have granted a spontaneous agreement <note>original: "spontanea conniuentia"</note> so that nothing may be the cause of the same thing both for itself and for others—we freely acquiesce: lest the soul, which is the cause of motion for others, should seem to be the cause of motion for itself. For it is the cause of motion to those things which would not move unless the soul itself provided it; but as for the soul's own movement, it does not bestow this upon itself, but it is of its very essence <term>essentia: the fundamental nature or "being" of a thing</term> that it is moved. 

From this, the question that follows is resolved. <margin>The sixth argument of Aristotle is solved.</margin> For perhaps I might concede that instruments are required for the exercise of motion when that which moves is one thing and that which is moved is another. But in the soul, not even a scurrilous joke could dare to seek this without a loss of modesty, for its motion is in its essence; just as fire, although it is moved by a cause hidden within itself, nevertheless uses no instruments to climb toward the heavens. Much less are these instruments to be sought in the soul, whose motion is its very essence. 

In the points that follow, so great a man <note>Referring to Aristotle</note>—who is elsewhere more serious than all others—is like one playing at sophistry. If the soul is moved, <margin>The seventh objection is refuted.</margin> he says, then among other motions it is also moved from place to place. Therefore, he says, it now exits the body, and now enters it again, and is often occupied in this exercise—which we do not see happen. Therefore, the soul is not moved. Against this, there is no one who does not respond without hesitation that not all things which move...

# BOOK II.

This all flows from one and the same cleverness <note>original: "astutia," implying a misguided or overly subtle ingenuity</note> of a poorly conceived definition. For because he once proposed to himself that "everything which is moved is moved by another," he seeks all these types of motion within the soul, in which one thing is that which moves and another is that which is moved. Yet none of these categories can apply to the soul, in which there is no separation between the mover and the moved.

"Who is it then," someone will ask, "or from where is the motion of the soul understood, if none of these exist?" Anyone who desires to know this will learn it, either from the words of Plato or from Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note>: **"Furthermore, for all other things that are moved, this is the source, this is the principle of moving."** <margin>By what motions the soul is driven.</margin> However, you will easily discover how great the expression of this word is—by which the soul is called the "source" <note>original: "fons," meaning a fountainhead or spring</note> of motion—if you conceive in your mind the motion of an invisible thing without an author <note>meaning without an external cause</note>, and therefore proceeding without beginning and without end, and moving all other things. Among visible things, nothing could be found more similar to this than a spring: which is the principle of water in such a way that, while it generates rivers and lakes from itself, it is said to be born from nothing itself. For if it were born from another, it would not be the principle itself.

And just as a spring is not always easily detected, yet from it are poured forth what becomes the Nile, or the Eridanus <note>The Po River</note>, or the Ister <note>The Danube</note>, or the Tanais <note>The Don River</note>. And as you admire their speed by seeing them, and seek within yourself the origin of such great waters, you return in thought to the spring: and you understand that all this motion flows from the first principle of the bubbling source. So, when by considering the motion of bodies—whether they be divine <note>referring to celestial bodies/planets</note> or earthly—you perhaps wish to seek the author, let your mind return to the soul as if to a spring. Its motion, even without the service of the body, is witnessed by thoughts, joys, hopes, and fears. For its motion is the discernment of good and evil: the love of virtues, and the desire for vices: from which flow all the channels of things born therefrom. For its motion is whatever we feel in anger, and when we are armed for the heap of mutual collision <note>referring to conflict or strife</note>: from which, little by little...

## ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO

Proceeding little by little, the madness of battles wavers. The motion of the soul is this: that we are snatched away by desires, and that we are bound by cravings. But these motions, if they are governed by reason, turn out to be beneficial; if they are abandoned by reason, they are both snatched headlong and snatch others away. You have learned the motions of the soul, which it exercises sometimes without the service of the body, and sometimes through the body. If, however, you seek the motions of the world-soul itself <note>The *Anima Mundi*, a concept where the universe is viewed as a living being with a soul</note>, look upon the celestial revolution and the rapid force of the underlying spheres, the rising or setting of the Sun, and the forward or backward courses of the stars—all of which occur because the soul moves them. Indeed, to call that which moves all things "immobile" does not suit Aristotle <note>original: "Aristoteli non conuenit"</note>—whose greatness in other matters is well proven—but it suits only one whom the force of nature and manifest reason do not move.

Scipio was urged by his grandfather Africanus toward both the virtues of leisure <note>contemplative or scholarly virtues</note> and the virtues of business <note>active political or military virtues</note>. Then, concerning the three parts of philosophy, none of which Cicero has passed over untouched.

->CHAPTER XVII.<-

Therefore, having taught and asserted the motion of the soul, Africanus commands and instructs in these words how its exercise must be equally employed: "Exercise this soul in the best of things." Now, the best cares are those concerning the safety of the fatherland; the soul that is stirred and exercised by these will fly more swiftly to this seat and to its own home. And it will do this more quickly if, even then while it is shut up in the body, it projects outward, and by contemplating those things which are outside itself, abstracts itself as much as possible from the body. For the souls of those who have surrendered themselves to the pleasures of the body and have offered themselves as their servants, as it were—and who, by the impulse of lusts obedient to pleasures, have violated the laws of Gods and men—once they have slipped out of their bodies, they are tossed about the earth itself, and do not return to this place unless they have been driven for many ages.

## BOOK II.

In the earlier part of this work, we stated that some virtues are "leisurely" <note>original: "otiosas"; referring to the contemplative or theoretical virtues of the mind</note> while others are "busy," <margin>On the two kinds of virtues</margin> <note>original: "negotiosas"; referring to the active or practical virtues of public life</note> and that the former belong to philosophers, while the latter belong to rulers. These virtues are sometimes separated, but at other times they are joined together when a mind is found capable of both by nature and by training. For if someone is considered a stranger to all formal teaching, yet in the republic he is <term>prudent, temperate, brave, and just</term> <note>The four cardinal virtues of classical philosophy</note>; such a man, though removed from the "leisurely" virtues, nonetheless stands out by the vigor of his **active virtues**, for which heaven is granted as a reward no less than for the others. If, however, someone is not suited for action due to an inherent quietness of nature, but—raised toward the heavens solely by the excellent gift of conscience—he spends his wealth of learning on the <margin>*snatched up</margin> exercise of **divine disputation**, a follower of heavenly things and a wanderer away from falling, earthly things, he too shall be carried up to the peak of heaven by the "leisurely" virtues. Yet it often happens that the same heart is sublime in the perfection of both acting and disputing, and attains heaven through the exercise of both types of virtue. Let **Romulus** be placed by us in the first category: his life never abandoned the virtues, but always exercised them in action. In the second category is **Pythagoras**, who, ignorant of public action, was a master of discourse; he followed only the virtues of learning and conscience. In the third and mixed category, among the Greeks, let there be **Lycurgus** and **Solon**; among the Romans, **Numa**, both **Catones**, and many others who both drank deeply of philosophy and provided a foundation for the republic. ->ON THE DREAM OF SCIPIO, BOOK II.<-

Moreover, the best concerns are those regarding the safety of the fatherland; driven and exercised by these, the soul will fly more swiftly to this seat and to its own home. Then, as if speaking to a man no less learned than brave, words suited to philosophers are added when it is said: *And it will do so more quickly if, even then while it is shut up in the body, it reaches outward; and contemplating those things which are outside, it abstracts itself as much as possible from the body.* <note>original: "Idq; ocyus faciet... se à corpore abstrahet." This refers to the practice of "philosophical death," or the detachment of the mind from physical sensations.</note> For these are the precepts of that teaching which says that "death" <note>The "death" mentioned here is the symbolic death of the philosopher—the separation of the soul's attention from the body's needs.</note> is to be sought by those practicing philosophy. From this it follows that while still placed within the body, they despise the body as a foreign burden (insofar as nature allows). And now, easily and opportunely, he urges the virtues, after he has declared how great and how divine the rewards owed to the virtues are. 

But because among laws, that one is also called "imperfect" in which no penalty is decreed for those who stray, he therefore decrees a penalty at the conclusion of the work for those living outside these precepts. Hermagoras the Platonic <note>A reference to a later Platonic commentator, likely Hermias or a similar figure associated with the school.</note> followed this topic more copiously, numbering the infinite ages in which the souls of the guilty, often rolled back into the same punishments, are permitted to emerge late from Tartarus <note>The deep abyss of torment in Greco-Roman mythology.</note> and, having finally obtained purification, to return to the principles of their nature, which is heaven. For it is necessary that every soul return to the seat of its origin. 

But those souls which inhabit the body as if they were foreigners return quickly after the body's death, as if to their fatherland. Those, however, which cling to the allurements of bodies as if to their own seats: the more violently they are separated from them, the later they return to the regions above. But let us now make an end to the "Dream" by restraining our discussion, adding this which will suit the conclusion: since there are three parts of all philosophy—moral, natural, and rational—and since the moral is that which teaches the refined perfection of character; the natural is that which disputes concerning divine bodies; and the rational is when the discourse concerns incorporeal things, which...

<meta>This page concludes Book II of Macrobius's Commentary on the Dream of Scipio, summarizing the three branches of philosophy found within Cicero's work.</meta>

# BOOK II.

those things which the mind alone embraces: <note>original: "quæ mens sola complectitur"</note> Cicero <note>original: "Tullius"</note> has omitted none of the three branches of philosophy in this dream. For that exhortation toward the virtues, the love of one's country, and the contempt of glory—what else does it contain but the moral principles of **ethical philosophy**? 

But when he speaks either of the measure of the spheres, or of the novelty and magnitude of the stars, and of the supremacy of the sun, the celestial circles, the terrestrial zones, and the location of the Ocean, and reveals the secret of the harmony of the spheres above: he is commemorating the secrets of **physics** <note>natural philosophy</note>. 

Yet when he disputes concerning the motion and immortality of the soul, in which it is established that nothing corporeal exists, and whose essence no sense perceives, but only reason: there he ascends to the heights of **rational philosophy** <note>metaphysics or logic</note>. Truly, therefore, it must be pronounced that nothing is more perfect than this work, in which the entire integrity of universal philosophy is contained.

<image-desc>Large ornate initial 'M' depicting a figure, possibly a satyr or similar mythological creature, within its design.</image-desc>Nature has won us over to many and various things in this life, my son Eustathius; but by no bond has she bound us more closely than by the love of those whom we have begotten.
