<page-num>179</page-num>
->BOOK I.<-

The material, which was previously disorganized and gathered at various times, has now been arranged into a single body. Those things which I had noted down indistinctly and in an ancient manner <note>original: "Priscuæ," referring to an archaic or old-fashioned style of note-taking</note> as an aid to memory, have now been brought together into an orderly sequence, cohering like the limbs of a body. 

Do not find fault with me if I often explain the matters I have borrowed from my varied reading using the very words in which they were narrated by the original authors. This present work does not promise a display of eloquence, but rather a collection of things worth knowing. You ought to take it in good part if you recognize the knowledge of antiquity—sometimes expressed clearly in our own words, and sometimes faithfully in the words of the ancients themselves—according as each matter suggested itself to be either narrated or translated. 

In a certain way, we ought to imitate the bees, which wander about and pluck flowers; then, whatever they have gathered, they arrange and distribute through their honeycombs. By a certain blending and the particular property of their own spirit, they change that varied nectar into a single flavor. We too shall commit to the pen whatever we have sought out through diverse reading.

our own mind: let it conceal all the sources by which it was aided, yet reveal the very thing it has produced. Just as those who compose fragrant perfumes <note>original: "odora pigmenta"</note> take care, above all, that the individual ingredients used in the preparation have no scent of their own; they aim, evidently, to blend the essences of all the aromatics into a single fragrance. Do you see how many voices make up a choir? Yet one sound is rendered from them all. In that group, some voices are high-pitched, some deep, and some in the middle; women are joined with men, and the pipe <note>original: "fistula," a reed pipe or flute</note> is played among them. Thus the voices of individuals remain hidden, but the voice of all is apparent, and a harmony <note>original: "concentus"</note> arises out of dissonant sounds.

I wish this present work to be such a thing. Within it are many arts, many precepts, and examples from many ages—but all breathing together as one. If you neither scorn those things which are already known to you, nor avoid those which are unknown, you will find many things that are either a pleasure to read, an enrichment to have read, or a use to remember. For I believe nothing has been inserted into this work that is either useless to know or difficult to perceive; rather, it contains everything by which your natural wit <note>original: "ingenium"</note> may become more vigorous, your memory better supported, your oratory more skillful, and your speech more pure—unless, perhaps, the vein of the Latin language fails us, having been born under another sky <note>Macrobius likely refers to his North African origins</note>.

I wish to ask and obtain this favor from those who might, by chance, have the time and the will to learn these things: that they judge fairly and kindly if the native elegance of the Roman mouth is found wanting in our discourse. But I must be careful not to heedlessly incur the same charm of a rebuke once directed by Marcus Cato toward Aulus Albinus, who was consul with Lucius Lucullus. <margin>Gellius, Book 11, Chapter 8.</margin> This Albinus wrote a history of Roman affairs in the Greek language. In the first part of that history, he wrote a passage to this effect: that it was proper for no one to be angry with him if anything in those books was written with little composure or less elegance. "For," he said, "I am a Roman man, born in Latium; therefore, Greek eloquence is entirely foreign to us."

## The theme of the entire work. ### CHAPTER I.
During the *Saturnalia* <note>The Roman winter festival in honor of Saturn, characterized by feasting and a reversal of social norms</note>, the leading men of the Roman nobility and other learned individuals gather at the house of Vettius Praetextatus. They devote this solemn holiday time to refined conversation, offering one another hospitality with mutual courtesy, and never departing from one another except for nightly rest. For through the entire duration of the holidays, they occupy the better part of the day with serious discussions, and at the time of dinner, they engage in convivial talk; thus, no time of the day is left void of producing something either learned or charming. However, the talk at the table will be more pleasant, so that it may have more of pleasure and less of severity. For both among others who have described banquets, and especially in that *Symposium* of Plato, the talk of the guests is not about some austere matter, but is a varied and charming description of Desire <note>original: "cupidinis"</note>. In that work, Socrates does not press and entangle his opponent with tighter knots (as is his custom), but in a manner of playing rather than fighting, he gives those he has caught a chance to slip away and escape. For it is proper that conversations at a banquet be as pure in their integrity as they are desirable in their grace. The morning discussion will be more robust, as befits men who are both learned and most distinguished. For neither did the likes of Cotta, Laelius, and Scipio <note>Famous figures of the Roman Republic often used as characters in philosophical dialogues</note> treat the most ample matters—so far as Roman letters...

Nor should it be held against me if one or two of these men, whom a mature age has gathered into this assembly, belonged to a later generation; that this is permitted is evidenced by the dialogues of Plato. Indeed, Parmenides was so much older than Socrates that the latter's boyhood barely reached the former's old age, and yet they are depicted disputing difficult matters. Socrates spends a famous dialogue in a dispute with Timaeus, though it is well known they did not live in the same century. Furthermore, Paralus and Xanthippus, whose father was Pericles, converse with Protagoras in Plato’s work during his second visit to Athens, even though that infamous plague had carried them off long before. Therefore, it is not fitting (with the example of Plato supporting us) to count the years of those meeting together on one's fingers. However, so that the things said by everyone might appear and be distinguished more easily, we have made Decius inquire of Posthumianus what that conversation was, and among whom it took place. Then Caecina spoke: "Since you, who lead me into this discussion, possess such knowledge that nothing from the labors of the ancients is denied to you by ignorance or withdrawn by forgetfulness, I see that it is somewhat redundant to bring forth well-known facts among the learned. However, lest anyone think I am burdened by the honor of your consultation, I will briefly recount whatever my thin memory suggests to me on this matter." After this, when he saw everyone alert and ready to listen, he began thus: "Marcus Varro <note>A prolific Roman scholar (116–27 BCE) often cited as an authority on Roman life.</note>, in the book of *Human Affairs* which he wrote concerning days, says: 'People who are born during these twenty-four hours, from midnight to the next midnight, are said to have been born on one single day.' By these words, he seems to have divided the observation of days such that a person born after sunset but before midnight is considered born on the day followed by that night; conversely, one born during the last six hours of the night is seen as born on the day that dawned after that night."

<margin>From Gellius, Book 3, Chapter 2, regarding the beginning of the day.</margin>

<margin>The Athenians.</margin> The same Varro wrote in that same book that the Athenians observe it differently: they say that the entire middle period from sunset to the next sunset constitutes one day.

<margin>The Babylonians.</margin> Furthermore, the Babylonians have another way: they call the space from sunrise to the beginning of the next sunrise by the name of one day.

<margin>The Umbrians.</margin> The Umbrians <note>An ancient people of central Italy.</note>, however, say that one and the same day lasts from noon until the following noon. "This," says Varro, "is quite absurd. For a person born among the Umbrians at the sixth hour <note>Noon.</note> on the Kalends <note>The first day of the Roman month.</note> would have a birthday that appears to be half on the Kalends and half on the day after the Kalends, lasting until the sixth hour of that day."

<margin>The Romans.</margin> However, that the Roman people count each day from midnight to the next midnight, just as Varro said, is shown by many proofs. For Roman sacred rites are partly diurnal <note>belonging to the day</note> and partly nocturnal. For those which are diurnal, the time is reckoned from the sixth hour of the preceding night; for the nocturnal rites, the following night is the limit. In addition to this, the ritual and custom of taking auspices <note>The practice of observing birds or other signs to determine the will of the gods.</note> teaches that the observation is the same. Furthermore, the Tribunes of the Plebs <note>officials elected to protect the rights of the common people</note>, who are not permitted to be absent from Rome for a single full day, are not considered to have been absent for a day when they depart after midnight and return after the first torches are lit but before the following midnight. This is because they returned before the sixth hour of the night <note>midnight</note> and thus spent some portion of that day within the city. I have also read that Quintus Mucius, the <term>Jurisconsult</term> <note>an expert in interpreting the law</note>, used to say that a woman had not legally "interrupted" her marriage <note>original: "usurpata esset"</note> if, having begun living with a man for the sake of marriage on the Kalends of January <note>January 1st</note>, she "interrupted" it on the fourth day before the following Kalends of January. For the "three-night" period <note>original: "trinoctium"</note> could not be completed, which <insert>according to the Twelve Tables</insert> <note>the foundation of Roman law, c. 450 BCE</note> she ought to be absent from the husband for the purpose of interrupting the legal possession <margin>interrupted, in the ancient sense</margin> of her person. This is because the final six hours of the third night would belong to the following year, which begins on the Kalends. Virgil also demonstrates this same point, as befits a man dealing with poetic matters, through a hidden and veiled reference to ancient ritual:

> The humid night, he says, turns its mid-course,
> And the cruel East Wind has breathed upon me with panting horses.
<margin>Aeneid, Book 5</margin>

With these words, he reminds us that the day which the Romans called "civil" begins from the sixth hour of the night. The same poet expressed when the night also begins in his sixth book. For when he had said:

> By this turn of conversation, Aurora in her rosy chariot
> Had already crossed the midpoint of the axis in her ethereal course.
<margin>Aeneid, Book 6</margin>

The prophetess soon added:

> Night rushes on, Aeneas; we spend the hours in weeping.

Thus, as a most careful observer of civil definitions, he described the beginnings of day and night. The day is divided as follows: the first period of the day is called the "inclination of midnight." Then follows "cock-crow" <note>original: "gallicinium"</note>. Then the "time of silence" <note>original: "conticinium"</note>, when the roosters fall silent and men [are asleep]...

...men are even then at rest. Then comes daybreak <note>original: "diluculum"</note>, that is, when the day begins to be distinguished. Then morning <note>original: "manè"</note>, while the day is bright. Now, "morning" is so called either because the beginning of light emerges from the lower places—that is, from the spirits of the dead <note>original: "manibus"; the author is playing on the linguistic connection between morning and the 'Manes' or ancestral spirits</note>—or (which seems truer to me) from an omen of a good name. For the people of Lanuvium also use "mane" to mean "good," just as among us the opposite is "immane" <note>monstrous or immense</note>: for example, a "monstrous beast" or a "monstrous crime," and other things of this kind, meaning "not good." Then follows the time from morning until midday <note>original: "meridiem"</note>, that is, the middle of the day. From then on, the time is called "setting" <note>original: "occiduum"</note>. And soon comes the "final season" <note>original: "suprema tempestas"</note>, which is the very last time of the day; as it is expressed in the Twelve Tables <note>The ancient foundation of Roman law</note>: *Let the setting of the sun be the final season.* Then comes evening <note>original: "uespera"</note>, which is derived from the Greeks; for they call it *hesperan* <note>original: ἑσπέραν</note> after the star Hesperus, from which Italy is also named "Hesperia," because it lies toward the West. From this time, it is called "first torch-light." Then "bedtime" <note>original: "concubia"</note>. And then "dead of night" <note>original: "intempesta"</note>, which has no fit time for conducting business. This is the division of the civil day observed by the Romans. Therefore, "on the coming night" <note>original: "noctu futura"</note>, when it begins to be midnight, will be the taking of the auspices for the Saturnalia, for which the custom is to begin "on the morrow" <note>original: "diecrastini"</note>.

### CHAPTER IV.

At this point, when everyone had praised Albinus's memory as if it were a storehouse of antiquity, Praetextatus, seeing Avienus whispering to Furius, said: "What is this, my dear Avienus, that you wish to be disclosed to Albinus alone, secretly from the rest of us?" For nouns that end in *-ibus* in the dative plural never allow the genitive of the same number to increase by a syllable: it either has the same number, as in *of necklaces* <note>original: "monilium"</note> from *necklaces* <note>original: "monilibus"</note>, or *of seats* <note>original: "sedilium"</note> from *seats* <note>original: "sedilibus"</note>; or it has one syllable less, as in *of songs* <note>original: "carminum"</note> from *songs* <note>original: "carminibus"</note>, or *of lights* <note>original: "luminum"</note> from *lights* <note>original: "luminibus"</note>. # OF THE SATURNALIA
<page-num>190</page-num>

<margin>Why authors preferred to say *Saturnaliorum* rather than *Saturnalium*.</margin>
You will ask, I seek to know whether this authority can be defended by any reasoning. Clearly, insofar as it is not out of place to pit a Grammarian <note>The author refers to the professional study of language rules</note> against his own analogy, I will attempt to unearth through conjectures what it was that turned them away from the usual pronunciation: so that they preferred to say *Saturnaliorum* <note>The genitive plural ending in -orum</note> rather than *Saturnalium* <note>The standard third-declension genitive plural ending in -ium</note>. And first, I estimate that they wished these names, which are neuter names of festival days and lack a singular number, to be of a different condition from those names which are formed in both numbers.

For *Compitalia*, and *Bacchanalia*, and *Agonalia*, and *Vinalia*, and others similar to these, are names of festival days, and are not named in the singular: or if you speak in the singular number, you will not signify the same thing unless you add "festival": such as the *Bacchanal* festival, and the *Agonal* festival, and the rest: so that it is no longer a substantive <note>A noun standing on its own</note>, but an adjective, which the Greeks call an *epitheton* <note>original: ἐπίδερν (likely a transcription error for ἐπίθετον), meaning an epithet or adjective</note>.

They were encouraged, therefore, to make a distinction in the genitive case, so that from this declension they might express the name of a solemn day: knowing that in several names, even when the dative ends in *-bus*, the genitive nonetheless ends in *-rum*, such as *domibus* / *domorum* <note>houses</note>, *duobus* / *duorum* <note>two</note>, *ambobus* / *amborum* <note>both</note>. So also *viridia* <note>green things</note>, when they are taken as an adjective <note>original: ἀντὶ ἐπιδέτο (instead of an adjective)</note>, they make the genitive in *-ium*, as in "green meadows" (*viridium pratorum*). But when we wish to signify the greenness of the place itself, we say *viridiorum*: as when it is said, "the beautiful appearance of the green spaces." For then *viridia* is placed as a substantive, not an accidental quality.

Moreover, there was such license among the ancients regarding this genitive that Asinius Pollio <note>A Roman orator and historian, 75 BC – AD 4</note> frequently used *vectigaliorum* <note>of the taxes</note>, because *vectigal* is said no less than *vectigalia*. But even when we read: "And on the left he carried the sacred shield (*ancile*)," nevertheless *anciliorum* has also been recorded. It must be seen, therefore, whether variety delighted them more than whether it was strictly true <note>original: *ad amussim*, meaning "according to the carpenter's rule" or perfectly exact</note> that the names of festival days were so called. For behold, even besides the names of solemn days, other words were also declined thus—

But I also find the names of the festivals themselves declined according to the rule among the ancients. For instance, Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a prolific Roman scholar</note> says in *On Festivals* that the day of the *Ferialia* <note>Festival of the Dead</note> is named from the bringing of feasts to the tombs. He did not say "of the *Ferialiorum*." And elsewhere he says "of the *Floralia*" <note>Festival of Flowers</note>, not "of the *Floraliorum*," even though in that context he did not mean the Floral Games, but the festival of the *Floralia* itself. Masurius also, in the 11th book of the *Fasts*, says: "The day of the *Liberalia* <note>Festival of Liber/Bacchus</note> is called the *Martial Agonium* by the priests." And in the same book: "That night thereafter, which leads into the following day, which is the *Lucaria* <note>Festival of the Grove</note>;" he did not say "of the *Lucariorum*." Likewise, many have said "of the *Liberalia*," not "of the *Liberaliorum*." From this, it must be pronounced that the ancients indulged in a wealth of variety: just as they used to say both *exanimos* and *exanimes* <note>lifeless</note>, *inermes* and *inermos* <note>unarmed</note>, and then *hilaros* as well as *hilares* <note>cheerful</note>. And therefore it is certain that it is <insert>permissible</insert> to say both *Saturnalia* and *Saturnaliorum*: since the rule and authority defend the one, while the authority of many—even if alone—defends the other.

However, the remaining words, which seemed new to our friend Avienus, must be asserted by us through the testimonies of the ancients. For Ennius <note>Quintus Ennius, the "father of Roman poetry"</note>—unless he is to be rejected for his lack of refinement by someone among the more polished of our age—used the phrase "at the time of first sleep" <note>original: *noctu concubia*</note> in these words:

> Which the Gauls, having stealthily attacked the heights of the citadel by night,
> At the **walls in the first sleep of night**, suddenly make the guards bloody.

<margin>By night.</margin>
In this passage, it should be noted not only that he said "at the time of first sleep by night," but also that he used the form "by night" <note>original: *noctu*</note>. And he placed this in the seventh book of the *Annals*, though in the third book he said the same thing even more clearly:

> On **this night** <note>original: *hac noctu*</note> the whole of Etruria will hang by a thread.

Claudius Quadrigarius also says in the 3rd book of his *Annals*: "But the Senate convened **by night**, and many were sent home late **at night**." I do not think it is out of place to mention here that the Decemvirs <note>The ten men who drafted the earliest Roman laws</note> in the Twelve Tables used the word *nox* <note>usually "night" as a subject</note> most unusually for *noctu* <note>"by night" as an adverb</note>. The words are these: "If **night** <note>meaning: by night</note> a theft should be committed, if anyone kills him, let it be held lawful..."

<margin>He used the word "conceived" because Cicero, struck by fear, did not deliver the speech exactly as it was written.</margin>...we should even beat him with rods; for even while you pretend to ignore your love for antiquity, you betray it all the more. For when you say, "it is of a thousand words," what else does your speech smell of but antiquity itself? For although Marcus Cicero, in the oration which he **conceived** <note>The speech "Pro Milone" was famously rewritten by Cicero after the actual trial, where he had been intimidated by Pompey's soldiers.</note> for Milo, left it written thus: *In front of the estate of Clodius, in which estate, on account of those insane foundations, easily a thousand of strong men were staying*—it was "were staying" [plural], not "was staying" [singular], as is often found in less accurately written books. And in the sixth speech against Antony: *Who was ever found at that arch of Janus who would charge a thousand of sesterces to Lucius Antony?* Although Varro also, a man of the same century, said in the seventeenth book of *Human Antiquities*: *It is more than a thousand and one hundred years*; nevertheless, they took the confidence for composing it this way only from the authority of those who came before them.

For Quadrigarius <note>Quintus Claudius Quadrigarius, a Roman annalist of the 1st century BC.</note> wrote thus in the third book of his *Annals*: *There, a thousand of men is killed.* And Lucilius in the third book of his *Satires*: *To the gate it is a thousand, from the gate it is six from there to Salernum.*

Elsewhere, indeed, he even carried out the declension <note>The grammatical inflecting of a word.</note> of this noun. For in the fifteenth book he says:
*The Campanian steed, the trotter, who has beaten this man by a thousand paces and two, will follow no more; he will seem to go at a greater distance and in a different direction.*
The same author in the ninth book:
*You can seek a hundred from one thousand of coins.*

He said "a thousand of paces" [milli passum] for "a thousand paces" [mille passibus], and he said "a thousand of coins" [milli nummum] for "a thousand coins" [mille numis], and he clearly showed that "thousand" is both a noun and is used in the singular number, and even takes the ablative case, and that its plural is "thousands" [millia]. For "thousand" is not used because of what is called *chilia* <note>original: "χίλια" - the Greek plural for thousands.</note> in Greek, but because of *chilias* <note>original: "χιλιάς" - the Greek singular noun for a group of a thousand.</note>. And just as one *chilias* and two *chiliades*: so the ancients, by a certain and direct reasoning, said one *mille* and two *millia*. And hey you! To these so learned men, of whom Marcus Cicero and Varro gloried in being imitators...

When she heard this, she trembled in her spirit; she left the house in a panic and brought the news to the other matrons. On the following day, a dense crowd of mothers-of-the-family rushed to the Senate; weeping and pleading, they begged that one woman might be married to two men rather than one man to two. The Senators, as they were entering the senate-house, were amazed at what this lack of restraint from the women meant, and what this petition of theirs intended; fearing that this shameless madness of the modest sex was a portent of no small matter. The boy Papirius removed the public fear. For, stepping forward into the middle of the senate-house, he related exactly as it had happened: what his mother had insisted on hearing, and what he himself had feigned to his mother. The Senate admired the boy's loyalty and wit; and it issued a decree that henceforth boys should not enter the senate-house with their fathers, except for that one Papirius. Later, as a mark of honor, the surname **Praetextatus** was bestowed upon the boy by decree, because of his wisdom in keeping silent and speaking during his "bordered-garment" years <note>original: 'praetextata aetate'. <margin>Sow</margin> But **Tremellius** was surnamed **Scropha** <note>original: 'Scropha', meaning a breeding sow.</note> due to the following event. This Tremellius was at his villa with his household and children. His slaves, when a sow from the neighbor's land went astray, snatched it and killed it. The neighbor, having called together his guards, surrounded the whole place so that it could not be carried out. He appealed to the master to have his livestock returned. Tremellius, who had learned of the matter from his bailiff, placed the carcass of the sow under the blankets upon which his wife was reclining. He then permitted the neighbor to conduct a search. When they came to the bedroom, he framed the words of an oath, swearing that there was no sow in his villa except the one, he said, which lies in those blankets—pointing to the bed. This most witty oath gave Tremellius the surname of **Scropha**.

Having improved that wild and crude way of life that existed before crops were known, Janus rewarded Saturn with a partnership in his kingdom. When he also became the first to strike bronze coins, he maintained his reverence for Saturn in this too: since Saturn had been brought by ship, Janus had an image of his own head stamped on one side, and a ship on the other, so that he might preserve the memory of Saturn for future generations. That the bronze was stamped in this way is understood even today in games of chance: when boys toss coins high into the air, they cry out "heads or ship" <note>The Roman version of "heads or tails." Roman coins often featured the two-faced head of Janus on the obverse and the prow of a ship on the reverse.</note>, with the game serving as a witness to antiquity. That these two reigned together in harmony and founded neighboring towns through their shared labor is clear, not only from **Maro** <note>The poet Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro).</note> <margin>Aeneid, Book 8</margin> who reports that **Janiculum** was the name for the one and **Saturnia** for the other, but also from the fact that descendants dedicated two consecutive months to them: so that December holds the festival of Saturn, and January the name of the other. 

When, amidst these events, Saturn suddenly disappeared, Janus devised an increase of honors for him. First, he named the entire land subject to his rule *Saturnia*. Then he established an altar with sacred rites, as if to a god, which he called the **Saturnalia**. Thus the Saturnalia precedes the age of the city of Rome by many centuries. He ordered him to be observed with religious majesty, as the author of a better life. His statue serves as evidence: to which he added a sickle, the symbol of the harvest. <margin>*grafting</margin> To this god they attribute the skills of grafting shoots <note>original: *infertiones* (likely a variant of *insitiones*)</note>, the cultivation of fruits, and all such fertile disciplines. The people of **Cyrene** <note>A Greek city in North Africa, famous for its agriculture.</note> also, when they perform divine rites for him, are crowned with fresh figs and send cakes to one another, considering Saturn the discoverer of honey and fruits. The Romans also call him **Sterculius** <note>A name derived from *stercus* (manure), crediting Saturn with teaching humans how to fertilize their fields.</note>...

<margin>Why the Temple of Saturn is the treasury.</margin>
The Romans intended for the **Temple of Saturn** to be the treasury because, during the time when he inhabited Italy, it is said that no theft was committed in his territories; or perhaps because under his rule nothing belonged to any individual as private property:

<margin>From the *Georgics*, Book 1, where it is read: "Nor indeed to mark..."</margin>
> *It was not lawful even to mark the ground, or divide the field with a boundary; they sought all things for the common store.* <note>original: "Nec signare solum, aut partiri limite campum / Fas erat: in medium quaerebant." Quotation from Virgil’s *Georgics*, 1.126-127, describing the Golden Age of Saturn.</note>

Therefore, the common money of the people was placed in the care of him under whom all things had been universal and common to all. I should not omit the fact that **Tritons** <note>Mythological sea-creatures, half-man and half-fish.</note> with trumpets were placed upon the roof of the Temple of Saturn, because from the <margin>*commemoration</margin> commemoration of his time down to our own age, history is clear and, as it were, vocal; but before his time, it was mute, obscure, and unknown. This is symbolized by the <margin>Why Tritons are on the Temple of Saturn.</margin> tails of the Tritons, which are plunged into and hidden in the earth. However, as to why **Saturn** himself <margin>Why Saturn has feet bound in wool.</margin> is seen in fetters, **Verrius Flaccus** <note>A famous Roman grammarian and teacher from the era of Augustus.</note> says he does not know the reason, but a reading of **Apollodorus** <note>Likely the Athenian mythographer.</note> suggests it to me. Apollodorus says that Saturn is bound throughout the year with a woolen bond, and is only released on his festival day—that is, in this month of December. And from this the proverb is derived: **"The gods have woolen feet."** <note>original: "Deos laneos pedes habere." This proverb suggests that divine vengeance or intervention arrives silently and slowly, but surely.</note> This signifies that in the tenth month, the seed animated in the womb grows toward life; until it breaks forth into the light, it is held by the soft bonds of nature. Furthermore, he is both **Kronos** and **Chronos**. <note>original: "κρόνος καὶ χρόνος." Praetextatus is using a common ancient Greek wordplay connecting the name of the Titan (Kronos) with the word for Time (Chronos).</note> For to the extent that myth-makers pull Saturn apart with their fictions, the natural philosophers <term>physici</term> <note>Scholars who explained myths as allegories for natural forces.</note> restore him to a certain likeness of the truth. They say that he cut off the private parts of his father **Caelus** <note>Heaven/Uranus.</note>; when these were cast into the sea, **Venus** was procreated, who received the name **Aphrodite** from the foam <note>original: "ἀφροδίτη" (Aphrodite), derived from the Greek word "aphros" meaning foam.</note> from which she was formed. From this, they <margin>What is Time.</margin> wish it to be understood that when there was **Chaos**, there was no time. Indeed, time is a fixed measurement, which is gathered from the revolution of the heavens. Time began from that point. From Caelus himself, **Kronos** is thought to have been born, who (as we have said) is **Chronos** (Time). And since the seeds of all things to be created after the heavens flowed down from the heavens, and the universal elements...

### BOOK I.

...also records in the first book of the *History of Italy* <note>Referring to the historian Xenon, mentioned earlier in the text</note> that **Janus** was the first in Italy to build temples to the gods and establish sacred rites. For this reason, he earned the honor of being named first in the preface of every sacrifice. Some think he is called "two-faced" <note>original: *bifrons*</note> because he knew the past and foresaw the future.

<margin>Who the god Janus was.</margin>
But the natural philosophers <term>Physici: scholars who sought the physical or scientific explanation behind myths</term> sanctify him with even stronger arguments for his divinity. For there are those who say that Janus is the same as both **Apollo** and **Diana**, and they affirm that both deities are expressed in this single divinity. Indeed, as **Nigidius** <note>Publius Nigidius Figulus, a famous Roman scholar and contemporary of Cicero</note> also reports, among the Greeks Apollo is worshipped as the "god of the door" <note>original: θυραῖος (*thyraios*)</note>. They celebrate his altars before their own doors, showing that he is powerful over exits and entrances. This same Apollo is also called by them the "god of the streets" <note>original: ἀγυιεύς (*agyieus*)</note>, as if he were the one placed in charge of urban roads. For they call the streets that are within the sacred city boundaries <note>original: *pomoeria*</note> "ways" <note>original: ἀγυιὰς (*agyiai*)</note>. To **Diana**, moreover, as the goddess "of the three ways" <note>original: *Trivia*</note>, they attribute power over all roads. But among us, the name **Janus** shows that he presides over all doors <note>original: *ianuis*</note>, which is similar to the Greek "god of the door." Indeed, he is also depicted with a key and a rod, as the guardian of all gates and the ruler of roads. Nigidius declared that Apollo is Janus, and Diana is **Iana**, with the letter 'D' added for the sake of elegance—a letter which is often added to the letter 'I' for such a reason, as in "is returned" <note>original: *reditur*</note>, "is held back" <note>original: *redhibetur*</note>, "is restored" <note>original: *redintegratur*</note>, and similar words.

Some wish to show that Janus is the **Sun**, and therefore he is "twin-faced," as if powerful over both celestial gates: opening the day as he rises and closing it as he sets. He is invoked first when a divine sacrifice is celebrated for any god, so that through him access to the specific god being sacrificed to might be opened—as if he himself transmits the prayers of the suppliants through his gates to the other gods. For this reason, his statue is also frequently fashioned holding the number three hundred in his right hand and sixty-five in his left <note>Roman numerals were often represented by finger counting or "digital notation"</note>, to demonstrate the measurement of the year, which is the chief power of the Sun. Others have wanted him to be the World—that is, the Heavens—and said that Janus is named from "going" <note>original: *ab eundo*</note>, because the world [is always moving]...

From this, the Phoenicians also, when expressing his image in their sacred rites, depicted a serpent coiled into a circle and devouring its own tail, to show that the world is both nourished from itself and revolves back into itself. For this reason, among us, he looks in four directions, as demonstrated by his statue brought from <margin>\*Falerii <note>The Latin text reads "Phalaris," but the marginal note and historical context suggest it refers to the town of Falerii</note></margin> **Falerii**. **C. Even **Marcus Messala**, who was the colleague of **Gnaeus Domitius** in the consulship and an **Augur** <term>a Roman priest who interpreted the will of the gods through the flight of birds</term> for fifty-five years, speaks thus concerning Janus:

> He who fashions all things and rules them, has joined together the heavy and downward-leaning nature of water and earth, which slides into the depths, with the light nature of fire and spirit, which flees into the immense heights; by surrounding them with the heavens, the greatest power of the sky has bound these two disparate forces together.

<margin>Various surnames of Janus.</margin>
In sacred rites, we also invoke **Janus the Twin**, **Father Janus**, **Junonian Janus**, **Consivian Janus**, **Quirinian Janus**, **Patultian Janus**, and **Clausian Janus**. Why we invoke him as "Twin," we have already said above. We call him "Father" as the "God of Gods." We call him "Junonian" because he holds the entrance not only to the month of January but to the beginning of all months. Indeed, all the **Kalends** <term>the first day of each Roman month</term> are under the jurisdiction of **Juno**. Hence **Varro** also writes in the fifth book of *Human Affairs* that twelve altars were dedicated to Janus for the twelve months. We call him "Consivius" from "sowing" <note>original: *a conferendo*</note>, that is, from the propagation of the human race, which is sown under the authority of Janus. We call him "Quirinus" as one powerful in wars, from the spear which the **Sabines** <note>An ancient Italic tribe</note> call a *curis*. The following reason is given for this practice: during the **Sabine** War, which was fought because of the abduction of the maidens, the **Romans** were hurrying to close the gate located at the foot of the **Viminal Hill** (which was afterwards named **Janualis** due to this event), because the enemy were rushing into it. After it was closed, it immediately flew open of its own accord. When this had happened a second and third time, many armed men stood as guards before the threshold since they were unable to close it. While a fierce battle was being fought on the other side, news suddenly arrived that our men had been routed by **Tatius** <note>Titus Tatius, King of the Sabines</note>. For this reason, the **Romans** who were guarding the entrance fled in terror. Just as the **Sabines** were about to burst through the open gate, it is said that from the Temple of **Janus** a massive torrent of water erupted through this gate, with gushing waves; many of the enemy bands either perished being scalded by the boiling water or were swallowed up by the swift whirlpool <gloss>whirl</gloss> <note>original: *uoragine*; gloss: *uortigine*</note>. Because of this event, it was decreed that during time of war the doors should be unlocked, as if the God had set out to aid the city. So much for **Janus**.

---

### On which day the Saturnalia were customarily celebrated, and that they were first celebrated for only one day, and later for several days.
->CAP. X.<-

But to return to the **Saturnalia**: it was considered a sin to begin a war during the **Saturnalia**. To demand punishment from a guilty person during those same days is a matter requiring atonement. Among our ancestors, the **Saturnalia** were finished in a single day, which was the fourteenth day before the **Kalends of January** <note>December 19th</note>. But after **Gaius Caesar** <note>Julius Caesar</note> added two days to this month, they began to be celebrated on the sixteenth day before the Kalends <note>December 17th</note>. It thus happened that because the common people did not know the specific day of the **Saturnalia**—some celebrating on the uncertain day introduced by **Gaius Caesar** and others according to the old custom—the **Saturnalia** came to be counted over several days. However, even among the ancients there was an opinion that the **Saturnalia** lasted for seven days—if that can be called an "opinion" which is confirmed by reliable authors.

### OF THE SATURNALIA
<header>OF THE SATURNALIA</header>

<margin>Nonius, writer of Atellan farces.</margin>
...confirmed by many authors. For **Nonius**, a most esteemed writer of **Atellan farces** <term>Atellan farces: early Italian comedic plays featuring stock characters and ribald humor</term>, says: *Long awaited come the seven days of the Saturnalia.* **Mummius** also—who, after **Nonius** and **Pomponius**, revived the long-dormant **Atellan** art—remarked: "Our ancestors, who established so many good things, did this best of all against the peak of winter: seven days of the **Saturnalia**." But **Mallius** says that those who (as we said above) defended themselves through the name and worship of **Saturn**, established three days of festival and called them the **Saturnalia**. Hence **Augustus**, following this opinion, ordered in his judicial laws that a three-day holiday be observed. **Masurius** and others believed the **Saturnalia** occurred on a single day, namely the fourteenth day before the **Calends** of January <note>December 19th; in the Roman calendar, dates were counted backward from the first of the following month</note>. **Fenestella** confirms their opinion, stating that the virgin **Aemilia** was condemned on the fifteenth before the **Calends** of January <note>December 18th</note>; if the **Saturnalia** were being celebrated on that day, she would not have pleaded her case at all <note>legal proceedings were forbidden during these festivals</note>. He then added: "The **Saturnalia** followed that day." Soon after he says: "On the next day, which was the thirteenth before the **Calends** of January <note>December 20th</note>, the virgin **Licinia** was ordered to plead her case." From this he shows that the festival had departed <note>original: *profectum*; meaning the festival had ended</note> by the thirteenth before the **Calends**.

<margin>The 12th.</margin>
On the twelfth <note>December 21st</note>, however, is the festival of the goddess **Angeronia**, to whom the priests perform a sacrifice in the chapel of **Volupia**. **Verrius Flaccus** says she is called **Angeronia** because, when appeased, she drives away anguishes <note>Latin: *angores*</note> and anxieties of the mind. **Masurius** adds that the statue of this goddess is placed on the altar of **Volupia** with her mouth bound and sealed for this reason: that those who conceal their pains and anxieties attain, through the benefit of patience, the greatest pleasure <note>original: *uoluptatem*; this explains why her statue was in the shrine of Volupia, the personification of pleasure</note>. **Julius Modestus** says that sacrifice is made to this goddess because the **Roman** people were delivered from the disease called *angina* <note>a throat infection or quinsy</note> after making a vow. On the eleventh before the **Calends** <note>December 22nd</note>, the festival is dedicated to the **Lares** <term>Lares: guardian deities of the household and the city</term>, for whom the praetor **Aemilius Regillus** vowed to oversee a temple in the **Campus Martius** during the war against **Antiochus**. On the tenth before the **Calends** <note>December 23rd</note> are the festivals of **Jupiter**, which are called the **Larentinalia**; concerning these, because to tell stories...

# BOOK I.

If one pleases, these are the opinions: For they say that during the reign of Ancus <note>Ancus Marcius, the fourth King of Rome</note>, the temple warden of Hercules, having nothing to do during the holidays, challenged the God to a game of dice <note>original: "tesseris"</note>, with himself playing for both sides. He added a condition: that whoever lost should pay for a dinner and a prostitute <note>original: "scorto"</note>. Thus, when Hercules won, the warden locked the famous prostitute of that time, Acca Larentia, inside the temple along with a dinner. The rumor spread the next day that after she had shared the bed of the God, she received a reward: that she should not spurn the first opportunity offered to her when she returned home.

<margin>Gellius, Book 6, Chapter 7.</margin>
And so it happened that as she left the temple, she was soon approached by a man named Carutius, who was captivated by her beauty. These holidays were also consecrated to Jupiter, because the ancients believed that souls are given by Jupiter and are returned to him again after death. Cato <note>Cato the Elder, the famous Roman statesman and historian</note> says that Larentia, having grown wealthy through the trade of a courtesan, left the lands of Turace, Semurium, <margin>* also: Litirium</margin> \* Lincerium, and Solinium to the Roman people after her death; and for this reason, she was deemed worthy of a magnificent tomb and the honor of an annual funeral rite. Macer <note>Licinius Macer, a Roman historian and politician</note> confirms in the first book of his *Histories* that Acca Larentia, the wife of Faustulus, was the nurse of Romulus and Remus. He states that during the reign of Romulus, she was married to a certain wealthy Etruscan named Carutius and was enriched by her husband's inheritance, which she later left to Romulus, whom she had raised. Because of this, he established a funeral festival and a feast day out of piety. From all these accounts, therefore, it can be gathered that the Saturnalia lasted for only one day and was celebrated only on the fourteenth day before the Calends of January <note>December 19th</note>. On that day alone, at the temple of Saturn, once the banquet was finished, "Saturnalia!" would be shouted. ### OF THE SATURNALIA

[The festival] is assigned <note>The word "nalia" in the OCR is the conclusion of "Saturnalia" from the previous page</note>, since it was first ascribed equally to Saturn and Ops. Now, they believed this goddess Ops to be the wife of Saturn; and for this reason, both the Saturnalia and the Opalia <note>A festival held on December 19th</note> are celebrated in this month, because Saturn and his wife are believed to be the discoverers of both grain and fruit. Therefore, once all the produce of the fields has been gathered, these gods are worshipped by men as the authors of a more civilized life. Some are even persuaded that these gods are Heaven and Earth: and that Saturn is named from "sowing" <note>original: "a satu"; a popular but scientifically doubtful Roman etymology</note>, the cause of which comes from heaven; and that the Earth is Ops, by whose help <note>original: "ope"</note> the nourishments of human life are sought, or from the "work" <note>original: "ab opere"</note> through which fruits and grains are born. To this goddess, they offer vows while seated, and they intentionally touch the earth, demonstrating that Mother Earth herself is to be sought by mortals. Philochorus <note>An Athenian historian of the 3rd century BCE</note> says that Cecrops <note>The mythical first king of Athens</note> first established an altar to Saturn and Ops in Attica, and worshipped those gods as Jupiter and the Earth. He also established that fathers of families, once the grain and fruit were gathered, should eat everywhere with their slaves, with whom they had endured the burden of labor in tilling the countryside; for the god is delighted by the honor shown to slaves in recognition of their labor. It is from this foreign custom that we perform the sacrifice to this god with an uncovered head <note>The "Greek rite" (ritua Graecus) involved sacrificing with the head bare, unlike the standard Roman practice of covering the head with a toga</note>. I believe we have now abundantly proved that the Saturnalia used to be celebrated on only one day, that is, the fourteenth day before the Calends <note>December 17th</note>. But later it was extended to three days, first from the days added to this month by Caesar <note>Julius Caesar's calendar reform added two days to December, which shifted the counting of days</note>, and then by an edict of Augustus, by which he assigned a three-day holiday to the Saturnalia. Thus, starting from the sixteenth day <note>December 15th</note> they end on the fourteenth, the only day on which they were previously accustomed to be held. But the added celebration of the Sigillaria <note>A festival of gift-giving, named for the "sigilla" or small clay figurines sold at the time</note> extends the public commotion and religious joy to seven days.

That the lot of slaves is not to be despised, since the gods themselves care for them, and many among them are faithful, foresightful...

<margin>Slaves are not to be despised by their masters, since they consist of the same elements; and slavery is a flaw of fortune, not of humanity.</margin>

Do you see how much care for a slave reached even the highest of the gods? But as for you, from where does such a vast and monstrous disgust for slaves arise? As if they do not consist of and are not nourished by the same elements as you; as if they do not draw the same breath from the same source. Will you not consider that those whom you call your property were born from the same seeds, enjoy the same sky, and live and die just as you do? They are slaves; rather, they are men. They are slaves; rather, they are fellow-slaves. If you consider that fortune has as much power over both, you can see that man as a free man just as easily as he might see you as a slave. Do you not know at what age Hecuba <note>The Queen of Troy, enslaved after the city fell</note> began her servitude, or Croesus <note>The famously wealthy King of Lydia</note>, or the mother of Darius, or Diogenes <note>The Cynic philosopher, reportedly captured by pirates and sold</note>, or even Plato himself? Finally, why do we shudder so at the name of slavery? A man is a slave, yes, but by necessity; yet perhaps he is a slave with a free mind. This status will only harm him if you can show me who is *not* a slave. One is a slave to lust, another to greed, another to ambition, and all are slaves to hope and all to fear. And certainly, no slavery is more disgraceful than that which is voluntary. Yet we trample upon a man lying under a yoke imposed by fortune as if he were wretched and vile; meanwhile, we do not allow ourselves to be criticized for the yokes we place upon our own necks. You will find among slaves someone stronger than money; you will find a master who, out of hope for profit, kisses the hands of other people's slaves. Therefore, I shall not value men by their fortune, but by their character. Each person gives themselves their own character, but chance assigns their status. Just as he is a fool who, intending to buy a horse, does not inspect the horse itself but rather its saddle and bridle; so he is the most foolish of all who values a man either by his clothes or by his status, which is merely a garment wrapped around us...

<margin>Why slaves are sometimes enemies to their masters.</margin>

<margin>*Alternatively: At home</margin>

Thus it happens that those who are not allowed to speak *in the presence* of the master speak *about* the master. <margin>The loyalty of slaves toward their masters</margin>
Shall we review those virtues practiced within the heart of a slave? First, let Urbinus occur to you. When he had been ordered to be killed and was hiding in Reate <note>A town in central Italy, modern-day Rieti</note>, his hiding place was betrayed. One of his slaves, having put on his master's ring and robe, lay in the bedroom toward which the pursuers were rushing. When the soldiers entered, he offered his neck and received the blow as if he were Urbinus himself. Afterward, when Urbinus was restored to his position, he built a monument to the slave, adding an inscription that spoke of such great merit. 

Aesopus, the freedman <term>libertus: a former slave who has been legally freed</term> of Demosthenes <note>likely referring to a Roman figure involved in the scandals of the Augustan era, rather than the famous Greek orator</note>, was aware of the adultery that his patron had committed with Julia <note>the daughter of Emperor Augustus</note>. Although he was tortured for a very long time, he persisted in not betraying his patron, until Demosthenes himself confessed when other accomplices proved the crime. 

And lest you think a secret can easily be hidden by just one person: when Labienus was hiding with the help of his freedmen, they could not be compelled by any kind of torture to reveal him. 

And lest anyone say that freedmen owed this loyalty more to the benefit of having received their freedom than to their natural character, hear now of a slave's kindness toward his master, even when he himself was being punished by that master. When Antius Restio was proscribed <term>proscriptum: placed on a public list of enemies of the state whose property was confiscated and who could be killed with impunity</term> and was fleeing alone at night while others were plundering his goods, a slave of his—who had been kept in chains and whose forehead had been branded <note>original: *inscripta fronte*. Branding was a common punishment for slaves who had attempted to run away</note>—followed him in his flight. After his master’s condemnation, the slave had been released from someone else’s custody. He urged the master not to fear him, saying he knew the insult to his person should be blamed on fortune, not on his master. He then hid and fed his master through his own efforts. Later, when he sensed the pursuers were near, he killed an old man who happened to be there by chance and threw him onto a constructed funeral pyre. Once it was lit, he met those who were searching for Restio, telling them that the condemned man had paid his penalty to him, and that he had tormented him much more severely than he himself had been tormented. Because his word was believed, Restio was saved.

# BOOK I.

...[the slave] carried [his master] to the Tiber in a chest. Having been conveyed to Ostia <note>The primary port city of ancient Rome</note> and into the Laurentine territory, he led him to his father's villa by a journey at night. Later, at Cumae, when his master was cast ashore by a shipwreck, the slave secretly hid him in Naples. Even when he was caught by a Centurion, he could not be induced by reward or threats to betray his master. Furthermore, when Asinius Pollio <note>A Roman statesman and historian (75 BC – AD 4)</note> was harshly forcing the people of Padua to contribute money and weapons—and because of this the masters were in hiding—a reward of freedom was offered to any slaves who would betray their masters. It is well known that not a single slave, overcome by the reward, betrayed his master.

Hear now, regarding slaves, not only of their loyalty, but also of a mind fertile in clever invention. When a siege was pressing the city of Grumentum <note>A city in Lucania, southern Italy, besieged during the Social War in 90 BC</note>, certain slaves left their mistress and fled to the enemy. Later, when the town was captured, they formed a conspiracy and made an attack on the house. They dragged their mistress out with faces threatening punishment, declaring loudly to anyone they met that at last the opportunity had been given to them to punish their cruel mistress. Having snatched her away as if for execution, they instead protected her with services full of devotion.

Observe also in this status of life a greatness of soul that treats the approach of death as a trifle. <margin>Gaius Vectius</margin> When Gaius Vectius Cluentius, a Paelignian of the Italian party, was seized by his own cohorts to be handed over to Pompey, his slave killed him; then, so that he would not survive his master, the slave killed himself. When Gaius Gracchus <note>The famous Roman populist reformer, died 121 BC</note> was fleeing from the Aventine Hill, his slave Euporus—or as some report, Philocrates—remained an inseparable companion as long as there was any hope of safety, protecting him by whatever means he could. Then, over the body of his slain master, he poured out his own life, his entrails torn by a self-inflicted wound. A slave placed Publius Scipio himself (the father of Scipio Africanus) upon a horse after he had fought with Hannibal and was wounded; and while all others were deserting, the slave alone led him back to the camp.

It would be a small thing to have served masters while they were living; what of the fact that in these men there is also found a spiritedness for exacting vengeance? For a slave of King Seleucus, when he was serving a friend...

Then, when the boys had reached adulthood, he handed over both the property and the power; he himself, having taken a small travel allowance, set out and grew old at Olympia with the greatest tranquility.

<margin>
The deeds and bravery of slaves in wars.
</margin>
How much the condition of slavery has benefited the public good is shown by many examples. In the Punic War <note>The great conflict between Rome and Carthage</note>, when there was a shortage of men to be drafted, slaves promised they would fight for their masters; they were admitted into the citizenry and called *Volones* <term>Volones: from the Latin 'volo', meaning 'I will' or 'I want', because they volunteered for service rather than being conscripted</term>. At Cannae also <note>A disastrous Roman defeat by Hannibal in 216 BC</note>, after the Romans were defeated, eight thousand slaves were purchased and served as soldiers; even though captives could have been ransomed for less, the Republic preferred to entrust itself to slaves in such a great storm. But also after the disaster at Lake Trasimene <note>Another major Roman defeat against Hannibal in 217 BC</note>, where a famous defeat was suffered, freedmen too were called to take the military oath. In the Social War <note>A conflict (91–87 BC) between the Roman Republic and several of its Italian allies</note>, the work of twelve cohorts recruited from freedmen appeared with memorable courage. We have learned that when Caesar was replacing soldiers in the place of those lost, he also accepted slaves from his friends and made use of their brave service. Augustus Caesar in Germany and Illyria chose several cohorts of freedmen, which he called "volunteers." Lest you think these things happened only in our Republic, the people of Borysthenes <note>A Greek colony on the Black Sea coast</note>, when Zopyrion <note>A general of Alexander the Great</note> was attacking, were able to withstand the enemy by freeing their slaves, giving citizenship to foreigners, and canceling debts <note>original: 'tabulis novis', literally 'new tablets', referring to the wiping clean of debt records</note>. # BOOK I.

<margin>The origin of the Sigillaria.</margin>
I think you have seen it proven that the name of "slave" should not be looked down upon with disdain; for even Jupiter has shown concern for slaves, and it is well established that many of them have proven to be faithful, far-sighted, brave, and even philosophers. Now I must briefly review the matter of the *Sigillaria* <note>The final days of the Saturnalia festival, named after the small clay figurines (*sigilla*) sold and gifted at that time</note>, lest you think I have spoken of jokes rather than sacred things. Epicadus <note>An ancient Roman grammarian</note> reports that after Hercules killed Geryon <note>A giant with three bodies whose cattle Hercules stole as one of his Labors</note> and led the herds through Italy as a victor, he built a temporary bridge (now called the Sublician Bridge) and threw human effigies into the river. He did this according to the number of companions he had lost by chance during his travels, so that the following current might carry them to the sea and return them, as it were, to their ancestral homes in place of their actual bodies. From this, the custom of fashioning such images remained as part of the religious rites.

But to me, a truer origin of this practice is the one I recall mentioning a little earlier: that after a more favorable interpretation of an oracle, the Pelasgians <note>A term for the ancient, pre-Greek inhabitants of the Mediterranean</note> were taught that "heads" meant not those of living men, but ones made of clay <gloss>fictitious</gloss>, and that the word *phota* <note>original Greek: φωτὰ</note> signified not only "man" but also "light." Thus, they began to light wax candles <note>original: *cereos*</note> for Saturn instead of sacrificing men, and they carried certain little masks <note>original: *oscilla*</note> to the chapel of Dis <note>The god of the underworld, also called Pluto</note>—which is joined to Saturn's altar—as a substitute for their own heads. From this comes the tradition of sending wax candles as gifts during the Saturnalia, and of crafting figurines <note>original: *sigilla*</note> from clay to be sold. These are things that men offer to Dis and Saturn as a propitiatory offering <note>original: *piaculum*</note> for themselves and their families. This is why the bustle of such trade began during the Saturnalia; it occupies seven days, which the law designates as holidays, though not all are official festival days. For we have proved that the festival itself falls in the middle, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends <note>December 17th</note>; this has been confirmed by the assertions of others who have more fully recorded the system of the year, months, and days, and the arrangement organized by Julius Caesar.

...to discourse so pleasantly on the nature of the year as well, before you experience the annoyance of someone asking you: for perhaps someone among those present is unaware of what order existed among the ancients, or by what more certain rules it was later renewed. To learn this, you yourself seem to me to have stirred the minds of the listeners by discussing the days added to the month. Then, with the same flow of speech, he wove together the remaining parts.

<margin>Uncertainty of the length of the year.</margin>
A certain measurement of the year existed always among the Egyptians alone; among other nations, the year wavered with an unequal number of days and an equal amount of error. To be content with reporting the custom of only a few regions: the Arcadians <note>An ancient people from the central Peloponnese in Greece</note> explained their year in three months; the Acarnanians <note>People from western Greece</note> in six; the rest of the Greeks calculated their own year as three hundred and fifty-four days. It is no wonder, then, in this variety, that the Romans also once had their year organized into ten months, under the authority of Romulus. This was because the year began in March and was completed in 304 days. Thus, six months—namely April, June, Sextilis <note>The "sixth" month, later renamed August in honor of Augustus Caesar</note>, September, November, and December—consisted of thirty days; while four—March, May, Quintilis <note>The "fifth" month, later renamed July in honor of Julius Caesar</note>, and October—were completed in thirty-one days. These latter four still today have their "Nones" <note>The Roman day-marker usually falling on the 5th or 7th of the month</note> on the seventh day, while the others have them on the fifth. 

For the months that had seven-day Nones, the Kalends <note>The first day of the following month</note> returned on the seventeenth day after the Ides <note>The midpoint of the month, falling on the 13th or 15th</note>. However, for those with five-day Nones, the start of the Kalends returned on the eighteenth day.

<margin>The first month, March.</margin>
This was the arrangement of Romulus, who dedicated the first month of the year to his father, Mars. That this was the first month of the year is proven most strongly by this: that Quintilis is the fifth month from it, and the following months were named according to their numerical order. Also, on the first day of this month, they used to light the new fire on the altars of Vesta <note>The goddess of the hearth; her sacred fire was essential to Rome's safety</note>, so that as the year began, the care of guarding the renewed fire would begin anew. Likewise, at the start of the same month, in the palace, the *curiae* <note>Ancient political and religious divisions of the Roman people</note>, and the houses of the Flamens <note>High-ranking priests dedicated to specific gods</note>, old laurels were replaced with new [laurels...] <note>The original text cuts off mid-word "laureis" at the end of the page</note>.

He details the specific day-counts and religious rituals, such as the lighting of Vesta's fire, that marked the new year.</summary>

Indeed, even in the twelve signs of the **Zodiac**, which are believed to be the specific dwellings of specific gods: while the first sign, **Aries** <note>The Ram</note>, is assigned to Mars, the following sign, **Taurus** <note>The Bull</note>, was immediately received by Venus. <margin>Cincius</margin> **Cingius** <note>likely Cincius Alimentus, an early Roman historian and legal scholar</note>, in the book he left behind *On the Calendar*, states that some people ignorantly think the ancients named the month of **April** after **Venus**, since no festival day and no significant sacrifice to Venus was established by our ancestors during this month. Furthermore, not even in the songs of the **Salii** <note>The "Leaping Priests" of Mars who sang ancient ritual hymns called the *Carmen Saliare*</note> is any praise of Venus celebrated, as is done for the other heavenly beings. <margin>Cincius</margin> **Varro** also agrees with Cingius, asserting that the name of Venus did not even exist among the Romans under the kings—in either Latin or Greek—and therefore the month could not have been named after Venus. 

But since, generally before the vernal equinox, the sky is gloomy and covered with clouds, and the sea is closed to sailors, and the lands themselves are covered by water, frost, or snow; and since all these things open up in the spring—that is, in this month—and the trees, no less than all other things contained in the earth, begin to open themselves into buds: for all these reasons, it is rightly believed that the month is called **April**, as if it were *Aperilis* <note>original: *Aperilem*; derived from the Latin verb *aperire*, meaning "to open"</note>. This is just as among the Athenians the same month is called **Anthesterion** <note>original: ἀνθεστηριών</note>, from the fact that at this time all things are in bloom. Nevertheless, **Verrius Flaccus** <note>A famous Roman grammarian of the Augustan age</note> does not deny that it was later established that on this day <note>the first of April</note> the matrons should perform a sacrifice to Venus. The reason for this, because it does not suit the current topic, must be passed over.

# BOOK I.

The priest of Vulcan <note>original: *Vulcanalis*; the *Flamen Vulcanalis* was the high priest of the god of fire</note> performs a sacred rite to this goddess on the **Kalends of May** <note>The first day of the month</note>. But **Piso** <note>Lucius Calpurnius Piso Frugi, a Roman historian and statesman</note> says the wife of **Vulcan** is called **Maiesta**, not **Maia**. Others contend that **Maia**, the mother of **Mercury**, gave her name to the month; they prove this primarily because in this month all merchants sacrifice to Maia and Mercury together. 

Some affirm—and **Cornelius Labeo** <note>A 3rd-century scholar of Roman religion and theology</note> agrees with them—that this **Maia**, to whom the sacred rite is celebrated in the month of May, is the **Earth**. She acquired this name from her magnitude <note>original: *magnitudo*; the author links the name Maia to *maior*, meaning "greater"</note>, just as she is called the "Great Mother" in sacred rites. They gather support for this opinion from the fact that a pregnant sow is sacrificed to her, which is a sacrificial victim specifically appropriate for the Earth. They also say that Mercury is joined to her in these rites because the human voice is given to a newborn upon contact with the earth. We know, moreover, that **Mercury** is the master of voice and speech. 

Cornelius Labeo is the authority stating that a temple was dedicated to this Maia (that is, the Earth) on the Kalends of May under the name of the **Good Goddess** <note>original: *Bona Dea*, a divinity associated with chastity and fertility whose rites were for women only</note>. He confirms that it can be shown from the more secret nature of the rituals themselves that the Good Goddess and the Earth are the same. He says that this same goddess is invoked in the books of the **Pontiffs** <note>The high priests who oversaw the Roman state religion</note> by the names **Good Goddess**, **Fauna**, **Ops**, and **Fatua**. 

She is called "**Good**" because she is the source of everything that provides for our sustenance; "**Fauna**" because she favors <note>original: *fauet*</note> every need of living creatures; "**Ops**" because life is sustained by her help <note>original: *auxilium*</note>; and "**Fatua**" from "speaking" <note>original: *fando*</note> because, as we stated above, infants brought forth in birth do not utter a sound before they have touched the earth. 

There are those who say this goddess has the power of **Juno**, and therefore a royal scepter is placed in her left hand. Others believe her to be **Proserpina**, and a sacred rite is performed for her with a sow, because the sow devoured the grain which **Ceres** gave to mortals. Others call her **Chthonic Hecate** <note>original: χθονίαν ἑκάτην; "Hecate of the Underworld"</note>. The Boeotians believe her to be **Semele**, and they also say she is the daughter of **Faunus**. They claim she resisted the will of her father when he had fallen in love with her, resulting in her being beaten by him with a myrtle rod; when she would not yield to her father's desire, even though he plied her with wine, she nevertheless transformed herself into a serpent

<margin>*Gynaikonitis*—the women's quarters, or a private room for women.</margin>
...it is believed [Faunus] was her father, and that he had relations with his daughter. As evidence for all this, they put forward the fact that it is a sacrilege to have a myrtle branch in her temple; that a vine is spread over her head—the method by which her father chiefly tried to deceive her <note>According to myth, Faunus beat his daughter with myrtle when she resisted his advances, and later seduced her by turning himself into a snake or by getting her drunk on wine (hence the vine and snake motifs)</note>; and that wine is usually brought into her temple not under its own name, but the vessel in which the wine is placed is called a **honey-jar** <note>original: *mellarium*</note>, and the wine is called **milk** <note>original: *lac*</note>. Furthermore, snakes appear in her temple, neither terrifying nor afraid, moving about freely. Some think she is **Medea** <note>The famous sorceress of Greek myth</note>, because every kind of herb is found in her shrine, from which the priestesses often provide medicines; and because no man is allowed to enter her temple on account of the injury she suffered from the ungrateful **Jason**. Among the Greeks, she is called the **women's goddess** <note>original: *theos gynaikeia*</note>. **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a prolific Roman scholar</note> recorded that she was the daughter of **Faunus**—so modest that she never stepped outside the **women's quarters** <note>original: *gynaikonitis*</note>, nor was her name ever heard in public, nor did she ever see a man or was she seen by one. For this reason, no man enters her temple. 

Similarly, women in Italy are not allowed to participate in the sacred rite of **Hercules**. This is because when Hercules was driving the cattle of **Geryon** through the fields of Italy, a woman told the thirsty hero that she could not provide water because the day of the **women's goddess** was being celebrated, and it was not divine law for men to taste anything from that preparation. Because of this, when Hercules was about to perform a sacrifice, he cursed the presence of women and ordered the **Potitii** and **Pinarii** <note>Two distinguished Roman families who traditionally served as priests of Hercules</note>, the guardians of the rites, not to allow any woman to be present. Here, then, is the origin of the name, by which we said **Maia** is the same as the **Earth** and the **Good Goddess**; the occasion has compelled us to bring forth whatever we have discovered about the **Good Goddess**.

<margin>The fourth month: June.</margin>

This was so much the case that (as **Nisus** says in his *Commentaries on the Calendars*)...

Among our ancestors as well, this naming of the month <note>June</note> remained for a long time; but later, after certain letters were worn away, it was called **June** <note>original: *Iunius*</note> instead of "Junonian" <note>original: *Iunonio*, after the goddess Juno</note>. For the temple to **Juno Moneta** <note>Juno "The Advisor" or "The Warner," where the Roman mint was located</note> was also dedicated on the **Kalends** <note>The first day</note> of June. Some have thought that the month of June was named after **Junius Brutus**, who was made the first consul of Rome: because in this month—that is, on the Kalends of June, after **Tarquin** <note>Tarquinius Superbus, the last king of Rome</note> was expelled—he fulfilled a vow by performing sacred rites for the goddess **Carna** on the Caelian Hill. They believe this goddess presides over the human vitals. From her, it is requested that she keep the liver, the heart, and whatever organs are within safe and sound. And because Brutus proved himself fit for the reform of the public state by the benefit of his "heart"—the concealment of which led to his reputation <note>Brutus's name means "dullard"; he feigned stupidity to survive the reign of the tyrant Tarquin</note>—he consecrated a temple to this goddess who presides over the vitals. She is sacrificed to with bean-mash and bacon, because bodily strength is greatly bolstered by these things. For the Kalends of June are also commonly called the **Bean Kalends** <note>original: *fabariæ*</note>, because in this month mature beans are used in religious rituals.

</margin>
**July** <note>original: *Iulius*</note> follows. According to the arrangement of **Romulus**, where March held the beginning of the year, it was called **Quintilis** <note>The Fifth</note> from its number. But later, in honor of **Julius Caesar** the Dictator, it was named July by a law proposed by the consul **Mark Antony**, son of Marcus: because in this month, on the fourth day before the **Ides** <note>The 12th of July</note> of Quintilis, Julius was born.

The month of **September** retains its original name <note>September comes from *septem*, meaning "seven"</note>, despite the attempted naming after **Germanicus** <note>Several emperors tried to rename September to honor Germanicus, the popular general, but the people reverted to the original name</note>.

<margin>
The eighth, October: which November and December follow.
</margin>
**Domitian** <note>An emperor often remembered as a tyrant</note> had indeed seized **October** for his own name. But when it was decided that his ill-omened name should be erased from every piece of bronze or stone <note>A reference to *damnatio memoriae*, where the memory of a disgraced ruler was officially erased from public records</note>, the months were also stripped of their usurped tyrannical titles. The caution of subsequent emperors, who avoided ill-omened names of disastrous memory, preserved the ancient names for the months from September through **December**.

This was the annual measurement ordained by **Romulus**, who (as we have already said above) established that the year should consist of ten months, comprising three hundred and four days. He arranged the months so that four of them had thirty-one days, while six had thirty. But since that number agreed neither with the course of the sun nor the logic of the moon, it sometimes happened through practice that the cold of the year occurred during summer months, and conversely, the heat occurred in winter months. Whenever that happened, they allowed as many days to pass without any month name as were necessary to reach that time of year where the appearance of the sky would be found appropriate for the month at hand.

# BOOK I.

<meta>catchword: Since</meta>

...sacrifices were believed to be necessary, the year should be extended. To these fifty days he had added, he joined another six, taken from those six months which previously had thirty days—that is, one day from each. These fifty-six days he divided equally into two new months. Of these two, he named the first **January** and wished it to be the first of the year, as the month of the **two-faced God** <note>original: *bicipitis Dei*; referring to Janus, the god of beginnings, gates, and transitions</note>, looking back toward the end of the past year and forward toward the beginnings of the future. The second month he dedicated to the god **Februus**, who is believed to have power over purifications <term>lustrations</term>. It was necessary for the city to be purified <note>original: *lustrari*; a ritual cleansing of the community</note> in that month, at which time he decreed that the proper rites should be paid to the **spirits of the dead** <note>original: *dijs manibus*; the Manes, or ancestral spirits</note>.

The neighboring peoples soon followed Numa’s arrangement; they began to calculate their own year with as many days and as many months as **Pompilius** <note>Numa Pompilius, the legendary second king of Rome</note> had decided. But they differed in this one respect: they alternated their months between twenty-nine and thirty days in number.

Shortly thereafter, Numa—with nature having brought forth this secret even before the time of **Pythagoras** <note>The Greek philosopher Pythagoras taught that odd numbers were masculine, finite, and divine, while even numbers were feminine and infinite</note>—added one day in honor of the **odd number**. He gave this day to January so that an odd number might be maintained in the total for the year as well as in the individual months, with the exception of February alone. For if the twelve months were each reckoned by either an even or an odd number, they would produce an even total; therefore, by establishing one month with an even number, he made the entire calculation odd.

**January**, therefore, along with **April**, **June**, **August** <note>original: *Sextilis*</note>, **September**, **November**, and **December**, were reckoned to have twenty-nine days, and their **Nones** fell on the fifth day. After the **Ides**, seventeen days were counted in all of these until the **Kalends** <note>The first day of the following month</note>. But **March**, **May**, **July** <note>original: *Quintilis*</note>, and **October** possessed thirty-one days each; in these, the Nones fell on the seventh day. Similarly, after the Ides, seventeen days were counted in each of these until the following Kalends. But **February** alone retained twenty-eight days, as if a diminished and even number were appropriate for the **gods of the underworld** <note>original: *Inferis*</note>.
