<margin>The reason for intercalation.</margin>
Since the Romans, following this distribution by **Pompilius** <note>Numa Pompilius, the legendary second king of Rome who established many of the city's religious laws</note>, calculated their own year according to the course of the **moon** <note>original: *Lunae cursum*</note> just as the Greeks did, it was necessary for them to establish an **intercalary month** <term>intercalation: the insertion of extra days or months into a calendar to keep it aligned with the seasons</term>, following the Greek custom. For the Greeks also, when they realized they had thoughtlessly organized the year with three hundred and fifty-four days—since it appeared from the course of the **sun** <note>original: *solis cursu*</note>, which completes the **zodiac** <note>original: *zodiacum*</note> in three hundred and sixty-five days and a quarter, that eleven days and a quarter were missing from their year—devised **intercalary periods** according to a set system. Thus, every eighth year, they would intercalate ninety days, from which they composed three months of thirty days each. The Greeks did this because it was laborious and difficult to intercalate eleven days and a quarter every single year. Therefore, they preferred to multiply this number eight times and insert the ninety days which are produced if the quarter and the eleven days are combined eight times, distributing them (as we said) into three months. They called these days **skipping days** <term>original: ὑπερβαίνοντας (*hyperbainontas*); days that "step over" the normal count</term>, but the months they called **insertions** <term>original: ἐμβολίσμυς (*embolismous*); months shoved into the calendar</term>.

The Romans decided to imitate this order as well, but in vain. Indeed, it escaped their notice that they had added one day—as we mentioned above—to the Greek number in honor of the **odd number** <note>Numa changed the lunar year from 354 to 355 days because odd numbers were considered lucky or "divine"</note>. Because of this, the total count and the order could not agree over the eight-year period. But since this error was not yet discovered, they continued for eight years to calculate ninety days as if they were to be added on, following the Greek example. Every other year, they would alternate between twenty-two and twenty-three intercalary days across four intercalations. However, every eighth year, eight extra days accrued because of those single days by which we have already said the Roman year exceeded the Greek number. Once this error was recognized, the following type of correction was introduced. In every third eight-year cycle, they distributed the intercalary days so that they would intercalate not ninety, but sixty-six days:

...compensating twenty-four days for those which had increased beyond the Greek count over as many years. Moreover, the month of **February** was assigned to all **intercalation** <term>intercalation: the insertion of extra days or months into a calendar to keep it aligned with the solar year</term>, because it was the last month of the year. In this, they were also imitating the Greeks. For the Greeks likewise inserted their extra days into the final month of their year, as reported by **Glaucippus**, who wrote about the sacred rites of the **Athenians**. However, they differed from the Greeks in one respect: the Greeks intercalated after the final month was completed, whereas the Romans did not wait for February to finish. Instead, they intercalated after the twenty-third day, specifically after the **Terminalia** <note>original: *Terminalibus*; the festival of Terminus, the god of boundaries, which traditionally marked the end of the old Roman year</note> had been performed. Then, they added the remaining five days of the month of February after the intercalation; I believe they did this according to an old custom of their religion, so that **March** would always follow February.

<margin>Regarding the day of the market.</margin>
But since it often happened that the **market days** <term>original: *nundinae*; the Roman market days that occurred every ninth day, when rural people came into the city</term> fell either on the first day of the year or on the **Nones** <note>original: *Nonas*; the 5th or 7th day of the month</note>, and both instances were considered harmful to the Republic, a remedy was devised to turn this away. We shall explain this, provided we first show why market days were avoided on both the **Kalends** <note>original: *Calendis*; the first day of every month</note> and all Nones. For whenever the year began on a day added for a market, that entire year was mournful with unfortunate events; this belief was especially strengthened by the **Lepidian tumult** <note>original: *Lepidiano tumultu*; a reference to the rebellion of Marcus Aemilius Lepidus in 78 BC, which coincided with such a calendar event</note>.

Furthermore, it was thought that a gathering of the entire multitude on the **Nones** should be avoided. This was because the Roman people, even after the kings had been driven out, celebrated this day of the Nones most significantly, as they believed it to be the birthday of **Servius Tullius** <note>The legendary sixth king of Rome, credited with many reforms favoring the common people</note>. Since it was uncertain in which month Servius Tullius had been born, yet certain that he was born on a Nones, they frequented every Nones with great *joy* <gloss>notitia / laetitia: the scribe has corrected 'fame/notoriety' to 'joy'</gloss>. Those in charge of the calendar feared that the masses, gathered together on a market day, might start a revolution out of a longing for the king; therefore, they took care to keep the Nones separate from the market days. The surplus of the year that we mentioned was left to the discretion of those who presided over the **calendar** <term>original: *fastis*; the official records of days when legal and public business could be conducted</term>. They were permitted to **intercalate** <term>intercalation: the insertion of extra days or months into a calendar to keep it aligned with the solar year</term> whenever they wished, provided they placed the extra time in the middle of the **Terminalia** <note>original: *Terminaliorum*; the festival of Terminus, god of boundaries, held on February 23rd</note> or within the intercalary month in such a way that they steered the celebration of the **market days** <term>original: *nundinarum*; the Roman market cycle occurring every ninth day</term> away from an unfavorable date. And this is what some of the ancient writers have reported: that among the Romans, there was not only an intercalary month but also an intercalary day.

<margin>When intercalation was first introduced.</margin>
As to when intercalation was first introduced, it is variously reported. **Licinius Macer** assigns the origin of this practice to **Romulus**. **Antias**, in his second book, contends that **Numa Pompilius** devised it for the sake of religious rites. **Junius** records that King **Servius Tullius** was the first to intercalate; **Varro** agrees that the market days were also instituted by him. **Tuditanus** reports in his third book on the *Magistrates* that the **Decemviri** <note>The "Ten Men" who drafted the earliest Roman law codes</note>—those who added two tables of law to the original ten—consulted the people about intercalation. **Cassius** writes that these same men were the authors of the practice. **Flavius** says that the consul **Martius** did this in the five hundred and sixty-second year from the founding of the city <note>original: *ab urbe condita*; approximately 191 BC</note>, shortly after the start of the Aetolian War. However, **Varro** disputes this, writing that a very ancient law was carved on a bronze column by the consuls **Lucius Pinatius** and **Furius** <note>circa 472 BC</note>, in which a mention of intercalation is included. Let these accounts regarding the beginning of intercalation suffice.

### How first **Julius**, then **Augustus** Caesar corrected the year. CHAPTER XIV.

However, there was a time when, due to superstition, all intercalation was omitted. At other times, it was manipulated through the favoritism of the priests, who wished to extend or shorten the days of the year to suit the interests of the **tax collectors** <term>original: *publicanis*; private contractors who collected taxes for the Roman state and benefited from longer or shorter fiscal years</term>. Thus, sometimes an increase and sometimes a reduction of days occurred, and under the guise of religious observation, there emerged a greater occasion for confusion.

But later, **Gaius Caesar** brought all this inconsistency of time—which had been wandering and uncertain up to that point—into the order of a fixed and de-

<margin>The Egyptians alone are privy to divine matters.</margin>
**Egyptians**—the only people who understand all divine matters—he strove to align the year to the measure of the sun, which completes its course in 365 days and a quarter. For just as a "lunar year" is essentially a month (because the Moon spends a little less than a month in its circuit of the zodiac), so the "solar year" must be calculated by the number of days it takes for the sun to return to the exact point from which it started. Hence it is called the **turning year** <note>original: *annus vertens*</note>; and it is considered "great," while the lunar year is thought of as "short." **Virgil** encompassed both of these:

> Meanwhile, the Sun rolls around the great year.
From this, **Atteius Capito** thinks the word "year" [*annus*] is named from the "circuit of time": because the ancients used to use the word *an* in place of *circum* [around], just as **Cato**
<margin>*An* used for "around" among the ancients.</margin>
wrote in his *Origins of the Orators*: *An terminum*, meaning "around the boundary" [*circum terminum*]; and *ambire* for "to go around" [*circumire*]. **Julius Caesar**, therefore, added ten days to the old system so that they might make the year 365 days, the time in which the Sun traverses the **zodiac**. And lest the quarter-day be missing, he established that every fourth year the priests who were in charge should **intercalate** <term>insert an extra day</term> one day into the months and days: specifically, in that month and place where the intercalary month was inserted among the ancients—that is, before the last five days of the month of February. ...and November, one day each. But he did not add a day to the month of **February**, lest the religious observance dedicated to the **god of the underworld** <note>original: *Deo infero*; referring to the fact that February was traditionally a month of purification and rituals for the dead, and its "unlucky" even number of days was tied to this religious status</note> be changed. Furthermore, for **March**, **May**, **July** <note>original: *Quintilis*</note>, and **October**, he preserved their original status, because they already had a sufficiently full number of days—that is, thirty-one days each. Therefore, these months also have their **Nones** <term>the 7th day of these specific months; usually the 5th in others</term> on the seventh day, just as **Numa** <note>Numa Pompilius, the legendary second king of Rome credited with the earlier calendar</note> established, because Julius changed nothing in these.

But **January**, **August** <note>original: *Sextilis*</note>, and **December**, to which Caesar added two days each, although they began to have thirty-one days apiece after Caesar’s reform, they nevertheless retain their **Nones** on the fifth day; and from their **Ides** <term>the 13th or 15th day of the month</term> to the following **Kalends** <term>the 1st of the next month</term>, they now count back from the nineteenth day. This is because Caesar did not want to insert the days he added either before the Nones or before the Ides, lest he corrupt the religious observance of those days—which were fixed—by a "new postponement" <note>original: *nouella cōperendinatione*; a legal term for delaying a trial, used here to mean shifting the sacred dates</note>. 

Neither did he wish to insert them immediately after the Ides, so that the scheduled announcement of any festivals would not be violated. Instead, once the established festivals of each month were completed, he made room for these "guest days" at the end of the month. 

Specifically, for **January**, he granted the days we call the fourth and third before the **Kalends of February**. For **April**, the third before the **Kalends of May**; for **June**, the third before the **Kalends of July**; for **August**, the fourth and third before the **Kalends of September**; for **September**, the third before the **Kalends of October**; for **November**, the third before the **Kalends of December**; and for **December**, the fourth and third before the **Kalends of January**. 

Thus it happened that, while all these months to which he added days had previously counted seventeen days back from the following month’s Kalends, they now changed: those that received two days now counted back from the nineteenth day, and those that received one day counted back from the eighteenth. Nevertheless, the order of the festivals for each month was preserved. For if a certain feast or holiday fell, for instance, on the third day after the Ides—which used to be called the "sixteenth day before the Kalends"—the same religious custom was maintained after the increase of days, so that it was still celebrated on the third day after the Ides, even if, due to the added days, it was no longer actually the sixteenth day before the Kalends.

For Caesar inserted the new days near the end of each month, at the point where he found the end of all the festivals that occurred in that month. He marked all the days added by him as **lawful** <term>fasti; days on which legal business and court sessions could be conducted</term> in order to provide greater freedom for legal actions. He established not only no **unlawful** days <term>nefasti; days on which public and judicial business was prohibited for religious reasons</term>, but he did not even make any of the added days an **assembly** day <term>comitialis; a day on which the people could meet for elections or passing laws</term>, so that the addition of days would not increase the political ambition of the magistrates <note>original: *ambitionē magistratuū*; Caesar wanted to avoid giving politicians more opportunities for campaigning or holding rallies</note>. Thus Caesar, having established the civil year based on solar measurements rather than the Moon, published it openly by a posted edict.

And the error could have stood at this point, had the Priests not created a new error for themselves out of the very amendment. For while it was necessary to intercalate <term>intercalate; to insert an extra day into the calendar, as in a leap year</term> the day which is made up of the "quarters" <note>the six hours or quarter-days that accumulate to a full day every four years</note> after every four years were completed and before the fifth began, those Priests performed the intercalation not when the fourth year was finished, but when it was beginning. This error persisted for thirty-six years, during which time twelve days were intercalated, even though only nine ought to have been intercalated <note>The Priests used "inclusive counting," mistakenly adding a leap day every three years instead of every four</note>.

<margin>The correction of the year performed by Augustus.</margin>
But **Augustus** also corrected this error after it was eventually discovered. He ordered twelve years to pass without any intercalary day, so that those three days—which had grown over the course of thirty-six years through the fault of the Priests' haste—might be "swallowed up" during the following twelve years when no day was intercalated. After this, he ordered one day to be intercalated according to Caesar’s original arrangement at the beginning of every fifth year <note>By Roman inclusive counting, the "beginning of the fifth year" is the same as our "every four years"</note>; and he committed this entire order to bronze tablets for eternal preservation by means of engraving.

# BOOK I.

...it was decided to be represented on the [following] day: and it was established that sixteen days should be counted between the **Ides** <term>Ides; the middle of the month, usually the 13th or 15th</term> and the following **Kalends** <term>Kalends; the first day of the month</term>. Therefore, the fuller month—those two days by which it was increased—had those days placed between its Kalends and **Nones** <term>Nones; the 5th or 7th day of the month</term>. Hence, for some months the fifth day from the Kalends marks the Nones, while for others it is the seventh. Caesar, however (as we said above), while guarding the fixed sacred rites, did not wish to change the order of the Nones in those months to which he added two days; because, once the festivals of the whole month were completed, he cautiously inserted his extra days for the sake of divine matters.

Therefore, in ancient times, before the calendars <note>original: *fasti*</note> were published by Gnaeus Flavius the scribe to the knowledge of all—against the will of the patricians <note>original: *invitis patribus*; the ruling class who previously kept the calendar secret to control legal business</note>—this duty was delegated to a minor **Pontiff**: to observe the first appearance of the new moon, and to report its sighting to the **King of Sacrifices** <term>Rex Sacrorum; a high priest who inherited the religious duties of the old Roman kings</term>. And so, after a sacrifice was celebrated by the King and the minor Pontiff, the same Pontiff, having <margin>*called</margin>—that is, summoned—the common people to the Capitoline Hill, next to the **Calabra Court** <margin>*Calabram</margin> (which is very close to the Hut of Romulus), would announce how many days remained from the Kalends to the Nones.

Indeed, for months where the Nones fell on the fifth day, he would proclaim it by saying the word *kalo* <note>original: *καλῶ*; Greek for "I call"</note> five times; for those on the seventh day, he would proclaim it by repeating the word seven times. <margin>How the Kalends were named.</margin> Now, the word *kalo* is Greek, meaning "I call"; and it was decided that this day, which was the first of those days being "called," should be named the **Kalends**. From this, the name "Calabra" was also given to the court itself where they were <margin>*called</margin> summoned; and also to the **Class** <note>original: *Classi*; the Roman assembly of citizens</note>, because the entire people were called into it.

The reason the minor Pontiff made public the number of days remaining until the Nones by "calling" <note>original: *calando*</note> was so that, after the new moon, it would be necessary for the common people who were in the fields to gather into the city to receive the reasons for the festivals from the King of Sacrifices, and to know what had to be done in that month. <margin>Nones</margin> From this, some believe the **Nones** were so named: as if it were the beginning of a "new" <note>original: *novae*</note> observation; or because from that day until the Ides, nine days are always counted. Just as among the Tuscans <note>the Etruscans</note>, more Nones were held: because these people, every ninth day, the King...

<margin>Origin of the name Ides</margin>
Furthermore, the name of the **Ides** <term>Ides; the middle day of the month, falling on the 13th or 15th</term> was taken from the *Etruscans* <note>original: *Tuscis*</note>, among whom that day is called *Itis*. They likewise interpreted the name as the "trust of *Jupiter*." For since we accept *Jupiter* as the author of light—whence the *Salii* <term>Salii; the "leaping priests" of Mars who sang ancient ritual hymns</term> sing of him as *Lucetius* <note>original: *Lucetium*; derived from *lux*, light</note> in their songs, and the *Cretans* call the day *Dia* <note>original: Δία</note>—the *Romans* themselves also call him *Diespiter*, as if he were the "father of the day" <note>original: *diei patrem*</note>. Rightly, then, is this day called the "trust of *Jupiter*," whose light does not end with the setting of the sun, but continues through the brilliance of day and night as the moon shines: which always happens during the **full moon** <note>original: *plenilunio*</note>, that is, in the middle of the month. The day which lacks the darkness of night they called by the *Etruscan* name "the trust of *Jupiter*."

<margin>The Ides as holidays for Jupiter</margin>
Hence antiquity decreed that all **Ides** should be observed as **festivals of Jupiter**. Others think the **Ides** were called *vidus* from "seeing" <note>original: *uidendo*</note>, because the full moon is seen on that day, and that later the letter "u" was removed. Just as, conversely, what the *Greeks* call *idein* <note>original: ἰδεῖν; to see</note>, we call "to see" <note>original: *uidere*</note> by adding the letter "v." Some prefer that the **Ides** were named from the *Greek* word for "form" <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ εἴδους (*apo tou eidous*)</note>, because on that day the moon shows its full appearance. There are those who believe the **Ides** are named after the *idulis* sheep—which the *Etruscans* call by this name—and on every **Ides** a sheep is sacrificed by the **Flamen** <term>Flamen; specifically the Flamen Dialis, the high priest of Jupiter</term>. But we consider that other reason for the name to be closer to the truth: that we call the day **Ides** because it "divides" the month. For in the *Etruscan* <note>original: *Hetrusca*</note> language, *iduare* means "to divide"; from which comes the word *vidua* [widow], as if it were "greatly divided" <note>original: *ualde idua*</note>, or a woman "divided" from her husband.

<margin>The Kalends sacred to Juno</margin>
Just as all **Ides** are assigned to *Jupiter*, so all **Kalends** <term>Kalends; the first day of the month</term> are attributed to *Juno*, as confirmed by the authority of both *Varro* and the *Pontifical* records. This is also observed by the *Laurentes* <note>The people of Laurentum, an ancient city of Latium near Rome</note> in their ancestral religious rites; they even added a surname to the Goddess from these ceremonies, calling her **Juno of the Kalends**. Moreover, on every **Kalends** from the month of *March* to *December*, they offer supplications to this Goddess on the day of the **Kalends**. In Rome also, on all **Kalends**, except that the **Pontiff**...

<margin>* Calabra</margin>
The **minor pontiff** <note>original: *fex minor*; the text likely intended *pontifex minor*, an official who assisted the higher priests</note> performs a sacred rite for **Juno** in the **Calabra Court** <term>Curia Calabra; a building on the Capitoline Hill where the start of the month was announced</term>. Also, the **Queen of Sacrifices** <term>Regina Sacrorum; the wife of the *Rex Sacrorum*, a high-ranking priest who inherited the religious duties of the ancient kings</term>, immolates a sow or a lamb to *Juno* in the royal palace. From this, we have also said that **Janus** was surnamed **Junonian**, because every entrance seems ascribed to that God, while all the days of the **Kalends** <term>Kalends; the first day of the month</term> are ascribed to this Goddess. For since our ancestors observed the beginning of the months from the rising of the moon, they rightly assigned the **Kalends** to *Juno*, believing the moon and *Juno* to be the same. This may also be because the moon travels through the air; hence the Greeks called the moon **Artemis** <note>original: ἄρτεμιν</note>, as if it were an **air-cutter** <note>original: ἀεροτόμην</note>, because she cuts the air. Since *Juno* is the mistress of the air, they deservedly consecrated the beginnings of the months—the **Kalends**—to this Goddess. <margin>Religious days for joining in marriage.</margin> Nor should I overlook that they judged the **Kalends**, **Nones**, and **Ides** to be **religious** <term>dies religiosi; days of religious restriction when certain secular or joyful acts were avoided</term>—that is, to be avoided—for joining in marriage. For these days, except the **Nones**, are holidays. It is an act requiring expiation for violence to be done to anyone on a holiday. Therefore, weddings are avoided then, in which violence seems to be done to virgins. But **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a prolific Roman scholar</note> reports that **Verrius Flaccus** <note>A famous Roman grammarian and teacher</note>, most skilled in Pontifical law, used to say that because it was permitted to clean old ditches on holidays, but not lawful to make new ones, holidays were therefore more suitable for **widows** than for **virgins** to marry. Someone might ask: Why then, if the **Nones** is not a holiday, is the celebration of weddings forbidden? The reason for this is also obvious. For because the first day of marriage is given to modesty, but on the day after, the bride ought to begin to take control of her husband's house and perform a sacred rite; yet all "day after" days—whether after the **Kalends**, **Nones**, or **Ides**—are equally **black** <term>dies atri; "black days" considered unlucky because they were associated with historical Roman defeats</term>. Therefore, they said the **Nones** were also unfit for weddings, lest the bride either inaugurate her wifely freedom on the following day or perform a sacrifice on a **black day**, on which it is forbidden for sacred rites to be celebrated.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of the Roman calendar. Having previously defined "religious" days as those of restriction, the author now transitions to Numa Pompilius’s foundational classification of all days in the Roman year into sacred, secular, and shared categories.</meta>

# SATURNALIA

<margin>Distinctions between days.</margin>
But because the order of our discourse has led us to a commemoration of the days, a few things must also be said concerning the consultation of our Horus <note>Horus is a character in Macrobius’s dialogue, representing an Egyptian perspective on Roman customs</note>. Numa <note>Numa Pompilius, the legendary second king of Rome, credited with establishing many of its religious institutions</note>, just as he divided the year into months, so he distributed each month into days. He called all days either **festive**, **working**, or **divided**.
<margin>Festive days.</margin>
**Festive** days <term>dies festi; days dedicated to the gods</term> are dedicated to the Gods. **Working** days <term>dies profesti; days for secular business</term> are granted to men for the administration of private and public affairs. **Divided** days <term>dies intercisi; "cut-between" days</term> are common to both Gods and men. On Festive days, there are sacrifices, sacred banquets, games, and holidays. On Working days, there are legal days <note>original: *fasti*; days when courts could meet</note>, assembly days <note>original: *comitiales*; days for voting</note>, adjournment days <note>original: *comperendini*</note>, set days, and days for battle. Divided days are split within themselves, rather than into other categories. For on those days, at certain hours it is lawful <term>fas; divinely permitted</term>, and at other hours it is not lawful, to pronounce the law. For while a sacrificial victim is being slaughtered, it is unlawful to speak the law; between the slaughter and the offering <note>original: *inter caesa et porrecta*; the interval while the organs were prepared</note>, it is permitted to speak; and again, when the sacrifice is being burned, it is not permitted. Therefore, the division of festive and working days must be discussed more broadly. A sacred celebration occurs either when sacrifices are offered to the Gods; or when a day is celebrated with divine feasts; or when games are performed in honor of the Gods; or when holidays are observed. There are four types of public holidays. They are either **fixed**, **movable**, **commanded**, or **market days**. **Fixed** holidays <term>feriae stativae</term> are common to the entire people on certain and established days and months, and are noted in the calendars with set observations; among these, the *Agonalia*, *Carmentalia*, and *Lupercalia* are especially observed. **Movable** holidays <term>feriae conceptivae</term> are those which are announced annually by the magistrates or priests on days that are either certain or even uncertain; such as the *Latin Festival*, the *Paganalia*, the *Sementinae* <note>The "Sowing Festival"</note>, and the *Compitalia* <note>The "Crossroads Festival"</note>. **Commanded** holidays <term>feriae imperativae</term> are those which the Consuls or Praetors proclaim at the discretion of their own power. **Market days** <term>nundinae</term> belong to the country folk—that is, the rustics—on which they gather to provide for their own business or merchandise.

There are besides holidays proper to specific families, such as those of the **Claudian** family, or the **Aemilian**, or the **Julian**, or the **Cornelian**, and any such ho-

# BOOK I.

Each family also observes its own specific **holidays**, according to the custom of their domestic celebrations. These belong to individuals, such as the observance of birthdays, or the rituals following a lightning strike, as well as funerals and rites of purification. Among the ancients, anyone who had invoked Salus <note>Goddess of safety and well-being</note>, Semonia <note>Goddess of sowing</note>, Seia <note>Goddess of seeds in the earth</note>, Segetia <note>Goddess of the standing grain</note>, or Tutilina <note>Goddess who protects the harvested grain</note> likewise observed a holiday. Similarly, the **Flaminica** <note>The wife of the Flamen Dialis, the high priest of Jupiter; her life was bound by many sacred restrictions</note>, whenever she heard thunder, was on holiday until she had appeased the gods.

Furthermore, the priests asserted that a holiday was polluted if any work was performed on festivals that were officially announced or appointed. Moreover, it was not permitted for the **King of the Sacred Rites** <term>Rex sacrorum; a high priest who carried out the religious duties formerly performed by the kings</term> or the **Flamines** <note>Priests dedicated to specific major deities</note> to see work being done on holidays. For this reason, they would announce through a herald that no such thing should be done, and anyone who ignored the instruction was fined. Beyond the fine, they asserted that a person who had done something unintentionally on such days must offer a pig as a **sin-offering** <term>piaculum; an expiatory sacrifice to atone for a ritual error</term>. However, Scaevola <note>Quintus Mucius Scaevola, a famous Roman jurist and Pontifex Maximus</note> the high priest maintained that one who acted intentionally could not be purified.

But Umbro <note>An author on religious law</note> denies that a person is polluted if they performed work pertaining to the gods or for the sake of sacred rites, or if they did something regarding an urgent necessity of life. Finally, when Scaevola was consulted on what was permitted to be done on holidays, he replied: "That which would cause harm if omitted." Therefore, if an ox fell into a pit and the head of the household rescued it using labor, he was not seen to have polluted the holiday; nor was he who saved a house from imminent ruin by shoring up a broken roof beam. Hence **Maro** <note>The poet Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro), whom Macrobius treats as an expert in all branches of learning</note>, being skilled in all disciplines and knowing that a sheep might be washed either for the sake of cleaning the wool or for curing the scab, pronounced that it was permitted for a sheep to be submerged during holidays if it were done for the sake of a remedy:

<margin>Georgics, Book 1.</margin>
->To dip the bleating flock in the healthful stream.<-

For by adding "healthful," he showed that it was permitted only for the sake of averting disease, and not also for the profit of cleaning the wool.

<margin>Working days.</margin>
These things concern **festive days** and those which arise from them, which are also called **unlawful days** <note>original: *nefasti*; days when legal business could not be conducted</note>. Now let us speak of **working days** <term>profesti dies; days available for secular business</term> and those that proceed from them.

[...divided] into: that is, lawful days, assembly days, adjournment days, fixed days, and battle days. **Lawful days** (*fasti*) are those on which the **Praetor** <note>A high-ranking Roman magistrate responsible for the administration of justice</note> is permitted to speak the three solemn words: "I give, I declare, I adjudge." <note>original: *do, dico, addico*. These were the formal legal utterances used to grant a trial, declare the law, or award property.</note> Opposite to these are the **forbidden days** (*nefasti*). **Assembly days** (*comitiales*) are those on which it is permitted to conduct business with the people. On lawful days, legal action can be taken according to the law, but business with the people cannot; on assembly days, both are permitted. **Adjournment days** (*comperendini*) are those on which a summons to appear in court may be issued. **Fixed days** (*stati*) are those established for a trial with a foreigner, as **Plautus** <note>The famous Roman comic playwright (c. 254–184 BC)</note> writes in *The Weevil*: *A fixed day, agreed upon with the foreigner, intervened.* <note>original: "Status, condictus cum hoste, intercessit dies."</note> He uses the word "enemy" <note>hostis</note> here in the ancient sense to mean "foreigner." I would not separate **battle days** (*praeliares*) from "proper" days; for the proper days are the thirty consecutive days during which, after the army has been ordered, a red flag is displayed on the Citadel. Battle days, however, include all those on which it is divinely permitted to demand restitution or to provoke the enemy. For when the *Latia*—that is, the solemn **Festival of the Latins**—is being observed; likewise during the days of the **Saturnalia**; and also when the **Mundus** is open: it is a religious violation to take up battle. For this reason, it was not fitting to begin a war during the time of the Latins, when in ancient times public truces were confirmed between the Roman people and the Latins; nor during the festival of **Saturn**, who is believed to have ruled without any military turmoil; nor when the *Mundus* was open, because that ritual is dedicated to **Father Dis** and **Proserpina** <note>The King and Queen of the Underworld</note>. They thought it better to go to battle only when the throat of **Pluto** <note>Another name for the god of the underworld</note> was closed. Hence **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a prolific Roman scholar</note> writes as follows: *When the Mundus is open, the door of the somber gods and the Underworld lies open, as it were.* <term>Mundus; a ritual pit in the center of Rome, believed to be an entrance to the underworld, which was opened only three times a year</term> Because of this, it is considered a religious violation not only to engage in battle, but also to hold a military levy, to set out as a soldier, to weigh anchor, or to take a wife for the sake of having children. The ancients also avoided calling men for service on days that were marked by misfortunes. They even avoided doing so on **holidays** (*feriae*), as Varro wrote in his *Books of the Augurs* in these words: *It is not proper to call men on holidays; if one has called them, let there be a sin-offering.* <term>piaculum; a sacrifice performed to atone for a ritual error or neglect of religious duty</term> It must be known, however, that the custom of choosing a day for fighting among the Romans...

For what place is there for religious observation when the power of choice no longer remains? Our ancestors thought that the "post-days" <note>Days immediately following the three main markers of the Roman month (the Calends, Nones, and Ides).</note> should be avoided for all matters: they even condemned them as **black days** <note>original: *atri*, meaning "gloomy" or "unlucky"</note>, as if by an ill-omened name. However, some have called these same days "common," perhaps to improve the name by using a more neutral term. Aulus Gellius, in the fifteenth book of his *Attic Nights*, and Cassius Hemina, in the second book of his *Histories*, report the reason for these days as follows:

In the 363rd year from the founding of the city <note>Approximately 391–390 BC.</note>, it was discussed in the Senate by the Military Tribunes—Virginius, Manlius, Caelius, Postumius, and their colleagues—what the reason was that the Republic had been so badly afflicted by misfortune so many times within a few years. By order of the senators, Lucius Aquinius, a <term>Soothsayer</term> <note>original: *Aruspex*, a priest who interpreted the will of the gods by examining the entrails of sacrificed animals.</note>, was ordered to come to the Senate to investigate religious failings. He stated that Quintus Sulpicius, the Military Tribune, when about to fight against the Gauls at the **Allia** <note>The River Allia, where the Romans suffered a catastrophic defeat by the Gauls in 390 BC, leading to the sack of Rome.</note>, had performed a religious sacrifice for the sake of the battle on the day after the **Ides of July** <note>original: *Idus Quintilis*. Quintilis was the fifth month in the early Roman calendar, later renamed July.</note>. Likewise, at the **Cremera** <note>A river where the clan of the Fabii was massacred by the Veientes in 477 BC.</note>, and at many other times and places, a conflict had turned out badly when a sacrifice was performed on the day following a festival. 

Then the senators ordered that these religious matters be referred to the College of <term>Pontiffs</term> <note>The high-ranking priests responsible for the state religion and the calendar.</note>. The Pontiffs decreed that all days following the **Calends**, **Nones**, and **Ides** should be held as "black days"; thus, these days should be neither <term>battle days</term> <note>original: *praeliares*, days on which war could be declared.</note>, nor "pure" days for legal business, nor assembly days for voting. Furthermore, Fabius Maximus Servilianus, a Pontiff, states in his twelfth book that one ought not to perform funeral rites for ancestors on a black day, because even then it is necessary to first invoke **Janus** and **Jupiter**, whose names it is not proper to utter on a black day.

<margin>Whether market days are holidays.</margin>
Regarding my statement that **market days** <term>Nundinae</term> <note>The Roman market day that occurred every ninth day by inclusive counting (every eight days by modern counting).</note> are holidays <note>original: *feriae*</note>, this can be debated. Titus <note>Livy, the famous Roman historian.</note>, when writing about holidays, did not include market days among them, but merely called them "solemn days." Julius Modestus also asserts that when Messala the Augur consulted the <term>Pontiffs</term> <note>The highest-ranking priests in Rome who governed religious law.</note> as to whether Roman market days and the Nones should be observed as holidays, they responded that market days did not seem to be holidays to them. Furthermore, Trebatius, in his first book of *On Religious Matters*, says that a magistrate can free slaves and hold court on market days. 

But on the contrary, Julius Caesar, in the sixteenth book of his *On Auspices*, denies that a public assembly can be called on market days—that is, business cannot be conducted with the people; therefore, elections <note>original: *comitia*</note> cannot be held on Roman market days. Cornelius Labeo also declares in his first book of the *Calendar* that market days are indeed holidays. 

The diligent reader will find the cause of this discrepancy in the second book of Granius Licinianus. He says that market days are holidays for Jupiter; indeed, on every market day, the <term>Flaminica</term> <note>The wife of the *Flamen Dialis*, the high priest of Jupiter.</note> is accustomed to sacrifice a ram to Jupiter in the *Regia* <note>The "Royal House" in the Roman Forum, which served as the headquarters for the Pontifex Maximus.</note>. However, it was brought about by the **Hortensian Law** <note>Passed in 287 BC, this law made the decisions of the plebeians binding on all citizens and altered the status of market days to allow legal business.</note> that they should be "lawful days" <note>original: *fastae*</note>, so that the country folk, who were coming into the city for the sake of marketing, could settle their lawsuits. For on an "unlawful day" <note>original: *nefasto*</note>, the <term>Praetor</term> <note>The Roman magistrate responsible for the administration of justice and the courts.</note> was not permitted to speak the formal legal words. Therefore, those who call them holidays are vindicated by the evidence of antiquity; those who think otherwise state the truth based on the perspective of the current age, which followed the law.

<margin>The origin of market days.</margin>
Some attribute the origin of these market days to Romulus; they record that after he shared his kingdom with Titus Tatius and established sacrifices and fellowships, he also added the market days—as Tuditanus asserts. But Cassius says that Servius Tullius <note>The sixth legendary king of Rome.</note> created the market days so that people would gather into the city from the fields for urban affairs... <note>The catchword "urbanas" links to the start of the next page.</note>

Geminius says that the day of the **market days** <term>nundinae</term> <note>The Roman market day cycle occurred every ninth day by inclusive counting (every eight days by modern reckoning). original: *nundinarum*</note> began to be celebrated once the kings had already been driven out: because many of the common people, recalling the memory of Servius Tullius <note>The sixth king of Rome, traditionally seen as a champion of the lower classes.</note>, would offer sacrifices to him on market days. Varro also agrees with this matter. Rutilius writes that the Romans established market days so that rural folk might work in the fields for eight days, but on the ninth day, pausing their country work, they would come to Rome for the market and to receive the laws. He also notes that decrees and resolutions were reported to a more crowded populace, which, having been proposed over a **three-market interval** <term>trinundinum</term> <note>A period covering three market days (about 24 days), used as a notice period for new legislation.</note>, were easily recognized by individuals and the whole community. From this the custom also developed that laws were promulgated over a three-market interval. For this reason, it was also the practice for candidates to come to the assembly place <term>comitium</term> <note>The public space where political and judicial assemblies met.</note> on market days and stand on a hill, where they could be seen by everyone in person. But all these things began to be handled more negligently and were later abolished, after the crowds began to be present in large numbers even during the three-market interval because of the multitude of common people. There is also a Roman Goddess, **Nundina**, named after the ninth day of the newborn, which is called the **day of purification** <term>dies lustricus</term> <note>original: *lustricus*. The day a child was ritually cleansed and named.</note>. The day of purification is when infants are purified and receive a name. However, this is the ninth day for males, but the eighth for females.

The arrangement of the year and months having been fully set out (as I believe), our friend **Horus** also has something to say regarding the names and observation of the days.

And I would certainly like to know whether there is anything that the clever **Son of the Nile** <note>Referring to Horus as an Egyptian. original: *Niligena*</note>—a neighbor to a nation powerful in numbers—might mock in this order of the Roman system, or if he agrees that the Tuscan Tiber <note>The river of Rome; "Tuscan" because it originates in Etruria. original: *Tuscum Tyberim*</note> has drawn something from his own disciplines. **Eustathius** replied: "Not only our friend Horus, a grave and distinguished man, but I think no one else could be of such shallow judgment that they would not approve of the order of the Roman year, corrected as they say 'to the fingernail' <note>An ancient idiom for something polished to perfection, like a sculptor checking a marble seam. original: *ad unguem*</note>; to which your tenacious memory and brilliant speech have added even greater grace."

# OF THE SATURNALIA

It is no wonder that this arrangement escaped the sting of criticism, since it summoned the authority of the final correction from Egypt. For Julius Caesar, just as he drew the motions of the stars—about which he left behind quite learned books—from Egyptian disciplines, so he also borrowed from the same institution the method of extending the duration of the year to match the course of the **sun**. But the ancient inhabitants of Latium <note>The region of Italy where Rome was founded.</note>, because it was not yet permitted to learn anything from Egypt (to which no passage was open to them), followed the custom of Greece in counting the days of the months: so that the calculation was resolved in a decrease, with the number receding backwards. For in this way we say the tenth day, then the ninth, and afterward the eighth, just as the Athenians were accustomed to say **the tenth and ninth of the waning month** <note>original Greek: *δεκάτω καὶ ἐνάτω φθίνοντος μηνὸς*. The Greeks and Romans often counted days backwards toward the end of a month or a specific division.</note>.

<margin>Odyssey, Book 14</margin>
Homer also says: **As this month wanes and the next begins** <note>original Greek: *Τοῦ μὲν φθίνοντος μηνὸς, τοῦ δ’ ἱσταμένοιο*</note>; what else does he mean by "waning" <note>original: *φθίνοντα*</note> except that month whose calculation, as it gradually fails, ends in the name of the one to follow? And "beginning" <note>original: *ἱσταμένον*</note> for the one which precedes the number that will succeed the previous one as it goes into decline? Our "Mantuan Homer" <note>A reference to the poet Virgil, who was born near Mantua and held in the same high regard as the Greek Homer.</note> 
<margin>Aeneid, Book 10</margin>
understanding this—that something is said to "stand" when it is being approached—says: **Each man has his set day** <note>original: *Stat sua cuiq; dies*. Virgil uses the word "stands" to imply a fixed destination.</note>, calling the final day "standing," as if it were the point toward which everyone travels through all their days. The same poet, equally noble in his learning and his modesty, knowing that the ancient Romans arranged their years according to the course of the moon and later generations according to the Sun, preserved respect for the opinions of both ages: 
<margin>Georgics, Book 1</margin>

*from the throwing of rays <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ βάλλειν τὰς ἀκτῖνας</note>: that is, from the casting of beams. Chrysippus <note>A Stoic philosopher (c. 279–206 BC) known for his work in logic and physics.</note> believes Apollo is so named because he is **not of the many and common substances of fire** <note>original: ὡς οὐχὶ τῶν πολλῶν καὶ φαύλων οὐσιῶν τοῦ πυρὸς ὄντα</note>. For he argues the first letter of the name retains the meaning of a negation <note>Referring to the "alpha privative" in Greek, where the 'A' in Apollo stands for "not," and 'polloi' means "many." Thus, Apollo = Not-Many, i.e., Unique.</note>, or **because he is alone, and not many** <note>original: ἢ ὅτι μόνος ἐστὶ, καὶ οὐχὶ πολλοί</note>. For even the Latin language called him the **Sun** <note>The Latin word for Sun is *Sol*.</note>, because he alone obtained such great brilliance. Speusippus <note>Plato's nephew and successor as head of the Academy.</note> argues that his power consists of many fires, **as if he were composed from many substances of fire** <note>original: ὡς ἀπὸ πολλῶν οὐσιῶν πυρὸς, αὐτῷ συνεστῶτος</note>. Cleanthes <note>A Stoic philosopher who succeeded Zeno.</note> suggests the name comes from his **making his risings from various and different places** <note>original: ὡς ἀπ᾿ ἄλλων καὶ ἄλλων τόπων τὰς ἀναβολὰς ποιουμένου</note>: that is, because he makes his sunrise from different declinations of locations. Cornificius <note>Likely Quintus Cornificius, a Roman scholar and contemporary of Cicero.</note> thinks Apollo is named **from revolving** <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀναπολεῖν</note>: that is, because within the circuit of the world, which the Greeks call the *pole* <note>original: πόλον</note>, he is carried by his force and returned to his rising. Others think Apollo is so named **as one who destroys living things** <note>original: ὡς ἀπολλύντα τὰ ζῶα</note>. For he kills and destroys animate beings when he sends a plague through the excess of his heat, as Euripides says in *Phaethon*: **"O golden-shining Sun, how you have destroyed me; hence mortals shall clearly call you Apollo"** <note>original: ὦ χρυσοφεγγὲς ἥλι᾿, ὡς μ᾿ ἀπώλεσας, ὅθεν σ᾿ Ἀπόλλων ἐμφανῶς κλήσει βροτός. A wordplay on 'Apollo' and 'apollumi' (to destroy).</note>. Archilochus <note>An early Greek lyric poet.</note> says the same: **"Lord Apollo, do you mark the guilty, and destroy them just as you destroy [others]"** <note>original: ἄναξ Ἀπόλλων, καὶ σὺ τοὺς μὲν αἰτίους σήμαινε, καὶ σφὰς ἔλλυ᾿ ὥσπερ ὀλλύεις</note>. Finally, those struck by disease are called **Apollo-struck** <note>original: ἀπολλωνοβλήτους</note> and **sun-struck** <note>original: ἡλιοβλήτους</note>. And because the effects of the moon are similar to the effects of the Sun, both in helping and in harming: therefore women afflicted by certain diseases are called **moon-struck** <note>original: σεληνοβλήτους</note> and **Artemis-struck** <note>original: ἀρτεμιδοβλήτους</note>. This is why the statues of Apollo are decorated with a bow and arrows: so that the power of the rays sent forth may be understood through the arrows. Whence*

For they believe he is named Apollo as much from **driving away diseases** <note>original: ὡς ἀπελαύνοντα τὰς νόσους</note> as from **destroying** <note>original: ἀπολλοῦντα</note> them. This opinion, which agrees with the pronunciation of the Latin name, has led us not to change the name of this god, so that you may understand "Apollo" as **the one driving away evils** <note>original: aspellentem mala</note>; whom the Athenians call **averter of evil** <note>original: ἀλεξίκακον (alexikakon)</note>. The same belief in a health-giving and healing God is maintained in our own Roman rites as well. For the Vestal Virgins <note>The priestesses of Vesta, responsible for maintaining the sacred fire of Rome.</note> address him thus: "Apollo the physician, Apollo the Paean." Since, therefore, there are two greatest effects of this star—that is, the Sun: one, by which he helps the life of mortals with tempered heat; the other, by which he sometimes sends a pestilential poison by the casting of his rays; they mark these two identical titles with specific pronunciations according to each effect, calling the God **Ieius** and **Paean**. 

These titles are suited to both effects: so that **Ieius** <note>original: ἰήϊος</note> comes from **healing** <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ ἰᾶσθαι</note>, and **Paean** <note>original: παιὰν</note> from **stopping distresses** <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ παύειν τὰς ἀνίας</note>. And conversely, **Ieius** may come from **hurling** <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ ἱέναι</note>, that is, from sending a **biting arrow** <note>original: βέλος ἐχεπευκές</note>; and **Paean** from **striking** <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ παίειν</note>. 

It has prevailed, however, that when they pray for health to be given to them, they pronounce **Ie Paean** <note>original: ἰὴ παιὰν</note> with the letter *eta* [η], which means "heal, Paean." But when they say **Hie Paean** <note>original: ἵε παιὰν</note> with the letter *epsilon* [ε] and an aspiration on the first letter, they signify that this is said against someone in a hostile prayer: **strike, Paean** <note>original: βάλλε παιὰν</note>, that is, "send by striking." 

They say Latona <note>The mother of Apollo and Diana.</note> used this cry when she urged Apollo to attack the Python <note>The monstrous serpent or dragon of Delphi.</note> with his arrows. I shall give the natural explanation for this matter in its proper place. The Delphic oracle is said to have confirmed this cry—that is, **Ie Paean**—to the Athenians when they sought the help of the God against the Amazons during the reign of Theseus <note>The mythical founder-king of Athens.</note>. For as they were about to enter war, the oracle ordered that the God be invoked and encouraged as a helper with these very words. <margin>Odyssey, Book 24</margin> They call this same God **Oulios** when he is responsible for healthful causes, which means the author of health: as Homer says, "**Hail to you, and may you be very well.**" <note>original: οὖλέ τε καὶ μάλα χαῖρε; The word "Oule" is related to "Oulios," meaning "be healthy" or "be whole."</note>

Menander writes that the people of Miletus sacrifice to **Apollo Oulios** for their own health. Pherecydes <note>An early Greek mythographer and historian.</note> records that Theseus, when he was being led to Crete to face the Minotaur, made a vow for his safety and return to **Apollo Oulios** and **Artemis Oulia**. Nor is it a wonder if twin effects are celebrated with various names, since we understand that other Gods also are judged by a double power and name arising from opposites in the same matter: such as **Neptune**, whom they sometimes call **Enosichthon** <note>original: ἐνοσίχθονα</note>, which means **shaking the earth**, and at other times **Asphalion** <note>original: ἀσφαλίωμα</note>, which means **stabilizing**. Likewise, Mercury both rouses and puts to sleep the minds and eyes of men, as the poet says:

<margin>Odyssey, Book 5</margin> "He took the rod with which he lulls the eyes of men."

Hence we worship Apollo—that is, the Sun—with titles signifying sometimes safety and sometimes plague; yet even the plague which he sends upon the wicked clearly signifies that this God fights for the good. <margin>The Libyan</margin> This is why, at **Pachynum**, a promontory of Sicily <note>Modern-day Capo Passero.</note>, **Apollo Libystinus** is celebrated with exceptional religious devotion. For when the Libyans, intending to invade Sicily, had brought their fleet to that promontory, Apollo, who is worshipped there, was invoked by the inhabitants; he sent a plague upon the enemies, and when nearly all were cut off by sudden death, he was given the surname **Libystinus**. Our own Roman annals also contain a similar instance of the present majesty of this same God. For when games were first celebrated at Rome in honor of Apollo, according to the prophecy of the seer Marcius...

### BOOK I.

...and by a Sibylline verse, at the sudden arrival of the enemy, the common people were roused to arms and met the foe. At that time, a cloud of arrows was seen to be carried against the adversaries, which both put the enemy to flight and brought the victorious Romans back to the spectacles of the God of Salvation <note>original: Dei sospitalis; a title for Apollo as a preserver or savior</note>. <margin>A brief note on the Apollinarian Games and their origin.</margin> From this, it is understood that the games were established for the sake of a battle, and not because of a plague (as some people think). Now, the reason for this common opinion is that at that time of year, the sun shines directly over the very summit of our habitation. For the sign of Cancer is in the summer solstice; as the sun passes through it, its rays illuminate our temperate zone, not from a distance, but sent down from above with direct brilliance. For this reason, it was estimated by some that the Apollinarian games were offered as a sacrifice to propitiate the God of Heat at that specific time. But I find in literature that these games were established for the sake of victory, not for health (as some writers of annals record). For during the Punic War <note>The series of wars between Rome and Carthage; these games were specifically instituted during the Second Punic War, around 212 BCE</note>, these games were first established based on the Sibylline books, on the advice of Cornelius Rufus the Decemvir <note>term: Decemviri; a "Board of Ten" men appointed for specific administrative or religious duties, in this case the oversight of sacred rites</note>, who for that reason was surnamed Sibylla, and afterwards, by a corruption of the name, first began to be called Sulla. Moreover, it is said that in the songs of the seer Marcius—two volumes of which were brought into the Senate—the following was found written:

> Romans, if you wish to drive the enemy from your territory,
> and the plague <note>original: vomicam; literally an ulcer or sore, used here metaphorically for the invading Carthaginian army</note> which comes from a distant nation,
> I advise that games be vowed to Apollo,
> which shall be performed annually in common for Apollo.
> The praetor who provides the highest justice for the people and the commons
> shall preside over the holding of these games.
> The Board of Ten <note>original: Decemviri</note> shall perform the sacrifices with sacred offerings according to the Greek rite.
> If you do these things rightly, you will rejoice forever,
> and the Republic will become better.
> For that god destroys your enemies
> who peacefully graze upon your fields.

From this verse, when one day had been spent on divine matters for the sake of performing the rituals, a decree of the Senate was afterwards made, that the Board of Ten—in order that they might be better instructed regarding the games to be held for Apollo and the proper performance of the divine rite—should consult the Sibylline books.

### SATURNALIA

...should approach <note>This continues the sentence from the previous page regarding the Senate approaching the Sibylline books</note>. When it was reported that the same instructions were found within them, the Senate <note>original: "patres," literally "the fathers," referring to the Roman Senators</note> decreed that games should be vowed and performed for Apollo. For this purpose, twelve thousand pieces of bronze money were given to the Praetor, along with two larger sacrificial victims. The Board of Ten <note>term: Decemviri; a ten-man committee responsible for overseeing sacred rites</note> was instructed to perform the sacrifice according to the Greek rite with these victims: for Apollo, a gilded bull and two white gilded goats; for Latona, a gilded cow. The people were ordered to watch the games in the circus while wearing crowns <note>original: "coronatus," referring to ceremonial garlands worn on the head</note>. This is the tradition primarily handed down regarding the origin of the Apollinarian Games.

Now let us prove, from the other names of this God as well, that Apollo and the Sun are the same being. <margin>Loxias.</margin> He is surnamed Loxias, as Aenopides <note>A 5th-century BCE Greek astronomer</note> says, "because he travels through the oblique circle from the West <margin>*Perhaps it should read "toward the East" because he proceeds through the oblique circle.</margin> toward the East" <note>original: "ὅτι ἐκπορεύεται τὸν λοξὸν κύκλον ἀπὸ δυσμῶν ἐπὶ ἀναβολὰς," referring to the sun's path along the ecliptic</note>. Or as Cleanthes <note>A Stoic philosopher</note> writes, "because he moves in spirals, which are themselves oblique," or "because he sends his oblique rays toward us <margin>being in the North</margin> while he is in the South" <note>original: "λοξὰς ἀκτῖνας ἵησι," meaning slanted or diagonal rays; this refers to the sun's angle relative to the Northern Hemisphere</note>.

<margin>Delius.</margin> He is surnamed Delius from the word for "clear" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ δῆλα"</note> because, by his light, he makes all things visible and clear. 

<margin>Phoebus.</margin> He is called Phoebus (as Cornificius says) from a word meaning "to move with force" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ φοιτᾶν βίᾳ"</note>. Most people, however, think he is called Phoebus because of his appearance and brightness, meaning "pure and shining" <note>original: "καθαρὸν, καὶ λαμπρὸν"</note>. 

<margin>Phanes.</margin> They also call him Phanes from the word for "shining" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ φαίνειν"</note>. And Phanaeus, "because he appears new" <note>original: "ἐπειδὴ φαίνεται νέος"</note>, since the Sun renews himself daily. Thus Virgil says:

> The day's first dawn. <note>original: "Mane nouum"; from Virgil's Georgics</note>

The people of Camirus <note>A city on the island of Rhodes</note>, who inhabit an island sacred to the Sun, sacrifice to Apollo as the "Always-born" <note>original: "ἀειγενετῇ" (Aeigenetes)</note>, because "he is always becoming the same and always generating" <note>original: "τῷ τὸν αὐτὸν ἀεὶ γί-νεσθαι καὶ ἀεὶ γεννᾶν"</note>; that is, because he is always being born as he rises, and because he himself generates all things by sowing, warming, bringing forth, nourishing, and increasing them. We receive several reasons for the name of Apollo "the Wolf-god" <margin>Lycius.</margin> <note>original: "Lycij"; associated here with light rather than wolves</note>. Antipater the Stoic writes that he is called Lycius "from the whitening of all things by light" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ λευκαίνεσθαι πάντα φωτί-"</note>.

# BOOK I.

...worshiping the burning rays of the sun. <note>original: "ζοντ@ ἡλίου," likely a fragment of a phrase describing the sun's heat or rays</note> Cleanthes <note>A Stoic philosopher known for his "Hymn to Zeus"</note> notes that Apollo was called "Lycius" <note>Wolf-like</note> because, just as wolves snatch up livestock, the sun likewise snatches up moisture with his rays. The ancient Greeks called the first light that precedes the rising of the sun *lyke* <note>light</note>, from the word *lykos*, <margin>* that is, the light of the time</margin> meaning time; even today they call this period *lycophos* <note>twilight; literally "wolf-light"</note>. Concerning this time, the poet writes:

<margin>Iliad, Book 7.</margin>
-> It was not yet dawn, but still the twilight of night. <-
<note>original: "ἦμος δ' οὔτ' ἄρ πω ἠώς, ἔτι δ' ἀμφιλύκη νύξ" (Iliad 7.433)</note>

-> Homer says the same: <-

<margin>Iliad, Book 4.</margin>
-> Pray to Apollo, the light-born, renowned for his bow. <-
<note>original: "Εὔχεο δ' Ἀπόλλωνι λυκηγένεϊ κλυτοτόξῳ" (Iliad 4.101)</note>

This title means "to the one generating the light," <note>original: "τῷ γεννῶντι τὴν λύκην"</note> that is, he who creates light by his rising. For the splendor of his rays, preceding the approaching sun by a great distance and breadth, gradually thins the darkness of the gloom and gives birth to light. No less do the Romans seem to have shaped their word for "light" (*lux*) from the Greek *lyke*, as they did with many other words. The most ancient Greeks also call the year *lykabanta*, meaning that which is "traversed and measured by the Sun" <note>original: "τὸν ἀπὸ τοῦ λύκου, id est, Sole, βαινόμενον καὶ μετρούμενον"</note>. That the Sun is called *lykos* <note>wolf</note> is also evidenced by the city of Lycopolis in the Egyptian Thebaid <note>A region in Upper Egypt</note>; that city worships Apollo and the wolf—that is, the *lykos*—with equal religious devotion. In both, they are venerating the Sun, because this animal snatches and consumes everything in the manner of the Sun; and, seeing with a very sharp eye, it overcomes the darkness of night. Some think that even wolves themselves <note>original: "λύκους"</note> were named from *lyke*—that is, from the first light—because these wild beasts observe that time as being most fit for snatching sheep, which are driven from their stalls to pasture before dawn after their nighttime hunger. <margin>Patrous.</margin> They also gave Apollo the surname *Patrous* <note>Ancestral or Fatherly</note>; not merely out of the religious devotion of a single race or city, but as the author of the procreation of all things, because the sun, having dried up moisture, provided the cause for all things to be generated. As Orpheus <note>The legendary poet and musician</note> says:
"Having the mind and the thoughtful counsel of the Father." <note>original: "Πατρὸς ἔχοντα νόον καὶ ἐπίφρονα βουλήν"</note> Hence we also call Janus "Father," venerating the sun under this title.

He also discusses the title "Patrous" (Fatherly) as a descriptor for the Sun's role in the creation of life.</summary>

### OF THE SATURNALIA

<margin>Nomius.</margin> ...worshiping him. They have given Apollo the name "Nomius" <note>Nomius means "of the pastures" or "the Shepherd."</note> not because of his role as a shepherd—as in the myth where he is imagined to have pastured the flocks of King Admetus—but because the Sun feeds all things that the earth brings forth. Thus, he is sung of as the shepherd not of just one kind, but of all flocks. 

<margin>Iliad 21.</margin> As in Homer, where Neptune says: 
> "Phoebus, you tended the shambling, curve-horned cattle." <note>original: "Φοῖβε, σὺ δ' εἰλίποδας ἕλικας βοῦς βουκολέεσκες" (Iliad 21.448)</note>

And the same poet signifies that Apollo is a shepherd of mares, when he says:
<margin>Iliad 2.</margin> > "The silver-bowed Apollo reared these in Pieria, 
> both of them mares, carrying the terror of Ares." <note>original: "Τὰς ἐν Πιερίῃ θρέψ' ἀργυρότοξος Ἀπόλλων / Ἄμφω θηλείας, φόβον Ἄρηος φορεούσας" (Iliad 2.766-767)</note>

Furthermore, temples dedicated to him as the protector of all shepherds exist among the people of Camirus under the name "guardian of the sheep" <note>original: "ἐπιμηλίου"</note> and among the Naxians as "protector of the herd." <note>original: "ποιμνίου"</note> Likewise, he is worshiped as the "lamb-haired" God, <note>original: "ἀρνοκόμης"</note> and among the Lesbians as "of the wooded glen." <note>original: "ναπαῖος"</note> There are many such titles throughout different cities that point toward the office of the God as a shepherd. For this reason, he is recognized as the overseer of every flock and truly a shepherd.

<margin>Eleleus.</margin> Apollo is called "Eleleus," from the word for "revolving around the earth," <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ ἑλίττεσθαι περὶ τὴν γῆν"</note> because he is seen to roll, as it were, in an eternal course around the earth. As Euripides says: "O Sun, whirling your flame with swift horses." <note>original: "ἥλιε θοαῖς ἵπποισιν ἑλίσσων φλόγα"</note> Or, because he travels about with a great mass of fire "gathered together"; <note>original: "συναλισθέντος"</note> or as Empedocles says: "wherefore, having been gathered together, you traverse the great heaven." <note>original: "οὕνεκ' ἀναλισθεὶς μέγαν οὐρανὸν ἀμφιπολεύεις"</note> Others derive the name from his "gathering and assembling" <note>original: "συναλίσκειν καὶ συναθροίζειν"</note> people when he rises, because his dawning brings men together into a company. 

<margin>Chrysocomas.</margin> Apollo is surnamed "Chrysocomas" <note>Golden-haired</note> from the brightness of his rays, which they call the "golden hair" of the sun. Hence he is also called "the one with unshorn hair," <note>original: "ἀκερσεκόμης"</note> <margin>* Unshorn hair</margin> because the rays can never be torn away from the forehead of his light. 

<margin>Argyrotoxus.</margin> Likewise, he is "Argyrotoxus" <note>Silver-bowed</note> because as he rises over the highest curve of the world’s circuit, he is shaped like a kind of white and silver bow; from this bow, his rays flash out in the manner of arrows. 

<margin>Smyntheus.</margin> He is surnamed "Smyntheus" <note>An epithet of Apollo usually associated with mice, but here given a solar etymology</note> because he "runs seething," <note>original: "ὅτι ζέων θεῖ," a pun on the heat of the sun</note> since he runs with burning heat. 

<margin>* Carneian.</margin> He is "Carneus," <note>original: "Καρνεῖος"</note> because he "is seen to be young while burning," <note>original: "καιόμενος ὁρᾶται νέος"</note> <margin>Carneus.</margin> or because, while all burning things are consumed, he—glowing with his own heat—remains always new. 

Likewise, he is Apollo "Skiollios," because he "makes his movements varied," <note>original: "ὅτι τὰς κινήσεις ἀλλοίας ποιεῖ"</note> always appearing to us from the South...

<margin>Philesius.</margin>

**Apollo Pythius** is thought by natural philosophers <note>The author uses "Physici" to refer to those who study the laws of nature rather than just myths.</note> to be named not from "consulting" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ πυθέσθαι"</note>—that is, not from the consultation

From this, they believe the name **Python** was derived, although the Greeks tell the myth that this name was given to the God because of his slaying of a dragon. 
Yet this myth does not shrink from an understanding of a natural secret. This will become clear if we review the sequence narrated about the birth of Apollo,
<margin>The natural reason for the myth of the serpent Python.</margin>
just as I promised a little earlier that I would explain. Juno is said to have opposed Latona when she was about to give birth to Apollo and Diana. But when the birth finally took place, they say a dragon called the **Python** attacked the cradle of the Gods, and Apollo, in his earliest infancy, killed the beast with his arrows. Natural reason demonstrates how this should be understood. 

For after chaos, when the confused deformity first began to shine forth into the shapes of things and the elements—and while the earth, still a moist substance, was swaying in its soft and unstable seat—as the ethereal heat gradually grew stronger and fiery seeds flowed down into it, these stars are believed to have been produced. The Sun was carried into the heights by the greatest force of heat, while the Moon, being of a more moist and, as it were, feminine nature, was pressed by a certain natural warmth and kept to the lower regions—as if the Sun consists more of the father's substance, and the Moon of the mother's. 

For indeed, natural philosophers hold that Latona represents the Earth. Juno long hindered her so that the deities we mentioned would not be brought forth; here, Juno represents the **Air**, <note>original: "aër"</note> which, being still moist and heavy at that time, stood in the way of the upper **Ether**, <note>original: "aetheri"</note> preventing the brilliance of the lights from shining through the density of the watery air, as if emerging from a kind of birth. # THE SATURNALIA

To confirm the truth of the story, the Temple of Providence—which they call the **Temple of Athena’s Foresight** <note>original Greek: "ναὸν προνοίας ἀθηνᾶς"</note>—is celebrated with appropriate religious devotion. For this reason, they are said to have been born on that island, because they seem to rise out of the sea for us. This island is called **Delos** for this reason: because the rising and, as it were, the birth of the twin lights <note>Apollo (the sun) and Diana (the moon).</note> makes all things **Delos** <note>original Greek: "Δῆλα," meaning manifest or visible</note>, that is, open and clear.

This, however, is the natural explanation for the death of the dragon, as **Antipater the Stoic** <note>A Stoic philosopher who sought to explain myths as metaphors for physical phenomena.</note> writes. For the exhalation of the still-damp earth, moving into the upper regions with a rolling force, and then—after it had been heated—rolling back down into the lower regions like a deadly serpent, was corrupting everything by the force of putrefaction. This decay is only generated from heat and moisture. By covering the sun itself with a cloud of thick darkness, it seemed in a way to steal away its light. But at last, weakened, dried out, and killed by the divine heat of the rays—as if by falling arrows—it gave rise to the myth of the dragon slain by Apollo.

There is also another reason for the slain dragon. For although the sun’s path never departs from the <term>ecliptic line</term> <note>The apparent path of the sun across the sky.</note>, it varies the shifts of the winds up and down with a certain deflection, winding its journey like the coil of a dragon. Hence **Euripides** says:

->The fire-born dragon who leads the way for the four-formed seasons, yoking the chariot’s many-peopled crowd in harmony.<- <note>A poetic description of the sun driving the seasons like a chariot, winding through the zodiac.</note>

Under this name of a "celestial journey," when the sun had completed its course, it was said to have **finished the dragon**.
<margin>*to have pierced</margin>
From this, the myth of the serpent’s death arose. Furthermore, by the name "arrows," nothing but the striking of the rays is shown. These are understood to be at their longest at the time when the sun is at its highest, on the longest days of the summer <term>solstice</term>, as it completes its annual course.

This is why he is called **Hekebolos** <note>original Greek: "ἑκηβόλος," the Far-Darter</note> and **Hekatebolos** <note>original Greek: "ἑκατηβόλος," the Far-Shooter</note>, from **casting his rays from afar** <note>original Greek: "ἕκαθεν τὰς ἀκτῖνας βάλλων"</note>, sending down his rays from the greatest distance and height all the way to the earth. ### BOOK I.

...completes [the sun's course], in which is the boundary of the longest day: and from there it performs a retreat toward the shortening of the days. At that time he is called **Pythius**: <note>original Greek: "ὡς πύματον θέων, ὅ ἐστι τὸν τελευταῖον δρόμον ἔχων"</note> as if "running to the end," which means "having reached the final part of the course." The same name fits him also when, entering **Capricorn** again, he is understood to have completed the final course of the shortest day. Therefore, in either of these signs, once the annual space has been traversed, Apollo is said to have finished the "dragon"—that is, his winding path. **Cornificius** <note>Quintus Cornificius, a Roman author interested in the origins of words.</note> reported this opinion in his *Etymologies*. Furthermore, these two signs, which are called the "gates of the sun"—**Cancer** and **Capricorn**—received these names for specific reasons: **Cancer** <note>The Crab.</note> is an animal that moves backward and sideways; by that same logic, the sun in that sign begins to perform its backward retreat obliquely, as is its custom. On the other hand, the habit of the **Goat** <note>Capricorn.</note> when grazing is to always seek high places as it feeds; similarly, the sun in Capricorn begins to return from the lowest depths to the heights.

<margin>Didymæus.</margin>
They call him **Apollo Didymæus** <note>original Greek: "Ἀπόλλωνα διδυμαῖον," meaning "Twin Apollo."</note> because he presents a double aspect of his own divinity: by illuminating and shaping the moon. For from a single source of light, he illuminates the spans of day and night with a twin celestial body. Thus, the Romans also worship the Sun under the name and form of the year <note>The text here is slightly fragmented in the original, likely referring to the sun's dual nature in governing time.</note> with the title of **Didymæan Apollo**.

<margin>Delphius.</margin>
They call him **Delphic Apollo** <note>original Greek: "Ἀπόλλωνα Δέλφιον."</note> because he reveals things that are hidden by the brightness of his light, <note>original Greek: "ἀπὸ τοῦ δηλοῦν ἀφανῆ," meaning "from making the unseen manifest"</note>; or—as **Numenius** <note>Numenius of Apamea, a philosopher who sought to link Greek thought with Eastern wisdom.</note> prefers—as if he were "one and alone." For he says that in the ancient language of the Greeks, *Delphos* meant "one"; from which, he says, a "brother" is called *adelphos*, as if no longer "one."

<margin>Description of the statue of Apollo among the people of Hieropolis, and its meaning.</margin>

The two equally female signs by which she is surrounded signify *hyle* <note>original: "hylen," a Greek term for "prime matter" or the raw substance of the universe.</note> and nature acting as his handmaidens. And the image of the dragon shows the winding path of the star; the eagles, because of the great speed of their flight, show the height of the sun. The Gorgon garment was added because Minerva, whom we accept as the guardian of this deity, is the power of the sun. As Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher who sought to find deep spiritual meanings in ancient myths.</note> also testifies, Minerva is the power of the Sun, which supplies wisdom to human minds. For this reason, this Goddess is remembered as being born from the head of Jove—that is, produced from the highest part of the ether, where the origin of the Sun is.

Orpheus clearly pronounces the Sun to be Liber in this verse:

> Consider **Iao** to be the supreme God of all:
> In winter he is **Hades**, and **Zeus** at the beginning of spring,
> The **Sun** in summer, and in autumn the delicate **Iao**.

### That not even Mars or Mercury are any other divinity than the Sun.

<meta>This page continues the discourse in Macrobius’s *Saturnalia*, Book 1, where the author argues through syncretism that all the major gods of antiquity are merely different names for the Sun.
