# BOOK I.

<margin>Liber is the same as the Sun.</margin>
What has been said concerning **Liber Pater** <note>The Roman name for Dionysus, the god of wine and ritual ecstasy.</note> demonstrates that **Mars** is also the same as the **Sun**. Indeed, many people associate Liber with Mars, showing them to be a single deity. This is why **Bacchus** is given the nickname <term>Enyalios</term>, <note>original: "ἐνυάλιος" (Enyalios), a title usually reserved for Mars or a specific war-spirit.</note> which is one of the names proper to Mars. Among the **Lacedaemonians**, <note>The Spartans, famous for their military culture.</note> an image of Liber Pater is even worshiped that is distinguished by a spear rather than a **thyrsus**. <note>A staff topped with a pinecone and wrapped in ivy, the traditional symbol of Bacchus.</note> Yet, even when he holds a thyrsus, what else is being carried but a hidden weapon, its point covered by creeping ivy? This signifies that the impulses of war must be restrained by a certain bond of patience—for ivy has a natural quality for binding and tying. Furthermore, the heat of wine, of which Liber Pater is the author, often drives men into a warlike fury. Therefore, because of the heat produced by both—which is of a similar nature—they wished Mars and Liber to be one and the same god.

Certainly, the Romans worship both with the title of "Father": calling one **Liber Pater** and the other **Marspiter**, <note>A contraction of "Mars Pater," similar to how "Jupiter" comes from "Iove Pater."</note> which is to say, "Father Mars." From this, Liber Pater is also proven to be a master of wars, because they recorded him as the first author of the **triumph**. <note>The ceremonial victory parade granted to successful Roman generals.</note> Since, therefore, Liber Pater is the same as the Sun, and Mars is the same as Liber Pater, who can doubt that Mars is the Sun? Even the **Acitani**, <note>The Accetani, a tribe in Roman Spain (Hispania).</note> a Spanish people, worship an image of Mars adorned with rays with the greatest religious devotion, calling him * **Neton**. <margin>* Neton</margin> And certainly, natural reason requires that the gods who are the parents of celestial heat should differ more in their names than in their substance and reality. Moreover, the fervor by which the mind grows hot, being excited at times toward anger, at times toward virtues, and sometimes toward the excess of a temporary madness—through which things wars are born—they have called Mars. The poet, expressing his power and comparing it to the likeness of fire, says:

> He raged as when spear-wielding Mars or a destructive fire [rages]. <margin>Iliad 15</margin>
<note>original Greek: "Μαίνετο δ᾿ ὡς ὅτ᾿ Ἄρης ἐγχείσπαλος ἢ ὀλοὸν πῦρ." From Homer's *Iliad*, Book 15, line 605.</note>

In short, it must be declared that the influence of the **Sun**, which rouses the fervor of our spirits and the heat of our blood, is called **Mars**.

<margin>That Mercury is the Sun.</margin>
To prove that **Mercury** is also the **Sun**, the evidence mentioned previously is supportive. Indeed, that **Apollo** and Mercury are the same is apparent from this: among many nations, the star of Mercury is referred to by the name of Apollo. Furthermore, Apollo presides over the **Muses**, and Mercury imparts speech, which is the gift of the Muses. Beyond this, there are many proofs that Mercury is considered to be the Sun. First, the statues of Mercury are adorned with feathered wings, a feature that demonstrates the speed of the Sun. Since we believe Mercury is the master of the mind—and we understand his name to be derived from the Greek *to interpret* <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ ἑρμηνεύειν" (apo tou hermēneuein), the etymological root of "Hermes."</note>—and since the Sun is the mind of the world, the speed of the mind is supreme, 
<margin>Odyssey, Book 7.
* wings
* winged</margin>
as **Homer** says: "as a wing or a thought." <note>original: "ὡσεὶ πτερὸν ἠὲ νόημα" (hōsei pteron ēe noēma). Macrobius is citing *Odyssey* 7.36.</note> Therefore, Mercury is adorned with wings as if he were the very nature of the Sun. The **Egyptians** illustrate this argument more clearly, fashioning winged statues of the Sun itself, which they represent with more than one color. 

They fashion one with a blue appearance and another with a bright appearance. Of these, they call the bright one "of the upper world" and the blue one "of the lower world." The name of the lower world is given to the Sun when it completes its course in the lower hemisphere—that is, in the winter signs—and the name of the upper world when it travels through the summer part of the **Zodiac**. The same fiction exists regarding Mercury under a different myth: he is considered the attendant and messenger between the gods of the upper and lower worlds. Furthermore, he is surnamed **Argiphontes** <note>Meaning "Slayer of Argus."</note>, not because he killed **Argus** (who they say was adorned with the light of many eyes around his head and, by the command of **Juno**, guarded the daughter of **Inachus** <note>Io, whom Jupiter had turned into a cow to hide her from his jealous wife, Juno.</note> after she had been turned into the form of a cow). <meta>This page continues the argument from page 268, where Macrobius identifies Mercury with the Sun. Having previously discussed the name "Hermes," he now explains the myth of Argus (the hundred-eyed giant) as an allegory for the starry sky being "extinguished" by the Sun's light.</meta>

# BOOK I.

...of eyes. Moreover, it was decided that the Sky should be called **Argus** because of its brightness and its speed, <note>original: "παρὰ τὸ ἀργὸν καὶ ταχύ" (para to argon kai tachu) — 'from [the words for] bright and swift.'</note>. And it seems to observe the earth from above; when the **Egyptians** wish to signify the earth in hieroglyphic letters, they use the figure of a bull. Therefore, that circuit of heaven, adorned with the lights of the stars, is thought to be slain by **Mercury** when the Sun, by observing the stars during the daytime, "kills" them as it were, by taking away the sight of them from mortals through the power of its light. Furthermore, many statues of Mercury are fashioned in a square shape, distinguished only by a head and with erect male genitalia.

This figure signifies that the **Sun** is the head of the world and the sower of all things: and that all its power consists not in some divided service of limbs, but in the mind alone, the seat of which is in the head. The four sides are fashioned for the same reason that the <term>tetrachord|A musical scale of four notes, or a four-stringed instrument, here representing cosmic harmony.</term> is believed to be attributed to Mercury. Indeed, this number signifies either the four regions of the world, or the four changes of the seasons by which the year is bounded; or it represents the fact that the system of the **Zodiac** is divided by two equinoxes and two solstices. In the same way, the seven strings of the lyre of **Apollo** allow us to understand the movements of the seven celestial spheres, over which nature established the Sun as the moderator. 

That the Sun is worshiped in the form of Mercury is also clear from the <term>caduceus|A staff entwined by two snakes, the traditional symbol of Mercury/Hermes.</term>, which the Egyptians fashioned in the likeness of male and female dragons joined together, to be consecrated to Mercury. These dragons are bound to each other in the middle part of their coil by a knot, which they call the **knot of Hercules**; and their front parts, bent back into a circle, join the circuit of the circle with pressed kisses; and afterwards the tails are brought back to the handle of the caduceus, and it is adorned with wings sprouting from that same part of the handle. The Egyptians extend the symbolism of the caduceus also to the generation of humans, which is called **genesis**: they say that four gods are present as protectors for a human being at birth...

OF THE SATURNALIA

...mentioning the **Guardian Spirit**, **Fortune**, **Love**, and **Necessity**. <note>original: "δαίμονα, τύχην, ἔρωτα, ἀνάγκην" (daimona, tychen, erota, ananken)</note> And they wish for the first two to be understood as the **Sun** and the **Moon**, because the Sun—as the author of the spirit, heat, and light—is the creator and guardian of human life; and therefore at birth he is believed to be the *daemon*, that is, a God. The Moon is *Fortune*, because she is the mistress of bodies, which are tossed about by the variety of chance occurrences. **Love** is signified by a kiss; **Necessity**, by a knot. Why wings are added to these figures has already been explained above. For these types of symbolic proofs, the coiling shape of dragons is especially chosen because of the winding path of both these celestial bodies.

->That **Aesculapius**, too, and **Health**, and **Hercules**, and along with **Isis**, even **Serapis** himself, are no other gods than the **Sun**. CHAPTER XX.<-

<margin>Aesculapius is the Sun.</margin>
This is why a dragon is placed alongside the statues of both **Aesculapius** and **Health**: because these deities are related to the nature of the Sun and the Moon. Indeed, Aesculapius is the health-giving power derived from the substance of the Sun, which brings aid to the souls and bodies of mortals. **Health** <note>The Roman goddess Salus.</note>, however, is the result of the Moon’s nature; by her, the bodies of living creatures are assisted, being strengthened by a health-bringing temperament. Therefore, the figures of dragons are joined to their statues because they demonstrate that human bodies—once the "skin" of weakness is cast off—may bloom again into their former vigor; just as dragons bloom again every single year after the skin of old age has been shed. For this reason, the appearance of the dragon is also attributed to the Sun itself: because the Sun always returns from a certain "old age" of its lowest descent <note>Referring to the winter solstice, the Sun's lowest point in the sky.</note> back to its height, as if into the strength of youth. Moreover, that the dragon is among the primary symbols of the Sun is shown even by the construction of its name: for it is named from the Greek word "to see." <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ δέρκειν" (apo tou derkein) — the word "dragon" (draco) is etymologically linked to the sharp sight of a serpent.</note> For they say that this serpent, with its extremely sharp and ever-watchful gaze, imitates the nature of this star; and for that reason, the guardianship of temples, shrines, oracles, and treasures is assigned to dragons. As for Aesculapius, the same...

# BOOK I.

That he <note>Aesculapius</note> is the same as **Apollo** is proved not only by this—that he is believed to have been born of him—but also because the power of divination is attributed to him. For **Apollodorus**, in his books titled <term>On the Gods <note>original: "πϵρὶ θϵῶν" (peri theon)</note></term>, writes that **Aesculapius** presides over divinations and auguries. And this is no surprise, since the disciplines of medicine and divination are closely associated. For a physician foreknows what will be either beneficial or harmful to the body in the future. <margin>This passage is in the *Prognostic* <note>Referring to the work by Hippocrates.</note>.</margin> Thus, as **Hippocrates** says, it is necessary for a physician to speak concerning the sick man about <term>the present, the past, and those things that are yet to be <note>original: "τά τϵ παρϵόντα, κὶ τὰ προγϵγονότα, καὶ τὰ μέλλοντα ἔσϵσθαι" (ta te pareonta, kai ta progegonota, kai ta mellonta esesthai)</note></term>: that is, what is, what has been, and what will soon follow. This matches the nature of divinations, which know <margin>Iliad, Book 1.</margin> <term>what is, what shall be, and what was before <note>original: "τά τ' ὄντα, τά τ' ἐσσóμϵνα πρὸ τ' ἐόντα" (ta t' onta, ta t' essomena pro t' eonta)</note></term>.

<margin>* The word "and" [atque] is not found in the ancient manuscripts.</margin> But **Hercules** is also not distinct from the substance of the **Sun**. Indeed, **Hercules** is that power of the **Sun** which provides virtue to the human race, making them like the gods. And you should not think that the one born of **Alcmene** at **Boeotian Thebes** was the only one, or even the first to be named **Hercules**; rather, after many others, he was the very last to be granted this title and honored with this name, because his immense bravery earned him the name of the God who governs virtue. Furthermore, the god **Hercules** is worshipped with great devotion at **Tyre**. But the **Egyptians** venerate him with the most sacred and august religion; and they worship him as one without a beginning, reaching back beyond memory, which among them is the longest of all records. He himself is believed to have slain the **Giants** when he fought on behalf of heaven, acting as the strength of the Gods. As for the **Giants**, what else should be believed other than that they were a certain impious race of men who denied the Gods, and were therefore thought to have wanted to drive the Gods from their celestial seat? Their feet ended in the coils of serpents, which signifies that they thought of nothing upright or heavenly, as the whole path and progress of their lives plunged toward the underworld. The **Sun** exacted the due punishments by the force of his pestilential heat. And indeed,
<margin>Glory of the air <note>original Greek: "ἦρας κλέος" (eras kleos)</note></margin> it is clear even from his name that **Hercules** is the **Sun**. For what else is **Heracles** but <term>Heras</term>—that is, "of the air"—and <term>cleos</term>—that is, "glory"? And furthermore, what other glory of the air is there except the illumination of the **Sun**, by whose retreat and depth the spirit of darkness is hidden?
Furthermore, the administration of sacred rites among the **Egyptians** asserts the manifold power of the God through manifold actions, signifying that this **Hercules** is <term>the sun who is in all things and through all things</term> <note>original Greek: "τὸν ἐν πᾶσι, καὶ διὰ πάντων ἥλιον" (ton en pasi, kai dia panton helion)</note>. From deeds performed elsewhere in the world, no small argument is gathered. For **Theron**, king of Nearer **Spain**, when he was driven by madness to storm the **Temple of Hercules** with an equipped fleet of ships, the **Gaditani** <note>The people of Gades, modern-day Cádiz, Spain.</note> came out against them, having set forth in long ships. Once battle was joined, while the fight still stood on equal terms, suddenly the royal ships were turned to flight and, at the same moment, were seized by an unexpected fire and burned. The very few enemies who survived were captured and reported that there had appeared to them lions standing upon the prows of the **Gaditan** fleet, and that suddenly their own ships were burned by emitted rays, just like those painted upon the head of the **Sun**.

<margin>That Serapis also and Isis are not distinguished from the sun.</margin> The city adjacent to this same **Egypt**, which boasts **Alexander the Macedonian** as its founder <note>Alexandria</note>, worships **Serapis** and **Isis** with a cult of almost breathless veneration. Yet it testifies that it bestows all that veneration upon the **Sun** under those names—whether by fixing a <term>calathus</term> <note>A basket-shaped crown, symbolizing the Sun's role in the fertility of the earth.</note> upon his head, or by adding to the statue the sign of a three-headed creature. This creature expresses in its middle (and also its largest) head the likeness of a **Lion**. On the right side, the head of a **Dog** rises up with a mild and fawning appearance; but the left part of the neck ends in the head of a ravenous **Wolf**. A **Dragon** <note>Used here in the classical sense of a large serpent.</note> connects these forms of animals with its coils, its head returning to the God's right hand, by which the monster is restrained. # BOOK I.

[The lion's] head represents the present time, because its condition, between the past and the future, is powerful and fervent in its present action. But the past is signified by the head of a **Wolf**, because the memory of things gone by is snatched and carried away. Likewise, the image of a fawning **Dog** designates the outcome of the future, regarding which hope—though uncertain—fawns upon us. To whom would these times be subservient, if not to their own author? His crown is marked by a <term>calathus</term> <note>A basket-shaped headdress, originally a grain measure, symbolizing the Sun's role in nourishing the world and the "capacity" of the universe to receive his heat.</note>, which both shows the height of the stars and demonstrates the power of his capacity: for all earthly things return to him when they are snatched up by his emitted heat. Hear now what is pronounced by an oracle regarding the **Sun**, or **Serapis**. For **Serapis**, whom the **Egyptians** have declared the greatest God, was asked by **Nicocreon**, king of the **Cyprians**, which of the gods he should be considered. The god instructed the king's anxious devotion with these verses:

> I am a god such as I shall tell you:
> The heavenly cosmos is my head, the sea my belly,
> The earth is my feet, and my ears are set in the ether;
> My far-beaming eye is the bright light of the sun.
<note>original Greek: Εἰμὶ θεὸς τοιόσ δε μαθεῖν, οἷον κ’ ἐγὼ εἴπω. / Οὐράνι@ κόσμ@ κεφαλὴ, κ’ ἀσὴρ ἡ θάλασσα, / Γαῖα δέμοι πόδες εἰσί, τὰ δ’ οὔατ’ ἐν αἰθέρι κεῖται. / Ὄμμά τε τηλαυγὲς, λαμπρὸν φά@ ἠελίοιο.</note>

From these things it is apparent that the nature of **Serapis** and the **Sun** is one and indivisible. **Isis** is celebrated in every religious rite, she who is either the earth or the nature of things subordinate to the **Sun**. Hence it is that the entire body of the **Goddess** is thick with continuous breasts, because the whole universe is nourished by the sustenance of either the earth or the nature of things.

# OF THE SATURNALIA

...but the lower hemisphere of the earth they called **Proserpina** <note>Also known as Persephone, the goddess associated with the underworld and the seasonal return of vegetation.</note>. Therefore, among the **Assyrians** or **Phoenicians**, a mourning Goddess is presented because the **Sun**, proceeding in its annual path through the order of the twelve signs, also enters a portion of the lower hemisphere. Of the twelve signs of the zodiac, six are considered "superior" and six "inferior." When the Sun is in the inferior signs, and thus makes the days shorter, the Goddess is believed to mourn, as if the Sun has been lost to a temporary death—snatched away and held by **Proserpina**, whom we have called the deity of the lower circle of the earth and of the **Antipodes** <note>Literally "those with feet opposite," referring to the inhabitants of the opposite side of the globe.</note>.

And again, they wish it to be believed that **Adonis** is restored to **Venus** when the **Sun**, having overcome the six annual signs of the lower order, begins to illuminate the hemisphere of our circle with an increase of light and of days. 

They say that **Adonis** was killed by a boar, fashioning in this animal an image of winter. For the boar is bristly and rough, delighting in damp and muddy places covered in frost; it feeds specifically upon a winter fruit, the acorn. Therefore, winter is like a wound to the **Sun**, which diminishes both its light and heat for us—both of which happen to living things at death.

A statue of this Goddess is fashioned on **Mount Lebanon** with her head <margin>Veiled, that is, covered.</margin> veiled and wearing a sad expression; she rests her face on her left hand beneath her cloak, and tears are believed to flow in the sight of those looking on. This image—besides representing the mourning Goddess (as we have said)—represents the wintry earth, at which time, veiled by clouds and widowed of the sun, it is numb. At this time, the springs (like the eyes of the earth) flow more abundantly, and the fields, again widowed of their own cultivation, show a mournful face. 

But when the **Sun** has emerged from the lower parts of the earth and crosses the boundaries of the vernal equinox by increasing the day, then **Venus** is joyful, and the fields grow beautiful and green with crops, the meadows with grass, and the trees with leaves. For this reason, our ancestors dedicated the month of **April** to **Venus**.

In a similar way, the **Phrygians**, in their myths and in the administration of their sacred rites...

# BOOK I.

...with only the names changed, the same principles are understood regarding the **Mother of the Gods** <note>Cybele, the ancient Phrygian earth goddess.</note> and **Attis**. For who could doubt that the **Mother of the Gods** is considered to be the **Earth**? This Goddess is carried by lions, animals known for their strength, impulse, and heat—qualities belonging to the nature of the heavens, whose embrace contains the air that carries the earth. The **Sun**, however, under the name of **Attis**, is adorned with both a shepherd’s pipe and a rod. The **pipe** <note>original: "fistula"</note> signifies the unequal nature of the breath of life, for the winds, which possess no equality or constancy, derive their proper substance from the Sun. The **rod** asserts the power of the **Sun**, who moderates and governs all things. Furthermore, it can be understood that the primary focus of these ceremonies is the **Sun** from this fact: after their ritual "descent" <note>original: "κατάβασις" (katabasis); referring to a ceremonial journey into the underworld or a period of mourning for a dying god.</note> is finished and the imitation of mourning is complete, the beginning of joy is celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of April <note>March 25th.</note>. This day they call the **Hilaria** <note>A festival of "rejoicing" marking the vernal equinox.</note>, the time when the **Sun** first makes the day longer than the night.

<margin>That Osiris is also the Sun.</margin>
The same religious effect, though under different names, is found among the **Egyptians** when **Isis** mourns **Osiris**. It is no secret that **Osiris** is nothing other than the **Sun**, and **Isis** is nothing other than the **Earth** (as we have said) or the nature of things. The same logic that applies to **Adonis** and **Attis** also alternates mourning and joy in the **Egyptian** religion according to the cycles of the annual administration. To assert that **Osiris** is the **Sun**, the **Egyptians**, whenever they wish to express his name in their hieroglyphic writing, engrave a scepter, and in it they depict the likeness of an eye. By this sign they show **Osiris**, signifying that this God is the **Sun**, looking down from on high with royal power upon all things, because antiquity calls the **Sun** the "eye of **Jupiter**" <note>Here referring to the sky or the supreme governing principle of the universe.</note>.

<margin>Horus is the same God as the Sun.</margin>
Among these same people, **Apollo**, who is the **Sun**, is called **Horus**. From this name, the twenty-four **hours** <note>original: "horae"</note> which make up the day and night received their name. Even the four seasons, which complete the annual circuit, are called **hours**. These same **Egyptians**, wishing to dedicate a statue in the name of the **Sun** itself, fashioned it with a shaved head,

# SATURNALIA

...but with the hair remaining on the right side. This preserved hair teaches us that the **Sun**, by the very nature of things, is never entirely hidden. Moreover, the removed hairs, though the roots remain, show that even during the time when this star is not visible to us, it still possesses the substance to emerge again, just as hair grows back. By the same logic, this also signifies the time when the light is "narrowed"—when the **Sun** reaches the shortest span of the day, as if its growth had been shaved away, leaving only a narrow presence. This time the ancients called the **winter solstice** <note>original: "brumale solstitium"</note>. They named this period *bruma* because of the "shortness of the days" <note>original: "bruma à breuitate dierū"; an ancient etymology linking *bruma* to *brevissima* (shortest day).</note>, which is the same as saying a **short day** <note>original: "βραχὺ ἦμαρ" (brachy emar)</note>. Emerging again from these hiding places or "narrows" toward the summer hemisphere, the Sun stretches out into greater increases as if being born anew; it is then believed to have reached its full kingdom.

For this reason, the **Egyptians** consecrated an animal in the **Zodiac** in that part of the sky where the **Sun**, in its annual course, boils with the strongest heat. They call the sign of the **Lion** <note>Leo</note> in that place the "home of the Sun," because that animal is seen to derive its very substance from the nature of the **Sun**. First, the lion surpasses other animals in impulse and heat, just as the **Sun** surpasses the other stars. Furthermore, the **Lion** is physically strong in its chest and the front part of its body, but its strength tapers off <note>original: "degenerat"</note> in its hindquarters. Likewise, the force of the **Sun** increases in the first part of the day until noon, or in the first part of the year from spring into summer; soon it weakens as it is led either toward sunset (the end of the day) or toward winter (which is seen as the "inferior" part of the year). The lion is also seen to always have open and fiery eyes, just as the **Sun** watches the earth with a perpetual, tireless, and open fiery eye.

<margin>That the signs of the zodiac are referred to nature.</margin>
But it is not only the **Lion**; indeed, all the signs of the **Zodiac** are rightly referred to the nature of the **Sun**. To begin with **Aries** <note>The Ram</note>, there is a great correspondence with him. For he lies upon his left side for the six months of winter, but from the vernal equinox <note>The start of spring.</note> he lies upon his right side—just like the **Sun**, which from that same time orbits the right hemisphere, having spent the rest of the time in the left. For this reason, the **Egyptians** also depict **Ammon** <note>The Egyptian god Amun-Ra, often depicted with ram's horns.</note>—whom they consider the setting sun...

...the Libyans believe, they fashion the Sun with **Ram’s horns**, with which that animal is especially powerful, just as the **Sun** is with its rays. For even among the Greeks, the **Ram** <note>original: "κριὸς" (krios)</note> is named from the **word for horn** <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ κέραος" (apo tou keraos). Ancient etymology linked the Greek word for ram to the word for horn.</note>. Moreover, Egyptian worship shows for many reasons that the **Bull** is related to the **Sun** <margin>from the head <note>original Greek: "ἀπὸ τῆς κάρας" (apo tēs karas); suggesting an etymology for the Bull/Taurus from the word for "head".</note></margin>, either because at **Heliopolis** <note>the "City of the Sun" in Egypt</note> they especially worship a bull consecrated to the **Sun**, which they name **Netiron** <margin>Netiron, Neuton</margin>; or because the bull **Apis** in the city of **Memphis** is received as an image of the Sun; or because in the town of **Hermonthis**, in a magnificent temple of **Apollo**, they worship a bull consecrated to the Sun, naming it **Bacchis** <margin>Bacin</margin>, distinguished by miracles corresponding to the nature of the sun. For it is claimed to change colors throughout every hour; and it is said to be shaggy with bristles growing in the opposite direction, contrary to the nature of all other animals. Whence it is held to be like an image of the **Sun** striving against the opposite part of the universe. Furthermore, what do the **Gemini** <note>the Twins, Castor and Pollux</note>, who are believed to live through alternating deaths, signify but one and the same **Sun**, now descending into the lowest parts of the world, now rising again to the highest altitude? What else does **Cancer** <note>the Crab</note>, with its sideways crawl, show but the path of the **Sun**? For the Sun's lot is never to travel a straight path, but always to move through that way <margin>as is usual; Virgil, Georgics 1</margin> *where the oblique order of the signs turns itself* <note>Quoting Virgil's *Georgics* 1.238. This refers to the ecliptic, the Sun's apparent path, which is tilted relative to the equator.</note>; and especially in that sign, the Sun begins to seek the lower regions from its highest course, moving obliquely. We have already spoken of the **Lion**. But **Virgo**, who carries an ear of grain in her hand, what else is she but the **solar power** <note>original Greek: "δύναμις ἡλιακὴ" (dynamis hēliakē)</note>, which is burdened <margin>cares for</margin> with fruits? And for this reason, she is believed to be **Justice**, who alone causes the growing fruits to reach the use of men. The whole of **Scorpio**, in which **Libra** <note>The Scales. In ancient astronomy, the Scales were originally the "Claws" of the Scorpion.</note> is located, represents the nature of the **Sun**, which grows sluggish in winter; and once this has passed, it raises its sting again by its own power, having suffered no loss of its nature from the winter torpor. **Sagittarius** <note>the Archer</note>, who is the lowest and last of all the dwellings of the **Zodiac**, for this reason degenerates from a man into a beast in its hindquarters; as if pushed down from the higher parts into the lower by its final sections: the arrow...

# OF THE SATURNALIA

...yet it suggests: which indicates that even then the life of all things depends on the rays of the **Sun**, even when it comes from the lowest point. **Capricorn**, in bringing the sun back from the lower regions to the upper ones, is seen to imitate the nature of the **goat**; for as it grazes, it always seeks the heights of the protruding cliffs from the lowest parts. Does not **Aquarius** show the very power of the Sun? For where would rain fall upon the earth, if the heat of the Sun did not draw moisture to the heights? The pouring back of this moisture provides an abundance of rain. In the final rank of the zodiac are located the **Pisces** (the Fish), which were consecrated to the Sun not by some likeness of their nature, as the others were, but as a display of the power of that star. For by it, life is given not only to creatures of the air and land, but also to those whose lives are submerged in the waters, as if exiled from the sight of the Sun. So great is the force of the sun that it gives life even by penetrating hidden places.

## That Nemesis, Pan (or Inuus), and Saturn are nothing other than the sun.
### CHAPTER XXII.

<margin>
That Nemesis is the sun.
</margin>
And, to return the discourse to the Sun's manifold power, **Nemesis**, who is worshiped as a check against pride, what else is she but the power of the Sun? For it is her nature to obscure bright things and remove them from sight, and to illuminate things in the dark and offer them to our view. 

<margin>
And that Pan is the sun god.
</margin>
**Pan** himself, whom they call **Inuus** <note>an ancient Roman deity of protector of herds, often identified with the Greek Pan</note>, allows himself to be understood by the wiser sort as the sun, under this appearance in which he is seen. The **Arcadians** <note>residents of a mountainous region in Greece</note> worship this god, calling him **the Lord of Matter** <note>original Greek: "τὸν τῆς ὕλης κύριον" (*ton tēs hylēs kyrion*). The Greek word "hyle" can mean both a forest/wood and the fundamental substance of the universe.</note>; they do not wish to signify a lord of the woods, but the ruler of all material substance. The power of this matter composes the essence of all bodies, whether they be divine or earthly. Therefore, the **horns of Inuus** and his long, flowing **beard** represent the nature of light, by which the sun both illuminates the circuit of the upper heaven and sheds light upon the lower regions. Whence **Homer** says of him:

<margin>
Iliad, Book XI.
</margin>
> He rose so that he might bring light to the immortals and to mortals. <note>original Greek: "Ὤρνυθ᾽ ἵν᾽ ἀθανάτοισι φόως φέροι, ἠδὲ βροτοῖσι" (*Ornyth' hin' athanatoisi phōōs pheroi, ēde brotoisi*)</note>

# BOOK I.

What the panpipe <note>Latin: *fistula*</note> or the staff signify, we have already explained above regarding the appearance of **Attis**. As for the fact that he ends in the feet of a **Goat**, the reasoning for this symbol is as follows: it is because matter, which is distributed into every substance by the Sun’s management, ends in the element of earth once the divine bodies have been formed from it. Therefore, the feet of this animal were chosen as a sign of this extremity: because the goat is an **earthly** creature, yet it always seeks the **heights** while grazing, just as the sun does—both when it sends its rays down to the lands from above, or when it gathers itself back and is seen upon the mountains. The love and delight of this **Inuus** <note>a Roman deity of the forests and herds, here equated with Pan</note> 
<margin>Echo.</margin>
is believed to be **Echo**, who is visible to no one's eyes. This signifies the **harmony of the heaven**, which is a friend to the Sun, acting as the moderator of all the celestial spheres from which that harmony is born; yet it can never be perceived by our human senses. **Saturn** himself, who is the author
<margin>Saturn is the same as the sun</margin>
of the seasons—and for this reason is called *Kronos* by the Greeks (changing a letter, as if he were *Chronos* <note>original: "κρόνος quasi χρόνος". The author is explaining an ancient etymology where the god's name, Kronos, is linked to the Greek word for "Time," *Chronos*.</note>)—what else is he to be understood as but the **Sun**? For the order of the elements is handed down to us as being distinguished by the count of the seasons, revealed by light, guided by the eternity of their connection, and separated by vision—all of which reveal the actions of the Sun.

That Jupiter and the **Assyrian Adad** are also the same as the Sun. Then, through the authority of both the theologians and **Orpheus**, it can be shown that all gods are referred back to the sun.

### CHAPTER XXIII.

Nor does **Jupiter** himself, the king of the Gods, seem to exceed the nature of the **Sun**. Rather, it is taught by clear evidence that Jupiter and the Sun are one and the same. For when **Homer** says:

<margin>Iliad 1.</margin>
> For Zeus went to the Ocean among the blameless Ethiopians
> yesterday for a banquet, and all the gods followed together;
> but on the twelfth day he will return to Olympus.
<note>original Greek: "Ζεὺς γὰρ ἐς ὠκεανὸν μετ’ ἀμύμονας αἰθιοπῆας / χθιζὸς ἔβη μετὰ δαῖτα, θεοὶ δ’ ἅμα πάντες ἕποντο, / Δωδεκάτῃ δέ τοι αὖθις ἐλεύσεται οὔλυμπόνδε."</note>

**Cornificius** writes that the Sun is understood by the name of Jupiter, for whom the waves of the **Ocean** provide a sort as a feast. For this reason (as both **Posidonius** and **Cleanthes** <note>Stoic philosophers who believed the sun was a "living fire" nourished by the evaporation of water</note> affirm), the Sun’s path does not withdraw from that region which is called "burnt," because it runs directly beneath it.

By these words, he intends the "great leader in heaven" to be understood as the **Sun** under the name of **Jupiter**, and he uses the "winged chariot" to show the speed of that celestial body. For because in whatever zodiac sign the Sun resides, he excels all other signs and stars—and the gods who preside over those signs—he is seen to go before all gods as their leader, ordering and adorning all things. Therefore, the other gods are regarded as his army, distributed through the twelve parts of the zodiac; for he himself holds and occupies the place of the twelfth sign, whichever sign he happens to be in. Moreover, he joins the name of **Spirits** <note>Daimones</note> with the title of **Gods**: either because gods are *daēmones*, that is, "those who know the future"; or (as **Posidonius** writes in his books titled *On Heroes and Spirits*) because they possess a quality produced and divided from the ethereal substance: whether from *daiein*, meaning "to burn,"

I have refrained from explaining why this was done, by what reasoning it departed from Egypt to the place where it now resides, or why it is worshipped according to Assyrian rather than Egyptian ritual, because it does not pertain to the present case. 

But now, that Jupiter and the Sun are the same is recognized both from the sacred ritual itself and from the deity's appearance. For the golden statue stands in the form of a beardless youth; the right hand is raised with a whip, in the manner of a **charioteer**; the left hand holds a thunderbolt and ears of grain. All these things demonstrate the combined power of Jupiter and the Sun. ...carried, not by their own will, but where the God impels those bearing them <note>The statues were carried on a litter by priests; the "divine impulse" directed their movements to indicate the god's will</note>: just as we have seen at Antium the statues of the **Fortunes** <note>The *Fortunae Antiates*, famous oracular goddesses in the city of Antium</note> move forward to provide their responses. Thus, even the Emperor **Trajan**, when he was about to enter **Parthia** <note>The Parthian Empire, Rome's great rival in the East</note> from that province with his army, was urged by friends of the most steadfast piety—who had witnessed great proofs of this divinity—to consult the god regarding the outcome of his undertaking. The priests were stunned by this action, for they were ignorant of the contents of the notebooks. Trajan received these with the greatest admiration, because he himself had also dealt with the God using blank tablets. Then, having written and sealed other notebooks, he consulted the god on whether he would return to Rome after the war was finished. The God ordered a **centurion's vine-staff** <term>Vitem centurialem: a branch of grapevine carried by a Roman centurion as a symbol of rank and used for discipline</term> to be taken from the gifts dedicated in the temple; he ordered it to be cut into pieces, wrapped in a shroud, and then carried out. The outcome of the matter became clear upon Trajan's death, when his bones were returned to Rome. For in the fragments of the staff, the likeness of remains <note>original: *reliquiarum* (relics or remains)</note> was visible, and by the symbol of the vine, the timing of the future event was shown.

When **Praetextatus** <note>Vettius Agorius Praetextatus, the host of the dialogue and a historical Roman senator known for his pagan piety</note> had made an end of speaking, all those present fixed their gazes upon him, revealing their admiration through their stunned silence. ...in our Virgil, who in my opinion excels the ancient teachers in learning, an injury is sought while excusing such things. But I ask whether, even if the poetry in such a great poet has displeased you, the oratorical sinews—which are most powerful in that same man—might yet seem to please you." At these words, **Evangelus** first broke into laughter. Then he added: "By Hercules, it finally remains for you to announce that **Virgil** <note>referred to in the text as "Vergilius"</note> is an orator! Nor is it a wonder, since your ambition carried him among the philosophers just a little while ago."

"If you are of the opinion," **Symmachus** said, "that **Maro** <note>Virgil's cognomen or family name</note> is thought by you to have intended nothing but the poetic—even though you might envy him even that name—hear what he himself pronounces about the manifold learning of his work. For a letter of Maro himself, in which he addresses **Augustus** <note>The first Roman Emperor, Virgil's patron</note>, begins thus: *'I truly receive frequent letters from you.'* and further down: *'Regarding my **Aeneas** <note>The hero of Virgil's epic, the Aeneid</note>, if by Hercules I already had something worthy of your ears, I would gladly send it. But the task begun is so great that I seem to myself to have entered upon such a work almost by a defect of mind; especially since, as you know, I am also imparting other studies to that work, and much more important ones.'*

Nor does the abundance of matter in Virgil's work disagree with these words, which most—nearly all—teachers of literature <term>literatores</term> pass by with unwashed feet <note>original: "pedibus illotis". A proverbial expression meaning to approach a subject without preparation, reverence, or proper initiation.</note>, as if a grammarian were allowed to know nothing beyond the explanation of words. Thus these 'elegant' men have set certain limits of knowledge for themselves, like certain <term>pomoeria</term> <note>The religious and legal boundary of a city, specifically Rome</note> and boundaries, beyond which if anyone should dare to step out, he must be thought to have looked into the temple of the goddess from which males are barred <note>An allusion to the "Bona Dea" (the Good Goddess), whose secret rites were strictly forbidden to men.</note>.

But let us, whom a 'thick Minerva' <note>original: "crassa Minerva". A Latin idiom referring to a dull, unrefined, or common-sense intellect; here, Symmachus argues they should strive for a more sophisticated, "thin" understanding.</note> does not suit, not allow the innermost shrines of the sacred poem to be hidden. Rather, having investigated the shrine of secret meanings, let us offer the opened inner sanctums to be celebrated by the devotion of the learned. Thus, stirred by mutual encouragement, they were easily and gladly moved to agreement; and looking at **Prætextatus**, they all begged that he be the first to reveal his judgment, with the others to follow in the order that the chance of their seating had created.

And **Vectius** said: "Indeed, among all the things for which the praise of ***Maro*** stands out, as a constant reader I admire this: that he has most learnedly preserved the law of the Pontiffs <term>ius Pontificum — the body of law governing the Roman state religion and its priests</term>, as if he were a professional in it, throughout many and varied parts of his work. After him, **Flavianus** said: "In our poet, I find such great knowledge of the law of the augurs <term>ius augurale — the sacred rules for interpreting the will of the gods through signs like bird flight</term> that, even if he were lacking in the learning of other disciplines, this profession alone would exalt him."

**Eustathius** then said: "I would especially proclaim how much he has carefully translated from the Greeks <note>referring to Virgil's debt to Homer and other Greek poets</note>—acting as if he were doing something else, now by the concealment of his art, now by open imitation—if I were not held by a greater admiration for the astrology and entire philosophy which, sparingly and soberly, he has sprinkled throughout his work in a way that can nowhere be criticized."

# BOOK I.

<page-num>287</page-num>

...he will make clear whatever seems obscure, being by far the greatest of all men of letters. After these words were spoken and pleased the whole assembly, **Prætextatus**, seeing the faces of everyone turned toward him, said: "Philosophy, which is the unique gift of the Gods and the discipline of disciplines, must be honored with the opening speech <note>original: "anteloquio"</note>. Therefore, let **Eustathius** remember that the first place for discourse has been granted to him, with every other profession stepping aside. You, my **Flavianus**, shall follow him; so that I may be refreshed by hearing you, and restore my strength for speaking through a period of silence."

Meanwhile, the steward in charge of the slaves <note>literally the 'moderator of servile obedience'</note>, whose task was to tend the household gods <term>Penates — the protective spirits of the Roman home</term>, arrange the provisions, and direct the domestic servants, reminded his master that the household slaves had already dined according to the solemnity of the annual custom. For during this festival <note>the Saturnalia, a midwinter festival where social roles were famously reversed</note>, religious households first honor the slaves with a feast prepared as if for the master's own use; and only then is the table reset for the father of the family. 

The head of the servants therefore suggested it was time for dinner and invited the masters to attend. Then **Prætextatus** said: "Our **Virgil** must therefore be reserved for a better part of the day, so that we may dedicate the fresh morning to examining his poem in order. Now the hour reminds us that this table should be graced by your presence. But let both **Eustathius** and, after him, **Nicomachus** remember that the duty of the opening speech is reserved for them in tomorrow's discussion." 

And **Flavianus** replied: "I now summon you according to our agreed rule, so that on the following day my own household gods <term>Penates</term> may boast of being blessed by the hospitality of such a great gathering." When everyone had agreed to this, they went to dinner with great cheerfulness of spirit, each man recalling and approving one point or another from the things they had shared among themselves.

Not to mention how many other things are missing in the meantime, and how confused everything is, as we shall point out in their proper places."

If you therefore approve of this plan, come now, let us recount whatever of such sayings comes to each man's mind, by turns stimulating our memory. Nothing could be said more charmingly or more bitingly. The king had asked about the size of the army and its matching strength; Hannibal answered regarding the plunder. <note>Hannibal implies the golden armor is merely expensive "loot" for the Romans to take, rather than a threat.</note>

For when a certain **Albidius** had eaten through his wealth and finally lost the remaining house he had to a fire, Cato said he had performed a *Protervia*: that which he could not eat, he had burned.

<header>OF THE SATURNALIA</header>

"If it had been in the union of a kiss,
Stirred by the fire of love,
It would have crossed over and left me.
And it would be a truly strange thing
That I would become dead to myself,
So as to live within the boy."
<note>This is a Latin translation of the Greek poem by Plato started on the previous page, where the speaker describes his soul flying to his lips during a kiss.</note>

### On the jokes of Marcus Tullius Cicero. CHAPTER III.

<margin>A joke of Cicero.</margin>
"But I am amazed," the speaker continued, "that you all have remained silent regarding the jokes of **Cicero**; in these he was most eloquent, as he was in all things. And if it seems right—just as a **shrine-keeper** <note>original: *Aedituus*. A temple official who explained the history and oracles of a sacred site to visitors.</note> proclaims the responses of his deity—so I shall relate the sayings of Cicero that my memory provides." Then, with everyone leaning in to listen, he began:

<margin>Against Damasippus.</margin>
When Marcus Cicero was dining at the house of **Damasippus**, and his host had put out a mediocre wine, saying, "Drink this **Falernian** <note>A famous and highly prized wine from Italy; Damasippus is caught lying about the quality of his cheap wine.</note>; it is forty years old," Cicero replied: "It carries its age well." <note>A double-edged remark: the wine is so poor that it hasn't improved at all over four decades, or perhaps it simply doesn't taste like a fine vintage should.</note>

<margin>Against Lentulus.</margin>
The same man, when he saw his son-in-law **Lentulus** <note>Publius Cornelius Lentulus Spinther. Historical accounts agree he was a man of very short stature.</note>—a man of very small height—buckled into a long sword, asked: "Who has tied my son-in-law to a sword?"

<margin>Against his brother Quintus.</margin>
Nor did he spare his brother **Quintus Cicero** from similar biting wit. For when he saw in the province that his brother had governed a **shield-portrait** <note>original: *clypeatam imaginem*. A style of portrait where the subject's head and chest were depicted within a circular frame resembling a shield.</note> of him, painted according to custom with massive features down to the chest—now, Quintus himself was of small stature—he said: "My brother is larger as a half than as a whole."

<margin>Against Vatinius.</margin>
During the consulship of **Vatinius** <note>Publius Vatinius, who served as consul for only a few days at the end of 47 BCE, a "reward" from Julius Caesar that was widely mocked.</note>, which he held for only a few days, a notable bit of Cicero’s **wit** <note>original: *urbanitas*. A Latin term for the refined, sophisticated humor expected of a city-dweller.</note> was being passed around. "A great miracle," he said, "occurred in the year of Vatinius: for while he was consul, there was neither winter, nor spring, nor summer, nor autumn." <note>The joke is that his entire term of office was so short that the seasons didn't even have time to change.</note>

Later, when Vatinius complained that Cicero had found it a burden to visit him at home while he was ill, he replied: "I wanted to come during your consulship, but the night overtook me." <note>Suggesting the consulship was so brief it was over before the day ended.</note>

Cicero, moreover, seemed to be avenging himself, as one who had responded...

<header>BOOK II.</header>

He remembered **Vatinius** <note>Publius Vatinius, a political climber and enemy of Cicero known for his physical deformities.</note>, who, when he was boasting that he had been carried back from exile on the shoulders of the Republic, was asked: "Where then did you get those varicose veins?" <note>Cicero implies that the weight of the Republic—or perhaps the "burden" of Vatinius himself—was so heavy or awkward that it caused physical strain, mocking Vatinius's physical ailments.</note>

<margin>Against Caninius.</margin>
**Caninius Rebilus** also, who (as Servius related) was consul for only a single day, when he had ascended the **rostra** <note>The speaker's platform in the Roman Forum.</note>, entered the office of the consulship and laid it down at the same time. Cicero, delighting in this, mocked him with every opportunity for wit, saying that Caninius was a "theoretical consul." <note>original: λογοθεώρητος (*logotheoretos*). A Greek term meaning "perceived only by the mind"—implying he was a consul in name only, not in practice.</note> Furthermore, the result for **Rebilus** was that people would ask under which "consuls" he had been a consul. <note>In Rome, years were named after the two consuls; because his term was so short, he didn't even "last" a whole year to have a term named after him.</note> Cicero did not stop saying: "We have a most vigilant **Consul** <note>original: *C O S.*, a standard abbreviation for *Consul*.</note> in Caninius, who during his entire consulship never saw sleep." <note>A pun: he wasn't "vigilant" because he was hardworking, but because his entire term lasted only a few hours during the day.</note>

<margin>Against Pompey.</margin>
**Pompey** was impatient with Cicero’s jokes. These sayings of Cicero about him were often repeated. "I truly know whom I should flee, but I do not know whom I should follow." <note>Cicero felt trapped between the tyranny of Caesar and the incompetence of Pompey.</note> Moreover, when he had arrived at Pompey’s camp and people said he had arrived late, he replied: "I am not at all late; for I see nothing prepared here." Then, when Pompey asked where his son-in-law **Dolabella** was, he replied: "With your father-in-law." <note>A sharp jab: Dolabella had joined Caesar’s side, and Caesar was Pompey’s former father-in-law.</note> And when Pompey had granted Roman citizenship to a deserter, Cicero said: "O, what a fine man! He promises the citizenship of another to the **Gauls**, yet he cannot restore our own to us." For these reasons, Pompey was seen to have rightfully said: "I wish Cicero would go over to the enemy, so that he might fear us."

<margin>Against Caesar.</margin>
The biting wit of Cicero also bared its teeth against **Caesar**. For first, after Caesar's victory, when asked why he had erred in choosing his side, he replied: "The way he wore his belt deceived me." <note>original: *Præcinctura*. Cicero joked about Caesar’s habit of wearing his toga loosely belted with trailing fringes, which was traditionally seen as a sign of effeminacy or a lack of discipline.</note> He joked about Caesar, who wore his toga belted in such a way that by trailing the fringe, he walked like a soft man. This went so far that **Sulla**, as if foreseeing the future, said to Pompey: "Beware that ill-girt boy."

Furthermore, when **Laberius** <note>Decimus Laberius, a famous writer of mimes whom Caesar forced to act on stage, which normally stripped a man of his status as a Knight.</note>, at the end of the games, was honored with a gold ring by Caesar and had immediately crossed over to the fourteen rows to watch the show—his rank having been violated—and when he had been pulled down...

->### SATURNALIA<-

...since he was a Roman knight. When the **Mime** <note>Decimus Laberius, a famous writer of mimes who was forced by Caesar to perform on stage, which cost him his knightly status.</note> was finished and was passing by, Cicero said to Laberius as he was looking for a place to sit: "I would have welcomed you to sit by me, were I not so cramped for space." He was both rejecting the man and joking about the new **Senate**, whose numbers Caesar had increased beyond what was right. But he did not get away with it: for Laberius replied: "It is a wonder that you are cramped, you who are accustomed to sitting on two stools." <note>original: *duabus sellis sedere*. This was a sharp rebuke of Cicero’s political reputation for "sitting on the fence" or trying to please both the Pompeian and Caesarian factions.</note> This was a reproach of Cicero’s inconsistency, for which this otherwise excellent citizen was unfortunately notorious.

Cicero also openly mocked Caesar's carelessness in selecting members for the Senate on another occasion. For when he was asked by his host, **Publius Mallius**, to secure a seat on the local council for his stepson, Cicero said in front of a large crowd: "In Rome, if **Pompey** regains his rights, it will be difficult; but currently, it is easy." <note>A jab at Caesar’s unilateral power to grant offices regardless of traditional law.</note>

Nor did his biting wit stop there. Indeed, when he was greeted by a certain **Andron of Laodicea**, Cicero asked the reason for his visit. When he learned that the man had come as an ambassador to Caesar to discuss the "liberty of his homeland," Cicero expressed the state of Rome's own public servitude by saying: "If you succeed in your mission, then go on an embassy for us as well." <note>original Greek: ἐὰν ἐπιτύχῃς, καὶ περὶ ἡμᾶς πρέσβευσον. Cicero is pointing out the irony of a foreigner asking Caesar for freedom when the Romans themselves have lost theirs.</note>

<margin>Against Mark Antony.</margin>
There was a great deal of excessive joking and sharp seriousness in him, such as this excerpt from a letter to **Gaius Cassius**, the assassin of the Dictator: "I wish you had invited me to dinner on the **Ides of March**; there certainly would have been no leftovers. As it is, your 'leftovers' are troubling me." <note>original: *reliquiarum nihil fuisset*. Cicero is joking that if he had been part of the conspiracy to kill Caesar, he would have insisted they kill Mark Antony as well. Antony is the "leftover" causing trouble for the Republic.</note> Cicero also mocked his son-in-law **Piso** and **Marcus Lepidus** with the greatest wit.

<margin>Transition to Chapter 4.</margin>
While **Symmachus** was still speaking and appeared ready to say more, **Avienus** interrupted him, as often happens in dinner-table conversations: "In this kind of wit," he said, "**Augustus Caesar** was second to none, and perhaps not even to **Tully** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note>. If you all wish, I shall relate some of his sayings as my memory suggests them." But **Horus** said: "Allow Symmachus to finish explaining the sayings of Cicero regarding those he has already named, and..."

<header>BOOK II.</header>

<margin>Against Piso</margin>
The things you wish to relate about **Augustus** <note>The first Roman Emperor, known for a specific style of refined, "urbane" wit.</note> will follow more opportunely. As Avienus fell silent, **Symmachus** said: "I recall that when Cicero’s son-in-law, **Piso**, was walking somewhat too softly, while his daughter was walking rather briskly, Cicero said to his son-in-law: 'Walk like a woman,' and to his daughter: 'Walk like a man.'"

And when **Marcus Lepidus** <note>A member of the Second Triumvirate alongside Octavian (Augustus) and Mark Antony.</note> had said to the Conscript Fathers in the Senate: "I would not have made so much of a similar deed,"
<margin>Against Lepidus</margin>
Tullius [Cicero] replied: "I would not have made so much of an **inflectional rhyme**." <note>original: ὁμοιόπτωτον (*homoeoptoton*). A rhetorical term for ending successive clauses with words in the same grammatical case. Cicero is mocking Lepidus’s repetitive and clunky phrasing.</note> "But continue, Avienus, lest I delay you further when you are so eager to speak."

### On the jokes of Augustus toward others, and of others in turn toward him. CHAPTER IV.

<margin>Augustus’s jokes toward many</margin>
And he continued: "Augustus Caesar, I say, affected a certain fondness for joking, provided his dignity and modesty remained intact; he took care not to descend into the behavior of a common buffoon. He had once written a tragedy titled *Ajax*, but had deleted it because he was dissatisfied with it. Later, **Lucius**, a serious writer of tragedies, asked him how his *Ajax* was doing. He replied: 'He has fallen upon the sponge.'" <note>A clever pun: the mythological hero Ajax committed suicide by falling on his sword; the Emperor's play "died" because he used a sponge to rub the ink off the parchment.</note>

The same Augustus, when a certain man was nervously offering him a petition—now extending his hand, now pulling it back—said: "Do you think you are giving a penny to an elephant?"

The same man, when **Pacuvius Taurus** was asking him for a gift of money, claiming that 'people were already commonly saying' that a large sum had been given to him by the Emperor, replied: "But do not you believe them."

When another man, who had been removed from his command of the cavalry and was demanding a pension, said: "I do not ask for this to be given to me for the sake of profit, but so that I may seem to have obtained the gift by your judgment, and thus to have laid down my office with honor," Augustus struck back with this saying: "You tell everyone that you received it, and I will not deny that I gave it."

His wit was also noted regarding **Herennius**, a young man given over to vices. When Augustus had ordered him to leave the camp, and the young man pleaded as a suppliant: "How shall I return to my father’s house? What shall I say to my father?" the Emperor replied: "Tell him that I displeased you."

To a soldier hit by a stone during a campaign, who was left with a disfiguring scar on his forehead yet boasted too much of his exploits, he gave this light rebuke: *“But when you run away,” he said, “never look back behind you.”* <note>The joke is that if the soldier had been hit in the face, he must have been facing the enemy; but Augustus suggests that if he had been fleeing, he wouldn't have been hit at all—or perhaps he's warning the boaster that his "war wound" is only visible from the front.</note>

To **Galba** <note>Sulpicius Galba, a renowned orator and father of the future emperor, who was a hunchback.</note>, whose body was deformed by a hump, while he was pleading a case before him and frequently saying, *“Correct me if you find anything to rebuke in me,”* Augustus replied: *“I can advise you, but I cannot **straighten** you.”* <note>original: "corrigere." Augustus puns on the double meaning of the Latin word: to correct a mistake and to physically straighten something crooked.</note>

When many people were being acquitted while **Severus Cassius** <note>A famously aggressive but often unsuccessful prosecutor.</note> was the accuser, and the architect of the **Forum of Augustus** was dragging out the completion of the work for a long time, Augustus joked: *“I wish Cassius had prosecuted my forum as well.”* <note>Implying that if Cassius had "accused" the forum, it would have been "discharged" or finished as quickly as the defendants he prosecuted.</note>

When **Vectius** had plowed up his father’s monument, Augustus said: *“This is truly cultivating your father’s memory.”* <note>original: "colere." A pun on the word meaning both to "till the soil" and to "honor or cherish."</note>

When he had heard that among the boys under two years old whom **Herod**, the King of the Jews, had ordered to be killed in Syria, Herod's own son had also been slain, he said: *“It is better to be Herod’s pig than his son.”* <note>This is a famous pun on the Greek words *hys* (pig) and *huios* (son). Since Herod was Jewish and observed dietary laws, his pigs were safe, whereas his sons were not.</note>

<margin>little honey</margin>
<margin>to tighten/stretch</margin>
<margin>all soft things.</margin>
The same Augustus, because he knew his friend **Maecenas** <note>Augustus's closest advisor and a famous patron of the arts, known for his luxurious and somewhat effeminate lifestyle.</note> possessed a style that was lax, soft, and loose, often displayed the same manner in the letters he wrote to him. In contrast to the disciplined speech he otherwise maintained in his writing, in a personal letter to Maecenas, he added several jokes poured out in jest: *“Farewell, honey of the people, my little honey-sweet, ivory from Etruria, silphium of Arezzo, heavenly diamond, Tiberine pearl, emerald of the Cilnii, jasper of the potters, beryll of Porsenna. May you have a carbuncle, so that I may **cut short all the soft indulgences** <note>original: ἵνα συντέμω πάντα μάλαγμα (hina syntemō panta malagma). Augustus is mocking Maecenas’s love of perfumes and soft poultices by using an absurdly florid and "effeminate" greeting.</note> of the harlots.”*

He was once received by a certain man for a dinner that was quite meager and ordinary. For he almost never refused anyone who invited him. Therefore, after the meal, departing from the host who had provided no display or grandeur, Augustus whispered this to him as he said goodbye: *“I did not realize I was such a close friend of yours.”* <note>A polite way of saying the food was so poor it was like a meal shared only between the most informal of family members.</note>

*When he complained about the darkness of the Tyrian purple <note>The most expensive and prestigious dye in the ancient world, extracted from sea snails.</note> that he had ordered, and the seller said, "Hold it up higher and look at it," he used this wit: "What then? So that the Roman people can say I am well-dressed, am I to walk only on the sun-deck?"* <note>original: "solario." A solarium was an open terrace or flat roof exposed to the sun; Augustus implies the color is only visible in harsh, direct light.</note>

*To his **nomenclator** <term>nomenclator: a servant whose job was to remember and whisper the names of citizens to his master during public greetings</term>, of whose forgetfulness he was complaining, and who asked: "Do you have any commissions for the forum?" he replied: "Take these letters of recommendation, since you don't know anyone there."*

*He elegantly insulted **Vatinius** in his youth. Vatinius, troubled by gout, nevertheless wanted to appear to have shaken off the ailment and boasted that he could walk a thousand paces. Caesar [Augustus] said: "I am not surprised; the days are somewhat longer now."* <note>A joke suggesting Vatinius's "mile" takes so long to walk that it only seems possible because the days have lengthened.</note>

<margin>20,000,000 sesterces</margin>
*When the massive size of the debt left by a certain Roman knight—which exceeded twenty million sesterces <term>sestertius: a silver coin and the basic unit of Roman currency; twenty million was a staggering, almost impossible fortune</term> and which he had concealed while alive—was reported to him, Augustus ordered that the man's bedroom mattress be bought for him at the auction. When people expressed surprise at the command, he gave this reason: "I must have for my sleep the mattress on which a man who owed so much was able to sleep."*

*One must not omit his remark in honor of **Cato** <note>Cato the Younger, the famous Stoic who committed suicide rather than live under Caesar's rule, becoming a symbol of Republican virtue.</note>. He happened to visit the house where Cato had lived. When **Strabo**, seeking to flatter Caesar [Augustus], spoke ill of Cato’s stubbornness, Augustus said: "Whoever does not wish the present state of the Republic to be changed is both a good citizen and a good man." In this way, he both seriously praised Cato and looked out for his own interests, so that no one would attempt a revolution.*

<margin>Jokes of others against Augustus.</margin>
*I am usually more amazed at the jokes Augustus endured than those he himself uttered, because the credit for patience is greater than that for eloquence—especially since he bore some jokes that were even sharper with an even temper. The harsh joke of a certain provincial man became well known. He had entered Rome looking exactly like Caesar, and had turned the eyes of everyone toward himself. Augustus ordered the man to be brought to him, and having seen him, questioned him in this way: "Tell me, young man..."*

...[the young] man, was your mother ever in Rome?" He denied it, but not content with that, he added: "But my father was, often." <note>Augustus was implying the young man looked so much like him that the boy's mother must have had an affair with Augustus's father; the boy cleverly flips the insult to suggest Augustus's own mother was the unfaithful one.</note>

During the times of the Triumvirate <term>Triumvirate: a political regime dominated by three powerful individuals; here referring to Augustus, Mark Antony, and Lepidus</term>, when Augustus had written **Fescennine verses** <term>Fescennine verses: a Roman tradition of ribald, improvisational, and often scurrilous poetry used to mock others</term> against **Pollio**, the latter said: "But I am staying silent; for it is not easy to write against a man who can proscribe." <note>original: "proscribere." A pun on the word "scribe": while Pollio could write (scribere) a poem, Augustus could "proscribe" (proscribere), which meant putting a name on a public list of those condemned to death and their property seized.</note>

**Curtius**, a Roman knight dissolved in luxury, when he had taken up a meager thrush <note>Thrushes were considered a great delicacy in Roman fine dining.</note> at Caesar’s banquet, asked if it might be permitted to "send" it. <note>original: "mittere." Curtius uses a double meaning: usually a guest might ask to "send" a gift from the table to a friend, but here he means "throw" it away.</note> The prince replied, "Why should it not be?" He immediately threw it out the window.

Augustus, without being asked, had paid off the debt of a certain senator dear to him, counting out four million sesterces. But that man, instead of giving thanks, wrote only this to him: "Nothing for me?" <note>The senator wittily complains that because the money went directly to his creditors, he did not actually "receive" any cash to keep for himself.</note>

His freedman **Licinius** was accustomed to contribute large sums of money to his patron when he was beginning new works. Following this custom, he promised a hundred [thousand] via a petition, in which a part of the over-drawn line <note>original: "uirgulæ superductæ." In Roman numeral notation, a horizontal bar placed over a number multiplied its value by one thousand.</note> extended beyond the end of the sum, leaving an empty space below. Caesar, taking the opportunity, joined another "hundred" to the first with his own hand, carefully filling the space and imitating the handwriting; thus he received a doubled sum while the freedman feigned ignorance. Later, when another work was begun, the freedman gently threw his own deed back at Caesar by giving him such a petition: "I contribute to you, Lord, for the expense of the new work, whatever shall seem fit." <note>By leaving the amount blank, Licinius prevented Augustus from forging a higher number by extending the lines of the numerals again.</note>

The patience of Augustus as **Censor** <term>Censor: a high-ranking official responsible for maintaining the census and supervising public morality and finances</term> was also remarkable and praised. A Roman knight was being reproached by the prince on the grounds that he had diminished his inheritance. But he proved right then and there that he had increased it. Soon after, Augustus objected to the same man that he had not obeyed the laws regarding entering into marriage. The man replied that he had a wife and three children. Then he added: "In the future, Caesar, when you make inquiries about honorable men, entrust the task to honorable men." <note>This was a sharp rebuke to the Emperor, suggesting his informants were dishonest or incompetent.</note>

He also bore not just the bluntness, but even the audacity of a soldier. In a certain villa he was spending restless nights, with the [sound] breaking his sle= <note>original: "somnum." The sentence continues on the next page.</note>

<margin>* elsewhere: it/her</margin>
...his sleep was frequently disturbed by the hooting of an owl. He ordered the owl to be caught. A soldier skilled in fowling <note>original: "aucupij." The art of catching birds.</note>, * and in hope of a great reward, brought it to him. The Emperor praised him and ordered a thousand coins to be given. The man dared to say: "I would rather it live," and he released the bird. Who did not marvel that the defiant soldier walked away without offending Caesar?

When a veteran was in legal danger on his appointed day of trial, he approached Caesar in public and asked him to stand by him. Caesar immediately gave him an advocate chosen from his own retinue and recommended the litigant to him. The veteran cried out in a loud voice: "But Caesar, when you were in danger during the **Battle of Actium** <term>Battle of Actium: the decisive naval battle in 31 BCE where Augustus defeated Mark Antony and Cleopatra</term>, I did not seek a substitute, but I fought for you myself!" and he bared the scars impressed upon him. Caesar blushed and personally attended the court session, as one who feared appearing not only arrogant, but also ungrateful.

<margin>Acroamata are festive performances and pleasant narrations among the Greeks.</margin>
During dinner, Caesar had been delighted by the young musician-slaves of Turonius Flaccus, a slave dealer; he had rewarded them with grain, even though he had been generous with coins for other **performances** <term>Acroamata: Greek for musical or theatrical entertainments intended for a banquet</term>. Later, when Caesar asked for the same boys during dinner, Turonius excused them by saying: "They are at the mills." <note>Working at the grain mills was a common and grueling punishment for slaves; Turonius is making a joke that since Caesar paid them in grain, they must be busy grinding it.</note>

He was returning in glory after the victory at Actium. Among those offering congratulations, a man met him holding a raven which he had trained to say: "Hail Caesar, Victor, Emperor!" Marveling at the dutiful bird, Caesar bought it for twenty thousand coins. The man’s partner, who had received none of that generosity, informed Caesar that the man had another raven, and asked that the man be forced to bring it. When it was brought, it uttered the words it had learned: "Hail, Victorious Emperor Antony!" <note>The bird-trainers were playing both sides of the civil war, preparing birds to greet whoever emerged as the winner—Augustus or his rival, Mark Antony.</note> Not at all provoked, Caesar thought it enough to order the man to share the reward with his partner. Having been greeted similarly by a parrot, he ordered it bought. Finding the same thing marvelous in a magpie, he purchased this one as well. There is also the example of a poor shoemaker...

[A neighbor] urged [a shoemaker] to train a raven for a similar greeting. The man, having exhausted his savings on the effort, used to say to the bird whenever it failed to respond: "The work and the expense are wasted." <note>original: "Opera & impensa perijt."</note> Eventually, however, the raven began to speak the dictated greeting. When Augustus heard it while passing by, he replied: "I have enough such greeters at home." The raven’s memory served it well, for it then added the words it used to hear its complaining master say: "The work and the expense are wasted." At this, Caesar laughed and ordered the bird to be bought for a price higher than he had ever paid for any bird before.

A certain **Greekling** <note>original: "Græculus." A diminutive term often used by Romans that could be either affectionate or slightly patronizing toward Greek intellectuals.</note> used to offer a fawning epigram to Caesar as he descended from the palace. When he had done this many times in vain, and Augustus saw him about to do it again, the Emperor quickly scribbled a short Greek epigram of his own on a piece of paper and sent it to the man as he approached. The man read it and began to praise it, expressing wonder in both his voice and his expression. As he drew near the Emperor's litter, he reached his hand into a meager pouch and pulled out a few small coins <note>original: "denarios."</note> to give to the prince. He added this remark: "Not according to your fortune, Augustus; if I had more, I would give more." <note>original Greek: "Μὴ κατὰ τὴν τύχην σου σέβαστέ εἰ πλέον εἶχον, πλέον ἐδίδουν."</note> Amidst general laughter, Caesar called his steward and ordered one hundred thousand **sesterces** <term>Sestertia: a high-value Roman currency; 100,000 sesterces was a small fortune, enough to qualify for certain social ranks</term> to be paid to the Greek.

### On the jests and character of Julia, daughter of Augustus. CHAPTER V.

Otherwise, she had a love of literature and much erudition (which was easy to acquire in that household), and furthermore, a gentle humanity, and...

<margin>Julia’s response.</margin>
Julia had come to him in a rather immodest outfit and had offended the eyes of her silent father. The next day, she changed the style of her dress and embraced her joyful father with an assumed severity. But he, who the day before had restrained his grief, could not restrain his joy. "And how much more appropriate," he said, "is this dress for a daughter of Augustus?" Julia did not fail in her own defense, saying: 

> "For today I dressed for my father's eyes; yesterday, for my husband's."

This also is well known: Livia <note>Augustus's wife and the stepmother of Julia.</note> and Julia had drawn the people’s attention to themselves at a gladiatorial show because of the difference in their entourages. For while serious, elderly men surrounded Livia, Julia was sat about by a flock of young men, and indeed quite extravagant ones. Her father warned her in writing that she should observe how much difference there was between two leading women. She wittily wrote back: 

> "And these men will grow old along with me."

This same Julia had begun to have gray hairs early, which she used to pluck out in secret. A sudden arrival of her father once surprised her hairdressers. There is a similar saying by Populia, daughter of Marcus. When someone wondered why other animals never desired a mate except when they wished to become pregnant, she replied: "Because they are beasts." <note>This implies that humans, unlike animals, enjoy intimacy for its own sake rather than just for reproduction.</note>

### Again, concerning the jokes and witty replies of men. CHAPTER VI.

But to return from women to men, and from lewd jokes to honorable ones: Casellius the legal consultant was considered a man of wonderful urbanity and freedom of speech. However, this particular joke of his became especially well known:

<margin>A celebrated story</margin>
Vatinius <note>Publius Vatinius, a politician much loathed by the Roman public for his corruption.</note> had once been pelted with stones by the people while he was presenting a gladiatorial show. He had managed to get the Aediles <gloss>public officials</gloss> to issue an edict that no one should throw anything into the arena except fruit. It happened during those days that Casellius was consulted by someone as to whether a pine cone was a fruit. 

<margin>Casellius's saying</margin>
He replied: "If you are going to throw it at Vatinius, it is a fruit." <note>A pine cone is hard and heavy; by legally classifying it as "fruit," Casellius wittily encouraged the public to continue pelting the unpopular Vatinius.</note>

Then, to a merchant who asked how he should divide a ship with his partner, he is said to have replied: "If you divide the ship, neither you nor your partner will have it." <note>A literal-minded legal joke; dividing a physical ship in half destroys it.</note>

<margin>Another version: "than," so that it refers to his eloquence.</margin>
Regarding Galba <note>Likely Servius Sulpicius Galba, an orator known for being physically deformed or hunched.</note>, who was famous for his eloquence but whose physical appearance <insert>as I mentioned above</insert> ruined the effect, a saying of Marcus Lollius was circulated: "Galba’s talent is poorly housed."

# BOOK II.

The Grammarian Orbilius <note>Orbilius Pupillus was a famous Roman teacher known for his harshness, famously described by the poet Horace as "the thrasher."</note> mocked the same Galba quite bitterly. Orbilius had appeared as a witness against a defendant; to confuse him, Galba pretended not to know his profession and asked: "What trade do you practice?" This is a sharp pun; as a teacher, he "rubbed" (polished) the heads of his students, but the phrase also implies he was so poor he had to sun himself like a beggar or a lizard.</note>

<margin>Caecilius.</margin>
When Gaius Caesar <note>Likely the Emperor Caligula, known for his erratic behavior and gambling.</note> ordered that one hundred thousand sesterces be given to the others who were playing ball with him, but ordered only fifty thousand to be given to Lucius Caelius alone, Caelius said: "What, do I play with only one hand and not two, so that I should receive more?"

<margin>Valerius’s mockery of the mime.</margin>
