Clodius was the man responsible for the exile of the great orator Cicero to Dyrrhachium; Valerius suggests that Clodius's greatest "threat" is merely a temporary exile from which one returns with more fame.</note>

Look how easily in old age he has dislodged me from my place,
The speech of an excellent man, delivered with a merciful mind,
Yet submissively, calmly, and with smooth-talking words.
Indeed, since the gods themselves could deny him nothing,
Who could bear for me, a mere man, to deny him?
I, having lived twice thirty years <note>Sixty years.</note> without a mark of disgrace,
Left my home a Roman Knight,
But shall return home a mime. Truly on this one day
I have lived longer for myself than I ought to have lived.
Fortune, excessive in good as well as in evil:
If it pleased you to shatter the flowering peak of my fame
With the praises of literature:
Why, when I was vigorous with youthful limbs,
When I was able to satisfy the people and such a man,
Did you not bend me when I was flexible, so that you might catch me?
Now where do you cast me down? What do I bring to the stage?
Beauty of form, or the dignity of my body?
Virtue of mind, or the sound of a pleasant voice?
As the creeping ivy kills the strength of trees:
So old age kills me with the embrace of years.
Like a tomb, I retain nothing but a name.

<margin>Pylades and Hylas, the actors.</margin>
But since I have once entered the stage by speaking of performers, we must not omit the actor Pylades. He was famous in his craft during the time of Augustus, and he raised his pupil Hylas to such a level of skill that he became his equal and rival. Consequently, the public was divided in their support between the two. When Hylas was performing a certain song <note>In Roman pantomime, the "actor" danced the narrative while a choir or singer provided the lyrics.</note> which ended with the words "the great Agamemnon," <note>original: "τὸν μέγαν Ἀγαμέμνονα"</note> Hylas gestured as if he were measuring someone of immense height.

<margin>“You make him tall.”</margin>
Pylades could not bear this, and shouted from the theater seats: "You are making him tall, not great!" <note>original: "σὺ μακρὸν οὐ μέγαν ποιεῖς" — a critique that Agamemnon's "greatness" was a matter of character and authority, not physical stature.</note> The audience then forced Pylades to perform the same song himself. When he reached the passage he had criticized, he represented a man lost in deep thought, believing that nothing better suited a great leader than to think on behalf of everyone. Later, Hylas was performing the role of Oedipus, and Pylades corrected the security of his movements by shouting, "You are looking!" <note>original: "σὺ βλέπεις" — Pylades was pointing out that Hylas was moving too confidently for a character who is famously blind.</note> When Pylades himself appeared as "Mad Hercules," and some felt he was not maintaining the gait appropriate for an actor, he took off his mask and scolded the laughers: "Fools, I am dancing as a madman!" <note>original: "μωροὶ, μαινόμενος ὀρχοῦμαι"</note> During this play, he even shot arrows into the audience. When he performed the same role at the request of Augustus in the dining room, he again drew his bow and released shafts. Nor was Caesar <note>Emperor Augustus</note> offended that Pylades treated him with the same lack of restraint he showed the Roman people. Because Pylades was said to have changed the old, crude style of dancing used by our ancestors and introduced a graceful new form, Augustus asked him what he had contributed to the art of dance. He replied: "The sound of flutes and pipes..." <note>original: "αὐλῶν συρίγγων"</note>

it is, which he deems in the first and second books of *The Laws* <note>Plato’s *Laws* is a late dialogue where he discusses the social and legal utility of drinking parties as a test of character.</note> to be not useless for men. For he judged that the spirits are refreshed and renewed for the restoration of the duties of sobriety through moderate and honorable relaxation during drinking; and he believed that men are rendered gradually more joyful and more fit to take up their intentions again. At the same time, he thought that if any deep-seated errors of the passions and desires were within them—which a reverent shame would otherwise hide—all these things might be uncovered without grave danger by the freedom granted by wine, and thus become more opportune for correction and healing.

<margin>*to this point</margin>
And Plato also says in the same place that these types of exercises <note>original: "exercitationes" — here meaning the "test" or "practice" of maintaining self-control while drinking.</note> against repelling the violence of wine ought not to be fled; nor has any person ever seemed sufficiently or faithfully continent or temperate whose life has not been tested amidst the very dangers of error and in the midst of the allurements of pleasures. For if all the Pleasures and Graces <note>original: "Libentiæ Gratiæq́;" — personifications of the joys of the banquet.</note> of feasts are unknown to someone, and if he is entirely devoid of them, and if by chance his will carries him, or chance leads him, or necessity drives him to participate in such pleasures, he is soon softened and captured, and neither his mind nor his spirit can hold firm. Therefore, one must join battle, as if in a certain line of cereal-combat, with pleasurable things; one must struggle hand-to-hand with that license of wine, so that we are safe against them not by flight nor by absence, but rather that we may protect our temperance and continence by vigor of mind, constant presence, and moderate use. And at the same time, with the soul warmed and refreshed, we may wash away whatever cold sadness or numbing shame might be within it.

<margin>From Gellius, Book 19, Chapter 2.</margin>
But because we have made mention of pleasures, Aristotle teaches which pleasures are to be guarded against. For there are five senses of men, which the Greeks call *perceptions* <note>original: "αἰσθήσεις" (*aisthēseis*).</note>, through which pleasure is seen to be sought for the mind or the body: touch, taste, smell, sight, and hearing. From all these, pleasure...

<header>B O O K  II.</header>
<sig>u 4</sig>

<margin>*Alternatively: disapproved</margin>
...which is taken immoderately, that pleasure is base and* shameful. For indeed, that which is excessive in taste and touch: that pleasure, as wise men have judged, is the foulest of all things. Those who have surrendered themselves most greatly to these two pleasures were called by the Greeks by names of the gravest vice, either <term>akrateis</term> <note>original: "ἀκρατẽς" — meaning "incontinent" or "powerless over oneself."</note> or <term>akolastous</term> <note>original: "ἀκολάστους" — meaning "intemperate" or "unrestrained."</note>; we call them either "incontinent" or "intemperate." We see that these two pleasures, taste and touch—that is, the pleasures of food and of lust—are the only ones shared by humans with the beasts. And for that reason, whoever is occupied by these wild pleasures is held in the number of the cattle and the fierce animals. The rest of the pleasures, proceeding from the other three senses, are proper to humans alone. I shall bring forward the words of the philosopher Aristotle on this matter, so that what such a famous and illustrious man thinks about these infamous pleasures may be made public:

<note>The following is a translation of the Greek text from Aristotle, likely drawing from his *Problemata* or *Nicomachean Ethics* regarding the nature of self-indulgence.</note>

"Why are those who exceed in the pleasure arising from touch or taste called 'incontinent'? For those concerned with sexual matters are 'intemperate,' as are those concerned with the enjoyment of food. Of the pleasures regarding food, for some the sweetness is in the tongue, but for others it is in the throat. This is why Philoxenus <note>Philoxenus of Leucas was a famous Greek glutton of the 4th century BCE; he famously wished for the neck of a crane so that he could enjoy the taste of his food for a longer duration as he swallowed.</note> prayed to have the throat of a crane. But as for the pleasure concerning sight and hearing, either it is not shared by us and the other animals, or we do not call someone 'intemperate' for those pleasures. Since those other pleasures [taste and touch] are shared with the beasts, subjection to them is shameful, and they are the most dishonorable; therefore, they are almost the only ones considered disgraceful. Thus, we blame the one who is defeated by these, and we call him 'incontinent' and 'intemperate,' because he is defeated by the basest of pleasures. Although there are five senses, the other animals only take pleasure from the two aforementioned; as for the others, they either take no pleasure at all, or they experience it only by accident. For a beast rejoices when seeing or smelling something only because it knows it will enjoy the meal, and when it is full, such things are no longer pleasant to it—just as the smell of salted fish is not pleasant to us when we are not hungry, but is most sweet when we are in need of food."

<header>O F  T H E  S A T V R N A L I A</header>

"But pleasure in the rose is always present." <note>original Greek: ἡ δ’ ἐν τῷ ῥόδῳ ἀεὶ ἡδονή. This likely refers to a more refined, aesthetic pleasure as opposed to the "animal" pleasures mentioned next.</note>

Who, then, possessing any sense of human shame, would take pride in those two pleasures—sexual union and eating—which man shares in common with the pig and the donkey? Socrates used to say that many men wish to live for the purpose of eating and drinking, but that he himself drank and ate in order to live. Hippocrates, moreover, a man of divine knowledge, held this view regarding sexual intercourse: that it is a certain part of a most foul disease, which our ancestors called the <term>comitial disease</term> <note>The Latin term for epilepsy, so named because an occurrence during a *comitia* (public assembly) was seen as a bad omen, requiring the meeting's adjournment.</note>. For these words of his are handed down: "intercourse <gloss>294</gloss> is a minor epilepsy" <note>original Greek: τὴν συνουσίαν εἶναι μικρὰν ἐπιληψίαν</note>; that is, sexual union is a minor form of the comitial disease.

### E N D  O F  T H E  S E C O N D  B O O K.

That this second book lacks its own conclusion, and the following book its beginning, is more easily seen than for the reader to need warning of it. Yet if any light can be added to such great darkness, I would think the connection of the books was this: at the end of the first book, mention was made of the poet Virgil. But since the time for dinner interrupted, it was decided that the discussion should be reserved for the conversation of the following day. Therefore, since the second book contains those things which were said during the meal, it remained for the third book to explain those things which were to be said about Virgil; no one fails to notice that a large part of these is certainly missing. But these losses can be lamented by us, yet they cannot be corrected.

Let us see, then, whether this same poet also preserved the propriety of custom regarding the worship of the gods of the underworld. It is well known that those about to perform sacred rites for the celestial gods are purified by a full washing of the body. However, when an offering is to be made to the gods below, it is considered sufficient if only a sprinkling occurs. Regarding the rites of the gods above, Aeneas says:
> Until I have washed myself in a living stream. <note>original: "Donec me flumine uiuo Abluero." From Aeneid, Book 2. Ritual law required "living" or running water for celestial purification.</note>

<margin>Aeneid, Book 4</margin>
> "Anna, dear nurse, bring my sister here to me. Tell her to hasten to sprinkle her body with river water." <note>original: "Annam chara mihi nutrix huc siste sororem. Dic corpus properet fluuiali spargere lympha."</note> And elsewhere:
> She had also sprinkled simulated waters of the spring of Avernus. <note>Avernus was a crater lake near Naples, believed by the Romans to be the entrance to the Underworld.</note>

<margin>*washed around</margin>
> — Three times he went around his companions with pure water, sprinkling them with a light dew. <note>original: "Ter socios pura circuntulit unda, Spargens rore leui." The margin note suggests a textual variant "circunluit," meaning he washed them around.</note>

And also when he describes Aeneas about to consecrate the branch to Proserpina <note>The "Golden Bough," an offering required to enter the realm of the dead.</note> in the underworld, he records it thus:
<margin>Aeneid, Book 6</margin>

How appropriately Virgil used the words pertaining to sacred rites!

### CHAPTER II.

The propriety of words is so familiar to this poet that such observation in Virgil almost ceases to be remarkable. Yet he used none more properly than his sacred or sacrificial words. And first, I should not omit a point in which many are mistaken: "And I shall <term>offer up</term> <note>original: "Porriciam." This is a highly technical term in Roman sacrifice.</note> the entrails into the salt waves." Most think Virgil said "I shall throw away" <note>original: "proiciam."</note>, believing he meant the entrails were simply to be discarded because he added "into the waves." But this is not so. For according to the <term>discipline of the Soothsayers</term> <note>The *disciplina Aruspicum*, the traditional Etruscan art of interpreting entrails and lightning.</note> and the decrees of the <term>Pontiffs</term> <note>The high priests of Rome who oversaw all state religious matters.</note>, this word is the solemn term for those performing a sacrifice. Just as Veranius, in the first book of Pictor, conducted a dissertation on this word as follows: "Let them <term>offer up</term> <note>original: "porriciunto"</note> the entrails, let them give them to the Gods upon the altars, or the shrine, or the hearth, or wherever the entrails ought to be given." To "offer up," therefore,

### BOOK III.

...not "to throw away," but "to offer forth" <note>original: "porricere." A technical term in Roman sacrifice for placing the internal organs of the victim upon the altar.</note> is the proper word for sacrifice. And because Veranius <note>A Roman scholar of the 1st century BCE who wrote on religious law and the meanings of words.</note> stated that this occurs "at the altar or the hearth, or wherever the entrails ought to be given," the sea must be understood to take the place of the altar and the hearth when a sacrifice is made to the gods of the sea. For the poet says:

<margin>Aeneid, Book 5</margin>
> Gods who hold dominion over the deep, whose waters I traverse, I shall joyfully set a white bull for you here upon this shore before your altars, as one bound by my vow; I shall cast forth <note>original: "porriciam"</note> the entrails into the salty waves and pour out liquid wine.

From these lines, we are taught that entrails could be "offered forth" <note>original: "porrici"</note> into the sea according to proper ritual, rather than merely "thrown" <note>original: "proijci"</note> away. "I shall set before the altars, as one bound by my vow." This phrase is specific to sacred matters: a person is called "Bound" <note>original: "Reus." While we use this today for a defendant in court, in Roman religion it meant someone who had made a promise to a god and was now "indebted" to perform the ritual.</note> who obligates himself to the deities by undertaking a vow; however, one is called "Condemned" <note>original: "Damnatus." This term surprisingly meant that the person's prayer had been answered, and thus they were "condemned" or strictly required to pay the promised sacrifice.</note> <margin>Bound. Condemned. * already</margin> when he has not yet paid the promised vows. But there is no need for me to provide more on this subject, since that most learned man, Eustathius <note>One of the scholars participating in this fictional dialogue.</note>, has just recently discussed this part quite fully. One can often find profound knowledge of this poet in a single word, which the common crowd might think was spoken by chance.

<margin>The custom of touching the altars.</margin>
For we read in many places that prayer alone cannot achieve a successful sacrifice <note>original: "litare." A technical term meaning to obtain a favorable omen or to sacrifice successfully.</note> unless the one who prays to the gods also grips the altar with his hands. For this reason, Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a prolific Roman scholar and contemporary of Cicero.</note> says in the fifth book of *Divine Affairs* that altars were first called "handles" <note>original: "ansas." This is a play on words: "aras" (altars) and "ansas" (handles), suggesting you must "handle" the altar for it to work.</note> because it was necessary for them to be held by those performing the sacrifice. Who could doubt that vessels are usually held by handles? Through a change of letters, they began to be called "aras" (altars), just as the families now called "Valerii" and "Furii" were previously called "Valesii" and "Fusii" <note>This refers to a linguistic process called rhotacism, where an 's' between two vowels turned into an 'r' in early Latin.</note>. The poet followed all of this in that verse:

<margin>Aeneid, Book 4</margin>
> As he prayed with such words and held the altars, the All-powerful heard him.

Should you not believe that he was heard specifically because he was not only praying, but also holding the altars? Likewise, when he says:

<margin>Aeneid, Book 6. Aeneid, Book 12.</margin>
> He prayed with such words and held the altars. Likewise: I touch the altars; I call to witness the fires between us and the divine powers.

He signifies the same force of the name derived from the act of gripping.

# OF THE SATURNALIA

The same poet [Virgil], as deep in knowledge as he is delightful in genius, interpreted several ancient words—which he knew pertained to the proper conduct of sacred rites—in such a way that while the sound of the word changed, the full meaning remained intact. For in the first book on Pontifical Law by Pictor <note>Likely Fabius Pictor, one of the earliest Roman historians and a writer on religious law.</note>, this word is found: *vitulari* <term>to celebrate or rejoice</term>. Regarding the meaning of this word, Titius <note>An orator or scholar, likely Gaius Titius, known for his descriptions of Roman customs.</note> reported thus: "To *vitulari* is to rejoice with the voice." Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, the most famous Roman scholar of the 1st century BCE.</note> also records in the fifteenth book of *Divine Antiquities* that the Pontiff is accustomed to *vitulari* in certain sacred rites, which the Greeks call *paianizein* <note>original: "παιανίζειν." To sing a paean, which is a song of triumph or thanksgiving, usually addressed to Apollo.</note>. With how few words the learned elegance of Maro [Virgil] expressed these many interpretive twists:

->And singing a joyful paean in chorus.<- <note>A quote from Virgil's Aeneid, Book 6, line 657.</note>

For if *vitulari* is to rejoice with the voice—which is to sing a paean <note>original: "παιανίζειν"</note>—then is not the perfect explanation of the word preserved in the phrase "joyfully singing a paean" <note>original: "παιᾶνα"</note>? And to dwell on this word a little longer: Hyllus <note>A scholar who wrote on the nature of the gods.</note>, in the book he composed *On the Gods*, says that a goddess named Vitula <margin>* Heifer-like/Of the calf</margin> presides over joy. Piso <note>Lucius Calpurnius Piso Frugi, a Roman historian and statesman.</note> says that Vitula is a name for Victory. He offers this proof for the matter: that on the day after the Nones of July <note>July 8th.</note>, following a successful action—when on the previous day the people had been put to flight by the Tuscans (the origin of the name *Populifugia* <term>the Flight of the People</term>)—after the victory, a *vitulatio* <term>a celebration of thanksgiving</term> is performed with specific sacrifices. Some think her name was derived because she has the power to sustain life <note>A wordplay in Latin connecting "Vitula" to "vitae tolerandae" (sustaining life).</note>. For this reason, sacrifices are said to be made to this goddess for the crops, because human life is sustained by crops. From this we notice what Virgil says:

<margin>Eclogues, 4 <note>The text cites Book 4, though this famous line is actually from Virgil’s Eclogue 3, line 77.</note></margin>
"When I make an offering with a heifer for the crops, come yourself."

So he used "with a heifer" (*vitula*) to mean "for a thanksgiving" (*vitulatio*); we explained above that this is the name of a sacrifice made on account of joy. We should remember, however, that it is to be read in the ablative case: "When I perform [the rite] with a heifer (*vitula*) for the crops"—that is, when I perform the divine rite, not with a sheep, not with a goat, but with a heifer. It is as if he were saying, "when I [sacrifice] a heifer for the cro-"

### On the sacred, the profane, the holy, and the religious, and what they are: and how diligently Maro [Virgil] expressed the proper meanings of these words. CHAPTER III.

And because among the decrees of the Pontiffs this is most frequently asked—what is sacred, what is holy, what is religious—we must inquire whether Virgil used these terms according to their definitions, and whether he preserved the specific property of each word in his usual manner.

<margin>Sacred</margin>
The "sacred" <note>original: "Sacrum"</note> is, as Trebatius <note>Gaius Trebatius Testa, a prominent Roman jurist and contemporary of Virgil.</note> records in the first book of *On Religions*, "anything that is held to belong to the gods." The poet, mindful of this definition, almost always added a mention of the gods whenever he named something sacred:

<margin>Also: Aeneid, Book 3</margin>
> *I was performing sacred rites to my Dionean mother and the gods.* <note>original: "Sacra Dioneæ matri, Diuisq; ferebam." Aeneid 3.19. Dionean mother refers to Venus.</note>
<margin>Aeneid, Book 4</margin>
> *The sacred rites to Stygian Jove which I have duly prepared and begun.* <note>original: "Sacra Ioui Stygio quæ ritè incœpta paraui." Aeneid 4.638. Stygian Jove refers to Pluto, king of the Underworld.</note>
<margin>Aeneid, Book 8</margin>
> *For to you, even to you, greatest Juno, she slays [the sow], offering sacred rites.* <note>original: "Tibi enim, tibi maxima Iuno Mactat sacra ferens." Aeneid 8.84.</note>

<margin>Profane</margin>
<margin>Furthermore: here meaning "far off."</margin>
Almost everyone agrees that the "profane" <note>original: "Profanum"</note> is that which is outside of a temple's jurisdiction <note>original: "extra fanaticam causam"</note>; as if it were "far from the shrine" <note>original: "porrò à fano"</note> and separated from religion. An example of this meaning followed when he [Virgil] spoke of both the grove and the sacred inner sanctum <note>original: "adyto"</note> of the inhabitants of the lower world:

<margin>* the entrance</margin>
> *Stay far, oh stay far away, you profane ones,*
> *the prophetess cries out, and withdraw from the whole grove.* <note>original: "Procul ô procul este profani / Conclamat uates, totoq; absistite luco." Aeneid 6.258.</note>

To this is added what Trebatius says: that "profane" is properly said of that which has been converted from a religious or sacred status into the use and ownership of men. This the poet most clearly observed when he said:

<meta>catchword: Faune (Faunus)</meta>

The "holy" <note>original: "Sanctum"</note> is, as the same Trebatius refers in the tenth book of *On Religions*, sometimes the same as the "sacred" and the same as the "religious"; at other times it is something else, that is, neither sacred nor religious. This relates to the second category.

For his soul was not held by the sacred or the religious; rather, he wished to show it as "holy," that is, uncorrupted. As also in this passage:

<margin>Aeneid, Book 12. <note>Actually Book 11, line 158.</note></margin>
> "And you, O most holy wife, happy in your death." <note>original: "Tuq; ô sanctissima coniux / Felix morte tua." Virgil, Aeneid 11.158-159.</note>

In this, he embraced the honor of the uncorrupted chastity of his wife. From this also come "holy laws" <term>sanctae leges</term>, which ought not to be corrupted by the "sanction" <term>sanctio</term> of a penalty. But as for what pertains to the definition of the first category of the holy—that is, that it is no different from the sacred or the religious:

<margin>Aeneid, Book 2.</margin>
> "Behold, a light crest was seen to pour forth light 
> from the very top of Iulus' head." <note>original: "Ecce leuis summo de uertice uisus Iuli / Fundere lumen apex." Virgil, Aeneid 2.682-683.</note>

And a little later:

> "We, trembling, were agitated by fear, and sought to shake out 
> the flaming hair and extinguish the holy fires with water." <note>original: "Nos pauidi trepidare metu, crinemq; flagrantem / Excutere, & sanctos restinguere fontibus ignes." Virgil, Aeneid 2.685-686.</note>

For here we shall understand "holy" as if it were "sacred," because they occurred by divine providence.

<margin>Aeneid, Book 6.</margin>
->Likewise:<-

> "And you, O most holy seer, foreknowing of the future." <note>original: "Tuq; ô sanctissima uates / Præscia uenturi." Virgil, Aeneid 6.65.</note>

He calls her nothing other than "sacred," for he saw she was both a seer, full of God, and a priestess.

<margin>The Religious, and Religion, on which also Gellius, Book 4, chapter 9.</margin>
It remains for us to share with Virgil what is "religious." Servius Sulpicius <note>Servius Sulpicius Rufus, a renowned jurist and friend of Cicero.</note> handed down that "religion" <note>original: "religionē"</note> was so named because it is removed and set apart from us on account of some holiness; as if it were named from "leaving behind" <note>original: "à relinquendo"</note>, just as "ceremony" is from "lacking" <note>original: "à carendo"</note>.

# BOOK III.

Virgil, observing this principle, says:

<margin>Aeneid, Book 8.</margin>
> "There is a vast grove near the cool stream of Caere, held sacred far and wide by the religion of our fathers." <note>original: "Est ingens gelidum lucus prope Cæretis amnem / Relligione patrum latè sacer." Virgil, Aeneid 8.597-598.</note>

And he added the following to express the specific nature of its religious character:

> "...On all sides hollow hills enclosed it, and a forest of dark fir surrounds the grove." <note>original: "Vndiq; colles / Inclusere caui, & nigra nemus abiete cingit." Virgil, Aeneid 8.598-599.</note>

This circumstance certainly made the grove secluded from the common interaction of the people. And to show that the place was left alone not only because it was difficult to reach, he also added its quality of holiness:

> "Rumor says the ancient Pelasgians <term>the earliest inhabitants of Greece and Italy</term> consecrated it to Sylvanus, the god of fields and cattle." <note>original: "Syluano fama est ueteres sacrasse Pelasgos / Agrorum, pecorisq; Deo." Virgil, Aeneid 8.600-601.</note>

According to Pompeius Festus <term>a 2nd-century Roman grammarian</term>, those things are "religious" which distinguish between what should be done and what should be avoided. From this, Maro <note>Virgil's family name</note> says:

<margin>Georgics, Book 1. "Deducere" [to drain/clean], as used in Virgil.</margin>
> "...No religious law has forbidden the draining of streams." <note>original: "Riuos deducere nulla / Relligio uetuit." Virgil, Georgics 1.269-270.</note>

Moreover, when he says "to drain" <note>original: "deducere"</note>, it means nothing other than "to clean out." For on festival days, it is permitted to clean out old, fouled streams, but it is not permitted to dig new ones.

In passing, this too should be noted, which the poet himself suggested as if in passing through the meaning of a single word. For it is cautioned in Pontifical law <term>the body of regulations governing Roman state religion</term> that since sheep are usually washed for two reasons—either to treat scabies or to clean the wool—on festival days it is not permitted to wash sheep for the sake of cleaning the wool; however, it is permitted if the washing is to cure scabies. Therefore, Virgil numbered this also among the permitted things:

<margin>In the same place [Georgics 1].</margin>
> "And to plunge the bleating flock into the healthful river." <note>original: "Balantumq; gregem fluuio mersare salubri." Virgil, Georgics 1.272.</note>

Now, if he had only said this much, he would have confused the permitted and the forbidden; but by adding "healthful" <note>original: "salubri"</note>, he expressed the specific reason for the permitted washing <note>since "salubri" implies a medicinal or health-related purpose, like curing scabies, rather than just cleaning wool for profit</note>.

What a shrine <term>delubrum</term> is, and who the household gods <term>dii penates</term> are. And how, even in these matters, Virgil did not deviate from his usual diligence.

->OF THE SATURNALIA<-

Let us inquire what the Pontiffs <term>the high priests of Roman state religion</term> properly call a *delubrum* <term>a shrine or sanctuary</term>, and in what way Virgil used this name. Varro, in the eighth book of his *Divine Antiquities* <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC) was Rome's greatest scholar; his "Divine Antiquities" is a lost but frequently cited work on Roman religion</note>, says: "Some consider a *delubrum* to be a place where, in addition to the temple building, a space (*area*) has been taken up for the sake of the gods, such as the temple of Jupiter Stator <note>Jupiter "the Stayer," who stopped the Roman retreat in battle</note> in the Flaminian Circus. Others consider it the place where the cult image of a god has been dedicated." And he added that, just as the place in which they fixed a candle was called a *candelabrum*, so the place in which they placed a god was named a *delubrum*. From these definitions provided by Varro, we can understand that he preferred the one he placed last (following his usual habit), suggesting that the word *delubrum* began to be used because of the dedicated image of the god. Virgil, however, carefully followed both definitions. To start with the latter, he was careful, when about to name a *delubrum*, to introduce either the specific names of the gods or things appropriate to the gods:

<margin>Aeneid, Book 2.</margin>
> "But the twin snakes escape with a gliding motion to the highest shrines." <note>original: "At gemini lapsu delubra ad summa dracones / Effugiunt." Virgil, Aeneid 2.225.</note>

And so that he might soon mention the cult image, he added:

> "—and they seek the citadel of fierce Tritonis <note>a title for Minerva</note>. Beneath the feet of the goddess and under the circle of her shield they are hidden." <note>original: "Sæuæq; petunt Tritonidis arcem. / Sub pedibusq; deæ, clypeiq; sub orbe teguntur." Virgil, Aeneid 2.226-227.</note>

Likewise:

> "We, wretched ones, for whom 그 day was to be our last, deck the shrines of the gods with festive foliage throughout the city." <note>original: "Nos delubra deûm miseri, quibus ultimus esset / Ille dies, festa uelamus fronde per urbem." Virgil, Aeneid 2.248-249.</note>

Truly, he did not disregard that other opinion regarding the open space which Varro had mentioned:

> "First they approach the shrines, and seek peace through the altars."
<margin>Aeneid, Book 4.</margin>
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; And soon after:
> "Or before the faces of the gods she walks to the rich altars." <note>original: "Aut ante ora Deûm pingues spatiatur ad aras." Virgil, Aeneid 4.62.</note>

For what else is "to walk" (*spatiari*) but to pace about in the space of a wide path? By adding "before the faces of the gods" <note>literally "before the mouths/faces of the gods"</note>, he shows that an area was taken up for the sake of the gods. Thus, in his usual manner, as if doing something else, he fulfills these secret meanings.

Concerning the gods proper to the Romans, that is, the Penates <term>household or state gods of the larder and the inner house</term>,

### BOOK III.

A diligent precision <term>subtilitas; a refined exactness in scholarship</term> is sprinkled throughout this work. Indeed, Nigidius <note>Nigidius Figulus (98–45 BC), a Roman scholar and contemporary of Cicero known for his works on science and religion</note>, in the nineteenth book of *On the Gods*, asks whether the **Penates** <term>the ancestral gods of the Roman state and household</term> of the Trojans are **Apollo** and **Neptune**, who are said to have built the walls for them, and whether **Aeneas** brought them into Italy. **Cornelius Labeo** <note>A third-century AD scholar who wrote extensively on Roman religious law</note> also holds the same opinion in his book *On the Penates*. **Maro** <note>Publius Vergilius Maro, commonly known as Virgil</note> follows this view when he says:

<margin>Aeneid, Book 3.</margin>
> "Having spoken thus, he offered the deserved honors at the altars: a bull to Neptune, a bull to you, fair Apollo." <note>original: "Sic fatus, meritos aris mactabat honores, / Taurum Neptuno, taurum tibi pulcher Apollo." Virgil, Aeneid 3.118-119.</note>

**Varro**, in the second book of his *Human Antiquities*, records that **Dardanus** brought the Penates from **Samothrace** <note>An island in the northern Aegean Sea, famous for its mystery cults</note> into **Phrygia**, and Aeneas brought them from Phrygia into Italy. However, Varro does not explicitly state who the Penates are in that mentioned book; but those who more diligently unearth the truth have said that the Penates are those through whom we breathe inwardly <note>original: "penitus spiramus"; the author is suggesting an etymological link between Penates and "penitus" (deeply/inwardly)</note>, through whom we possess a body, and through whom we hold the reason of our mind. They also use the argument that **Jupiter** is the middle ether, **Juno** is the lowest air together with the earth, and **Minerva** is the highest peak of the ether; they cite as proof that **Tarquinius** <note>Tarquinius Priscus, the fifth King of Rome</note>, the son of **Demaratus the Corinthian**, who was mystically initiated into the religious rites of Samothrace, joined these three mentioned divinities in one temple and under the same roof. **Cassius Hemina** <note>An early Roman historian of the 2nd century BC</note> says that the Samothracian gods, who are the same as the Roman Penates, are properly called the **Great Gods**, the **Good Gods**, and the **Powerful Gods** <note>original: "θεοὺς μεγάλους, θεοὺς χρηστούς, θεοὺς δυνατούς" (theous megalous, theous chrēstous, theous dynatous)</note>. Our poet <note>Virgil</note>, knowing these things, says:

<margin>Aeneid, Book 3.</margin>
> "With comrades and son, the Penates and the Great Gods." <note>original: "Cum socijs, natoq;, Penatibus & magnis Dijs." Virgil, Aeneid 3.12.</note>

This phrase expresses the Greek term **Great Gods** <note>original: "θεοὺς μεγάλους" (theous megalous)</note>. But he also preserves all these names when referring to one of the aforementioned divinities, confirming beyond doubt his own learning regarding this entire opinion. For when he says:

<margin>Aeneid, Book 3.</margin>
> "First adore the divinity of great Juno with prayer," <note>original: "Iunonis magnæ primùm prece numen adora." Virgil, Aeneid 3.437.</note>

he names her **the Great** <note>original: "τὴν μεγάλην" (tēn megalēn)</note>; and here:

<margin>Aeneid, Book 1.</margin>
> "May Bacchus the giver of joy be present, and good Juno," <note>original: "Adsit lætitiæ Bacchus dator, & bona Iuno." Virgil, Aeneid 1.734.</note>

he names her **the Good** <note>original: "τὴν χρηστήν" (tēn chrēstēn)</note>; and he calls her "powerful mistress," naming her **the Powerful** <note>original: "τὴν δυνατήν" (tēn dynatēn)</note>. In the same...

> "So he spoke: and with his hands he brought out the headbands, and mighty Vesta, and the eternal fire from the innermost shrines." <note>original: "Sic ait: et manibus vittas, Vestamque potentem, / Aeternumque adytis effert penetralibus ignem." Aeneid 2.296-297.</note>

**Hyginus** <note>Gaius Julius Hyginus, a scholar and librarian under Emperor Augustus</note> added in the book he wrote *On the Penate Gods* that they are called **ancestral gods** <note>original Greek: θεοὺς πατρῴους (theous patrōous)</note>. Virgil was not ignorant of this either:

> "Gods of my fathers, preserve my house, preserve my grandson." <note>original: "Di patrii servate domum, servate nepotem." Aeneid 2.702.</note>
And elsewhere:
<margin>Aeneid, Book 2.</margin>

## CHAPTER V.

<margin>Two types of victims: one animal, the other for consultation</margin>
Virgil reveals his diligence concerning the practice of sacrifices no less than his knowledge of the Gods. For when **Trebatius** <note>Gaius Trebatius Testa, a prominent Roman jurist and contemporary of Cicero</note> teaches in the first book of *On Religions* that there are two types of sacrificial victims: one, in which the will of God is investigated through the **entrails** <term>exta; the internal organs, specifically the heart, lungs, and liver, used for divination</term>; the other, in which only the life-force is consecrated to God—which is why the **Soothsayers** <term>Haruspices; priests who interpreted the will of the gods by inspecting entrails</term> call these "**animal victims**" <term>animales hostias; sacrifices where the animal's 'anima' or breath/life is the focus rather than divination</term>. Virgil demonstrates both types of victims in his poetry.

First, indeed, he shows that type by which the will of the divinities is revealed through the entrails:
<margin>Aeneid, Book 4.</margin>
> "—He slays chosen ewes of two years according to custom." <note>original: "Mactat lectas de more bidentes." Aeneid 4.57. 'Bidentes' refers to sheep reaching maturity, marked by two prominent teeth.</note>
And soon after:
> "—And peering into the opened breasts of the beasts, he consults the breathing entrails." <note>original: "Pecudumque reclusis / Pectoribus inhians spirantia consulit exta." Aeneid 4.63-64.</note>

He shows that other type, which is called an "animal victim" because only its life is consecrated, when he depicts **Entellus** as victor slaying a bull for **Eryx**. To fulfill the definition of an "animal victim," he used the very name itself:
> "This better life <note>original: animam</note>, Eryx, I offer to you in place of the death of Dares." <note>original: "Hanc tibi Eryx meliorem animam pro morte Daretis." Aeneid 5.483-484. Entellus sacrifices the bull as a substitute for his defeated opponent, Dares.</note>

### BOOK III.

And to signify that vows had been formally pronounced, he says, "I pay" <note>original Latin: *perfoluo*</note>: a term used specifically in relation to a vow. And to show that the debt was paid to the Gods, he indicated it by saying:

<margin>Aeneid, Book 5.</margin>
> "The ox is laid low, and falls to the earth lifeless and trembling." <note>original: "Sternitur, exanimisq; tremens procumbit humi bos." Aeneid 5.481.</note>

We must also consider whether he does not identify that sacrifice as a **victim of life** <term>hostia animalis—a sacrifice where only the life/breath of the animal is offered to the deity, rather than the meat being shared</term>:

<margin>Aeneid, Book 2.</margin>
> "With blood you appeased the winds, and with a maiden slain,
> when first you Greeks came to the shores of Troy.
> With blood your return must be sought, and you must sacrifice with a Greek life." <note>original: "Sanguine placastis uentos, & uirgine cæsa: / Cùm primum Iliacas Danai uenistis ad oras. / Sanguine quærēdi reditus, animaq; litādū Argolica." Aeneid 2.116–118.</note>

For he used the word **life** <note>original: *anima*</note> as the name for the victim, and used the term **to sacrifice favorably** <note>original: *litare*</note>, which means to appease the divine power once the sacrifice has been duly performed.

<margin>Unyoked oxen.</margin>
Among these very victims—whether they are "animal sacrifices" or "consultative" ones <note>sacrifices where the entrails are consulted for omens</note>—there are some called **unyoked sacrifices** <term>hostiae iniuges</term>: that is, animals that have never been tamed or submitted to the yoke. Our poet [Virgil] mentions these as well:

<margin>Aeneid, Book 6.</margin>
> "Now it would be better to slaughter seven bullocks from an untouched herd,
> and as many ewes chosen according to custom." <note>original: "Nunc grege de intacto septem mactare iuuencos / Præstiterit, totidem lectas de more bidentes." Aeneid 6.38–39.</note>

And to express "unyoked" even more clearly, he added:

> "And as many heifers with untouched necks." <note>original: "Et intacta totidem ceruice iuuencas." Aeneid 6.39.</note>

<margin>Exceptional sacrifices.</margin>
The word **exceptional** <note>original: *eximius*</note> in the context of sacrifices is not a poetic **epithet** <term>ἐπίϑετον—a descriptive literary tag</term>, but a technical priestly term. For **Veratius** <note>A Roman writer on religious law</note> teaches in his *Pontifical Questions* that those victims are called **exceptional** which are "set apart" <note>original: *eximantur*</note> from the flock for the purpose of sacrifice, or because they are chosen for their **exceptional** appearance to be offered to the deities. Hence Virgil says:

> "Four exceptional bulls of surpassing body." <note>original: "Quatuor eximios præstanti corpore tauros." Aeneid 4.60.</note>

Where he showed they are "exceptional" because they are set apart, and "of surpassing body" because they are selected. An **Ambarval victim** is, as **Pompeius Festus** <note>A 2nd-century Roman grammarian</note> says,
<margin>Ambarval sacrifices.</margin>
one that is led around the fields <note>from *amb-* (around) and *arva* (fields)</note> for the sake of a divine rite, by those who perform sacrifices for the benefit of the crops. Virgil mentions this sacrifice in his *Eclogues*, where he speaks of the deification of Daphnis:

> "These things shall ever be yours, both when we pay our solemn vows
> to the nymphs, and when we purify the fields." <note>original: "Hæc tibi semper erunt, & cùm solennia uota / Reddemus nymphis, & cum lustrabimus agros." Eclogues 5.74–75.</note>

# SATURNALIA

Where "to purify" <note>original Latin: *lustrare*</note> signifies to "circle around." Indeed, it is evident that the name for a sacrificial victim <note>original: *hostia*</note> was acquired from this practice of "going around" <note>original: *ambiendis*</note> the fields. This is also found in the *Georgics*, Book 1:

->And thrice let the auspicious victim go around the new crops.<- <note>original: "Terq; nouas circum felix eat hostia fruges." Georgics 1.345.</note>

It was a rule observed by those performing sacrifices that if a victim, while being led to the altars, struggled violently and showed that it was being brought to the shrine against its will, it should be removed. This was because they believed the offering was being made to a God who did not want it. However, a victim that stood still when offered was thought to be given to a willing deity. Thus our poet [Virgil] writes:

->And led by the horn, the sacred goat shall stand at the altar.<- <note>original: "Et ductus cornu stabit sacer hircus ad aras." Georgics 2.395.</note> And elsewhere:
->And I shall set a bullock with gilded brow before the altar.<- <note>original: "Et statuam ante aras aurata fronte iuuencum." Aeneid 9.627.</note>

<margin>Why Mezentius was a "scorner of the gods."</margin>
Furthermore, Virgil placed such great emphasis on the piety to be shown to the Gods in sacrifices that he called Mezentius a "scorner of the gods" <note>original: *contemptorem divum*</note> for the opposite reason. For he was not called a "scorner of the gods" (as the grammarian Asper believes) simply because he was impious toward men without regard for the Gods. Otherwise, Virgil would have said this much more of Busiris <note>A mythical Egyptian king who sacrificed visitors; Virgil calls him "unpraised" (*illaudatus*) in Georgics 3.5</note>, whom he was content to call "unpraised," though he was far more cruel. But the diligent reader will find the true cause of this reproachful title in the first book of Cato’s *Origins*. For Cato says that Mezentius ordered the Rutulians to offer to him the **first fruits** <term>primitiae—the first part of the harvest or the first-born of livestock, traditionally reserved for the gods</term> which they used to offer to the Gods; and all the Latins, fearing a similar command, made this vow: "Jupiter, if it is more pleasing to your heart, let us give these to you rather than to Mezentius, so that you may make us victors." Therefore, because he had demanded divine honors for himself, he was deservedly called by Virgil a "scorner of the gods." Hence that pious mockery by the Priest:

<margin>Aeneid, Book 11.</margin>
->—These are the spoils and the first fruits from a proud king.<- <note>original: "Hæc sunt spolia & de rege superbo Primitiae." Aeneid 11.15-16.</note>

By using the term associated with his defiance, for which he paid the penalty, the priest marked the armor stripped from him as "first fruits" reclaimed for the gods.

Virgil’s learning regarding both Roman and foreign sacred rites was truly marvelous, as seen from Apollo's...

He also corrects a common misconception about the character Mezentius, explaining that his "contempt" was specifically the act of usurping offerings meant for the gods.</summary>

BOOK III. 325
Evidence from the rites of Delos and Hercules the Victor.

### CHAPTER VI.

<margin>Where a victim is not slain for Apollo.</margin>
The learning of this poet [Virgil] regarding both our own Roman rites and those of foreign nations is truly wonderful. For it is not without reason that when Aeneas arrives at Delos, he slays no sacrificial victim; a religious offering was only made to Apollo and Neptune as he was preparing to depart. It is well established (as Cloatius Verus teaches in the second book of his *Arranged Matters* <note>original: *Ordinatorum*</note>) that there is an altar at Delos where no victim is ever killed, but the people worship the God only with solemn prayer. These are the words of Cloatius: "At Delos there is an altar to Apollo of the Birth <note>original Greek: *γενέθλιος* (genethlios); the title refers to Apollo as the god of origins or birthdays</note>, at which no animal is sacrificed; it is said that Pythagoras worshipped at this altar because it was undefiled by blood." The poet demonstrates that this is the Altar of the Birth <note>original: *γενέθλιον* (genethlion)</note> which Aeneas worships. Indeed, having entered the temple, the high priest <note>original: *Pontifex*</note>, without performing any blood sacrifice, immediately begins his prayer; and to address the Father more specifically, he says: *Grant, Father, an omen.* <note>Virgil, Aeneid 3.89</note> But when he later sacrifices a bull to Apollo and Neptune, we are to understand that this was done at a different altar. He wisely refers to him only as "Father" at the first altar, which is proper there, and uses the name "Apollo" at the second, which is a common address. Cato also mentions this altar in his work *On Raising Children* in these words: "The nurse performed all these rites with sacred branches and pipes, without victims, just as is done at the Altar of the Birth-Giving <note>original: *genitiui*</note> Apollo at Delos."

<margin>Why he said the temple was built of ancient stone.</margin>
In the same verse, I think it should not be overlooked why he said the temple was built *of ancient stone*. Velius Longus claims this is a "change of epithet" <note>a grammatical term where a quality of the thing itself—antiquity—is applied to its material</note>; he argues Virgil simply wants to emphasize the age of the temple. Many other commentators have followed this view. However, it is a dull interpretation to merely note the age of a building. Epaphus, a man of extensive reading, states in his seventeenth book that while the famous temple at Delphi was once plundered and burned despite being considered sacred and untouchable, the island of Delos remained unique. He adds that although many cities and islands near Corinth were swallowed by earthquakes, Delos was never troubled by such a disaster, neither before nor since.

In Rome, however, there are two temples of Hercules the Victor: one at the Triple Gate <note>original: *porta trigemina*</note>, and the other in the cattle market <note>original: *foro boario*</note>.

<margin>* Sabinus</margin>

He says: "Marcus Octavius Herennius, a flute-player in his early youth, turned to trade after losing confidence in his art. Having conducted his business well, he dedicated a tenth <note>It was a common Roman custom to offer a "tithe" (one-tenth) of profits or spoils to Hercules.</note> of his profits to Hercules. Later, while sailing for the same purpose, he was surrounded by pirates, fought most bravely, and emerged victorious. Hercules informed him in his dreams that he had been saved by the god's help. Having obtained a site from the magistrates, Octavius dedicated a temple and a statue to him, and called him 'the Victor' in an inscription. Thus he gave the God an epithet which contains both the argument for the ancient victories of Hercules and a commemoration of the new story which gave cause for this recent Roman sacred rite." Nor was it for nothing that he [Virgil] said in the same place:

### OF THE SATURNALIA

> *But the ram himself in the meadows shall change his fleece, now with*
> *sweet-blushing purple, now with saffron-yellow.* <note>original: "Ipse sed in pratis aries iam suaue rubenti / Murice, iam croceo mutabit uellera luto." From Virgil's Eclogue 4, lines 43-44. Virgil is describing a Golden Age where sheep naturally produce colored wool.</note>

It is recorded in the book of the Etruscans <note>The Etruscans were famed in the ancient world for their "discipline" or art of interpreting omens, especially lightning and animal entrails.</note> that if an animal should be clothed in an unusual color, it portends the greatest happiness and prosperity for the ruler of all things. There is a book by Tarquinius <note>Likely Tarquitius Priscus, a famous scholar of Etruscan lore who translated their ritual books into Latin.</note> transcribed from a Tuscan book of omens; there it is found: "If a sheep or a ram is sprinkled with a purple or golden color, it increases the wealth and generosity of the leader of the order and the clan with the highest happiness; it propagates his line and progeny in fame, and makes them more joyful." Therefore, Virgil prophesies this state of affairs for the Emperor in a passing remark. We may also observe from this point how deeply he seeks his meanings, even in individual words concerning sacred ritual:

<margin>Aeneid, Book 10.</margin>
> *The Fates laid their hands upon him, and consecrated him to the spears*
> *of Evander.* <note>Virgil, Aeneid 10, line 419. This describes the death of Halaesus.</note>

For whatever is destined for the gods is called "sacred." However, it cannot reach them unless the soul is freed from the burden of the body, which cannot happen except through death. Thus, Virgil appropriately makes Halaesus "sacred," because he was about to meet his death. And here, Virgil has followed the specific technicalities of both human and divine law. For by using the phrase "laying on of hands" <term>manus iniectio: a Roman legal procedure where a claimant physically seized a person to assert ownership or debt</term>, he designated something nearly like an enslaved property; and by the word "consecration," he fulfilled the requirements of divine law. At this point, it does not seem out of place to report on the condition of those men whom the laws command to be "sacred" to certain gods. For I am not unaware that it seems strange to some people that, while it is a sin to violate other sacred things, it was legally permitted for a "sacred man" to be killed. The reason for this is as follows: The ancients did not allow any sacred animal to remain within their borders, but drove them away to the territories of the gods to whom they were sacred; they considered the souls of consecrated men—whom the Greeks call the living ones <note>original: *ζωάνας* (zoanas). This likely refers to those dedicated to the gods while still living.</note>—to be owed to the gods. Therefore, just as they do not hesitate to send away from themselves that which is sacred and cannot be sent to the gods themselves, so they thought that souls, which they believed could be sent to heaven when sacred, should be stripped of their bodies—

### CHAPTER VIII.

We ruin the dignity of several passages which were most learnedly presented, simply by reading them incorrectly. For example, some read:

<margin>Aeneid, Book 2.</margin>
> *I depart, and with the Goddess guiding me, I pass through the flames and the enemies.* <note>Virgil, Aeneid 2, line 632. This refers to Aeneas being guided by his mother, Venus, during the fall of Troy.</note>

But he actually wrote with great learning: *with the God guiding* <note>original: "ducente Deo"</note>, not "the Goddess." For Acterianus affirms that in the works of Calvus <note>Gaius Licinius Macer Calvus, an orator and poet of the late Republic.</note>, one should read: *And Venus, the powerful God* <note>original: "Pollentemq; Deum Venerem"</note>, not "Goddess." There is even a statue of this deity in Cyprus with a bearded body, but in a woman’s dress, with a scepter and the stature of a man. They believe that this same deity is both male and female. Aristophanes <note>Likely referring to the scholar Aristophanes of Byzantium.</note> calls her <term>Aphroditus</term> <note>original: "ἀφρόδιτος." This is a masculine form of the name Aphrodite, used to describe her hermaphroditic or masculine aspect.</note>. Levinus also says: *Worshipping, therefore, the nourishing Venus, whether she is female or male: just as the nourishing Moon-light is.* Philochorus also affirms in his *History of Attica* that she is the Moon: for he says that men perform sacrifices to her in women's clothing, and women in men's clothing, because she is considered to be both male and female.

This was also said by Virgil with religious prudence:

> *It fell breathless, and left its life among the stars of the air.* <note>Virgil, Aeneid 5, line 517. This describes the death of a dove in an archery contest.</note>

<margin>Birds given to the stars for sacrifice.</margin>
For Hyginus, in his work *On the Properties of the Gods*, when he was speaking of the stars and heavenly bodies, says that birds ought to be sacrificed to them.

<margin>Aeneid, Book 5.</margin>
Thus, Virgil spoke learnedly when he said the soul of the bird remained among those deities to whom it was given for a <term>successful sacrifice</term> <note>original: "litandum." In Roman religion, "litatio" was a sacrifice that obtained a favorable omen.</note>. Nor does he allow any name in his work to be without purpose, even if it could seem accidental:

> *-And by his mother's name he called...* <note>Virgil, Aeneid 5, line 564. Referring to the young Atys naming a town after his mother.</note>

Following the previous page's discussion on the gender of deities and the correct reading of "God" vs "Goddess," the author now explores the etymology of the name "Camilla" and the legalistic definitions of "custom" (mos) versus "habit" (consuetudo).</meta>

<header>SATVRNALIA</header>

<margin>
Why Camilla was so named.
</margin>

*By changing a part of the name Casmilla, he called her Camilla.* <note>Virgil, Aeneid 11, line 543. The poet is explaining how the name of the warrior maiden was derived from her mother’s name, Casmilla.</note>
For Statius Tullianus, in the first book of his *On the Vocabulary of Things*, says that Callimachus <note>A famous Greek poet and scholar from Alexandria.</note> claimed the Etruscans <note>original: "Tuscos"</note> call Mercury "Camillus," a name they use to signify a minister of the Gods. This is why Vergil says Metabus called his daughter Camilla, as she was a minister to Diana. Even Pacuvius <note>An early Roman tragic poet.</note>, when speaking of Medea, says: *Welcome, guest, the long-awaited attendant of the inhabitants of heaven.* <note>original: "Cœlitum Camilla expectata aduenis, salue hospita."</note> The Romans also call noble, prepubescent boys and girls "Camilli" and "Camillae" <term>Camilli: young ritual assistants who served the priests and priestesses</term>, who serve the <term>Flamines and Flaminicae: high-ranking priests and their wives in Roman religion</term>. It is also not fitting to overlook this observation of his:

<margin>
Custom.
Aeneid, Book 7.
</margin>

> *There was a custom in Hesperian Latium, which the Alban cities*
> *continuously held sacred, and now Rome, the greatest of things,*
> *observes:—* <note>Virgil, Aeneid 7, lines 601–603. This refers to the ritual opening of the Gates of War.</note>

Varro, in his work *On Customs*, says that "custom" <note>original: "mos"</note> is a judgment of the mind which "usage" <note>original: "consuetudo"</note> ought to follow. Julius Festus, in the thirteenth book of his *On the Signification of Words*, says: "Custom is an ancestral institution, pertaining to the religions and ceremonies of the forefathers." Therefore, Vergil followed both authors: first Varro, because Varro had said that custom precedes and usage follows. After saying: *There was a custom*, Vergil added, *which the Alban cities continuously maintained*, and *now Rome, the greatest of things, observes*, by which he shows the perseverance of "usage." And since Festus says that it pertains to ceremonies, Vergil <note>original: "Maro," referring to Publius Vergilius Maro.</note> taught this same thing by adding the word "Sacred":
> *—Which the Alban cities*
> *continuously held sacred.*

Therefore, "custom" came first, and the "cultivation of custom" followed, which is "usage." And here he fulfilled Varro’s definition. Then, by adding "Sacred," he showed that custom is dedicated to ceremonies, which is what Festus asserted. He maintained this same distinction in the twelfth book, when he says:
> *The custom and the rites of the sacred things.* <note>Aeneid 12, line 836.</note>

Indeed, first the Latins reigned, then the Albans, and then the Romans. Therefore he said, first, *it was a custom in Hesperian Latium*; and afterwards, *which the Alban cities continuously held sacred*; and then he added, *now Rome, the greatest of things, observes it.* <note>Macrobius is citing Virgil, Aeneid 7, lines 601–603, to show Virgil’s awareness of the historical transition of power from the early Latins to Rome.</note>

->Concerning the chant by which the tutelary Gods were usually summoned, and by which either cities or armies were devoted to destruction.<-

### CHAPTER IX.

<margin>On summoning the tutelary Gods.</margin>
**All the Gods by whom this empire stood have departed, leaving their shrines and altars.** <note>Virgil, Aeneid 2, lines 351–352. This describes the gods abandoning Troy before its fall.</note>

This statement was brought forth both from the most ancient Roman custom and from the most secret rituals. For it is well known that all cities are under the protection <term>tutela: the religious and legal guardianship of a deity over a specific place or people</term> of some God. It was a secret Roman custom, unknown to many, that when they were besieging an enemy city and believed it could finally be taken, they would summon the tutelary Gods <note>original: "tutelares Deos"</note> with a specific chant <term>evocatio: a formal ritual "calling forth" of an enemy's gods to desert them and move to Rome, where they were promised new temples and worship</term>. They did this because they either believed the city could not be captured otherwise, or even if it could, they considered it a sacrilege to hold Gods as captives. For this reason, the Romans themselves wished both the God under whose protection the city of Rome exists and the Latin name of the city itself to remain unknown. But the name of the God has indeed been recorded in several books of the ancients (though they differ among themselves), and so it has become known to those who investigate antiquity, whatever the prevailing opinion may be. For some have believed it to be Jupiter, others Luna. There are those who suggest Angerona <note>An early Roman goddess associated with the winter solstice and silence.</note>, who commands silence with a finger placed to her mouth. Others, however, whose reliability seems stronger to me, have said it is Ops Consivia <note>original: "Opem Consiviam," an ancient goddess of the earth and abundance.</note>. However, the name of the city itself was unknown even to the most learned, as the Romans were careful lest they themselves suffer the same fate they knew they had often inflicted upon the cities of their enemies, namely...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the secret Roman ritual of summoning an enemy city’s protector gods (evocatio) and the subsequent consecration of that city to destruction (devotio). <header>THE SATURNALIA</header>

...they themselves might also be vulnerable to a hostile summoning, if the name of their own protector <term>tutelae: the divine guardianship or protection of a city</term> were to be made public. But we must be careful that the mistake made by some does not confuse us as well—those who think that by a single chant the Gods are both summoned from a city and the city itself is devoted to destruction. For I found in the fifth book of the *Hidden Matters* of Sammonicus Serenus <note>Serenus Sammonicus was a renowned scholar and tutor in the 2nd and 3rd centuries AD, famous for his massive library.</note> both chants, which he claimed to have found in a very ancient book by a certain Furius.

<margin>Chant for summoning the Gods.</margin>
The chant by which the gods are summoned when a city is surrounded by a siege is of this kind: "Whether it be a God or a Goddess under whose protection the people and state of Carthage are held, and you especially, who have taken upon yourself the protection of this city and people, I pray to you, I venerate you, and I ask for your favor, that you might desert the people and state of the Carthaginians; that you might leave their places, temples, sacred objects, and city, and depart from them; and that you might cast fear, dread, and forgetfulness upon that people and state; and having been surrendered, that you come to me and my people at Rome; and that our places, temples, sacred objects, and city may be more acceptable and approved by you; and that you may be set over me, the Roman people, and my soldiers, so that we may know and understand it. If you do this, I vow that I will build temples and hold games in your honor."

<margin>Words for the devotion of cities and armies.</margin>
One must perform sacrifices with these same words, and the authority of the entrails <term>extorum: the internal organs of a sacrificed animal, used by Roman priests to determine the will of the gods</term> must be observed to see if they promise these future events. Truly, cities and armies are "devoted" <note>original: "devoventur"; here meaning a ritual consecration to the powers of the underworld for total destruction.</note> in this way, once the divine powers have already been summoned. But only dictators and commanders-in-chief have the power to devote with these words: "Father Dis <note>original: 'Dis pater'; the Roman god of the underworld, similar to the Greek Pluto.</note>, or Jupiter of the underworld <note>original: 'Iovis manes'; literally 'the spirits of Jupiter,' referring to the chthonic or underworld aspect of the king of the gods.</note>, or by whatever other name it is lawful to call you, I ask that you fill that city of Carthage, and the army which I feel myself to be naming, with flight, dread, and terror; and those who carry arms and weapons against our legions and army, may you lead away those armies, those enemies, those men, their cities and fields, and those who dwell in those places, regions, fields, and cities, from the light above..."

<meta>The catchword "ro prin" likely suggests a continuation of the ritual formula, perhaps "depriving them of the light" (lumine supero privetis).</meta>

### BOOK III

At this point, while everyone, with unanimous testimony, was ranking the poet <note>Virgil</note> as equal in learning to the one he was narrating <note>meaning the character or historical source he describes</note>, Euangelus exclaimed that he had succumbed to patience for a long time, and could no longer hide the fact that he must expose the wounds of Virgil’s ignorance to everyone. "We too," he said, "once withdrew our hands from the schoolmaster’s rod <note>original: "manum ferulæ aliquando subduximus" — a Roman idiom meaning 'we have finished our primary education'</note>, and we too have received instruction in Pontifical law <term>Pontificium ius: the body of law and regulations managed by the Roman high priests concerning sacred rites</term>. From those things known to us, it will be established that Maro <note>Virgil's cognomen</note> was ignorant of the discipline of this law. For when would he say:

> To the king of the heaven-dwellers I was sacrificing a bull upon the shore:

Indeed, Labeo <note>Antistius Labeo, a rival jurist to Capito, known for his vast learning</note> stated in his sixty-eighth book that a bull is not to be sacrificed to anyone except Neptune, Apollo, and Mars. Behold your 'Pontiff' <note>Euangelus is mocking those who call Virgil a master of religious law</note>! At this, Prætextatus replied with a smile: "As to which of the gods a bull should be sacrificed, if you wish to share a word with Virgil, he himself will teach you:

> A bull for Neptune, a bull for you, beautiful Apollo.
<note>original: "Taurum Neptuno, taurum tibi pulcher Apollo" — Aeneid 3.119</note>

Therefore, looking toward things to come, he made the sacrificial victim an inappropriate one. But he also knew that this error was not beyond atonement. The act is committed, then, not as something that cannot be purified, yet it is unusual. And it is committed not out of ignorance, but so that he might make a place for the monster that was to follow."

## SATURNALIA

...sacrifices are completed. Among these things, the table <term>mensa: here referring to a ritual table used for offerings</term> holds the primary place, upon which the feasts, libations, and small offerings are placed. The ornaments, truly, are shields, crowns, and votive gifts of this sort. For votive gifts are not dedicated at the same time as the shrines are consecrated; however, the table and the small altars are usually dedicated on the same day as the temples themselves. Hence, a table dedicated with this rite in a temple takes on the function of an altar and the sanctity of a ritual couch <term>pulvinar: a cushioned seat for the statues of gods to "attend" a banquet</term>. Therefore, in Evander’s case, the libation is performed correctly: namely, at that table which had been dedicated along with the Great Altar <note>original: "ara maxima" — the famous altar of Hercules in Rome</note> according to religious custom; it was performed in a sacred place and during the actual rites in which they were feasting.

<margin>How Dido pours a libation on the table.</margin>
In Dido’s banquet, however, which is established as being merely royal and not also sacred—held at a human table, in a dining room, not in a temple—since it was not a religious libation but a customary one <note>original: "usurpata libatio" — a libation used by social custom rather than strict religious law</note>, he [Virgil] had only the queen pour the libation. In her person, there was no necessity for strict religious observance, and she had much power to adopt customary practices as she pleased.

But here:
<margin>Aeneid, Book 8.</margin>
> *Joyfully they pour libations upon the table, and pray to the gods.*

Because he knew what was done correctly, he recorded that it was done by everyone feasting together in a temple, sitting at a single consecrated table. Regarding that other verse:

> *To whom you dilute the honeycombs with milk and mild Bacchus,* <note>original: "miti Baccho" — Bacchus is used metonymically for wine</note>

I shall briefly resolve the accusation against Maro <note>Virgil's cognomen</note>. For the poet, being equally a seeker of learning in matters of doctrine and elegance in words, knowing that a libation of mead <term>mulsum: a mixture of wine and honey</term> is made to Ceres, added: "dilute the honeycombs with mild Bacchus," clearly saying that the wine grows mild when it begins to become mead. For he called the wine "mild" here just as elsewhere he calls it "tamed":

<margin>Georgics, Book 4.</margin>
> *—And destined to tame the harsh flavor of Bacchus.*

<margin>*on the day</margin>
\* You will not deny it is well known that on the * twelfth day before the Kalends of January <note>December 21st, the feast of Divalia or Angeronalia</note>, they perform a sacrifice to Hercules and Ceres with a pregnant sow, loaves of bread, and mead.

### Why Virgil assigned the Salii to Hercules, and why he depicted them crowned with poplar branches. CHAPTER XII.

"By Hercules, Praetextatus, you have most opportunely mentioned Hercules, for in his sacred rites this Virgil of yours has committed a double error:

<margin>Aeneid, Book 8</margin>
> Then the Salii come to the songs around the smoking altars,
> their temples bound with poplar branches.

For he assigned the Salii <note>The Salii were a college of priests famous for their rhythmic dancing and "leaping" rituals, traditionally dedicated to Mars.</note> to Hercules, whom antiquity dedicated only to Mars; and he mentions poplar crowns, even though at the Great Altar <note>original: "aram maximam" — the Ara Maxima, the oldest and most important altar to Hercules in Rome, located in the Forum Boarium.</note>, they bind their heads only with laurel, and no other foliage. We also see a laurel crown on the head of the Urban Praetor <note>The high-ranking Roman magistrate responsible for the administration of justice within the city.</note> when he performs a sacrifice to Hercules. Marcus Terentius Varro also testifies in that satire titled *About the Thunderbolt* <term>original Greek: περὶ κεραυνὗ — "peri keraunou"</term> that our ancestors used to vow a tithe to Hercules; nor did ten days ever pass without them inviting the people to a banquet provided without cost <term>original Greek: ἀσύμβολον — "asymbolon," meaning a meal where guests do not contribute money or food</term>, at which time they would go to bed wearing laurel crowns."

<margin>Poplar crowns in the rites of Hercules.</margin>
"Is this," Vettius replied, "a double error? I, for one, say Virgil erred in neither. For to speak first regarding the type of foliage: it is well established that those sacrificing at the Great Altar are now crowned with laurel. But this custom began a long time after the founding of Rome, after the laurel grove on the Aventine Hill began to grow green; Varro teaches us this in the second book of his *Human Affairs*. Therefore, the laurel plucked from the nearest hill was taken by those performing the rites because the nearby location offered the opportunity. Thus our Maro <note>A common name for the poet Virgil, whose full name was Publius Vergilius Maro.</note> correctly looked back to the times when Evander, before the city was founded, celebrated the rites at the Great Altar and used the poplar, which was certainly most pleasing to Alcides <note>A traditional epithet for Hercules, referring to his grandfather Alceus.</note>. 

<margin>Why the Salii are assigned to Hercules.</margin>
Furthermore, he assigns the Salii to Hercules because of the richness of deeper learning: for among the Pontiffs, this god is considered to be the same as Mars. And indeed, a Menippean satire of Varro affirms this, titled *This Is Another Hercules* <term>original Greek: ἄλλος οὗτος ἡρακλῆς — "allos houtos heraklēs"</term>; in this work, while speaking much about Hercules, he proves that he and Mars are the same. The Chaldeans <note>A term often used by Romans to refer to Babylonian astronomers and astrologers.</note> also call the star of Hercules...

BOOK III.

## On the extravagance or luxury of Quintus Hortensius, Fabius Gurges, Metellus Pius, and Metellus the Chief Pontiff: Then concerning the "Trojan Pig," and the fattening of hares and snails.

### CHAPTER XIII.

<margin>The luxury and effeminacy of Q. Hortensius.</margin>
Hear also the words of Marcus Varro, from the third book of his *On Agriculture*: when he was speaking about raising peacocks at a country estate, he said: *“Quintus Hortensius is said to have been the first to serve these at an inaugural banquet <note>original: "augurali adijciali cœna" — a lavish feast held when a new member was co-opted into the college of Augurs (priests who interpreted the will of the gods).</note> for an augur. Men of good character praised this act more as an instance of luxury than of strict morality. Many soon followed him, driving up their price, so that their eggs now sell for five denarii <note>A silver coin; five denarii was a significant sum, roughly several days' wages for a laborer.</note> each, and the birds themselves easily for fifty.” Behold a matter not only to be wondered at, but to be ashamed of: that peacock eggs sell for five denarii, which today—I will not say are cheaper—but are simply not for sale at all.* This same Hortensius was accustomed to watering his plane trees with wine; so much so that in a certain legal action which he had undertaken against Cicero, he urgently requested that Tullius <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note> swap his turn to speak with him. He claimed he needed to go to his villa immediately to personally pour wine over a plane tree he had planted on his Tusculan estate. 

But perhaps Hortensius does not sufficiently represent the character of his age—a man who was otherwise openly effeminate <note>original: "mollis" — literally "soft," a term used to criticize men who lacked traditional Roman ruggedness or "virilitas."</note> and placed all his honor in his outward appearance. He was indeed meticulously careful in his dress. To ensure he went out perfectly attired, he would study his reflection in a mirror; looking at himself there, he would arrange the toga upon his body so that an "artistic knot" <note>term: "artifex nodus" — a carefully constructed tie or fold in the toga that required professional skill to execute.</note> would bind the folds, placed there not by chance but by industry. The fold of the garment, flowing down by design, would wrap around his side just so. Once, when he was walking along having been elaborately prepared for show, he filed a lawsuit against a colleague for damages because, having met him in a narrow passage, the colleague had accidentally bumped him and ruined the structure of his toga. Hortensius considered it a capital offense that a fold had shifted its place on his shoulder. 

Therefore, setting him aside, let us turn to those men of triumphal status, who, though victors over nations, were conquered by luxury. I shall pass over "Gurges," a man nicknamed for "devouring" his inheritance <note>original: "Gurges" — meaning "the Whirlpool," a nickname given to Fabius for his youthful spendthrift habits.</note>, because—

Indeed, how shameful even the names of these foods are to speak!
For Cincius, in his speech supporting the <term>Fannian Law</term> <note>original: "legis Fanniæ" — A law passed in 161 BCE to limit the amount of money spent on banquets and the types of food served.</note>, re-
proaches his own age because they brought "Trojan pigs" to the tables.
They called them this because they were stuffed with other animals
inside them, just as that Trojan Horse was pregnant with armed men.
This lack of restraint in gluttony also demanded that even
hares should be fattened; as witnessed by Varro, who in the
third book of his *On Agriculture*, when speaking of hares, says:

> This too has been recently established: that hares should be fattened, since some people take them from the <term>leporarium</term> <note>A hare-enclosure or walled park for keeping wild animals.</note> and make them fat in cages and enclosed spaces.

If this seems strange to anyone—what Varro says about hares being
commonly fattened in that age—let him hear another thing more worthy
of wonder: that snails were fattened, which the same Varro
reports in that same book. I have indicated where those who wish
to read his exact words ought to look. Nor do I now say that we
should be preferred or compared to antiquity; but I have re-
sponded to the complaining Horus, asserting, as the matter stands,
that those centuries had a greater care for delights than our own.
