### CHAPTER XIV.

Furius Albinus, who was no less skilled in antiquity than Cecinna, added: "I wonder that you have not related how great an abundance of sea-riches used to be procured for them; by the reporting of which, you might have shown the extreme sobriety of our own banquets." And Cecinna said: "Bring forth into the open those things which <margin>* and you</margin> have also found in your reading * about this matter. For you surpass all others in your memory of old times." And so Furius began: "Antiquity indeed must always be worshipped by us (if we are wise). For those were the ages that gave birth to this Empire through either blood or sweat, which only a fertile abundance of virtues could achieve. But it must be confessed that in that abundance of virtues, that age was not without its vices: some of which have been corrected in our own age by the sobriety of our manners. I had intended to speak of the luxury of that time regarding sea-riches; but because, in the assertion of our own improvement, one thing suggests another to be brought forward, I shall not omit the fishes, but I will postpone them, <margin>The custom of dancing before dining rooms and elsewhere.</margin> while I remind you of another form of playfulness which we now lack. Tell me, Horus <note>A character in the dialogue, likely Horus the Cynic philosopher.</note>, you who throw antiquity in our faces, before whose <term>triclinium</term> <note>original: "triclinium" — A Roman dining room, typically featuring three couches for reclining during a meal.</note> do you remember recently seeing a female or male dancer? But among the ancients, dancing was eagerly sought after even by honorable people. For look, to start from that time which possessed the best morals—the period between the two <term>Punic Wars</term> <note>The great conflicts between Rome and Carthage (264–146 BCE) that defined Roman character and expansion.</note>—freeborn children, what am I saying, freeborn? The sons of Senators went to dancing school, and there they learned to dance while carrying <term>crotala</term> <note>original: "crotala" — Ancient clappers or castanets used to keep rhythm during dances.</note>. I say nothing of the fact that matrons also did not think dancing was dishonorable, but even among the respectable women there was a care for dancing: provided it was not too elaborate, to the point of professional perfection. For what does Sallust <note>Gaius Sallustius Crispus, a famous Roman historian. This quote refers to his description of the scandalous Sempronia.</note> say? 'To play and sing, and to dance more elegantly than is necessary [for a respectable woman]' <note>original: "Psallere, saltare elegantius, quàm necesse est [probæ]" — Sallust used this to critique women who behaved like stage performers rather than modest wives.</note>

### BOOK III.

...was she [not] honorable? <note>original: "probæ?" The text continues from a previous sentence discussing the reputation of a woman.</note> Thus even Sallust himself reproached Sempronia, not because she knew how to dance, but because she knew how to do it too well. Scipio Africanus Aemilianus <note>A famous Roman general and statesman (185–129 BC).</note> is a witness that the sons of nobles and—shameful to say—even their virgin daughters were numbered among those practicing the study of dancing. In his speech against the judicial law of Tiberius Gracchus, he says:

> They are taught dishonest tricks: with effeminate dancers <note>original: *cinædulis*, referring to shameful or provocative performers</note>, and with the sambuca <note>original: *sambuca*, a triangular stringed instrument of oriental origin</note> and the psaltery <note>original: *psalterióq;*, a stringed instrument</note>, they go to the school of actors. They learn to sing, which our ancestors wanted to be considered a disgrace for free-born citizens. They go, I say, to the dancing school among effeminate dancers—virgins and free-born boys.

When someone told me these things, I could not bring myself to believe that noble men were teaching such things to their children. But when I was taken to a dancing school, by my faith <note>original: *mediusfidius*, a common Roman oath</note>, I saw more than five hundred boys and girls in that school. Among them, I saw one (for whom I most greatly pitied the Republic) a boy wearing a bulla <note>original: *puerum bullatum*, a boy wearing the protective amulet worn by free-born Roman children</note>, the son of a candidate for office, not less than twelve years old, dancing with castanets <note>original: *crotalis*, rhythmic instruments similar to castanets</note>—a dance which a shameful little slave could not have performed with any decency.

You see how Africanus groaned because he had seen the son of a candidate—that is, a man seeking office—dancing with castanets. Even the hope and the plan of obtaining a magistracy, a time when he should have defended himself and his family from every disgrace, could not restrain him from doing what was clearly not considered shameful. Furthermore, he complained that for the most part, the nobility celebrated these disgraceful acts. In a similar way, Marcus Cato called the well-known Senator Caecilius a "loiterer" and a "Fescennian" <note>likely referring to the Fescennine verses, which were bawdy and mocking</note>. He said that he performed rhythmic dances in these words:

> He dismounts from his horse, and from there he performs rhythmic dances <note>original: *staticulos*, a type of mime-like or rhythmic dance</note> and pours out ridiculous things.

And elsewhere against the same man:

> Moreover, he sings whenever he pleases, sometimes he performs Greek verses, tells jokes, changes his voice, and performs rhythmic dances.

Thus said Cato. To him, as you see, even singing does not seem to be the act of a serious man, although among others...

<margin>Actors</margin>
...to such an extent was it not counted among shameful things <note>original: *turpia*; referring to activities considered beneath the dignity of a Roman citizen</note>: that **Lucius Sulla**, a man of such great reputation, is said to have sung excellently. Moreover, **Cicero** provides testimony that actors were not held among the disgraceful: for no one is ignorant that he was so familiar with the actors **Roscius** and **Aesopus** that he protected their interests and accounts with his own legal skill. This is declared not only by many other instances, but also from his letters. For who is there who has not read that speech in which he rebuked the Roman people because they raised a disturbance while Roscius was performing? And it is certainly well established that Cicero used to compete with the actor himself to see whether the actor could express the same thought more often through various gestures, or whether he himself, through his abundance of eloquence, could deliver it in different ways through speech. This matter drew Roscius to such confidence in his art that he wrote a book in which he compared eloquence with acting. This is the Roscius who was also very dear to Lucius Sulla and was presented with a gold ring by the same dictator. So great, moreover, was his favor and glory that he alone received a daily wage from the public treasury of a thousand denarii <note>A standard silver coin; a thousand denarii per day was an astronomical sum for a single performer</note>, not including his troupe. It is also known that Aesopus, through equal skill, left twenty million sesterces to his son. But why do I speak of actors, when **Appius Claudius**, a man who celebrated a triumph and who was a **Salian** <note>The Salii were "leaping priests" of Mars who performed ritual dances through the streets of Rome</note> until his old age, considered it a point of glory that he danced better than any of his colleagues? And before I depart from the subject of dancing, I will add this: at one and the same time, three very noble citizens possessed not only a passion for dancing, but even (if it please the Gods) a skill in which they might take pride: **Gabinius**, the former consul and enemy of Cicero—which Cicero openly reproached him for—and **Marcus Caelius**, a man well known in times of political turmoil, whom the same Cicero defended, and **Licinius Crassus**, the son of that Crassus who perished among the Parthians.

### CHAPTER XV.

<margin>Of Lucius Philippus</margin>
**B**ut from the dancing of the ancients, the name of the **Licinii** reminds me to transition to the luxury of marine spoils: for it is well established that they were surnamed *Murenae* <note>original: *Murænas*; the Latin name for the moray eel</note> because they took the most extravagant delight in this fish. **Marcus Varro** agrees with this opinion, stating that the **Licinii** were called *Murenae* in the same way that **Sergius** was surnamed *Orata* <note>The gilt-head sea bream, known for the gold mark between its eyes</note>: because those fish, which are called *auratae* [golden breams], were most dear to him. This is the **Sergius Orata** who first possessed "hanging baths" <note>original: *balneas pensiles*; these were floors suspended over heating chambers, an early form of underfloor heating</note>, first established oyster beds in the **Baian** district, and was the first to judge the **Lucrine** oysters <note>Oysters from the Lucrine Lake near Naples, a famous Roman luxury spot</note> as having the finest flavor. He lived, moreover, in the age of the famous and eloquent **Lucius Crassus**, whom even **Cicero** teaches us was considered grave and serious. Yet that **Crassus** was a man of censorial rank <note>A "censorius" was a former Censor, one of the highest and most morally authoritative offices in Rome</note>. For when he was Censor with **Gnaeus Domitius**, though he was considered more eloquent than all others and was a leader among the most distinguished citizens, he nevertheless put on mourning clothes and wept for a moray eel that had died in the fishpond of his home, as if it were a daughter. Nor was this kept secret, for his colleague **Domitius** cast this in his teeth in the **Senate** as if it were a shameful crime. But **Crassus** did not blush to admit it; instead (if you can believe it!) the Censor even boasted of it, bragging that he had done a pious and affectionate thing. 

Moreover, as evidence of how packed those most noble Roman leaders—**Lucius Philippus** and **Hortensius**, whom **Cicero** calls the "fishpond-fanciers" <note>original: *piscinarios*; a derisive term for aristocrats more interested in their pets than the Republic</note>—kept their ponds with the most precious fish, there is that which **Marcus Varro** records in his book *On Agriculture*. He writes that **Marcus Cato**, who later died at **Utica**, when he was left as heir in the will of **Lucilius**, sold the fish from his ponds for forty thousand sesterces <note>A very large sum, illustrating that even the stern "Stoic" Cato was not above profiting from the luxury he often criticized</note>. Furthermore, moray eels were summoned to the fishponds of our city all the way from the **Sicilian** Strait, which looks down upon **Messana** from **Rhegium**. For there, by Hercules, the very best are believed to be found by the extravagant, as are the eels. And both from that place are called *floaters* in Greek <note>original: πλῶτες (*plōtes*)</note> and *flutae* in Latin, because they swim on the very surface, [warmed by] the sun...

### On the sturgeon, mullet, parrotfish, and wolf-fish.
#### CHAPTER XVI.

Nor did the sturgeon <note>original: *acipenser*; a highly prized and rare fish in Roman luxury</note>, which the seas nourish for the extravagant, escape the delicacies of that age. And so that it may be clear that the name of this fish was famous during the Second Punic War, hear how **Plautus** mentioned it in the play titled *Baccharia* <note>Likely a reference to the play *Bacchides*</note>, in the character of a parasite:
> Who is the mortal ever blessed with such fortune,
> As I am now, for whose belly this parade is being carried?
> Even now, for the sturgeon that lay hidden from me in the sea until now,
> Whose flank I shall return to the hiding places of my teeth and hands?

But as to what **Pliny** says regarding the scales of the sturgeon, that most great investigator of natural things, **Nigidius Figulus**, shows it to be true. In the fourth book of his *On Animals*, it is written: "Why some fish have scales following the body, while the sturgeon has them facing the opposite way." These are the words of **Sammonicus**, who marks the shamefulness of his prince's banquet by praising it: revealing the veneration in which the fish was held, so that it was brought in by crowned men with the song of a flute-player, as if it were some procession not of delicacies, but of a deity. ...that the sturgeon used to be valued at a heavy price: Afinius Celer, a man of consular rank (as the same Sammonicus reports), purchased a single red mullet <note>original: *mullum*; a highly prized delicacy in Rome known for its changing colors as it died</note> for seven thousand sesterces. fleet, knowing that the parrotfish <note>original: *scarum*; likely the Mediterranean parrotfish, *Sparisoma cretense*</note> was so unknown to Italian shores that we did not even have a Latin name for the fish, had an incredible multitude of parrotfish brought here in various ships and scattered into the sea between Ostia <note>The harbor city of ancient Rome</note> and the coast of Campania. When it is the tenth hour <note>Roughly 4:00 PM; the end of the Roman business day</note>, they order a boy to be called to go to the Comitium <note>The public meeting space in the Roman Forum</note> to ask: what has been done in the forum, who supported the law, who opposed it, how many tribes voted "yes," and how many "no." Then they head to the Comitium themselves, lest they lose their own case by default. As they go, there is no jar in the narrow alleyway that they do not fill, for they have bladders full of wine. They arrive at the Comitium looking somber and order the case to proceed. The advocates tell their story. The judge calls for witnesses. He himself goes out to urinate. When he returns, he claims he has heard everything. He asks for the tablets and inspects the writing. He can hardly keep his eyelids open because of the wine. Going into deliberation, this is the speech: "What business do I have with these triflers? <insert>rather, why don't we drink?</insert> Why don't we instead have honey-wine mixed with Greek wine? Let us eat a fat thrush, a good fish—a true wolf-fish <note>original: *lupum germanum*; 'germanus' here means 'genuine' or 'authentic' rather than 'German'</note> that was caught between the two bridges?"

So says Titius. But Lucilius, a sharp and violent poet, also shows that he knows this fish of excellent flavor caught between the two bridges; he calls it a "plate-licker" <note>original: *catillonem*</note>, as if it were a scavenger; specifically, one that hunts for filth <note>original: *stercus*; waste or excrement</note> near the riverbanks.

<margin>Who were called Plate-lickers.</margin>
Properly, however, those were called "Plate-lickers" <note>original: *Catillones*</note> who, when they came to the final sacrificial feast of Hercules, would lick the small plates <note>original: *catillos*</note>. The verses of Lucilius are these:

> Moreover, imagining that whatever each person wanted was being brought.
> This man was led by sow's udders and a platter of fattened birds:
> That man by the plate-licker caught between the two Tiber bridges.

<header>OF THE SATURNALIA</header>

### CHAPTER XVII.

<margin>*Just as*</margin>
<margin>*The Orchian law.*</margin>
It would be a long task if I wished to list how many instruments of gluttony <note>original: *instrumenta gulæ*; refers to the specialized tools, exotic ingredients, and elaborate cooking methods developed by gourmands</note> were either devised by their wit or produced by their diligence. And these, to be sure, were the reasons why so many laws concerning dinners and expenses were brought before the people. It even began to be ordered that people should eat lunch and dinner with their doors standing open. Thus, with the eyes of the citizens acting as witnesses, a limit might be placed on luxury. Now, the first of all laws regarding dinners reached the people as the **Orchian Law**, which Gaius Orchius, Tribune of the Plebs, proposed upon the advice of the Senate, in the third year after Cato had been Censor <note>Cato the Elder, famous for his strict morality and opposition to Greek influences, served as Censor in 184 BCE</note>. I pass over its specific words, as they are lengthy. However, its essence prescribed the number of guests. And this is the Orchian Law about which Cato soon shouted in his speeches: because more guests were then being invited to dinner than was permitted by its decree.

<margin>The Fannian law.</margin>
And when increased necessity cried out for the author of a new law, twenty-two years after the Orchian Law, the **Fannian Law** was passed, in the year 588 <note>The transcription reads *lxxxviii* (88), but in the context of Roman history and the founding of the city, this refers to 588 AUC, or roughly 161 BCE</note> after the founding of Rome, according to the opinion of Gellius. Regarding this law, Sammonicus Serenus <note>A 3rd-century scholar and tutor to the emperor’s son, known for his vast library and writings on history and medicine</note> reports as follows: "The Fannian Law reached the people with the vast consent of all classes. And it was not proposed by Praetors or Tribunes, like most other laws, but the Consuls themselves proposed it following the counsel and opinion of all good men; for the Republic was suffering greater damages from the luxury of banquets than can be believed. Indeed, things had come to such a state that many free-born boys, enticed by gluttony, were selling their modesty and their freedom; many of the Roman commoners would come to the Comitium <note>The public assembly area in the Roman Forum</note> soaked in wine, and while drunk, would deliberate on the safety of the Republic." Thus far Sammonicus. Moreover, the severity of the Fannian Law surpassed the Orchian Law in this: that in the earlier law, only the number of diners was restricted, and according to it, anyone was allowed to consume their property among a few people; but the Fannian Law [restricted] both the costs...

<page-num>351</page-num>
<header>BOOK III.</header>

...[the law] set a limit of one hundred *asses* <note>The *as* was a bronze Roman coin; a hundred *asses* was a modest sum intended to restrain luxury</note>. For this reason, in his characteristic festive manner, the poet Lucilius calls it the "hundred-as law" <note>original: *centussis*; a term for a hundred-unit value</note>.

<margin>The Didian law.</margin>
The **Didian Law** followed the Fannian Law eighteen years later. There were two reasons for its introduction: First and most importantly, so that all of Italy, and not just the city [Rome], would be bound by sumptuary law; for the Italians believed that the Fannian Law had been written only for the citizens within the city, not for themselves. Secondly, it ensured that not only those who hosted lunches or dinners at great expense would be liable, but also those who had been invited to them and were present at all, would be held under the penalties of the law.

<margin>The Licinian law.</margin>
After the Didian, the **Licinian Law** was introduced by Publius Licinius Crassus the Rich. So much zeal was invested by the aristocrats in proposing and approving it that the Senate issued a decree: as soon as the law was posted <note>original: *promulgata*; the formal public announcement of a proposed law</note>, even before it was confirmed after the three-market-day period <note>original: *trinundino*; the legal interval of roughly 24-27 days required before a vote</note>, it should be observed by everyone just as if it had already been approved by the vote of the people. In truth, this law agrees with the Fannian Law in most respects, with only a few changes. For in its proposal, the authority of a new law was sought because the fear of the older law was fading away. Indeed, by Hercules, it was just as happened with the **Twelve Tables** <note>The foundational code of Roman law from c. 450 BCE</note> themselves: when their antiquity began to be held in contempt, those same restrictions provided by those ancient laws were transferred into the names of new legislators. 

But the gist of the Licinian Law was that on the Kalends, the Nones, and Roman market-days <note>The 1st and 5th/7th of the month, and the recurring *nundinae* or market days</note>, anyone was permitted to spend only thirty *asses* for the sake of eating. On other days that were not exempted, no more should be served than three pounds of dried meat and one pound of salted fish <note>original: *salsamentorum*; generally referring to preserved fish or salted meats</note>, along with whatever else is produced from the earth, the vine, or a tree. I see what causes a prick of conscience. Is it therefore a sign of a sober age when the expense of dinners is restrained by such a legal prescription? Not so. For sumptuary laws were proposed by individuals to correct the vices of the entire state. Yet, unless people were living with the worst and most extravagant habits, there certainly would have been no need for passing such laws. As the old saying goes:
*Good laws are born from bad habits.*

# SATURNALIA

<margin>The Cornelian Law.</margin>
This is followed by the **Cornelian Law**, also a sumptuary law, which was brought forward by the Dictator Cornelius Sulla <note>Lucius Cornelius Sulla (c. 138–78 BCE), a Roman general and statesman who held the office of dictator to reform the constitution</note>. In this law, the magnificence of banquets was not prohibited, nor was a limit placed on gluttony; rather, lower prices were imposed on goods. And for what things (good Gods!), and for what exquisite and almost unknown types of delicacies did he set these prices? What fish and what little morsels <note>original: *offulas*; small, dainty cuts of meat or savory bites</note> does he name there? And yet he established lower prices for them—I would even dare to say that the cheapness of these foodstuffs might incite men's minds to procure even greater quantities of provisions <note>original: *opsoniorum*; a term for side dishes, especially fish or gourmet items eaten with bread</note>. This allowed even those with small means to serve their own gluttony. I will say plainly what I feel: he seems to me remarkably luxurious and wasteful if these great things are provided for feasts even for free. Indeed, this present age is so much more prone to every kind of indulgence that most of the things included in Sulla’s law (though it is widely known) are things none of us have even heard of.

<margin>The Law given by Lepidus.</margin>
After Sulla's death, the Consul Lepidus also brought forward a food law <note>original: *legem cibariam*</note>. For Cato <note>Cato the Elder, a famous Roman statesman known for his traditionalism and opposition to Greek luxury</note> calls sumptuary laws "food laws."

<margin>The Law of Antius Restio.</margin>
A few years later, another law reached the people, introduced by **Antius Restio**. Although this law was excellent, the stubbornness of luxury and the firm alliance of vices rendered it useless, even without anyone formally repealing it. However, a memorable story is told about Restio, the author of the law himself: for as long as he lived, he never dined out at someone else's house <note>original: *non recænasse*; to dine out or go to a dinner party</note>, so that he would not become a witness to the contempt shown for the law he himself had passed for the public good.

<margin>Antony’s edict.</margin>
I would count among these laws the edict on expenses proposed by **Antony**, who was later a Triumvir <note>Mark Antony, the famous general and lover of Cleopatra, who was part of the Second Triumvirate</note>, were I not to believe it unworthy to give Antony a place among those who restrained spending. His usual expenses for a single dinner were surpassed only by the valuation of the single great pearl <note>original: *Unionis*; a "union" pearl was a large, unique pearl of such high quality it was said to be "one of a kind"</note> consumed by his wife Cleopatra. For Antony—considering that whatever was born of the sea, the earth, or even the sky was created only to satisfy his own voracity <note>original: *ingluuiem*; excessive greed or an insatiable gullet</note>—would shove it all between his jaws and teeth. And having been captivated by this habit...

It concludes by mocking Mark Antony's hypocrisy in issuing an edict on spending despite his own legendary extravagance with Cleopatra.</summary>

### BOOK III.

Cleopatra, the wife <note>original: *uxor*; though not legally his wife by Roman law, she was his partner</note> who wished to make the Egyptian kingdom a part of the Roman Empire, was a woman who could not be outdone by the Romans even in luxury. She challenged Antony with a bet, claiming she could spend ten million sesterces <note>A massive sum: 10,000,000 sesterces was roughly equivalent to the annual property qualification for ten Roman senators</note> on a single dinner. This seemed miraculous to Antony. Without delay, he took up the bet.
<margin>*Other versions: "a worthy judge." Some read it as a pledge guarded by Munatius Plancus.</margin>
The judge chosen for this honorable contest was Munatius Plancus, a man worthy of the kitchen <note>A sarcastic remark implying Plancus was a glutton or overly concerned with food</note>. On the following day, Cleopatra, testing Antony, prepared a truly lavish meal, but it was not one that Antony found particularly marvelous; indeed, he recognized everything being served as part of their daily abundance. Then the queen, smiling, called for a small bowl, poured into it a bit of sharp vinegar, and quickly dropped into it a large pearl <term>unio; a rare, large pearl named for being "unique" or "one of a kind"</term> taken from one of her ears. As it was quickly dissolved—as is the nature of that stone—she swallowed it. And although she had won the bet by this act alone—since that pearl was easily worth ten million sesterces without any argument—she nevertheless moved her hand toward her other ear to take the second pearl. She would have done the same had not Munatius Plancus, acting as a most severe judge, quickly pronounced Antony defeated. As for the size of that pearl, it can be gathered from this: the one that remained after the queen was defeated and Egypt was captured was brought to Rome and cut in two. These two halves, made from a single pearl, were placed upon the statue of Venus in the temple called the Pantheon, as objects of monstrous size.

But first, I want you to finish explaining the nuts which your memory...

And Servius <note>Servius was a famous 4th-century grammarian known for his commentary on Virgil</note> says: That walnut <margin>The Walnut.</margin> [iuglans], according to the opinion of some, is thought to be named from "helping" <note>original: *iuuando*</note> and from "acorn" <note>original: *glans*</note>. But Caius Bassus <note>A Roman writer on grammar and law from the early Empire</note>, in his book *On the Meaning of Words*, records this: The walnut tree is so named because it is, as it were, "Jupiter’s acorn" <note>original: *Iouis glans*</note>. # BOOK III.

Walnuts produce their buds and flowers at the same time as "Greek nuts."

<margin>The Greek Nut. * And showing it, he said, "This is the Greek nut, and..."</margin>
Now we must discuss what the "Greek nut" is. And as he said this, he took an almond from a dish * and showed it: "The Greek nut is that which is also called the almond <note>original: *amygdala*</note>. But the same nut is also called the 'Thasian' nut." Cloatius <note>Cloatius Verrius, an Augustan-era scholar who wrote on Greek influence in Roman life</note> is a witness to this in the fourth book of his *Arrangement of Greek Terms*, where he says: "The Greek nut is the almond." Likewise, the character Acca says in the *Supplication*: "Add a Greek nut and as much honeycomb as you please."

<margin>The Mollusca Nut.</margin>
Although the winter season denies us the fruit itself, nonetheless, since we are speaking of nuts, we should not leave the "mollusca" nut unmentioned. Plautus <note>The most famous Roman comic playwright, active c. 200 BCE</note> mentions it in his play *The Little Shoe* [Calceolus] in this way: "He said the mollusca nut hung over its roof-tiles." Behold, Plautus names it, but does not explain what the mollusca nut actually is. It is, however, that which is commonly called the "Persian fruit" <note>original: *persicum*. We know this today as the peach, which the Romans often classified as a type of nut because of its hard pit or 'stone'</note>, and it is called the "mollusca" [softish] nut because it is softer than all other nuts. A suitable witness for this fact is Suevius <note>A Roman poet known for his work on food and nature</note>, a very learned man, in his poem on food titled *The Salad* [Moretum]. For when he speaks of a gardener making a salad, among the other things he says are put into it, he mentions that this fruit is added with these words:

> "Now mix in some of these Royal nuts, Acca,
> And some Persian fruits: which name is so given
> Because those who once, with the powerful King
> Named Alexander the Great, brought fierce battles
> Against the Persians in their war, upon their return
> Spread this genus of tree through the chosen lands of Greece,
> Giving new fruits to mortal men.
> This is the 'mollusca' nut, lest anyone should err in ignorance."

<margin>The Tarentine Nut.</margin>
The "Tarentine" nut is so named because it is so soft that it breaks with the slightest touch. Regarding this, we find the following in the book of Favorinus <note>A philosopher and orator of the 2nd century CE, often a character in these dialogues</note>: "Likewise, some speak of Tarentine sheep or nuts, which are actually 'Terentine,' named after *Terenus*, which is the word for 'soft' in the Sabine language <note>The Sabines were an ancient Italic tribe whose language influenced early Latin</note>."

### Chapter XIX. On the varieties of apples and pears.

<margin>How nuts and apples differ.</margin>
And because we see apples mixed among the dessert delicacies <note>original: *bellarijs*, referring to the final course of a Roman banquet consisting of nuts, fruit, and sweets</note>, after discussing nuts we must now treat the various kinds of apples. There are writers on agriculture who divide nuts and apples in this way: *they call a "Nut" any fruit that is covered by a hard shell on the outside and has the edible part within; but they call an "Apple" [malum] that which has the edible part on the outside and encloses something hard within. According to this definition, the peach—which the poet Suevius previously numbered among the nuts—should instead be numbered among the apples.*

<margin>Varieties of apples.</margin>
With these things established, we must list the varieties of apples <note>original: *mala*. In Latin, this term often applied broadly to many fleshy fruits, not just what we call apples today</note>, which Cloatius <note>Cloatius Verrius, an expert on Roman and Greek vocabulary</note> catalogs so diligently in the fourth book of his *Arrangement of Greek Terms*. The varieties of apples are: the <term>Armenian</term> [apricot], the <term>Cydonian</term> [quince], the <term>citron</term>, the <term>plum</term> <note>original: *coccymelium*</note>, the <term>preserved apple</term>, the <term>medlar</term> <note>original: *ἐπιμηλίς* (epimelis)</note>, the <term>must-apple</term> [sweet], the <term>Mattian</term>, the <term>round-apple</term>, the <term>grainy-apple</term>, the <term>early-ripener</term> [apricot], the <term>shriveled-apple</term>, the <term>Punic apple</term> [pomegranate], the <term>Persian apple</term> [peach], the <term>Quirian</term>, the <term>Prostian</term>, the <term>red-apple</term>, the <term>Scandian</term>, the <term>wild-apple</term>, the <term>sparrow-quince</term> <note>original: *struthium*</note>, the <term>Scantian</term>, the <term>Tibur-apple</term>, and the <term>Verian</term>. You see that the peach was numbered among the apples by Cloatius; it has kept the name of its place of origin <note>Persia</note>, even though it has long been a product of our own soil. Moreover, Cloatius says that the citron is also a type of "Persian apple," following the view of Virgil <note>Publius Vergilius Maro, the Roman epic poet</note>:

<margin>Georgics, Book 2.</margin>
> *Of the blessed fruit <note>original: *felicis mali*</note>, than which none is more excellent.*

And so forth. And so that no one may doubt that Virgil said these things about the citron, listen to what Oppius says in his book *On Forest Trees*: "The citron tree and the peach are other kinds..."

And a little later, speaking of the citron <term>citreum (Citrus medica)</term>, he says: "It is indeed most fragrant, and when placed among clothing, it kills moths. It is also said to be an antidote to poisons; when crushed and drunk with wine, it saves the drinkers by the purging power of its natural properties. Citrons grow in Persia at all times of the year; for while some are being harvested, others are ripening." You see here that it is both called a Citron and that all the characteristics are provided which Virgil <note>The famous Roman poet (70–19 BCE)</note> mentioned, even though Virgil did not use the name "citron." Indeed,
<margin>Note that in Odyssey Book 5, it is written: "and the scent of thyon spread through the island," just as in another closing of the following verse we read "and having washed."</margin>
Homer, who calls the citron *thyon* <note>original Greek: θύον</note>, shows that it is a fragrant fruit when he says: "a beautiful scent of thyon breathed from it" <note>original Greek: θύ' δ' ἀπὸ καλὸν ὀδώδει</note>. And what Oppius <note>Gaius Oppius, a friend of Julius Caesar who wrote on natural history</note> says about the citron being placed among clothing, Homer also signifies when he says:
> And she put on fragrant, shining garments. <note>original Greek: Εἵματα δ' ἀμφιέσατα θυώδεα σιγαλόεντα</note>
Hence the poet Naevius <note>Gnaeus Naevius (c. 270–201 BCE), an early Roman epic poet and playwright</note> also speaks of a "citron-scented garment" in his work on the Punic War.

<margin>Kinds of Pears.</margin>
As for these pears <note>original: *Pyra*</note> that we see, a numerous variety of names distinguishes them. For the same Cloatius <note>Marius Cloatius, a Roman scholar who wrote on food and language</note> describes their names as follows: the Antian, the gourd-pear, the ciritum, the service-berry pear, the stony-pear, the Crustumine <note>from Crustumerium, an ancient city near Rome</note>, the deciman, the little Greek, the Lollian, the Lanuvian, the laurel-pear, the Laterasian, the marapium, the Milesian <note>from Miletus in Ionia</note>, the myrtle-pear, the Naevian, the round-pear, the Praecian, the reddish-pear, the Signine <note>from Signia, famous for its pears</note>, the Tullian, the Titian, the Turrinian, the thyme-pear, the early-ripening, the hand-filling pear <note>original: *uolemium*, literally "filling the palm"</note>, the medlar-pear, the late-pear, the late-sown, the late-Sextilian, the late-Tarentine, and the late-Valerian.

### Chapter XX. On the varieties of figs, olives, and grapes.

<margin>Kinds of Figs.</margin>
Dried figs also prompt us to list the various kinds of figs; our same source Cloatius instructs us on these as he did on the others. In his usual diligent manner, he enumerates the different figs thus: the African, the whitish, the reed-fig, the wild-donkey fig, the black, the marsh-fig, the Augustan, the twice-bearing <note>producing fruit twice a year</note>, the Carian <note>the *carica*, or dried fig from Caria</note>, the Caldic, the white, the black, the Calpurnian,
<margin>*the Livian</margin>
the Chian <note>from the island of Chios</note>, the gourd-fig, the hard-skinned, the Herculean, the Livian, the stage-player fig, the little-stage fig, the Marsic, the Numidian, the dark-fig, the Pompeian, the early-ripening, the Tellane, and the black. It should be known that the white fig is produced from fortunate trees... <note>original: *ex felicibus... arboribus*. In Roman religious law, certain trees were "lucky" or "auspicious" while others were "unlucky."</note>

...[from happy] trees; on the other hand, black ones are from the unhappy trees. The Pontiffs <note>The high priests of ancient Roman religion</note> teach us both. For Veranius says in his work *On Pontifical Words*:

<margin>* Others say "sapinus," the fir-tree</margin>
"Happy" trees <term>arbores felices (trees of good omen)</term> are considered to be the oak, the winter oak, the holm oak, the fir-tree <margin>sapinus</margin>, the beech, the hazel, the service tree, the white fig, the pear, the apple, the vine, the plum, the cornelian cherry, and the lotus. However, Tarquinius Priscus <note>The fifth king of Rome (reigned 616–578 BCE)</note>, in his book on tree portents <term>ostentarium arborario</term>, speaks thus: The trees which are under the protection of the gods of the underworld and those who turn away evil <note>original: *avertentium*</note>, he names "unhappy" <term>infelices (trees of ill omen)</term>. 

<margin>* Alder: or, but the myrtle</margin>
<margin>* Alternative: blood-colored</margin>
He considers the [red dogwood] <margin>blood-colored</margin> happy, but the black fig, and whichever trees bear a black berry or black fruit, as well as the holly, the wild pear, the butcher's broom <margin>Others: the plum</margin>, the bramble, and thorns are unhappy; it is proper to order that evil omens and prodigies be burned with these. 

What of the fact that we find the fig is distinguished from "fruit" <term>poma</term> among reliable authors? Afranius <note>A Roman comic poet of the 2nd century BCE</note> says in his play *Selia*: "Fruit, vegetable, fig, grape." And also Cicero in the third book of his *Oeconomicus* <note>A translation of Xenophon's work on household management</note>: "He neither plants the vine, nor carefully tends what is sown; he has no oil, no figs, no fruit." Nor should it be ignored that the fig is the only tree of all that does not flower. The term "milk" is properly used for figs.

<margin>Others: of milk</margin>
Unripe figs are called *grossi* when they do not mature; the Greeks call these *olynthoi* <note>original Greek: ὄλυνθους</note>. Marcus Attilius says: "In so many thousands of figs you will not see an unripe one." And a little later he says: "You might take from another the unripe figs overflowing with milk." And Postumius Albinus, in the first book of his *Annals*, says regarding Brutus <note>Lucius Junius Brutus, who feigned stupidity to survive the reign of Tarquin the Proud</note>: "For that reason he made himself out to be a fool and stupid <note>The name 'Brutus' translates to 'dull' or 'stupid' in Latin</note>, and he ate little unripe figs with honey."

### END OF THE THIRD BOOK.

## VESALIENSIS ON THE
## FOURTH BOOK.

Just as in the preceding book Prætextatus showed Virgil to have been most expert in pontifical law <term>pontificii iuris (the sacred laws governing religious rites)</term>, so in this book Eusebius <note>A character in the dialogue, a teacher of rhetoric</note> demonstrates how great a master of Rhetoric that same poet was. But how small a portion of these things has been saved from destruction? Since both the beginning and the end, along with so many other passages, are missing, it is likely that scarcely a sixth part of this book survives. 

I truly wish that, either by chance or by the diligent industry of scholars, it might one day happen that these works—if not in every way, then at least in some part—might be restored to their original integrity. This can only be done if, by some luck, a more corrected copy is unearthed from some dusty library. Otherwise, either I am completely foolish, or such a thing simply cannot be done.

### On moving the emotions through the physical bearing of a character. CHAPTER I.

<margin>Pathos from physical bearing.</margin>
<image-desc>Historiated decorative initial 'N' depicting several figures in classical attire within an architectural setting.</image-desc>Neither is she more moved in her expression by the speech he had begun:
> Than if she stood as hard flint or a Marpesian crag. <note>original: "Nec magis incœpto uultu sermone mouetur: Quàm si dura silex, aut stet Marpesia cautes." From Virgil’s *Aeneid* (6.470–471), describing Dido’s stony silence when she meets Aeneas in the Underworld. "Marpesian" refers to the famous marble quarries of Mount Marpessus on the island of Paros.</note>

At last she tore herself away, and fled back as an enemy. <note>original: "Tandem corripuit sese, atq; inimica refugit." *Aeneid* 6.474.</note>

Likewise, there is <term>pathos (the rhetorical portrayal of emotion or suffering)</term> in this verse:
> I was struck dumb, my hair stood on end, and my voice stuck in my throat. <note>original: "Obstupuit, steteruntq; comæ, & uox faucibus hæsit." *Aeneid* 2.774. Aeneas describing his physical reaction to seeing the ghost of his wife, Creusa.</note>

But also the entire exhaustion of Dares is depicted through his physical bearing:
> But his faithful companions [led] him away, dragging his weak knees,
> Shaking his head to either side, and spitting out thick blood
> From his mouth. <note>original: "Ast illum fidi æquales genua ægra trahentem, / Quassantemq; utroq; caput, crassumq; cruorem / Ore eiectantem." *Aeneid* 5.468–470, describing the defeated boxer Dares.</note>

He also briefly shows the trepidation of Dares' companions:
> —Called forward, they receive 
> The helmet and the sword. <note>original: "—Galeamq;, ensemq; uocati Accipiunt." *Aeneid* 5.471–472.</note>

As if they were receiving the prize not of their own will, but as something that had to be granted out of a sense of shame.

Of the same kind is this passage: —And from the whole face of the speaker
Sparks fly out, and fire flashes from his fierce eyes. <note>original: "—Totoq; loquentis ab ore / Scintillæ absistunt, oculis micat acribus ignis." *Aeneid* 12.101–102, describing the rage of the character Turnus.</note>

There is also <term>pathos</term> in the description of physical weakness <note>original: "languoris habitus"</note>: such as the entire description of the plague in the works of Thucydides <note>The Greek historian who famously detailed the symptoms and social collapse caused by the Plague of Athens in the 5th century BCE.</note>. And:
> The winning horse falls, unlucky, forgetful of his exercises 
> And the grass. <note>original: "Labitur infelix, studiorum, atq; immemor herbæ Victor equus." From Virgil’s *Georgics* (3.498–499), a didactic poem on farming; here Virgil describes a plague affecting livestock.</note> And,
> —Drooping ears, a fitful 
> Sweat appears there, and indeed it is cold for those about to die. <note>original: "—Demissæ aures, incertus ibidem Sudor, & ille quidem morituris frigidus." *Georgics* 3.500–501.</note>

Shame is also numbered among the <term>pathe (emotions or sufferings)</term>, as in:
> Around Deiphobus, who was trembling and hiding his cruel punishments. <note>original: "Circa Deiphobum pauitantem, & dira tegentem / Supplicia." *Aeneid* 6.498–499. Deiphobus, a son of Priam, was hideously mutilated by the Greeks; his physical trembling and his attempt to cover his wounds manifest his shame and suffering.</note>

And grief is revealed by physical habit, as with the mother of Euryalus:
> The shuttles were shaken from her hands, her wool-work was unrolled, and the unhappy woman flew out. <note>original: "Excussi manibus radij, reuolutaq; pensa, / Euolat infelix." *Aeneid* 9.476-477. This describes the mother’s physical shock and immediate abandonment of her domestic work upon hearing of her son’s death.</note>

> He held his face fixed in a steady gaze. <note>original: "Defixa obtutu tenet ora." *Aeneid* 12.70. A description of the King’s stunned reaction to his daughter Lavinia’s blush and the impending duel.</note>

And Venus, because she is about to ask a favor:
> Sadder, her bright eyes filled with tears. <note>original: "Tristior, & lachrymis oculos suffusa nitentes." *Aeneid* 1.228. Venus here uses her physical display of sorrow to move Jupiter to pity for her son Aeneas.</note>

And the Sibyl, because she is in a frenzy:
> Suddenly her face changed, her color was not one, and her hair did not remain combed. <note>original: "Subitò non uultus, non color unus, / Non comptae mansere comae." *Aeneid* 6.47-48. The physical transformation of the Sibyl as she is possessed by the god Apollo.</note>

->How emotion is expressed by the very flow of speech.<-

### CHAPTER II.

<margin>On emotional speech.</margin>
Now let us see by what flow of speech <term>pathos (emotion)</term> is expressed. And first, let us ask what is taught by the rhetorical art concerning such speech. For it is necessary that emotional speech be directed either toward indignation or toward pity; these are called <term>oiktos (pity)</term> and <term>deinosis (indignation or heightening of a wrong)</term> by the Greeks. One of these is necessary for the accuser, the other for the defendant. And it is necessary that it have an abrupt beginning, since it is not fitting for those who are sufficiently indignant to begin gently. Therefore, in Virgil’s work, Juno begins in this way:
> —"Why do you force me to break my deep silence?" <note>original: "Quid me alta silentia cogis / Rumpere?" *Aeneid* 10.63.</note> And elsewhere:
> —"Must I desist from my undertaking, defeated?" <note>original: "Me'ne incoepto desistere uictam?" *Aeneid* 1.37.</note> And elsewhere:
> <margin>In other versions it is read as "deeds" [factis]: that is, "attempts" [conatibus].</margin>
> "Alas, hated race, and the fates of the Phrygians contrary to our own!" <note>original: "Heu stirpem inuisam, & fatis contraria nostris / Fata Phrygum." *Aeneid* 7.293-294. Phrygians is a common poetic name for the Trojans.</note> And Dido:
> —"Shall we die unavenged? But let us die," she says. <note>original: "Moriemur inultae? Sed moriamur, ait." *Aeneid* 4.659.</note> And the same:
> —"By Jupiter, will this man go [from here]?" <note>original: "Prò Iuppiter ibit / Hic ait." *Aeneid* 4.590-591.</note> And Priam:
> —"But to you, for your crime," he cries out, "for such daring deeds." <note>original: "At tibi pro scelere exclamat, pro talibus ausis." *Aeneid* 2.535.</note>

# THE SATURNALIA

<page-num>362</page-num>
<header>OF THE SATURNALIA</header>

Not only should the beginning be like this, but if it is possible, every emotional speech should fluctuate with short sentences and frequent changes of rhetorical figures, as if tossing amidst the surges of anger. Let one speech from Virgil, therefore, serve as our example:

<margin>An example of an emotional speech from *Aeneid* Book 7.</margin>
> *Alas, hated race!* <note>original: "Heu stirpem inuisam." Juno, the Queen of the Gods, begins her famous soliloquy in *Aeneid* 7.293, expressing her fury that the Trojans have reached Italy despite her attempts to stop them.</note>

The beginning starts from an <term>ecphonesis</term> <note>An emotional exclamation used to express strong feelings like outcry or grief.</note>. Then follow short interrogations:

> — Could they not have fallen on the Sigean plains? Could they not have been captured once taken? Did burning Troy not consume these men? <note>original: "Num Sigeis occumbere campis? / Num capti potuere capi? num incensa cremauit / Troia uiros?" Juno sarcastically asks if the Trojans are impossible to kill or conquer.</note>

Then follows a <term>hyperbole</term> <note>An intentional exaggeration used for emphasis rather than literal truth.</note>:

> — Through the middle of the ranks, and through the middle of the fires, they found a way. <note>original: "Medias acies, mediosq; per ignes / Inuenere uiam."</note>

Then <term>irony</term> <note>The use of words to convey a meaning that is the opposite of its literal meaning, often for sarcastic effect.</note>:

> — But I suppose my divine powers at last lie exhausted; satiated with hatred, I have come to rest. <note>original: "At credo mea numina tandem / Fessa iacent: odijs haud exaturata quieui." Juno mocks the idea that she has given up or lost her power.</note>

Then she complains that her daring efforts were ineffective:

> — Daring to follow through the waves, and to oppose myself to the exiles across the whole sea. <note>original: "Per undas / Aufa sequi, & profugis toto me opponere ponto."</note>

After this, a second <term>hyperbole</term>:

> The powers of heaven and sea are exhausted against the Trojans. <note>original: "Absumptæ in Teucros uires cœliq;, marisq;."</note>

Then, scattered complaints:

> Of what use to me were the Syrtes or Scylla, or what did vast Charybdis profit me? <note>original: "Quid Syrtes aut Scylla mihi, quid uasta Charybdis / Profuit?" These refer to the famous mythological sea-monsters and hazards Juno sent against Aeneas.</note>

Then an <term>argument from the lesser</term> <note>original: <term>argumẽtum à minore</term>. A logical move arguing that if a lesser power could achieve a great feat, a greater power certainly should be able to.</note> is joined to it, so that the <term>pathos</term> <note>The quality of a speech that appeals to the audience's or speaker's emotions.</note> may be increased:

> — Mars was able to destroy the giant race of the Lapiths. <note>original: "Mars perdere gentem Immanem Lapithûm ualuit." Juno compares her struggle to Mars’s successful destruction of his enemies.</note>

Mars is a lesser personage than she, and therefore this follows:

> But I, the great consort of Jove. <note>original: "Ast ego magna Iouis coniux." Juno emphasizes her status as Queen of the Gods to highlight her frustration.</note>

Then, when she had also compared their motives, with what great force the Goddess said:

> — Unhappy woman that I am, who have turned myself to every shift! <note>original: "Infelix quæ memet in omnia uerti?"</note>

And she did not say, "I cannot destroy Aeneas," but rather: "I am conquered by Aeneas." Then she steels herself to cause harm; and, as is characteristic of one who is angry, even if she despairs that it can be fully accomplished, she nevertheless intends to im—

<meta>The catchword "pedire" (to impede/hinder) indicates that the sentence continues on the next page with Juno's plan to delay the Trojans even if she cannot stop them permanently.</meta>

<summary>This page analyzes the rhetorical structure of Juno's angry monologue in Virgil's Aeneid, demonstrating how she uses exclamation, irony, and logical arguments to express divine fury. The author highlights how a truly emotional speech should "fluctuate" through different rhetorical figures to mimic the instability of anger.</summary>

# BOOK IV

<page-num>363</page-num>
<header>BOOK IV</header>

...content to hinder them:
> If I cannot bend the gods above, I will stir the Underworld. <note>original: "Flectere si nequeo superos, Acheronta mouebo." *Aeneid* 7.312. Juno, frustrated that the celestial gods will not stop Aeneas, famously vows to summon the powers of Hell (Acheron).</note>
> It will not be granted to me, let it be so, to bar him from the Latin kingdoms,
> But I may drag it out, and add delays to such great matters.
> But I may cut down the peoples of both kings. <note>original: "Non dabitur regnis, esto, prohibere Latinis, / At trahere, atq; moras tantis licet addere rebus. / At licet amborum populos excindere regum." Juno admits she cannot change destiny, but she can cause carnage in the meantime.</note>

After these things, at the very end, as angry people are prone to do, she utters a curse:
> With Trojan and Rutulian blood you shall be dowered, O maiden. <note>original: "Sanguine Troiano, & Rutulo dotabere uirgo." Juno predicts that the marriage between Aeneas and Lavinia will result in a bloody war between their peoples.</note>

And immediately she follows with a fitting argument based on a similar case from the past:
> —Nor was Cisseus’ daughter the only one pregnant with a torch to bring forth wedding fires. <note>original: "—Nec face tantum / Cysseïs prægnans ignes enixa iugales." Hecuba, daughter of Cisseus, dreamed she gave birth to a torch (Paris) who burned Troy. Juno suggests Lavinia’s marriage will be equally destructive.</note>

You see how often she changed her style of speech and varied it with frequent rhetorical figures: because anger, which is a "brief madness," cannot maintain a single consistent thought while speaking. Nor are there lacking in the same poet speeches that stir up <term>misericordia</term> <note>A rhetorical term for the appeal to pity or mercy.</note>. For example, Turnus speaking to his sister Juturna:
> Was it so you might see the cruel death of your wretched brother? <note>original: "An miseri fratris letum ut crudele uideres?" *Aeneid* 12.636.</note>

And the same character, when he increases the odium of his friends being killed on his behalf:
> I myself saw Muranus before my very eyes, calling me with his voice. <note>original: "Vidi oculos ante ipse meos me uoce uocãtẽ Muranum." *Aeneid* 12.638. Muranus was a close comrade of the hero Turnus.</note>

And the same, when he makes his own fortune appear pitiable so that he might be spared as a defeated man:
> —You have conquered, and the Ausonians have seen me, defeated, stretching out my hands. <note>original: "—Vicisti, & uictum tendere palmas / Ausonij uidere." *Aeneid* 12.936. The Ausonians were the ancient inhabitants of Italy.</note>
The same character:
> Those whom I least wanted. <note>original: "Quos minime uellem."</note>

And the prayers of others begging for their lives:
> By you, by the parents who bore such a child as you. <note>original: "Per te, per qui te talem genuere parentes." *Aeneid* 10.597. A common rhetorical appeal to a conqueror’s own family ties.</note> and similar passages.

<term>Pathos</term> <note>The quality in a work of art or speech that stirs up emotions of pity, sympathy, or sorrow.</note> can be derived from age, from fortune, from weakness, from place, or from time.

### CHAPTER III

<margin>Pathos derived from age.</margin>
Now let us speak of the condition of <term>pathos</term>, whether it resides in age, or in physical weakness, and the other factors that follow. Virgil elegantly observed this, so that he might stir the pathos of pity from every stage of life.

*While I drag out a life in the woods among the desert dens and homes of wild beasts.* <note>original: "Cùm uitam in ſyluis inter deſerta ferarum / Luſtra, domosq; traho." *Aeneid* 3.646–647. Spoken by Achaemenides, who was abandoned in the land of the Cyclopes.</note> And:

And this is expressed excellently and briefly:
*Thrice he had dragged Hector around the walls of Troy.* <note>original: "Ter circum Iliacos raptauerat Hectora muros." *Aeneid* 1.483.</note>
"Of Troy" (*Iliacos*), meaning the walls of his own fatherland, which he himself had defended, and for which he had fought effectively for the span of ten years. And also:
*We flee our fatherland.* <note>original: "Nos patriam fugimus." *Eclogues* 1.4.</note> And:

*Dying, he remembers sweet Argos.* <note>original: "Dulces moriens reminiſcitur Argos." *Aeneid* 10.782. Antores, a Greek fighting in Italy, thinks of his distant home as he dies.</note>

Pathos is created by the distance between where a hero was born and where he is buried.</note>

And to show that Agamemnon was killed shamefully, he utilized the "place":
*He perished at the very first threshold.* <note>original: "Prima inter limina dextra Oppetijt." *Aeneid* 11.267. Agamemnon was murdered inside his own palace immediately upon his return from the war.</note> And:
*Within his father's walls, and amidst the safety of homes.* <note>original: "Mœnibus in patrijs, atq; inter tuta domorum."</note>

*And through the houses, and the sacred thresholds of the gods.* <note>original: "Perq; domos, & relligioſa Deorum Limina." *Aeneid* 2.764.</note>

Does a sacred place make a scene more pitiable? 
> *Look, the virgin daughter of Priam, Cassandra, was being dragged from the temple and sanctuary of Minerva with her hair disheveled.* <note>original: "Ecce trahebatur passis Priameïa uirgo / Crinibus à tēplo Cassandra, adytisq́; Mineruae." From Virgil’s *Aeneid*, 2.403–404. The horror is magnified because she is a priestess being seized in a holy place.</note>
And elsewhere:
> *—He fell before the altar of the goddess powerful in arms.* <note>original: "Diuæ armipotentis ad aram Procubuit." *Aeneid* 2.425. This describes the death of a warrior at the very feet of Minerva's statue.</note>

And Andromache, when she spoke of the death of Pyrrhus, expressed the shamefulness of the killer by highlighting the location:
> *He caught him off guard and butchered him at his father's altars.* <note>original: "Excipit incautum, patriasq́; obtruncat ad aras." *Aeneid* 3.332. The cruelty is doubled because the victim is killed where his father was also slain.</note>

And Venus, when she indignantly complains to Neptune about Aeneas being tossed about on the sea by Juno’s rage, makes a point about the location:
> *Did she dare this in your own realms?* <note>original: "In regnis hoc ausa tuis?" *Aeneid* 5.789. Venus argues that Juno’s interference in the ocean is an insult to Neptune’s sovereign territory.</note>

Virgil often creates <term>pathos</term> <note>A rhetorical technique used to stir deep emotions, especially pity or sorrow, in the audience.</note> from the timing or the duration of an event: 
*—Before they had tasted the fodder of Troy or drunk from the Xanthus.* <note>original: "Priusquàm / Pabula gustassent Troiæ, Xanthumq́; bibissent." *Aeneid* 1.472–473. This refers to the horses of Rhesus; if they had eaten or drunk in Troy, the city could not have fallen. The tragedy is in how close they were to safety.</note>

And Orpheus, made pitiable by his long-lasting grief:
> *They say he wept for seven whole months in a row, beneath a towering cliff by the waters of the lonely Strymon.* <note>original: "Septem illum totos perhibent ex ordine menses, / Rupe sub aëria, deserti ad Strimonis undam Fleuisse." From Virgil’s *Georgics* 4.507–509. The duration of seven months emphasizes the depth of his loss.</note>

And Palinurus: *Scarcely on the fourth light did I catch sight of Italy.* <note>original: "Vix lumine quarto Prospexi Italiam." *Aeneid* 6.356. Palinurus survived three days at sea only to be killed just as he reached the shore.</note> And Achaemenides: 
*Now for the third time the horns of the moon are filling with light.* <note>original: "Tertia iam Lunæ se cornua lumine complent." *Aeneid* 3.645. Meaning he has been hiding in terror for three months.</note> And:
<margin>* summer</margin>
*The seventh summer since the fall of Troy is now turning.* <note>original: "Septima post Troiæ excidium iam uertitur ætas." *Aeneid* 1.755. The margin note suggests "æstas" (summer) is the correct reading over "ætas" (age/time).</note>

### Pathos from cause, manner, and material. CHAPTER IV.

<margin>* creates</margin>
In his work, <term>pathos</term> is frequently derived from the "cause." In truth, a cause often *creates* <note>The Latin text notes "efficit" (effects/brings about), while the margin suggests "conficit" (completes/makes).</note> the sense that a matter is either atrocious or pitiable. For example, Cicero in his speech against Verres says: *“He was asked for money by the parents just for the burial of those he had killed in prison.”* <note>From Cicero's *In Verrem* 2.5.118. The "cause" of the payment—merely to bury a murdered child—makes Verres' greed appear monstrous.</note> It was not so much the demanding of money that was shameful, but the fact that it was demanded for this specific cause. And when Demosthenes complains that someone was 
<margin>* by Midias</margin>
trapped by malice, <note>Referring to Demosthenes' oration *Against Midias*.</note> he increases the indignation through the cause: *“He circumvented,” he says, “the arbitrator who had judged between me and him with total integrity.”* Therefore, Virgil also frequently drew out emotion from this source. *“Galesus,” he says, “is killed in the battle line.”* <note>*Aeneid* 7.535.</note> This in itself is not especially worthy of pity in a time of war, but he added the cause:

### BOOK IV.

->While he offers himself as a mediator for peace,<-
->The unhappy man is laid low.<-
<note>original: "Dum paci medium se offert. / Sternitur infelix." From Virgil’s *Aeneid*, 2.426. This describes the death of Coroebus, a young man who dies while trying to intervene during the fall of Troy.</note>

The same author in another place then adds a pitiable cause:
->By another's wound:<- <note>original: "Alieno uulnere". From *Aeneid* 10.781. The tragedy here is that the victim, Antores, was struck by a spear intended for someone else; his death is an accidental waste.</note> 
that is, when the weapon had been sent against someone else. And when he wished to show that Palamedes was unworthily slain:
> —Whom the Greeks, through a false charge of treason, 
> though innocent, by unspeakable testimony, because he forbade the wars, 
> sent down to death.
<note>original: "Quem falsa sub proditione Pelasgi / Infontem, infando indicio, quia bella uetabat, / Demisere neci." From *Aeneid* 2.82–84. Palamedes was a Greek hero framed by Ulysses with planted evidence of bribery; his "cause" for being killed was his desire for peace.</note>

And Aeneas, in order to show the magnitude of his own fear, established the cause well:
> —Fearing equally for both his companion and his burden.
<note>original: "Et pariter comitiq́, oneriq́; timentem." *Aeneid* 2.729. As Aeneas flees the burning city, he is not afraid for himself, but for his father Anchises (the burden) and his son Ascanius (the companion).</note>

What of <term>Iapyx</term>? <note>In the *Aeneid*, Iapyx was a healer and a favorite of Apollo.</note> To live without glory, having set aside all other skills (as the poet says), what kind of cause is presented?
> So that he might prolong the life of his dying parent.
<note>original: "Ille ut depositi proferret fata parentis." *Aeneid* 12.395. Iapyx chose the "silent art" of medicine over more prestigious gifts like prophecy or archery specifically to save his father’s life.</note>

From the same category is: *Your piety deceives you, unwary one.* <note>original: "Fallit te incautum pietas tua." *Aeneid* 10.812. This is spoken to Lausus as he is killed by Aeneas; his "cause" of death was his devoted attempt to protect his father, Mezentius.</note> For this cause made him pitiable even to his enemies. But when Aeneas urges that the slain be buried, what cause does he propose?
> —Those who have won this homeland for us with their own blood.
<note>original: "Qui sanguine nobis Hanc patriam peperere suo." *Aeneid* 11.24–25.</note>

Furthermore, indignation is also demonstrated by the cause, as in this passage:
> Groaning much at the ignominy and the blows of the proud 
> victor, then the loves he lost unavenged.
<note>original: "Multa gemens, ignominiam, plagasq́; superbi / Victoris, tum quos amisit inultus amores." From Virgil’s *Georgics* 3.226–227, describing a bull that has lost a fight for a mate. The cause of his sorrow is the shame of defeat and the loss of his love.</note>

And this passage draws from the cause to show the effect of indignation:
> —Does that grief touch only the sons of Atreus? 
> Is it permitted for Mycenae alone to take up arms? 
<note>original: "An solus tangit Atridas / Iste dolor? solisq́; licet capere arma Mycenis?" *Aeneid* 9.138–139. Turnus argues that the Italians have as much "cause" to fight for their brides as the Greeks (the sons of Atreus) did at Troy.</note>
And that:
> —But you, Alban, should have stood by your word. 
<note>original: "At tu dictis Albane maneres." *Aeneid* 8.643. A reference to Mettius Fufetius, an Alban leader who betrayed his alliance with Rome; his betrayal is the "cause" for his gruesome punishment.</note>
And all those:
> This one sold his country for gold.
> And those slain on account of adultery.
> Nor did they set aside a portion for their own kin.
<note>original: "Vendidit hic auro patriam... Quiq́; ob adulterium cæsi... Nec partem posuere suis." *Aeneid* 6.621–623. These are descriptions of souls in the underworld; their suffering is justified by the "cause" of their crimes.</note>

To stir <term>pathos</term>, <note>A rhetorical technique used to evoke pity or sadness.</note> he did not omit those two topics which rhetoricians call "from the manner" and "from the matter." "Manner" is when I describe how someone died...

—he kills, whether openly or secretly. "Matter" is when I say: "by the sword" or "by poison." Regarding the "manner," Demosthenes stirs up resentment against Midias <note>Demosthenes was a famous Greek orator; his speech *Against Midias* concerns an assault he suffered while organizing a festival.</note> by saying he was struck by a *cothurnus* <note>a thick-soled boot worn by tragic actors; the detail of being hit by a "theatrical boot" adds to the indignity of the assault.</note>. <note>original: "Capulo tenus abdidit ensem." From *Aeneid* 2.553.</note>

<note>original: "Rostroq; immanis uultur adunco / Immortale iecur tondens." From *Aeneid* 6.597. This describes the punishment of the giant Tityos in the underworld.</note>

<note>original: "Quos super atra silex iamiam lapsura cadenti / Imminet assimilis." From *Aeneid* 6.601–602.</note>

<margin>From the matter.</margin> Furthermore, among rhetoricians, the "matter" or means also moves the <term>pathos</term> <note>the quality in a work of art that stirs up emotions of pity, sorrow, or anger.</note>, as when Cicero complains of a fire being made from green wood, and there 
<margin>* killed</margin> he kills the man enclosed within the smoke. For this is from the "matter," since in this case he used smoke as the "matter" for killing, just as another might use a sword or another poison; and therefore a very sharp <term>pathos</term> was moved by this. He does the same when he complains of a Roman citizen being beaten with rods. You will find the same in Virgil:
> But the omnipotent father hurled his bolt through the thick clouds, 
> not he with torches or smoky fire-brands.

Pathos arises among the orators <note>original: "apud rethores pathos nascitur"</note> in various ways, and we have shown that Virgil <note>The text refers to him by his cognomen, Maro.</note> followed their practice. But sometimes Virgil uses two or more combined circumstances in a single instance to increase the emotional impact. For example, regarding Turnus <note>The primary antagonist of the *Aeneid*.</note>, he draws pathos from his age:

> —Pity a father in his old age. 
<note>original: "Miserere parentis Longæui." From *Aeneid* 12.932.</note> 
And from his location:
> —Whom now his native Ardea, far away, separates from him in his sorrow. 
<note>original: "Quem nunc mœstum patria Ardea longe Diuidit." From *Aeneid* 7.411–412.</note>

And regarding Cassandra <note>The Trojan princess and prophetess who was cursed never to be believed.</note>, he draws from the manner of the act: 
> —Behold, she was being dragged. 
<note>original: "Ecce trahebatur." From *Aeneid* 2.403.</note> 
From her physical state: 
> —The maiden daughter of Priam with disheveled hair. 
<note>original: "Passis Priameïa uirgo Crinibus." From *Aeneid* 2.403–404.</note> 
From the location: 
> —From the temple and inner sanctuaries of Minerva. 
<note>original: "A' templo, adytisq́; Mineruæ." From *Aeneid* 2.404.</note>

And regarding Agamemnon <note>The leader of the Greek forces in the Trojan War, murdered upon his return home.</note>, he draws from his homeland: 
> —The Mycenaean himself. 
<note>original: "Ipse Mycenæus." From *Aeneid* 11.266.</note> 
From his status: 
> —Leader of the great Achaeans. 
<note>original: "Magnorum ductor Achiuûm." From *Aeneid* 11.267.</note> 
From the necessity of his fate: 
> —The unspeakable crime of his wife. 
<note>original: "Coniugis infandum." From *Aeneid* 11.267–268.</note> 
From the location: 
> —At the very threshold, on the right. 
<note>original: "Prima inter limina dextra." From *Aeneid* 11.267.</note>

Pathos is also often moved silently, as if by a definition <term>definition (definitio): a rhetorical device where the meaning of a term is implied through context rather than stated directly</term>. This occurs when a matter that evokes pity is not stated clearly but is given to be understood. For instance, when Mezentius <note>An exiled king and ally of Turnus; he is portrayed as a "scorner of the gods" but suffers deeply over the death of his son, Lausus.</note> says:

> —Now the wound is driven deep. 
<note>original: "Nunc altè uulnus adactum." From *Aeneid* 10.850.</note>

For what else is to be understood from this, except that losing a son is a "deep wound"? And again, the same character says:

> —This was the only way you could destroy me. 
<note>original: "Hæc uia sola fuit, qua perdere posses." From *Aeneid* 10.879.</note>

But here, too, we must obviously understand "to be destroyed" as meaning "to lose a son." And when Juturna <note>A water nymph and the sister of Turnus; she was granted immortality by Jupiter but laments it because she must watch her brother die.</note> complains that she is forbidden from helping her brother:

> —Am I immortal? 
<note>original: "Immortalis ego." From *Aeneid* 12.882.</note>

For what follows? It is not true "immortality" to live in grief. These instances, as I have said, have the force of a definition and are elegantly introduced by the poet.

## *Pathos through Similarity.*

### CHAPTER V.

There are also these "topics" <term>topics (loci): standard categories or themes used by orators to find arguments or emotional appeals</term> in the rhetorical art for moving pathos, which are said to concern the "circumstances of the matter" and are very useful for stirring the emotions. The first of these is "from similarity." There are three types of this: the example, the parable, and the image. In Greek:

->*Example, comparison, image.*<- <note>original: "παράδειγμα, παραβολή, εἰκών"</note>

->From example, Virgil writes:<-

<margin>Pathos from example.</margin>
> *If Orpheus could summon the spirits of his wife,* <note>original: "Si potuit manes accersere coniugis Orpheûs"</note>
> *relying on his Thracian lyre and tuneful strings;*
> *if Pollux redeemed his brother by alternating death.* <note>Pollux, being immortal, shared his life with his mortal brother Castor, each spending half their time in the underworld.</note>
> *—Why mention Theseus? Why the great Hercules?* <note>original: "Quid Thesea? magnum Quid memorem Alciden?" Hercules is often called Alcides after his grandfather Alcaeus.</note>
> *Antenor could escape from the midst of the Greeks, etc.*

For all these examples move the listener to mercy, since it seems unfair to be denied what has been granted to others. Next, see how he increases the sense of indignation <note>The rhetorical term *inuidia* here refers to a sense of injustice or ill-will regarding the disparity of treatment.</note>:

> *If Orpheus could summon the spirits of his wife.*

You have a different case here: there it was the spirits of a wife, here it is the spirits of a father; there it was to summon them back, here it is merely to see them.

> *Relying on his Thracian lyre,*

<margin>* the subject matter</margin>
Here he made light of <note>original: "irrisit." The author suggests Virgil uses the "Thracian lyre" as a modest instrument to show that if such a small thing worked for Orpheus, Aeneas’s greater cause deserves even more pity.</note> his pity.

> *If Pollux redeemed his brother by alternating death,*
> *And goes and returns along the path so often.*

This now pertains to the manner of the act. For it is a greater thing to go often than to go only once.

> *—Why mention Theseus? Why the great*
> *Hercules?*

Here, because of their distinguished status, he had nothing to diminish or increase; instead, he boasts that the greatness which shone in them is shared by him:

> *—And my lineage is also from supreme Jove.*

There is a similar instance arising from indignation:

> *What indeed (says Juno)*
> *could Pallas burn the fleet of the Argives?* <note>Juno is complaining that Pallas Athena was allowed to destroy an entire fleet, while she, the queen of the gods, is thwarted by the Trojans.</note>

Now this is a greater thing: a victorious fleet, rather than the remnants of those fleeing. Then she diminishes the cause:

> *On account of the crime and madness of one man, Ajax son of Oileus.*

See how she diminished it by calling it a "crime" <note>The Latin *noxa* is used here as a term for a lighter fault or offense.</note>, which is the name for a minor offense: and

<margin>From comparison.</margin>
Indeed, the <term>comparison</term> <note>original: "parabola." In rhetoric, a comparison or simile used to illustrate a point through resemblance.</note>, since this is more suited to the poet, very frequently stirs <term>pathos</term> <note>The emotional appeal or power of a work to evoke pity or sorrow.</note>, whether the poet wishes to introduce a pitiable character or an angry one. A pitiable one like this:
> *Just as the grieving nightingale under the poplar’s shade.* <note>original: "Qualis populea mœrens philomela ſub umbra." (Georgics 4.511).</note>

> \* *Just as when a wounded bull flees the altar, bellowing.* <note>original: "Mugitus ueluti fugit cùm faucius aram Taurus." (Aeneid 2.223).</note>

<margin>\* In Virgil himself: "A bellowing, such as when he flees."</margin>
And whoever seeks will find many more similar things. <margin>From the image.</margin> Also the <term>image</term> <note>original: "imago." Here referring to *iconismus*, a vivid physical description of a person or creature.</note>, which is the third part of the category of similarity, is suitable for moving the emotions. This occurs when either the form of an absent body is described, or one that does not exist at all is imagined. Virgil did both elegantly. The former regarding Ascanius:
> *O, the only remaining image of my Astyanax to me!*
> *Just so he carried his eyes, his hands, his face.* <note>original: "O mihi ſola mei ſuper Aſtyanactis imago, / Sic oculos, ſic ille manus, ſic ora ferebat." (Aeneid 3.489-490). Andromache speaks to Ascanius, who reminds her of her dead son.</note>

But the first form provides <term>pity</term> <note>original Greek: "οἶκτον" (oikton).</note>, while this one provides <term>indignation</term> <note>original Greek: "δείνωσιν" (deinosin), referring to a rhetorical heightening of the horror or gravity of a subject.</note>; that is, the first—

### Pathos from the Greater and the Lesser. CHAPTER VI.

We have spoken of pathos from comparison; now let us speak of <term>pathos</term> placed by the poet from the "lesser." Truly, when something is proposed which is great in itself, and then it is shown to be less than that which we wish to heighten, an infinite pity is undoubtedly moved. As in that passage:
> *O happy alone before all others, daughter of Priam,*
> *ordered to die at the enemy's tomb, beneath the high walls of Troy.* <note>original: "O' felix una ante alias Priameia uirgo, / Hostilem ad tumulum, Troiæ sub mœnibus altis, / Iussa mori." (Aeneid 3.321-323). Andromache refers to Polyxena, who was sacrificed by the Greeks.</note>

First, because he says "happy," he made a comparison to his own state: then he placed it by location, "at the enemy’s tomb." And by manner, which is no less bitter, "ordered to die." Thus these things are to be understood: "although at the enemy's tomb, although ordered to die, she is nonetheless happier than I, because she did not endure any lots <note>Refers to the drawing of lots for the distribution of female Trojan captives as slaves.</note> of slavery." Similar also is that:
> *— O three and four times blessed!* <note>original: "O' terq; quaterq; beati." (Aeneid 1.94). Aeneas laments that those who died at Troy were luckier than he, who faces a storm at sea.</note>

And what he says of Pasiphaë:
> *The daughters of Proetus filled the fields with false lowing.* <note>original: "Prœtides implerunt falsis mugitibus agros." (Eclogues 6.48). The daughters of King Proetus were punished with a madness that made them believe they were cows.</note>

Then, to show this was "lesser":
> *Yet none of them followed such shameful unions*
> *with cattle.* <note>original: "At non tam turpes pecudum tamen ulla secuta est / Concubitus." (Eclogues 6.49-50). Virgil argues that Pasiphaë’s actual lust for a bull was worse than the Proetides' delusion.</note>

What of this? Is it not vehemently emotional, from the "lesser"?
> *Neither the prophet Helenus, when he warned of many horrors,*
> *nor the dread Celæno, foretold these griefs to me.* <note>original: "Nec uates Helenus, cùm multa horrenda moneret, / Hos mihi prædixit luctus: non dira Celæno." (Aeneid 3.712-713). Aeneas mourns the death of his father, Anchises, noting it was a sorrow greater than even the worst prophecies of the Harpy Celæno.</note>
