*What do we understand here, except that everything they had suffered seemed less to them than their father's death?* <note>original: "Quid hic intelligimus, nisi omnia, quæ passus erat, minora illis uisa, quàm patris mortem?" The author refers to a moment in epic poetry where a personal loss outweighs all previous collective hardships.</note>

*Some have denied that a matter can be magnified from something already "greater." But Virgil skillfully introduced this regarding Dido:*
> *Not otherwise than if, the enemy having been let in, all*
> *Carthage or ancient Tyre were falling.* <note>original: "Non aliter, quàm si immissus ruat hostibus omnis / Carthago, aut antiqua Tyrus." (Aeneid 4.669-671). Virgil compares the lamentation for Dido's suicide to the destruction of an entire civilization.</note>

*For he said that the grief from one death was no less than if the entire city—which would undoubtedly be a greater event—had fallen. And Homer did the same:* <note>original: "ὡς εἰ ἅπασα ἴλιος ὀφρυόεσσα πυρὶ σμήχοιτο κατ’ ἄκρης." (Iliad 22.410-411).</note> *as if all beetling Troy were smoldering in fire from its summit. Among orators, that topic is also suitable for moving <term>pathos</term>, which is called "beyond expectation" [praeter spem]. Virgil employed this frequently:*
> *We, your offspring, to whom you promised the citadel of heaven.* <note>original: "Nos tua progenies, cæli quibus annuis arcem." (Aeneid 1.250). Venus complains to Jupiter that the suffering of the Trojans is unexpected, given his divine promise of glory.</note>

*And so forth. And Dido:*
> *If I was able to foresee such great grief,*
> *I shall also be able to endure it, sister. Aeneas concerning Evander:*
> *And now indeed, greatly deceived by empty hope,*
> *perhaps he even makes vows. And that other passage: —A stranger to our land*
> *(which we never feared), so that the possessor of our little field*
> *should say, "These things are mine; move on, old settlers."* <note>original: "Aduena nostri / (Quod nunquam ueriti sumus) ut possessor agelli / Diceret, hæc mea sunt, ueteres migrate coloni." (Eclogues 9.2-4). This refers to the shock of farmers losing their land to veterans.</note>

*I find, however, that someone can move pathos from that which they have already hoped for, as Evander does:*
> *I was not unaware how much influence new glory in arms,*
> *and the sweetest honor, can have.* <note>original: "Haud ignarus eram, quantum noua gloria in armis, / Et prædulce decus." (Aeneid 11.154-155). Evander reflects on his son's fatal pursuit of glory, which he had anticipated but which still brings pain.</note>

<margin>From the similarity of suffering.</margin>
*Orators call it <term>homoiopatheia</term> <note>From the Greek 'homoios' (similar) and 'pathos' (suffering); a rhetorical device where a character recognizes their own pain in another's situation.</note> whenever <term>pathos</term> arises from a similarity of suffering, as in Virgil:*
> *Your father Anchises was such a man to you as well. and,*
> *The image of fatherly devotion touched him. and,*
> *The image of his dear father came to mind. And Dido:*
> *A similar fortune has willed that I too, tossed through many*
> *hardships, should at last settle in this land.* <note>original: "Me quoq; per multos similis fortuna labores / Iactatam, hac demum uoluit consistere terra." (Aeneid 1.628-629). Dido welcomes the Trojans by identifying with their exile.</note>

<margin>From speech addressed to inanimate objects.</margin>
There is also that technique for stirring emotion (<term>pathos</term> <note>the quality in a work of art that evokes pity or sadness</note>), in which speech is directed either to inanimate objects or to those that are mute—a device that orators frequently employ. Virgil handled both very skillfully and with great emotional power (<term>pathetically</term> <note>In this rhetorical context, "pathetic" refers to the ability to evoke deep emotion or "pathos," rather than its modern negative connotation.</note>), such as when Dido says:
> Sweet relics, while the fates and God allowed. <note>original: "Dulces exuuiæ, dum fata, Deusq; sinebant" (Aeneid 4.651). Dido addresses the clothing and bed left behind by Aeneas before her suicide.</note>
Or when Turnus says:
> —And you, best Earth, hold the iron fast. <note>original: "Tuq; optima ferrum Terra tene" (Aeneid 12.777). Turnus prays to the earth to keep Aeneas’s spear stuck so he cannot retrieve it.</note>
And the same poet elsewhere:
> —Now, O spear that never failed my calls... &c. <note>original: "Nunc ô nunquam frustrata uocatus Hasta meos" (Aeneid 10.773). Mezentius speaks to his weapon as if it were a conscious ally.</note>
> Rhoebus, we have lived a long time, if anything is long for mortals. <note>original: "Rhebe diu, res si qua diu mortalibus ulla est, Viximus" (Aeneid 10.861). The warrior Mezentius addresses his horse, Rhoebus, before their final battle.</note>

<margin>From hesitation.</margin>
Hesitation also creates <term>pathos</term> among orators; the Greeks call this <term>aporia</term> <note>original: ἀπόρησιν; a rhetorical device where the speaker expresses doubt or a sense of being at a loss for words or actions</note>. For it is characteristic of one who is grieving or angry to doubt what to do next.
> See, what do I do? Shall I, mocked, again try my former suitors? <note>original: "En quid ago? rursus'ne procos irrisa priores Experiar?" (Aeneid 4.534-5). Dido debates her options after being abandoned.</note>
And that regarding Orpheus:
> What should he do? Where should he go, his wife twice snatched away? <note>original: "Quid faceret? quò se rapta bis coniuge ferret?" (Georgics 4.504). Describing Orpheus's despair after losing Eurydice a second time.</note>
And regarding Nisus:
> What should he do? By what force, by what weapons should he dare to rescue the youth? <note>original: "Quid faciat? qua ui iuuenum, quibus audeat armis Eripere?" (Aeneid 9.399-400). Nisus sees his friend Euryalus captured and feels helpless.</note>
And Anna is moved:
> What shall I, deserted, first complain of? Should it be the companion, my sister...? &c. <note>original: "Quid primū deserta querar? comitem'ne sororē" (Aeneid 4.677-8). Anna's lament upon finding her sister Dido dying.</note>

<margin>From witnessing.</margin>
The witnessing (<term>attestatio</term> <note>vividly recounting a scene as if observed firsthand to make the listener feel present</note>) of a sight also stirs emotion among rhetoricians. Virgil carries this out as follows:
> When he saw the head of snowy Pallas supported and his face, and the wound open in his smooth chest. <note>original: "Ipse caput niuei fultum Pallantis & ora Vt uidit, leuiq; patens in pectore uulnus" (Aeneid 11.39-40). Aeneas looks upon the body of his fallen young ally.</note>
And that:
> And blood filled her lap. <note>original: "Impleuitq; sinum sanguis" (Aeneid 4.685).</note>
And:
> —And dying, he rolls in his own blood. <note>original: "Moriensq; suo se in sanguine uersat" (Aeneid 9.333).</note>
And:
> He sees the cruel mother showing the wounds of her son. <note>original: "Crudelis nati monstrantem uulnera cernit."</note>
And:
> The pale faces of men hung with grim gore. <note>original: "Ora uirūm tristi pendebant pallida tabo" (Aeneid 8.197). Describing the gruesome trophies in the cave of the giant Cacus.</note>
And:
> Euryalus rolls in death, and blood goes through his beautiful limbs. <note>original: "Voluitur Euryalus leto, pulchrosq; per artus It cruor" (Aeneid 9.433-4).</note>
And:

*I myself saw two of our number, when their bodies...* <note>original: "Vidi egomet duo de numero cùm corpora nostro." From Aeneid 3.623, describing the Cyclops seizing Odysseus’s men.</note>

<margin>Through hyperbole.</margin>
The use of <term>hyperbole</term> <note>rhetorical exaggeration used for emphasis</note>—that is, excess—creates <term>pathos</term> <note>the quality that evokes pity or sadness</note>: through this, either anger or mercy is expressed. Anger is expressed, for instance, when we might say: "He ought to have died a thousand times," as found in Virgil:
> *I myself would have given my guilty life through every kind of death.* <note>original: "Omnes per mortes animam sontem ipse dedissem." Aeneid 10.854. King Mezentius expresses deep regret and self-loathing over his son's death.</note>

Pity is expressed when he says:
> *Daphnis, they say even the Carthaginian lions groaned at your death.* <note>original: "Daphni tuum Pœnos etiam ingemuisse leones Interitum." Eclogues 5.27. An exaggerated image of nature mourning a beloved youth.</note>

Beyond these, an emotional effect (<term>pathos</term>) of an amorous or other kind can also arise from excess:
> *If this light is not already longer to me than a whole year.* <note>original: "Si mihi non hæc lux toto iam longior anno est." Catullus 66.3; though quoting Virgil, the author often draws on other poets to illustrate these shared rhetorical figures.</note>

And these separate examples:
> — *That Turnus be allowed to burn the seas before the sacred pines.* <note>original: "Maria antè exurere Turno, Quàm sacras dabitur pinus." Aeneid 9.115. Referring to the transformation of Aeneas’s ships into sea nymphs to save them from fire.</note>
> — *Not even if he should pour the earth into the waves.* <note>original: "Non si tellurem effundat in undas." Aeneid 12.204. Latinus swearing an unbreakable oath by the elements.</note>

<margin>Through exclamation.</margin>
Exclamation, which is called <term>ekphonesis</term> <note>from the Greek ἐκφώνησις, an emotional outcry</note> by the Greeks, stirs the emotions. This is done sometimes from the persona of the poet himself, and sometimes from the persona of the character he brings in to speak. From the poet’s own persona, we find:
> *Mantua, alas, too near to wretched Cremona!* <note>original: "Mantua uæ miseræ nimium uicina Cremonæ." Eclogues 9.28. Virgil laments the land confiscations that affected his home region.</note>
> *Unhappy man! However posterity shall report those deeds.* <note>original: "Infelix, utcunq; ferent ea fata nepotes." Aeneid 6.822. Referring to Brutus, who executed his own sons for the sake of the Republic.</note>
> *Love was your crime.* <note>original: "Crimen amor uestrum." Aeneid 10.188.</note> And other similar examples.

But from the persona of another character:
> — *May the gods bring this back upon his own head and his race.* <note>original: "Dij capiti ipsius,generiq; referuent." Aeneid 8.484. Evander's curse upon the tyrant Mezentius.</note>
> *O gods, repay the Greeks with such things, if with a pious mouth I demand punishment.* <note>original: "Dij talia Graijs Instaurate, pio si pœnas ore reposco." Aeneid 2.190. Sinon, the Greek spy, pretending to curse his own people.</note>
> *O gods, ward off such a plague from the lands.* <note>original: "Dij talem terris auertite pestem." Aeneid 3.620. A prayer against the horror of the Cyclops.</note>

The opposite of this figure is <term>aposiopesis</term> <note>from the Greek ἀποσιώπησις</note>, which is silence. For just as in the previous figure we say certain things by exclaiming, here we withdraw certain things by keeping silent, which the listener can nevertheless understand. This is especially fitting for those who are angry, such as Neptune:

> *Whom I—! But it is better to calm the troubled waves.* <note>original: "Quos ego. sed motos præstat componere fluctus." From Aeneid 1.135. This is a famous example of aposiopesis, where Neptune stops mid-threat to focus on restoring order.</note>
And *Mnestheus:* —*Nor do I strive to win.*
> *Although oh—! But let them conquer, to whom you, Neptune, have granted this.* <note>original: "Nec uincere certo. Quanquã ô. sed superẽt..." From Aeneid 5.195-6. Mnestheus breaks off his wish for victory, showing humble resignation.</note>
And *Turnus:*
> *Although—oh, if only some of our accustomed courage were present!* <note>original: "Quanquam. ô si solitæ quicquam uirtutis adesset." From Aeneid 11.415.</note>
And in the *Bucolics:*
> *We know—while the he-goats looked askance—and in what shrine*
> *(but the easy-going Nymphs only laughed)...* <note>original: "Nouimus, & qui te transuersa tuentibus hircis..." From Eclogues 3.8-9. A playful use of breaking off a sentence to imply a scandalous secret.</note>
But pity is also stirred by this figure through *Sinon:*
> —*Until, with Calchas as the servant—*
> *But why do I revolve these unwelcome things in vain?* <note>original: "Donec Calchante ministro. Sed quid ego hæc..." From Aeneid 2.100-101. Sinon, the Greek spy, uses a calculated pause to manipulate the Trojans' emotions.</note>
Emotion (<term>pathos</term>) <note>the quality in a work of art that evokes pity or sadness</note> also arises from repetition, which the Greeks call <term>epanaphora</term> <note>original: ἐπαναφωρὰν; a rhetorical device where the same word or phrase is repeated at the beginning of successive clauses</note>, when sentences begin with the same names.
Hence *Virgil:*
> —*The voice itself and the cold tongue called:*
> *“Eurydice!”—Ah, poor Eurydice!—as the soul fled;*
> *the riverbanks echoed “Eurydice!” all along the stream.* <note>original: "Eurydicen uox ipsa & frigida lingua..." From Georgics 4.525-527, describing the death of Orpheus.</note> And this:
> *Of you, sweet spouse, of you alone on the lonely shore,*
> *of you at the coming of the day, of you at its departure, he sang.* <note>original: "Te dulcis coniux..." From Georgics 4.465-466.</note> And this:
> *For you the grove of Angitia, for you the Fucinus with its glassy wave,*
> *for you the liquid lakes wept.* <note>original: "Te nemus Angitiæ..." From Aeneid 7.759-760, mourning the death of the healer Umbro.</note>
<term>Epitimesis</term> <note>original: ἐπιτίμησις; a rhetorical figure consisting of a sharp rebuke or reproach</note>, which is a scolding, also contains emotion: that is, when we refute things presented with the same words:
> *Aeneas is away in ignorance; let him be away in ignorance!* <note>original: "Aeneas ignarus abest, ignarus & absit." From Aeneid 10.85. Juno uses this repetition to mock Venus's excuses.</note>

### If for no other reasons, Virgil is certainly to be preferred over Cicero in this: that while the latter excelled in only one, the former excelled in all styles of speaking; concerning the four types of speaking and the dual style. CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'P' containing an image of a lion or wolf in a garden setting.</image-desc>
After these things, when Eusebius had rested for a short while, everyone declared with a harmonious murmur that Virgil should be considered no less an orator than a poet: in whom both such great discipline of ornament and such diligent observation of the rhetorical art <note>The art of persuasive speaking or writing</note> were shown. And Avienus said: "I wish you would tell me, best of teachers, if we grant (as is necessary) that Virgil was an orator: if someone now wished to pursue the art of oratory, would he profit more from Virgil or from Cicero?" 

"I see what you are doing," said Eusebius, "what you intend, and where you are trying to pull me: namely, to where I least want to go, to a comparison of Maro <note>original: "Maronis"; refers to Virgil's family name, Publius Vergilius Maro</note> and Tully <note>original: "Tullij"; refers to Marcus Tullius Cicero</note>. For you have asked modestly which of them is more excellent: since necessarily he will contribute the most who himself excels the most. But I wish you would release me from that necessity, for it is a lofty and profound matter: because it is not for us to settle such great disputes between those men, nor would I dare to appear as the author of such an opinion in either direction. This only I will dare to have said: that the eloquence of the Mantuan <note>original: "Mantuani"; refers to Virgil, who was born near Mantua</note> is manifold and multiform, and embraces every kind of speaking. For behold, in your Cicero there is one tenor of eloquence—that abundant, and rushing, and copious. Of orators, however..."

Virgil uses this style when Latinus <note>The king of the Latins in the *Aeneid*</note> gives counsel to Turnus <note>The prince of the Rutuli and Aeneas’s primary rival</note>:
> O youth of outstanding spirit, the more you yourself excel in fierce

The other style is the opposite of this: burning, lofty, and hostile, such as Marcus Antonius <note>Mark Antony, the Roman general known for his forceful oratory</note> used. You will not look for this in Virgil's work in vain:
> —You did not give such 
> words a moment ago: die, and do not let a brother desert a brother.
<note>original: "Haud talia dudum / Dicta dabas: morere, & fratrem ne desere frater." From Aeneid 10.599-600; Aeneas speaks these harsh words to Lucagus and Liger.</note>

Do you see how his eloquence is distinguished by every variety? It seems to me that Virgil—not without a certain foresight by which he prepared himself to be of use to everyone—mixed these styles on purpose. He foresaw this not with a mortal, but with a divine genius; and so, following no other guide than nature itself, the mother of all things, he wove this together like a harmony of discords in music. Indeed, if you look closely at the world itself, you will find a great similarity between that divine work and this poetic work. For just as the eloquence of Maro <note>Virgil's family name, Publius Vergilius Maro</note> is whole and adapted to the character of everyone—now brief, now copious, now dry, now flowery, sometimes all at once, occasionally smooth or rushing—so the earth itself is here lush with crops and meadows, there rough with woods and rocks; here dry with sands, there watered by springs, while part is opened up to the vast sea. Forgive me, and do not think me excessive for comparing Virgil to the nature of things. For it seemed to me I would be falling short of the truth if I were to say only that he had blended the diverse styles of the ten orators <note>The "Attic Canon," a group of ten ancient Greek orators including Demosthenes and Lysias, considered the models of rhetorical excellence</note> who flourished in Attic Athens into this one man.

"You compare a poet from the Mantuan countryside to a god," <note>Evangelus is speaking here, acting as the skeptic in the dialogue.</note> said Evangelus. "I would even assert that he never at all read those Greek rhetoricians whom you mentioned. For how could a man from the Veneto region, born to rustic parents and raised among woods and thickets, have even a slight knowledge of Greek literature?"

And Eustathius <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and one of the more learned participants in the dialogue.</note> replied: "Be careful, Evangelus, lest you believe that any of the Greeks—even their greatest authors—drank so deeply from the well of Greek learning as the diligence of Maro <note>Virgil's family name; the name Maro was often used to refer to him as a master poet.</note> either attained or organized within his own work. For besides that vast abundance of philosophy and astronomy which we discussed above, there are no small number of other things which he drew from the Greeks and sowed into his own poem as if they had been born there."

And Praetextatus <note>Vettius Agorius Praetextatus, the host of the Saturnalia and a prominent Roman statesman.</note> said: "I pray you, Eustathius, that you would be willing to share these things with us as well, as much as your memory, suddenly prompted, may provide." Following Praetextatus, everyone urged Eustathius to begin his discourse. 

He began thus: "Do you think that I am going to speak of those things Virgil took from the Greeks which are already common knowledge? Such as how he made Theocritus <note>A Greek poet from Sicily, the father of pastoral poetry.</note> the model for his pastoral work, or Hesiod <note>An early Greek poet; Virgil's *Georgics* follows his *Works and Days*.</note> for his agricultural work? Or that in the *Georgics* themselves, he took the signs of fair weather and storms from the *Phenomena* of Aratus <note>A Greek didactic poem about the stars and weather.</note>? Or that he transcribed the destruction of Troy—along with his Sinon, the wooden horse, and all the other things that make up the second book—almost word-for-word from Pisander <note>A Greek epic poet whose work is now mostly lost; Virgil used his accounts for the Fall of Troy.</note>? 

Pisander is a poet who stands out among the Greeks for a work that, beginning from the marriage of Jupiter and Juno, gathered all the histories that occurred in all the intervening ages down to Pisander’s own time into a single series, creating one body of work out of the various gaps in time. In this work, among the other histories, the destruction of Troy was related in this manner. By faithfully translating these things, Maro constructed for himself the ruin of the Trojan city. But these and similar things are repeated over and over to schoolboys—"

# THE SATURNALIA

I shall pass over things already well-known. Now indeed, has not the *Aeneid* itself borrowed from Homer first the wanderings <note>original: "errorem"; referring to the travel adventures in the first half of the *Aeneid* modeled on the *Odyssey*.</note> from the *Odyssey*, and then the battles from the *Iliad*? This is because the order of events necessarily changed the order of the work: for in Homer, the Trojan war was waged first, and then the wanderings happened to Ulysses as he returned from Troy; while in Maro <note>A common name for the poet Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro).</note>, Aeneas's voyage preceded the wars which were later waged in Italy. Again, when Homer in the first book wished to make Apollo hostile to the Greeks, he built the cause <margin>* From here</margin> *from the injury done to the priest. <note>Referring to the priest Chryses in the *Iliad*, whose daughter Agamemnon refused to return.</note> Here [Virgil], so that he might make Juno hostile to the Trojans, prepared a vast collection of causes for himself. Nor shall I recount this with great care—although, as I think, it has not been noticed by everyone—that while he promised in the first verse that he would bring forth Aeneas from the shores of Troy:

->*Who first from the shores of Troy,*<-
->*a refugee by fate, came to Italy and the Lavinian shores:*<-
<note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.1–3.</note>

yet when he comes to the threshold of the narration, he brings forth Aeneas’s fleet not from Troy, but from Sicily:

->*Hardly out of sight of the Sicilian land,*<-
->*they were joyfully spreading their sails into the deep.*<-
<note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.34–35.</note>

All of this he wove with Homeric threads. For Virgil himself, avoiding the likeness of historians in his poem—whose law is to begin from the very start of matters and lead a continuous narrative through to the end—followed poetic discipline: he began from the middle of things and later returned to the beginning. Therefore, Homer does not begin to describe the wandering of Ulysses from the Trojan shore; instead, he first shows him sailing from the island of Calypso, and in his own persona <note>A term from ancient literary criticism meaning the narrator's voice.</note> leads him to the Phaeacians. There, at the banquet of King Alcinous, Ulysses himself narrates how he traveled from Troy all the way to Calypso. After the Phaeacians, the poet again describes Ulysses’s voyage all the way to Ithaca in his own persona. Following him, Maro [Virgil] brings Aeneas forth from Sicily, whose voyage—
<meta>catchword: voyage-</meta>

<summary>Eustathius explains how Virgil modeled the structure of the Aeneid on Homer, specifically by starting the narrative "in the middle of things" (in medias res) and mirroring the Odyssey's wanderings and the Iliad's battles.</summary>
<keywords>Virgil, Homer, Aeneid, Odyssey, Iliad, poetic structure, in medias res, narrative technique, Juno, Apollo</keywords>

# BOOK V.

...[voyage] by describing it, he leads the reader to Libya. There, at Dido's banquet, Aeneas himself narrates his own navigation from Troy all the way to Sicily: and he added in a single verse what the poet had already described in detail:

->*From here, having departed, a god drove me to your shores.*<-
<note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 3.715. After Aeneas finishes his long narration of his travels to Dido, this line marks his arrival in Carthage.</note>

After Africa, the poet again describes in his own voice the fleet's journey all the way to Italy itself:

->*Meanwhile Aeneas was already holding his steady course*<-
->*mid-sea with the fleet.*<-
<note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 5.1–2.</note>

What of the fact that the entire Virgilian work is formed as if from a certain mirror of the Homeric work? For even the storm is described with marvelous imitation. Whoever wishes may compare the verses of both. Just as Venus took the place of Nausicaa, the daughter of Alcinous <note>In the *Odyssey*, the princess Nausicaa discovers the shipwrecked Odysseus; in the *Aeneid*, the goddess Venus (in disguise) meets Aeneas after his shipwreck.</note>. Dido herself reflects the image of King Alcinous, hosting a banquet. Scylla also, and Charybdis, and Circe are fittingly touched upon; and instead of the Cattle of the Sun <note>The sacred livestock of Helios which Odysseus's men infamously ate.</note>, the Strophades islands are fashioned <note>The home of the Harpies in the *Aeneid*.</note>. And instead of the consultation of the dead, a descent to them with the company of a priestess is introduced. There, Palinurus corresponds to Elpenor; moreover, to the hostile Ajax, the hostile Dido responds; and to the counsels of Tiresias, the warnings of Anchises correspond.

Now, the battles of the *Iliad*, and the description of wounds (not without technical perfection), and the double enumeration of reinforcements, and the forging of arms, and the variety of the funeral games <note>original: "ludicri certaminis"; referring to the athletic competitions in *Aeneid* 5 and *Iliad* 23.</note>, and the treaty struck between kings and the broken covenant, and the nocturnal scouting <note>original: "speculatio nocturna"; referring to the mission of Nisus and Euryalus, modeled on the "Doloneia" in *Iliad* 10.</note>, and the embassy reporting a rejection from Diomedes after the example of Achilles; and the lamentation over Pallas, as over Patroclus; and the dispute: just as between Achilles and Agamemnon, so between Drances and Turnus (for in both cases, one was thinking of his own advantage, the other of the public good); the single combat of Aeneas and Turnus, like that of Achilles and Hector; and the captives destined for the underworld—as there for Patroclus, here for Pallas:

-> —those born of Sulmo— <-
<note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 10.517. This refers to the four youths Aeneas captured to sacrifice at Pallas's funeral, mimicking Achilles' sacrifice of twelve Trojans for Patroclus.</note>

"Four youths here, as many as Ufens raised, he seizes alive as funeral offerings, to sacrifice to the shades." <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 10.517–519. In this scene, Aeneas captures prisoners to be human sacrifices at the funeral of his friend Pallas, directly imitating Achilles’ actions in the *Iliad*.</note> What of the fact that for the Homeric Lycaon—who was caught among the fugitives (and so it is no wonder if he resorted to prayers, yet Achilles did not spare him because of his grief for the slain Patroclus)—Magus is substituted in a similar condition in the midst of the battle? <margin>strove</margin> From there he leveled <note>original: *tenderet*</note> the deadly spear at Magus from afar. -> The commerce of war Turnus <-
-> ended first, even then when Pallas was slain. <-
<note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 10.532–533. Aeneas argues that by killing Pallas, Turnus has forfeited the traditional "rules" of war that might allow for mercy or ransom.</note>

But also the insult of Achilles toward Lycaon himself, once he was slain, is transferred by Virgil to Tarquitius. Achilles says:
<margin>Iliad 21.</margin> "Lie there now among the fish, who will lick the blood from your wound, unconcerned; nor shall your mother place you on a bier and mourn you, but the swirling Scamander <note>The river god and river of Troy.</note> will carry you into the broad lap of the sea," etc. <note>Homer, *Iliad* 21.122–125.</note>
<margin>your poet</margin> But here our poet <note>original: *noſter*; meaning Virgil, as the speaker is addressing Romans.</note> writes: "Lie there now, you who were so feared," and the rest. <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 10.557. Aeneas speaks these words to the decapitated corpse of Tarquitius.</note>

And when Avienus <note>Gennadius Avienus, one of the younger participants in the dialogue.</note> had requested that he should not comment sporadically, but follow the order from the beginning, he <note>Eustathius.</note> drew the pages back toward the start with his hand and began thus:

and with her the Nymphs, daughters of Zeus who holds the aegis,
the daughters of the wild, join in the sport, and Latona rejoices in her heart;
and she towers above them all with her head and brow,
and she is easily recognized, though all are beautiful:
so did the unwed maiden shine among her handmaidens.
<note>original Greek: Odyssey 6.102–109. This is Homer’s description of Princess Nausicaa, which Virgil adapted for Dido. Latona (Leto) is the mother of Artemis and Apollo.</note>

Aeneas stood forth and shone in the clear light,
in face and shoulders like a god; for his mother herself had breathed 
upon her son beautiful hair, and the glowing light of youth,
and had given his eyes a joyous luster:
such grace as hands add to ivory, or when silver 
or Parian marble is set in yellow gold.
<note>original Latin: "Restitit Aeneas, claraque in luce refulsit... Pariusve lapis circumdatur auro." (Aeneid 1.588-593). Venus, the mother of Aeneas, magically enhances his beauty as he appears before Dido.</note>

Odyssey, Book 6.
In this place, 
verses similar 
to these are 
cited from an 
ancient manuscript, 
but from 
Odyssey Book 23.

Athena, the daughter of Zeus, made him
taller to look upon and mightier, and from his head

And as when a man pours gold over silver—
a skilled man whom Hephaestus and Pallas Athena
have taught every art, and he completes beautiful works—
so then she shed grace upon his head and shoulders.
<note>original Greek: Odyssey 6.229–235 (also found in 23.156-162). Homer describes Athena enhancing Odysseus's appearance after his bath. Virgil’s "Parian marble" and "ivory" imagery directly mirrors Homer’s description of gold-plated silver.</note>

—"I am here before you, the one you seek, 
Trojan Aeneas, snatched from the Libyan waves."
<note>original Latin: "Coram quem quaeritis, adsum / Troius Aeneas, Libycis ereptus ab undis." (Aeneid 1.595-596). Aeneas reveals himself to Dido.</note>

I have come in the twentieth year to my native land."
<note>original Greek: Odyssey 21.207-208. Odysseus reveals his true identity to his loyal servants, the swineherd and cowherd, after twenty years away from home.</note>

<note>original Greek: Iliad 3.33–37. Alexander (Paris) retreats from Menelaus (the son of Atreus) just as Virgil’s Androgeus retreats from Aeneas.</note>

*Scylla haunts the right side, and insatiable Charybdis the left:*

### *Homer on Charybdis and on Scylla:*

<margin>Odyssey, Book 12.</margin>
For on one side was Scylla, and on the other divine Charybdis
terribly sucked down the salty water of the sea.
Indeed, when she vomited it forth, like a cauldron on a great fire,
she would all seethe up, bubbling, and the spray on high
would fall upon the tops of both cliffs.
But when she swallowed back the salty water of the sea,
she appeared all churning within, and the rock around
roared terribly, and beneath the earth appeared
with its dark-blue sand.
<note>original Greek: Odyssey 12.235–243. Macrobius provides this to show the source of Virgil’s "sucking" and "vomiting" imagery for the whirlpool Charybdis.</note>

### *Homer on Scylla,*

And there within Scylla dwells, yelping terribly;
her voice is truly as great as a newborn puppy’s
but she herself is an evil monster, nor would anyone
rejoice at seeing her, not even if a god should meet her.
She has twelve feet in all, dangling deformed;
and she has six very long necks, and on each...
<note>original Greek: Odyssey 12.85–91. Homer emphasizes Scylla's bizarre anatomy and her high-pitched, puppy-like yelp (the name Scylla is related to the Greek word for puppy, *skylax*).</note>

The kindly light rouses Evander from his humble roof, along with the morning songs of birds beneath the eaves. He woke and sat upright, and put on a soft tunic, beautiful and new; and around him he threw a great cloak. Beneath his glistening feet he bound his fair sandals. O, if Jupiter would restore my past years to me, such as I was when I laid low the front rank beneath Praeneste <note>An ancient city in Latium, modern-day Palestrina.</note> itself, and as victor burned the heaps of shields; and with this right hand sent King Herilus down to the Underworld, to whom at birth his mother Feronia <note>An Italian goddess of wilderness and fertility.</note> had given—terrible to say—three lives: three sets of armor to be wielded, three times he had to be laid low in death; yet then this right hand took all those lives from him and stripped him of as many sets of armor.

Thus he speaks weeping; at the same time he takes from his shoulder the gilded sword, which Lycaon of Gnosus <note>Crete</note> had made with wondrous skill,
<margin>ivory for the sheaths, Iliad 10.</margin>
and had fitted it with a handy ivory sheath. Mnestheus gives to Nisus a skin and the spoils of a shaggy lion; faithful Alethes exchanges helmets with him.
<note>original Greek: "Τυδείδῃ μὲν δῶκε Μενεπτόλεμος Θρασυμήδης / Φάσγανον ἄμφηκες... Καὶ σάκος... Μηριόνης δ' Ὀδυσῆϊ δίδου βιὸν, ἠδὲ φαρέτρην / Καὶ ξίφος." From Homer’s *Iliad* 10.255-60.</note>
To the son of Tydeus <note>Diomedes</note>, Thrasymedes, steadfast in battle, gave a two-edged sword—for his own had been left at the ships—and a shield; and upon his head he placed a helmet of bull’s hide, without peak or crest, which is called a <term>kataytyx</term> <note>a low-fitting leather skullcap used for stealth</note>, and it protects the heads of vigorous young men. And Meriones gave to Odysseus a bow, a quiver, and a sword.

Immediately they advance armed; as they go, the whole band of leaders, both young and old,
<margin>Iliad 10.</margin>
follows them with prayers; and also the handsome Iulus <note>the son of Aeneas</note>.
<note>original Greek: "Τώ δ' ἐπεὶ οὖν ὅπλοισιν ἐνὶ δεινοῖσιν ἐδύτην / Βᾶν ῥ' ἴεναι, λιπέτην δὲ κατ' αὐτόθι πάντας ἀρίστους." From Homer’s *Iliad* 10.272-73.</note>
When the two of them had donned their dread armor, they set out to go, and left behind all the best of the men.
Having gone forth, they cross the ditches, and through the shadows of the night they seek the enemy camp; yet first they are to be the death of many. Everywhere they see bodies scattered through the grass in sleep and wine, and chariots tilted on the shore.

<margin>Iliad, Book 10</margin>
<note>original Greek: "τὼ δ' βάτην προτέρω διά τ' ἔντεα καὶ μέλαν αἷμα / Αἶψα δ' ἐπ' ερῃκῶν ἀνδρῶν τέλοσ' ἷξον ἰόντες. / Οἱ δ' εὗδον καμάτῳ ἀδδηκότες, ἔντεα δέ σφιν / Καλὰ παρ' αὐτοῖσιν χθονὶ κέκλιτο, εὖ κατὰ κόσμον / Τριστιχὶ, παρὰ δέ σφιν ἑκάστῳ δίζυγος ἵπποι." Dawn rose from her bed beside noble Tithonus, so that she might bring light to the immortals and to mortal men.

The reaction of Euryalus’s mother to the dreadful news—how the shuttles <note>tools for weaving</note> were knocked from her hands and she dropped her wool, how she ran wailing through the walls and the ranks of men with her hair torn, and how she poured out her grief in lamentations—Virgil took all of this from Andromache's mourning for the death of her husband <note>Hector</note>.

# BOOK V.

Fame, the messenger, rushes forth and glides into the ears of Euryalus’s mother. Suddenly, heat leaves her wretched bones; the shuttle is shaken from her hands, and her weaving is unrolled. The unhappy woman flies out, and with a womanly wail and torn hair, she frantically seeks the walls and the front ranks in her course. She is unmindful of men, unmindful of danger and weapons; then she fills the heavens with her laments: "Do I behold you thus, Euryalus? You, that late-arriving rest of my old age, could you leave me alone, cruel one? Nor was the opportunity given to your wretched mother to address you one last time as you were sent into such great dangers?" <note>This passage from Virgil's *Aeneid* (9.473–482) describes the mother of Euryalus discovering her son's death.</note>

<margin>Iliad, Book 22.</margin>
So she spoke, and rushed through the halls like a madwoman <note>original Greek: μαινάδι, a "maenad" or ecstatic follower of Dionysus</note> with a throbbing heart. Her handmaidens went with her. But when she reached the tower and the crowd of men, she stood looking from the wall, and she perceived him <note>her husband, Hector</note> being dragged before the city. <note>This is Homer's description of Andromache's grief (Iliad 22.460–464), which Virgil used as a model.</note>

<margin>For this, that verse in the ancient poet is cited: "O weaklings, evil shames, Achaean women, no longer Achaean men." Iliad, Book 2. Aeneid, Book 9.</margin>

"Oh me, you boastful Achaean women, no longer Achaean men!" <note>original Greek: "Ὤ μοι ἀπειλητῆρες ἀχαιΐδες, ὐκ' ἔτ' ἀχαιοῖ." Homer uses a nearly identical insult against the Greeks.</note>

### CHAPTER X.

> *They hurl weapons from their hands: just as beneath dark clouds Strymonian <note>The Strymon was a river in Thrace, famous in antiquity for its large population of migrating cranes.</note> cranes give signals and traverse the air with sound, and flee the South Winds with a following cry.* <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 10.264–266. Virgil uses the image of noisy cranes to describe the shouting of the Trojans as Aeneas returns to the battle.</note>

<margin>Iliad, Book 3.</margin>
> The Trojans went with a clamor and a cry like birds, even as the clamor of cranes arises before the sky, which, after they have fled winter and the unspeakable rain, fly with a clamor toward the streams of the Ocean. <note>original Greek: "Τρῶες μὲν κλαγγῇ..." Homer uses this simile to contrast the noisy advance of the Trojans with the silent, disciplined march of the Greeks.</note>

> *A flame burns upon his head, and from the crest of his helmet fire is poured, and the golden boss of his shield vomits forth vast fires. Not otherwise than when in a clear night bloody comets glow mournfully, or the heat of Sirius <note>The "Dog Star," associated by the Romans with the "dog days" of midsummer and the spread of disease.</note>—that star which, bringing thirst and disease to weary mortals, rises and saddens the sky with its ill-omened light.* <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 10.270–275. This describes the terrifying appearance of Aeneas as he reaches the shore.</note>

<margin>Iliad, Book 5.</margin>
> She <note>The goddess Athena</note> kindled from his helmet and shield an unwearied fire, like the star of autumn, which shines most brightly after being bathed in the Ocean. Such a fire she kindled from his head and shoulders. <note>original Greek: "Δαῖέ οἱ ἐκ κορυθός..." This describes the hero Diomedes entering battle.</note>

<margin>Iliad, Book 22.</margin>
> Gleaming like the star that rushes across the plain. The one that comes at harvest time, and its rays appear most clear among many stars in the dead of night; they call it by the name of Orion’s Dog. It is the brightest of all, but it is made an evil sign, and it brings much fever to wretched mortals. <note>original Greek: "Παμφαίνονθ’ ὥς τ’ ἀστἐρ’..." Homer uses this to describe Achilles as he approaches Hector.</note>

> To each his own day stands: brief and irreplaceable is the time of life for all. <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 10.467–468. Jupiter speaks these words to comfort Hercules regarding the impending death of Pallas.</note>

<margin>Iliad, Book 6.</margin>
> For I say that no man has escaped fate, neither the coward nor the brave man, once he has first been born. <note>original Greek: "Μοῖραν δ’ οὔ τινά..." Hector’s famous words to his wife, Andromache.</note>

> Most dread son of Cronus <note>Zeus</note>, what a word you have spoken!

### BOOK V.

*The fates call, and he has reached the goal of his allotted age.* <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 10.472. This refers to the young hero Pallas, whose death is predestined by Fate despite the prayers of Aeneas's allies.</note>
<margin>Iliad, Book 13.</margin>
But an evil fate led him, where was the end of death. <note>original Greek: "Ἤϊτόν δ' ἄγε μοῖρα κακὴ, θανάτοιο τέλος ᾗ." Homer, *Iliad* 13.602.</note>

*By the spirits of your father, and the hopes of rising Iulus, I pray you, preserve this life for both a son and a father. I have a lofty house; talents <note>A talent was a massive unit of weight for precious metals, often used in ancient ransoms.</note> of engraved silver lie buried deep; I have weights of gold, both worked and unworked. The victory of the Trojans does not turn on this, nor will one life create such a difference.*
*He had spoken; Aeneas in turn gave him these words: "Those many talents of silver and gold you mention, save them for your children. Turnus first abolished those commerce-dealings of war, even then when Pallas was slain. This the spirit of my father Anchises feels, and this Iulus knows."*
*So having spoken, he held the helmet with his left hand, and, as the suppliant's neck was bent back, he buried the sword up to the hilt.* <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 10.524–536. Here, the Latin warrior Magus begs Aeneas for mercy, offering wealth. Aeneas refuses, arguing that the death of his friend Pallas has ended the possibility of taking prisoners for ransom.</note>
<margin>Iliad, Book 6.</margin>
<margin>In place of these, in the ancient [original source], there are many more verses from Iliad, Book 11, regarding the sons of Antimachus.</margin>
Take me alive, son of Atreus, <note>Menelaus</note> and accept a worthy ransom. Many treasures lie in my wealthy father’s house: bronze, and gold, and well-wrought iron. From these my father would grant you a boundless ransom, if he should learn I were alive at the ships of the Achaeans. <note>original Greek: "Ζώγρει ἀπ' εἴος ὑιέ..." Homer, *Iliad* 6.46–50. Virgil uses this Homeric motif of the "ransom plea" to highlight Aeneas's transition into a state of vengeful fury.</note>

*Just as a hungry lion, often roaming the high stalls (for maddening hunger drives him), if by chance he has spotted a fleeing goat or a stag with rising horns: he rejoices, gaping immensely, and has raised <margin>*has raised (variant reading)</margin> his mane, and clings, crouching over the entrails; foul blood washes his wicked mouth.*
*So Mezentius rushes eagerly into the thick of the enemy.* <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 10.707–711 and 713. Mezentius is a "scorner of the gods" and one of Aeneas’s primary antagonists, compared here to a savage lion.</note>
<margin>Iliad, Book 3. In the ancient [text] the whole passage is set out: adding also six others from Iliad, Book 12: "he went like a mountain-bred lion," which we indicated were cited a little earlier.</margin>
As a lion rejoices when he happens upon a great carcass, having found either a horned stag or a wild goat, <margin>Iliad, Book 23.</margin> being hungry. <note>original Greek: "Ως τε λέων ἐχάρη... Πεινάων." Homer, *Iliad* 3.23–25. Virgil adopts the visceral details of the lion's hunger and its "gaping" mouth from these lines.</note>

*The earth is sprinkled with tears, the armor is sprinkled too.* <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 11.191. This line describes the mourning for the fallen Pallas.</note>

And these matters, indeed, must be left to the judgment of the readers, so that they may judge for themselves what they ought to feel regarding the comparison of both poets. However, if you should consult me, I will not deny that sometimes Virgil, in the process of translating <note>The author uses the term "translating" (transferendo) to describe Virgil's creative adaptation of Homeric Greek into Latin.</note>, has refined the material more densely, as in this passage:

> *Just as labor busies the bees in early summer through the flowery countryside under the sun, when they lead out the grown offspring of the race, or when they pack the liquid honey and stretch the cells with sweet nectar; or receive the burdens of those arriving, or having formed a column...* <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.430–434. <meta>This page continues the philological comparison between Homer and Virgil, specifically examining how Virgil "enriches" or expands upon Homeric models. # BOOK V.

*They drive the drones, a lazy herd, from the stalls.*
*The work seethes, and the fragrant honey smells of thyme.*
<note>Virgil, *Georgics* 4.168–169. Virgil uses this to describe the industrious nature of bees, which he often treats as a metaphor for a well-ordered human society.</note>

<margin>Iliad, Book 2.</margin>
> Even as the tribes of thronging bees go forth from some hollow rock, ever coming anew, and in clusters they fly over the flowers of spring; some fly in heaps here, some there. <note>original Greek: "Ἠΰτε ἔθνεα εἶσι μελισσάων ἁδινάων / Πέτρης ἐκ γλαφυρῆς..." Homer, *Iliad* 2.87–90. Homer uses this to describe the Greek army swarming out of their ships.</note>

Do you see how the bees are described as workers by Virgil, but as wanderers by Homer? The latter expresses their dispersal and the mere variety of their flight; the former expresses the duty of their innate craft. In these verses also, Maro <note>Publius Vergilius Maro, known simply as Virgil.</note> proved to be the more enriched interpreter.

*O companions (for we are not ignorant of evils before),*
*O you who have suffered heavier things: God will give an end to these also.*
*You have approached both the Scyllaean rage and the deep-sounding*
*rocks; you have also experienced the Cyclopean crags.*
*Recall your spirits, and dismiss your gloomy fear;*
*perhaps one day it will be a pleasure to remember even these things,*
*through various misfortunes... and the rest.*
<note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.198–204. Aeneas is comforting his men after a shipwreck.</note>

<margin>Odyssey, Book 10.</margin>
<note>While the margin says Book 10, the passage is actually from *Odyssey* 12.208–212.</note>
> O friends, for in no way are we ignorant of evils; surely this is no greater evil than when the Cyclops penned us in his hollow cave by his stark might. But even from there, by my excellence and counsel and wit, we escaped; and I think that one day we shall remember these things. <note>original Greek: "Ὦ φίλοι, οὐ γάρπω τι κακῶν ἀδαήμονες εἰμέν..."</note>

Ulysses mentioned a single hardship to his companions. Here [Virgil], to encourage hope for release from the present evil, exhorts them by the outcome of a double misfortune. Next, while the former said somewhat obscurely, "and I think that one day we shall remember these things" <note>original Greek: "καὶ που τῶν δε μνήσεσθαι οἴω"</note>, the latter spoke more clearly: **"Perhaps one day it will be a pleasure to remember even these things."** Moreover, what our poet added provides a stronger consolation. For he encouraged his men not only with the example of escaping, but also with the hope of future happiness—promising through these labors not just quiet homes, but kingdoms.

Virgil described the frequent turning of the neck in the character of Palinurus as he consulted the stars: *Arcturus*, he says, *behold, he gazes toward the North. Then at the Pleiades and Hyades. Behold, he turns toward the South. And the Twin Bears <note>original: "Triones," referring to the constellations Ursa Major and Minor</note>, he turns his gaze back to the North again. And he looks around at Orion, armed with gold; once more he turns himself toward the South.* Indeed, even with the word *looks around*, Virgil shows the variety of a man repeatedly turning himself back and forth. Homer introduces his pilot looking only once at the *Pleiades*, which are in the Southern region, and once at *Boötes and the Bear*, which are at the North Pole.

> No goddess was your mother, nor was Dardanus the founder

<margin>Iliad, Book 16.</margin>
> Pitiless man, the horseman Peleus was not your father, 
> nor was Thetis your mother; rather, the gray sea bore you, 
> and the steep rocks, because your mind is so harsh.
<note>original Greek: "Νηλεές, οὐκ ἄρα σοί γε πατὴρ ἦν ἱππότα Πηλεύς. / Οὐδὲ Θέτις μήτηρ, γλαυκὴ δέ σε τίκτε θάλασσα, / Πέτραι τ’ ἠλίβατοι, ὅτι τοι νόος ἐστὶν ἀπηνής." from *Iliad* 16.33–35. Patroclus says this to Achilles to highlight his lack of empathy for the suffering Greeks.</note>

Clearly, *Virgil* does not only criticize the lineage, as the poet he was following did, but also the upbringing and nursing, characterizing it as beast-like and harsh. For he adds of his own accord: *and Hyrcanian tigers offered you their teats.* He does this because, evidently, in the molding of character, a great part is played by the disposition of the nurse and the nature of her milk. This milk, infused into the tender infant and mixed with the still-fresh seed of the parents, shapes a single nature from this twin blending. This is why the providence of nature, preparing a likeness between children and those who beget them from the very act of nursing, caused an abundance of nourishment to be born at the same time as the birth itself.

<margin>A similar discussion is found in Aulus Gellius, Book 12, Chapter 1.</margin>

Wherefore it is not believed without reason that, just as the force and nature of the seed <note>original: *seminis*—the OCR reads *feminis*, but in early modern printing, the "long s" (ʃ) is often mistaken for "f"; the context of procreation and "fabricator" (maker) confirms "seed" is intended</note> is effective in shaping the likenesses of body and mind, the character and properties of milk are no less effective for the same purpose. And this has been observed not only in humans, but also in cattle. For if kids are perhaps nourished on the milk of sheep, or lambs on the milk of goats, it is generally agreed that in the former the wool becomes harder, while in

<margin>*bristle</margin>
the latter the * hair <note>original: *capillum*—referring here to the finer coat of the goat</note> produced is softer. Even in trees and crops, the force and power of the water and soil that nourish them is often greater for either diminishing or increasing their natural quality than the nature of the seed itself that is sown. Indeed, you may often see a lush and shining tree, if transferred to another place, wither due to the inferior sap of the soil. Thus, in describing behaviors, Homer lacked what Virgil added:

> With the whip he always drove them from the shoulder, and the horses

The Greek poet mentions only the horses running under the animating whip: although it could not be said more elegantly than what he added, *lifted on high* <note>original Greek: *ὑψόσ’ ἀερέσθην*</note>, by which he expressed the greatest impetus of speed that nature could provide. > As a cauldron boils within, urged by a great fire,
> Melting the fat of a tender-fed hog,
> Bubbling up on all sides, and dry wood lies beneath it.

<margin>*steaming</margin>
The Greek verses regarding the bronze vessel <note>original: *aheni*—a bronze cauldron or pot</note> mention it bubbling over a great fire, and these words—*bubbling up on all sides* <note>original: πάντοθεν ἀμβολάδην</note>—adorn the whole passage. For he has elegantly expressed the springs of water emerging from every part. In the Latin verses, the entire pageantry of the event is described, including the sound of the flame. And in place of what the former had said—*bubbling up on all sides*—[Virgil] used "waters leaping with heat," and a "*steaming* river overflowing with foam," and "raging within." You will not find the same dignity in a single word, but he compensated for what was lacking in abundance with the variety of his description. He added, after all: "Nor can the wave now contain itself," by which he expressed what always happens in practice when there is an excess of heat placed beneath. Thus, the style of the poetic trumpet <note>a metaphor for the grand, epic style of poetry</note> holds itself well, encompassing everything that occurs in such a matter.

# THE SATURNALIA

They stood as high-headed oaks on the mountains, 
Which abide the wind and the rain through all days, 
Firmly fixed with great, stretching roots; 
So these two, trusting in their hands and their strength, 
Awaited great Asius as he approached and did not flee.
<note>original Greek: *Iliad* 12.132–136. This passage describes the Greek heroes Polypoetes and Leonteus defending the gates of their camp against the Trojan ally Asius.</note>

The Greek soldiers Polypoetes and Leonteus stand before the gates and, unmoving, await the approaching enemy Asius like fixed trees. This concludes the Greek description. However, the Virgilian version makes Bitias and Pandarus open the gate of their own accord, offering themselves to the enemy, which was exactly what the enemy desired: to gain possession of the camp, even if it meant being in the enemy's power. And the poet <note>Virgil</note> now calls the twin heroes "towers," and now describes them as "flashing with the light of their crests." Nor did he omit the comparison to trees, like the former poet, but he described it more abundantly and more beautifully. Nor would I deny that these lines were brought forth more refinedly by Maro <note>a common name for Virgil, from his full name Publius Vergilius Maro</note>:

> A harsh rest and iron sleep press upon his eyes,

<meta>This page continues the philological comparison between Homer and Virgil, specifically focusing on how Virgil (referred to as Maro) attempted to capture the speed, vividness, and physical details of Homeric descriptions, often finding that the Greek original possessed a unique "weighty" swiftness that was difficult to replicate in Latin.</meta>

->BOOK V.<-

These two verses were translated from that source:
<margin>Iliad, Book 10.</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἦ καὶ ὁ μέν μιν ἔμελλε γενείου χειρὶ παχείῃ, ἁψάμενος λίσσεσθαι, ὁ δ’ αὐχένα μέσσον ἔλαυσε φασγάνῳ ἀΐξας· ἀπὸ δ’ ἄμφω κέρσε τένοντε. φθεγγομένου δ’ ἄρα τοῦγε κάρη κονίῃσιν ἐμίχθη. (*Iliad* 10.454–457)</note>
He spoke, and was just about to touch the other's chin with his stout hand in supplication, but the other, springing forward, struck him in the middle of the neck with his sword and shore through both tendons; and while he was still speaking, his head was mingled with the dust.

Observe the excessive speed combined with a sense of weight, a quality which Virgil's <term>Maro</term><note>Virgil's full name was Publius Vergilius Maro; Macrobius frequently refers to him simply as "Maro."</note> efforts could not quite reach. In the chariot race, see with what vividness Homer described one chariot slightly ahead and the other following so closely they were almost joined:
<margin>Iliad, Book 23.</margin>
<note>original Greek: Πνοιῇ δ’ Εὐμήλοιο μετάφρενον εὐρέε τ’ ὤμω θέρμετ’· ἐπ’ αὐτῷ γὰρ κεφαλὰς καταθέντε πετέσθην. (*Iliad* 23.380–381)</note>
The back and broad shoulders of Eumelus grew warm with their breath; for their heads seemed to rest right upon him as they flew along.
*They grow wet with foam and the breath of those following.*
<note>original Latin: *Georgics* 3.111 or *Aeneid* 5.342. Virgil's adaptation of the Greek imagery above.</note>

Even more marvelous is the speed of the one following the leader in the foot race, as described by the same poet:
<margin>Iliad, Book 23.</margin>
<note>original Greek: ἴχνια τύπτε πόδεσσι πάρος κόνιν ἀμφιχυθῆναι. (*Iliad* 23.763)</note>
...and he struck his tracks with his feet before the dust could settle over them.

Now, the sense of this verse is as follows: if one happens to run through loose dust, a clearly marked footprint is undoubtedly seen the moment the runner's foot is lifted from the earth; and yet, faster than thought, the dust that had been kicked up by the impact of the foot settles back over the track. Therefore, the divine poet says that the one following was so close that he occupied the leader's footprint before the dust could fall back into it. But Virgil, wishing to signify the same thing, says: *And now Diores rubs heel against heel.* <note>original Latin: *Aeneid* 5.324.</note> Observe the elegance of Homer even in this.
<margin>* ...he lay with his thick neck bent back.</margin>
<note>original Greek: * κεῖτ’ ἀποδοχμώσας παχὺν αὐχένα. (*Odyssey* 9.372, describing the Cyclops Polyphemus)</note>
\* He spoke, and leaning back he fell on his back — — The other [Virgil] says:
\**He laid down his bent neck.*\**
<note>original Latin: *Ceruicem inflexam posuit.* From *Aeneid* 9.327.</note>

Let us also compare these verses, if it seems well:
<note>original Greek: Ἅρματα δ’ ἄλλοτε μὲν χθονὶ πίλνατο πουλυβοτείρῃ Ἄλλοτε δ’ ἀΐξασκε μετήορα. (*Iliad* 23.368–369)</note>
The chariots at one time would graze the bounteous earth, and at another would leap up into the air.
*And now low, and now raised high, they seem to be carried through the thin air.*
<note>original Latin: *Georgics* 3.108–109. Virgil's description of the bouncing motion of racing chariots.</note>

<header>OF THE SATURNALIA</header>

<margin>Odyssey, Book 6.</margin>
<note>original: "παϲάων δ᾽ ὑπὲρ ἥγε κάρη ἔχει ἠδὲ μέτωπα"</note>
She holds her head and brow above them all.
<note>Homer describes the goddess Artemis standing out among her nymphs.</note>
—And as she walks, she towers above all other goddesses.
<note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.501. Virgil uses this to describe Queen Dido walking among her people, likening her to Diana (Artemis).</note>

<margin>Iliad, Book 2.</margin>
<note>original: "Ἔϲπετε νῦν μοι μῦϲαι ὀλύμπια δώματ᾽ ἔχουϲαι, ὑμεῖϲ γὰρ θεαί ἐϲτε, πάρεϲτέ τε, ἴϲτε τε πάντα."</note>
Tell me now, Muses, who dwell in Olympian homes—for you are goddesses, you are present, and you know all things.
<note>Homer's invocation to the Muses before the famous "Catalogue of Ships."</note>
For you, O goddesses, remember, and you have the power to recount.
<note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 7.645. Virgil's version of the invocation.</note>

<margin>Iliad, Book 19.</margin>
<note>The marginal note says Book 19, but the passage is actually from *Iliad* 20.403–405.</note>
<note>original: "Αὐτὰρ ὃ θυμὸν ἄϊϲθε, καὶ ἤρυπεν, ὡϲ ὅτε ταῦροϲ ἤρυπεν ἑλκόμενοϲ ἑλικώνιον ἀμφὶ ἄνακτα κούρων ἑλκόντων, γάνυται δέ τε τοῖϲ ἐνοϲίχθων."</note>
But he breathed out his life and bellowed, as a bull bellows when he is dragged around the lord of Helicon <note>The "Lord of Helicon" refers to Poseidon (Neptune) or perhaps a specific local title for the god.</note> by young men dragging him; and the Earth-shaker delights in them.
At the same time he raises horrendous cries to the stars. Like the bellowing of a wounded bull when it has fled the altar and shaken the uncertain axe from its neck.
<note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 2.222–224, describing the death of Laocoön. Macrobius is comparing the sound of a dying man to Homer's sacrificial bull.</note>

When the style of both poets is examined here, how great a distance do you find? Nor is this handled with less elegance by Homer: in speaking of the bull dragged for sacrifice, he mentions both Apollo, *around the lord of Helicon*, and also Neptune, *and the Earth-shaker delights in them*. That the bull is the primary victim used in divine rites for these two gods is testified by <term>Vergilius</term> <note>The poet Virgil.</note> himself:

->A bull for Neptune, a bull for you, fair Apollo.<-
<note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 3.119.</note>

<margin>Iliad, Book 2.</margin>
<note>original: "Ἠΰτε πῦρ ἀΐδηλον ἐπιφλέγει ἄϲπετον ὕλην Οὔρεοϲ ἐν κορυφῆϲ ἕκαθεν δέ τε φαίνεται αὐγή."</note>
Even as a destructive fire consumes a boundless forest on the mountain peaks, and the glare is seen from afar.

<margin>Iliad, Book 4.</margin>
<margin>
In place of these, two other passages are cited in the old copies: one from Iliad, Book 11 <note>represented by the Greek letter 'λ' (lambda)</note> regarding Agamemnon: *as when destructive fire...* etc. The other regarding Diomedes: *for he rushed across the plain like a river swollen by winter storms...* etc. Iliad, Book 5 <note>represented by the Greek letter 'ε' (epsilon)</note>.
</margin>
<note>original: "Ὡϲ δ᾽ ὅτε χείμαῤῥοι ποταμοὶ κατ᾽ ὄρεϲφι ῥέοντεϲ Ἐϲ μιϲγάγκειαν ϲυμβάλλετον ὄβριμον ὕδωρ Κρουνῶν ἐκ μεγάλων κοίληϲ ἔντοϲθε χαράδρηϲ Τῶν δέ τε τηλόϲε δοῦπον ἐν οὔρεϲιν ἔκλυε ποιμήν."</note>
As when winter-flowing rivers, rushing down from the mountains, join their heavy waters in a meeting of valleys, from great springs within a hollow ravine, and the shepherd hears their thunder in the mountains from afar.

Just as when a flame falls upon the standing corn when the South winds are raging, or a rapid torrent from a mountain stream levels the fields, levels the lush crops and the labors of the oxen, and drags down the forests headlong; the bewildered shepherd, hearing the sound from the top of a high rock, is struck senseless.
<note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 2.304–308. Virgil is describing Aeneas watching the fall of Troy.</note>

And Virgil has "violated" two <term>parables</term> <note>Used here in the sense of "similes" or "extended metaphors."</note> so that he might make one, drawing fire from one source and a torrent from the other; yet he has not fulfilled the dignity of either.

# BOOK V.

<margin>Iliad, Book 9</margin>
<note>original: "Ὡς δ᾿ ἄνεμοι δύο πόντον ὀρίνετον ἰχθυόεντα, Βορέης καὶ Ζέφυρος, τώ, τε Θρῄκηθεν ἄητον. Ἐλθόντ’ ἐξαπίνης, ἄμυδις δέ τε κῦμα κελαινὸν Κορθύεται, πολλὸν δὲ παρὲξ ἅλα φῦκος ἔχευαν."</note>
As when two winds stir the fish-filled sea, Boreas and Zephyrus, which blow from Thrace, coming suddenly; and at once the dark wave swells high and casts much seaweed along the shore.

<note>original: "Aduersi rupto ceu quondam turbine uenti Confligunt, Zephyrúsq; Notúsq; & laetus Eois Eurus equis: stridunt syluae, saevitq; tridenti Spumeus, atq; imo Nereus ciet aequora fundo."</note>
As when sometimes, in a bursting whirlwind, opposing winds clash—Zephyrus, Notus, and Eurus, joyful with his Eastern horses; the woods shriek, and foamy Nereus rages with his trident, stirring the waters from their lowest depths.
<note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 2.416–419.</note>

He <note>Virgil</note> removes this fault, which occurs rather frequently, by constructing one passage more clearly out of two Greek <term>parabolis</term> <note>parables or similes</note>.

<margin>Odyssey, Book 11</margin>
<note>original: "Ἡμῖν δ᾿ αὖ μετόπισθε νεὼς κυανοπρῴροιο Ἴκμενον οὖρον ἵει πλησίστιον ἐσθλὸν ἑταῖρον."</note>
But for us, behind our dark-prowed ship, a good companion sent a favorable wind that filled the sails.

<note>original: "Prosequitur surgens à puppi uentus eunteis."</note>
A rising wind follows them from the stern as they go.
<note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 3.130.</note>

What our poet <note>Homer</note> called *ikmenon* <note>original: "ἴκμενον" - favorable or following</note>, your poet <note>Virgil</note> calls "rising from the stern," quite decorously. However, those <term>epitheta</term> <note>epithets or descriptive adjectives</note> which our poet applied to the wind are so many and so apt that they exalt the passage.

<note>original: "Σὺν δὲ δύω μάρψας ὥς τε σκύλακας ποτὶ γαίῃ. Κόπτ’, ἐκ δ’ ἐγκέφαλος χαμάδις ῥέε, δεῦε δὲ γαίαν. Τοὺς δὲ διαμελεϊστὶ ταμὼν ὥπλίσατο δόρπον. Ἤσθιε δ’, ὥς τε λέων ὀρεσίτροφος, οὐδ᾿ ἀπέλειπεν Ἔγκατά τε σάρκας τε, καὶ ὀστέα μυελόεντα."</note>
Snatching two at once like puppies, he dashed them to the ground; their brains flowed out on the earth and wet the ground. Cutting them limb from limb, he prepared his supper. He ate like a mountain-bred lion, leaving nothing—neither entrails, nor flesh, nor marrow-filled bones.
<note>Homer, *Odyssey* 9.289–293, describing the Cyclops eating Odysseus’s men.</note>

<note>original: "Visceribus miserorum, & sanguine uescitur atro. Vidi egomet duo de numero cum corpora nostro, Prensa manu magna medio resupinus in antro Frangeret ad saxum."</note>
He feeds on the vitals of the wretched men and their dark blood. I myself saw when he, lying back in the middle of the cave, grabbed two bodies of our number in his great hand and crushed them against the rock.
<note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 3.622–624.</note>

Maro <note>Virgil</note> provided a bare and brief account of the deed; Homer, by contrast, mixed in <term>pathos</term> <note>emotional appeal or suffering</note>, and through the sorrow of the telling, he matched the indignation caused by such cruelty.

<note>original: "Τὴν δὲ μετ᾿ Ἰφιμέδειαν Ἀλωῆος παράκοιτιν Εἴσιδον, ἣ δὴ φάσκε Ποσειδάωνι μιγῆναι."</note>
After her I saw Iphimedeia, the wife of Aloeus, who said she had lain with Poseidon.
<margin>Odyssey, Book 11</margin>
<note>original: "Καὶ ῥ’ ἔτεκεν δύο παῖδε μινυνθαδίω δὲ γενέσθην."</note>
And she bore two sons, though they were to be short-lived.

-># SATURNALIA<-

<note>original: "Ωτόν τ' Αντίθεον, τηλέκλειτόν τ' Εφιάλτην, Οὕς δὴ μηκίστους θρέψε ζείδωρος ἄρουρα, καί πολὺ καλλίστους, μετά γε κλυτὸν Ωρίωνα. Ἐννέωροι γὰρ τοί γε καὶ ἐννεαπήχεες ἦσαν Εὖρος, ἀτὰρ μῆκος γε γενέσθην ἐννεόργυιοι. Οἵ ῥα καὶ ἀθανάτοισιν ἀπειλήτην ἐν Ὀλύμπῳ φυλόπιδα στήσειν πολυάϊκος πολέμοιο. Ὄσσαν ἐπ' Οὐλύμπῳ μέμασαν θέμεν, αὐτὰρ ἐπ' Ὄσσῃ Πήλιον εἰνοσίφυλλον, ἵν' οὐρανὸς ἀμβατὸς εἴη."</note>
And godlike Otus and far-famed Ephialtes, whom the grain-giving earth nourished to be the tallest, and by far the fairest, after famous Orion. For at nine years old they were nine cubits in breadth, and in height they reached nine fathoms. They even threatened the immortals on Olympus that they would raise the din of furious war. They strove to set Mount Ossa upon Olympus, and upon Ossa leafy Pelion, that heaven might be accessible.
<note>Homer, *Odyssey* 11.307–313.</note>

*Here also I saw the twin sons of Aloeus, monstrous*
*bodies, who attempted with their hands to tear down the great heaven,*
*and to thrust down Jupiter from his high realms.*
<note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 6.582–584.</note>

Homer measured the size of their bodies in height and breadth, and depicted their limbs with a circuit of words. Your poet <note>Virgil</note> says "monstrous bodies," and added nothing further, not daring to touch the names of measurements. The former <note>Homer</note> expressed the attempt of their insane construction regarding the stacking of mountains; the latter <note>Virgil</note> was content to have said they "attempted to tear down heaven." Finally, if you compare passage to passage, you will find a shameful difference.

<margin>Iliad, Book 4.</margin> <note>original: "Ὡς δ' ὅτ' ἐν αἰγιαλῷ πολυηχέϊ κῦμα θαλάσσης. Ὄρνυτ' ἐπασσύτερον ζεφύρου ὑποκινήσαντος, Πόντῳ μὲν τὰ πρῶτα κορύσσεται, αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα Χέρσῳ ῥηγνύμενον, μεγάλα βρέμει, ἀμφὶ δέ τ' ἄκρας Κυρτὸν ἐὸν, κορυφοῦται, ἀποπτύει δ' ἁλὸς ἄχνην."</note>
As when on an echoing shore a wave of the sea rises, one after another, under the stirring of the West Wind; at first it gathers a crest out at sea, but then, breaking on the land, it roars loudly, and arching around the headlands, it rises to a peak and spits out the salt spray.
<note>Homer, *Iliad* 4.422–426.</note>

*Just as when a wave begins to whiten in the deep sea:*
*the sea gradually raises itself, and lifts its waves higher,*
*then rises from its lowest depths to the heavens.*
<note>Virgil, *Georgics* 3.237–239.</note>

When the former <note>Homer</note> describes the marine motion and the shore-breaking waves from the very beginning, the latter <note>Virgil</note> flies past this. Then, where the former says, "at first it gathers a crest out at sea," Maro <note>Virgil</note> has turned this into, "the sea gradually raises itself."

# BOOK V.

The former <note>Homer</note> says that the wave, by its own growth, is driven to dash loftily curved against the shores, and to spit out the foam of the collected filth: a thing which no picture could more expressively represent. Your poet <note>Virgil</note> leads the sea from the bottom all the way to the heavens.

> He had spoken, and he confirmed it by the rivers of his Stygian brother, 
> by the banks with boiling pitch and black whirlpool 
> he gave his nod: and he made all Olympus tremble with that nod.
<note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 9.104–106. The "Stygian brother" is Pluto, god of the underworld.</note>

<margin>Iliad, Book 1.</margin>
> <note>original: "ἦ, καὶ κυανέῃσιν ἐπ' ὀφρύσι νεῦσε κρονίων. Ἀμβρόσιαι δ' ἄρα χαῖται ἐπεῤῥώσαντο ἄνακτος Κρατὸς ἀπ' ἀθανάτοιο, μέγαν δ' ἐλέλιξεν ὄλυμπον."</note>
> The son of Cronos spoke, and nodded with his dark brows; 
> and the divine locks of the king shook upon his immortal 
> head, and he made great Olympus tremble.
<note>Homer, *Iliad* 1.528–530.</note>

->And elsewhere:<-

<margin>Odyssey, Book 5.</margin>
> <note>original: "Καὶ τὸ κατειβόμενον στυγὸς ὕδωρ ὅς τε μέγιστος Ὅρκος δεινότατος τε πέλει μακάρεσσι θεοῖσι."</note>
> And the down-flowing water of the Styx, which is the 
> greatest and most terrible oath for the blessed gods.
<note>Homer, *Odyssey* 5.185–186.</note>

<margin>*borrowed</margin>
When Phidias <note>The most famous sculptor of classical antiquity, roughly 480–430 BCE.</note> was fashioning the Olympian Jupiter, and was asked from what model he would imitate the divine likeness, he replied that he had found the archetype of Jupiter in these three verses of Homer:

<margin>Iliad, Book 1.</margin>
> <note>original: "ἦ καὶ κυανέῃσιν ἐπ' ὀφρύσι νεῦσε κρονίων Ἀμβρόσιαι δ' ἄρα χαῖται ἐπεῤῥώσαντο ἄνακτος Κρατὸς ἀπ' ἀθανάτοιο μέγαν δ' ἐλέλιξεν ὄλυμπον."</note>
> The son of Cronos spoke, and nodded with his dark brows; 
> and the divine locks of the king shook upon his immortal 
> head, and he made great Olympus tremble.

For he said he had gathered the whole countenance of Jupiter from the eyebrows and the hair. You see that both of these were omitted by Virgil. Truly, he did not remain silent regarding the majesty of the nod that shook Olympus. But he took the oath from another place in Homer, so that the sparseness of his translation might be compensated by this addition: <margin>Odyssey, Book 10.</margin> <note>original: "πρῶτον ὑπηνήτῃ ᾧ περ χαριεστάτη ἥβη."</note> "A youth first showing a beard, when youth is most graceful."

->*A boy marking his face with the first unshorn youth.*<-
<note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 9.181.</note>

By omitting the grace of beginning puberty—the phrase "when youth is most graceful"—he made the Latin description less pleasing.

of Peleus on the 
other side sprang

<meta>The previous page established the framework for this literary critique: Macrobius is systematically comparing the works of the Greek poet Homer (8th century BCE) and the Roman poet Virgil (1st century BCE). He has been arguing that while Virgil is a master of the Latin language, he often falls short of the "majesty" and descriptive "abundance" found in Homer's original Greek verses.</meta>

# SATURNALIA

> <note>original: "Αἰχμὰς ἐκ χειρῶν, τοῦ δ’ οὔποτε κυδάλιμον κῆρ / Ταρβεῖ, οὐδὲ φοβεῖτ’, ἀγηνορίη δέ μιν ἔκτα / Ταρφέα τε τρέσε’ στίχας ἀνδρῶν πειρητίζων / Ὅππητ’ ἰθύσει, τῇ τ’ εἴκουσι στίχες ἀνδρῶν."</note>
> Spears fly from hands, yet his noble heart never 
> fears nor is he afraid; his own courage brings him to his death. 
> Often he turns, testing the ranks of men; 
> wherever he charges, there the ranks of men give way.
<note>Homer, *Iliad* 12.41–44. This describes a boar or lion at bay, used as a metaphor for a warrior's bravery.</note>

> *Like a wild beast, which, surrounded by a dense circle of hunters,*
> *rages against the weapons: knowing she is doomed, she flings herself*
> *and is carried by a leap over the hunting spears.*
<note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 9.551–553.</note>

Do you see how the Latin parable has been so contracted into a narrow space that nothing could be more meager? Do you see how the Greek, on the contrary, has fulfilled the grandeur of a true hunt with an abundance of both words and details? In the face of such a great difference, it is almost embarrassing to compare them.

<margin>Iliad, Book 13.</margin>
> <note>original: "φράξαντες δόρυ δουρί, σάκος σάκει προθελύμνῳ / Ἀσπὶς ἄρ’ ἀσπίδ’ ἔρειδε, κόρυς κόρυν, ἀνέρα δ’ ἀνήρ."</note>
> Fencing spear with spear, shield with shield in close array; 
> buckler pressed on buckler, helmet on helmet, and man on man.
<note>Homer, *Iliad* 13.130–131. A famous description of the "phalanx" formation.</note>

> *In no other way do the Trojan ranks and the Latin ranks*
> *clash: foot clings to foot, and man is packed against man.*
<note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 10.360–361.</note>

How great the difference is between each passage, I leave to the reader to judge.

<margin>Iliad, Book 12.</margin>
> <note>original: "Ὄρνις γάρ σφιν ἐπῆλθε περησέμεναι μεμαῶσιν, / Αἰετὸς ὑψιπέτης ἐπ’ ἀριστερὰ λαὸν ἐέργων / φοινήεντα δράκοντα φέρων ὀνύχεσσι πέλωρον / ζωὸν ἔτ’ ἀσπαίροντα, καὶ οὔπω λήθετο χάρμης. / κόψε γὰρ αὐτὸν ἔχοντα κατὰ στῆθος περὶ δειρὴν, / ἰδνωθεὶς ὀπίσω. ὁ δ’ ἀπὸ ἕθεν ἧκε χαμάζε / Ἀλγήσας ὀδύνῃσι, μέσῳ δ’ ἐνὶ κάββαλ’ ομίλῳ / Αὐτὸς δὲ κλάγξας πέτετο πνοιῇσ’ ἀνέμοιο."</note>
> For a bird came upon them as they were eager to cross— 
> a high-flying eagle, skirting the host on the left, 
> bearing in its talons a monstrous, blood-red snake, 
> still alive and gasping, and it had not yet forgotten the joy of battle. 
> For the snake struck the bird on the breast near the neck, 
> as the bird held it, by bending itself backward. The bird, stung 
> by the pain, cast it from him to the ground, dropping it 
> in the midst of the crowd; then the eagle, with a cry, 
> flew away on the gusts of the wind.
<note>Homer, *Iliad* 12.200–207.</note>

> *And as when a tawny eagle, flying high, carries a snatched-up snake,*
> *and has entwined its feet and clung with its claws;*
> *but the wounded serpent twists its sinuous coils,*
> *and bristles with raised scales, and hisses with its mouth,*
> *rising up tall: the eagle nonetheless attacks the struggling creature*
> *with its hooked beak, while simultaneously beating the air with its wings.*
<note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 11.751–756.</note>

Virgil

<summary>In this excerpt, Macrobius compares specific passages from Homer and Virgil, arguing that Virgil's Latin imitations are often "meager" or overly condensed compared to the rich, descriptive detail of the original Greek. He specifically examines metaphors of wild animals, the clashing of armies, and the omen of an eagle battling a snake.</summary>
<keywords>literary criticism, epic similes, Homeric vs. Virgilian style, Aeneid, Iliad, eagle and snake omen, ancient philology</keywords>

--- Page 425 ---
<meta>The previous page concluded a comparison between Virgil and Homer regarding their use of animal metaphors for warriors. Macrobius argued that Virgil’s descriptions of a hunted beast were "meager" and "contracted" compared to Homer’s "abundance" and "grandeur." This page continues the critique, moving from general metaphors to specific omens and personifications, specifically comparing Virgil’s description of Rumor to Homer’s description of Strife.</meta>

# BOOK V.

Virgil reports only the eagle’s prey, and does not take notice of the omen of Homer’s eagle, which, coming from the left, was preventing the advance of those who were winning; and, having received a bite from the captive snake, it dropped its prey in pain: and with a <term>favorable omen</term><note>original: "tripudio solistimo"; here referring to a specific divinatory sign where an object falls to the ground, usually associated with sacred chickens, but applied here to the eagle dropping the snake.</note>, it flies away with a cry testifying to its pain. By all these things, the "collusion" <note>original: "praevaricatio"; here suggesting a reversal or betrayal of victory.</note> of victory was signified. Because these details were omitted, which gave "soul" to the comparison, only a lifeless body remained in the Latin verses.

*Small at first through fear, soon she lifts herself into the air,*
*And walks upon the ground, and hides her head among the clouds.*
<note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 4.176–177. This describes "Fama" (Rumor or Fame).</note>

<margin>Iliad, Book 4.</margin>
> <note>original: "Ἥ τ’ ὀλίγη μὲν πρῶτα κορύσσεται, αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα / Οὐρανῷ ἐστήριξε κάρη καὶ ἐπὶ χθονὶ βαίνει."</note>
> *She who is small at first when she rears her head, but afterwards*
> *she plants her head in heaven while she walks upon the ground.*
<note>Homer, *Iliad* 4.442–443. This describes "Eris" (Strife or Contention).</note>

Homer said that Strife—that is, contention—begins from a small start, and afterwards grows upward even unto heaven. Virgil said the same thing about Rumor, but incongruously. For the characteristics of Contention and Rumor are not equal: because Contention, even if it proceeds all the way to mutual devastations and wars, is still Contention, and remains the same thing that grew. Rumor, however, when it goes out into the immense world, ceases to be Rumor, and becomes a known fact. For who would still call it "rumor" when a matter has become known from the earth to the sky? Furthermore, he could not even equal the <term>hyperbole</term><note>an intentional exaggeration for emphasis.</note> itself: Homer said "heaven," while Virgil said "the air and clouds." But this was the reason for not equaling everything he transcribed from his author: because in every part of his work he wished to introduce an imitation of some Homeric passage, yet he was not always able to equal that divinity with human strength. Consider this passage, which I want us to weigh together in our common judgment: Minerva added the glow of flames to her Diomedes while he was fighting, and the flash of his head and armor threatens for the soldier amidst the slaughter of the enemy.

<margin>Iliad, Book 5.</margin>
> <note>original: "Δαῖέ οἱ ἐκ κόρυθός τε καὶ ἀσπίδος ἀκάματον πῦρ"</note>
> *She kindled from his helmet and shield an unwearied fire.*
<note>Homer, *Iliad* 5.4. Referring to the goddess Athena (Minerva) assisting the hero Diomedes.</note>

->In the scales he placed two fates of death that brings long grief:<-

->For although Juno had already prophesied concerning Turnus:<-
->“Now I see the youth join battle with unequal fates;<-
->The day of the Fates and the hostile light approach.”<-
<note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 12.149–150. Macrobius argues that since the outcome was already stated, the following scene of weighing the fates is redundant.</note>
