->Jupiter himself holds up two scales with equal balance,<-
->and places in them the different fates of the two.<-
<note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 12.725–727. Virgil adapts Homer's scale-weighing scene.</note>

But these and other things must be forgiven in Virgil, who, through an excess of zeal for Homer, oversteps the limit. And in truth, he could not help but seem lesser in some respects, since he used this one <term>archetype</term> <note>A primary model or original pattern from which copies are made.</note> throughout all his poetry. For he fixed his eyes sharply on Homer, so as to rival not only his greatness, but also his simplicity, the immediacy of his speech, and his quiet majesty. From this comes the varied magnification of the different characters among his heroes; from this the intervention of the Gods; from this the authority of mythical elements; from this the expression of natural emotions; from this the pursuit of ancient monuments; from this the expansion of parables; from this the sound of a rushing torrent of speech; and from this the peak of splendor in individual things.

> Virgil found the imitation of Homer so sweet that he even wished to rival some of his faults. Furthermore, consider how much he imitated his <term>epithets</term> <note>Descriptive terms or phrases accompanying a name, like "swift-footed Achilles."</note> and other things that make speech more pleasing.

### CHAPTER XIV.

So sweet is the imitation of Homer to Virgil that he even imitated faults in the verses which are ignorantly criticized by some. I mean those lines which the Greeks call **acephalous**, **lagarous**, and **hypercatalectic**. He did not shun these here either, approving of the Homeric style, as they appear in his work:
<note>These are technical terms for irregular hexameter lines: **acephalous** (headless) lines are missing a syllable at the start; **lagarous** (hollow/weak) lines have a short syllable where a long one is expected in the middle; **hypercatalectic** lines have an extra syllable at the end.</note>

<term>Headless lines</term> <note>original Greek: ἀκέφαλοι. In poetry, these are lines of verse missing the first syllable, creating a sudden, jarring start.</note>, such as: "He rams against the gates," or "A path woven with blind walls," <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 11.890 and 5.589.</note> and similar examples. There are also <term>hollow lines</term> <note>original Greek: Λάγαροι. These are verses that contain "weak" or short syllables in the middle where a long, heavy beat is expected.</note>, which have short syllables in the middle of the verse instead of long ones: "And bar the stubborn doors," or "The father Latinus himself takes counsel and great undertakings." <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 11.881 and 7.249.</note> Then there are <term>over-full lines</term> <note>original Greek: ὑπερκαταληκτικοί (hypercatalectic). Verses that have one or more extra syllables at the end.</note>, which are a syllable longer than usual: "Nay, immediately all things..." or "Vulcan boils off the moisture." <note>Virgil, *Georgics* 1.281 and 1.295.</note> And also:

> They mix the froth of silver and living sulfur. <note>Virgil, *Georgics* 3.449.</note>

And, "The rough strawberry tree." <note>Virgil, *Georgics* 2.69.</note> In Homer, there are certain verses that seem "shaven" or "plucked" <note>Verses that sound more like casual speech than formal, rhythmic poetry.</note>, differing not at all from the common way of speaking. Virgil fell in love with these as well, despite their unpolished appearance in heroic verse:
<margin>Iliad, Book 11</margin> "one hundred and fifty chestnut horses, all of them mares." <note>Homer, *Iliad* 11.680.</note>

> Love conquers all, and let us yield to love. <note>Virgil, *Eclogues* 10.69.</note>
> Naked you will lie, Palinurus, on an unknown shore. <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 5.871.</note>

There are also pleasant repetitions which he did not avoid, such as:

->Even if Pan were to compete with me with Arcadia as judge,<-
->Even Pan would say he was defeated with Arcadia as judge.<-
<note>Virgil, *Eclogues* 4.58–59. Virgil repeats the phrase "Arcadia as judge" to mimic a rustic song style.</note>

How much he admired Homeric <term>epithets</term> <note>Descriptive nicknames or adjectives traditionally attached to a person or thing, like "swift-footed" Achilles.</note> is proven by his own imitation of them. Homer uses: "Child of fate, blessed by fortune"; "Bronze-armored"; "Bossed shields" <note>Shields with a central metal projection or "boss."</note>; "of breastplates"; "Newly polished"; "Dark-haired" <note>An epithet for Poseidon, the sea god.</note>; "Earth-shaker"; "Earth-shaker" <note>Homer uses two different Greek words for this, *Enosichthon* and *Enosigaios*.</note>; "Cloud-gatherer"; "The shady mountains and the echoing sea"; "Dark-hued." And there are a thousand such words, with which the varied majesty of that divine song sparkles like the stars. To these, your poet [Virgil] responds with his own: "Evil-counseling hunger"; "Golden-haired branches"; "Hundred-fold Briareus." <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 6.276, 6.137, and 6.287.</note> Add also: "Smoke-bearing night"—and many others which the diligent reader will recognize in almost every single verse. Often Homer, in the middle of a narrative, directs his speech as if to someone:

<margin>Iliad, Book 3</margin> "You would say he was a surly person and a fool besides."
<margin>Iliad, Book 10</margin> "You would not know which side the son of Tydeus belonged to."
<margin>Iliad, Book 4</margin> "Then you would not see the noble Agamemnon slumbering."

Nor did Virgil omit this technique:

*Likewise, that divine poet <note>Homer</note> brings back events that happened either a little or much earlier at opportune moments in the sequence of his narrative. He does this to avoid a purely historical style—which would mean simply listing events in the order they happened—while still ensuring he does not deprive us of the knowledge of the past. Achilles had destroyed Thebe, a city in Asia, and many others before he became angry. But Homer’s work took its starting point from the anger of Achilles. Therefore, so that we would not be ignorant of what happened before, he provides a timely narration of those events.*

### The differences in the catalogues between Virgil and Homer. CHAPTER XV.

<margin>of traveling</margin> When, however, the allies are enumerated—what the Greeks call a **catalogue**—Virgil attempted to imitate that same author of his <note>Homer</note>, but in several respects he deviated slightly from Homeric gravity. First, because Homer, bypassing Athens, Lacedaemon, and even Mycenae (the home of the army’s commander), placed **Boeotia** at the head of his catalogue. He did this not because of any superior dignity of that place, but because he chose a very well-known promontory as the starting point for his list. Proceeding from there, he describes now the inland parts, now the adjacent coastal areas. Then, by the disciplined method of one describing a route, he approaches each location among the connected places just as if he were a traveler making a journey. Nor does he allow the continuity of the regions to gap by any "leap" in his book; rather, proceeding in this <margin>manner of walking</margin> way, he returns to where he first departed, and thus everything his enumeration encompasses is completed in a circle.

In contrast, Virgil preserves no such order in commemorating the regions, but tears apart the sequence of locations with leaps. He first brings forward **Massicus** from **Clusium** and **Cosa**. **Abas** follows him, accompanied by a band from **Populonia** and **Elba**. After these, **Pisa** sent **Asilas**. It is too well known to need noting how far apart these places are in different parts of Etruria <note>Etruria is modern Tuscany. Macrobius is pointing out that Virgil’s list jumps geographically from the north to the south rather than following a map.</note>. Then he soon returns to **Caere**, **Pyrgi**, and **Graviscae**—places very near the city <note>Rome</note>—to which he gave **Astur** as leader. From here he hur-

<meta>The catchword "pit illum" (hurries him) completes the word "rapit." This suggests the text continues to describe the rapid pace of Virgil's poetic movement compared to Homer's steady "walking" pace.</meta>

<summary>Macrobius compares the "Catalogues of Ships/Heroes" in Homer and Virgil, arguing that while Homer follows a logical, geographical "traveler’s path," Virgil purposefully leaps between distant locations to create a more fragmented, poetic structure.</summary>

...takes Cygnus to Liguria, and Ocnus to Mantua. But even in the catalogue of Turnus's allies, if you wish to run through the layout of the places in your mind, you will find that he did not follow the geographical continuity of the regions. Furthermore, Homer mentions everyone he lists in his catalogue, recording them in battle whether they meet with good or bad fortune. And when he wishes to speak of those killed whom he did not include in the catalogue, he introduces them not by a specific man's name, but by a collective term for a multitude. And whenever he wants to signify a great slaughter, he says a "harvest of men" <note>original Latin: "messem hominū"</note> was made; he rarely gives a specific name outside the catalogue, whether adding them to the battle line or removing them.

But our Maro <note>A common medieval and Renaissance nickname for Virgil, taken from his cognomen Maro.</note> neglected the strictness of this observation. For he both passes over those named in the catalogue during the actual war, and names others in the war who were not mentioned before. He said that under the leader Massicus, a band of a thousand youths came who left the walls of Clusium and the town of Cosae. Later, Turnus flees on a ship on which King Osinius had been carried from the shores of Clusium—yet he had never named this Osinius before. And it is nonsensical for a king to serve under Massicus. Moreover, neither Massicus nor Osinius appears at all in the war itself. 

Furthermore, those whom he does mention—the "brave Gyas and brave Serestus," the "beautiful Equicolus," "Maivortian Haemon," "the most brave Umbro," and "Virbius, the most beautiful offspring of Hippolytus"—deserved no place among the ranks of the fighters, neither in glorious nor shameful mention. Astur, likewise Cupavo, and Cygnus (famous for the legends of Cygnus and Phaethon) provide no service in the battle; meanwhile, the obscure Halaesus <note>spelled "Alesus" in the source</note> and Sacrator do fight, as does Atinas, who was not mentioned before. 

Furthermore, among those he does name, there is often a careless confusion on his part. In the ninth book, Asilas lays low Corynaeus. Then, in the twelfth book, Corynaeus kills Ebusus:

> Confronting him, Corynaeus snatched a charred brand from the altar,
> and as Ebusus came and dealt a blow,
> he struck him in the face. <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 12.298–300. The critic is pointing out that Corynaeus appears to have died in Book 9 only to reappear in Book 12.</note>

*In this same way, Numa, whom Nisus kills <note>In Book 9 of the Aeneid.</note>, is later pursued by Aeneas—the "brave Numa." <note>In Book 10. This implies Virgil mistakenly used the same name for two different characters or forgot he had already killed him off.</note> Aeneas strikes down Camers in the tenth book, yet in the twelfth, the goddess Juturna takes on the appearance of Camers. Cloreus is killed by Camilla in the eleventh book, and then by Turnus in the twelfth. Regarding Palinurus, son of Iasus, and Iapyx, son of Iasus <note>term: Iasides (a patronymic meaning "son of Iasus")</note>, I wonder if they are meant to be brothers. Then there is the "son of Hyrtacus" <note>term: Hyrtacides</note>: he is Hippocoon, and yet again a "son of Hyrtacus" kills Corynaeus, and Asilas does the same. It is possible, of course, that two men simply shared one name. But where is that famous Homeric caution in these instances?*
<margin>Iliad, Book 2.</margin> *In Homer’s work, since there are two men named Ajax, he always distinguishes them; sometimes he says: "swift Ajax, son of Oileus" <note>original Greek: δϊλῆος ταχὺς Αἴας</note>; at other times, "Ajax, son of Telamon" <note>original Greek: Τελαμώνιος Αἴας</note>. Likewise, elsewhere he says:*
> *They were namesakes, possessing a single soul.* <note>original Greek: ἶσον θυμὸν ἔχοντε ὁμώνυμοι. Referring to the two Ajaxes fighting together in Iliad 13.704.</note>

*He never ceases to separate with identifying marks those whom he joins by name, so that the reader is not forced to struggle with suspicions regarding a variety of identities. On the other hand, in his own catalogue, Virgil took care to avoid causing boredom—a problem Homer did not guard against in the same way, as he frequently repeated the same phrasing: "And those who dwelt in Aspledon..." <note>original Greek: οἱ δ' ἄσπληδόν' ἔναιον</note>; "And those who held Euboea..." <note>original Greek: οἱ δ' εὔβοιαν ἔχον</note>; "And those who held Argos..." <note>original Greek: οἱ τ' ἄργοστ' ἔχον</note>; "and those who held hollow Lacedaemon, full of sea-monsters" <note>original Greek: οἵ τ' ἔχον κοιλὴν λακεδαίμονα κητώεσσαν</note>. Virgil, however, varies his phrasing as if avoiding repetition like a disgrace or a crime:*

> First Asper <note>In the standard text of Virgil, this is Mezentius; "Asper" may be a variant or a specific reference used by Macrobius.</note> enters the war from Tyrrhenian shores.
> Next to him, his son Lausus.
> After these, a chariot famous in renown through the fields.
> Then the twin brothers.
> Nor was the founder of Praeneste absent.
> But Messapus, tamer of horses.
> Behold, from the ancient blood of the Sabines.
> From here, the son of Agamemnon.
> And you, from the mountainous [lands].
> Indeed, there came also a priest from the Marrubian folk.
> And the offspring of Hippolytus went.

*Perhaps someone might think these varied forces are to be preferred over that divine simplicity* <note>The author is comparing Virgil's sophisticated variety to Homer's plain, repetitive style.</note>

<meta>catchword: to be preferred [preferendas]</meta>

Instead, he remains in the habit of those taking a census, enumerating them as if they were drawn up in a battle line. This is done through no other means than the names of the numbers <note>The author is referring to the rhythmic, almost mathematical way Homer counts out his heroes.</note>. Virgil <note>referred to here by his family name, Maro</note> so admired that massed enumeration in Homer that he expressed it in a way that I would almost say he translated it more elegantly.

->And similar passages.<-

Following that example are these lines from Virgil:

> *The ranks are thickened on the plains: the Argive youth, the Auruncan bands, the Rutulians, and the ancient Sicanians; the Sacranian lines stand ready, and the Labicians with their painted shields; those who plow your glades, O Tiber, and the sacred shore of Numicius, and who work with the plowshare the Rutulian hills and the Circeian ridge, over whose fields Jupiter Anxur <note>A local Italian form of Jupiter worshipped at Anxur, modern Terracina.</note> presides, etc.* <note>Aeneid 7.793-799.</note>

What a similarity there is in the catalogs of both poets, and how frequent are the maxims found in each! Then there are those points in which Virgil—whether by chance or by design—departs from Homer, and in which he disguises the imitation itself.

<margin>Iliad, Book 2</margin>
> And those who inhabited Pylos and lovely Arene, and Thryon, the ford of the Alpheius, and well-built Aipy, and those who lived in Kyparisseïs and Amphigeneia, and Pteleos, and Helos, and Dorion; there it was that the Muses met Thamyris the Thracian as he was coming from Oechalia, from the house of Eurytus the Oechalian, and put a stop to his singing. > Of these, Tlepolemus, famous with the spear, was the leader; he whom Astyocheia bore to the might of Hercules, the woman Hercules had brought from Ephyra, from the river Selleïs. <note>original Greek: Τῶν μὲν Τληπόλεμος δουρικλυτὸς ἡγεμόνευε... Iliad 2.653-659.</note>

And so on, by which means he extended the reader's delight. Virgil <note>referred to here as Maro</note> followed his master in this; in his first catalog, he tells stories now of Aventinus, now of Hippolytus; in the second catalog, the story of Cygnus is his theme. Thus, this interwoven charm cures the weariness of the narrations. Indeed, in all the books of the *Georgics* <note>Virgil's "Farming Poems," which are essentially instructional manuals in verse.</note>, he did this same thing with the greatest elegance. For after the technical instructions—which by their nature are a dry subject—he concluded each book by inserting a theme summoned from outside the main topic, so that he might renew the reader’s mind or hearing. The first book ends with the signs of storms; the second with the praise of country life; the third finishes with a plague among the cattle; and the end of the fourth is the famous—and far from idle—narrative of Orpheus and Aristeus. Thus, in every work by Maro, his <margin>*shines forth</margin> imitation of Homer shines. Homer so stuffed his entire poetry with meaningful thoughts that his individual <term>apophthegms</term> <note>From the Greek *apophthegmata*: concise, pithy sayings or maxims.</note> serve as proverbs in everyone’s mouth, such as:

In some matters, I know not whether by chance or by design, he <note>Virgil</note> has departed from the Homeric school. Homer preferred to be ignorant of Fortune, and commits all things to be ruled by the single decree which they call <term>μοῖραν</term> <note>Moira: the Greek word for Fate or "one's portion."</note>; so much so that this word <term>τύχη</term> <note>Tyche: the Greek word for Luck or Fortune.</note> is not named in any part of the Homeric volume. Conversely, Virgil not only knows and remembers Fortune, but even attributes omnipotence to her; though the Philosophers who name her intend that she can do nothing by her own power, but is the servant of the decree, or rather of providence.

And in myths or in histories he sometimes does the same. Aegeon in Homer's work provides aid to Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note>. The verses of Maro <note>Virgil</note> arm him against Jove. Eumedes, the son of Dolon, famous in war, reflects his parent in spirit and hand; whereas in Homer, Dolon is a coward. Homer admits no mention of the Judgment of Paris. Virgil did not act with enough skill in beginning the war between the Trojans and the Latins. From there, the things he translated from Apollonius and Pindar. How he delighted in Greek words as well as their inflections. 
->CHAPTER XVII.<-

*What Virgil <note>original Latin: *Vergilio*</note> gained from Homer is most obvious from this: when the necessity of the plot forced Maro <note>Virgil's cognomen, or family name</note> to arrange a beginning for the war—something Homer did not have to do, as he took the "Wrath of Achilles" as his starting point, which occurred only in the tenth year of the war—Virgil labored to bring forth something new. He made the accidental wounding of a deer the cause of the riot. But seeing this was too slight and much too childish, he heightened the sorrow of the country folk so that their impulse would be sufficient to start a war. But the servants of Latinus <note>The king of the Latins</note>, and especially those in charge of the royal stable, were not ignorant of the treaty Latinus had entered into with the Trojans, nor of the gifts of horses and the chariot team; therefore, they should not have brought war upon the offspring of the gods. What happens then? The greatest of the goddesses <note>Juno</note> is brought down from heaven, and the greatest of the Furies <note>Allecto</note> is summoned from Tartarus. Snakes are scattered about as if on a stage, giving birth to madness. The Queen <note>Amata</note> is not only led out from the inner rooms of matronly modesty, but is forced to run wild through the middle of the city. Not content with this, she seeks the woods, calling the other mothers into a partnership of madness. A chorus that was once modest now goes wild in a <term>Bacchic</term> <note>pertaining to Bacchus, the god of wine and frenzy</note> frenzy, and insane <term>Orgia</term> <note>secret, ecstatic religious rites</note> are celebrated. Why say more? I would have preferred that Maro, in this part as well, had followed his own master <note>Homer</note>, or any other of the Greeks.*

*I did not say "another" without reason, because he did not harvest his vintage from the clusters of just one vine. Rather, he turned to his own use whatever he found worth imitating anywhere: so much so, that from the fourth book of the <term>Argonautica</term> <note>An epic poem about Jason and the Argonauts</note>, whose author is Apollonius, he took a book of the Aeneid...*

Now listen to Virgil’s verses, so that you might say he rather began them than brought them to perfection.

> *The port is sheltered from the approach of winds, and vast*
> *in itself, but nearby Etna thunders with terrifying ruin.*

Now, in the first place, Pindar followed the truth and described the matter as it actually is, and as can be witnessed there with one's own eyes: that Etna smokes by day and flames by night. Virgil, however, while laboring to find noisy and resounding words, confuses the two times of day without making any distinction. Furthermore, Pindar, imitating Greek sources, brilliantly described how the mountain "vomits fire," how "rivers flow with smoke," and how "tawny and twisting volumes of flame" are carried into the reaches of the sea like fiery serpents. But here, your poet [Virgil], wishing to interpret "a glowing stream of smoke" <note>original Greek: ῥόον καπνοῦ αἴθωνα (*rhoon kapnou aithona*)</note>, has piled things up clumsily and excessively; he also translated "fountains" <note>original Greek: κρουνὸς (*krounos*)</note> as "balls of flame," which is a harsh and inaccurate <note>original Greek: ἀκύρως (*akyros*), a rhetorical term meaning the word is used improperly or does not fit the context</note> choice. It is beyond words that he described a black cloud smoking with a pitch-black whirlwind and "white-hot" ash. <note>Macrobius is critiquing Virgil’s description of Etna in *Aeneid* III.572–573.</note> For things that are white-hot are not usually smoky, nor are they black—unless, perhaps, he used the word "white-hot" <note>original Latin: *candente*</note> in a common and improper sense to mean "boiling" rather than "shining." For the term *candens* is derived from brightness <note>original: *candor*</note>, not from heat. 
<margin>to be raised up</margin> Moreover, as for his statement that crags are "belched forth and raised up," <note>The margin note *erectari* (to be raised up) contrasts with the text's *eructari* (to be belched forth), noting a textual variant or a specific point of criticism regarding Virgil's verb choice.</note> and that these same rocks are immediately liquefied and groan, and gather into balls toward the air: this was neither written by Pindar nor ever heard of in any account; of all the things called "monsters" in poetry, it is the most monstrous. 

Finally, consider how willingly he yielded himself to the Greek tongue, as you may judge from the frequent Greek-derived words he employs: *Dread Ulysses*, *Caves of wild beasts*, *Daedalian roofs*, *Rhodopean towers*, *High Panchaea*, and the *Getae*, and the *Hebrus*, and *Actian Orithyia*. <note>Virgil frequently used Greek-style epithets and geographic names to give his Latin poetry an elevated, epic tone.</note> And:

> Where the Maenad, hearing the cry of Bacchus, is stirred by the triennial
> rites, and nocturnal Cithaeron calls with a shout. <note>A reference to the Bacchic revels on Mount Cithaeron.</note> And,

->He says:<-

> *Glaucus, and Panopea, and Melicertes, son of Ino.* And,
> *The swift Tritons, and the monstrous sea-creatures.* <note>original: *cete*. Virgil uses the Greek neuter plural ending here rather than a Latin one.</note>

Indeed, he is so delighted by Greek declensions <note>term: declensions — the way noun endings change to show their role in a sentence, such as the subject or the object.</note> that he said *Mnesthea* <note>Greek accusative ending</note> instead of *Mnestheum*. Just as he said elsewhere: *Not by his brother Mnestheus*. And he preferred to say *Orphi* <note>original: *Orphi*, a Greek-style grammatical form</note> instead of *Orpheus*, declining it in the Greek fashion, as in:

> *Orpheus born of Calliopea, and lovely Apollo born of Linus.* And,
> *— O citizens, we have seen Diomedes.*

In these names, the accusative <note>term: accusative — the "object" case in grammar, indicating who or what receives the action.</note> follows the Greek form ending in *e*. For if anyone thinks he spoke in Latin by saying *Diomedem*, the rhythmic health of the verse would be found wanting. Finally, he preferred to entitle all his poems in Greek: *Bucolica* <note>Pastoral poems</note>, *Georgica* <note>Agricultural poems</note>, and the *Aeneis* <note>The Story of Aeneas</note>, the very formation of which name is foreign to the rules of the Latin language.

### Things that Virgil translated so secretly from the Greeks that it is difficult to recognize their origin. CHAPTER XVIII.

<margin>*those things</margin>
But enough regarding those matters, most of which are known to all Romans, and some to at least a few. I come now to * other things, which, having been unearthed from the inner shrines of Greek literature, are known to no one except those who have drank deeply from Greek learning. For this poet was as scrupulously and anxiously learned as he was disguised and almost secretly so; he translated many things in such a way that it is difficult to know where they were translated from. In the opening of the *Georgics*, he placed these verses:

> *Liber and nourishing Ceres, if by your gift the earth* <note>Liber is the Italian god identified with the Greek Bacchus/Dionysus; Ceres is identified with Demeter.</note>
> *Exchanged the Chaonian acorn for the rich ear of grain,*
> *And mixed the cups of Achelous with the discovered grape.* <note>Achelous was a Greek river god; Virgil uses his name here as a poetic way to say "water."</note>

The crowd of grammarians <note>A "crowd of grammarians" refers to the standard schoolteachers of the time.</note> delivers nothing more to their students regarding these verses than this: that it was by the work of Ceres that humans ceased their ancient diet and used grain instead of acorns; and that Liber was the discoverer of the vine.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Chapter 18 regarding Virgil’s "hidden" Greek borrowings. The previous page ended by introducing a specific instance where Virgil uses a Greek poetic device to describe water.</meta>

<header>OF THE SATURNALIA</header>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<meta>catchword: to be called</meta>

...that wine was provided for human drink, to which water should be mixed. But why did Virgil name the **Achelous** <note>Achelous was a major river in Greece, often personified as a river-god.</note> river in particular when he wished water to be understood? No one even asks, or even suspects that something more learned lies beneath. Having scrutinized this more deeply, we have noticed that the learned poet spoke in the manner of the most ancient Greeks (as authority will show), among whom **Achelous** was properly used to signify water. Nor was this without reason, for the cause of this matter has also been recorded with care. But before I set forth the cause, I will show by the testimony of an ancient poet that this manner of speaking was widespread, so that they spoke of "Achelous" for any water. Aristophanes, the old comic writer, says this in his comedy *Cocalus*: <note>original Greek: Ἤμην ἄξιον βάρος. Ἤπειρε γάρ τοι μὴ οἴνου καὶ μιγεὶς πόμα Ἀχελώῳ.</note>

> I was a heavy load.
> For indeed, the drink was not mixed
> of wine and **Achelous**.

I was weighed down, he says, by wine to which water had not been mixed—that is, by pure wine. <note>term: *mero* — undiluted wine, which the Greeks and Romans usually mixed with water for social drinking.</note> Why they were accustomed to speak this way, Ephorus, a most famous historical writer, shows in his second book with these words: <note>original Greek passage from Ephorus follows.</note>

> While neighboring people sacrifice to other rivers, it has happened that all humanity honors **Achelous** alone. They do not use common names in place of specific ones, but rather they transfer the specific name of **Achelous** to the common noun. For we call water in general—which is the common name—"Achelous," after that specific river's name. We often name common things after specific ones, such as calling the Athenians "Greeks," or the Lacedaemonians "Peloponnesians." Regarding this puzzle, we can say nothing truer than that the oracles from **Dodona** <note>Dodona was the site of the oldest Greek oracle, where Zeus's will was interpreted through the rustling of oak leaves.</note> almost always added the instruction to sacrifice to **Achelous**; so that many, thinking the oracle meant not the river flowing through **Acarnania** <note>A region in western Greece.</note>, but water as a whole [called it] **Achelous** by the oracle...

# BOOK V.

...to be called, they appropriate) the names of the god. The proof is that we are accustomed to speak this way when referring to the divine. For we most often call water **Achelous** in oaths, in prayers, and in sacrifices, all of which pertain to the gods. <note>This concludes the quote from the historian Ephorus, explaining that because the Achelous was so revered, his name became a holy synonym for all water used in religious rites.</note>

Can it be shown more clearly that **Achelous** was commonly used by the ancient Greeks to mean any water whatsoever? This is why Virgil, with great learning, wrote that **Father Liber** <note>term: *Liber Pater* — an ancient Italian god of fertility and wine, identified with Bacchus.</note> mixed wine with the **Achelous** <note>Referencing Virgil's *Georgics* 1.9: *poculaque inventis Acheloia miscuit uvis* ("and mixed the Achelous [water] with the discovered grapes [wine]").</note>. Although the evidence of the comic poet Aristophanes and the historian Ephorus already provided is sufficient proof of this, we shall go even further. For **Didymus**, easily the most learned of grammarians, having set out the reason mentioned above by Ephorus, added another in these words: <note>Didymus "Chalcenterus" was a prolific scholar in Alexandria known for his vast output of commentaries.</note>

> It is better to say that because the **Achelous** is the oldest of all rivers, men pay him honor by calling all flowing streams simply by his name. At any rate, **Hegesilaus** has shown in the first book of his *History* that **Achelous** is the oldest of all rivers; for he said: "**Ocean** marries **Tethys** his own sister, and from them are born three thousand rivers, but **Achelous** is the oldest of them and is most honored."

Although these examples are more than enough to prove the ancient custom where **Achelous** was used as a general name for all water, we should also add the authority of **Euripides**, the most noble writer of tragedies. The grammarian Didymus cited him in his books titled *On the Language of Tragedy* <note>original Greek: τραγῳδουμένης λέξεως (*Tragoidoumene Lexis*)</note> with these words:

> Euripides says that all water is **Achelous** in his play *Hypsipyle*. Speaking of water that is very far from **Acarnania** <note>The region in western Greece where the physical Achelous river is located.</note> where the river **Achelous** is located, he says: "I will show the silver stream of Achelous."

In the seventh book [of the *Aeneid*] are those verses in which the **Hernici** people and their most noble city, as it was then, **Anagnia**, are listed: <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 7.682-684. The author is transitioning to a new example of Virgil's antiquarian precision.</note>

<margin>Aeneid, Book 7</margin>
> —Those whom wealthy Anagnia feeds,
> And you, Father Amasenus: not all of them have arms,
> Nor do shields or chariots ring. The greater part scatter
> Slugs of bluish lead; a part carry two darts 
> In hand; and tawny wolf-skin caps 
> They have as covering for the head; they set down 
> The bare tracks of the left foot; a raw-hide boot covers the other.
<note>original: "Quos diues Anagnia paſcit... uestigia nuda ſiniſtri Inſtituere pedis, crudus tegit altera pero." These lines from Virgil describe the Hernici, an ancient tribe of Latium.</note>

That this custom existed in Italy—to go to war with one foot shod and the other bare—I have nowhere yet found, as far as I know. However, I shall now make it plain by a most reliable author that this was a custom among some of the Greeks. In this matter, one must marvel at the most hidden diligence of this poet. For since he had read that the **Hernici** <note>An ancient Italic tribe living in the valley of the Sacco River.</note> (to whom Anagnia belongs) were descended from the **Pelasgians** <note>term: *Pelasgians* — a term used by ancient Greek writers to refer to the prehistoric indigenous inhabitants of the Greek world and their descendants.</note>, and were named so after a certain leader of theirs named Hernicus: he assigned to the Hernici a custom which he had read regarding **Aetolia**, as the Hernici are an ancient colony of the Pelasgians. 

Indeed, **Julius Hyginus** <note>A scholar and friend of Ovid who served as the head of the Palatine Library under Emperor Augustus.</note> proves with no few words in the second book of his *On Cities* that the man Hernicus was a Pelasgian leader of the Hernici. Moreover, the most famous tragic writer **Euripides** shows that it was the custom for the Aetolians to go into battle with only one foot shod. In his tragedy entitled *Meleager*, a messenger is brought in describing the attire of each of the leaders who had gathered to catch the boar. <note>Referring to the Calydonian Boar hunt, a famous episode in Greek myth.</note> In that play are these verses:

> Telamon held a golden eagle upon his small shield,
> A defense against the beast, and crowned his head with grapes,
> Honoring Salamis, his blessed fatherland.
> And there against the hated beast was the Arcadian Atalanta, 
> With her dogs and holding her bow, and the double-mouthed 
> Blade of her axe; her robes were simple. But the sons 
> Of Thestius had the left track of their foot unshod...
<note>original Greek: "Τελαμὼν δ' χρυσοῦν αἰετὸν πέλτης ἔπι... Παῖδες τὸ λαιὸν ἴχνος ἀνάρβυλοι ποδὸς." Euripides explains that the sons of Thestius left the left foot bare to ensure a firm, non-slip grip on the earth while pivoting.</note>

BOOK V.

> And one man went in sandals, that he might have
> a light knee, as is the custom for all Aetolians.
<note>original Greek: "Τὸν δ' ἐν πεδίλοις, ὡς ἐλαφρίζον γόνυ ἔχοιεν, ὅς δὴ πᾶσιν Αἰτωλοῖς νόμος." This is a fragment from a lost play of Euripides, likely *Meleager*, describing the Aetolians, a people from central Greece.</note>

Do you notice how very carefully the words of Euripides were preserved by Virgil? For that poet says:

> The left track of the foot was unshod.
<note>original Greek: "Τὸ λαιὸν ἴχνος ἀνάρβυλοι ποδός."</note>

And Virgil likewise described the same foot as being bare: *They set down the bare tracks of the left foot.* In this matter, so that our devotion to study may be better proved to you, we shall not remain silent about a fact known to very few: that Euripides was criticized by Aristotle, who contended that this was a result of Euripides’ ignorance. He argued that the Aetolians do not have the left foot bare, but rather the right. So that I may prove this rather than merely asserting it, I will provide the words of Aristotle from the second book of his treatise *On Poets*, in which he says, speaking of Euripides:

> Euripides says the sons of Thestius <note>Thestius was a legendary king of Aetolia; his sons were uncles to the hero Meleager.</note> came with their left foot unshod; at least he says that "unshod was the left track of the foot, and the other in sandals so that they might have a light knee," although the custom for the Aetolians is exactly the opposite. For they shoe the left foot and leave the right foot unshod; for I believe it is thought that the leading foot should be light, rather than the one that remains fixed.
<note>original Greek: "Τοὺς δ' Θεστίου κούρους... τὸν δὲ δέξιον ἀνυποδετῆσαι..." Aristotle’s point is that the foot used for kicking or stepping forward (the right) should be light/bare, while the stabilizing foot (the left) should be protected by a shoe.</note>

Since these things are so, you see nevertheless that Virgil preferred to use Euripides as his authority rather than Aristotle. For I would hardly believe that a man so painstakingly learned was ignorant of these facts. He rightly <margin>* or Aristotle</margin> preferred Euripides. For he possessed a great familiarity with the writers of Greek tragedies, a fact which can be inferred either from what has already been said or from what will be said shortly.

[She] had taken it away, and had condemned her head to the Stygian Underworld.

Then Iris, sent by Juno, cut her hair and brought it to the Underworld. Virgil did not invent this story out of nothing, as **Cornutus**—otherwise a very learned man—estimates, who wrote a note of this kind on these verses: *It is unknown where this story comes from, that hair must be taken from the dying. But he was accustomed to inventing things in the poetic manner, such as the story of the golden bough.* These are the words of Cornutus. But I am ashamed that such a great man, and one most learned in **Greek literature**, was ignorant of the most famous play of **Euripides**, the *Alcestis*. For in this play,
<margin>* elsewhere: Charon</margin> **Orcus** <note>The Roman personification of Death, here representing the Greek Thanatos.</note> is brought onto the stage carrying a sword, with which he cuts a lock of hair from Alcestis, and he speaks thus:
<margin>Charon speaks.</margin>
> You may speak much, yet you will gain nothing more.
> The woman shall indeed go down to the halls of Hades.
> I go toward her, so that I may begin the rite with my sword.
> For he is sacred to the gods beneath the earth,
> Whosoever’s hair this blade shall hallow.
<note>original Greek: "Πόλλ᾽ ἂν σὺ λέξας, οὐδὲν ἂν πλέον λάβοις. Ἡ δ᾽ οὖν γυνὴ κάτεισιν εἰς ᾅδου δόμους. Στείχω δ᾽ ἐπ᾽ αὐτὴν, ὡς κατάρξωμαι ξίφει. Ἱερὸς γὰρ οὗτος τῶν κατὰ χθονὸς θεῶν, Ὅτου τόδ᾽ ἔγχος κρατὸς ἁγνίσει τρίχα." From Euripides, *Alcestis*, lines 70–76.</note>

This tradition was handed down, I believe, and Virgil followed it when he introduced the story of the cutting of the hair. Moreover, the Greeks use the word <term>hallow</term> <note>original: ἁγνίσαι (*hagnisai*)</note> to mean "to consecrate to the gods." Hence your poet says, speaking in the character of Iris:
> —This I carry as sacred to **Dis**,
> as commanded, and I release you from that body.
<note>original: "—Hunc ego Diti / Sacrum iussa fero, teq; isto corpore soluo." From *Aeneid* 4.702-3. "Dis" is another name for Pluto/Hades.</note>

Now, because I have proved almost everything I said above by the authority of the **Tragedians**, I shall also note that which was handled by **Sophocles**. For in the fourth book, Virgil depicts **Elissa** <note>Another name for Queen Dido of Carthage.</note>—after she has been abandoned by Aeneas—fleeing as if to the incantations and devotions of priests and sorceresses; and among other things, he says that for the sake of calming her love, herbs were sought which were to be "cut with bronze sickles." Moreover, a tragedy by Sophocles displays the very thing we are looking for even in its title. For it is inscribed <term>The Root-Cutters</term> <note>original Greek: ῥιζοτόμοι (Rhizotomoi). <note>original Greek: "Ἡ δ’ ἐξοπίσω χερὸς ὄμμα τρέπουσα / Ὀπὸν ἀργινεφῆ σάζοντα τομῆς / Καλκείοισι κάδοις δέχεται."</note>

Thus says Sophocles: from whose authority Virgil undoubtedly brought forth the **bronze sickles**. In general, however, many things indicate that bronze was commonly used for divine matters: and especially in those sacred rites by which they wished to soothe some, or devote <note>In a ritual sense, "devoting" someone usually meant a religious curse or consecration to the gods of the Underworld.</note> them, or finally to drive out diseases. I pass over that line of **Plautus**, when he says: *The village, the disease, and bronze dwell with me:* and what Virgil says elsewhere,
> —the sounds of the Curetes, and the clashing bronze.
<note>original Latin: "—Curetum sonitus, crepitantiaq; æra." From Virgil's Georgics, 4.151, referring to the clashing of shields to protect the infant Jupiter.</note>

But I shall set down the words of the most diligent and learned **Carminius**: who in the second book of his *On Italy* speaks thus: *And so I find that formerly even the **Tuscans** [Etruscans] were accustomed to use a bronze plowshare when cities were founded, in their traditional rites: and among the **Sabines** there were bronze knives with which the priests were shorn.* After these words of Carminius, it would be a long task if I wished to review in how many places the most ancient of the Greeks were accustomed to use the sounds of bronze as a most powerful thing. But for the present work, it is enough for us to have shown that sickles

> reared in his mother's grove around the Symethus
> rivers, where the altar of Palicus is rich and unappeasable.
<note>original Latin: "Stabat in egregijs Arcentis filius armis, / Pictus acu chlamydem, & ferrugine clarus Ibera, / Insignis facie : genitor quem miserat Arcens, / Eductum matris luco Symætia circum / Flumina, pinguis ubi implacabilis ara Palici." From Aeneid 9.581-585.</note>

Who this god Palicus is—or rather, who these Palici gods are, for there are two—I have found in no Latin author at all, as far as I know. But Maro [Virgil] drew this story out from the most hidden literature of the Greeks. For just as the Symethus river, which he mentions in these verses, is in Sicily, so too are the Palici gods worshipped in Sicily. Aeschylus the tragedian—a man who was certainly Sicilian <note>Aeschylus spent the final years of his life in Sicily and died there; Macrobius considers him an expert on local lore.</note>—was the first of all to commit them to writing. He also expressed the interpretation of their name—which the Greeks call <term>etymology</term> <note>original Greek: ἐτυμολογίαν</note>—in his verses. But before I provide the verses of Aeschylus, the history of the Palici must be explained in a few words. 

In Sicily, there is the Symethus river. Near it, the Nymph Thalia, pregnant by the embrace of Jove, prayed that the earth might gape open for her because she feared Juno. This was done. But when the time for the maturity of the infants she had carried in her womb arrived, the earth opened again, and two infants came forth from the womb of Thalia and emerged. They were called the Palici, <term>from coming back again</term> <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ πάλιν ἱκέσθαι (apo tou palin hikesthai). This is a folk etymology connecting the name to 'returning' from the earth.</note>, because having first been immersed in the earth, they then returned from there. Not far from that place are small but immensely deep lakes, always bubbling with a spring of waters, which the inhabitants <margin>Craters</margin> call "craters," and they name them the Dellos. They believe these are the brothers of the Palici, and they are held in the highest worship. Especially regarding the demanding of an oath near them, a present and effective divine power is shown. For when a person is sought to be trusted in a case of a denied theft or a similar matter, and an oath from...

<header>OF THE SATURNALIA</header>

...[of the swelling] rivers <note>original: μαζομένων ποταμῶν</note>, he says: Those called the Palici <note>The Palici were twin Sicilian deities associated with volcanic springs and the sanctity of oaths.</note> by the inhabitants are considered indigenous gods. They have brothers, which are low-lying craters <note>These "craters" are the Lago di Naftia, volcanic vents that bubbled with gas.</note>; those approaching them must be pure from all pollution and sexual intercourse, and must wear new garments. A heavy smell of sulfur arises from them, which causes a terrible heaviness in the head <note>original: καρηβαρίαν; a reference to the toxic effects of volcanic gases like carbon dioxide or sulfur dioxide.</note> to those standing nearby. The water is murky, and in color very similar to white earth. It is carried up in billows and bubbles, like the eddies of boiling water being cast up. They say the depth of these craters is infinite, so that even oxen falling in disappear, as well as a driven pair of mules, and even leaping livestock. 

There is a most great oath for the Sicilians there, once those challenged have been purified. Those administering the oath, holding a tablet, proclaim to those being sworn the matters for which they demand the oath. The one being sworn—waving a branch, veiled, unbelted and wearing only a single tunic <note>original: μονοχίτων; this ritual undressing and the use of a branch signify a state of religious vulnerability and purity.</note>—and touching the crater, recites the oath dictated to him. If he keeps the spoken oaths, he goes home unharmed; but if he becomes a transgressor against the gods, he dies on the spot. When these things happen, they promise to provide guarantors to the priests; if any new circumstance occurs, they owe a purification to those who remain. Around this place, the Palikani inhabited a city named after these spirits, Palikane.

Thus says Polemon. But Xenagoras also writes thus in the third book of his *History* concerning the divination of the place: "And when the land of the Sicilians was barren, they sacrificed to a certain hero, as the oracle of the Palici had directed them; and after the return of fertility, they filled the altar of the Palici with many gifts."

The explanation of the Virgilian passage <note>Referring to Aeneid 9.585.</note> is now complete (I believe) and supported by suitable authorities. Our men of letters <note>original: literatores; here referring to schoolmasters or grammarians who might provide only superficial explanations.</note> do not think this passage is obscure, being content either to know themselves or to suggest to their pupils that "Palicus" is the name of a certain god. But who he might be...

### On Gargarus and Mysia from the first book of the Georgics.

#### CHAPTER XX.

**N**or shall we leave those verses untouched which are found in the first book of the *Georgics* <note>original: γεωργικῶν; Virgil's famous didactic poem on agriculture</note>:

> O farmers, pray for moist summers and serene winters;
> For in winter dust the grain is most joyful,
> And the field is glad. In no other cultivation does Mysia so greatly
> Boast, and Gargarus itself wonders at its own harvests.

Although the meaning here seems somewhat obscure and expressed a bit more intricately than is the habit of this poet, it nevertheless contains a point to be noted which comes from Greek antiquity: what are these "Gargara" <note>Usually referred to as Gargarus in the singular, it refers to both a mountain peak and a city</note> which Virgil intended to be a model of fertility? These Gargara, then, are in Mysia, which is a province of the Hellespont. However, the meaning of the name and the location is twofold. For both a peak of Mount Ida and a town situated beneath that same mountain are called by this name. Homer established the meaning of the peak in this way:

<margin>Iliad, Book 8</margin>
> And he came to Ida, mother of wild beasts, rich in springs, 
> To Gargarus. <note>original: Ἴδην δ' ἵκανεν πολυπίδακα μητέρα θηρῶν / Γάργαρον.</note>

Here, the context itself indicates that it is appropriate for Gargarus to be understood as the most prominent point of the mountain, for he is speaking about Jupiter. But elsewhere too, as Homer himself testifies, it is expressed more clearly:

> Thus the Father slept peacefully upon the height of Gargarus. <note>original: ὣς ὁ μὲν ἀτρέμας εὗδε πατὴρ ἀνὰ γαργάρῳ ἄκρῳ</note>

And Epicharmus <note>A Greek dramatist and philosopher often credited with the invention of comedy</note>, a very ancient poet, in the play entitled *The Trojans*, put it thus:

> Zeus, dwelling upon snowy Gargarus. <note>original: Ζεὺς ἀνα ναίων γάργαρ᾽ ἀγάννιφα</note>

From these examples, it is crystal clear that the peak of Mount Ida is called Gargarus.

to be called <note>completing the word *appellitari* from the previous page</note>. As for those who have spoken of Gargarus as a town, I shall enumerate them. Ephorus, a most famous writer of histories, says in his fifth book:

> After Assos is the city of Gargarus nearby. <note>original: Μετὰ δὲ τὴν Ἄσσον ἐστὶ Γάργαρα πλησίον πόλις.</note>

Not only Ephorus, but also Phileas, an ancient writer, in that book titled *Asia*, mentions it thus:

> After Assos is a city named Gargarus,
> And next to this is Antandrus. <note>original: Μετὰ Ἄσσον πόλις ἐστὶν ὄνομα Γάργαρα, Ταύτης ἔχεται Ἄντανδρος.</note>

A book of *Elegies* by Aratus is also cited, in which he says this about a certain poet named Diotimus:

> I mourn Diotimus, who sits among the rocks 
> teaching the children of the Gargarans their alpha and beta. <note>original: Αἰάζω Διότιμον ὃς ἐν πέτρῃσι κάθηται / Γαργαρέων παισὶ βῆτα καὶ ἄλφα λέγων. A reference to a poet reduced to teaching the basic alphabet.</note>

From these verses, the name of the citizens also becomes known, because they are called **Gargarans**. Since, therefore, it is established that Gargarus is to be understood now as a mountain peak and now as a town situated beneath that same mountain, Virgil is speaking not of the mountain top, but of the town.

Let us inquire, however, why he placed Gargarus as a place so fertile in crops. It is well enough established that all of Mysia was considered to have rich crops, evidently on account of the moisture of the soil. Whence Virgil, in the aforementioned verses, having said "Moist summers," added, "In no other cultivation does Mysia so greatly 
<margin>* as if he were saying</margin>
boast"; * as if to say: Every region that has opportune moisture will equal the fertility of the fields of Mysia. But when Homer says: "And he came to Ida, rich in springs" <note>original: Ἴδην δ' ἵκανε πολυπίδακα</note>, he designates the moist field lying beneath the mountain. For *polypidaca* <note>original: πολυπίδακα; a Greek epithet for Mount Ida</note> signifies "abounding in springs."

From this, these Gargarans possessed such a great abundance of crops that whoever wished to express a large number of anything would name "Gargara" to represent an immense multitude. Alcaeus is a witness, who says thus in the tragedy *The Heavens* <note>original: Cœlo; Alcaeus was a lyric poet, but this likely refers to a lost dramatic work</note>:

> I happened to be bringing more from nearby... <note>original: Ἐτύγχανον μὲν ἀγχόθεν πλείους φέρων</note>

# BOOK V

->To the festival, as much as is likely,<-
->I see from above a **multitude** of men in a circle.<-
<note>original: Εἰς τὴν ἑορτὴν ὅσον οἷον εἰκὸς / Ὁρῶ δ’ ἄνωθεν γαργαρά ἀνθρώπων κύκλῳ. The poet uses the word "gargara"—the name of the city—to mean a vast number or a "heap."</note>

He clearly used the word **Gargara** (as you can see) to mean a multitude. The comic poet Aristomenes did the same in his *Tales*: "For we have within a **gargara** of men." <note>original: ἔνδον γὰρ ἡμῖν ἐστὶν ἀνδρῶν γαργαρα.</note> However, the comic playwright Aristophanes tries to express an even more uncountable number—in his characteristic witty style—by inventing a word composed of "sand" and "Gargara." In his play *The Acharnians*, he says:

> How much my very heart has been bitten!
> I have been pleased by few things—very few, only four.
> But the things that pained me were **sand-hundred-gargaras**.
> Come, let me see: what have I enjoyed that was worth a "hello"?
<note>original: Ὅσα δὴ δέδηγμαι... ψαμμοκοσιογάργαρα. This is a comedic "mashing" of words: sand (*psammo*), hundreds (*-kosia*), and the city of Gargara, used to mean "squillions."</note>

<margin>*sand-hundreds</margin>
<note>original: *ψαμμοκόσια</note>
The Roman scholar Varro often used the word "sand" by itself to represent a large amount in his *Menippean Satires*. But Aristophanes added **Gargara** to signify a number that is truly beyond counting. According to these examples, the meaning of Virgil's verses is as follows: when the weather of the year is such that the winter is dry and dusty, but the summer solstice is rainy, the crops come forth most excellently. These conditions are so necessary for the fields that, without them, even those fields of **Mysia** <note>A region in northwest Asia Minor (modern Turkey) famed for its fertility.</note>—which are by nature most fertile—would not live up to their reputation for productivity. 

He mentions **Gargara** in Mysia by name for a specific reason: because that city is situated at the very base of Mount Ida, it is naturally irrigated by the waters flowing down from above. One might therefore think it does not particularly need the summer rains. To provide further evidence that not only Gargarus but the fields of the entire province of Mysia are naturally moist, we can call Aeschylus <note>The famous Greek tragedian.</note> as a witness: "**The overflows of Mysia.**" <note>original: Μύση ἐπιῤῥοαί.</note> We have already discussed what Virgil borrowed from the Greeks in this passage. We will add this further point for the sake of interest, and to show how our Virgil drew ornaments for his work from every source among the ancients, from which he said:

> —**Spelt is most joyful in the winter dust.**
<note>original: Hyberno letissima puluere farra. This is from Virgil’s *Georgics* (1.101), suggesting that a dry winter leads to a better harvest.</note>

# On the Types of Drinking Vessels. CHAPTER XXI.

<margin>From various passages of Virgil.</margin>
Virgil frequently uses Greek names for drinking vessels, such as *carchesia*, *cymbia*, *canthari*, and *scyphi*.

->Regarding *carchesia*, he writes:<-
->*"Take up the carchesia of Maeonian Bacchus,"*<-
->*he says, "let us pour a libation to the Ocean." And elsewhere:*<-
->*“Here, duly pouring a libation of two carchesia of pure Bacchus.”*<-
<note>original: "Cape Mæonij carcheſia Bacchi... Hic duo rite mero libans carcheſia Bacchi." A *carchesium* is a tall, slender Greek drinking cup with handles extending from the rim to the base.</note>
->Regarding *cymbia*:<-
->*“We bring in bowls [cymbia] foaming with warm milk.”*<-
<note>original: "Inferimus tepido ſpumantia cymbia lacte." A *cymbium* is a boat-shaped vessel, named after "cymba," a small boat.</note>
->Regarding the *cantharus*:<-
->*“And the heavy pitcher [cantharus] hung by its worn handle.”*<-
<note>original: "Et grauis attrita pendebat cantharus ansa." A *cantharus* is a large, deep drinking cup with two high vertical handles, often associated with Bacchus.</note>
->Regarding *scyphi*:<-
->*“And the sacred cup [scyphus] filled his right hand.”*<-
<note>original: "Et ſacer impleuit dextram ſcyphus." A *scyphus* is a deep, two-handled bowl or cup used by the common people and in ritual.</note>

<margin>Various types of vessels.</margin>
No one asks what shapes these might be, or who has mentioned them; people are content merely to know that they are types of cups. One might tolerate it if *scyphi* and *canthari*—names common even among the general public—passed without inquiry. But as for *carchesia* and *cymbia*, which I doubt you would ever find in Latin writers and are extremely rare even among the Greeks, I do not see why people are not compelled to ask what these strange and foreign Greek names signify.

<margin>The Carchesium.</margin>
The *carchesium* is a vessel known only to the Greeks. *Pherecydes* <note>A 5th-century BC Greek mythographer.</note> mentions it in his books of histories; he says that Jupiter gave a golden *carchesium* to Alcmene as a gift for their union. But the playwright *Plautus* left out this unfamiliar name; in his play *Amphitruo*, he says a *patera* was given, even though the shape of these two vessels is vastly different.

<margin>The Patera.</margin>
For a *patera*, as the name itself indicates, is flat and open <note>The word *patera* comes from *patere*, meaning "to lie open." It is a shallow dish used for libations.</note>, whereas a *carchesium* is tall...

...vessels, and compressed around the middle part, with moderate handles that reach from the top to the very bottom. Moreover, Asclepiades, a man among the Greeks of the highest learning and diligence, believes that *carchesia* <note>Tall, slender Greek drinking cups with handles from rim to base.</note> were named after a nautical object. For he says that the lower part of a ship's sail is called a *patera* [bowl]; but around the middle part it is called the <term>neck</term> <note>Greek: *trachēlon*</note>, while the topmost part is named the *carchesium* <note>In a nautical context, this refers to the mast-head or the scuttle around the mast.</note>. From there it spreads out into each side of the sail, and these are called the "horns" [yardarms]. Asclepiades is not the only one to mention this cup; other illustrious poets do as well, such as Sappho, who says:
> "Then they all held *carchesia*,
> And poured libations. They prayed for all
> Good things for the bridegroom." <note>original: "Κοινᾶ δ’ ἄρα πάντες καρχήσι’ ἔχον, Καὶ ἔλειβον. δράσαντο δ’ πάμπαν Ἐσλὰ τῷ γαμβρῷ."</note>

Cratinus writes:
> "A thyrsus, a multi-colored saffron robe, and a *carchesium*." <note>original: "Θύρσον, κροκωτὴν ποικίλον καρχήσι."</note>

Sophocles, in the play entitled *Tyro*:
> "Claiming that the serpents
> Had approached the table and
> Were among the food and the 
> *Carchesia*." <note>original: "Πρὸς τὴν τράπεζαν φάσκων Προσεληλυθέναι τὸς δράκοντας καὶ Γένεσθαι περὶ τὰ σιτία καὶ τὰ Καρχήσια."</note>

These things are said regarding *carchesia*, which are unknown to the Latin language and celebrated only by Greece. But you will not find *cymbia* <note>A small, boat-shaped drinking vessel, from "cymba," a skiff.</note> in our common speech either. Indeed, it has been mentioned by only a few of the Greeks. Philemon, the very famous comic poet, says in *The Ghost*:
> "Since pleasure has shaken down for you 
> From above a *cymbium* of unmixed wine." <note>original: "Ἐπεὶ δ’ ἡ ἡδονὴ κυμβίον ἀκράτο Κατασέσεικεν ὑμῖν ἄνω."</note>

Anaxandrides, also a comic poet, in the play *The Rustics*:
> "Perhaps great cups were offered as toasts,
> And with unmixed wine,
<margin>*harmed</margin>
> The *cymbia* *overcame you." <note>original: "Μεγάλ’ ἴσως ποτήρια, προπινόμνα Καὶ μετ’ ἀκράτο Κυμβί’ ἐκάρωσεν ὑμᾶς." The marginal note *ἐκάκωσεν* (ekakōsen) provides an alternative reading: "the bowls harmed you" instead of "the bowls overcame/stupefied you" (ekatōsen).</note>

Demosthenes also mentions it in the speech *Against Midias*:
> "riding on a mule-saddle from Euboea, wearing fine cloaks
> and having *cymbia*, which the tax-collectors were seizing." <note>original: "ἐπ’ ἀσράβης δ’ ὀχούμενον ἐξ ἀργύρας εὐβοίας χλανίδας δὲ καὶ κύμβia ἔχον, ὧν ἐπελαμβάνοντο οἱ πεντηκοστολόγοι."</note>

# OF THE SATURNALIA

These **cymbia** <note>Small, boat-shaped drinking vessels.</note> (as the shape of the name itself indicates) are named as a diminutive of **cymba** <note>A small boat or skiff.</note>: which is a type of vessel among both the Greeks and us (who borrow the term from them). Indeed, I have noticed among the Greeks many types of cups named after naval objects, just as I explained above regarding *carchesia*, so too these *cymbia* are tall cups similar to ships. Eratosthenes, a most deeply learned man, mentions this cup in a letter to Agetor the Lacedaemonian, in these words:

<margin>In the ancient version, the following are cited in this way: "They set out a mixing bowl, not of silver nor set with jewels, but of the earth of Colias <note>A promontory in Attica famous for its fine pottery clay.</note>, which, having filled to the brim six times, they poured for the gods in order, dipping into it with the *cymbium*." This entire passage is explained by Athenaeus in Book 11.</margin>

"I wonder how those same people, not possessing a ladle <note>Greek: *kyathos*</note>, but having acquired only the boat-cup <note>Greek: *kymbion*</note> as their only vessel, seem to me to have taken it into their possession for the sake of human need on one hand, and for the honor of the gods on the other." <note>original: "Θαυμάζω δὲ οἱ αὐτοὶ καὶ πῶς κύαθον μὴ κεκτημένοι, ἀλλὰ κυμβίον μόνην φιάλην προσεκέκτητο, δοκεῖ δή μοι, τὸ μὲν τῆς τῶν ἀνθρώπων χρείας ἕνεκα, τὸ δὲ τῆς τῶν θεῶν τιμῆς εἰς τὴν κτήσιν παρειληφέναι."</note> There were some who thought *cymbium* was an abbreviation <note>The technical term is *syncope*, the loss of sounds from the middle of a word.</note> of *cissymbium*. Many mention the **cissymbium** (to say nothing of Homer, who remembers this cup being given to the Cyclops by Ulysses); some wish for the *cissymbium* to be properly a wooden cup made from **ivy**, that is, *kissos*. And a certain Nicander of Colophon in the first book of the *Aetolica* <margin>*Hyalicon</margin> says:

"In the sacred rites of Didymaean Zeus <note>Referring to the sanctuary at Didyma; although famous for the oracle of Apollo, Zeus was also worshipped there.</note>, they make libations with ivy leaves. From this, the ancient drinking vessels are called *kissubia*." <note>original: "Ἐν τῇ ἱεροποιϊᾳ τοῦ Διδυμαίου Διὸς κισσῷ σπονδοποιεῦνται πετάλοισιν. Ὅθεν τὰ ἀρχαῖα ἐκπώματα κισσύβia φωνέεται."</note>

But Callimachus also mentions this cup:

> "For indeed he rejected the Thracian-style gulping <note>Greek: *amystin*, a way of drinking a large amount in one breath.</note> of unmixed wine, but was delighted by a small **ivy-cup** [*kissubion*]. To him I said this, as the third goblet <note>Greek: *aleisou*</note> went around." <note>original: "Καὶ γὰρ ὁ Θρηϊκίην μὲν ἀπήνατο χανδὸν ἄμυστιν ζωροποτειν. ὀλίγῳ δ' ἥδετο κισσυβίῳ Τῷ μὲν ἐγὼ τὸ δ' ἔλεξα περιστείχοντος ἀλείσου Τὸ τρίτον."</note>

Those who think the *cissymbium* is a cup made from ivy and called as if *kissinon* [of ivy] seem to rely on the authority of Euripides, who in the *Andromeda* <margin>*Andromache</margin> says:

> "All the shepherd folk are rushing: one bringing an **ivy-wood bowl** [*kissinon skuphos*] of milk, a refresher from labors, and another the joy of the vines [wine]." <note>original: "Πᾶς δ' ποιμένων ἔρρει λεώς Ὁ μὲν γάλακτος κίσσινον φέρων σκύφος, Πόνων ἀναψυκτήρ, ὃ δ' ἀμπέλων γάνoς."</note>

<margin>Scyphus.</margin>
"And the sacred **scyphus** <note>A deep, handle-less or two-handled drinking bowl.</note> filled his right hand." The *scyphus* is the cup of Hercules, just as the *cantharus* belongs to Father Liber <note>Another name for Bacchus.</note>. Indeed, the ancient sculptors depicted Hercules with a cup for good reason: sometimes he is shown reeling and drunk. This is not only because that hero is said to have been a heavy drinker, but also because there is an ancient story that Hercules crossed the vast seas in a cup as if it were a ship, carried by the winds. But I shall say a few things from Greek antiquities regarding both points. That this hero was a "great drinker"—to say nothing of what is commonly known—is clearly argued by the fact that Ephippus, in his play *Busiris*, introduces Hercules speaking thus: "I know not, by the gods, whether I am a Pythian or an Orgian; for those who are drunk always fight their battles with passion." <note>original Greek: "οὐκ οἶδα μ’ ὄντα πρὸς θεῶν... οἱ μεθύοντες αἰὲν τὰς μάχας πάθος μάχοντ’."</note>

### On certain other passages of Virgil. CHAPTER XXII.

Virgil also occasionally borrows names from the most ancient Greek histories. You know that in his work, one of the companions of Diana is called **Opis** <note>In the *Aeneid*, Opis is a nymph and attendant of the goddess Diana/Artemis.</note>. While those who are ignorant might think this name was perhaps applied at random or even invented, the ingenious poet wished to assign to her companion a surname that had been given to Diana herself by the ancient Greek writers. But Virgil says this:

> Meanwhile, in the heavenly dwellings, Latonia <note>Diana, daughter of Leto (Latona in Latin).</note>
> addressed the swift Opis, one of the virgin
> companions and her sacred band, and with her 
> lips uttered these sorrowful words.

->And below:<-

> But Opis, the guardian of Trivia <note>An epithet for Diana, referring to her role as goddess of the "three ways" or crossroads.</note>, had long since been in the mountains.

He calls Opis, as he says, a companion and associate of Diana. But hear where Virgil received this name; for (as I said) he applied to her companion an epithet that he had read belonging to the goddess herself. Alexander Aetolus <note>A Greek poet and scholar of the 3rd century BCE who worked at the Library of Alexandria.</note>, an excellent poet, in his book entitled *The Muses*, relates with what great zeal the people of Ephesus, after dedicating the temple of Diana, took care to offer prizes so that the most talented poets of the time might compose various songs to the Goddess. In these verses, Opis is not called the companion of Diana, but Diana herself is called Opis. He is speaking (as I said) of the people of Ephesus:

> But he, learning that Timotheus <note>A famous and innovative Greek musician and poet.</note>, the son of Thersander, 
> skilled in the lyre and in song, was held in high 
> esteem by all the Greeks, rewarded the man with 
> a sacred thousand of golden shekels <note>original Greek: *siglōn*, a Persian coin often mentioned in Greek texts regarding the East.</note> 
> to sing a hymn to Opis, the archer of swift arrows.
<note>original Greek: "Αλλ’ ὅγε πευθόμενος πᾶγχυ γραικοῖσι μελέσθαι / Τιμόθεον κιθάρης ἴδμονα καὶ μελέων / Υἱὸν θερσάνδροιο τὸν ἤνεσεν ἀνέρα σίγλων / Χρυσέων ἱερὴν πάντοτε χιλιάδα / Ὑμνῆσαι ταχέων ὦπιν ἐρητῆραν ὀϊστῶν."</note>

# BOOK V.

It appeared, if I am not mistaken, that **Opis** was a name once used for **Diana** herself, and that Virgil, out of his excessive learning, transferred this name to her companion.

> All the gods departed, leaving behind their shrines and altars.
> <note>original: "Excessere omnes adytis arisq; relictis Dij." From Virgil's *Aeneid*, Book 2. It refers to the "evocatio," a ritual where the gods were believed to leave a city before its fall.</note>

<margin>Neptune</margin>
No one inquires from where Virgil might have said this, but it is certain that he drew it from **Euripides** <note>A famous Athenian playwright (c. 480–406 BC) known for his tragedies.</note>, who, in his play *The Trojan Women*, introduces **Apollo** speaking these words when Troy was about to be captured:

<margin>In ancient copies, only the beginning of the third verse is cited: *I leave famous Ilium.* These are the words of Neptune in the poet.</margin>
> But I—being overcome by the Argive goddess
> Hera, and by Athena, who together have overthrown the Phrygians—
> I leave behind famous Ilium and my altars.
> For when a city is seized by a wretched desolation,
> the things of the gods fall sick, and they no longer care to be honored.
> <note>original: Ἐγώ δὲ νικῶμαι... This passage from Euripides describes the gods abandoning the city of Troy as it falls to the Greeks.</note>

These verses show from where Virgil adopted the idea that the gods had departed from a city that had already been captured. Nor is the following passage without the authority of Greek antiquity:

> She herself hurled Jupiter's rapid fire from the clouds.
> <note>original: "Ipsa Iouis rapidum iaculata è nubibus ignem." Referring to Minerva (Athena) using her father's lightning.</note>

For Euripides introduces **Minerva** asking **Neptune** for winds against the Greek fleet, saying that she ought to do what **Jupiter** had done, from whom she had received the thunderbolt to use against the Greeks.

In Virgil's work, **Pan** is said to have enticed **Luna** <note>The personification of the Moon.</note> with a gift of snowy wool, calling her into the deep woods: *With such a snowy gift of wool, if it is worthy of belief*, and so forth. In this passage, **Valerius Probus** <note>A famous Roman grammarian and critic of the 1st century AD.</note>, a most accomplished man, notes that he does not know this history or myth, nor to which author it refers. I am surprised that such a point escaped so great a man. For **Nicander** <note>Nicander of Colophon (2nd century BC), a Greek poet who wrote about natural history and mythology.</note> is the author of this history—a poet whom **Didymus** <note>Didymus Chalcenterus (c. 63 BC – 10 AD), a prolific scholar in Alexandria who wrote thousands of books.</note> (the most learned of all grammarians who are or ever were) calls "myth-making." Knowing this, Virgil added the phrase, *If it is worthy of belief*: thus he confesses that he used a myth-making author. In the third book, the following is read cursorily, and the source of its translation is not sought:

> What things the almighty Father told Phoebus, and Phoebus Apollo told me

<image-desc>A large historiated decorative initial 'H' containing a classical figure seated within a frame of floral and architectural motifs.</image-desc>**H**ERE Praetextatus <note>Vettius Agorius Praetextatus, a prominent historical figure and leader of the traditional Roman pagan aristocracy, depicted here as the host of the Saturnalia gathering.</note> said: "Eustathius has arranged in a wonderful manner those things which **Virgil** <note>original: Vergilius; the author of the *Aeneid* and the central subject of the group's literary analysis.</note> inserted into his poem from Greek antiquity. But we remember that the men who are by far the most learned of our age, **Furius** and **Caecina Albinus**, promised that they would reveal what the same Maro <note>A common name for Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro).</note> drew from the ancient Roman writers. The time now reminds us that this should be done." When this was pleasing to everyone, **Furius Albinus** then spoke: 

"Even though I fear that, while I desire to show how much our Virgil profited from his reading of the ancients—and which 'flowers' he gathered from everyone, or what ornaments he tasted from various sources for the beauty of his poem—I may provide an opportunity for the unlearned or the malicious to find fault. They might reproach such a great man for the 'usurpation' of another’s work <note>original: alieni usurpationem; a legalistic term for taking possession of something belonging to someone else.</note>, failing to consider that this is the very fruit of reading: to emulate those things which you approve of in others, and to turn those things which you most admire among the sayings of others to your own use through a timely derivation. This is something our own writers have often done among themselves as well as from the Greeks, and the most excellent of the Greeks have done the same among themselves. To say nothing of foreigners, I could demonstrate with many examples how much the authors of the old library <note>Referring to the collective body of classical literature.</note> have plundered one another. However, I will prove this at another convenient time (if it is your wish). For now, I will bring forward one example which is for..."

# OF THE SATURNALIA

to be proven, the evidence which I bring forward will almost suffice. For **Afranius** <note>Lucius Afranius, a Roman comic poet of the 2nd century BCE.</note>, a writer of *togatae* <term>togata: A genre of Roman comedy where characters wore the Roman toga, distinguishing it from 'palliata' comedies based on Greek models.</term>, in that *togata* which is titled the *Compitalia* <term>Compitalia: An ancient Roman festival celebrated in honor of the Lares, the guardian spirits of the crossroads.</term>, not at all shamelessly responding to those accusing him of having taken too much from **Menander** <note>The most famous Greek writer of New Comedy, whom many Roman playwrights imitated.</note>, says: "I confess," he says, "I took it, not only from him, but from anyone who had what suited me, and what I believed I could not do better myself; even from a Latin author." Now, if this partnership and community of material is granted to be practiced among all poets and writers, who would consider it a crime in **Virgil** <note>original: Vergilius.</note> if he borrowed certain things from the ancients to refine his own work? Indeed, gratitude should be shown to him on this account: that by transferring some things from them into his own work—which is destined to remain forever—he ensured that the memory of the ancients would not be entirely erased. For (as the present *time* <margin>*the sense</margin> shows) we have already begun to regard them not only with neglect, but even with laughter. Finally, through both his judgment in transferring and his manner of imitating, he achieved this: that whatever *other* <margin>*another's*</margin> thing we read in his work that belongs to another, we either prefer it to be *his*, or we marvel that it sounds better here than where it was born. I will say, therefore, first, which lines he drew from others, whether from a half-verse or almost in their entirety; after this, whole passages transferred with some small change; or themes so transcribed that it is clear where they came from; others altered, yet in such a way that their origin is not unknown. After these, I will show some of those things taken from **Homer**—not that he took them from **Homer** himself, but that others had taken them from there first, and he transferred them from those writers whom he had undoubtedly read.

->Accius in the *Judgment of Arms*. <note>Lucius Accius (170–c. 86 BC) was a celebrated Roman tragic poet. This play concerned the contest between Ajax and Ulysses for the armor of Achilles.</note><-

*For it is a fine thing for me to bear away a trophy from a brave man. If, however, I am also defeated: to be defeated by such a man is no disgrace.* <note>original: "Nam trophæum ferre me à forti uiro, pulchrum est. Si autem & uincar : uinci à tali, nullum est probrum."</note>

->Ennius in his tenth book, when he was speaking of the citadel of Troy. <note>Quintus Ennius (239–169 BC) is often called the "Father of Roman Poetry." Pergamis refers to Pergamum, the citadel of Troy.</note><-

### CHAPTER II.

Which passages Virgil translated from the ancient Latin writers, either in their entirety or with very few changes: and which he changed in such a way that their origin can still be easily detected.

After the verses translated from others, either entirely or in part—or by changing certain words as if they were tinged with a different juice—it now pleases my mind to compare passage with passage, so that you may recognize from where they were formed, as if in a mirror.

->Virgil.<-

> Nor am I doubtful in my mind how great a task it is to master 
> these things in words, and to add this honor to narrow themes. 
> But a sweet love seizes me through the deserted heights of Parnassus: 
> it is a joy to go along the ridges where none of my predecessors... <note>original: "Nec sum animi dubius, uerbis ea uincere magnum Quam sit, & angustis hunc addere rebus honorem. Sed me Parnassi deserta per ardua dulcis Raptat amor : iuuat ire iugis, quà nulla priorum." From *Georgics* 3.289-292. Virgil acknowledges the difficulty of writing poetry about lowly agricultural subjects.</note>

# BOOK VI.

->Virgil in the *Georgics*<-

> Neither the shadows of deep woods, nor soft
> meadows can move his mind; nor the river which, rolled through the rocks,
> seeks the plain, purer than amber <note>original: "electro." Electrum can refer to amber or a bright alloy of gold and silver; here it emphasizes the crystalline purity of the water.</note>.

->Lucretius in Book 2<-

> Nor can tender willows, and herbs growing green with dew,
> and any rivers gliding by the tops of their banks
> delight the mind, and turn away sudden care.

Indeed, the entire tone and nearly all the outlines of the plague itself, which appears in the third book of the *Georgics*, are drawn from the description of the plague in the sixth book of Lucretius <note>Macrobius is comparing Virgil’s description of a cattle plague in Noricum to Lucretius’s famous account of the Plague of Athens.</note>. For Virgil's account begins:

> Here once, from a corruption of the air, a wretched season
> arose, and burned with all the heat of autumn;
> and it gave over to death every kind of cattle, and every kind of wild beast.

->And Lucretius’s begins thus:<-

> This cause of diseases once, and this death-bearing heat,
> rendered the fields funeral-filled within the borders of Cecrops <note>original: "Cecropis." Cecrops was the legendary first king of Athens; Lucretius uses this to refer to the territory of Attica.</note>:
> and it laid waste the roads, and drained the city of its citizens.

But since it would be quite long to set down the entire passage of both poets, I will select some excerpts from which the similarity of the twin descriptions appears. 

->Virgil:<-

> Then indeed their eyes were burning, and the breath, drawn from deep
> within, was sometimes heavy with a groan; and with a long
> sob they strained their lowest flanks; black blood flows
> from their nostrils, and a rough tongue presses against their obstructed throats.

->Lucretius:<-

> At the beginning, they had their heads burning with heat,
> and their two eyes red with suffused light.
> The throats also sweated within with black
> blood, and the path of the voice was blocked and closed by ulcers.
