#### Virgil.

> And yet, though these have been the labors of men and oxen in turning the earth through experience, the shameless goose does nothing [less to harm them]. <note>original: "Nec tamen, hæc cum sint hominumq́; boumq́; labores / Versando terram experti, nihil improbus anser." This passage from Virgil's *Georgics* (Book 1) describes the various pests and weather events that ruin a farmer's hard work.</note>

#### Lucretius in his fifth book. <note>Lucretius was a Roman poet and philosopher known for *On the Nature of Things*.</note>

> But yet sometimes, things sought with great labor, when they are already leafing throughout the lands and everything is in flower, either the parching sun from the sky burns them with excessive heat, or sudden rains and cold frosts destroy them, and the blasts of the winds harass them with a violent whirlwind. <note>original: "Sed tamen interdum magno quæsita labore..."</note>

There are other passages of many verses which Maro <term>Maro: The family name of the poet Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro)</term> transferred from the ancient poets into his own work with the change of only a few words. And because it would be a long task to transcribe every single one from both sources, I will note the ancient books, so that whoever wishes may marvel at the equality of the passages by comparing the readings there. In the first book of the *Aeneid*, a storm is described; and Venus complains to Jupiter about the dangers facing her son; and Jupiter consoles her with the prospect of future prosperity. This entire passage is taken from Naevius, from the first book of the *Punic War*. <note>Gnaeus Naevius (c. 270–201 BCE) wrote an epic on the First Punic War; Macrobius argues Virgil modeled the opening of the *Aeneid* on Naevius's work.</note> For in that work, Venus likewise complains to Jupiter while the Trojans are struggling in a storm, and the words of Jupiter consoling his daughter with the hope of the future follow. Likewise, concerning Pandarus and Bitia opening the gates, the passage is taken from the fifteenth book of Ennius, who introduced two Istrians <note>The Istrians (Histri) were a tribe from the Adriatic peninsula of Istria.</note> who, during a siege, burst through a gate and caused a slaughter among the besieging enemy. Nor did he abstain from plundering Tullius, <term>Tullius: Marcus Tullius Cicero, the famous Roman orator and statesman</term> provided he could gather ornaments for himself from every side. *O fame immense, greater still in arms, Trojan man!* <note>original: "O fama ingens, ingentior armis Vir Troiane." A quote from *Aeneid* 11.124.</note> To be sure, he says this: that Aeneas [surpassed] his own fame by his brave deeds...

<meta>This page continues Macrobius's discussion of Virgil's literary predecessors. On the previous page, Macrobius was listing specific phrases Virgil adapted from poets like Ennius and Lucretius. Here, he moves into a more complex argument: that Virgil often borrowed from Homer not directly, but by way of earlier Roman poets who had already translated those Homeric scenes into Latin.</meta>

<page-num>478</page-num>
<header>OF THE SATURNALIA</header>

...surpassed [it], since for the most part reputation is greater than reality. <note>original: "fama sit maior rebus."</note> This sentiment appears in Cicero’s *Cato* with these words: "It happened to him—which for most people is usually the opposite—that everything seemed greater in reality than by reputation, something that does not happen often; thus expectation was overcome by experience, and the ears by the eyes." <note>Cicero is remarking that Cato the Elder was even more impressive in person than his legend suggested.</note> Likewise: "Next to this one after a long, but still next, interval." <note>original: "Proximus huic longo, sed proximus interuallo." This refers to Virgil's description of a race in the *Aeneid* (5.320).</note> Cicero says in his *Brutus*: "Therefore, Lucius Philippus approached closest to the two greatest orators, Crassus and Antonius, but at a long interval; nevertheless, he was the next."

### On the passages which others first translated from Homer, and from there Virgil adopted for his own work. CHAPTER III.

There are certain things in Virgil which are believed to have been translated directly from Homer; but I will show that these were actually taken from our own [Roman] authors, who earlier had drawn these passages from Homer into their own poems. This indeed is the greatest tribute to Homer’s fame: that although so many have kept watch against him <note>Meaning many poets have tried to compete with or surpass him.</note> and the combined strength of everyone has joined hands against him, he remains unmoved like a rock in the sea. Homer says regarding the brave fight of Ajax:

<margin>Iliad 16.</margin>
> Ajax no longer stood his ground, for he was overwhelmed by the missiles; the will of Zeus and the noble Trojans subduing him with their throws. Around his temples his bright helmet, when struck, rang with a terrible clatter, and it was struck continually on the well-made cheek-pieces. He grew weary in his left shoulder, always holding firm his flashing shield; nor were they able to drive him back, though they pressed him with missiles. Always he was gripped by painful gasping, and much sweat flowed from his limbs on every side. Nowhere was he able to catch his breath; on every side evil was heaped upon evil. <note>original Greek: "Αἶας δ' οὐκέτ' ἔμιμνε..." Macrobius provides the Greek text from the *Iliad* (16.102–111) to show the source of the "weary warrior" motif.</note>

Ennius, in his fifteenth book, translates this passage regarding the fight of the Tribune Caelius <note>Caelius was a Roman military officer; Ennius replaces the Greek hero Ajax with a Roman figure to make the epic history of Rome feel "Homeric."</note> with these words:

> From everywhere the weapons gather upon the Tribune like a rainstorm; they pierce his shield, and the boss rings from the spear-shafts, <note>original: "Vndiq; conueniunt, uelut imber, tela Tribuno / Configunt parmam, tinnit hastilibus umbo."</note>

<meta>The text continues on the next page with the word "Aerato" (bronze), completing the description of the Tribune's armor.</meta>

->From this, Virgil says:<-
> *Not if I had a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths.* <note>original Latin: "Non mihi si linguæ centum sint, oráq; centum." This is a famous trope of "unspeakability," where the poet claims even a hundred mouths wouldn't be enough to describe the scene.</note>

->The Homeric description of a fleeing horse is in these words:<-

<margin>Iliad, Book 6</margin>
> *Just as when a horse, kept at the manger and well-fed on barley, having broken his bond, runs galloping across the plain, accustomed to bathe in the fair-flowing river, exulting; he holds his head high, and around his shoulders his mane tosses, and trusting in his splendor, his knees easily carry him to the haunts and pastures of the mares.* <note>original Greek: "Ως δ' ὅτε τις στατὸς ἵππος ἀκοστήσας ἐπὶ φάτνῃ...". This is one of Homer's most celebrated similes, used to describe Paris returning to battle.</note>

->Ennius drew from this:<-

<margin>* spoken</margin> <note>The marginal note "* fatus" likely refers to a textual variant or a gloss on the word "actus" (driven) in the poem.</note>
> *And then just like a horse, who, driven from the stalls, has broken the bonds with his great spirit, and thereafter carries himself through the deep blue of the field and the happy meadows with a high chest; often he shakes his high mane, and the breath from his warm soul drives white foam.* <note>original Latin: "Et tum sicut equus, qui de præsepibus actus...". Ennius was the first to adapt Homer's Greek hexameters into Latin.</note>

->Virgil:<-
> *Just as when, having broken his bonds, he flees the stalls, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Qualis ubi abruptis fugit præsepia uinclis, &c." Virgil refined the "rough" Latin of Ennius into a smoother, more rhythmic form in Aeneid 11.492.</note>

Let no one think the ancient poets are worthless because their verses seem rough to us. For that style alone pleased the ears of Ennius’s century: and the following age labored long so that this softer style might be more accepted. But I will no longer delay Cecinna, so that he himself may set forth what he remembers Maro <note>The poet Virgil’s full name was Publius Vergilius Maro.</note> to have transferred from antiquity.

### Concerning Latin, Greek, and foreign words which Virgil might seem to have been the first to use, when the ancients had nevertheless used them before.
### C H A P T E R I V.

Then Cecinna spoke: Furius has discussed how much Maro sought from antiquity in his verses or passages, as one mindful of the abundance of both old and new authors. I shall endeavor to show that this most diligent poet both judged the individual words of the ancients most fittingly, and inserted chosen words into his work which the neglect of antiquity makes seem new to us. For example:

<header>BOOK VI.</header>

Look at the word **Added** <note>original: *Addita*</note>, used to mean "hostile" and "dangerous." Who would not think the poet wished to manufacture a new word for himself by his own choice? But it is not so; for when he says: *Nor will Juno, **added** as a foe, ever be far away*—meaning "affixed" and therefore "hostile"—Lucilius had already said this in his 14th book in these verses:
> If a leader is not **added** to me, and does not drive me,
> Not badly has that one man, as I say, tormented me.

->Virgil.<-

In the morning [the palace] vomits a wave of callers from its whole structure.
<margin>To vomit a wave.</margin> He uses the phrase "vomits a wave" beautifully and in an archaic style, for Ennius says:
*And the river Tiber vomits into the salty sea.*
<margin>Vomitoria.</margin> From this we even now call the **Vomitoria** in theaters <note>original: *spectaculis*. These were the wide passages that allowed large crowds to "spew" into or out of their seating areas quickly.</note>, from which people entering in a mass pour themselves into the seats.
<margin>A column of motion.</margin> To use the word *Agmen* <term>Agmen: usually a column of marching soldiers, here used for a flow of water</term> for the act and certain motion of a thing is not inelegant; as in, *The Tiber flows in a gentle column*: indeed, it is an ancient usage. For Ennius says in his fifth book:
> Because through the pleasant city the river flows in a gentle column.

<margin>With crackling flames.</margin> When he says "to burn with crackling flames," he did not employ a new word, but Lucretius previously used it in his sixth book:
> Nor does any thing burn more with the crackling of the flame
> with a terrible sound than the Delphic laurel of Apollo.

<margin>The field bristles.</margin> Then the field **bristles** with iron spears. This use of "bristles" <note>original: *horret*</note> is wonderfully employed. But Ennius also says in his fourteenth book:
> The army bristles with weapons, sharp on both sides.

->And in the Erechtheus:<-

The arms are stiff, the weapons bristle. And in the *Scipio*:
With long spears scattered, the field shines and bristles.

->But before all others, Homer:<-

<margin>Iliad, Book 13.</margin> The man-destroying battle bristled with the long, flesh-cutting spears which they held. <note>original Greek: "Ἔφριξεν δὲ μάχη φθισίμβροτος ἐγχείῃσι Μακρῇς, ἃς εἶχον ταμεσίχροας."</note>
<margin>Trembling light.</margin> —The sea shines beneath the **trembling light**.

The author, Macrobius, through his characters, continues to demonstrate that Virgil’s poetic vocabulary—far from being "invented" or "improper"—is rooted in the respected traditions of earlier Roman poets like Ennius, Lucretius, and Furius, as well as the prose of Cicero and Varro.</meta>

<header>SATURNALIA</header>

The phrase "tremulous light" <note>original: *tremulum lumẽ*</note> is expressed from the very image of the thing itself. But Ennius used it earlier in *Menalippe*:

> Thus the earth and the hollow blue skies gleam with such **tremulous light**.

And Lucretius in his sixth book:

> Furthermore, the moisture of water is tossed about by the Sun's rays, and thins into light from the **tremulous heat**.

<margin>Sunshades.</margin> *Here the white poplar leans over the cave, and the supple vines weave **umbracula**.* <term>Umbracula: literally "little shadows," usually referring to leafy bowers or sunshades.</term> There are those who think this word *umbracula* was composed by Virgil as its author, even though Varro says in the 10th book of his *Divine Things* that a certain type of **umbraculum** <note>original: *umbraculi*</note> was granted to some magistrates in the town. And Cicero says in the fifth book of *On the Laws*: "Do you wish then (since the Sun already seems to have declined a little from noon, and all this place is not yet sufficiently shaded by these young trees) that we go down to the Liris; and pursue what remains in those **umbracula** <note>shady retreats</note> of the alders?" Similarly in the *Brutus*: "But just as with the **umbracula** of that most learned man, Theophrastus," etc.

<margin>To cross over.</margin> *They **cross** the plains at a run, and the herds of deer mass their dusty columns in flight.* He uses "they cross" <note>original: *transmittunt*</note> elegantly in place of "they pass through." So too Lucretius in his second book:

> And the horsemen fly around, and suddenly **cross** the middle of the plains, shaking them with powerful force.

But also Pestanus Vibonensis <note>An otherwise obscure author or source cited by Macrobius</note> says: "We **crossed** the horses on foot," which means, we passed over. The whole cohort, imitating this,

<margin>To flow down.</margin> *leaving their horses, **flowed down** to the ground.* <note>Virgil uses *defluxit* ("flowed down") to describe the soldiers dismounting.</note> So Furius says in his first book:

> Suddenly overcome by a heavy wound, he let go of the horse's reins, and sliding down he **flowed down** to the ground, and gave back a sound from his bronze armor.

<margin>To separate.</margin> *Then the soil began to harden, and to **separate** Nereus from the deep.* <note>original: *discludere Nerea*. Nereus, a sea god, is used here to represent the sea itself.</note> This word **separate** strikes our ears,

<meta>This page continues the philological analysis of Virgil’s poetry from Book VI. Macrobius is currently demonstrating how Virgil’s specific word choices—such as "deductum" for a refined song—are not innovations but are rooted in the technical and literary language of earlier Roman authors like Lucretius, Cato the Elder, and various playwrights.</meta>

<page-num>483</page-num>
<header>BOOK VI.</header>

...as if it were new. But Lucretius did this earlier in his fifth book:

> From that place the parts began to fly apart, and like things 
> To join with like, and to mark out the world's divisions.
> —Tityrus, it behooves a shepherd to feed fat 
> Sheep, but to sing a **refined song**:

<margin>A refined song.</margin>
The word **refined** <note>original: *deductum*</note> is elegantly used here to mean "thin and subtle." Likewise, Afranius says in *The Virgin*: "She responded with very few words, with a sad, **drawn-out** <note>original: *deducta*</note> voice, and said she would rather not have rested." Also in Cornificius: "To me, babbling with a **drawn-out** voice." But these usages flowed from what Pomponius says in his Atellan farce <term>Atellan farce: a form of low-brow, improvised Roman comedy featuring masked stock characters</term> titled *The Calends of March*: "You must **draw out** <note>original: *deducas*</note> the voice so that it sounds like the words of a woman; just order one to be brought, and I shall make the voice thin and tinkling." And further down: "Even now I shall **draw out** the voice."

<margin>Projecting / Jutting.</margin>
> —And we scrape past the **jutting** rocks of Pachynus.

The word **jutting** <note>original: *proiecta*</note>, if spoken according to common custom, is understood as "cast away" or "abject"; but according to the ancients, it means "cast forward." Elsewhere Virgil says:

> —While he readies himself for the fight with his left foot **extended**.

But Sisenna <note>Lucius Cornelius Sisenna: a 1st-century BCE historian known for his archaic style</note> also said in his second book: "And the Marsi <note>The Marsi: an Italic people known for their bravery in the Social War</note> drew closer. And so, with their shields **extended** <note>original: *proiectis*</note> and held as a roof, they vied to hurl heavy stones with their hands against the enemy." And in the same book: "There was an ancient and massive holm-oak tree which, with its **projecting** branches, covered the greater part of the summit." And Lucretius in his third book:

> However much he stands out with a monstrous **projection** of the body.

<margin>The seasonable pine.</margin>
> And to fell the **seasonable** pine from the woods.

He took this term **seasonable** <note>original: *tempestiva*</note> regarding the pine from Cato, who said: "When you dig up a pine nut, take it out when the moon is waning, after midday, and without a south wind. Then truly it will be **seasonable** when its own seed is mature." He also inserted Greek words into his work, but he was not the first to dare this. For he followed the boldness of the ancient authors. *Lamps hang from the golden paneled ceilings.* Just as Ennius says in his 9th book: "The lights of the **lamps**..."

<margin>Lamps.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of Virgil’s poetic influences, moving from specific verbs like "draw out" and "jutting" to nouns and adjectives that Virgil adopted from earlier Roman poets like Ennius and Lucretius, as well as his use of foreign loanwords from Gallic and Oscan origins.</meta>

<page-num>484</page-num>
<header>THE SATURNALIA</header>

...the twice-six signs <note>original: "mina bis sex"; likely a reference to the twelve signs of the zodiac mentioned by Lucretius</note>. And Lucretius in his fifth book says:
> Moreover, those nightly lights of yours that belong to the earth,
> The hanging **lamps** <note>original: *lychni*</note>.

Lucilius in his first book says: "Furthermore, the **goose-footed** <note>original: *chaenopodas*</note> and **bed-footed** <note>original: *clinopodas*</note> supports, and the **lamps** <note>original: *lychnos*</note>; and we spoke of the **stools** <note>original: *cennos*</note> before the feet of the bed and the lamps." And where Virgil said, "Nor is the pole of the sky bright with the **starry ether**," Ennius had said it first in his sixteenth book: "Meanwhile the torch [of the sun] sets, and the red expanse of the **ether** <note>original: *aethra*</note> overwhelms the tracts of the Ocean."
<margin>Ether.</margin>
And Accius in his play *Theutras*: "To be carried high, a glowing torch through the fiery **ether**."
<margin>Daedala.</margin>
Virgil uses the phrase "**skillful** Circe" <note>original: *Daedala Circe*</note> because Lucretius had said: "the **skillful** earth" <note>original: *Daedala tellus*</note>.
<margin>To re-echo.</margin>
The phrase "the forests and great Olympus **re-echo**" <note>original: *reboant*</note> appears because it is found in Lucretius: "Nor do the coffered and gilded ceilings **re-echo** with the lyre." But the older poets used this license more broadly, while Virgil used it more sparingly. Indeed, those ancients used words like *pausa* <note>a pause or stop</note>, *machaera* <note>a sword</note>, *acotia* <note>a rare term for a type of vessel or perhaps a Greek medical term</note>, *malace* <note>a term for softness or luxury</note>, and other similar terms.
<margin>*acacian</margin>
Furthermore, the ancients used Punic and Oscan words, and in imitation of them, Virgil did not reject foreign words, as in that line: "the woodland **wild oxen** <note>original: *uri*</note> continually."
<margin>Wild oxen.</margin>
For **wild oxen** is a Gallic word used to signify wild cattle. Also: "shaggy ears beneath **curved** horns."
<margin>Curved. Chamber/Vault.</margin>
**Curved** <note>original: *camuris*</note> is a foreign word, meaning "turning back on themselves." And perhaps we also name a **vaulted chamber** <note>original: *camera*</note> according to this same logic.

->**Chapter V: That the epithets which seem new in Virgil were also in use among the older authors.**<-

There are also many epithets in Virgil which are believed to have been created by him; but I shall show that these too were drawn from the ancients. Some of these are simple, such as **Gradius** <note>an epithet of Mars, "The Strider"</note> and **Mulciber** <note>an epithet of Vulcan</note>; others are compound, such as **bow-bearing** <note>original: *arcitenens*</note> and **vine-planter** <note>original: *vitisator*</note>. But first I shall speak of the simple ones: "And the loosely-clad Africans of **Mulciber**."
<margin>Mulciber.</margin>
Mulciber is Vulcan: because he is fire, and fire **softens** <note>original: *mulceat*</note> and tames all things. Accius says in his *Philoctetes*: "Alas, Mulciber, you have forged invincible arms with your unskilled hand." And Egnatius in the first book of *On the Nature of Things*: "Finally, Mulciber himself, bearing the fires, reaches the highest parts of heaven."

<header>BOOK VI.</header>

<margin>Lucretius in Book 2. **Butting**.</margin>
"And the **butting** <note>original: *petulci*; describes young animals that butt with their heads</note> kids leap upon the flowers."
"Furthermore, the tender kids with their trembling voices know their horn-bearing mothers, and the **butting** lambs."
<margin>**Liquid fire**.</margin>
It might seem an act of the greatest boldness when Virgil says in the *Bucolics*:
"And at the same time **liquid fire**" <note>original: *liquidi ignis*</note>. Here "liquid" is used to mean pure or bright, or perhaps flowing and abundant; yet this would be bold indeed had not Lucretius used this epithet first in his sixth book:
> "For this reason it happens that the mobile,
> golden heat of **liquid fire** flies down to the earth."
<margin>**Harsh** for **bitter**.</margin>
Using "**harsh**" <note>original: *tristis*</note> to mean "bitter" is a fitting metaphor. For example: "the **harsh** lupins." Similarly, Ennius says in the fourth book of his *Sabines*: "He seeks neither **harsh** mustard nor **sad** onion."
<margin>**Long-eared** hare.</margin>
Maro <note>Virgil's cognomen</note> was not the first to use the phrase "**long-eared** <note>original: *auritos*</note> hares," but he follows Afranius, who says in his prologue in the persona of Priapus:
> "For what the common folk declare—that I was
> born of a **long-eared** parent—is not so."
And to include compound words, consider what
<margin>**Incense-burning**.</margin>
Virgil said: "I saw her when she placed gifts on the **incense-burning** <note>original: *turicremis*</note> altars."
Lucretius had already said in his second book:
> "For often before the beautiful shrines of the gods, a calf
> falls slaughtered beside the **incense-burning** altars."
<margin>**Bow-bearing**.</margin>
"As the pious **bow-bearing** [god]." Naevius used this epithet in the second book of his *Punic War*: "Then the mighty, famous **bow-bearing** <note>original: *arcitenens*</note> one, powerful with arrows, the holy Pythian Apollo, son of Delphi." He says elsewhere:
> "When you, **bow-bearing** goddess, are powerful with arrows."
So too Hostius in the second book of his *Istrian War*:
> "Divine Minerva,
> and at the same time unconquered Apollo, **bow-bearing** son of Latona."
<margin>**Forest-dwelling**.</margin>
"Also the **forest-dwelling** Fauns." Naevius in the first book of the *Punic War*:
"**Forest-dwelling** <note>original: *syluicolæ*</note> men, unskilled in war."
Accius in his play *The Bacchants*:
"**Forest-dwelling** ones visiting unknown places."
<margin>**Sail-flying**.</margin>
"Looking down upon the **sail-flying** <note>original: *ueliuolum*; often used to describe the sea when covered in ships</note> sea." Livius [Andronicus] in his *Helena*:
"You who have traversed the deep, **sail-flying** seas of the ocean."
Ennius in his fourteenth book:
> "When from afar they see the enemies approach
> with **sail-flying** ships."

### BOOK VI.

<meta>catchword: word</meta>

...will suffice, which you desire to hear. Now, do not delay any longer in opening the way for Servius to discuss Virgil. Then Avienus, turning entirely toward Servius, said: "I wish you to tell me, greatest of teachers, why it is that while Virgil was always anxiously careful in choosing words according to the merit or the severity of the subject, he used a word carelessly and meanly in these verses:

> Her white loins girded with barking monsters,
> To have harassed the Dulichian ships.
> <note>original: *Candida succinctam latrantibus inguina monstris, / Dulichias uexasse rates*; from *Eclogues* 6.75–76. Scylla is described attacking the ships of Odysseus, who is referred to by his home, Dulichium.</note>

<margin>Gellius, book 2, chapter 6.</margin>
For 'harassed' [*vexasse*] is a word for a light and small inconvenience, not suited to such a terrible event, where men were suddenly snatched and torn apart by a most savage beast. But I have also discovered another instance of this kind:

> Who knows not of hard Eurystheus,
> Or the altars of the unpraised Busiris?
> <note>original: *Quis aut Eurysthea durum, / Aut illaudati nescit Busiridis aras?*; from *Georgics* 3.4–5. Busiris was a mythical Egyptian king who sacrificed all foreigners who entered his country.</note>

For this word, 'unpraised' [*illaudatus*], is not suitable to express the detestation of a most wicked man. Since he was accustomed to sacrifice people of all nations, he is not merely 'unworthy of praise,' but worthy of the detestation and execration of the whole human race. Furthermore, this word also does not seem to me to come from Virgil’s usual diligence: 'Through the tunic stiff with gold' <note>original: *Per tunicam squallentem auro*; from *Aeneid* 10.314.</note>. For it is not fitting to say 'filthy with gold' [*squallentem*], since the foulness of squalor is the opposite of the brightness and splendor of gold."

<margin>To harass [*vexare*].</margin>
And Servius replied: "Regarding the word 'harassed' [*vexasse*], I believe it can be answered in this way. 'Harassed' is actually a weighty word; it is derived from the word 'to carry' [*vehere*], which implies the force of another's will, for one who is carried is not in control of himself. But 'harassed' [*vexasse*], which is the intensive form of the word, undoubtedly implies a much more violent force and movement. For he who is carried off, snatched away, and pulled hither and thither, is properly said to be 'harassed' [*vexari*]. This is similar to how 'to appraise' or 'to tax' [*taxare*] is a more forceful and frequent action than 'to touch' [*tangere*], from which it is undoubtedly derived. And 'to toss' [*iactare*] is much more extensive and broader than 'to throw' [*iacere*], from which it...

--- Page 494 ---
<meta>This page continues the response to Avienus’s challenge regarding Virgil's vocabulary. The speaker (likely Servius or another learned guest) is explaining why the words "harassed" (vexatus) and "unpraised" (illaudatus) are actually far more powerful than they appear in modern common usage.</meta>

<page-num>492</page-num>

<header>THE SATURNALIA</header>

<margin>* original</margin>the word is derived. To "shatter" [quassare], for instance, is heavier and more violent than to "shake" [quatere]. Therefore, just because it is commonly said that someone is "harassed" by smoke, wind, or dust, the true force and * nature of the word should not be lost; it was observed correctly by the ancients, who spoke with both precision and figurative power. We find the words of Marcus Cato <note>Cato the Elder (234–149 BCE), a Roman statesman known for his austere character and his influential history and oratory.</note> in the speech he wrote *Concerning the Achaeans*: "And when Hannibal was tearing apart and **harassing** the land of Italy." Cato said Italy was "harassed" [*vexatam*] by Hannibal at a time when no kind of calamity, cruelty, or inhumanity could be found that Italy did not endure. Marcus Tullius [Cicero] says in the fourth book of his *Against Verres*: "Which was so despoiled and plundered by that man, that it seems to have been **harassed** not by some enemy—who might still respect religious law and the customs of war—but by barbarian pirates." <note>Cicero argues that "harassed" implies a level of total, lawless devastation beyond mere warfare.</note>

<margin>Unpraised.</margin>Regarding the term "unpraised" [*illaudatus*], however, two answers seem possible. One is of this sort: No person is of such ruined character that they do not occasionally do or say something that can be praised. Hence, this very ancient verse is celebrated like a proverb:

<margin>* For even a fool</margin>
> Often even a gardener speaks a word very much to the point.
> <note>original: Πολλάκι καὶ κηπωρὸς ἀνὴρ μάλα καίριον εἶπεν. The Latin translation provided in the source text is: *Sæpe etiam est holitor ualdè opportuna locutus*.</note>

<margin>* So indeed</margin>But indeed, he who in every matter and at every time is devoid of all praise—he is "unpraised" [*illaudatus*]; and such a person is the worst and most despicable of all. * Just as the absence of all fault makes one "blameless" [*inculpatus*]—and being blameless is the equivalent of perfect virtue—so too being "unpraised" is the very limit of extreme malice. Thus Homer is often accustomed to praise not by naming virtues, but by removing vices. <note>This is a rhetorical device called litotes, where an affirmative is expressed by the negative of its contrary.</note> For instance:

> The **blameless** seer spoke. <note>original: Ἤυδα μᾶντις ἀμύμων.</note> And:
> They flew **not unwillingly**. <note>original: Τώ δ’ οὐκ ἀκονte πετέσθη. *Iliad* 4.512.</note>
> They flew not unwillingly.
> <margin>Iliad, Book 4.</margin>There you would not see divine Agamemnon **slumbering**. <note>original: Ἔνθ’ οὐκ ἂν βρίζοντα ἴδοις Ἀγαμέμνονα δῖον. *Iliad* 4.223.</note>

<meta>catchword: Then</meta>

<summary>This page defends Virgil’s use of "harassed" and "unpraised" by showing how ancient authors used these terms to describe extreme devastation and total wickedness through the rhetorical device of litotes.</summary>

<header>BOOK VI.</header>

Then one would not see divine Agamemnon sluggish,
<note>original Greek: Οὐδὲ καταπτώσοντ’ οὐδ’ οὐκ ἐθέλοντα μάχεσθαι</note>
Nor cowering, nor unwilling to fight,
Nor fearful, nor hesitant to decide the matter with the sword.
<note>This is a translation of Homer’s Iliad (4.223–225), used here to show how poets define greatness by the absence of negative qualities.</note>

<margin>From Gellius.</margin>
Epicurus also in a similar way defined the greatest pleasure as the privation and removal of all pain, in these words: "The limit of the magnitude of pleasures is the removal of everything that causes pain." <note>original Greek: ὅρος τοῦ μεγέθους τῶν ἡδονῶν παντὸς τοῦ ἀλγοῦντος ὑπεξαίρεσις. Epicurus argued that true happiness is simply the absence of suffering.</note>

By the same reasoning, the same Virgil called the Stygian marsh "unlovely" <note>original: *inamabilem*</note>. For just as "unpraised" <note>original: *illaudatum*</note> is defined by the <term>privation of praise</term> <note>original: κατὰ στέρησιν</note>, so he expressed detestation for the Styx through the <term>privation of love</term>. In another way, "unpraised" is defended thus: in the ancient language, "to praise" <note>original: *laudare*</note> means to name or to call upon. Thus, in civil legal actions, a witness or guarantor is said to be "praised," which means to be named. Therefore, "unpraised" <note>original: *illaudatus*</note> is as if it were "unmentionable"—that is, someone who should never be named. This is just as it was once decreed by the common council of Asia that no one should ever mention the name of the man who had burned the temple of Diana at Ephesus. <note>The council sentenced the arsonist Herostratus to "damnatio memoriae," or the erasure of his name from history, to deny him the fame he sought.</note>

<margin>To be stiff or scaly.</margin>
The third point remains from those things which were criticized: that he called a tunic "stiff with gold" <note>original: *tunicam squallentem auro*</note>. This, however, signifies the abundance and density of gold woven in the appearance of scales. For "to be stiff" <note>original: *squallere*</note> is derived from the frequency and roughness of "scales" <note>original: *squamae*</note>, which are seen on the hides of serpents or fish. This usage is demonstrated both by others and by this same poet in several places:
> Whom a skin, he says, fastened with scales of bronze
> and gold, covered in a plume-like fashion. <note>Aeneid 11.770–771</note>
And in another place:
> And now he had already put on his glowing breastplate,
> bristling with scales of bronze. <note>Aeneid 11.487–488</note>

Accius writes thus in his *Pelopidae*: *The scales of that serpent were bordered with stiff gold and purple.* Therefore, whatever was excessively thick or covered with something so that it struck viewers with a shuddering sensation from its strange appearance was said "to be stiff" <note>original: *squallere*</note>. Just as on unkempt and "scaly" bodies a deep accumulation of filth is called "squalor" <note>original: *squallor*</note>. Of which meaning, much...

<header>SATURNALIA</header>

...and through constant use that whole word has become so corrupted that now "squalor" <note>original: *squallor*</note> has begun to be used for nothing else but filth.

### Three other passages in Virgil explained. CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>Gellius, Book 5, ch. 3.</margin>
"I am grateful," Avienus said, "that my poor opinion of those excellent sayings has been corrected. But in this verse, it seems to me that something is missing:
> *He himself sat with the Quirinal staff, and girt*
> *In a short robe.*
<note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 7.187–188. The passage describes King Picus as an ancient Roman ruler and priest.</note>

<margin>The staff.</margin>
For if we concede that nothing is missing, the result is that he is 'girt with a staff and a robe,' which is utterly absurd. Since a staff <note>original: *lituus*</note> is a short rod, curved at its thicker end, which the <term>Augurs</term> <note>Priests who interpreted the will of the gods by observing the flight of birds.</note> use, I do not see how he could be seen as 'girt' with a staff. Servius responded: This was said in the way that many things are commonly expressed through <term>ellipsis</term> <note>original: *defectionem*; the omission of a word that is understood from context.</note>. For example, when it is said: 'Marcus Cicero, a man of great eloquence,' and 'Roscius the actor, of the highest charm.' Neither of these is a full or perfect phrase, yet it is understood as if it were full and perfect. Just as Virgil says in another place:
> *Victorious Butes with a massive body,*
that is, *having* a massive body. And likewise elsewhere:
> *Into the center he threw twin gauntlets of massive weight.*
And similarly:
> *A house of gore and bloody feasts.*

Thus, therefore, that passage too ought to be seen in this way: *He himself with the Quirinal staff*, that is, *holding* the Quirinal staff. This would be not at all surprising if it had been said thus: 'Picus was with a Quirinal staff,' just as we say, 'the statue was with a large head.' Indeed, 'is,' 'was,' and 'has been' are often elegantly omitted without any loss to the meaning. But since mention has been made of the staff <note>original: *lituus*</note>, it must not be passed over; for we notice it can be asked whether the staff [took its name] from the trumpet...

<header>B O O K VI.</header>

Whether the staff of the <term>Augurs</term> <note>Priests in ancient Rome who interpreted the will of the gods by observing the flight of birds.</note> is called a trumpet <note>original: *tuba*</note>, or whether the trumpet is named after the staff <note>original: *lituus*</note>, is a matter of debate. For both have an equal form, and both are equally curved at the top. But if (as some think) the trumpet is called a *lituus* because of its sound—following that verse of Homer, "the bow twanged" <note>original: *λιγξε βιός* (*ligxe bios*); Virgil and others often sought Greek roots for Latin sounds.</note>—then it must be that the augural rod is called a *lituus* because of its resemblance to the trumpet. However, Virgil uses this word to mean a trumpet, as in this line:

->*And distinguished by the trumpet and the spear he went to battle.*<-

<margin>Gellius, Book 10, chapter 11.</margin>Avienus then added: "Regarding the phrase 'Hasten your flight,' <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.137; Neptune's command to the winds to leave his sight.</note> it is not quite clear to me what it means. For flight seems to me to be the opposite of 'ripening' or 'maturing' <note>original: *maturitati*; Avienus is confused because *maturare* usually means to ripen slowly, but here it is paired with flight.</note>. Therefore, I ask you to teach me how this word should be understood." And Servius replied: Nigidius, a man <margin>To hasten or ripen.</margin> distinguished in the disciplines of all the noble arts, said that "to hasten" <note>original: *maturare*</note> is to do something neither too quickly nor too slowly, but it is a sort of middle and tempered state. Nigidius spoke well and accurately. For in both grain and fruit, those things are called "mature" which are neither raw and unripened, nor fallen and overcooked, but have grown to strength in their proper time. The divine Augustus used to express this interpretation of Nigidius elegantly with two Greek words. For they say he was accustomed both to say in conversation and to write in his letters: "Make haste slowly" <note>original: *σπεῦδε βραδέως* (*speude bradeos*); a famous motto often translated into Latin as *Festina lente*.</note>. By this, he advised that both the speed of industry and the slowness of diligence should be applied to an action at the same time. From these two opposites, "maturity" is created. Thus Virgil introduces Neptune commanding the winds to depart: that they should depart so quickly as if they were in flight, and yet maintain a middle ground of stability in their retreat, going away as if "maturely"—that is, in a tempered manner. For he fears that in the very departure they might harm the fleet, should they return with excessive force, as if through a panicked flight. The same Virgil most skillfully separated those two words, "to hasten" <note>original: *maturare*</note> and "to hurry" <note>original: *properare*</note>, as if they were complete opposites, in these verses:

*If ever the cold rain keeps the farmer indoors,*

<header>THE SATURNALIA</header>

"Many things which, under a clear sky, would soon need to be hurried, may be finished in good time." <note>A reference to Virgil’s *Georgics* 1.260-261, discussing farm work during rainy weather.</note> He has distinguished these two words well and elegantly. For in the preparation of rural affairs, during storms and rains—since leisure is forced upon us—work can be **matured** <note>original: *maturari*; meaning to complete a task steadily and in its proper season.</note>; but during clear weather, because the time is pressing, it is necessary to **hasten** <note>original: *properari*</note>. Indeed, when we must describe something done with more compulsion and speed, it is more correctly said to be done **prematurely** rather than **maturely**. As Afranius said in his *Togata* <note>A Roman comedy featuring Roman characters and settings, named for the *toga* worn by the actors.</note> titled *The Name*:

->You seek power, you madman, prematurely, before it is ripe.<-

In this verse, it should be noted that he says "ripe" <note>original: *praecocem*</note>, not *praecoquem*. For its nominative case is not *praecoquis*, but *praecox*. At this point, Avienus asked again: "Since Virgil protected his Aeneas—as a man of such piety—from the contact of that grim sight among the inhabitants of the Underworld, making him hear the groans of the guilty rather than see the tortures themselves, yet freely led him into the very Fields of the Pious: why, then, does he show him in this verse the entrance to the places where the wicked were confined?

->Before the vestibule itself, and in the very jaws of Hades?<-

<margin>Gellius, Book 16, chapter 5.</margin>
For he who sees the vestibule and the jaws has undoubtedly already entered the house itself. Or, if something else is to be understood by the word **vestibule**, I wish to know." To this Servius replied: "There are many words that we use commonly, yet we do not clearly notice what they signify according to their true property. Such is **vestibule** <note>original: *vestibulum*</note>, a word frequent and obvious in conversation, yet not clearly understood by everyone who uses it easily. For they think a vestibule is the front part of the house, which they call the **atrium** <note>The central hall or court of a Roman house.</note>. But Caecilius Gallus, a most learned man, in the second book of his work *On the Signification of Words Pertaining to Civil Law*, says that a vestibule..."

<page-num>497</page-num>

<header>BOOK VI.</header>

[He] says it is not within the house itself, nor even a part of the house, but a vacant space before the door of the building, through which there is an entrance and access to the doors of the house from the street. For the door itself was set far back from the street, with an empty area placed between them. Furthermore, there is often much inquiry into the reasoning behind this word <note>The word being "vestibulum" or vestibule.</note>. But I will not hesitate to bring to light what I have read in the writings of reliable authors. 

The particle **ve-** <note>original: "Ve-"</note>, just like certain others, signifies sometimes an intensification and sometimes a reduction. For **Vetus** <note>original: "Vetus" (Old)</note> and **Vehemens** <note>original: "Vehemens" (Vehement)</note> are examples: the former is composed from and shortened by a "greatness of age" <note>The author suggests "vetus" comes from "ve" (intensive) + "aetas" (age).</note>; the latter is built from an "excessive impulse and force of mind" <note>original: "ve-" (intensive) + "mens" (mind).</note>. On the other hand, **Vecors** <note>meaning senseless or foolish</note> and **Vesanus** <note>meaning insane</note> signify a deprivation of sanity and heart <note>original: "cor" (heart/mind) and "sanus" (healthy/sane).</note>. 

Now, as we said above, those who built grand houses in ancient times were accustomed to leaving a vacant space before the door, which was situated in the middle between the doors of the house and the street. In that place, those who had come to greet the master of the house would stand before being admitted. Thus, they stood neither in the street, nor were they inside the building. <margin>* standing together</margin> Therefore, from that "standing together" <note>original: "consistione"</note> in a large place, and as it were a kind of "stabling" or gathering point, those spaces were called **Vestibules** <note>original: "Vestibula"</note>, in which many people would stand as they arrived before being let into the house. 

Others, while agreeing that vestibules are what we have described, disagree on the sense of the word. For they relate it not to those who arrive, but to those who live in the house: because they never "stand" there <note>Using "ve-" as a negative prefix</note>, but come to this place only for the sake of passage, whether leaving or returning. Whether, therefore, it should be understood according to the first group as an intensification <note>Meaning a place of much standing.</note> or according to the second as a reduction <note>Meaning a place of no standing.</note>, it is nevertheless established that the "vestibule" is the name for the area that divides the house from the street. 

The **Fauces** <note>original: "Fauces," literally "the throat," referring here to a narrow entrance passage.</note>, however, is the narrow path through which one turns from the street toward the vestibule. Therefore, when Aeneas sees the **fauces** and the **vestibule** of the house of the ungodly, he is not *inside* the house: nor is he polluted by the cursed and cruel contact of the building, but—

### CHAPTER IX.

<margin>Gellius <note>Aulus Gellius, a 2nd-century Roman author known for his miscellany "Attic Nights."</note> Book 16, Chapter 6.</margin>

But I wish to know the reasoning for this epithet applied to sheep.' And he, without any hesitation, said: 'Sheep are called *bidentes* <note>Literally: "two-toothed."</note> because they have only two teeth.' Then I asked: 'Where on earth, I pray you, have you ever seen sheep that by nature have only two teeth? For that would be a <term>monstrous omen</term> <note>original: "ostentum"</note>, and would require rituals of atonement!' At this, he became agitated and angry with me, saying: 'Seek instead those things which a grammarian ought to be asked; for you should ask shepherds about the teeth of sheep.' I laughed at the wit of that worthless man and left him."

"But," Avienus continued, "I am questioning you, Servius, as one who is well-acquainted with the very nature of words." <header>BOOK VI.</header>

...indeed, to prevent the collision of two vowels, the letter "d" is usually inserted. Therefore, they were first called *bidennes* <note>original: "bidennes," likely meaning "two-yearly" or "two years old."</note>, as if to say *biennes* <note>original: "biennes," from "bis" (twice) and "annus" (year).</note>; then, through long usage of speech, the pronunciation was corrupted, and from *bidennes* they were called <term>bidentes</term> <note>Literally "two-toothed."</note>. Hyginus, however, who was well-versed in the Law of the Pontiffs <note>The religious laws governing Roman priests.</note>, wrote in the fifth of the books he composed regarding Virgil that those sacrificial victims are called *bidentes* which, because of their age, have two teeth taller than the others, by which it is clear they have transitioned from a younger to an older age. Again, Avienus asks regarding these verses:

<margin>Gellius Book 18, Chapter 5.</margin>
> The Pelethronian Lapiths <note>A mythical tribe from Thessaly, credited in legend with inventing the bridle and the art of riding.</note> gave us the bit and the turning-circle,
> Mounted on the horse's back; and taught the horseman under arms
> To gallop over the ground and to gather his proud strides.

why Virgil attributed the action of the horse to the horseman. For "galloping over the ground" and "gathering strides" are agreed to be the actions of the horse, not the rider.

"Rightly so," said Servius, "this question of yours arises from a neglect of ancient reading. For because our age has abandoned Ennius <note>Quintus Ennius (c. 239–169 BC), often called the father of Roman poetry.</note> and the entire ancient library, we are ignorant of many things that would not be hidden from us if the reading of the ancients were familiar to us."

<margin>Horseman.</margin>
For all the ancient writers used the term <term>eques</term> <note>Usually translated as "horseman" or "knight."</note> for the man sitting on the horse, and also for the horse itself when it carried the man; and they said that not only the man "rides" <note>original: "equitare"</note>, but the horse does as well. Ennius says in the seventh book of his *Annals*:

> Finally, with great force, the four-footed horseman and the elephants
> Hurl themselves forward.

Is there any doubt that here he called the horse itself a "horseman" <note>original: "equitem"</note>, since he had added the adjective "four-footed" to it? In the same way, the word "to ride" <note>original: "equitare"</note>, which is a verb derived from the noun for horseman, was used for both the man using the horse and the horse walking under the man. For Lucilius <note>Gaius Lucilius, the 2nd-century BC inventor of Roman satire.</note>, a man exceptionally skilled in the Latin language, says that a horse both "runs" and "rides" in this verse:

> Surely we see this horse running and riding.

Therefore, in the work of Maro <note>original: "Maronem," referring to the poet Virgil.</note>, who was a diligent student of ancient Latin, it must be understood in this way: *And they taught the horseman under arms* <note>original: "Atque equitem docuere sub armis," from Virgil's Georgics 3.116.</note>; that is, they taught both the horse and the man carrying him to leap upon the ground and to gather his proud strides. ### V E S A L I E N S I S <note>This heading likely refers to a commentator or editor from Wesel or a specific 16th-century humanist scholar.</note>

It would certainly be a cause for grief that even this book is not preserved in its entirety, if the parts missing from the previous books were not of such great importance. Now, just as more serious diseases are sometimes the reason why subsequent ailments that arrive are not easily felt: so the gaps in the preceding books affect all scholars with such great pain that there can hardly be any room for further grief over this one.

ONCE THE FIRST courses were removed after the feast, and as smaller cups were circulating with varying rounds of wine, Prætextatus <note>Vettius Agorius Prætextatus, a high-ranking Roman official and leader of the pagan intellectual circle in the 4th century AD.</note> said: "Food usually makes men quiet when it is consumed, while drink makes them talkative. But we remain silent even amidst the cups, as if such a banquet ought to be devoid of serious or even philosophical discussions." And Symmachus <note>Quintus Aurelius Symmachus, a famous Roman statesman and orator known for his defense of traditional Roman religion.</note> replied: "Do you really feel this way, Vettius, that Philosophy should be present at banquets? Should she not rather be kept within her inner chambers like some censorious and overly <margin>modest</margin> <note>original: *verecunda*, correcting the printed text *reuerenda*</note> mistress of the house? Nor should she mix with Liber <note>A Roman name for Bacchus, the god of wine.</note>, to whom even commotions are familiar, since she herself is of such modesty that she admits not only the noise of words, but not even the noise of thoughts into the sanctuary of her peace? Let us learn even from foreign institutions and the discipline sought from the customs of the Parthians <note>An empire in ancient Iran; Romans often viewed their customs as exotic or luxury-oriented.</note>, who are accustomed to enter banquets with concubines, not with wives—as if it were fitting for the former to be brought before the public and even to behave wantonly, while it is right for the latter to protect their hidden modesty only when secluded at home. Should I think that Philosophy should be brought out to a place where even the rhetorical art—a popular profession—has blushed to come? For Isocrates <note>A famous Greek orator (436–338 BC) known for his polished, rhythmic prose.</note>, the Greek orator, who first compelled words (which were previously free) to follow rhythmic measures, when he was begged by his companions at a banquet to bring forth something from the fountain of his eloquence, refused with this excuse: 'Those things which are now [fitting]...' <note>original: "Quæ præsens," leading into the famous quote: "What is now appropriate, I am not skilled in; what I am skilled in, is not now appropriate."</note>

<summary>This page begins the final book of the Saturnalia, shifting the dialogue to whether philosophy and serious intellectual debate have a rightful place at a dinner party. Symmachus argues that philosophy is too "modest" for the rowdiness of wine, citing the orator Isocrates and Parthian social customs as examples.</summary>

<margin>The Greek says: "In matters where I am skilled, it is not the right time; in matters where it is the right time, I am not skilled." <note>original: "ἐν οἷς μὲν ἐγὼ δεινὸς οὐκ ὁ νῦν καιρός, ἐν οἷς δὲ ὁ νῦν καιρός οὐκ ἐγὼ δεινὸς." This refers to a common proverb about the difficulty of matching one's expertise to the social occasion.</note></margin>
*...what the place and time demand, I do not know; what I know is suited neither to the present place nor the time. To this, Eustathius replied: "I approve of your intention, Symmachus, in that you venerate Philosophy with that great reverence you think it deserves, so much so that you believe it should only be adored within its inner sanctuary. But if it is to be exiled from banquets for this reason, then let its foster-daughters depart far from here too—I mean Honesty and Modesty, and no less Piety along with Sobriety. For which of these would I say is less venerable? Thus it happens that if this chorus of noble matrons <note>Here, Eustathius personifies the virtues as "noble matrons" (matronarum) to contrast them with the "concubines" of vice.</note> is banished from such gatherings, the freedom of banquets is surrendered solely to concubines—that is, to vices and crimes.*

*But far be it from Philosophy, which treats so carefully of the duties of dining in its own schools, to dread banquets itself—as if it could not maintain in practice what it is accustomed to teach in words, or did not know how to observe a limit, the boundaries of which it has established in all acts of human life. For I do not invite Philosophy to the table so that she might not moderate herself, she whose discipline is to teach the moderation of all things. Therefore, so that I may settle the matter between you and Vettius as if by an arbitral judgment, I shall indeed open the doors of the dining rooms <term>triclinia</term> <note>The Roman dining room, named for the three couches (*tri-cline*) arranged around a central table.</note> to Philosophy. But I promise she will be present in such a way that she does not exceed the measure of the arrangement known to her and her followers." Then Furius said: "Since our age has produced you, Eustathius, as the unique follower of Philosophy, you are requested to reveal to us the manner of the arrangement which you grant even to a banqueter."*

<margin>A philosopher must first observe the temperaments of the fellow-guests: and according to their quality, must sometimes be silent and sometimes speak.</margin>
*And Eustathius said: "I know she will observe this first: that she weighs within herself the temperaments of the guests present. And if she finds several who are skilled, or at least lovers of her, in the company of the banquet, she will allow herself to be the subject of discussion. Because just as a few mute letters <note>A reference to consonants, which in ancient grammatical theory were "mute" unless accompanied by a vowel.</note>, scattered among many vowels, are easily softened into the fellowship of a voice, so the few unlearned rejoice in the company of the learned..."*

<meta>catchword: or</meta>

<summary>Eustathius argues that Philosophy belongs at a banquet because it teaches the very moderation and virtue needed to prevent a feast from descending into vice. He suggests that a philosopher's participation depends on the character of the other guests, using a grammatical analogy of vowels and consonants.</summary>

# BOOK VII.
I 4
<meta>catchword: things,</meta>

...they harmonize, if they are able; or they are captivated by the hearing of such things. If, however, the majority of the guests are strangers to the training of this discipline <note>Referring to the study of Philosophy.</note>, Philosophy will command the few wise men present to conceal their true nature. She will allow a level of talkativeness that is more agreeable to the majority to prevail, so that the rare nobility of thought is not disturbed by the rowdy commoners. And this is one of the virtues of Philosophy: because while an orator is only proven by his speaking, a Philosopher philosophizes no less by keeping silent when the time is right than by speaking. Thus, the few more learned men present will shift their behavior to match the unrefined group, while keeping the notion of truth safe and quiet within themselves, so that any suspicion of discord vanishes.

<margin>A deed of Pisistratus <note>A 6th-century BCE ruler (tyrant) of Athens known for his cleverness and public works.</note> worthy of note.</margin>
Nor is it surprising if a learned man does what Pisistratus, the tyrant of Athens, once did. When he had given his sons right counsel but failed to obtain their agreement—and was therefore at odds with his children—he discovered that this was a cause of joy for his rivals. They hoped that from that discord, a revolution might arise in the house of the ruler. Having summoned the whole body of citizens together, Pisistratus announced that although he had been angry with his sons for not yielding to their father’s will, it later seemed to him more fitting for fatherly devotion to yield to his children’s opinion himself. He wanted the city to know, therefore, that the king’s offspring were in harmony with their father. By this artifice, he stripped away the hope of those plotting against the ruler’s peace.

So, in every walk of life, and especially in the joy of a banquet, everything that seems out of tune must be brought into a single harmony of sound, provided integrity is preserved. Thus Agathon’s banquet <note>The setting of Plato's famous *Symposium*, a philosophical discussion on Love.</note>, because it included Socrates, Phaedrus, Pausanias, and Eryximachus—and likewise that dinner which the most learned Callias gave for Carneades, Antisthenes, and Hermogenes, and others like them—heard not a single word that was not philosophical. But indeed, the tables of Alcinous or Dido <note>Alcinous is the king of the Phaeacians in Homer’s *Odyssey*; Dido is the Queen of Carthage in Virgil’s *Aeneid*. Both are famous literary hosts.</note>, being suited only for luxuries, featured Ioppas or Demodocus singing to the lyre.

<margin>*Polyphemus <note>The original margin notes "Polyphemum" here, possibly as a scholarly cross-reference to Homeric themes of unrefined vs. refined dining.</note></margin>
Nor were there lacking at the court of Alcinous men who danced—

# THE SATURNALIA

...things; and at Dido’s table, Bitias <note>A character from Vergil’s *Aeneid* who drinks deeply from a gold bowl at the feast given for Aeneas.</note>, gulping down the unmixed wine so that he soaked himself entirely in its excessive overflow. Would it not be true that if someone, either among the Phaeacians <note>A peaceful, seafaring people in Homer's *Odyssey* known for their hospitality and feasts.</note> or among the Carthaginians, had mixed discourses dug out from deep wisdom with the light stories of a banquet, he would both lose the charm appropriate to those gatherings and <margin>*justly</margin> rightly move the guests to mockery?

<margin>On which matters one should philosophize at a banquet, if only the opportunity for philosophizing is given.</margin>

Therefore, his first observation will be to evaluate the guests. Then, when he sees an opening for himself, he will not speak of the secrets of his own depth amidst the cups; nor will he raise knotty and anxious questions, but rather those that are useful and easy. For just as among those who make it a type of exercise to dance in the middle of banquets, if someone—in order to exercise himself further—should challenge his companions to a race or to boxing, he would be cast out from the lively group as foolish; so at the table, when it is permitted, one must philosophize about fitting things. In this way, the mixing-bowl of liquid born for joy may be tempered not only by the Nymphs <note>In antiquity, wine was almost always diluted with water; the "Nymphs" here symbolize the water used for dilution.</note>, but also by the addition of the Muses <note>The goddesses of the arts and sciences, representing intellectual conversation.</note>.

For if (as must be admitted) in every gathering one must either keep silent or speak, let us ask whether silence or an opportune conversation is better suited to banquets. For if, just as at Attic Athens the Areopagites <note>The elite and somber judicial council of Athens.</note> judge in silence, it were necessary always to be silent during feasts, then there would be no further question of whether one should philosophize at the table or not. But if banquets are not to be silent, why should honorable speech be forbidden where dishonorable speech is permitted? Especially since words gladden a banquet no less than the sweetness of wine.

For if you scrutinize Homer’s hidden wisdom more deeply, that soothing drug which Helen mixed into the wine—"lulling all sorrow and anger, and bringing forgetfulness of every evil" <note>original: νηπενθές τ᾿ ἄχολόν τε κακῶν τ᾿ ἐπίληθες ἁπάντων</note>—was not a herb, nor a juice from India, but the opportunity for storytelling, which turned the guest, forgotten of his sorrow, toward joy. For she was recounting the famous deeds of Ulysses <note>The Roman name for the Greek hero Odysseus.</note> while his son <note>Telemachus, who was visiting Helen and Menelaus in Sparta.</note> was present:

<margin>Odyssey, Book 4.</margin>

"I could not tell or name all [the struggles of bold-hearted Odysseus]" <note>original: Πάντα μὲν οὐκ ἂν ἐγὼ μυθήσομαι οὐδ᾿ ὀνομήνω</note>

<summary>This page argues that philosophy is appropriate for banquets as long as it is "tempered" to suit the company, comparing intellectual conversation to the way water (Nymphs) tempers wine.</summary>

# BOOK VII.

I 5

> All the many trials that stout-hearted Odysseus endured.
> But what a deed this was that the strong man performed and dared
> in the land of the Trojans, where you Achaeans were suffering.
> <note>original: "Ὅσσοι Ὀδυσσῆος ταλασίφρονος εἰσὶν ἄεθλοι. / Ἀλλ' οἷον τόδ' ἔρεξε καὶ ἔτλη καρτερὸς ἀνὴρ / Δήμῳ ἔνι Τρώων, ὅθι πάσχετε πήματ' Ἀχαιοί." From Homer’s *Odyssey*, Book 4.242, 244-5. Helen tells these stories to Odysseus's son, Telemachus, to hearten him.</note>

Therefore, by recounting his father’s glory and his individual deeds of bravery, she made the son’s spirit more cheerful; and so it was believed that she mixed a remedy for sorrow into the wine. "What," he asks, "does this have to do with Philosophy?" On the contrary, nothing is so closely related to wisdom as adapting one's speech to the time and place, based on an assessment of the persons present. For some are inspired by related examples of virtues, others by examples of benefits, and several by examples of modesty—so that those who were acting otherwise might often come to self-improvement upon hearing such things. If the order of conversation at a banquet requires it, Philosophy will strike those entangled in vices without them even feeling it. It is like how Father Liber <note>A Roman name for Bacchus (Dionysus), the god of wine and theater.</note> strikes with his thyrsus <note>A staff tipped with a pine cone and wrapped in vine leaves or ivy. It was the ceremonial wand of Bacchus and his followers.</note> by the slanting of the surrounding ivy, while the sharp point remains hidden. For a philosopher will not present himself at a banquet as a Censor <note>A high-ranking Roman official responsible for public morality and the census.</note>, openly punishing vices. Otherwise, those liable to such faults would fight back, and the banquet would be thrown into such an uproar that the guests would seem to have been invited under an edict like this:

> "For what remains, men, now that things are well done,
> joyfully tend to your bodies and, being ready, look forward to the fight."
> <note>original: "Quod superest, læti bene gestis corpora rebus / Procurate uiri, & pugnam sperate parati." From Vergil’s *Aeneid* IX, 157-158.</note>

Or as Homer said more briefly and clearly:

<margin>Iliad 19.</margin>
> "Now go to dinner, so that we may join the battle."
> <note>original: "Νῦν δ' ἔρχεσθ' ἐπὶ δεῖπνον, ἵνα ξυνάγωμεν Ἄρηα." From the *Iliad*, Book 19.275.</note>

Therefore, if the opportunity for a necessary reprimand arises, it should come from the Philosopher in such a way that it is both veiled and effective. What wonder is it if the wise man (as I said) strikes those who do not feel it? For sometimes he may reprimand in such a way that the person being corrected is actually gladdened. Yet he will demonstrate the power of Philosophy—which speaks nothing foolish—not only through his stories, but also through his inquiries. Therefore, let no honorable act, no place, and no assembly exclude her; she adapts herself so that she appears necessary everywhere, as if it would have been a sin for her to be absent.

### On what topics each person may be asked about with pleasure. CHAPTER II.

<margin>The matters about which one might desire to be questioned.</margin>

*AND Avienus said: You seem to be introducing two new disciplines to me—that of questioning, and even that of criticizing—so that excitement may be stirred up on both sides in those being addressed. For pain usually follows criticism, even when it is just. Therefore, I beg you to make these matters, which you have only lightly touched upon, clearer through a full explanation.*

*“First,” said Eustathius, “I want you to understand that I was not speaking of that kind of criticism which has the appearance of a formal accusation, but rather that which takes the form of a light-hearted reproach. The Greeks call this a **skōmma** <note>original: "σκῶμμα"; a witty taunt or playful jab intended to provoke a reaction without being truly malicious.</note>. It is indeed no less bitter than a formal accusation if it is brought forth at the wrong time. But it will be presented by a wise man in such a way that it is not lacking in sweetness.*

*And to answer you first regarding questioning: he who wishes to be a pleasant inquirer asks those things which are easy for the person questioned to answer, and which he knows that person has learned through diligent practice. For everyone rejoices when they are invited to bring their learning into the open; no one wants what they have learned to remain hidden—especially if the knowledge they sought with great effort is familiar to only a few and unknown to most, such as astronomy, or logic <note>original: "dialectica"; the art of investigating or discussing the truth of opinions through logical argument.</note>, and other similar subjects.*

*For then they seem to reap the fruit of their labor when they obtain the opportunity of making public what they have learned without the mark of showing off—a mark which is absent from one who does not force his knowledge upon others, but is invited to bring it forth. On the contrary, it is a cause of great bitterness if you question someone in front of many people about something they have not mastered with the best knowledge. For they are forced either to deny they know it—which they consider the ultimate loss of dignity—or to answer recklessly, committing themselves to the chance outcome of being right or wrong. From this, the betrayal of their ignorance often arises, and they blame the inquirer for all this misfortune to their reputation.*

*Likewise, those who have traversed the seas and lands rejoice when they are asked about the location of lands or the curves of the coastline unknown to many; they respond gladly, and describe...* <meta>catchword: ...bunt (they will describe)</meta>

<summary>Eustathius explains the etiquette of conversation, arguing that a polite guest should ask others about subjects they know well to allow them to share their expertise without appearing boastful. He also distinguishes between harmful accusations and "skōmma," or witty, constructive social critiques.</summary>

# BOOK VII.

<page-num>507</page-num>

...many, they describe <note>The text begins mid-sentence, completing the thought that people with rare knowledge enjoy sharing it.</note> locations, sometimes with words and sometimes with a pointer <note>original: "radio"; a geometer's rod used for measuring or pointing to diagrams</note>, thinking it a most glorious thing to present to the eyes of others what they themselves have seen. What of generals and soldiers, who are always eager to speak of their brave deeds, yet remain silent for fear of appearing arrogant? If they are invited to recount these things, do they not feel that the reward for their labor has been paid in full? They consider it a recompense to tell of their actions to a willing audience. Indeed, this kind of storytelling has such a taste of glory that if envious people or rivals happen to be present, they disrupt such questioning by making noise; by inserting other tales, they prevent the telling of things that usually bring praise to the narrator. Also, one who has escaped past dangers or hardships that are now completely over is most pleasantly invited to recount them. For one who is still even slightly entangled in them shudders at the reminder and fears the account. Euripides expressed this well: "How sweet it is for one who has been saved to remember his troubles" <note>original: "ὡς ἡδύ σωθέντα μεμνῆσθαι πόνων"</note>. He added the word "saved" <note>original: "σωθέντα"</note> to show that the pleasure of the telling begins only after the end of the evils. And your poet <note>A reference to Virgil, highly esteemed by the characters in the Saturnalia.</note>, by adding the word "someday," says that the memory of settled labor will bring pleasure in the future only after misfortunes have been endured:

-> "Perhaps someday it will be a joy to remember even these things." <-
<note>Virgil, Aeneid, 1.203</note>

<margin>*others read: attached or fixed</margin>
Nor would I deny that there are types of evils that the one who endured them does not wish to remember even after they are over; he is no less offended when questioned than when he was in the midst of the evils themselves. Such as one who has experienced the executioners and the torture of his limbs, or one who has suffered unlucky bereavements, or one on whom a <term>Censorial mark (nota censoria): a public mark of disgrace or demotion in rank imposed by the Roman Censors</term> was once *afflicted. Take care not to ask about such things, lest you seem to be throwing them in his face. If you can, frequently invite him to speak who was favorably received in a public recitation, or who carried out a diplomatic mission <term>legationem: an official embassy or mission on behalf of the state</term> with freedom and success, or who was welcomed by the Emperor courteously and affably, or if someone escaped alone—whether by wit or by strength—when almost the entire fleet was captured by pirates; for [the questioner] hardly satisfies the speaker's desire...

<summary>Eustathius discusses the psychology of conversation, noting that people enjoy being asked about their successes or past (but resolved) hardships, while certain traumas and social disgraces should never be mentioned.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discourse of Eustathius on the art of conversation at a banquet. -># OF THE SATURNALIA<-

...or even a long narration of such things. It is pleasing if you bid someone to speak of a friend's sudden good fortune, which he did not dare to mention or keep silent of his own accord—fearing now the appearance of boasting, now the appearance of malice. Let the man who delights in hunting be asked about the extent of the forest, the winding paths of the coverts, and the outcome of the hunt. If a religious man is present, give him the opportunity to relate by what observances he earned the help of the Gods, and what great fruit he gathered from his ceremonies; for people also consider it a form of religious duty not to keep silent about the benefits of the Divine Powers. Add to this that they wish to be thought of as friends to the Gods. If, however, an old man is also present, you have an occasion where you may seem to have conferred the greatest favor upon him if you question him even about things that do not concern him at all. For talkativeness is a familiar trait of this age. Homer, knowing this, had a whole cluster of questions offered to Nestor at once:

<margin>Odyssey, Book 3</margin>
> "Now I wish to inquire and ask Nestor about another matter, since he knows justice and the wisdom of others beyond all men. For they say he has reigned over three generations of men; thus he seems to me like an immortal to look upon. O Nestor, son of Neleus, tell me the truth. How did the son of Atreus, wide-ruling Agamemnon, die? Where was Menelaus? What kind of destruction did the crafty Aegisthus plot for him, since he killed a man much better than himself? Was he not in Achaean Argos, but wandering somewhere else among men, so that the other grew bold and slew him?" <note>original: This is a translation of the Greek passage from Homer's Odyssey, 3.243–252. Telemachus is asking the aged King Nestor for news of his father and the other heroes of the Trojan War.</note>

He heaped together so many seeds for speaking by his questioning that he might satisfy the "itch" <note>original: "pruritum"; here used metaphorically for a restless urge or desire to talk</note> of old age. And Virgil's Aeneas, showing himself grateful for everything toward Evander, provides him with various occasions for narrative. For he does not inquire about only one thing or another, but **gladly seeks out and hears, one by one, the monuments of earlier men.** <note>original: "Exquiritq; audit'que uirūm monumenta priorum"; a quote from Virgil's Aeneid, 8.312. Aeneas is being shown the sites of what would eventually become Rome by the local king, Evander.</note> And Evander, captivated by these consultations, you know how many things he then recounted.

He cites the classical examples of Nestor in Homer and Evander in Virgil to show how satisfying a person's desire to share their history creates a pleasant atmosphere.</summary>

### On the various kinds of jests, and how cautiously they must be used among banquet guests. CHAPTER III.

<margin>* a touch</margin>
As he spoke these words, the favor of all greeted him. But soon Avienus added: "I would ask all of you, the most learned of the learned who are present, that by your encouragement Eustathius might be emboldened to reveal what he spoke of a little earlier regarding the jest." With everyone urging this, he continued: "Besides *kategoria* <note>original: κατηγορία; a formal accusation</note>, which is an accusation, and besides *diabole* <note>original: διαβολὴν; slander or backbiting</note>, which is a false report, there are two other names among the Greeks: *loidoria* <note>original: λοιδορία</note> and *skomma* <note>original: σκῶμμα</note>. I do not find exact Latin names for these, unless perhaps you say that *loidoria* is a 'reproach' aimed at a direct insult. For I might almost call a *skomma* a 'figured bite' <note>Latin: *morsum figuratum*; a metaphorically stinging remark</note>, because it is often covered by deceit or wit, so that it sounds like one thing while you understand another. Yet it does not always lead to bitterness; sometimes it is even pleasant to those at whom it is thrown. The wise man, or otherwise the witty one, practices this kind of talk especially among tables and cups, where provocation to anger is easy. For just as even a light breeze <margin>* touch</margin> pushes one standing on a precipice, so too when one is soaked or sprinkled with wine, even a small pain incites a person into a frenzy.

<margin>Another kind of jest.</margin>
Therefore, one must abstain more cautiously from the jest <term>skomma|A witty, indirect, or metaphorical jibe that masks its sting.</term> at a banquet, which holds a hidden injury within itself. Such sayings stick much more tightly than direct insults <term>loidoria|A direct and open verbal attack or reproach.</term>, just as barbed hooks are fixed more tenaciously than straight points; and such sayings especially move those present to laughter, and by this kind of assent, the injury is confirmed. An insult of this kind is: 'Have you forgotten that you used to sell salted fish?' <note>In antiquity, selling salted fish was considered a lowly, manual trade; this remark serves to shame someone for their humble origins.</note> But a jest, which we said is often a concealed insult, is like this: 'We remember when you used to wipe your nose on your arm.' <note>Before the common use of handkerchiefs, wiping one's nose on a sleeve was a sign of a rustic or unrefined upbringing.</note> For though the same thing is said in both cases, the former is an insult because it is an open objection and reproach; the latter is a jest because it is phrased figuratively. Octavius, who by birth <gloss>* noble</gloss> appeared to be a Libyan...
