To Cicero, while he was reciting, he [Octavius] said: "I do not hear what you are saying." Cicero replied, "Certainly you used to have well-pierced ears." <note>original: "Certè solebas bene foratas habere aures."</note> This was said because Octavius was said to be of Libyan origin, and it is their custom to pierce the ear. <note>In Rome, pierced ears were associated with people from North Africa or slaves, whereas Cicero’s joke plays on the idea that someone with "holes" in their ears should be able to hear better.</note> Laberius used a similar jest against Cicero; when Cicero would not receive him into the seating area, saying, "I would receive you, were we not sitting so narrowly," <note>original: "nisi angustè sederemus"</note> Laberius replied quite bitingly: "And yet you used to sit on two chairs," <note>original: "Atqui solebas duabus sellis sedere"</note> throwing a jab at so great a man for his slippery loyalty. <note>Laberius is mocking Cicero for being a "fence-sitter" between the political factions of Caesar and Pompey.</note> But that which Cicero said—"were we not sitting so narrowly"—was a taunt <term>scomma<gloss>a witty but stinging jest</gloss></term> against Gaius Caesar, who was admitting so many people into the Senate from everywhere that the fourteen rows of seats could not hold them. Therefore, a wise man must always abstain from this kind of talk, which is the offspring of insult, and others should especially avoid it at a banquet.

<margin>* From chapter 2 of book 2, we have restored this passage thus: "as Marcus Votacilius against the Consul, who completed his consulship in only a single day. They used to," etc.</margin>

There are other jests that are less harsh, like the bites of a toothless beast; * such as what Cicero said regarding the consul who served for only a single day. <note>This refers to Caninius Rebilus, who was appointed consul by Caesar for the final few hours of a year.</note> "Usually," he said, "we have Priests of Jupiter <note>original: "Flamines Diales"; a pun on "Dialis" (belonging to Jupiter) and "dies" (day)</note>; now we have Daily Consuls." And regarding the same man: "Our Consul is most vigilant, for in his entire consulship he never saw sleep." <note>Since his term lasted less than 24 hours, he literally didn't sleep through it.</note> And to that same man who reproached him for not having come to visit him during his consulship, Cicero said, "I was coming, but night overtook me."

These and such things are those which have more refinement and less bitterness. So too are those remarks about certain bodily defects that produce little or no pain: such as if you speak of someone’s baldness, or their nose—whether it is a curved hook or a Socratic flatness. <note>Socrates was famously described as having a snub or "depressed" nose.</note> For the less these things are considered "misfortunes," the lighter the pain they cause. On the other hand, the loss of an eye is never mentioned without provoking an outburst of emotion. Indeed, King Antigonus <note>Antigonus the One-Eyed, a general of Alexander the Great.</note> killed Theocritus of Chios—whom he had sworn he would spare—because of a jest Theocritus made about him. For when he was being hurried toward Antigonus as if to be punished, and his friends were consoling him and promising hope, saying he would surely experience the king's mercy when he came before his eyes...

Nor would I deny that philosophers also sometimes stumbled into this kind of taunting out of indignation. For when a king’s freedman <note>A former slave who had gained freedom and often significant wealth or political power.</note>, recently raised to new riches, had gathered philosophers for a banquet and, by mocking their trivial questions, said he wished to know why a porridge of one color is produced from black and white beans; Aridices the philosopher, taking it poorly, said: "You explain to us why similar welts are produced from white and black thongs." <note>Aridices is implying that the freedman was whipped as a slave by both light and dark leather straps, leaving the same scars regardless of the color of the strap.</note>

<margin>Again, two kinds of taunts.</margin>
There are taunts <term>scommata<gloss>witty but biting jests</gloss></term> which on the surface have the appearance of an insult, but meanwhile do not affect the listeners, whereas if the same things were said to a guilty person, they would distress him. Conversely, there are those which have the appearance of praise, but render the character of the listener full of disgrace.

<margin>The first kind.</margin>
I shall speak of the first kind first: Lucius Quintus the Praetor had recently returned from his province, having observed—which you might wonder at—the greatest integrity during his praetorship in the time of Domitian <note>The Emperor Domitian (r. 81–96 AD) was known for his harsh and often corrupt administration; Quintus is noted for remaining honest in a corrupt era.</note>. When he, being ill, said to a friend sitting by him that he had cold hands, that friend, smiling, said: "And yet you brought them back 'hot' from the province just a little while ago." <note>A pun on "hot hands": to have "hot hands" in a province meant to be greedy or to embezzle money. Since Quintus was famously honest, the joke is a backhanded compliment.</note> Quintus laughed and was delighted, since he was entirely free from any suspicion of theft.

On the other hand, if this were said to one with a guilty conscience, reflecting on his own thefts, it would have provoked the listener. When Socrates challenged Critobulus, a youth of famous beauty, to a contest of looks, he was joking, not mocking. Certainly, if you say to a man of consummate wealth, "I am stirring up your creditors against you," or to an exceedingly chaste man, "Prostitutes are grateful to you because you have enriched them with continuous generosity," they will certainly be delighted, knowing that their conscience is not burdened by these words. Just as, conversely, there are those that distress under the appearance of praise, as I divided a moment ago. For if I say to a very fearful man, "You are to be compared to Achilles or Hercules," or...

->## BOOK VII.<-

...to a man of notorious iniquity: "I prefer you to Aristides <note>Aristides (c. 530–468 BC) was an Athenian statesman nicknamed "the Just," famous for his rigid integrity.</note> in equity." Without doubt, both parties will interpret these words—which sound like praise—as a mark of their own reproach. These same witty jests <term>scommata<gloss>clever but stinging jokes</gloss></term> can at one time be helpful and at another time bite the very same people, depending on the diversity of the persons present. For there are things which, if they were cast at us in the presence of friends, we might hear gladly. Yet, we do not want any such jest to be said against us when a wife, parents, or teachers are present—unless perhaps the joke is of such a kind that their own judgment would receive it gladly.

For example, one might mock a youth in the presence of his parents or teachers by saying he is "going mad" from constant vigils and nightly readings; or, in the presence of a wife, one might say her husband acts "foolishly" by being so devoted to her that he ignores all other beautiful women. Such remarks drench both the subject of the joke and the onlookers with cheerfulness.

The condition of the speaker also recommends the jest if they share the same circumstance: for instance, if a poor man mocks another for his poverty, or one of obscure birth mocks another who is obscurely born. Consider Tharsius Amphias <note>A figure mentioned in Greek anecdotal history, likely a parvenu or successful commoner.</note>, who, having become powerful after starting as a gardener, said something to a friend as if mocking his low status, but then immediately added: "But we too are grown from the same seeds." Thus, he made everyone equally happy.

Indeed, those "direct" jests fill the one they are aimed at with joy: for instance, if you should reproach a brave man as if he were reckless with his own safety and too willing to die for others; or if you should object to a generous man that he "squanders" his possessions by looking less to his own needs than to those of others.

In this way, Diogenes used to praise his teacher, Antisthenes the Cynic <note>Antisthenes was the founder of Cynic philosophy; Diogenes of Sinope was his most famous pupil, known for living in a ceramic jar (often called a "tub").</note>, by appearing to reproach him. For he used to say, "He himself made me a beggar instead of a rich man, and made me dwell in a tub instead of a spacious house." He expressed this much better than if he had simply said, "I am grateful to him because he made me a philosopher and a man of perfected virtue." Therefore, while there is only one name for a witty jest, many different effects are contained within it. For this reason, among the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans, known for their disciplined lifestyle and "laconic" wit.</note>, amidst their other institutions for a disciplined life, this also...

...this kind of exercise was instituted by Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta, traditionally credited with the city's rigid social and military system.</note>: so that young men might learn both to tell jokes <term>scommata<gloss>witty, biting jests</gloss></term> without malice, and to endure them when said by others against themselves. And if any of them should fall into indignation because of such a remark, he was no longer permitted to joke at another's expense. Therefore, since you see, my dear Avienus (for your youth must be instructed, being so eager to learn that it invites teaching), since you see, I say, that every kind of witty jest is double-edged, I advise that at banquets—where anger lies in wait for joy—you keep away from such sayings. Instead, you should either propose dinner-table questions <note>original: "quaestiones conviviales"</note> or solve them yourself. The ancients did not consider this genre so trivial, for even Aristotle wrote something about them, as did Plutarch and your own Apuleius <note>The famous North African Roman author of "The Golden Ass" and various philosophical works; the speaker calls him "yours" to emphasize his Latin heritage.</note>. Nor should that be held in contempt which has earned the attention of so many philosophers.

### CHAPTER IV. That simple food is to be preferred to varied food, as being easier to digest.

<margin>Whether simple or varied food is easier to digest.</margin>

Come now, all of you who are present, let us talk of things appropriate for a banquet—not only about food itself, but also perhaps something concerning the nature of our bodies, or other matters. This is especially fitting since our friend **Disarius** <note>A prominent physician in the dialogue, representing the medical perspective.</note> is present, whose skill and learning can contribute most to this kind of inquiry. Then he said: I ask whether a simple or a varied meal is easier to digest, because we see many people following the former, and not a few the latter. Indeed, a restrained diet is proud and stubborn, and as it were, a display of itself; on the other hand, a hearty appetite wishes to appear pleasant and companionable. ->## BOOK VII.<-

...nature, to digest <note>original: 'concoquenda', literally "to cook together," reflecting the ancient belief that digestion was a process of heating or cooking food in the stomach</note> all that has been gathered. And first, let us look at the quality of the juice <note>referring to chyle or chyme, the fluid produced by digestion</note>. He who takes simple food easily learns, by experience, whether his body is helped or burdened by its juice. For he is not in doubt as to which food's quality has taken possession of him, since he has taken only one. And so it happens that the harm, once its cause has been discovered, is easily avoided. But he who is nourished by varied food suffers diverse qualities from the diversity of juices; nor do the humors arising from a variety of matter agree, nor do they produce clear or pure blood when they are transformed by the service of the liver, but they pass into the veins with their own tumult. From this comes a spring of diseases, which are born from the discord of humors repugnant to each other. Next, because the nature of all things that are eaten is not the same: not all are digested at the same time, but some faster, and others slower. And so it happens that the order of the subsequent digestions is disturbed. For the digestion of the food we take is not a single process; but in order to nourish the body, it undergoes four digestions. One of these everyone—even the dull-witted—perceives, while more hidden reasoning detects the others. To make this clear to all, I must trace the cause back a little further.

<margin>The four digestions.</margin>

There are four powers <term>virtutes<gloss>innate faculties or forces within the body</gloss></term> in us which have received the duty of administering nourishment. One of these is called the "attractive" power <note>original Greek: 'kathelktikē'</note>, which draws down the food prepared by the jaws. For what would push such thick matter through the narrow passages of the throat unless a more hidden force of nature swallowed it? Once swallowed, however, the foods do not descend all the way to the bottom in a continuous fall through the succeeding openings of the body, being passed out just as they were received; rather, they await the beneficial service of digestion. This is the care of the second power, which the Greeks call "retentive" <note>original Greek: 'kathektikēn'</note>, because it holds the food back. The third, because it changes food from one thing into another, is called "transformative" <note>original Greek: 'alloiōtikē'</note>. To this, the others are subservient...

everyone, because nature herself takes care of these things through the various stages of digestion. For there are two openings of the belly: the upper one, standing erect, receives what is swallowed and stores it in the bag of the belly. This is the stomach <note>original: 'stomachus'. In ancient anatomy, this often referred to the esophagus or the cardiac orifice of the stomach</note>, which has deserved to be called the master of the house <note>original: 'pater familias'</note>, as if it alone governs the whole animal. For if it becomes ill, life hangs in the balance, as the passage for nourishment falters; to this organ, nature has granted a will and a refusal, as if it were capable of reason. The lower opening, however, is turned downward and joined to the adjacent intestines, and from there lies the path for discharging waste. 

Therefore, the first digestion takes place in the belly, where a transformative power <term>alloeotica<gloss>from the Greek 'alloio-,' meaning to change or alter the nature of a substance</gloss></term> turns whatever has been received into juice. The dregs of this are the refuse which, passed along by the lower orifice, slide through the intestines; the expulsion is managed by the service of a fourth power, called the expulsive power <note>original: 'ἀποκριτική' (apokritiki)</note>. 

Therefore, after the food is reshaped into juice, the care of the liver now follows. Now, the liver is congealed blood, and for that reason, it possesses a native heat which turns the finished juice into blood. And just as the turning of food into juice is the first digestion, so the transition of juice into blood is the second digestion. The heat of the liver distributes this blood, administered through the channels of the veins, into each of the limbs. The part of the digested matter which is coldest is poured back into the spleen; for just as the liver is the home of heat, the spleen is the dwelling-place of cold. Indeed, this is why all the parts on the right side are stronger and the left side parts are weaker: because the former are ruled by the heat of their own organ [the liver], while the latter are dulled by the contact of the cold that holds sway on the left [the spleen]. 

In the veins and arteries, however, which are the receptacles of blood and spirit <note>original: 'spiritus' or pneuma, the vital force carried through the body</note>, the third digestion takes place. For it cleanses the received blood in a certain way, and the veins pour back into the bladder what is watery within it; but they provide the liquid, pure, and nourishing blood to the individual members of the whole body. And so it happens that while the belly alone receives the food, its nourishment is dispersed through all the passages of the limbs, feeding even the bones, the marrow, the nails, and the hair. And this is the fourth digestion, which takes place in the individual

### BOOK VII. ###

...individual limbs, while that which is given to each limb becomes nourishment for that limb. Yet even for this nourishment, which has been purified so many times, its own waste products <note>original: 'retrimenta'. In ancient medicine, every stage of digestion produced its own 'dregs' or 'waste' that needed to be expelled.</note> are not lacking; when all the limbs are in their proper health, these vanish through hidden channels. But if any part of the body grows sick, those final waste products we mentioned slip into it, as if into the weaker part. And from here arise the causes of diseases, which it is the custom of doctors to call <term>rheumata<gloss>Greek ῥεύματα, literally 'fluxes' or 'flows'. Ancient doctors believed fluids 'flowed' from healthy parts of the body to settle in weak ones.</gloss></term>. 

For if there is a more abundant quantity of the final juice than is proper, the part of the body that is healthier repels it from itself; and without doubt, it slides into the weak part, which lacks the strength to repel it. Consequently, the reception of this foreign matter distends the place into which it has fallen, and from here pains are created. This, then, is the triple cause either of <term>podagra<gloss>Gout, specifically of the foot.</gloss></term>, or of any disease arising from a confluence: that is, the abundance of humor <note>The 'humors' were the vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that ancient doctors believed must stay in balance for health.</note>, the strength of the limb repelling it, and the weakness of the limb receiving it. 

Since, therefore, we have asserted that four digestions occur in the body, of which one depends on the other—and if the preceding one is hindered, the following has no effect—let us return in our minds to that first digestion which is completed in the belly. We will find what sort of hindrance arises from a varied diet <note>original: 'multiformi naſcatur alimonia'. Disarius is arguing against eating many different types of food at once.</note>. For different foods have different natures: and there are those which are digested more quickly, and others that are digested more slowly. 

When, therefore, the first digestion is turned into juice, because all things taken together are not transformed at the same time, that which is transformed first turns sour while other things are transformed more slowly; and we often sense this even by belching. Other things also, for which digestion is slow, are like damp wood, which creates smoke when pressed by fire: so those things, while the "fire of nature" <note>Ancient physiology viewed the body's internal heat as a literal fire that 'cooked' food into nutrients.</note> hangs over them, produce a kind of smoke while they are cooked more slowly. Indeed, nor does this escape the sense of one belching. But simple food does not have a conflicting delay, since it is turned into a simple juice all at once; nor is any digestion disturbed, while all the [allotted] measures of time...

If anyone—since nothing is more impatient than ignorance—should deign to ignore these reasons, thinking that digestion is hindered only by the sheer quantity of food and does not wish to consider its quality: even here, a multi-faceted diet is found to be the cause of diseases. For a variety of dishes requires various seasonings, by which the palate <note>original: 'gula', literally 'the throat'</note> is provoked more than is necessary for nature. From this, a mass of undigested food is formed, as one tastes a little of everything through the "itch of desire." 

For this reason, Socrates used to advise that those foods and drinks should be avoided which lead to an appetite beyond the quenching of thirst or hunger. Finally, let a variety of eating be rejected for this reason alone: because it is full of pleasure, which must be avoided by those who are serious and studious. For what is so contrary as Virtue and Pleasure? But I shall put an end to my dispute, lest I seem to accuse this very banquet in which we are—for although it is sober, it is nevertheless a varied feast.

### Against the previous view: that a variety of foods is more suitable than a single kind. CHAPTER V. ###

When these points had been approved by Praetextatus and the rest with ready agreement, Evangelus <note>Evangelus is depicted in the *Saturnalia* as a harsh, cynical guest who frequently interrupts the scholarly discussions with biting remarks.</note> cried out: "Nothing is so unbearable to tolerate as the fact that the Greek language holds our ears captive. Let him share with us whatever can be said in favor of a varied diet, so that this violent tongue may fall by its own weapons. Let a Greek snatch this applause from a Greek—as the saying goes, let 'a crow peck out the eyes of a crow' <note>original: 'cornix cornici oculos effodiat'. An ancient proverb meaning that like usually does not harm like; Evangelus is spitefully hoping the Greek scholars will turn on one another.</note>."

And Symmachus said: "Evangelus, you have requested a pleasant thing quite bitterly. For to dare to speak against such copiously and elegantly devised arguments is a matter..."

Does this "simplicity" of food seem so plain to you, where so many trees and shrubs are listed—plants that differ no less in their sap than in their names? As for the claim that humans are more easily seized by diseases than cattle: I am satisfied with the testimony of **Homer**. He records that the plague began with the cattle; indeed, before the disease could creep into the human population, it fell more easily upon the seized herds. <note>In Book I of the *Iliad*, the plague sent by Apollo strikes mules and dogs before it reaches the Greek soldiers.</note> Furthermore, the brevity of their lives is proof of how great the infirmity of mute animals truly is. For which of those animals with which we are familiar can equal the lifespan of a man? Unless, perhaps, you resort to those fables told about crows and ravens. Yet we see these birds gaping at every corpse, lying in wait for every seed, and pursuing the fruits of the trees. Indeed, they possess no less greediness than the legends tell of their longevity.

The second example (if I remember correctly) is that doctors usually offer simple food to the sick, not a variety. In my opinion, this is offered not because it is easier to digest, but because it is less appetizing; the goal is that, through the boredom of a uniform diet, the desire to eat might grow faint. It is as if nature, through its current weakness, were insufficient to cook and process many different things. <note>The "cooking" of food refers to the ancient medical theory of 'pepsis' or concoction, where the stomach was thought to "cook" food using internal heat.</note> Therefore, if any of the sick should crave even a simple dish too eagerly, you doctors still withdraw that desire. Thus, in your practice, it is not the quality of the food that matters, but the quantity. 

However, just as in drinking, the variety of food should be avoided because it contains the snares of a hidden deception, colored by a deceptive similarity. Otherwise, the logic of food is far different. For who was ever satisfied in their *mind* by eating a great deal—a thing which does happen in drinking? One stuffed with food is merely weighed down in the stomach or belly; but one soaked in wine becomes similar, I believe, to an insane man...

### BOOK VII.

Because the bulk of food stays in one place, awaiting the process of digestion, and only then, once fully processed, does it gradually flow into the limbs. Drink, however, being lighter by nature, soon seeks the heights; it strikes the brain, which is located at the crown of the head, with a spray of warm vapor. And for this reason, mixing various wines is avoided, so that a substance which is so quick to seize the head does not wound the seat of counsel <note>A poetic way of referring to the brain or the mind's rational center.</note> with heat that is as diverse as it is sudden. No similarity or reason persuades us that this same danger is to be feared in a variety of foods.

In that discussion, however, where you laid out the order of digestions in a discourse both clear and varied, I do not deny that everything you said regarding the nature of the human body was eloquently stated and does no harm to the question at hand. I only disagree with this one point: your claim that the various juices produced from a variety of foods are harmful to our bodies. In fact, our bodies themselves are manufactured from contrary qualities. For we consist of the hot and the cold, and of the dry and the moist. 

But a simple food, when eaten, emits a juice of only a single quality from itself. We know, moreover, that like is nourished by like. Tell me, I ask you, from where would the other three qualities of the body be nourished? That individual elements are drawn to what is similar to them is testified by **Empedocles** <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who proposed that the universe is composed of four elements: earth, air, fire, and water.</note>, who says:

> So the sweet snatched the sweet, and the bitter rushed to the bitter, the sharp went to the sharp, and the hot coupled with the hot. <note>original: "Ως γλυκὺ μὲν γλυκυμάρπτε, πικρὸν δ’ ἐπὶ πικρὸν ὄρουσε, ὀξὺ δ’ ἐπ’ ὀξὺ ἔβη, θερμὸν δ’ ἐποχεύετο θερμῷ."</note>

Furthermore, I often hear you quoting the words of your **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine."</note> with admiration: 

> If man were a single thing, he would not feel pain; but since he feels pain, he is not one. <note>original: "εἰ ἓν ἦν ὁ ἄνθρωπος οὐκ ἂν ἤλγεεν, ἀλγᾷ δ’ ᾗ οὐκ ἄρα ἓν ἐστὶ."</note>

<margin>
We now read this in the book *On the Nature of Man*: "I say that if man were a single thing, he would never feel pain, for there would be nothing by which he could be pained." <note>original: "ἐν τῶ περὶ φύσιος ἀνθρώπου. ἐγὼ δέ φημὶ εἰ ἓν ἦν ὁ ἄνθρωπος οὐ δέποτ’ ἂν ἤλγεεν οὐδὲ γὰρ ἦν ὑπὸ τοῦ ἀλγήσειεν."</note>
</margin>

Therefore, if man is not a single thing, he must not be nourished by a single thing. For even God, the maker of all things, did not wish the air which surrounds us—and which we draw in by breathing—to have a simple quality, such as being always cold or always hot. Nor did He confine it to continuous dryness or perpetual moisture. This is because He could not nourish us with a single quality, since we are manufactured from a mixture of four. Thus, He made Spring warm and moist; Summer is dry and hot;

### BOOK VII

*Indeed: autumn is dry and cold; winter is equally moist and cold. So too the elements, which are our first principles, consist of these very diversities and nourish us. For fire is hot and dry; air is moist and hot; water is likewise moist and cold; earth is both cold and dry. Why then do you restrict us to a uniform diet, when nothing in us, nor around us, nor in those things from which we are made, is uniform? As for the fact that food turns sour or sometimes "smokes" <note>original: "fumare." This refers to the rising of vapors or "nidor" from the stomach during indigestion.</note> in the stomach, which you wish to attribute to variety: to make us believe this, you must declare either that one who eats a varied diet always suffers these things, or that one who eats a simple diet never suffers them. But if he who enjoys a rich table often does not feel this defect, and he who restricts himself to a single food often endures what you complain of: why do you attribute this to variety and not to gluttony? For even from simple food, a greedy man suffers the harm of indigestion <note>original: "cruditatis." A technical medical term in antiquity for undigested food in the stomach.</note>, and in a varied diet, a moderate man enjoys the benefit of digestion. But you say, this very lack of moderation arises from the variety of foods: with the gluttony tickling the throat and provoking one to take more than is necessary. I return again to what I have already said: indigestion arises from the quantity, not from the quality. For he who is master of himself keeps the measure <margin>* even</margin> even at a Sicilian or Asian table. <note>The tables of Sicily and Asia Minor were proverbial in Rome for their extreme luxury and excess.</note> The person lacking restraint exceeds it even if he feeds only on olives or garden-herbs. And yet that wealthy man, if he maintained moderation, is in possession of health; on the other hand, he becomes unhealthy whose food is pure salt, if he has attacked this very thing voraciously. Finally, if you think variety in what we eat is harmful: why do you compose medicinal potions, which you pour through the mouth into human vitals, from such contrary and mutually repelling mixtures? # BOOK VII.

of the camp, and the venomous bodies of vipers <note>original: "uenenata corpora uiperarum." This refers to the "theriac," a famous ancient medicinal compound that used viper flesh as an anti-venom ingredient.</note>: with which you mix whatever India nourishes, and whatever herbs are carried from the noble lands of Crete. Since, therefore, these remedies do for the protection of life the same thing that food does—insofar as the former recalls life while the latter maintains it—why do you labor to provide variety for those remedies, yet impose the squalor of uniformity upon food?

After all this, you have attacked **pleasure** with the censure of a tragic style <note>original: "cothurnati sermonis," literally "buskined speech," referring to the high boots worn by tragic actors; thus, a formal or overly solemn tone.</note>, as if pleasure were always an enemy to virtue—and not only when it has collapsed into luxury by scorning moderation. For what does even a slave do, who eats only when compelled by hunger and drinks only when thirsty, except to take pleasure from both? Therefore, **pleasure** is not immediately infamous by its name alone, but becomes either honorable or blameworthy based on the manner of its use. It is not enough if pleasure is merely accused; it should also be praised. For food that is taken with pleasure, drawn by desire, is stored in the belly as it is seized with a wide-open expectation; and while the body spiritedly enjoys it, it soon digests it. This does not happen equally with foods that are not recommended by any sweetness of their own.

Why then do you accuse variety as if it were an irritation to the throat <note>original: "gulæ iritamentum," referring to gluttony or the provocation of the palate.</note>, when it is the very health of a man for his appetite to be vigorous? When the appetite fails, he languishes and draws closer to danger. For just as at sea, **helmsmen** <note>original: "gubernatores."</note> fly past by drawing in their sails to a smaller size when their wind is blowing, even if it is too much—and they can restrain a gust when it is too great, but they cannot stir it up when it is sleeping—so too the appetite, when it is tickled and grows, is tempered by the **rudder of reason**. If it should once fail, the living creature is extinguished.

If, therefore, we live by food, and only appetite makes food commendable, we must labor through the invention of variety so that appetite may always be provoked, provided that **reason** is at hand to temper it within the boundaries of its own moderation. Remember, however, that I am present at a charming banquet, not an anxious one. Nor do I admit variety in such a way that I approve of luxury—where summer snows are sought,

## CHAPTER VI.

<margin>Wine is cold by nature.</margin>
After this, Flavianus spoke: "I have always heard other physicians saying the same thing—that wine should be counted among hot things. But even now, when Eustathius touched upon the causes of drunkenness, he proclaimed the heat of wine. To me, however, reflecting often on this, the nature of wine has seemed closer to cold than to heat. And I bring forward into the open the reasons that draw me to this opinion, so that it may be your judgment upon my estimation. Wine (as far as my opinion goes), just as it is naturally cold, so it becomes capable of or even seeking heat when it has been brought near hot things. For even iron, though cold to the touch—**'he bit the cold bronze with his teeth'** <note>original: "ψυχρὸν δ᾽ ἔle χαλκὸν ὄδοντι." A quote from Homer's Iliad, describing the coldness of metal weapons.</note>—if it endures the sun, it grows warm, and the external heat expels the native cold. Let us ask whether reason may persuade us that this is so. Whether wine is introduced to the internal parts by drinking, or applied as a compress to care for the surface when it is poured on the skin, even physicians do not deny that it is cold. However, they claim it is hot in the internal parts, although it does not go down as such, but grows warm when mixed with hot things. Indeed, I want them to answer why they offer wine to a sick person whose stomach is failing from exhaustion, in order to restore strength through constriction <note>In ancient medicine, "constriction" (stypsis) was a cooling action used to firm up "loose" or failing tissues.</note>, unless it were because it forces together exhausted parts by its coldness, and gathers together those things that have become loosened <meta>The text continues with "solutas" on the next page.</meta>

### BOOK VII.

...dissolved? And since (as I said) they apply nothing hot to a weary stomach, lest the weariness increase further, they do not prohibit the drinking of wine, changing weakness into strength by this treatment. I will give another indication that belongs more to the nature of wine than to an innate heat. For if someone unknowingly drinks aconite <note>original: "aconitum"; a highly poisonous plant also known as monkshood, believed in antiquity to kill by chilling the body</note>, I do not deny that he is usually cured by drinking a great deal of undiluted wine. For when poured into the internal organs, it draws heat to itself and, acting like something already hot, resists the cold poison. If, however, the aconite itself is ground up and given in wine to drink, no treatment saves the drinker from death. For then the wine, being cold by nature, increased the coldness of the poison by being mixed with it; nor does it then grow warm in the internal parts, because it descended into the organs not freely, but mixed with another substance—or rather, turned into something else. Moreover, wine is given to those exhausted by excessive sweating or a loose belly, so that it may constrict the passages against both ailments. 

Physicians rub sleepless people with cold things, sometimes with poppy juice, sometimes with mandrake <note>original: "mandragora"</note>, or similar things, in which there is also wine. For sleep is usually brought back by wine, which is nothing if not evidence of a great coldness. Furthermore, all hot things provoke sexual desire <note>original: "venerem"; referring to Venus, the goddess of love</note>, stimulate the semen, and favor procreation. However, after drinking a great deal of undiluted wine, men become more sluggish for intercourse. They even say it is not suitable for conception, because an excess of wine, being cold, makes the semen thin or weak. 

This, indeed, offers the most manifest proof of my opinion: that whatever happens to those who are excessively chilled, the same things happen to the drunk. For they become trembling, pale, and heavy; and their joints and limbs are shaken by a tossing of the agitated spirit. There is the same numbness of body in both, and the same stammering of the tongue. For many, that disease which the Greeks call paralysis <note>original: "παράλυσιν"</note> happens just as much from too much wine as from great cold. Look also at what kinds of treatments are applied to the drunk. Is he not ordered to lie under many blankets, so that his extinguished heat may be revived? And is he not...

# SATURNALIA

...are they led to hot baths? Is not the heat of the body excited for them at the time of their anointings? Finally, those who frequently become drunk age quickly. Others, before the time of their appropriate age, are marked either by baldness or by a premature graying of the hair, which occur only through a lack of heat. What is colder than vinegar, which is simply wine that has gone bad? For of all liquids, this alone violently extinguishes a growing flame, while its coldness overcomes the heat of the element <note>The "element" here refers to fire.</note>. Nor do I overlook this: that of the fruits of trees, those are colder whose juice imitates the taste of wine, such as apples—whether common apples, or pomegranates, or quinces, which Cato calls *cotonea* <note>original: "cotonea"; an ancient Roman term for quinces, a fruit related to apples and pears</note>. I have said this because it has often moved and exercised me while I debated within myself; for I wished to bring into the open what I thought should be felt about wine. For I address you, Disarius, so that you may resolve what has occurred to me to ask. I remember reading in a Greek philosopher (unless I am mistaken, it was Aristotle) in the book he composed *On Drunkenness* <note>original: "de Ebrietate"; refers to a lost work by Aristotle</note>, that women rarely fall into drunkenness, but old men do so frequently. Nor did he add the cause of either this frequency or that rarity. And because this entire question pertains to the nature of bodies—which to know is the duty of both your diligence and your profession—I want you to reveal the causes of the matter which he stated as an opinion, provided you agree with the philosopher. 

Then he [Disarius] said: Aristotle is correct in this as in other things. Nor can I fail to agree with a man with whose findings nature itself does not disagree. 

<margin>Why women get drunk less often.</margin> 

Women, he says, rarely get drunk, but old men often do. That double-sided sentence is full of reason, and one part depends on the other. For once we have learned what defends women from drunkenness, we already hold what frequently drives old men to it. For the female body and the aged body have been allotted contrary natures. A woman's body is of a very moist nature. This is shown by both the smoothness and the brilliance of the skin; it is shown...

BOOK VII

...they are helped especially by frequent purgings <note>original: "purgationes"; a reference to the menstrual cycle, which ancient medicine viewed as a necessary cleansing of excess fluids</note>, which relieve the body of superfluous moisture. Therefore, when the wine they drink falls into such a great amount of moisture, it loses its power and becomes diluted; it does not easily strike the seat of the brain, as its strength has been extinguished. This reasoning also supports the truth of the opinion: that the female body, destined for frequent purgings, is filled with many pores—so that it stands open with channels and provides paths for the moisture flowing toward its exit in the discharge. Through these pores, the vapor of the wine quickly evaporates.

<margin>Why old men are easily intoxicated.</margin>
In contrast, the bodies of old men are dry, which is proven by the roughness and scaly nature <note>original: "squallor"; refers to the dry, flaky appearance of aged skin</note> of their skin. This is also why this age is less prone to weeping, which is a sign of dryness. Within these men, wine suffers no opposition from a resisting moisture; it clings to the dry body with its strength intact, and soon occupies the places that serve the human capacity for wisdom. There is no doubt that the bodies of old men are also hard; and for that reason, the natural passages in their harder limbs are blocked. Once wine is swallowed, no exhalation occurs; instead, the whole of it ascends to the very seat of the mind. Thus it happens that even healthy old men suffer from the evils of the drunk: trembling of the limbs, faltering of the tongue, talkativeness, and outbursts of anger.

<margin>Stumbling, of the first declension.</margin>
Young men when drunk are just as subject to these conditions as old men are when sober. Therefore, if old men endure even a light impulse of wine, they do not "receive" these evils, but rather the wine agitates the conditions by which they are already gripped by reason of their age.

## *Whether the nature of women is colder than that of men, or hotter. And why new wine does not intoxicate.*

### CHAPTER VII.

<margin>Women are cold.</margin>
When Disarius’s discourse had been approved by all, Symmachus added: "Just as the entire reasoning Disarius found regarding the rarity of female drunkenness has been examined, so too has one thing been omitted by him: that by the excessive cold which is in their bodies, the wine grows cold...

...the swallowed wine cools down; it is so weakened that its power, having faded, cannot stir up any heat from which drunkenness might arise. To this, Horus replied: "Indeed, Symmachus, you are mistaken in thinking that the nature of women is cold.

<margin>That the nature of women is hotter than that of men.</margin>

If you are willing, I will easily prove to you that it is hotter than the nature of men. The natural moisture in the body, once a person has passed childhood, becomes harder and is sharpened into hair. This is why at that age the pubic area, the cheeks, and other parts of the body are covered <note>A reference to the growth of body and facial hair during puberty</note>. But in the female body, because heat dries up this moisture, there is a lack of hair; for this reason, the body of this sex remains continuously bright and smooth. There is also this proof of heat in them: an abundance of blood, the nature of which is warmth <note>original: "fervor"; ancient medicine viewed blood as the primary carrier of vital heat</note>. So that this blood does not burn the body if it stays put, it is drawn away through frequent purging <note>A reference to menstruation, which Horus argues is a necessary release of excess thermal energy</note>. Who then would call them cold, whom no one can deny are full of heat, since they are full of blood?

Furthermore, although the custom of burning the bodies of the deceased is no longer used in our age, literature <note>original: "lectio"; referring to historical texts</note> teaches that in the time when it was considered an honor for the dead to be given to the fire, if it ever happened that several bodies were to be burned together, the funeral attendants used to add one female body to every ten male bodies. Aided by that one body—which acted like a natural flame and therefore burned quickly—the others would catch fire. Thus, the heat of women was not unknown to the ancients. I will not remain silent on this either: since heat is always the cause of reproduction, women become fit for childbearing sooner than boys because they are hotter. Indeed, even according to <term>public laws</term> <note>iura publica; refers specifically to Roman civil law</note>, the twelfth year for a girl and the fourteenth for a boy defines the age of <term>puberty</term>. What more? Do we not see women, when the cold is extreme, content with moderate clothing, and not wrapped in as many coverings as men usually are? This is surely because their natural heat fights back against the cold brought by the air." At this, Symmachus smiled and said: "Well..."

<margin>
On the contrary, that the nature of women is colder than that of men.
</margin>

Our friend Horus attempts to appear as an Orator instead of a Cynic <note>The Cynics were a school of philosophers known for their blunt, often rude honesty; here, Horus is being praised for his rhetorical skill in arguing the opposite of his previous point</note>, for he turns his reasoning to the contrary to prove the coldness of the female body. For the fact that they are not covered in hair as men are is due to a lack of heat. It is heat, after all, that creates hair. This is why hair is also lacking in eunuchs <term>eunuchis</term>, whose nature no one would deny is colder than that of men. Furthermore, in the human body, those parts which contain more heat are the ones most covered in hair. But the female body is smooth, as if it were thickened by a natural cold. For density accompanies coldness, and smoothness accompanies density. 

The fact that they are frequently purged <note>original: "purgantur"; a reference to menstruation</note> is not a sign of an abundance of blood, but of a faulty humor <term>uitiosi humoris</term>. For that which is expelled is undigested and raw, flowing out because it is weak; it has no fixed place, but is driven out by nature as something harmful and rather cold. This is best proven by the fact that women happen to feel a chill when they are being purged. From this, it is understood that what flows out is cold, and therefore does not remain in a living body, as if it were extinguished by a lack of heat. 

As for the fact that the female body used to aid "burning" men <note>Horus is addressing a previous point that women's bodies were used to help ignite funeral pyres because they supposedly burned more easily</note>, this was not due to heat, but to fatty flesh that is more like oil, which in their case does not result from heat. That they are quickly brought to the age of reproduction is not a sign of excessive heat, but of a weaker nature; just as small, thin apples ripen faster, while robust ones ripen later. 

But if you wish to understand the true measure of heat in reproduction: consider that men persevere far longer in the act of procreating than women do in the act of giving birth. Let this be your certain proof of either cold or heat in both sexes: for the same force is extinguished more quickly in a colder body, but lasts longer in a warmer one. That they endure the cold of the air more easily than men is caused by their own coldness; for like rejoices in like. Therefore, the habit of their nature, which they have been granted as colder, prevents their bodies from shuddering at the cold.

But regarding these matters, let each individual judge as they wish; I, however, turn toward the...

...opportunity for consulting; and what I consider worthy of knowing, I ask from the same **Disarius**, who is a very dear friend to me and most learned in these as well as other matters. <margin>Why must does not inebriate.</margin>
To this **Disarius** replied: Everything that is sweet quickly satiates, nor does it maintain a long-lasting desire for itself; instead, a feeling of revulsion <note>original: "horror"; here meaning a physical rejection or distaste that prevents over-consumption</note> succeeds satiety. In must, however, there is only sweetness <term>dulcedo</term>, but no pleasantness <term>suavitas</term>. > Nurse, come now, draw wine for me in jars, the pleasant kind. <note>original Greek: "Μαῖ' ἄγε δήμοι οἶνον ἐν ἀμφιφορεῦσιν ἄφυσσον Ηδύν"</note>

For he calls honey "sweet" <note>original: "glukeros"</note> and wine "pleasant" <note>original: "hedys"</note>. Therefore must, since it is not yet pleasant but only sweet, by a certain revulsion does not allow enough of itself to be consumed to cause drunkenness. I add another point: by natural reason, sweetness is repugnant to drunkenness; so much so that doctors compel those who are distended by too much wine to the point of danger to vomit; and after vomiting, to counter the fumes of the wine remaining in the veins, they offer bread smeared with honey; and thus sweetness <margin>*defends</margin> defends the man from the evil of drunkenness. Therefore, must does not inebriate, because it contains only sweetness. But it also follows from a suitable reason that must is heavy, both from the mixture of gas <term>flatus</term> and water, and from its weight...

By its own weight, it quickly descends into the intestines and flows through, nor does it remain in those places susceptible to drunkenness <note>The ancients believed drunkenness was caused by vapors rising from the stomach to the head; Disarius argues that must passes through the stomach too quickly to release these fumes.</note>. Moreover, that there is water in must is proven by this: that as it ages, it becomes less in measure but sharper in strength. This is because once the water—which softened it—has evaporated, the nature of the wine remains alone with its own strength, no longer softened by any mixture of diluted moisture.

### On the ease or difficulty of digestion of certain
### foods: and regarding certain other quite clever
### little questions. CHAPTER VIII.

**A**fter these things, **Furius Albinus** said: I also, for my manly part, will not leave our **Disarius** unexercised. <margin>Why minced meat is difficult to digest.</margin> Tell me, please, what cause makes a <term>minced meat dish</term> <note>original: "isitium"; a dish made of finely pounded meat, similar to a sausage or forcemeat ball</note> difficult to digest? It is called *insitium* from the word for "insertion" <note>original: "infectione"; Albinus suggests the name comes from "inserting" or "stuffing" the meat into a casing</note>, though it later obtained the name it has now by the loss of a letter. Why is this so, when the very diligent grinding <term>tritura</term> should have greatly aided the future digestion, and should have removed whatever was heavy in the meat, completing a large part of the processing in advance?

And **Disarius** replied: This type of food is difficult to digest for the very reason you think its digestion was previously provided for. For the lightness which the grinding provided causes it to float upon the liquid food which it finds in the middle of the stomach; thus it does not adhere to the lining of the stomach, by whose heat digestion is promoted. Similarly, when it is freshly ground and pressed together and then cast into water, it floats. From this, it is understood that it does the same in the moisture of the stomach, withdrawing itself from the necessity of digestion; and it is cooked there as slowly as those things which are finished more tardily by steam...

If this heat encounters a suitable material, it engages with it freely and quickly consumes it in the struggle; but it sometimes passes over light material as if it were hidden, or sometimes turns it into ash rather than into nourishing juice. Just as huge oak logs are turned into glowing chunks of charcoal by fire, yet if chaff falls into the fire, soon only ash remains to be seen. You have also this similar example: a more powerful millstone crushes larger grains, but lets through those smaller ones that remain whole. By a great wind, the fir or the oak is torn up, but no gale easily breaks a reed."

...I asked: <margin>Why wines are cold in Egypt</margin> Why is it that in Egypt, which is the warmest of all regions, the wine produced is not hot, but, I might almost say, of a cold quality? To this **Disarius** said: "You have found through experience, **Albinus**: waters which are drawn either from deep wells or from springs steam in winter and grow cold in summer. This happens for no other reason than that the air surrounding us, due to the season, is hot, and so the cold sinks into the depths of the earth and affects the waters whose source <term>scaturigo</term><note>The bubbling source or spring of a body of water.</note> is at the bottom. Conversely, when the air presents winter, the heat sinks into the interior and gives vapor to the waters rising from the bottom. Therefore, what alternates everywhere according to the change of season is always the case in Egypt, whose air is always hot. For the cold, seeking the depths, wraps itself around the roots of the vine and gives such a quality to the juice rising from there. Thus, the wines of a hot region are lacking in heat."

"Our discourse," **Albinus** said, "once it has entered into the subject of heat, does not easily depart elsewhere. I wish you to say, then, why a person who descends into <margin>Why hot water becomes hotter when moved.</margin> hot water is burned less if he does not move; but if he moves the water by his own agitation, he feels a greater heat; and the water burns more every time a new motion is added to it." And **Disarius** said: "The hot water that adheres to our body soon offers a gentler touch; either because it has become accustomed to the skin, or because it has received cold from us. But motion applies new water to the body; and since the habituation of which I just spoke ceases, the novelty always increases the sensation of heat."

"Why then," **Albinus** said, "<margin>Why in summer air moved by a fan feels cooler.</margin> in summer when the hot air is moved by a fan <term>flabrum</term><note>A fly-flap or fan used to move air.</note>, does it not acquire heat, but cold? For by the same reasoning, motion ought to increase the heat in this case too." "The reason is not the same," **Disarius** said, "for the heat of water and of air. For the former is of a more solid body; and thick matter, when it is moved, attacks the surface to which it is moved with its full force. Air, by motion, is dissolved into wind, and becoming more liquid...

### CHAPTER IX.

<margin>Why those rotating in a circle suffer from dizziness.</margin>
**E**vangelus <note>Evangelus is the most skeptical and combative guest at the banquet, often challenging the experts.</note> interrupted the proceeding consultation and said: "I will put our friend **Disarius** to the test, to see if he can satisfy an inquirer with those minute and revolving responses of his. Tell me, **Disarius**, why is it that those who turn themselves so as to rotate frequently in a circle suffer from both dizziness of the head and a darkening of the eyes? Finally, if they persist, they fall, although no other bodily motion imposes this necessity?" To this **Disarius** said: "There are seven bodily motions. For one either moves forward, or retreats backward, or turns to the right or the left, or is moved upward, or downward, or is rotated in a circle. Of these seven motions, only one is found in divine bodies: I mean the spherical motion, by which the heaven is moved, by which the stars and the other elements are moved. For terrestrial animals, those six are primarily familiar, but sometimes the seventh is also employed. But those six, being direct, are harmless. The seventh, however, which creates circles, disturbs the head by its frequent turning and entangles the <term>spiramentum</term><note>original: "spiramentum." In ancient medicine, this refers to the vital breath or "animal spirits" believed to travel through the nerves to facilitate sensation and movement.</note> within the humors of the brain; it is this which serves the soul in the brain, which governs almost all the senses of the body. For it is this <term>spiramentum</term> which, surrounding the brain, provides power to each of the individual senses; it is this which provides strength to the nerves and muscles of the body. Therefore, when it is disturbed by the spinning and simultaneously oppressed by the agitated humors, it grows weak and abandons its service. From this it happens to those who are caught in rotations that their hearing becomes duller—

Fat, marrow, and the brain are so steeped in moisture and softness that this same effect of the soul, which dryness does not receive, this softness does not hold. Therefore, sensation is found to be absent from teeth, nails, bones, and hair, as well as from fat, marrow, and the brain...

It could. And just as the cutting of hair brings no pain, so too if a tooth, or a bone, or fat, or the brain, or marrow were to be cut, all sense of pain would be absent. But you will say, "We see people afflicted with torments when their bones are cut, and men tortured by the pain of teeth." Who would deny this is true? But for a bone to be cut, the membrane <note>original: "omentum" – in this context, Disarius refers to the periosteum, the sensitive tissue covering the bone, rather than the abdominal membrane usually called the omentum today</note> which is placed over the bone brings the torture while it suffers the cutting. When the physician's hand passes through this, the bone—along with the marrow it contains—possesses an insensibility similar to the cutting of hair. And when there is pain in the teeth, it is not the bone of the tooth that feels it, but the flesh <note>Likely referring to the gums or the dental pulp</note> which contains the tooth. For even a nail, as far as it grows out beyond the flesh, is cut without sensation. That which adheres to the flesh causes pain if it is cut, not by its own body, but by the body of its seat. Just as the upper part of the hair feels no pain while being cut, but if it is pulled, it receives sensation from the flesh it leaves behind. And the brain—which either tortures a man when touched or frequently kills him—does not bring this pain through its own sensation, but through that of its clothing, that is, the membrane <note>original: "omentum" – here referring to the meninges, the protective layers surrounding the brain</note>. Therefore, we have named those things in man which are without sensation, and the reason for this has been shown. The remaining
<margin>How the brain, lacking sensation, governs the senses of the body.</margin>
part of my debt is to explain why the brain, though it has no sensation, governs the senses. But I will attempt this too, if I am able to pay what I owe. The senses of which we speak are five: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. These are either in the body or around the body, and are familiar only to perishable <term>caducis</term> <note>Bodies that are mortal or subject to decay</note> bodies. For no sensation exists in a divine body. The soul, however, is more divine than any body, even if that body be divine. Therefore, if the dignity of divine bodies disdains sensation as something suited to the perishable, much more is the soul of a greater majesty than to need sensation. However, for a man to exist and be a living animal, the soul provides this, illuminating the body. Furthermore, it illuminates it by inhabiting it, and its habitation is in the brain.

<meta>The catchword at the bottom of the original page is "est" (is), which begins the next page: "Et hinc est..." (And it is from here...).</meta>

<summary>Disarius explains that while the brain and bones lack sensation themselves, the membranes covering them feel pain. He then argues that the soul, residing in the brain, governs the five senses because it "illuminates" the body from its seat of power.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the medical lecture by Disarius in Macrobius's Saturnalia. Following the discussion on why the brain itself lacks sensation despite being the source of it, Disarius now explains the anatomical structure of the nervous system and the specific "pairs" of nerves that govern the five senses and bodily functions.</meta>

<page-num>537</page-num>
<header>BOOK VII.</header>

It is. \*For the spherical nature, coming to us from on high, has claimed the high and spherical part of man <note>Referring to the head and brain as reflections of the celestial spheres</note>, and it lacks the kind of sensation that is not necessary for the soul. But because sensation is necessary for the living creature, nature places within the hollows of the brain a "breath of life" <note>original: "spiramentum" — a term for the "pneuma" or vital spirit believed to carry signals through the nerves</note> derived from its own powers. The nature of this breath is such that it both introduces and governs sensation. From these hollows, therefore, which our ancestors called the "ventricles" <note>original: "ventres cerebri," literally "bellies of the brain"</note> of the brain, seven **pairs of nerves** <note>original: "συζυγίαι" (syzygiai) — a Greek term for a "yoking" or "pairing"</note> are born; you may give this thing whatever Latin name you wish. We call them a **pairing** of nerves when two nerves emerge together and end in a specific location.

Therefore, the seven pairs of nerves arising from the ventricle of the brain fulfill the role of pipes, leading the sensation-bearing breath to each of its proper places by natural law, so that they may pour sensation into the nearby and distant members of the living creature.

1.  The **first pair** of such nerves seeks the eyes, providing them with the recognition of forms and the distinction of colors.
2.  The **second** spreads into the ears, through which the knowledge of sounds is born in them.
3.  The **third** is inserted into the nostrils, providing the power of smelling.
4.  The **fourth** occupies the palate, through which tastes are judged.
5.  The **fifth**, by its own power, fills the whole body; for every part of the body distinguishes between soft and rough, cold and hot.
6.  The **sixth**, traveling from the brain, seeks the stomach <note>In ancient anatomy, this often referred to the esophagus and the upper digestive tract</note>, for which sensation is most necessary: so that it may crave what is lacking, reject what is superfluous, and, in a sober man, regulate itself.
7.  The **seventh pair** of nerves pours sensation into the **spinal marrow** <note>original: "spinali medullæ" — the spinal cord</note>, which is to a living creature what a keel is to a ship.

Indeed, it is of such great use and importance that it has been called the "extended brain" by physicians. Finally, from this—as if from the brain itself—various passages arise, serving the three purposes set forth by the soul’s foresight. For there are three things which the body of a living creature receives from the providence of the soul: that it may live, that it may live fittingly, and that immortality may be sought for it through succession <note>Referring to reproduction and the continuation of the species</note>.

Having set forth these three things, as I said, the action of the soul is provided through the spinal cord <note>original: "spinalem medullam," literally "spinal marrow"</note>. For the heart, the liver, and the organs of breathing—all of which pertain to the maintenance of life—are supplied with strength from the spinal passages we have mentioned. Strength is also provided from there to the nerves of the hands, the feet, and other parts through which one lives a dignified life. And so that the succession of generations may be ensured, nerves from that same spinal cord are supplied to the genitals and the womb so they may fulfill their work. Thus, no part of the body in man exists without the breath of life <term>spiramento: the "pneuma" or vital spirit believed to carry signals through the nerves</term>, which is located in the ventricle of the brain, and without the benefit of the spinal cord. So it happens that, although the brain itself lacks sensation, sensation nevertheless proceeds from the brain into the entire body. "Well done!" said our little Greek <note>original: "Græculus noster" — a familiar, sometimes slightly patronizing term for a Greek scholar</note>, Evangelus. "He has shown us the things <margin>*hidden</margin> covered by nature so clearly that we seem to see with our eyes whatever he has described in speech." Eustathius replied: "Now let either Eusebius, that most eloquent of men, or whoever else wishes, approach this exercise of consultation. We shall meet later in a time of more free leisure."

### Why it happens that baldness as well as greyness first invade the front parts of the head. Then, why the voice of women and eunuchs is thinner than that of men. CHAPTER X.

<margin>Greyness and baldness: why they occupy the front part of the head at the start.</margin>
**E**usebius said: "Therefore, Disarius, I must have a conversation with you about old age, at whose door we are both now nearly knocking. Since Homer calls old men **grey-templed** <note>original: "πολιοκροτάφους" (poliokrotaphous)</note>, I ask whether he wishes to signify the whole head in the poetic manner by naming a part, or if by some reason he assigns grey hair specifically to this part of the head?" Disarius replied: "In this, too, that divine poet acted as wisely as in all other things. For the front part of the head is more humid than the back <note>original: "occipitio"</note>, and it is from there that greyness usually begins." Eusebius replied: "And if the front part is more humid, why does it suffer from baldness? Which does not occur except...

...unless it happens because of dryness? "A timely objection," said Disarius, "but the reason is not hidden. Nature made the front parts of the head more porous so that whatever excess or smoky vapor exists around the brain might escape through many passages. This is why we see in the dry skulls of the dead certain sutures <note>original: "suturas" — the fibrous joints where the bones of the skull meet</note> by which the **hemispheres** (if I may call them that) of the head are bound together. In those for whom these passages are wider, the moisture is transformed by dryness; and for this reason, they turn gray later, but they do not escape baldness.

If, therefore, dryness causes men to be bald—as you said the back parts of the head are drier—why is it that we never see a bald **occiput** <term>occiput: the back of the head or skull</term>?" 

He replied: "The dryness of the back of the head is not from a defect, but from nature. Therefore, the back of the head is dry in everyone. However, baldness arises from that specific dryness which happens through a 'bad temperament' <note>original: "δυσκρασίαν" (dyscrasia) — a Greek medical term for an imbalance or 'bad mixture' of the four bodily humors</note>, as the Greeks usually call it. This is why those with curly hair turn gray slowly but pass quickly into baldness, because they are so balanced that they have drier heads. On the other hand, those with thinner hair are not easily stripped of it, as they are nourished by the moisture called **phlegm** <note>original: "φλέγμα"</note>; yet they turn gray quickly. For they are gray for this very reason: they imitate the color of the moisture that nourishes them.

If, then, an abundance of moisture tints the hair of the elderly with grayness, why has old age acquired the reputation of being extremely dry? Because," he said, "old age becomes cold when the natural heat is extinguished by age; and from that cold, chilly and excess humors are born. Otherwise, the vital liquid has been dried up by long life. Thus, old age is dry from a lack of natural moisture, but it is moist from an abundance of defective humor produced by the cold. This is why a more advanced age is made heavier by wakefulness; for sleep, which happens mostly because of moisture, is born from what is not natural. Just so, there is much sleep in infancy, which is moist from an abundance of natural—not excess—moisture. The same reasoning applies to why childhood [is prevented] from turning gray..."

...does not allow for this, since it is extremely moist. It is not humid because of a **phlegm** <note>original: "phlegmate" — one of the four traditional humors, associated with cold and dampness</note> produced by cold, but is nourished by that natural and vital moisture. Therefore, they are easily bent, for they cannot bear the weight of the body placed upon them, just as a reed bends when a weight is placed on it. 

And Eusebius said: "Since the discussion of excess moisture has dragged us from old age all the way to eunuchs, I want you to tell me why their voices are so shrill—so much so that unless you see them, you would not know if a woman or a eunuch was speaking?" 

<margin>Why the voice in women and eunuchs becomes thinner.</margin>

Disarius replied that the abundance of excess moisture also causes this. For the moisture itself, by making the <term>trachea</term> <note>original: "ἀρτηρίαν" (artērian) — in ancient anatomy, this term was often used for the windpipe or "rough artery" through which air and sound pass</note> through which the sound of the voice rises thicker, narrows the passage of the voice. This is why the voice is shrill in both women and eunuchs; it is deep in men, for whom the passage of the voice has a free and entirely open path. Moreover, it is clear that an almost equal abundance of troublesome moisture arises in eunuchs and in women from a similar lack of heat, since both their bodies often grow fat; certainly, the breasts of both grow large in nearly the same way.

...bringing less instruction than if you yourself were to answer others when they consult you. And when he <note>Likely Eusebius or another guest</note> prompted Servius <note>Servius was a famous 4th-century grammarian and commentator on Virgil</note>, who had been silent for a long time, with frequent encouragements, Servius said: "I ask this of you, which you said had happened to me: What cause makes a **blush** arise in the body from the soul's **shame**?"

<margin>Gellius book 19, chapter 6.</margin>

And he [Disarius] replied: "Nature, when it encounters something worthy of honorable shame, penetrates the blood by seeking the depths. Once this blood is stirred up and spread out, the skin is stained, and from there the blush arises. Natural philosophers <note>original: "physici" — those who study the physical world and the laws of nature</note> also say that Nature, touched by shame, stretches the blood before itself like a veil—just as we see anyone who blushes frequently place their hand before their face. Nor will you be able to doubt these things, since a blush is nothing else but the *color* <note>The main text uses "color," but the margin suggests "heat" as an alternative reading.</note> of the blood."

<margin>*heat</margin>

Servius added: "And those who rejoice—why do they turn red?" Disarius said: "**Joy** happens from the outside. Nature hurries toward this with a spirited encounter, and the blood, accompanying it—as if possessing the eagerness of its own wholeness—stains the skin. And from there, a similar color arises."

<margin>Why those who fear grow pale.</margin>

He [Servius] also asks: "On the other hand, for what reason do those who **fear** grow **pale**?" Disarius said: "This is not hidden either. For when Nature fears something happening from the outside, she plunges entirely into the depths, just as we also, when we are afraid, seek hiding places and spots to conceal ourselves. Therefore, descending entirely so as to hide, she drags the blood with her—which she always rides like a chariot. With this blood submerged, a thinner fluid <note>original: "humor" — one of the bodily fluids believed to control health and temperament</note> remains in the skin, and from that, it grows pale. This is why those who fear also tremble: because the power of the soul <note>original: "anima" — the vital life force responsible for movement</note>, fleeing inward, leaves the nerves behind, which used to hold the strength of the limbs; and from that, they are shaken by the 'leaping' of fear. From this also, a loosening of the bowels accompanies fear: because the muscles, by which the passages of waste were closed, are abandoned by the power of the soul as it flees inward. They loosen the bonds by which the waste was held until the proper time for <term>digestion</term> <note>In ancient medicine, "digestion" or *pepsis* referred to the overall processing and distribution of food and waste in the body</note>." Having respectably agreed with these words, Servius fell silent.

### On thirteen minor questions proposed to Disarius by Avienus. CHAPTER XII.

<margin>The first question proposed by Avienus.</margin>
Then Avienus said: "Since the order of the day brings me to the task of consulting you, I must bring the conversation back to the banquet itself, as it has wandered far from the table and moved toward other inquiries. Seeing as salted meat—which we call *laridum* <note>Bacon or salted fat; the term is related to the modern 'lard'</note>, I believe, as if it were 'abundantly dry' <note>original: *large aridum*</note>—is often served, I decided to ask myself by what logic the addition of salt preserves meat for long-term use. Although I might form an opinion on this myself, I prefer to be informed by one who heals bodies."

And Disarius replied: "Every body is by its very nature dissolvable and prone to decay; unless it is held together by a certain bond, it easily falls apart. Bodies are held together as long as the soul <note>original: *anima*</note> is present by the exchange of air <note>respiration</note> by which the vessels of the spirit are nourished, so long as they are fed by a constant supply of fresh breathing. When this ceases through the departure of the soul, the limbs decay, and the entire body is worn down, crushed by its own weight. At that point, even the blood (which, as long as it possessed heat, gave vigor to the limbs) turns into a corrupt discharge <note>original: *saniem* — a thin, foul-smelling liquid from a wound or decaying flesh</note> as the heat departs; it does not remain within the veins but is squeezed out. Thus, as the breathing-pores are loosened, a foul waste flows out.

"The addition of salt to the body prevents this from happening. Salt is by nature dry and hot; through its heat, it contracts the flow of the body, and through its dryness, it either checks or absorbs the moisture. Certainly, it is easy to recognize that moisture is dispersed or consumed by salt from this fact: if you make two loaves of bread of equal size, one sprinkled with salt and the other without salt, you will find the one lacking salt to be heavier in weight—evidently because 
<margin>Second.</margin>
the moisture remains in it due to the lack of salt. I also wish to ask this of my friend Disarius: why is wine that has been cleared of its dregs stronger in its effects, but weaker in its ability to last? Why does it move the drinker so quickly, yet if it is left alone, it spoils so easily?"

...changed? "As for why it changes so quickly," Disarius said, "this is the reason: the more the wine is purified of its dregs <note>original: *fæce purgata*; the 'lees' or sediment of the wine</note>, the more liquid it becomes and the more easily it penetrates the veins of the drinker. However, it spoils easily because, lacking any firm support to lean on, it is exposed to harm from every side. For the dregs are like a root for the wine, sustaining it, nourishing it, and providing it with sufficient strength."

<margin>The third question.</margin>
"And I ask this as well," Avienus said. "Why do the dregs sink to the bottom of every liquid except honey? For honey is the only substance that spits its dregs to the top." To this Disarius replied: "The material of the dregs, being thick and earthy, is heavier than other liquids, but it is surpassed by honey. Therefore, in those other liquids, it sinks to the bottom by its own weight; but in honey, being lighter <note>The physician explains this through relative density: honey is denser than its own impurities</note>, it is displaced and pushed upward."

<margin>The fourth question.</margin>
"Since similar questions arise from what has been said: Why, Disarius, are honey and wine considered best at different ages? Honey is best when very fresh, but wine when it is very old. This is the source of the proverb used by gourmands: 'A honey-wine <note>original: *mulsum*; a popular Roman drink made by mixing wine and honey</note> that you would blend properly should be mixed with new Hymettian honey <note>Honey from Mount Hymettus in Greece, famous for its quality</note> and old Falernian wine <note>A prestigious wine from Campania, Italy, known for its longevity</note>.'

"This is because," Disarius replied, "their inherent natures are different. The nature of wine is moist, while that of honey is dry. If you doubt my word, consider the effects seen in medicine. For those parts of the body that need moistening are treated with wine, while those that need drying are cleansed with honey. Therefore, as time passes and draws something out of both, the wine becomes purer <note>original: *meracius*; more concentrated or potent as water evaporates</note> and the honey becomes drier. Thus, honey is deprived of its vital juice just as wine is freed from its excess water."

<margin>The fifth question.</margin>
"Nor is the following question unlike those already asked: why is it that if you keep vessels of wine and oil half-full for a long time, the wine almost always spoils into sourness, but the oil, by contrast, acquires a sweeter flavor?"

Disarius said, "Both observations are true. Into that empty space which lacks liquid at the top, outside air enters; it draws out and absorbs all the thinnest moisture. Once this moisture is dried out, the wine—as if stripped of its strength—depending on whether it was naturally weak or strong, either turns sharp with sourness or becomes harsh and constricted."

Oil, however, once its excessive moisture has been dried up—as if the mold <note>original: *mucore*; referring here to the dregs or impurities that cause spoilage</note> that lay hidden within it were wiped away—acquires a new sweetness of flavor.
