<margin>Seventh [Question].</margin>
<margin>*under a roof</margin>
but in honey, the best is at the bottom. I ask, therefore, why is it believed that oil is best at the top, wine in the middle, and honey at the bottom? Without hesitation, Disarius said: The honey that is best is heavier than the rest. Therefore, in a vessel of honey, the part at the bottom certainly excels in weight, and is thus more precious than that which floats above. Conversely, in a vessel of wine, the lower part is not only turbid due to the mixture of dregs, but is also inferior in flavor. The top part, however, is corrupted by its proximity to the air, and becomes thinner through that mixture. For this reason, farmers are not content to have stored their jars <note>original: *dolia*; large earthenware storage jars</note> sub *tecto <note>original: *sub tecto*; under a roof or in a covered building</note>, but they bury them; and after smearing the lids on the outside, they fortify them, removing, as much as possible, the contagion of the air from the wine. The wine is so clearly harmed by the air that it can barely protect itself even in a full vessel, which is less accessible to the air. Furthermore, if you draw wine from it and open a space for the air to mix in, all the liquid that remains is corrupted. Therefore, the middle part is as far removed from the boundaries of both extremes as it is from harm, being neither turbid nor diluted.

<margin>Eighth [Question].</margin>
Avienus added: Why does the same drink seem stronger <note>original: *meracior*; more undiluted or potent</note> to a person who is fasting than to one who has taken food? To which Disarius replied: Hunger empties the veins, while satiety obstructs them.

Therefore, when a drink flows deep within through that emptiness—since it finds the veins neither dulled by food nor made thinner by mixture—traveling through the vacuum, it is perceived by a stronger sense of taste.

it relieves hunger slightly; however, he who takes food while thirsty not only fails to tame his thirst, but further ignites the craving for drink. The reason, said Disarius, is well known. For liquid is not hindered from passing through to all parts of the body, flowing in every direction to fill the veins. And so, the hunger that had created a state of emptiness is refreshed by the remedy of drink, as if it were no longer entirely vacant. Food, however, being more solid and bulky, is not admitted into the veins except gradually as it is digested. Therefore, it provides no relief to the thirst it encounters; on the contrary, it absorbs whatever moisture it finds outside itself, and thus the scarcity of moisture, which is called thirst, is increased.

<margin>Tenth [Question].</margin> I shall not leave myself ignorant of this either, Avienus said: why is there greater pleasure when thirst is extinguished by drink than when hunger is settled by food? And Disarius replied: This is also clear from what was said before. For the entire draft of a drink penetrates the whole body at once, and creates a single, very great, and perceptible pleasure for the senses of all the parts; food, however, consoles the scarcity bit by bit with a meager supply. Therefore, the pleasure of it is diminished by being spread out in many ways.

<margin>Eleventh [Question].</margin> I also add this to my inquiries, if you please: why does satiety <note>The feeling of being full or satisfied.</note> take hold more easily of those who devour greedily than of those who have eaten the same things more quietly? That response is brief, he said. For when one devours greedily, a great deal of air is brought in with the food because of the gaping of the mouth <note>original: *rictus*; referring to the wide opening of the jaws</note> and the frequency of breathing. Therefore, when the air has filled the veins, it acts as a substitute for food to drive away the appetite.

<margin>Twelfth [Question].</margin> If I am not being troublesome, Disarius, pray endure a man who babbles excessively out of a desire for learning, and tell me: why can we tolerate quite hot food more easily in the mouth than we can hold it in the hand? And if some of it is too hot to be chewed for any length of time, we swallow it immediately—and yet the stomach is not dangerously burned? And he replied: The internal heat that is in the stomach is, as it were, much greater and more powerful, and whatever heat it receives, it...

<margin>Thirteenth [Question].</margin> However, so that the hand might be able to bear a burning-hot thing, it is aided by no internal heat of its own. For a long time, said Avienus, I have desired to know why water, which is brought to a snowy stiffness through being covered with spheres of <margin>* of snow</margin> clouds, is no less harmful in a drink than water melted from the snow itself. Therefore, snowy water is not ruinous by its stiffness alone, but for another reason, which I shall not be reluctant to reveal, on the authority of Aristotle: who posed this in his *Physical Problems*, and (unless I am mistaken) settled it in this sense: <margin>Gellius, Book 19, chapter 5.</margin>

> Every water, he says, has in itself a portion of the thinnest air, by which it is healthy: it also has earthy dregs, which are heavy matter compared to the air. Therefore, when it grows cold and is driven together by the chill of the air and by frost, it is necessary that through evaporation that thinnest breeze be squeezed out of it, as it were: and when that <margin>* departing</margin> *descending* <note>The marginal note corrects "descedente" (descending) to "discedente" (departing/leaving).</note> air has left, the water comes together into a frozen mass, with only the earthy nature remaining in itself. This is apparent from the fact that when the same water has been melted by the heat of the sun, a smaller measure of it is found than there was before it froze. For that which evaporation consumed—the only healthy part of the water—is missing. 

Snow, therefore, which is nothing other than water thickened in the air, lost its fineness when it was thickened: and therefore, from the drinking of it when melted, various kinds of diseases are sown in the internal organs.

This is proven by the fact that floating things which (as I said above) are thrown into the Black Sea, are pushed outward; but if a column should fall in, it swims inward. And this has often been proven by experience: that the heavier things at the bottom of the Sea of Marmara are pushed into the inner parts of the Black Sea.*

# On the three questions which Horus proposed to Disarius.
## CHAPTER XIII.

<margin>Why those who are fasting are more thirsty than they are hungry.</margin>
Horus took his turn: "Since Avienus," he said, "has asked many things concerning drink and food, he has passed over one thing that is most necessary—whether intentionally or because he forgot, I do not know—namely, why those who are fasting are more thirsty than they are hungry. Resolve this for our common benefit, Disarius, if you please."

And he replied: "You have asked a matter worthy of discussion, Horus, but one whose reasoning is plain. For since a living creature <note>original: animal</note> consists of various elements, there is one among those which make up the body that, either alone or especially beyond the others, seeks for itself its own suitable nourishment: I speak of heat <note>original: calorem</note>, which always demands that liquid be supplied to it. Indeed, among the four elements <note>The classical elements: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note> themselves as we see them externally, we see that neither water, nor air, nor earth requires anything by which it is nourished or which it consumes, nor do they cause any harm to things neighboring or placed near them. Fire alone, out of a desire for perpetual nourishment, consumes whatever it encounters.

Look also at the infancy of the first stage of life, how much food it processes <note>original: conficiat; implying digestion and growth</note> because of excessive heat; and on the contrary, consider how the elderly easily endure fasting, as if the heat that is usually restored by nutrients has been extinguished in them. But even those in middle age, if they have stirred up their natural heat through much exercise, seek food more eagerly. Let us also consider animals lacking blood <note>original: animalia sanguine carentia; in ancient biology, blood was the primary carrier of vital heat, so bloodless animals like insects were thought to be 'cold.'</note>, which seek no food due to a lack of heat. Therefore, if heat is always in a state of appetite, and liquid is the proper nourishment of heat, it is right that in us, when nutrients are sought for the body after fasting, heat especially demands its own share. Once this is received, the whole body is refreshed and waits more patiently for more solid food."

Having said these things, Avienus picked up his ring from the table, which had suddenly fallen off from the shortest finger <note>original: brevissimo... digito; referring to the pinky or little finger.</note> of his right hand. And when...

<margin>
Why a ring is worn on that finger which is next to the smallest on the left hand.
</margin>
...it was asked by those present why, when he was putting it <note>Referring to a ring.</note> on a different hand and finger than those usually assigned for this ornament, he showed that his left hand was swollen from a wound. From this arose the opportunity for Horus to ask a question. "And tell me," he said, "Disarius—for the entire arrangement of the body pertains to the physician’s knowledge, and you have achieved a learning even beyond what medicine requires—tell me, I say, why has common consent persuaded everyone that a ring should be worn on the finger next to the smallest <note>The ring finger.</note>, which they even call the 'medicinal finger' <note>original: medicinalem; the ring finger was historically associated with healing and doctors.</note>, and specifically on the left hand?"

And Disarius replied: "Regarding this very question, a certain report had come to us from Egypt, about which I was doubtful whether to call it a fable or a true reason. But after later consulting the books of the anatomists, I found it to be true: that a certain nerve, originating from the heart, proceeds forward as far as the finger of the left hand next to the pinky, and there it ends, intertwined with the other nerves of that same finger. And therefore it seemed right to the ancients that this finger should be encircled by a ring, as if by a crown."

<margin>
Gellius, Book 10, Chapter 10.
</margin>
And Horus said: "Indeed, Disarius, it is so true that the Egyptians believe what you say, for when I saw their priests—whom they call Prophets <note>In ancient Egypt, the 'Prophet' was a high-ranking rank of priest (hem-netjer).</note>—in the temple around the altars of the Gods, they would anoint this finger on each person with prepared perfumes. When I inquired into the reasons for this, I learned from their leader what has already been said about the nerve, and furthermore about the number signified through it. For when folded, this finger demonstrates the number six <note>Refers to ancient finger-counting (dactylonomy), where specific bends of the fingers represented numbers.</note>, which is in every way full, perfect, and divine. He asserted many reasons why this number is 'full'; I will leave those aside now as being less suited to our present tales. These are the things I learned in Egypt, the master of all divine disciplines, as to why a ring is preferentially placed on this finger."

Meanwhile, Caecina Albinus said: "If it pleases you all, I will bring into our midst what I have found regarding this same cause in the writings of Ateius Capito <note>A famous Roman jurist of the Augustan age.</note>, who was among the foremost experts in Pontifical law..."

# BOOK VII

...I remember reading that while he ordained it a sacrilege for the forms of the Gods to be carved into rings, he went so far as to explain why the ring is worn on this finger or on this hand. The ancients, he says, carried a ring with them not for decoration, but for the purpose of sealing. Hence it was not permitted to have more than one, nor was it allowed to anyone except a free man; for only the free were deemed worthy of "trust" <note>original: *fides*; in Roman culture, the ability to sign or seal a document was a mark of legal standing and integrity.</note>, which is maintained by a seal <note>original: *signaculo*</note>. Therefore, servants did not have the right to wear rings. 

The engraving was pressed into the material of the ring itself, whether it was made of iron or gold; and it was worn however one wished, on whichever hand and on whichever finger. Afterward, he says, the customs of a more luxurious age began to carve seals into precious gems; and everyone competed in this imitation, boasting of the increased price they paid for the stones to be carved.

From this it happened that the use of rings was taken away from the right hand, which performs much work, and was relegated to the left, which is more idle; this was done lest the precious stones be broken by the frequent movement and labor of the right hand. Moreover, he says, the finger next to the smallest was chosen on the left hand itself, as being more suitable than the others to be entrusted with the value of the ring. 

For the thumb—which took its name from the fact that it "prevails" <note>The Latin *pollex* (thumb) was etymologically linked to *pollere* (to be powerful or prevail).</note>—does not rest even on the left hand; it is no less active than the whole hand itself. Hence among the Greeks it is called the *anticheir* <note>original: αντιχειρ, literally "against the hand" or "another hand."</note>, as if it were a second hand. But the finger next to the thumb <note>The index finger.</note> seemed bare and without the protection of another finger placed next to it, for the thumb is positioned so much lower that it barely reaches past the base of the index finger. 

They avoided the middle finger and the smallest finger, he says, as being unsuitable—one for its excessive size, the other for its shortness. And so the finger was chosen that is enclosed by both neighbors, performs less work, and is therefore better adapted for keeping the ring safe. These are the details contained in the Pontifical records. Let each person follow either the Etruscan or the Egyptian opinion as he wishes.

During this, Horus, having turned back <margin>turned back</margin> to consult [Disarius], said: "You know..."

<margin>Why fresh water is more suitable for washing away dirt than salt water.</margin>
*...by the name of Disarius <note>Disarius is a physician and one of the learned guests at the banquet described in the *Saturnalia*.</note>, that beyond this clothing which covers me, I have nothing else in my entire estate. For which reason, I have no servant, nor do I wish to have one; but every service that must be provided for a living man, I provide for myself. Recently, therefore, when I was staying in the town of Ostia <note>Ostia was the harbor city of ancient Rome, located where the Tiber River meets the Mediterranean Sea.</note>, I washed my soiled cloak <note>original: *pallium*; a rectangular outer garment draped over the shoulder.</note> in the sea for a long time, and dried it in the sun upon the shore; nevertheless, the very same stains of dirt were visible upon it after the washing. And while this matter amazed me, a sailor who happened to be standing by said, "Rather, wash your cloak in the river if you want it cleaned of spots." I obeyed, to test the truth of it; and having washed and dried it in fresh water <note>original: *aqua dulci*, literally "sweet water."</note>, I saw it restored to its former brilliance. And from this, I sought the cause: why is fresh water more suitable for washing away dirt than salt water?

"Long ago," Disarius said, "this question was both proposed and solved by Aristotle. For he says that sea water is much thicker <note>original: *spissiorem*</note> than fresh water—indeed, that it is full of dregs—whereas fresh water is pure and subtle. For this reason, he says, the sea supports even those who are unskilled in swimming; whereas river water, being weak and unsupported by any aid, soon gives way and sends the weights it has received to the bottom. Therefore, he said that fresh water, being light by nature, sinks more quickly into those things that are to be washed; and while it dries, it draws the stains of dirt away with it. But sea water, being thicker, does not easily penetrate for the purpose of cleaning because of its density, and since it hardly dries, it does not carry much dirt away with it."

When Horus <note>A Cynic philosopher present at the discussion.</note> seemed to agree with these things, Eustathius <note>A highly respected philosopher and orator in the group.</note> said: "Please, do not deceive a trusting man who has committed himself and his question to your good faith. For Aristotle discussed these matters, as he did several others, more acutely <note>meaning with cleverness or sharp wit</note> than truly. In fact, the density of water is so far from being a hindrance to washing that often those who wish to have certain items cleaned, lest they achieve this too slowly with fresh water alone, mix ash into it—or, if that is lacking, earth dust—so that it might be thicker..."

# BOOK VII

...so that it might more quickly wash away what has been done <note>original: *facta*; referring to the dirt or stains mentioned on the previous page</note>. Therefore, the density of sea water is not the actual hindrance. Nor is it less effective because it is salty. Indeed, saltiness usually splits and, as it were, opens up the channels <note>original: *meatus*; the tiny pores in fabric or skin</note>, and for that reason, it ought to have been more capable of drawing out the things to be washed away. But there is this one reason why sea water is not fit for washing: it is "fatty" <note>original: *pinguis*; in ancient science, "fatness" referred to a literal oily or sticky quality believed to be present in certain liquids</note>, just as Aristotle himself often testified; even the salts themselves show this, for no one is ignorant of the fact that there is something fatty within them. There is also this evidence of the fatness of sea water: when it is sprinkled upon a flame, it does not extinguish it so much as it is ignited along with it, because the fatness of the water provides nourishment to the fire. Finally, let us follow Homer, who alone was conscious of the inner workings of nature. For he depicts Nausicaa <note>In Homer’s *Odyssey*, Nausicaa is the Phaeacian princess who discovers the shipwrecked Odysseus</note>, the daughter of Alcinous, washing clothes when she was *beside* the sea, but not *in* the sea—rather, she washed them in a river. That same passage of Homer teaches us that there is a certain fatty substance mixed into sea water. For Ulysses <note>The Roman name for the Greek hero Odysseus</note>, when he had finally escaped the sea and stood with his body dried, said to the handmaids of Nausicaa:

<margin>Odyssey, Book 6</margin>
> "Handmaids, stand over there, far enough away so that I might wash the brine from my shoulders myself, and rub myself with oil; for truly, it has been a long time since ointment has touched my skin." <note>original: Ἀμφίπολοι στῆθ' οὕτω...; Homer, *Odyssey* 6.218-220</note>

After this, when he had gone down into the river: "From his head, he washed away the crust of salt." <note>original: Ἐκ κεφαλῆς ἔσμιχεν ἁλὸς χνόον; Homer, *Odyssey* 6.224-225</note> For the divine poet, who followed nature in every matter, expressed what usually happens: those who come up out of the sea, if they stand in the sun, find that the water is indeed dried quickly by the sun, but there remains on the surface of the body a sort of "flower" <note>original: *flos*; here referring to the thin, powdery film or crust of salt left behind</note>, which can be felt even when wiping it away. And this is the fatness of sea water, which alone hinders the process of washing.

### CHAPTER XIV.

<margin>Why images appear larger than they truly are in water.</margin>
"And since, being freed from other matters, you are indulging me for a little while—and as our conversation just now concerned water—I ask why images in water appear larger than they truly are. We see this sort of thing displayed by tavern-keepers <note>original: *popinatores*; these were sellers of prepared food or wine-shop owners</note> in many of their delicacies <note>original: *scitamentorum*; choice appetizers or tidbits</note> which are set out, appearing larger in sight than they are in substance. For we see in small glass jars filled with water: eggs appearing as larger spheres, little livers with more swollen fibers, and shellfish <note>original: *beluas*; literally "beasts," here referring to aquatic creatures like prawns or snails</note> with massive coils. And more generally, I ask by what principle the act of seeing itself is established for us; for some are accustomed to hold views on this matter that are neither true nor even likely." 

And Disarius said: "Water is denser than the thinness of air, and therefore the sight penetrates it more slowly. Once struck by this resistance, the sharp edge of the vision <note>original: *acies*; ancient science often viewed vision as a physical 'ray' or 'beam' emitted by the eye</note> is split and turns back upon itself. Having been split as it returns, it no longer strikes in a direct line, but rushes upon the outlines of the image from every side; thus it happens that the image appears larger than its archetype <note>original: *archetypo*; the actual object being viewed</note>. For the morning disk of the Sun also appears larger than usual to us because the air, still dewy from the night, lies between us and it; its image grows larger as if it were being viewed in a mirror of water. 

<margin>*clumsily. On the nature of seeing. Gellius, Book 5, Chapter 16.</margin>
Indeed, Epicurus did not immediately <note>The marginal note *insubide* suggests 'foolishly' or 'clumsily,' indicating the commentator's disagreement with Epicurus, though the main text uses *subinde*, meaning 'immediately' or 'repeatedly'</note> look into the nature of seeing itself. However, in my opinion, his view is not to be rejected in this matter, especially since Democritus agrees; for in this, as in other things, they held similar views. Epicurus therefore believes that certain images <note>original: *simulachra*; these are the 'eidola' or thin films of atoms proposed by Epicurean physics</note> flow from all bodies in a perpetual stream. He believes that there is never even the slightest delay, but that these 'shucking skins' <note>original: *exuviae*; literally 'cast-off skins,' describing the thin layers of atoms that peel off objects</note> of bodies, held together by an empty form, are carried forth of their own accord. The receptacles for these are in our eyes, and thus they return to the seat of their own sense assigned to them by nature. These are the things which that man relates; if you have arguments against them, I am waiting for what you might say in reply."

At this, Eustathius smiled and said: "It is quite obvious what deceived Epicurus. For he has fallen away from the truth,"

### BOOK VII.

...following the example of the other four senses: for in hearing, tasting, smelling, and touching, we emit nothing from ourselves, but rather receive from the outside that which moves the sense. Indeed, the voice comes to the ears of its own accord, scents flow into the nostrils, what produces flavor is pressed upon the palate, and things to be felt are applied to our bodies by touch. From this, he <note>Likely referring to Epicurus or Democritus, who championed the "image" theory of vision</note> thought that nothing proceeds outward from the eyes either, but that the images of things travel into the eyes of their own accord.

<margin>The first reason why vision occurs by the emission of rays from the eyes, not the reception of images.</margin>
This opinion is contradicted by the fact that in mirrors, the reflected image faces its own observer; whereas (if it indeed originated from us and proceeded in a straight path) it ought to show its back as it departs—just as a person's left side should correspond to the left, and the right to the right. For an actor <note>original: *histrio*</note> sees the mask he has pulled off from the side he wore it—that is, not the face, but the hollow cavity behind it.

<margin>The second reason.</margin>
Next, I would like to ask this man whether these images fly off from things only when someone wishes to see, or do these likenesses <note>original: *simulachra*; thin "films" or "idols" that ancient atomists believed objects shed to be seen</note> flash out from every side even when no one is looking? For if he holds to my first point, I ask by whose command are the images ready for the viewer: and do they turn themselves as often as a person wishes to turn their face? But if he clings to the second point, saying that images flow in a perpetual stream from all things: I ask how long they remain joined together, when they are held by no binding agent <note>original: *coagulo*; literally a "curd" or "rennet," used here as a metaphor for glue</note> to ensure their permanence? Or, even if we grant that they remain, how will they retain any color? For the nature of color, while being incorporeal, can nonetheless never exist without a physical body.

<margin>The third reason.</margin>
Furthermore, who can be convinced that, the moment you turn your eyes, the images of the sky, the sea, the shore, the meadow, the ships, the flocks, and countless other things besides—all of which we see in a single glance—rush in at once, especially since the pupil, which holds the power of sight, is so very small?

<margin>The fourth reason.</margin>
And in what manner is an entire army seen? Do the images proceeding from individual soldiers crowd themselves together, and thus arranged, do so many thousands penetrate the eyes of the beholder...

*...ments? But why do we labor to strike such a hollow opinion with words, when the very emptiness of the matter refutes itself? It is well established that vision occurs for us by this reasoning: A natural light flashes forth from the pupil in a straight line, wherever you turn it. This internal flow of the eyes, if it finds light in the air surrounding us, proceeds through that light in a direct path until it strikes an object. And if you turn your face to look around, the sharp edge of sight proceeds directly in either direction. Furthermore, this very beam, which we said flashes out from our eyes, starts from a thin root* <note>original: *tenui radice*; Disarius describes the visual ray as a cone that is narrow at the eye and widens as it travels</note> *and becomes wider at its furthest point, just as rays are depicted by a painter. This is why the eye, looking through even the smallest hole, can see the depth of the heavens. Therefore, those three things are necessary for us to achieve the act of seeing: the light which we emit from ourselves; that the intervening air be luminous; and an object which, when struck, brings the stretching of the ray to an end. If this stretching should continue for too long, it becomes exhausted and cannot maintain a straight path, but instead is split and spreads out to the right and the left. It is from this that, wherever on earth you stand, you seem to see a certain boundary of the sky; and this is what the ancients called the "horizon." Their investigation faithfully discovered that the sightline directed from the eyes across a flat surface toward those looking back does not proceed beyond 180 stadia* <note>A "stadium" was a unit of length; 180 stadia is roughly 20 to 22 miles. Ancient scientists calculated this as the limit of human vision across a flat plane before the curvature of the earth or the "tiring" of the visual ray intervened.</note>*, and from there it now curves back into a circle. I added "across a flat surface" because we can look at heights from a very great distance, since we can even see the sky. Therefore, in every circle of the horizon, the observer himself is the center* <note>original: *centron*</note>*. And because we have stated how far the sightline extends from the center to the edge of the circle, without a doubt the diameter* <note>original: *διάμετρος* (diametros)</note> *of the circle in the horizon is 360 stadia; and if the observer moves further forward or retreats backward, he will see a similar circle around himself. Thus, as we have said, when the light which proceeds from us falls upon an object through the light of the air, the duty of seeing is fulfilled. But so that the thing seen can be understood, the sense of the eyes reports the appearance it has seen to the reason; and*

# BOOK VII.

...memory recognizes it once it is summoned. Therefore, to see belongs to the eyes, to judge belongs to reason, and to remember belongs to memory. For the function that completes the process of distinguishing a shape is a triple one: sense, reason, and memory. Sense feeds the thing seen back to reason. Then reason remembers <note>original: *recordatur*; in this context, it implies the mind identifying the object based on prior knowledge</note> what has been seen. Indeed, the function of reason is so necessary in the act of seeing that often, within the single sense of sight, reason detects another sense because memory suggests it. 

For if fire appears, reason knows it is hot even before it is touched. If it is snow that is seen, reason understands the coldness of touch within it. If reason is absent, sight is ineffective; so much so that the fact that an oar appears broken in water, or that a tower seen from a distance appears round when it is actually angular, is caused by the negligence of reason. If reason focuses itself, it recognizes the angles in the tower and the integrity of the oar. It distinguishes all those things which gave the Academics <note>The 'Academics' were followers of the Skeptical school of philosophy who argued that because the senses could be deceived by illusions, certain knowledge was impossible.</note> the opportunity to condemn the senses. In truth, a single sense should be held among the most certain of things, provided that reason accompanies it; for sometimes a single sense is not sufficient for reason to distinguish an appearance. 

For if from a distance the shape of the fruit called an apple is seen, it is not definitely an apple; for a likeness of an apple could be fashioned out of some other material. Therefore, a second sense must be summoned, so that smell may judge. But it could have been placed among a pile of real apples and thus caught the aura of that scent. At this point, touch must be consulted, which can judge by the weight. But there is a fear that touch itself might be deceived, if a deceptive craftsman chose a material that imitated the weight of an apple. One must therefore flee to taste; if it agrees with the form, there is no doubt it is an apple. Thus it is proved that the effectiveness of the senses depends on reason. For this reason, God the Craftsman <term>Deus opifex: the divine 'worker' or 'architect' of the universe, a concept central to Platonic thought</term> located all the senses in the head—that is, around the seat of reason.

### CHAPTER XV.

<margin>Gellius, Book 17, Chapter 11.</margin>
Once these things were said, favor arose from everyone, who marveled at the soundness of his words; so much so that even Evangelus <note>Evangelus is one of the more cynical and argumentative guests at the banquet described in the *Saturnalia*.</note> himself did not hesitate to agree. Disarius then added: "Those are the cheers that provoke Philosophy to claim for herself discussions belonging to another’s art, which often leads her into obvious errors."

<margin>Against Plato.</margin>
"Just as your Plato, while he did not abstain from anatomy (which is the proper domain of medicine), left a cause for laughter to posterity. For he said that there were separate paths for swallowing food and drink: and that food is drawn through the esophagus <note>original: *stomachum*; in ancient anatomy, this term frequently referred to the gullet or esophagus rather than the organ we call the stomach today</note>, while drink actually slips into the lungs through the *windpipe* <note>original: *ἀρτηρίαν* (arterian); the ancients believed the 'arteries' carried air/spirit</note>, which is called the 'rough' one <note>original: *τραχεῖα* (tracheia)</note>, and glides into the fibers of the lungs. It is a cause for wonder, or rather grief, that so great a man either believed this or recorded it in his books. From this, Erasistratus <note>Erasistratus (c. 304–250 BCE) was a famous Greek anatomist and royal physician in Alexandria known for his pioneering work on the circulatory and nervous systems.</note>, the most noble of the ancient physicians, rightly attacked him, saying that he recorded things far different from what reason has discovered.

For there are two tubes like channels, and these start from the back of the throat and go downward. Through one of them, all food and drink are introduced and slide down into the esophagus, and from there are carried into the belly, which in Greek is called the 'lower cavity' <note>original: *κάτω κοιλία* (kato koilia)</note>, and there they are worked upon and digested. Then the drier remains from these gather in the bowel, which in Greek is called the *colon* <note>original: *κῶλον* (kolon)</note>. The more liquid parts, however, are drawn through the kidneys into the bladder. Through the other of the two upper tubes, which in Greek is called the 'rough artery' <note>original: *τραχεῖα ἀρτηρία* (tracheia arteria); this is the origin of the modern term <term>trachea</term></note>, the breath passes from the top of the mouth into the lungs, and from there back out through the mouth and nostrils; and through this same path the passage of the voice is made. And lest drink or drier food, which ought to go into the esophagus, should fall from the mouth and slip into that tube through which the breath moves back and forth—and by that obstruction the 'path of the soul' <note>original: *animae via*; referring to the airway which sustains life</note> be shut off—there was placed, by a certain art and the help of nature, the **epiglottis** <note>original: *ἐπιγλωττίδα* (epiglottida)</note>, as if it were a mutual gate for both tubes, which are joined together..."

...and that the epiglottis <note>original: *ἐπιγλωττίδα*</note> covers and protects the trachea <note>original: *τὴν τραχεῖαν* (ten tracheian), literally the "rough one"</note> during eating and drinking, so that nothing from the food or drink might fall into that path of the surging breath. Because of this, no moisture flows into the lungs, as the mouth of the windpipe <note>original: *arteriæ*; the ancients used this term for the windpipe because it was believed to carry air or "spirit" (*pneuma*)</note> is fortified.

These are the views of Erasistratus, with which (as I judge) true reason agrees. For since food should not be introduced to the belly in a dry or rough state, but softened by the tempering of moisture, it is necessary that the same path be open to both, so that the food, tempered by drink, may be stowed in the belly through the esophagus <note>original: *stomachum*; in this context, it refers to the gullet or passage to the stomach</note>. Nor would nature have arranged it otherwise, except as it would be healthy for the animal. 

Furthermore, since the lung is both solid and smooth, if anything thick should fall into it, how could it penetrate or be transmitted to the place of digestion? For it is well known that if, by chance, something a little too dense falls into the lung because of the violent drawing of the breath, a very harsh cough and other convulsions immediately arise, even to the point of endangering one's health. 

If, however, the natural path drew drink into the lungs, then when thick liquids are drunk, or when one swallows drink mixed with grains or some denser substance, what would the lung suffer from those things? Hence the epiglottis <note>original: *ἐπιγλωττὶς*</note> was provided by nature to serve as a cover for the windpipe when food is consumed, so that nothing slips through it into the lungs while the breath is being drawn in.

<margin>*allows</margin>
Just as when speech is to be emitted, it [the epiglottis] inclines to cover the path of the esophagus, so that it allows* the windpipe <note>original: *ἀρτηρίαν* (arterian)</note> to lie open for the voice. This is also known from experience: those who swallow drink slowly have more moist bellies, as the moisture taken in bit by bit remains there longer. If, however, someone gulps it down more greedily, the moisture passes through to the bladder with the same force by which it is drawn in, and a slow digestion results for the drier food. This difference would not occur if the passages for food and drink had been divided from the start. As for what the poet Alcaeus <note>Alcaeus was a lyric poet from Lesbos (c. 600 BCE) known for his drinking songs.</note> said, and what is commonly sung: "With wine, the lungs... <note>original: *Οἴνῳ πνεύ[μονα]*; this is a fragment of a poem suggesting wine moistens the lungs, which Disarius is about to critique.</note>"

The epiglottis <note>original: *ἐπιγλωττὶς*</note> which you mention is an invention of nature for covering and uncovering the paths of food and drink with a certain alternation, so that it may transmit the former to the gullet <note>original: *stomachum*; in ancient anatomy, this often refers to the esophagus.</note> and the lung may receive the latter. It is for this reason that the lung is divided by so many passages and stands open with gaps: not so that the breath might have a way out (for a hidden exhalation would suffice for that), but so that if any part of the nourishment falls into the lung, its juice may soon migrate through them into the seat of digestion. ...because those whose lungs are diseased are inflamed with the greatest thirst; this would not happen unless the lung were the reservoir for drink. Consider also this: that animals which do not possess a lung do not know how to drink. For Nature made nothing superfluous, but created each individual limb for some specific service of living; when the organ is absent, the use for it is not required. Or consider this: if the stomach <note>The author uses *stomachus* here to refer to what we now call the esophagus or the digestive tract leading to the belly.</note> received both food and drink, the use of the bladder would be superfluous. For the stomach could deliver the waste of both substances to the intestine, to which it now delivers only the waste of food; nor would there be a need for different passages through which each substance is delivered, but one would suffice for both, transmitted from the same station. As it is, however, the bladder and the intestine serve our health separately: because the stomach delivers to the latter, and the lung to the bladder. Nor should this be overlooked: that in urine, which is the waste of drink, no trace of food is found; nor is it tainted by any quality of those food-wastes, whether in color or odor. But if they had been in the belly together, they would be tainted by some quality of that filth. Finally, why do the stones that are born from drink in the bladder never form in the belly? Since they are produced only from drink, they ought to have been born in the belly as well, if the belly were the receptacle for drink. Even noble poets are not ignorant that drink flows down into the lung. For Eupolis says in the play titled <margin>*</margin> *The Flatterers*: "For Protagoras used to urge us to drink so that he might keep his lungs soaked before the Dog-star rises." <note>original: Πίνειν γὰρ ὁ πρωταγόρας ἐκέλευεν ἵνα πρὸ τοῦ κυνὸς τὸν πνεύμον’ ἔκλυτον φορῇ (*Pinein gar ho Prōtagoras ekeleuen hina pro tou kunos ton pneumon’ eklyton phorē*). The "Dog-star" (Sirius) refers to the hottest days of summer.</note> And Eratosthenes testifies to the same: "And soaking his deep lung with unmixed wine." <note>original: Καὶ βαθὺν ἀκρήτῳ πνεύμονα τεγγόμενος (*Kai bathyn akrētō pneumona tengomenos*).</note> Euripides, indeed, is the most obvious supporter of this matter: "Wine having passed through the channels of the lungs." <note>original: Οἶνος περάσας πλευμόνων διαῤῥοάς (*Oinos perasas pleumonōn diarrhoas*).</note> Since, therefore, both the logic of the body's structure and the noble authority of witnesses support Plato, is not anyone who thinks otherwise insane?

"You think you are mocking us," said Disarius, "and yet the question you have raised is worthy of both inquiry and knowledge. For you have consulted me about the <margin>worthlessness</margin> worthlessness <note>original: *vilitate*; referring to the perceived triviality of the subject matter.</note> of a matter: whether the chicken first came from the egg, or the egg from the chicken. But this should be included in our holiday festivities in such a way that it ought to be discussed even with great care. And I will bring forward those points that occur to me to be said on either side, leaving it to you to decide which of them you prefer to see as more true. 

If we concede that all things that exist began at some point, the egg will rightly be judged to have been made first by nature. For that which begins is always still imperfect and unformed, and it is shaped toward its own perfection through the additions of advancing skill and time. Therefore, nature, in crafting the bird, began from an unformed beginning and produced the egg, in which the appearance of the living creature does not yet exist. From this, the appearance of the perfect bird emerged as the effect of maturity gradually advanced. 

Next, whatever has been provided by nature with various ornaments undoubtedly began from something simple, and was thus diversified by the addition of structure. Thus the egg is simple to the sight and created with a uniform appearance on all sides; and from that, the variety of ornaments of which the bird's appearance consists was completed. For just as the elements existed first, and <margin>I say that the word "thus" [ita] does not contribute anything to the matter, nor is it found in the ancient copies.</margin> *thus the remaining bodies were created from their mixing—so the seminal reasons <term>seminal reasons: known in Latin as *rationes seminales*, these were thought to be the latent "blueprints" or formative principles within matter that guide the development of living things</term> which are in the egg must be believed to be, if you will pardon the metaphor, like certain "elements" of the chicken. 

Nor would I inappropriately compare the egg to the elements from which all things are made. For in every kind of living creature that is born from sexual union, you will find that for some, the egg is the beginning, like an element. For living creatures either walk, or crawl, or live by swimming or flying. Among those that walk, lizards and similar creatures are created from eggs. Those that crawl are born from eggs. From the beginning, all flying things are born from...

<header>BOOK VII.</header>

...come forth from eggs, except for one, which is of an uncertain nature. For the **bat** <note>original: *vespertilio*</note> indeed flies with skin-covered wings, but it is not to be counted among the flying creatures: because it walks on four feet, gives birth to formed offspring, and nourishes those it begets with milk. Almost all swimming things arise from eggs of their own kind; the **crocodile**, however, also arises from hard-shelled eggs, like those of flying creatures. 

And lest I seem to have excessively praised the egg by calling it an "element," consult those initiated into the mysteries of **Father Liber** <note>original: *Liberi patris*; a Roman name for Bacchus or Dionysus. The Orphic mysteries associated with him famously used the "World Egg" as a symbol of the universe's creation.</note>; in these rites, the egg is revered with such veneration that, because of its smooth and almost spherical shape, closed on all sides and enclosing life within itself, it is called a **likeness of the world**. Now, by the consensus of all, it is established that the world is the beginning of the universe.

Let him come forward who wants the **chicken** <note>original: *gallina*</note> to be first, and let him attempt to bring forth his defense in these words: The egg is neither the beginning nor the end of the thing to which it belongs. For the beginning is the seed, and the end is the formed bird itself. The egg, however, is a development <note>original: *digestio*; in ancient physiology, this refers to the "concoction" or maturation of biological fluids into a more complex form.</note> of the seed. Since, therefore, the seed belongs to the animal, and the egg belongs to the seed, the egg could not have existed before the animal, just as the digestion of food cannot occur before there is one who eats. 

And it is like saying the egg was made before the chicken, as if someone were to say the **womb** <note>original: *matricem*</note> was made before the woman. And he who asks how the chicken could exist without the egg is like one asking in what way humans were made before the **genitals** <note>original: *pudenda*</note> from which humans are procreated. Thus, just as no one rightly says the human belongs to the seed, but the seed to the human, so neither does the chicken belong to the egg, but the egg belongs to the chicken.

Next, if we concede (as was said by the opposing side) that these things which exist took some beginning in time: nature first formed individual animals as perfect beings; then she gave a perpetual law so that the succession might be continued through procreation. Moreover, that perfect things could be produced at the beginning is evidenced even now by not a few living creatures which are born perfect from the earth and rain: as in...

<header>OF THE SATURNALIA</header>

<margin>\* he perceived</margin>
...mice in Egypt, and in other places frogs, snakes, and similar creatures [arise spontaneously from the earth]. Eggs, however, were never procreated from the earth, because there is no **perfection** <term>perfection: in ancient Aristotelian biology, this refers to a fully developed or "complete" state of being; an egg was considered "imperfect" because it is only a potential animal</term> in them. But Nature forms perfect things, and those eggs proceed from perfect things, just as parts proceed from a whole. For even if I grant that the eggs of birds are the "nurseries" of life, let us see what the definition of the Philosophers testifies about the **seed** itself, which it decrees thus <note>original: *sancit*</note>: *Seed is a generation proceeding toward the likeness of that from which it comes.* One cannot proceed toward the likeness of a thing that does not yet exist; just as a seed does not emanate from that which does not yet subsist. Therefore, let us understand that in the first origin of things—along with the other living creatures that are born from seed alone, about which there is no doubt that they existed before their own seed—birds also existed as **perfected** beings by the hand of Nature the artisan. And because the power of generating was inserted into each individual, from these now proceed the modes of being born, which Nature has varied according to the diversity of living things. You have, Euangelus, both sides of the argument to hold onto; and having set aside your mockery for a little while, deliberate with yourself which you should follow.

> And Euangelus said: Since the force of your speaking makes even serious matters out of jokes, I want this resolved for me, a matter which has long occupied my own deliberation. For recently, wild boars from my **Tiburtine** <note>original: *Tyburti*; referring to Tibur, the modern Tivoli, where many wealthy Romans held country estates</note> estate were presented to me, which the woods had offered up to the hunters. Because the hunt was continued for quite a long time, some were brought home during the day, and others at night. Those which the daylight brought stayed fresh with the integrity of their meat unharmed; but those which were carried through the night while the **moon was at its full** <note>original: *lunari plenitudine*; ancient science believed the full moon accelerated the decomposition of organic matter by increasing moisture</note> became rotten. When this was discovered, those who were bringing them the following night stuck a sharp **bronze** <note>original: *æneo*; referring to bronze or copper, which was often thought in antiquity to have "drying" or preservative powers</note> instrument into various parts of the body, and thus brought the boars through with their meat intact. I ask, therefore, why the lunar light caused the harm to the slaughtered beasts which the rays of the Sun did not?

> Disarius said: That response is easy and simple. For the rotting of no thing ever occurs unless heat and moisture come together. Now, the rotting of slaughtered beasts is nothing other than when a certain flowing away...

<header>BOOK VII.</header>

...[a certain] hidden destruction <note>original: *pernicies*, completed from the previous page's catchword</note> dissolves the solidity of the flesh into liquid. Moreover, if heat is temperate and moderate, it nourishes the **humors** <term>humors: the four vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed in ancient medicine to control health and temperament</term>; but if it is excessive, it dries them out and thins the constitution of the flesh. Therefore, in the case of dead bodies, the sun—possessing a greater heat—draws out the moisture; but lunar light, in which there is no obvious heat but rather a hidden warmth, spreads the moisture further. Thus, by the injection of this warmth and the increase of moisture, rot arises. Having said these things, Euangelus looked toward Eustathius:

> "If you agree with the reasoning stated," he said, "you ought to nod in assent; or if there is something that troubles you, do not be reluctant to bring it forward, for the power of your discourse has ensured that I shall not listen with an unwilling ear."

> Eustathius replied, "Everything has been said by Disarius both brilliantly and truthfully. But we must look more closely at whether the *measure* of heat is the sole cause of rot—namely, the claim that it does not occur from greater heat, but proceeds from a lesser and more temperate warmth. For the sun’s heat, which burns intensely during the summer and grows lukewarm in winter, causes meat to rot in summer, not in winter. Therefore, it is not simply because of a lower heat that the moon spreads moisture. Rather, there is a certain specific property <note>original: *idioma*</note>, a certain nature inherent in the light that flows from her, which moistens bodies and makes them damp as if with a hidden dew. When the lunar heat itself is mixed with this, it rots the flesh into which it has been infused for a long time. For not all heat is of a single quality, such that it differs only by being greater or lesser; rather, it is proven by clear evidence that there are very different qualities in fire that have no fellowship with one another.

> <margin>For melting and strengthening glass</margin>
> Goldsmiths, for the purpose of shaping gold, use no fire except that made from straw, because other fuels seem unsuitable for working this material. Physicians, when decocting remedies, require a fire from brushwood rather than from any other wood. Those who see to the melting and strengthening of glass provide their fire with fuel from the tree called the **tamarisk** <term>tamarisk: a flowering shrub or tree; in antiquity, specific woods were believed to produce different "qualities" of flame suited for specific industrial tasks</term>. The heat from olive wood, while it is healthy for bodies, [is...]

<page-num>366</page-num>
<header>OF THE SATURNALIA</header>

[This humidity] is destructive to baths: and is effectively harmful for dissolving the joints of marble <note>original: *marmorū*. This sentence concludes the thought from the previous page regarding the "hidden destruction" of humidity</note>. Therefore, it is no wonder if, by the nature of the property inherent in each, the heat of the sun dries, while that of the moon moistens. Hence also nurses, when nourishing children, cover them with wrappings when they pass under the moon: lest the lunar light further moisten those who are already full of natural moisture 

<margin>*Humectum*, in the neuter gender, for humidity.</margin>

due to their age <note>Ancient medicine believed children were naturally "wet" or "moist" in their constitution, and excessive moisture was thought to cause physical deformities</note>: and just as wood that is still wet with its greenness is bent when heat is applied, so too does the addition of moisture twist their limbs. This too is well known: if anyone gives himself over to sleep for a long time under the moon, he is woken with difficulty and becomes close to insane: weighed down by the pressure of the moisture which has been diffused and dispersed throughout his whole body by the lunar property: which, in order to flood the body, opens and loosens all its **passages** <term>passages: *meatus*, the pores or internal channels through which fluids and spirits were thought to flow in the body</term>. Hence it is that Diana, who is the moon, is called **Artemis** <note>original Greek: *Ἄρτεμις*</note>, as if it were **aerotomis** <note>original Greek: *ἀεροτόμις*</note>, that is, "cutting the air." She is invoked as **Lucina** by those in labor: because her specific task is to stretch the cracks of the body and give way to the passages, which is beneficial for accelerating childbirth. And this is what the poet Timotheus expressed elegantly: "Through the bright vault of the stars and through the moon that brings swift birth" <note>original Greek: *Διὰ λαμπρὸν πόλον ἄστρων διά τ᾿ ὠκυτόϰοιο σελάνας*</note>. Nor is the property of the moon shown any less regarding inanimate things. For timber that is felled either when the moon is already full or still waxing is unsuitable for construction: as if softened through the absorption of moisture. And farmers take care not to harvest grain from the fields except when the moon is waning, so that it remains dry. Conversely, you should deal with things you want to keep moist while the moon is waxing. Then you will also plant trees more effectively: especially when the moon is above the earth: because for the growth of shoots, the nourishment of moisture is necessary. The air itself both suffers and reveals the property of lunar moisture. For when the moon is full, or when it is born (for even then it is full on the side facing upward), the air either dissolves into rain: or if it is clear, it emits a great deal of dew from itself. Hence the lyric poet Alcman said:

<page-num>567</page-num>

### BOOK VII.

[They call] Dew the son of Air and the Moon. Thus it is proven from every direction that there is a property in lunar light for moistening and dissolving flesh: a fact which practical experience has grasped more than theory. 

As for what you said, Evangelus, concerning the sharp bronze instrument (if my conjecture does not fail me), it does not deviate from the truth. For there is in bronze a sharper power, which physicians call **styptic** <term>styptic: from the Greek *styptikos*, meaning a substance that contracts tissues to stop bleeding or secretions</term>. For this reason, they add its scales to remedies used against the destruction caused by **putrefaction** <note>original: *putredinis*; the process of decay or rotting</note>. Furthermore, those who spend their time in copper mines always enjoy healthy eyes: even those whose eyelids had previously been bare of lashes find them covered with hair again there. For the vapor that proceeds from the bronze, falling upon the eyes, draws out and dries up the harmful fluids. For this reason, Homer calls bronze sometimes "man-ennobling" <note>original Greek: *εὐήνορα* (*euēnora*), implying strength-giving or splendid</note>, and sometimes "flashing" <note>original Greek: *νώροπα* (*nōropa*)</note>. 

Aristotle is the authority for the fact that wounds made by a bronze point are less harmful than those made by iron, and are more easily cured. This is because, he says, there is a certain remedial and drying power in bronze which it leaves behind in the wound. Therefore, by the same logic, a bronze instrument fixed into the body of a beast resists the lunar moisture.

->THE EDITOR FROM WESEL<- <note>original: *VESALIENSIS*. This is a marginal or concluding note by the printer or editor, likely Johannes Oporinus or a contemporary scholar associated with the city of Wesel</note>

Whoever compares the end of the first book with the end of this one will easily notice that certain things are still missing for the completion of this work. But whether the author himself did not add them because he was hindered by other matters or snatched away by death, or whether they were lost through the negligence of scribes, cannot easily be said.

->T H E  E N D.<-
